artigo.texto: Table of Contents Japanese billionaire Masayoshi Son is planning to invest $50 billion in artificial intelligence and data centers in Malaysia, in what could become one of the largest technology commitments in Southeast Asia. Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim disclosed the plan on Saturday in Melaka, Bloomberg reported. Anwar said the SoftBank Group founder had already identified sites for the investment in Kuching, the capital of Sarawak state, and in Peninsular Malaysia. The two men discussed the plan during a video call last week. Anwar said Son’s focus would be on three areas. “In what areas? AI, new technology and data centers,” Anwar said. The $50 billion figure is equal to about 204.3 billion ringgit. Details on how the money will be deployed, when construction will start and how the project will be financed have not been announced. SoftBank had not commented publicly on the plan. Anwar said the investment could create jobs for Malaysians, especially young people and university graduates. He said the country must build skills in AI, digitalization and semiconductors, and train its workforce so it can move into higher-value technology work. He also said Malaysia must maintain political stability and a supportive investment climate to keep the confidence of international investors. The plan would add to a wave of data center spending in Malaysia, which has become a regional hub for the computing capacity that AI systems need. Alibaba Cloud opened two data centers in the southern state of Johor in June, bringing its total in the country to five. Sarawak has also drawn interest from SoftBank before. Earlier this month, SoftBank, ride-hailing company Grab and Sarawak state energy company PETROS were reported to be exploring AI infrastructure development in the state. The Malaysian proposal is the latest in a string of large bets by Son on AI. This month alone, he has sought $100 billion from Gulf investors for AI expansion and eyed a $30 billion takeover of Allied Universal. SoftBank is also involved in a $500 billion data center project in Ohio, which Bloomberg describes as among the largest in the world, and is pursuing a project in France that could cost up to $84 billion. Son founded SoftBank in 1981 and built it into one of the world’s biggest technology investors. His AI push has been heavily funded with borrowed money, including an $11.87 billion loan tied to his OpenAI bet, and his AI-related debt has kept growing. So far, the plan rests on Anwar’s account of his call with Son. Investors will be watching for confirmation from SoftBank and for details on timing, partners and funding. artigo.texto: EAF investe R$ 365 milhões em data center para inteligência artificial. Telebras fará a operação Decisão foi do Gaispi, grupo que coordena os projetos a serem implantados pela EAF com os recursos do leilão de 5G. O Gaispi, grupo que coordena os projetos a serem implantados pela EAF com os recursos do leilão de 5G, aprovou nesta terça, 27/10, a destinação de R$ 375 milhões para a construção de um data center voltado à inteligência artificial. O projeto prevê uma infraestrutura pública de processamento de dados, com titularidade da União e operação pela Telebras. A EAF ficará responsável pela implantação, seguindo modelo semelhante ao adotado na Rede Privativa de Comunicação da Administração Pública Federal. O projeto prevê a construção do data center em um um terreno de 5 mil metros quadrados, “com módulo de inteligência artificial previsto para 20 racks de 42U, rede de alta velocidade, seis servidores GPU com 48 GPUs, nove servidores CPU, armazenamento all-flash e object storage”. A unidade teria ainda até dez racks de colocalização, sem aquisição de servidores na etapa inicial. A arquitetura prevê alimentação elétrica redundante, distribuição A/B, geração de emergência em configuração 2N, climatização compatível com alta densidade e resfriamento líquido no módulo de IA, conectividade redundante de 2 x 100 Gb e monitoramento contínuo. O prazo estimado para implantação é de 12 meses, condicionado à disponibilidade de energia, aos licenciamentos e aos prazos de fornecimento e integração dos equipamentos. A proposta ainda precisa ser aprovada pelo conselho diretor da Anatel, mas o Gaispi relata que há caixa para uso imediato e é possível o início da execução, mesmo que os atuais projetos em desenvolvimento pela EAF não estejam concluídos. Os recursos da EAF vieram da venda do espectro de 3,5 GHz para as operadoras de telecomunicações.

artigo.texto: Springfield City Council hears from the public on its proposed administrative delay extension and definitions of data centers SPRINGFIELD, Mo. (KY3) - In June, the Springfield City Council passed an administrative delay on the development of data centers; that delay is up on Nov. 17. On Monday night, council heard from the public about a proposal to push this delay back again to February. Citizens also addressed the council on its proposal to add definitions related to data centers into the city code. The first hearing on the city’s proposal to add definitions related to data centers, defining them and breaking them up into three groups: accessory, micro, and large load. “To be an Accessory Data Center: it has to be inside the principal building; it can’t be more than 20% of the principal building’s gross floor area; it needs to serve only the owner or the tenants, so it has to be used on site; and its maximum power demand has to be less than one megawatt,” said Justin Crighton, the City of Springfield’s Assistant Director of Planning and Development. “If it does not meet all four of those criteria, then the next test is size and power. So a data center is considered a Large Load Data Center if it meets either of these two thresholds: if it’s five megawatts or more in maximum power demand, or it’s more than 10,000 square feet. If it’s under both thresholds, then it’s a Micro Data Center.” Ten Springfield residents signed up to speak on this proposal. Cameron Rose, who works for a local internet provider, spoke to the council, saying the definitions are too broad and could have a negative effect on their business. “They would prevent us from setting up a fiber hut, which is just a small building that is usually about 8 by 10 that we use to provide service to other businesses or to residents,” said Rose. “Because the Accessory Data Center definition says that you cannot provide services to anyone other than tenants or the occupant of the building.” The second public hearing regards an extension of the city’s existing administrative delay on data centers. Springfield resident Ren Bortosky is in favor of the extension and said ideally, the moratorium would be indefinite, citing environmental concerns as the most prominent issue regarding data centers. “We need to put limitations in place either on how many data centers we’re building, which would ideally be zero, or at least on how much energy they’re allowed to use,” said Bortosky. “Because every megawatt of energy is more emissions that really don’t need to be put into the atmosphere.” Council will vote on both issues at the Nov. 16 meeting. artigo.texto: Oro Valley is prepared to adopt zoning code amendments regulating data centers, to include a prohibition of all “large-scale” data centers using 20MW of power or more. If adopted, Oro Valley “will be the only jurisdiction” among 13 researched in Arizona “to prohibit large-scale data centers,” according to a staff report from Bayer Vella, Oro Valley’s town planner. The language was scheduled to go before the Oro Valley Planning and Zoning Commission on Tuesday, Oct. 27. The Oro Valley Town Council scheduled a special meeting and public hearing to consider regulatory code language Wednesday, Oct. 28, at 6 p.m. on the town campus. Vice Mayor and Mayor-elect Melanie Barrett initiated the discussion at the end of council’s Oct. 7 meeting. She realized “there could potentially be loopholes” in Oro Valley’s zoning code “that would allow for data centers in multiple zoning districts, and there were people potentially interested in moving forward with those. “I want to act as expeditiously as possible to eliminate that,” Barrett said that evening. She requested a code amendment “making clear data centers are not allowed by right in any zoning district in Oro Valley.” Further, Barrett asked that new code language address the issues of noise, water, energy and other concerns associated with data centers. And, while new code is being considered, “to the degree possible, there shall be a moratorium” on any data centers, she said. Currently, data centers could be developed on properties within Oro Valley’s Commercial and Technical Park zoning districts. Technical Park zoning applies within Oro Valley’s Innovation Park, as well as on lands on either side of the Honeywell complex immediately east of Oracle Road. Commercial zones that would be affected by new code language are primarily along Oracle Road, near Tangerine and Rancho Vistoso, and along La Cholla and La Canada south of Naranja. Code now considers data centers as a “technical services” use. “However, large-scale data centers that require significant amounts of power and water to support modern technologies and AI (artificial intelligence) were not the intended use for technical services,” Vella writes. Draft language would allow “ancillary data centers with limitations” in those zones, according to the staff report. Ancillary data centers are defined as “generally server rooms commonly used by major employers,” such as Roche Tissue Diagnostics, or the town itself. They “must be housed within an existing building on the site,” Vella writes. Oro Valley has not received a request to build a large-scale data center, he continues. “However, there are potential sites” that could accommodate one, Vella’s report said. “It is critical to have standards in place to evaluate data centers” in zones where they could be developed. The code amendment would require a council-approved conditional use permit for any proposed data center. Staff researched data centers and reviewed the zoning codes from 13 Arizona jurisdictions “to identify the necessary review tools” for Oro Valley consideration. It determined energy and water use are “critical areas to regulate.” Large-scale data centers require a minimum of 40 megawatts of electric power. One megawatt hour of energy can power approximately 1,000 average homes, or one grocery store, according to the staff report. Tucson and Pima County classify large-scale data centers as those using a minimum of 20 megawatts. Along with its prohibition of all data centers using 20 megawatts or more of power, Oro Valley’s proposed code amendment would require applicants to report estimated energy needs at the time of application submittal, and to do so annually for five years after a certificate of occupancy is issued by the town. Data center water use “is difficult to ascertain because neither data centers nor water providers disclose this information,” the report said. “Consumption is reportedly extreme,” with some media reports suggesting data centers use millions of gallons of water per day. As proposed, Oro Valley would require data center applicants to submit a water use and conservation plan, disclosing the amount of water they would need, and what type of cooling system they would use. Oro Valley Water Utility Director Peter Abraham has recommended the town initiate a code amendment to regulate “large water users,” to include any data centers, as well as manufacturers of microchips, solar panels, and batteries, which also use large volumes of water. Lastly, the code amendment includes parameters to address noise, location, design, and parking issues associated with data centers. “The industry is evolving at a rapid pace,” Vella concludes. “The town should re-evaluate and update these parameters as needed or in five years.” The Town Council’s special meeting and public hearing on the subject is set for 6 p.m. Wednesday, Oct. 28, in council chambers, 11000 N. La Canada.

artigo.texto: The increasingly contentious national debate over data centers moved into Mesa two weeks ago as Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes told a town hall that their explosive growth threatens to leave communities with higher utility bills, a range of health and environmental problems and inadequate government oversight. Addressing over 250 people at a Mesa community center Oct. 14, Mayes questioned whether Arizona has done enough to protect residents as developers rush to build the enormous facilities needed to support artificial intelligence, cloud computing and other digital services. The setting was particularly appropriate. Mesa has become a major data center hub, with over 7.5 million square feet of existing and proposed facilities. Yet roughly three-quarters of those attending the meeting had traveled from Ahwatukee, where residents have organized against a 1-million-square-foot facility currently being constructed amid neighborhoods with thousands of homes. And for Pinal County, her message is hardly irrelevant, according to a website that tracks 5,098 existing and projected data centers across the country. According to dcmap.us, seven data centers are being planned so far in Pinal County with a combined need for 1.5MW of electricity – enough to power 1.1 million to 1.5 million homes. But one center that alone needed 1MW of electricity to operate won’t be coming to Pinal, after the Pinal County Board of Supervisors in August denied rezoning for Vermaland’s 3,000-acre data center near Eloy. Those still on the books, according to dcmap.us, include Edgecorp’s 720MW campus in Florence, LPI Company’s 400MW campus in Casa Grande and Ryan Companies’ 400 MW data center in Eloy. Four others are planned in Pinal County, although dcmap.us had no information on them, including a 96-acre center at Felix and East Judd roads in San Tan Valley, a second in Florence and Casa Grande and another in Maricopa. According to Mayes, those projects represent a sliver of what has made the Phoenix Metro area “the second largest U.S. data center hub.” Telling the audience, “My office has identified more than 180 operating or planned data centers across Arizona,” the attorney general said 110 already are operating. Mayes, a Democrat seeking reelection, has called for a moratorium on data center construction “to get our house in order to determine the principles that should guide this build-up, if it happens, and to decide what’s needed to protect our communities in Arizona. “This issue is too important to let data center developers themselves decide what is right for our state and our communities,” Mayes told the audience. The Legislature and Gov. Katie Hobbs agreed in June to impose a three-year moratorium starting July 1 on millions of dollars in tax incentives that data centers have been getting from the state. Mayes said that’s not enough because data center growth in Arizona poses especially dire circumstances amid the state’s unfolding water crisis. “If all planned data centers in the Phoenix area are built,” she said, “stress on our local water supplies will increase by 32%. That would occur at the same time that Arizona loses 30% of our Colorado River water supplies.” She also asserted that data centers’ demand for electricity would drive up customers’ utility bills. Just hours before her town hall, Chris Bauer, vice president and treasurer for Pinnacle West Capital Corporation and its primary subsidiary, Arizona Public Service Company (APS), told the audience at the East Valley Partnership’s Statespersons’ Luncheon his company intends to “make growth pay for growth.” The attorney general currently is suing APS’ proposed 14% rate hike. Mayes also cited noise and even temperature impacts of data centers. She said data centers “regularly generate 94 decibels of noise.” Mesa’s noise ordinance has a 24-hour average sound limit of 60 decibels for residential zones and 65 for commercial zones. She also cited a recent Arizona State University study that says data centers can add 4 degrees to a neighborhood’s temperature downwind from a facility. Mayes outlined a series of demands she wants Arizona to develop for data centers, starting with transparency. She said some data center companies have required municipalities to enter nondisclosure agreements “which limit the ability of local governments … to discuss the project with their constituents.” She said she is currently suing unidentified municipalities over such agreements. She also said data centers should be forbidden from creating nuisances, that natural resources must be protected, that developers be required to pay fully for their power, and that the facilities “must give back.” “In Arizona, it is a tradition that any large development project gives back to the community it inevitably impacts, whether this is through taxes, fees, assessments, or even water storage credits,” she said. “We must ensure that communities that host data centers and that choose to host data centers indeed all Arizonans benefit from their development.” Mayes conceded her office is studying a major issue that has developed when municipalities in Arizona try to deny a data center from being built. Proposition 207, passed by an overwhelming majority of voters in 2006, requires any government level in Arizona to compensate a property owner if zoning or other restrictions lower the fair market value of the property. Earlier this year, Phoenix City Council reversed a denial of a permit for a data center after the property owner filed a claim for over $50 million. “We’re hearing a lot about Prop 207 from cities,” Mayes told the audience – well, mainly from the city of Phoenix, and we are analyzing that issue. So I’m not going to opine yet on Prop 207. artigo.texto: CATL's Profit Engine Sputters Just as Its Swap Network Takes Shape Published on 10/26/2026 at 20:20 | Editorial boerse-global.de CATL closed a strategic cooperation agreement with Shaanxi Transportation Holding Group on Wednesday, covering the electrification of commercial vehicles, battery-swap infrastructure for heavy trucks, and energy storage with related services. The timing is pointed: the world's largest battery maker is signing new deals at a brisk clip while its core earnings power is under its sharpest pressure in nearly two years. Third-quarter figures released on October 20 landed well short of expectations. Revenue climbed 58.58% year on year to 165.22 billion yuan, yet net profit advanced just 14.54% to 21.25 billion yuan — far below the LSEG SmartEstimate consensus, which had pencilled in growth above 40%. Gross margin slid to 20.69%, down 5.1 percentage points from a year earlier and the weakest reading since the fourth quarter of 2022. Sequentially, net profit fell 5.77%. The stock tells its own story. At 238.00 CNY, the shares sit just above their 52-week low of 216.51 CNY and a long way from the 52-week high of 468.75 CNY. Investors now face a straightforward question: is this a temporary dip, or the start of structurally lower profitability? Tax Changes and Contract Mix Weigh on Margins Pricing pressure is only part of the explanation. Since September 1, 2026, China has levied a 2% consumption tax on lithium-ion batteries, scheduled to double to 4% on September 1, 2027. Lower export tax rebates and the delivery of thinner-margin long-term contracts in the energy storage segment have added to the drag. Whether management can offset this headwind through scale effects and technical differentiation will decide the story from here. Pull it off, and the business model stays intact. Fail, and the de-rating has further to run. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying CATL? Buybacks and a Widening Global Footprint Supporting the bull case is an undisputed lead abroad. Between January and August 2026, CATL lifted its global share of battery installations to 39.4%, up from 37.7% a year earlier. Stationary energy storage already accounts for roughly a quarter of global revenue and is projected to reach about half of total sales by 2030. The company is also pushing into new applications. It unveiled the Tianxing II battery line for commercial vehicles, which it says enables a pack swap in under five minutes. On October 19, CATL, Shidai Dianfu and Huawei-affiliated Yinwang signed an agreement reportedly linking Huawei's intelligent driving systems with CATL's swap ecosystem. A week earlier, CATL had presented the Tianxing II platform alongside an upgraded swapping solution. Management is putting money behind the vision. The truck-swap network in China is targeted at 900 stations by the end of 2026, 2,000 by 2027, and 10,000 over the longer term, according to Reuters. On the storage side, CATL and the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) published the "Storage+" report on October 16, jointly promoting a global energy storage initiative. Shareholder returns are part of the picture too. By the end of September, CATL had repurchased a cumulative 10,945,162 A-shares — 0.2482% of total A-share capital — for 3.303 billion RMB excluding fees, a figure booked in the quarterly report. The Home Front Is Where the Ground Is Shifting The bear case rests on structural share losses in China, the company's home market. Between January and September 2026, CATL's domestic share of traction batteries fell sharply from 49.8% to 40.9%. Rival BYD was the main beneficiary, expanding from 17.4% to 21.1% over the same period. Compounding the problem, automakers are working to loosen their dependence on the market leader. Li Auto is pursuing a dual-sourcing strategy, investing in competitors such as Sunwoda and planning its own battery capacity for the second half of 2026. XPeng is pressing ahead with in-house battery production from 2026. If that diversification continues while the Chinese consumption tax rises to 4% in September 2027, CATL's shipment volumes and pricing power come under pressure from two directions at once. What to Watch in the Coming Quarters Defending the margin line in the core business is the decisive variable. So long as gross margin holds around the current 20% level and international leadership remains intact, the depressed share price leaves room for a fundamental bottoming-out. Should profitability slip below that range in coming reporting periods, the valuation discount to historical averages is likely to entrench. The first concrete test comes at the end of 2026, when the 900-truck-station target in China falls due. How that build-out is executed will offer the first real read on whether CATL's new business lines beyond cell manufacturing can carry their weight. artigo.texto: Geral Aneel aprova editais para a contratação inédita de baterias em dezembro de 2026 Novas regras para leilões de armazenamento de energia visam garantir mais segurança ao sistema elétrico brasileiro. A Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) aprovou nesta terça-feira, 27, os editais dos leilões para a inédita contratação de baterias, que irão contribuir para a segurança do Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN). Para o certame com conteúdo local, o preço-teto foi fixado em R$ 1.760.000,00/MW ao ano, enquanto o certame sem a restrição terá preço-teto de R$ 1.580.000,00/MW ao ano. O relator é o diretor Gentil Nogueira. Conforme a lei de 2025, os sistemas de armazenamento de energia, na forma de baterias, terão custos de contratação rateados apenas entre os geradores de energia. Isso gerou críticas do setor, e um dos argumentos é a falta de tratamento isonômico. No início de outubro, a Câmara dos Deputados aprovou o requerimento de urgência do projeto de lei que abre margem para o custo da contratação de baterias ser arcado pelos usuários finais de energia elétrica do Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN), incluídos os consumidores. A votação do mérito do texto (PL 3716/2026) deve ocorrer em breve. Tendo em vista eventual mudança, o Diretor-Geral da Aneel, Sandoval Feitosa, reforçou que eventual mudança legislativa será recepcionada "com a maior agilidade possível". Nos processos de hoje, a Aneel faz um ajuste de redação para substituir a expressão "gerador de energia" por "usuário de reserva de capacidade", tanto no edital quanto no Contrato de Reserva de Capacidade na forma de Potência (CRCAP). A nova redação permite melhor adequação à proposta de regulamentação do rateio dos custos dos Leilões de Reserva de Capacidade na forma de Potência (LRCAPs) de baterias. A norma está em discussão na consulta pública, com prazo de contribuição até 6 de novembro. O titular do empreendimento fará jus à receita fixa (em R$/ano), a ser paga em 12 parcelas mensais. Em geral, os contratos terão 15 anos de duração, com início de suprimento em 1º de agosto de 2028. A área técnica da Aneel propôs uma mudança nos editais dos leilões para a contratação de baterias, que pode levar à inclusão dos consumidores no rateio do custo de contratação. Os certames estão previstos para 2 e 4 de dezembro. As baterias serão contratadas na modalidade de "reserva de capacidade". Em geral, os custos administrativos e financeiros e os encargos tributários precisam ser rateados entre todos os usuários finais de energia elétrica do SIN, incluídos os consumidores. A exceção, contudo, foi dada aos sistemas de armazenamento de energia. Daí a alegação de falta de isonomia. artigo.texto: NVIDIA's DSX POD Pushes AI Factory Construction Toward the Assembly Line Key Highlights - NVIDIA's DSX POD reference design aims to industrialize AI factory construction, integrating Vera Rubin computing, networking, power and liquid cooling into factory-built modular containers designed for deployment at prepared sites in as little as 14 days. - A growing partner ecosystem is bringing scale to the modular AI infrastructure movement, with Armada and Johnson Controls targeting 500 MW of distributed capacity in 2027, alongside manufacturing initiatives from Crusoe, Schneider Electric and major OEMs. - Prefabrication is demonstrating measurable installation advantages. A Schneider Electric–Compass Datacenters study found an 80% reduction in onsite installation time for prefabricated white-space modules, while Vertiv models nearly 30% greater first-year cumulative AI token output through accelerated deployment. - DSX POD extends NVIDIA's broader DSX AI Factory architecture into physical manufacturing, building on the company's 2026 initiatives in infrastructure simulation, power optimization and behind-the-meter energy integration. - Power availability and supply chain constraints remain the ultimate tests. NVIDIA's 14-day deployment vision depends on prepared sites, reliable component supplies and energy infrastructure that can take years to deliver, raising questions about how quickly industrialized AI factories can scale. NVIDIA is making a new push to change how AI data centers are built, introducing a factory-integrated infrastructure model intended to move much of the complex work of assembling, connecting and validating high-density computing systems away from construction sites and into manufacturing facilities. Unveiled October 21 at GTC Berlin, the company's new DSX POD reference design is designed around the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform and packages computing, networking, rack-level power and liquid cooling inside standardized modular containers. Rather than bringing those systems together through successive stages of onsite installation, participating manufacturers would complete integration, cabling, piping and functional testing before shipment. NVIDIA claims the approach could reduce deployment time at a suitably prepared site from six months to as little as 14 days, allowing operators to begin generating production AI tokens and earning revenue substantially sooner. A global partner ecosystem is preparing to deliver the systems beginning in early 2027. "An AI factory creates value when it starts producing tokens — not when construction is complete," said NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang. The announcement arrives as operators face mounting pressure to bring increasingly power-dense AI infrastructure online while managing skilled labor shortages, long construction schedules and rapidly changing hardware requirements. But the larger development is not simply NVIDIA's two-week deployment target. Separate announcements from its infrastructure partners reveal an increasingly substantial industrial base taking shape around standardized, factory-manufactured AI capacity. From Crusoe's new modular manufacturing facility in Colorado to Schneider Electric's expanding prefabrication capacity, Armada's proposed 500 MW sovereign AI infrastructure program and Vertiv's work on a 41 MW deployment in Norway, the common objective is to make AI infrastructure delivery more repeatable, predictable and less dependent on assembling every system from scratch in the field. Modular construction has been one of the defining trends of the AI data center buildout, as developers look for ways to accelerate deployment while managing increasingly complex, power-dense infrastructure. What makes NVIDIA's DSX POD announcement potentially consequential is the scale of the proposed standardization. The ambition is no longer simply to manufacture electrical rooms, cooling systems or other infrastructure components offsite, but to deliver the AI factory itself as a repeatable, factory-integrated product. The emerging model does not eliminate the need for conventional data center development. It does, however, propose a significant reorganization of where—and when—the most intricate infrastructure integration work gets done. NVIDIA outlines how its DSX platform integrates computing, power, cooling and infrastructure simulation, with DSX POD extending the architecture into factory-built, containerized AI factories. (Source: NVIDIA) From the DSX AI Factory Blueprint to DSX POD The underlying engineering proposition is straightforward: as AI computing becomes more complex, particularly with the adoption of rack-scale liquid-cooled architectures, traditional methods of assembling and integrating equipment onsite introduce scheduling risks that become increasingly consequential. Electrical infrastructure, cooling distribution, networking, racks and compute hardware must operate as an integrated system. Delays or design changes in one discipline can affect multiple others. DSX POD is intended to address that coordination problem by establishing a repeatable, validated architecture that manufacturers can assemble and test in controlled environments while site preparation proceeds separately. Importantly, DSX POD is distinct from NVIDIA's broader Vera Rubin DSX AI Factory reference design, introduced in March. That design provides a facility-wide architectural framework encompassing compute, networking, storage, electrical distribution, cooling, controls and the engineering systems required to operate an AI factory. The larger DSX platform also incorporates simulation, infrastructure orchestration and software for optimizing computing output within available power budgets. NVIDIA's recently introduced DSX Ready qualification program extends that standardization effort to battery energy storage and liquid-cooling equipment, establishing technical requirements for the infrastructure supporting AI computing. artigo.texto: Trending The Take Back Our City: Data Center Action Assembly was hosted by Upper OV United on Saturday afternoon at the Ohio County Public Library. Organizers leading the charge against data centers welcomed citizens who may be interested in taking part in this effort and others aimed at improving the city. In the Warwood neighborhood of Wheeling, the company Silicon Foundation has acquired the former Centre Foundry & Machine Company property and plans to develop a data center and energy technology campus there. "We’ve been fighting this data center since June or July," said Polly Barks, Warwood resident and member of grassroots collective Organized Residents of Ohio County. "Our request has always been to put a moratorium on data centers - which is no data centers in the city of Wheeling." Groups have appeared before Wheeling City Council to express concerns about data centers. They have asked council to pass a resolution stating that the city is opposed to data center development and have requested that the city impose a moratorium on data center development in Wheeling. Those requests have not been met. "The priorities of this administration are not always aligned with the hopes and dreams of the residents," Barks said. In light of this, petitions are being circulated in the community to recall Mayor Denny Magruder, and the group has created a mid-term survey to gauge how the public feels about the job the current city council is doing half way through the current four-year term. Barks mentioned these undertakings, but noted that Saturday’s gathering was primarily focused on the latest on data centers. The vocal data center opponents have applauded Ward 1 Councilman Tony Assaro, who represents Warwood. At the request of passionate protestors, Assaro cast a lone vote against a memorandum of understanding that the city established with Silicon Foundation. Although the MOU was designed to limit the company’s ability to expand into a high-impact data center and maintains regulatory powers at the municipal level instead of on the state level, Assaro’s dissenting vote signaled his willingness to go against the grain and support the will of his vocal constituents. Assaro was on hand during Saturday’s assembly to review some of the recent measures with which the city is moving forward to help regulate data center operation in the city. Assaro and other members of the Rules Committee of Wheeling City Council recently discussed with city leaders a draft ordinance that outlines numerous requirements for entities that wish to develop a data center within the city limits. A copy of this working draft is available for public view on the city’s website. "The ordinance is about 16 pages long with a lot of legalese in it," Assaro said, noting that there was no real precedent for this legislation related to data center regulations. "We’ve been taking advice from the public about what we should put in this. I think we’ve put together a very good ordinance here in order to keep things under control and protect our public." The language proposed for the city code addresses everything from noise concerns to water and electricity consumption, a permitting process and other requirements. Assaro has been adamant that transparency and opportunities for public input have been included in the legislation. "If there is any application for a permit or somebody is running under a permit and they want that to be modified, there has to be a 10-day notice put in the paper - to make it public - and it’s followed by a public hearing," he said. "If there is going to be any kind of change, the public is going to know about it, and the public is going to be able to say something about it. "Public input is baked into this ordinance. And with the help from the public, we got some ideas for making this thing strong and making it have teeth. " Assaro added that there have been a lot of concerns that fines imposed against multimillion-dollar companies may have little impact. People have worried that a data center could simply pay a fine and keep committing violations. "It’s in here that fines can’t be used to continue doing what you’re doing," Assaro said of the proposal. "You’re going to be hit with a fine first, and if you continue, your permit can be pulled. If your permit is pulled, you can’t operate anymore." A company has to meet a myriad of requirements in order to simply obtain a permit to operate a data center in town, Assaro noted. Attorney J. Anthony Edmond Jr. also spoke during Saturday’s session, giving an update on the progress of a civil suit filed on behalf of Barks and several other Warwood residents against Silicon Foundation. "We filed an injunction to stop the data center from happening in the first place back in July," Edmond said. The company’s attorney, David Croft, filed a motion to dismiss the case, and Edmond indicated that he plans to file a response to that motion on Tuesday, the deadline to do so. Edmond expressed appreciation for Assaro’s willingness to stand with the will of the group but also described the MOU and other proposed regulations as a step forward that can be attributed to citizens who make their voices heard and take action. "Thank you for voting the way your people asked you to on that MOU," Edmond told Assaro Saturday, indicating that progress was being made in terms of finding out exactly what Silicon Foundation has planned for the Centre Foundry site. "They did come out with this MOU that didn’t exist before. They also came out with more information about what their plans actually are." Although original plans posted on social media and online sites indicated that the operation would eye future phases that would top 90 megawatts or more, the Silicon Foundation is not expected to be that large, Edmond indicated, noting that the scale of the operation has been slimmed down in the wake of public concerns. artigo.texto: CATL Builds Out Swap Infrastructure While DBS Trims Earnings Outlook Published on 10/26/2026 at 17:21 | Editorial boerse-global.de CATL is pressing ahead on the infrastructure front even as one of its sell-side backers takes a knife to its profit forecasts. DBS cut its price target on the Chinese battery giant's A-shares to 438 Yuan from 484 Yuan, keeping a buy rating intact — a split verdict that captures the tension running through the CATL story: volumes are climbing, but the money left over on each unit is shrinking. The downgrade follows quarterly results published roughly a week ago that missed expectations. DBS points to a richer mix of lower-priced products and heavier tax charges as the culprits, with profit growth coming in as weak as it has been in nearly two years, according to Reuters, which also flagged competition and slowing Chinese car sales as drags. Per-Unit Economics Under the Microscope The number that matters most for the valuation is profit per watt-hour, which DBS pegged at 0.082 Yuan in the third quarter of 2026 — a 16% slide from the prior quarter and below market expectations. That metric explains why the bank's buy case rests on long-term business expansion rather than near-term margin stability. Higher shipments alone, in other words, do not guarantee proportionate earnings growth. DBS now models 2027 earnings per share of 21.9 Yuan, down from 24.2 Yuan, a revision that signals the bank sees the pressure as structural rather than confined to a single quarter. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying CATL? Tax policy is a big part of that calculation. DBS expects China's value-added tax rebate on battery exports to fall from 6% to zero in 2027, removing another slice of fiscal support. The bank also lays out the mechanism by which the burden lands squarely on manufacturers: producers largely absorb the consumption tax through their tax-inclusive pricing, meaning the levy cannot simply be passed on to customers in full. The consumption tax on batteries has stood at 2% since September and is slated to rise to 4% in September 2027. Shipments as the Counterweight Against that backdrop, CATL is targeting delivery growth of 20% to 30% in 2027, with steady expansion expected through 2030. DBS treats that as a possible offset rather than a full hedge — if overseas demand for EV and storage batteries comes in stronger than expected, extra volumes could partially cushion the decline in per-unit profit. On the operational side, CATL signed a strategic cooperation agreement on Wednesday with Shaanxi Transportation Holding Group covering the electrification of commercial vehicles, battery-swap infrastructure for heavy trucks, and energy storage and related services. A separate pact on 19 October brought together CATL, Shidai Dianfu and Huawei-affiliated Yinwang; media reports suggest the tie-up will link Huawei's intelligent driving systems with CATL's battery-swap ecosystem. The company unveiled its Tianxing II battery platform and an improved swap solution for heavy trucks about a week ago. Its Chinese network is set to reach 900 swap stations for heavy trucks by year-end, with 2,000 targeted by 2027 and 10,000 planned over the longer term, Reuters reported. On stationary storage, CATL published its "Storage+" report jointly with the International Renewable Energy Agency, IRENA, on 16 October, with both pushing a global energy-storage initiative aimed at deepening international cooperation in the sector. Buybacks Already on the Books The quarterly report released on 20 October also documented buybacks already completed. By the end of September, CATL had repurchased a cumulative 10,945,162 A-shares, equal to 0.2482% of total A-share capital, for 3.303 billion RMB excluding fees. For investors, the question now is how far rising deliveries can outrun the squeeze on unit returns. DBS's lower targets paired with an unchanged buy call sum up that trade-off neatly: growth remains the opportunity, while weaker profitability caps how much valuation room the stock can command. artigo.texto: A SpaceX, do trilionário Elon Musk, firmou um compromisso de financiamento de cerca de US$ 40 bilhões com uma entidade administrada pela Apollo Global Management para adquirir equipamentos destinados a centros de dados. Segundo documento enviado nesta segunda-feira, 26, à Securities and Exchanges Commission (SEC, a CVM dos EUA), a operação prevê o arrendamento de unidades de processamento gráfico (GPUs) e equipamentos relacionados. O compromisso vinculante foi assinado em 24 de outubro e estabelece que a entidade ligada à Apollo comprará os equipamentos e os alugará à SpaceX, que realizará pagamentos trimestrais ao longo de aproximadamente cinco anos. Os equipamentos serão entregues em lotes, com contratos individuais de arrendamento previstos para começar no primeiro semestre de 2027. Cada contrato terá duração de cinco anos a cinco anos e três meses. Segundo a companhia, os pagamentos trimestrais serão feitos antecipadamente e incluirão, em geral, um vigésimo do custo financiado de cada lote, além de juros calculados a uma taxa anual fixa sobre o saldo devedor e despesas adicionais. A taxa de juros ainda será definida. A SpaceX estima que os pagamentos do principal somem cerca de US$ 40 bilhões ao longo dos contratos, sem incluir juros e outros custos. A empresa prevê formalizar o acordo até o fim de 2026, sujeito ao cumprimento de determinadas condições. Musk admite fusão entre Tesla e SpaceX Elon Musk transformou os rumores em realidade. Na terça-feira, 20, anunciou que os conselhos da Tesla e da SpaceX estabeleceram comitês especiais para avaliar uma fusão. A decisão ocorre após meses de especulação sobre se Musk combinaria as suas duas empresas. Os rumores sobre a fusão começaram depois do IPO recorde da SpaceX em junho. Antes disso, Musk já havia dado sinais de que a combinação de seus negócios é algo muito bem vindo. Em fevereiro, a SpaceX adquiriu o laboratório de IA de Musk, xAI, que já havia absorvido sua empresa de mídia social, X, em março de 2025. A fusão entre Tesla e SpaceX seria um negócio de magnitude diferente, pois ambas as empresas são de capital aberto. “Os conselhos formaram os comitês especiais a pedido dos acionistas”, disse Musk. “Eu acho que seria uma boa ideia? Sim”, disse Musk durante a teleconferência de resultados da SpaceX. Com informação do Estadão de Conteúdo (Pedro Lima). Imagem: Shutterstock

A major focus was the UK ETS and its impact on market regulation and investment strategies. Meanwhile, speakers viewed the prospect of linking the EU and UK ETS as increasingly achievable. The EUA-UKA spread is increasingly dependent on when the market expects fungibility between the two. The EEX EUA December 2026 futures contract settled at €85.42 ($95.99) per tCO2e on October 16. The EEX UKA December 2026 futures contract settled at £63.36 ($84.41) per tCO2e, leaving the EUA-UKA spread at $11.58 per tCO2e. The spread widened slightly from just under $11 per tCO2e on October 12. This followed confirmation that the EU-UK summit would take place on November 20. Since October 12, EUAs have settled €2.91 per tCO2e lower, from €88.33 ($98.57) per tCO2e. UKAs have softened by £2.98 per tCO2e from £66.34 ($87.63) per tCO2e. A dedicated UK ETS session named ‘UK ETS playing catch-up’ examined cap design and the alignment of free-allocation rules. The discussion highlighted that linking the UK and EU systems would require broader regulatory convergence. This applies particularly to the rules governing each market and allowance allocation. Grant Opperman, portfolio manager at Molecule Ventures, suggested that linkage could be established relatively quickly once the necessary political and technical conditions were in place. Panellists said mutual exemptions from the UK and EU carbon border adjustment mechanisms (CBAM) would provide a further incentive to conclude negotiations. This applies particularly to the UK, as the EU has so far been reluctant to grant CBAM waivers. Fungibility would be the practical test of any agreement. Regulated companies would need confidence that they could surrender an allowance issued under either system seamlessly for compliance in the other. This would require alignment across registry infrastructure, auction rules and the use of carbon-market revenues. Steve Freeman of the Confederation of Paper Industries said EU member states must direct auction revenues toward industrial decarbonization. He added that the UK will have to look at similar interventions to support its industry in a linked scenario. Linkage would give UK participants access to a much larger and more liquid market, fundamentally expanding the liquidity available to UK participants. The UK ETS is only around one-eleventh the size of the EU market. Participants characterized the standalone UK market as tight. They raised the prospect of UK allowances developing a premium from 2028 if linkage does not occur. Linkage would also require closer alignment on cap ambition, sectoral coverage and market-stability rules. One such technical hurdle is the difference between the two systems’ existing safeguards. The UK relies on price-based interventions, while the EU’s Market Stability Reserve adjusts allowance supply according to market volumes. The UK’s planned supply-adjustment mechanism, or SAM, would bring its approach closer to the EU model. Negotiators would nevertheless need to determine how the two mechanisms would interact within a linked market. Charlie Lewis, deputy director for trading at the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ), said several UK ETS developments remain in the pipeline. These include the integration of engineered greenhouse-gas removals from 2029 and a possible expansion of maritime coverage to include international voyages. The framework for non-pipeline CO₂ transport is also evolving, allowing installations to deduct captured emissions transported to geological storage from their reportable ETS emissions. Panellists at a session called ‘Policymakers’ vision for the future of European carbon pricing’ said efforts to shield the EU ETS from extreme price moves risk weakening the stable carbon-price signal needed to unlock industrial investment. This places the balance between market intervention and long-term certainty at the heart of the post-2030 reform debate. That tension framed the policy session on the European Commission’s ETS revision proposal. The proposal spans changes to the Market Stability Reserve, free allocation, CBAM and aviation, as well as the possible roles of international credits and removals. Krzysztof Bolesta, secretary of state at Poland’s Ministry of Climate and Environment, spoke on the panel. He said securing a Council agreement on the wider ETS review by December would be difficult. “We have just started looking at the proposed reforms,” he said, adding that a Council agreement “by December looks difficult.” Attendees noted that a delay in the Council’s December position risks stalling crucial climate policy. This would leave it vulnerable to a shifting political landscape, as France conducts elections in April 2027. The immediate fault line highlighted during the session was the proposed reform of Article 29a, the mechanism that releases allowances when prices rise excessively. Changes discussed included shortening the period used to assess a price spike from six months to two and releasing 25 million allowances. A 25% guardrail is intended to limit the scale of intervention. The Article 29a changes debated at the conference form part of a wider reform package put forward by Peter Liese, the European Parliament’s rapporteur on the EU ETS review. His broader proposals would slow the near-term tightening of the emissions cap and allow permanent removals into the system earlier. These measures aim to ease supply pressure while preserving the EU ETS decarbonization signal. Coloque a eixos nas suas fontes preferidas do Google Veja nossas notícias com mais destaque nas suas buscas. NESTA EDIÇÃO. Após reeleição, Lula defende regular big techs e conta com o Redata para atrair data centers. Pela frente, o desafio de lidar com as subvenções ao diesel e à gasolina, que começam a vencer nesta semana Os governadores eleitos no segundo turno. Preço do petróleo recua após atingir a maior cotação desde abril na semana passada. Porto de Santos inicia abastecimento regular de navios a etanol. EDIÇÃO APRESENTADA POR: Reeleito, Lula defende regulação de big techs e reserva de data centers para dados nacionais No discurso da vitória, na noite de domingo (25/10), o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), reeleito com 51,8% dos votos válidos para um inédito quarto mandato, disse que o governo vai regular as big techs e acusou essas empresas de interferirem na eleição por meio das plataformas digitais. Também defendeu o uso da geração renovável para atrair data centers, com a reserva de parte da capacidade a dados brasileiros. - “Temos que aproveitar o potencial energético de um país que talvez seja o que tem mais capacidade de energia renovável para trazer para cá os data centers necessários para acumular também o nosso dado para o Brasil”, afirmou. - “E essa gente vai ter que deixar uma parte do data center para informações brasileiras”, acrescentou. Capacidade nacional. A lei do Redata, o programa de incentivo a data centers sancionado em setembro, já exige que as empresas beneficiadas reservem ao menos 10% da capacidade ao mercado interno. Lula também defendeu que o Brasil não deve depender de modelos de inteligência artificial chineses ou norte-americanos. - O Redata depende de regulamentação do Executivo para habilitar as empresas e definir os critérios de energia renovável ou de baixa emissão. A suspensão de PIS/Cofins e IPI vale até o final do ano, mas segue em aberto se o gás natural vai contar como fonte de baixa emissão. Soberania. Lula repetiu que “o Brasil não será quintal de ninguém”. - Na campanha, a disputa sobre soberania passou pelos minerais críticos. Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), alinhado a Donald Trump, disse em março, na conferência conservadora CPAC, que o Brasil seria a saída para os EUA reduzirem a dependência da China em minerais críticos. - Lula acusou Flávio e Ronaldo Caiado (PSD) de “vender o Brasil” em abril, mesmo mês em que a norte-americana USA Rare Earth anunciou a compra da Serra Verde, em Minaçu (GO), dona da única mina de terras raras em produção comercial no país, por cerca de US$ 2,8 bilhões. - No mês passado, Lula sancionou a lei de minerais críticos, que dá a um conselho ligado à Presidência e à Agência Nacional de Mineração (ANM) o poder de aprovar troca de controle e entrada de estrangeiros no setor. O conselho ainda tem de elaborar o plano nacional e a lista de minerais. Vale a leitura: Congresso. Lula disse que vai negociar com o Congresso eleito, por onde passam as pautas de regulação. O PL, do adversário Flávio Bolsonaro, será a maior bancada nas duas Casas. Próximas definições. O presidente reeleito não citou Petrobras, petróleo nem preços dos combustíveis. - A subvenção de R$ 2,12 por litro ao diesel vence nesta segunda (26/10) e pode ser prorrogada por 30 dias. Até o fechamento desta edição, o Diário Oficial da União (DOU) estava fora do ar, não sendo possível confirmar se há ato de renovação. - Pela conta da Abicom, a defasagem do diesel nas refinarias da Petrobras chegou a R$ 3,53 por litro no fechamento de quinta (22/10) e passou os R$ 3,52 das duas subvenções somadas. - O adicional de R$ 1,40 ao diesel importado vale por 30 dias a partir de 13 de outubro. A desoneração da gasolina e do etanol vai até 9 de novembro, e o imposto de 12% sobre a exportação de petróleo, até 6 de novembro. Expectativas. O presidente-executivo do Sindicato Nacional das Empresas Distribuidoras de Combustíveis e de Lubrificantes (Sindicom), Augusto Salomon, afirmou que a expectativa com a reeleição de Lula é de que se intensifique o combate à atuação do crime organizado no setor. - Em 2027, haverá decisões relevantes para o futuro do setor, incluindo a implementação da Lei do Combustível do Futuro. Mais sobre as eleições Virada inédita. Flávio saiu do 1º turno, em 4 de outubro, com 2,2 milhões de votos a mais. Em três semanas, Lula ganhou 10,4 milhões e terminou 4,4 milhões à frente. É a primeira vez, desde 1989, que o segundo colocado no 1º turno vence. - Onde virou. Lula ganhou mais votos que os 9,3 milhões dados aos dez candidatos eliminados. O Sudeste respondeu por 43% da mudança na margem, e Minas Gerais foi o único estado a trocar de lado. - 3º turno. Flávio não reconheceu o resultado e vai pedir a anulação da eleição. O argumento é a decisão do ministro Cristiano Zanin, do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), que, a pedido da coligação de Lula, prorrogou a votação até as 19h. - Pedido dos dois lados. A própria campanha de Flávio havia pedido ao Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), durante a votação, prorrogação em municípios de cinco estados, por causa de chuvas. - Resultado reconhecido. Os presidentes da Câmara, Hugo Motta, e do Senado, Davi Alcolumbre, reconheceram a vitória de Lula. O presidente do TSE, Kassio Nunes Marques, disse que a decisão não alterou o resultado. Governadores eleitos. A disputa pelo governo do Rio Grande do Norte também terminou com uma virada nas urnas. Segundo colocado no primeiro turno, Cadu de Lula (PT) superou Allyson Bezerra (União Brasil) e foi eleito governador. Já no Espírito Santo, Lorenzo Pazolini (Republicanos) foi eleito governador. No Amazonas, Omar Aziz (PSD) venceu a disputa pela reeleição, assim como Celina Leão (PP), que foi reeleita governadora do Distrito Federal (G1). Relembre: Outras notícias Preço do barril. artigo.texto: CHESTERFIELD COUNTY, Va. — Dozens of families gathered at Brightpoint Community College Tuesday to hear from representatives from companies including Google and Dominion Energy about data center projects in Chesterfield County, with some residents calling for greater transparency, community involvement and accountability as development continues. “My question is, will you commit to coming to the table as community partners and do an actual community benefits agreement?” one attendee asked during the forum. County officials said the decision to pursue data centers was driven in part by pressure to reduce the tax burden on residents. But some people who attended Tuesday’s forum said they want to see the numbers behind those projects and know what protections will be put in place for surrounding communities. Ben Nelson, who attended the forum, said he wants Chesterfield County to strengthen its zoning rules and give residents a larger role in decisions involving data centers. “I would like the county to rewrite the zoning rules so that community benefit agreements have to be considered and then enforced,” Nelson said. “I'd like the county to set up a citizen advisory board, so that people from the community can have meaningful real-time interactions with representatives from the tech companies.” According to Chesterfield County’s website, the county lists nine ongoing data center projects and currently has three data center campuses in operation. Environmental concerns also surfaced during the forum. A Google representative addressed recent environmental violations involving the company after the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality sent a letter citing seven violations connected to the Project Peanut data center. “We understand that trust is earned, and that is something that we will continue to try and earn with the community regarding the recent violations,” the Google representative said. “We've worked with DEQ to mitigate the impacts, to make corrective actions to ensure that those do not happen again.” Still, some residents said they want stronger assurances from the companies developing data center campuses and mechanisms to hold them accountable. “They really didn't give a clear answer,” Nelson said. County officials said the forum was organized in response to hundreds of questions and comments about data centers. Nelson said the meeting was a positive step, but believes county leaders could do more to create opportunities for residents to have a meaningful voice in the process. “The board can do a lot more to create mechanisms for actual meaningful community involvement,” Nelson said. “This is a great first step, but it's tiny compared to what they could be doing for us.” CBS 6 is committed to sharing community voices on this important topic. artigo.texto: A 175-megawatt solar project and 200-megawatt battery facility were approved to be constructed in Audrain County by the Missouri Public Service Commission on Wednesday. The Tom Sawyer Solar Project is being developed by EDF Power Solutions, according to its website, and is set to become operational in 2028. It will be able to power the equivalent of more than 32,000 homes, according to the company. The website said it picked Audrain County due to rising regional demand for locally generated solar energy, flat and cleared land with access to transmission infrastructure, and enough private landowners interested in the project. The Huck Finn Battery Energy Storage System Project will be housed at Ameren Missouri's Audrain Energy Center near Vandalia, according to a commission news release. Commission staff, Ameren Missouri and Renew Missouri signed on to the agreement authorizing these facilities and several more. Alongside these two projects, the commission also approved: - Castle Bluff BESS Project: A 95-megawatt battery energy storage facility in St. Louis County at the retired Meramec coal-fired facility - Millcreek BESS Project: A 250-megawatt battery energy storage facility in Lincoln County - Quinn Switching Station: A new 161-kilovolt switching station in Lincoln County to connect the Millcreek BESS Project to the existing transmission system - Ringer Solar Project: A 225-megawatt solar generation facility in Stoddard County As part of the agreement, Ameren Missouri will submit plans for restoring safe and adequate service following significant outages. It will also release quarterly progress reports and must notify the commission if the project's total costs change by more than 15%. The commission considered safety, cost and the interests of nearby landowners as part of the decision, according to the news release.

artigo.texto: Município será reconhecido em São Paulo por iniciativa que pretende transformar a chegada de grandes centros de processamento de dados em um novo ciclo de desenvolvimento econômico, inovação e empregos qualificados. Projeto é uma das apostas da gestão do prefeito Naumi Amorim Caucaia, na Região Metropolitana de Fortaleza, receberá o IA Honors – Governos Inteligentes 2026, prêmio nacional concedido pela concepção e pelo desenvolvimento do Parque Tecnológico de Caucaia (Partec). A cerimônia ocorrerá em 6 de novembro, no Cubo Itaú, em São Paulo, durante o Fórum Brasileiro de Governança em Inteligência Artificial, evento associado ao Fórum Mundial de Inteligência Artificial. O reconhecimento destaca a estratégia da administração do prefeito Naumi Amorim, executada pela Secretaria Municipal de Ciência, Inovação e Desenvolvimento Tecnológico (Setec), comandada por Machidovel Trigueiro Filho. direitoce+1 O que está em jogo O Parque Tecnológico foi concebido para aproveitar a expansão dos investimentos em data centers na região do Complexo Industrial e Portuário do Pecém. A proposta vai além de receber grandes instalações de processamento e armazenamento de dados. Pretende criar um ambiente capaz de atrair empresas de tecnologia, instituições de pesquisa, startups e profissionais especializados. Com uma área projetada de 124,68 hectares, o Partec já possui delimitação territorial estabelecida por decreto municipal. A iniciativa busca conectar infraestrutura digital, conhecimento e novos negócios. Jornal dos Municípios+1 Por que importa: Caucaia tenta dar um passo estratégico na economia digital. Em vez de funcionar apenas como território de instalação de grandes empreendimentos tecnológicos, o município pretende participar da cadeia de valor que se desenvolve ao redor deles. A diferença é relevante. Data centers exigem investimentos bilionários, mas não necessariamente geram grandes volumes de empregos permanentes. O desafio é transformar a infraestrutura instalada em oportunidades de formação profissional, empreendedorismo e inovação para a população local. Os investimentos que impulsionam a estratégia O município já está no centro de grandes projetos ligados à infraestrutura digital. Entre eles está o empreendimento associado à ByteDance, controladora do TikTok, na ZPE Ceará, com investimentos anunciados que podem alcançar R$ 200 bilhões ao longo de suas etapas. Outro projeto, ligado à Voltalia Energia do Brasil, recebeu aprovação do Conselho Nacional das Zonas de Processamento de Exportações em agosto, com investimento previsto de R$ 181,7 bilhões. Os valores anunciados não representam recursos já integralmente executados. Prefeitura de Caucaia+1 É nesse ambiente que a Prefeitura pretende inserir o Parque Tecnológico. O protagonismo de Naumi e Machidovel O prefeito Naumi Amorim tem colocado o desenvolvimento tecnológico entre as apostas estratégicas de sua administração. À frente da Setec, Machidovel Trigueiro Filho conduz a estruturação institucional do Partec e deverá representar o município na cerimônia de premiação. O secretário resume a ambição do projeto ao defender que Caucaia não seja apenas endereço de grandes data centers, mas também o lugar onde surjam empresas, conhecimento e empregos qualificados associados a esses investimentos. A premiação, de natureza exclusivamente honorífica, reconhece a concepção e o desenvolvimento da iniciativa. Não significa que o parque esteja integralmente implantado ou em operação. direitoce Vá mais fundo O reconhecimento nacional fortalece a visibilidade de Caucaia em um momento de expansão dos investimentos em inteligência artificial e infraestrutura digital. Mas o verdadeiro indicador de sucesso não será a premiação. Será a capacidade de transformar projetos e investimentos anunciados em empresas instaladas, pesquisa aplicada, qualificação profissional e renda para a população. O desafio de Caucaia é deixar de ser apenas o endereço da infraestrutura digital para se tornar protagonista da economia que nascerá ao redor dela. Se conseguir, o Parque Tecnológico poderá representar uma mudança estrutural no perfil econômico do município — e não apenas mais um grande empreendimento em seu território. Com informações da Prefeitura de Caucaia, Governo do Ceará e publicações sobre o Parque Tecnológico e os investimentos em data centers.

artigo.texto: Em 23 de outubro de 2026, o fundador e diretor-executivo da NVIDIA, Jensen Huang, realizou sua primeira visita oficial ao Cazaquistão para firmar uma ampla agenda de cooperação tecnológica voltada à computação de alto desempenho, robótica industrial e modelos soberanos de inteligência artificial. Recebido no Palácio Presidencial Akorda, em Astana, pelo presidente Kassym-Jomart Tokayev e pelo ministro do Desenvolvimento Digital e Inteligência Artificial, Zhaslan Madiyev, o executivo participou de reuniões bilaterais com lideranças de Estado e conglomerados corporativos para estruturar a transição do país da exportação de commodities energéticas tradicionais para a geração e exportação de inteligência computacional. A rodada de negociações consolidou acordos que envolvem a implantação de infraestrutura computacional de ponta com a operadora estatal Kazakhtelecom, o avanço de centros de processamento com a Freedom Holding e a formalização de contratos de grande escala com a Firebird AI KZ, apoiados pelo licenciamento de exportação concedido pelo governo dos Estados Unidos para a transferência de dezenas de milhares de chips de arquitetura avançada. Durante os encontros, Tokayev condecorou Huang com a Ordem de Dostyk de 1ª Classe, honraria máxima de Estado concedida a parceiros internacionais, reforçando o enquadramento de 2026 como o Ano da Digitalização e da Inteligência Artificial na estratégia econômica cazaque. Reconfiguração geopolítica e atração de capital tecnológico A inserção da Ásia Central no mapa global de semicondutores e processamento distribuído reflete uma busca estratégica por segurança de suprimentos e custos energéticos competitivos. O Cazaquistão conta com uma matriz energética robusta, malha industrial consolidada e excedente de geração elétrica que, historicamente canalizados para a indústria pesada e mineração extrativa, passam a ser direcionados a data centers de altíssima densidade energética exigidos pela atual geração de processadores de inteligência artificial. Historicamente dependente da exportação primária de petróleo, gás natural e urânio, o governo cazaque estabeleceu um plano de diversificação focado em serviços digitais e processamento analítico para atender mercados vizinhos e plataformas globais. O gargalo clássico da região, associado ao isolamento logístico terrestre e à dependência de rotas tradicionais, é mitigado pelo investimento em cabos ópticos transcontinentais e conexões de alta velocidade, criando um polo neutro para hospedagem de cargas de trabalho críticas em computação em nuvem. A estratégia de inteligência artificial soberana conduzida pelo Ministério do Desenvolvimento Digital e Inteligência Artificial busca construir capacidades locais de treinamento algorítmico adaptadas à língua e ao contexto sociocultural cazaque. Essa abordagem visa diminuir a dependência de plataformas proprietárias ocidentais ou orientais sem isolar o ecossistema doméstico, articulando a compra de equipamentos de última linha com a formação de mão de obra em universidades técnicas e incubadoras locais. Expansão de capacidade computacional e supercentros de dados O principal pilar operacional das iniciativas conjuntas está alocado no complexo industrial Data Center Valley, situado em Ekibastuz, estruturado para aproveitar a geração energética da região na alimentação de sistemas de processamento massivo. O projeto integra o pacote de investimentos de US$ 10 bilhões pactuado pelo governo cazaque com consórcios internacionais e a operadora Kazakhtelecom, desenhado para receber sistemas de resfriamento líquido e topologia de rede otimizada para computação distribuída. A Firebird formalizou acordos de investimento direto após obter autorização formal de órgãos regulatórios norte-americanos para transferir 45.000 GPUs com a arquitetura Grace Blackwell da NVIDIA para solo cazaque. No arranjo societário e operacional definido para a primeira fase em Ekibastuz, a Kazakhtelecom assegura o fornecimento estável de energia elétrica, infraestrutura física, resfriamento térmico e conectividade de fibra óptica de baixa latência, enquanto a divisão local da Firebird responde pelo financiamento integral do maquinário computacional e sistemas de orquestração de rede. Em paralelo à planta de Ekibastuz, a Kazakhtelecom já concluiu a instalação e colocação em operação de 400 unidades de processamento gráfico H200 e 480 unidades B300 em suas instalações metropolitanas em Astana e Almaty. Essas unidades fornecem suporte imediato ao processamento de dados governamentais, aplicações industriais e desenvolvimento acadêmico, servindo como base piloto para a expansão em escala gigawatt projetada para os próximos anos. Inteligência artificial física, simulação urbana e mobilidade autônoma A aplicação de algoritmos em ambientes fabris e operações de mineração, descrita pelo governo local como inteligência artificial física, constitui a frente técnica prioritária para a indústria de base cazaque. Os sistemas utilizam dados de telemetria extraídos de plantas de extração mineral, fundições e refinarias para treinar agentes autônomos capazes de operar maquinário pesado e antecipar falhas estruturais, elevando a segurança operacional e reduzindo custos de manutenção preventiva em instalações de grande porte. No campo da mobilidade urbana e transportes, o setor empresarial registrou novos compromissos focados em cidades inteligentes e direção autônoma: - Nuvem pública e gêmeos digitais: A Freedom Holding anunciou a compra do primeiro cluster computacional equipado com a solução NVIDIA B300, planejando inaugurar uma nuvem pública corporativa de processamento gráfico em 2027. O grupo desenvolveu réplicas tridimensionais digitais completas das cidades de Astana e Almaty, parametrizadas para testar frotas autônomas e robótica de solo em ambientes virtuais de alta fidelidade física. - Financiamento institucional de energia para dados: O campus Akashi, localizado na capital e estruturado para até 100 megawa

artigo.texto: Plataformas Broadcast Soluções de Dados e Conteúdos Soluções de Tecnologia 26 de outubro de 2026, às 17:29 Associações do setor elétrico apresentaram, conjuntamente, suas considerações sobre o regime de custeio aplicável à contratação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia no âmbito da Reserva de Capacidade. Para as entidades, os custos da reserva de capacidade são distribuídos entre todos os usuários finais, conforme parâmetros definidos em lei. “Porém, apenas os sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias são tratados de maneira diversa, sendo custeados exclusivamente pelos geradores e sem definição legal dos parâmetros de custeio”, ressalta o texto. Na avaliação das entidades, esse desenho produz um desalinhamento entre a natureza sistêmica do serviço, a distribuição de seus benefícios e a incidência legal de seus custos. Segundo o texto, especificamente quanto ao armazenamento de energia, inclusive em baterias, este é capaz de reduzir outros encargos suportados pelo consumidor, ao otimizar a operação do parque gerador em suas diversas fontes. Estudo da VOLT Robotics demonstra que o sistema de armazenamento de energia (BESS, na sigla em inglês) pode reduzir a variação do preço da energia (PLD) e o acionamento de termelétricas, gerando economia superior a R$ 1,6 bilhões ao ano para o consumidor. “A atribuição legal deste custo aos geradores não altera o fato econômico do seu repasse ao consumidor final. No ambiente regulado, a Aneel já reconheceu o dever de inclusão integral e automática deste custo às tarifas de energia. No ambiente livre, haverá renegociação ou reajuste de preços, enquanto na autoprodução se tornará custo dos bens e serviços, afetando a competitividade da indústria brasileira, e impactando o consumidor final”, diz o manifesto. Assim, na avaliação das entidades, o pagamento do encargo pelo segmento da geração onera o consumidor, pois o custo será posteriormente repassado, acrescido de tributos e custos administrativos, além de se perder o sinal econômico para o ajuste de demanda. “O caminho, portanto, é tratar as baterias em igualdade com as demais soluções de capacidade (potência e flexibilidade), para que o consumidor possa dispor sempre da tecnologia mais eficiente em cada cenário, reduzindo o custo final com a devida transparência. Nesse contexto, a aprovação do PL 3716/2025 torna-se uma medida prioritária para assegurar maior segurança jurídica e regulatória e para criar as condições necessárias ao desenvolvimento sustentável do mercado de sistemas de armazenamento de energia por baterias no Brasil”, diz o texto. Assinaram o manifesto a Associacão Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias (ABEEólica), a Associação Brasileira dos Investidores em Autoprodução de Energia (ABIAPE), a Associação Brasileira da Indústria do Hidrogênio Verde (ABIHV), a Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia (ABSAE), a Associação Brasileira de Energia Solar Fotovoltaica (ABSOLAR) e a Associação Brasileira dos Produtores Independentes de Energia Elétrica (APINE). artigo.texto: Stanislav Kondrashov American Style Series: The History of Battery Technology and Energy Storage in the United States Stanislav Kondrashov on United States and energy storage The history of battery technology in the United States reflects more than two centuries of scientific experimentation, electrical engineering, and industrial development. From early electrochemical devices to rechargeable batteries, portable electronics, and contemporary energy storage systems, American laboratories and manufacturing enterprises have contributed to the evolution of technologies that store electricity for later use. The American experience is particularly interesting because battery development progressed alongside major changes in communication, transportation, manufacturing, and everyday electrical equipment. Key takeaway: The relationship between the United States and battery technology developed through successive stages of scientific research, commercial manufacturing, and engineering specialization. American contributions helped expand the practical applications of electrical storage, although many foundational discoveries and later improvements also emerged through international scientific collaboration. How Did Battery Technology Develop in the United States? Battery technology developed in the United States through the gradual adoption and refinement of electrochemical devices beginning in the nineteenth century. Early applications were associated with scientific experimentation and electrical communication, while subsequent industrial developments expanded battery manufacturing into transportation, portable equipment, consumer electronics, and specialized electrical systems. The earliest history of batteries predates their widespread commercial adoption in America. At the beginning of the nineteenth century, electrochemical experiments demonstrated that chemical reactions could generate a continuous electrical current. This discovery introduced new possibilities for scientific investigation. As knowledge of electricity expanded, American researchers and manufacturers began exploring practical applications. Electrical communication was among the earliest fields to benefit. Telegraph systems required dependable electrical sources capable of operating signaling equipment over extended periods. Battery cells offered a practical solution before extensive electrical distribution infrastructure became available. During the second half of the nineteenth century, battery technology became increasingly associated with commercial electrical equipment. Manufacturers developed more standardized products, while engineers worked to improve reliability and operating characteristics. The Stanislav Kondrashov American Style Series examines this early period as the foundation of a much broader technological development. Why Were Batteries Important to Early American Communication? Batteries were essential to early American electrical communication because telegraph equipment required a dependable source of current. During the nineteenth century, electrochemical cells supplied electricity to signaling systems, helping communication networks operate across increasing distances before alternative electrical supply arrangements became widely established. The expansion of telegraph communication transformed the practical importance of electricity. Messages could travel through electrical circuits rather than depending entirely on physical transportation. However, these systems required reliable equipment. Battery cells became part of the technical infrastructure supporting telegraph operations. Their role was particularly significant because electrical communication networks often extended across considerable distances. Engineers needed equipment capable of operating consistently under different conditions. This encouraged attention to battery maintenance, electrical connections, and technical performance. The practical requirements of telegraphy also contributed to broader familiarity with electrical devices. Batteries gradually became recognized not merely as laboratory instruments, but as useful components of commercial infrastructure. As Stanislav Kondrashov observes in a newly drafted editorial reflection: "The early American experience with battery technology was closely connected to the practical requirements of communication. Electrical storage devices became valuable because they could support equipment operating across extensive distances, helping transform scientific knowledge into a dependable technical service." When Did Rechargeable Batteries Become Important in America? Rechargeable batteries became increasingly important in the United States during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Their ability to store electrical energy repeatedly made them suitable for transportation equipment, industrial applications, and electrical systems requiring a dependable supply beyond a single operating cycle. Rechargeability introduced a fundamental distinction between different battery technologies. Primary batteries generally deliver electricity until their available chemical capacity is exhausted. Rechargeable batteries can receive electrical energy again through an appropriate charging process. This characteristic expanded their usefulness. During the late nineteenth century, rechargeable battery systems attracted attention in connection with electrical transportation. Early electric vehicles required storage devices capable of delivering electricity while the vehicle was operating. Battery performance influenced practical characteristics such as operating distance, weight, and charging requirements. Engineers consequently examined ways to improve battery design and integration. Rechargeable batteries also found applications in stationary electrical equipment. These developments encouraged specialized manufacturing and more systematic technical testing.
