artigo.texto: ASEIC Expands Carbon Market Cooperation with Vietnam Cooperation in Waste Heat Recovery, ESS, Solar Power, and Medical Waste Treatment The ASEM SMEs Eco-Innovation Center (ASEIC) said on October 27 that it held the opening ceremony of the 2026 Korea-Vietnam Eco-Innovation Partnership Week on October 26, attended by officials from the Department of Climate Change (DCC) at Vietnam’s Ministry of Agriculture and Environment. The program is part of ASEIC’s “Eco-Innovation Consulting and Capacity Building for Vietnamese SMEs” project. It was designed to strengthen Vietnam’s capacity to implement its carbon market system and expand cooperation between the two countries by sharing Korea’s policy and technological experience. At the opening ceremony, the DCC and ASEIC exchanged a letter of intent (LOI), and four Korean green technology companies signed memorandums of understanding (MOUs) with Vietnamese companies. Jeong Gwangcheon, chairman of ASEIC and president of the Korea Innovation Business Association, and Bui Duc Hieu, deputy director of the Department of Climate Change at Vietnam's Ministry of Agriculture and Environment, pose for a commemorative photo after exchanging a letter of intent (LOI) at the opening ceremony of the 2026 Korea-Vietnam Eco-Innovation Partnership Week on the 26th. ASEM SMEs Eco-Innovation Center View original image The agreements involved four Korean companies working in waste heat recovery and power generation; energy storage systems (ESS) and waste battery diagnostics; ESS and solar panels; and steam sterilization treatment of medical waste. ASEIC expects the agreements to expand opportunities for technology exchange and cooperation between companies in the two countries across various fields, including improving energy efficiency, using renewable energy, and managing waste. During their visit to Korea, Vietnamese officials plan to visit domestic institutions, including the Greenhouse Gas Inventory and Research Center of Korea (GIR) and the Korea Environment Corporation, to learn about Korea’s greenhouse gas management system and experience operating related policies and systems. They will also explore policy implications for implementing Vietnam’s carbon market system and ways for the two countries to cooperate. artigo.texto: XPeng's IRON Robot Solid-State Battery Rolls Off in Small-Batch Production, Scale Manufacturing Targeted by Year-End On October 28, at the 2026 Embodied Intelligence Robot Conference and Embodied Intelligence Main Forum hosted by the China Society of Automotive Engineers, Gu Jie, vice president of XPeng Group, revealed that the solid-state battery used in its IRON robot has completed small-batch production and rolled off the line, and the overall robot project is in the sprint phase before SOP (standard operating procedure). Gu Jie made the remarks while speaking at the forum. SOP is typically seen as the key milestone marking a product's transition from engineering validation to volume manufacturing, and the statement signals that the IRON robot's core power component has already cleared the mass-production stage ahead of the rest. XPeng Robotics is regarded as one of the group's most important business segments outside of new energy vehicles, and its pace of progress has clearly accelerated recently. On September 22, XPeng Group held its first robot supply chain partner conference, drawing leading suppliers of core components including actuators, dexterous hands, sensors and AI chips. XPeng Robotics has completed supply chain factory audits and designated core components, further solidifying mass-production readiness. Under the established plan, the IRON robot will enter large-scale production by the end of 2026 and officially go on sale and begin deliveries in 2027. The solid-state battery is the core selling point that sets the IRON robot apart from similar products. XPeng Group announced at its 2025 Tech Day that its new-generation humanoid robot IRON would be the industry's first to use an all-solid-state battery. In February this year, the group disclosed related technical progress: all-weather road testing had concluded, the battery pack's volume utilization had risen to 78%, 23 percentage points higher than conventional liquid battery packs, while weight was reduced by 35%. On the battery self-development front, XPeng Group Chairman He Xiaopeng said in September that the group has invested in three battery cell companies and that all its batteries will be made in-house starting in 2026. This arrangement provides a common foundation for the power solutions of both the robot and vehicle businesses. In terms of application scenarios, the IRON robot is slated to enter XPeng stores and commercial settings worldwide starting in 2027, taking on service functions such as sales assistance and product presentations, forming a closed loop of "mass production—delivery—scenario deployment." In the secondary market, XPeng-W (09868.HK) rose HK$1.18 (approximately $0.15) that day, a gain of 3.347%. For XPeng Group, the significance of the solid-state battery's small-batch rollout extends beyond the robot itself. Humanoid robots have far higher requirements than passenger cars for battery energy density, safety and lightweighting. If this technology path is validated on robots, it could in the future feed back into the company's vehicle products. However, the journey from "small-batch rollout" to "large-scale production and delivery" still requires clearing two hurdles: yield ramp-up and cost control. Whether the end-2026 mass-production target can be met on schedule will be a key observation point for testing the company's execution.

artigo.texto: China's NIO taps EVE Energy, Gotion High-tech to make its in-house large cylindrical cells, with small-volume output due by year-end NIO's multi-year push into in-house batteries has finally produced tangible progress. According to Jipian Lab, the large cylindrical cells independently designed by NIO have been confirmed for contract manufacturing by EVE Energy (300014.SZ) and Gotion High-tech (002074.SZ), with small-volume output due by the end of the year. At the same time, NIO continues to use CATL (300750.SZ) batteries in models under its Firefly and Onvo brands, and cooperation between the two sides has not cooled despite the in-house push. The significance of this news goes beyond one automaker's supply chain choices. It means that after Geely, Li Auto and Leapmotor, another vehicle manufacturer has extended its reach into the core segment of power batteries, and the supplier-dominated structure of the power battery industry is gradually being pried open by automakers' own R&D. NIO did not start late on in-house cell development. The company launched the business in 2021, planned a battery plant with 100 GWh of annual capacity, and internally set a 2024 target for installing self-developed cells in vehicles in 2022. But buffeted by business volatility, the effort stalled for a time. The 46105 large cylindrical cell unveiled at NIO Day 2023, originally intended for the 120 kWh battery pack in the NIO ET9, ultimately did not materialize, and the production version of the ET9 switched to CATL cells. The turning point came in the second half of last year. As sales recovered and its financial position improved, NIO restarted the in-house battery business. In February this year, NIO Battery Technology (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. was established, deepening its R&D footprint. A NIO representative previously told media that the company is accelerating R&D on solid-state battery technology and expects to achieve large-scale application after 2027. For now, NIO's battery strategy works both ends: near-term deployment of large cylindrical cells and a medium- to long-term bet on solid-state batteries. Compared with Li Auto's approach, NIO is not yet able to significantly reduce its reliance on outside suppliers. Li Auto announced in September that within the year it will switch all models except the L9 to its own batteries, but the cells are developed by Li Auto itself and contract-manufactured by Sunwoda (300207.SZ) and CALB (3931.HK), and the company does not yet have cell production capacity of its own. Leapmotor, meanwhile, has already put its in-house cell line into production, with first-phase capacity sufficient to meet the needs of 500,000 to 600,000 vehicles. The only company that has truly achieved fully in-house battery development and production is BYD (002594.SZ), which built its business on batteries. Most automakers' in-house battery operations are still in their early stages, either lacking cell production capacity or unable to cover all model demand with their own batteries, ultimately still relying on suppliers as a backstop. For NIO, in-house batteries carry an additional test. As one of the few companies in the industry committed to battery swapping, NIO needs batteries from different suppliers, with varying capacities and specifications, to circulate efficiently through its swap network while balancing differences in performance and density. This year NIO also announced a partnership with Geely in charging and swapping, and how Geely-family swap-capable models will be integrated into NIO's swap network once launched will likewise test its operational capabilities. That means NIO is taking on more risk than brands without battery swapping. At the industry level, automakers' in-house batteries are unlikely to threaten battery suppliers' room to survive in the short term, but the bargaining landscape is already changing. With battery R&D and production capabilities in hand, automakers gain more initiative in negotiations with suppliers and find it easier to secure capacity when supply is tight. That in turn forces battery makers to speed up technology iteration and improve product competitiveness. Still, developing and producing power batteries in-house requires enormous investment, and without economies of scale it is hard to generate clear economic benefits, making it a burden for automakers instead. The more likely path for the industry is this: a handful of automakers that have already achieved results will continue in-house development, while more companies fall back to a model of jointly defining products with suppliers, with automakers leading product definition and deeply participating in battery pack and cell design while core technology still comes from battery suppliers. Worth noting is that as NIO advances in-house batteries, the downstream race to build charging infrastructure for power batteries is also heating up. BYD, Geely, Chery and Li Auto have successively announced plans to build megawatt-level fast-charging stations, and battery maker Sunwoda has also proposed building 10,000 megawatt-level fast-charging stations by the end of 2027 together with industrial capital, automakers and charging operators. Vehicle-side charging rates have been pushed from 5C to 10C, 12C and even 15C, while charging piles remain mostly below 250 kW. Data from the China Charging Alliance shows that as of August 2026, charging piles below 120 kW accounted for 67.8% and those between 120 and 250 kW for 22.5%, with the two combined making up more than 90%. The gap between vehicle-side capability and charging infrastructure means large-scale application of ultra-fast charging will still take time. For NIO, whether its in-house cells can be smoothly integrated into the swap system and keep the network efficient and safe across batteries from different suppliers will be a harder challenge than building a set of reliable cells.

artigo.texto: - The second-generation Seal 07 grows to 5,080 mm in length and will feature the DiSus-M intelligent magnetorheological body control system. - Reservation holders will receive priority production and delivery, with deposits fully refundable before orders are locked in. BYD (HKEX: 1211) has opened reservations for the second-generation Seal 07, a larger electric sedan equipped with its second-generation Blade Battery and flash charging technology. Zhang Zhuo, general manager of BYD's Ocean lineup sales division, announced the opening of reservations on Weibo on Monday, without disclosing pre-sales prices — a practice known as blind reservations. An official poster shows that reservation holders will receive priority production and delivery, with deposits fully refundable before orders are locked in. The reservations serve only as expressions of purchase intent, allowing customers to change colors and configurations after the launch. BYD is also offering exclusive gifts to customers who place reservations and take delivery. The move follows a series of previews. Zhang first unveiled the exterior on September 28 and shared cabin details on October 23. The second-generation Seal 07 will feature the second-generation Blade Battery and flash charging, with BYD promoting its charging capability as "ready in 5 minutes, full in 9 minutes." The car will also feature the DiSus-M intelligent magnetorheological body control system, front double-wishbone and reinforced rear 5-link suspension, and BYD's Smart Ecosystem 2.0. The second-generation Seal 07 adopts the Ocean Aesthetics 2.0 design language, with styling consistent with the Seal 08. It offers 6 exterior colors and 3 interior color schemes. The car measures 5,080 mm in length, 1,960 mm in width and 1,495 mm in height, with a wheelbase of 2,960 mm. It is 85 mm longer than the Seal 07 EV launched in March, with a 60 mm longer wheelbase. The cabin features front zero-gravity seats with massage, ventilation and heating functions, along with a 20-speaker Devialet audio system. BYD lists trunk and front-trunk capacities of 618 liters and 160 liters, respectively. The vehicle shown is equipped with roof-mounted LiDAR, though BYD has yet to detail its driver-assistance capabilities or how equipment will vary across trims. Earlier filings with China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) showed that the second-generation Seal 07's battery-electric version offers peak motor outputs of 245 kW (329 hp) and 300 kW, both above the 240 kW of the model launched in March. Alongside the battery-electric model shown in the poster, the filings included a plug-in hybrid retaining the Seal 07 DM-i name, with a 1.5-liter turbocharged engine and a 160 kW electric motor. The plug-in hybrid has a 38.029-kWh battery and a WLTC electric range of 245 km (152 miles). The latest official poster did not specify reservation arrangements for that version. For reference, the Seal 07 EV launched on March 5 was offered in 2 variants priced at 169,900 yuan ($25,300) and 189,900 yuan. The redesign comes as the Seal lineup faces sales pressure. Data compiled by CnEVPost shows that the series sold 46,718 vehicles in September, down 9.04% year-on-year and 1.57% from August. In the first 9 months of the year, Seal-series sales totaled 304,723 vehicles, down 14.11% year-on-year. The lineup includes the Seal 07 and several other battery-electric and plug-in hybrid models. ($1 = 6.7162 yuan)

artigo.texto: BAIC Group and CATL signed an expanded battery-swapping agreement on October 22, 2026, to connect compatible models from multiple BAIC brands to CATL’s Choco-Swap network. The partners’ reported ambition is a mature Chinese ecosystem serving vehicles at the million-vehicle scale, with BAIC dealerships helping support station locations. How the agreement is meant to work CnEVPost reported, citing a BAIC statement, that the cooperation covers vehicle and battery development, swap-station network construction, battery-energy services and new business models. BAIC is to connect compatible vehicles from several of its brands to Choco-Swap. Its dealership network is to help identify station sites, and the companies are exploring joint development and operation of stations with dealers. The partners also aim to consolidate swap assets under specialized management and promote unified standards and interoperable networks. For drivers, compatibility depends on the vehicle and battery system: a CATL-supplied battery alone does not establish that a vehicle can use a CATL swap station. A million-vehicle ambition, alongside CATL’s existing network The million-vehicle figure describes the scale of the partners’ ambition, not a dated deployment target. CATL’s network was reported at 2,520 battery-swap stations across 200 Chinese cities as of September 29, 2026, before the agreement was signed. Battery swapping replaces a depleted pack with a charged one at a station. The agreement sets out cooperation on vehicles, stations and related services, while its stated goal describes the scale the partners hope the Chinese ecosystem will reach. BAIC and CATL had already worked on swap-compatible vehicles The October agreement builds on earlier BAIC-CATL cooperation signed in June 2024, which covered swap-compatible vehicles, battery-block development and battery-data management, according to CnEVPost. CnEVPost reported that the Arcfox Beta S3 swap version, using CATL’s Choco-SEB system, launched on May 22, 2026. A swap version of the Arcfox Beta T1 appeared in an August 2026 filing with China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology.

artigo.texto: - The companies plan to deploy Tener Sodium energy storage systems in markets including Germany, Switzerland and Austria. - The agreement marks another step in CATL's European sodium-ion storage commercialization push, following partnerships with Alfen and Solarpro. CATL (HKEX: 3750) has signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with German energy storage solutions provider Intilion to deploy 3 GWh of sodium-ion energy storage systems in Europe over the next 5 years. The world's largest battery supplier announced the partnership on Wednesday, saying the companies would introduce its Tener Sodium energy storage systems in markets including Germany, Switzerland and Austria for grid-scale, commercial and industrial applications. The agreement builds on CATL's push into European sodium-ion storage this year and extends its existing project partnership with Intilion to a new battery technology. The companies have deployed more than 30 energy storage projects in Germany since 2022 and will promote the large-scale adoption of multiple battery technologies, including sodium-ion and lithium-ion, in Europe, CATL said. Designed for Europe's harsh winter conditions, the Tener Sodium system offers a cycle life of more than 15,000 cycles and 25 years of stable operation, while maintaining high discharge power at -20°C (-4°F), according to CATL. These features can support frequency regulation on European power grids and the long-term stability of energy storage systems, the company said. CATL unveiled Tener Sodium on June 22, describing it as the world's first field-validated sodium-ion energy storage solution. The system has a modular design that allows storage duration to be configured to suit project requirements. The system is dimensionally compatible with lithium-ion batteries. CATL previously said the design gives customers greater flexibility in choosing battery technologies and reduces their exposure to lithium price volatility. Before the latest agreement, CATL signed an MOU in July with European new energy integrator Alfen N.V. to deploy 5 GWh of sodium-ion energy storage systems in Western European countries, including the Netherlands, starting in 2027. That same month, the company signed a 2 GWh Tener Sodium energy storage cooperation agreement with Eastern European renewable energy company Solarpro, further expanding its regional partnerships. In China, CATL signed a 3-year supply agreement in April with energy storage system provider HyperStrong for 60 GWh of sodium-ion batteries for energy storage. The partnerships come as Europe's energy storage market expands rapidly. European lithium-ion energy storage battery shipments reached 72.7 GWh in the first half of 2026, up 74% year-on-year, according to South Korean market research firm SNE Research. Over the same period, CATL's global lithium-ion energy storage battery shipments rose 81% year-on-year to 125.0 GWh, giving it the leading market share of 27.1%.

artigo.texto: Segundo o TecMundo, no primeiro discurso após ser reeleito, Lula (PT) sinalizou que pretende usar a capacidade de geração renovável do Brasil como atrativo para empresas de computação e criar uma inteligência artificial nacional. Ele venceu Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) no segundo turno, com 51,74% dos votos válidos, ante 48,26% do adversário, conforme os números do TSE divulgados no domingo (25). O novo mandato começa em janeiro de 2027. A proposta, de acordo com o plano de governo disponível no TSE, inclui investimentos em infraestrutura digital, formação de profissionais e reforço da indústria tecnológica local. Para os centros de dados, o documento prevê contrapartidas: parte da capacidade computacional deve ficar à disposição do mercado brasileiro. Também menciona exigências socioambientais, como eficiência no consumo de energia, avanço para fontes renováveis e análise dos efeitos sobre recursos hídricos, rede elétrica e moradores das áreas vizinhas. Na área de inteligência artificial, Lula quer ampliar o ensino de matemática e engenharia para diminuir a dependência de soluções dos Estados Unidos e da China. O plano cita sistemas de linguagem natural voltados ao português e a outros idiomas, uma base nacional de dados destinada a treinar e testar esses sistemas, além de apoio a pesquisas públicas e a fabricantes nacionais de equipamentos e programas de computação de alto desempenho. Agronegócio, saúde e serviços financeiros aparecem como setores de aplicação. O documento também prevê conectar instituições de ensino, laboratórios e companhias. Ele também retomou a defesa de regras para as grandes plataformas digitais e relacionou o tema à atuação dessas empresas no processo eleitoral. Lula criticou companhias que, segundo ele, faturam no país sem recolher impostos e tentam influenciar resultados eleitorais. No discurso, associou a necessidade de regulação à influência das plataformas no pleito e disse que delitos no ambiente digital devem receber tratamento equivalente ao de crimes cometidos fora da internet.

artigo.texto: BOTETOURT CO., Va. – Mike Herwald gives a tour of the Munters plant located in the Botetourt Center at Greenfield. He points to the massive space filled with workers and equipment. “We’re receiving raw metal. We’re bending it, forming it, painting it, welding it. It all happens within this factory,” Herwald said. Mike Herwald knows data center cooling inside and out. He is the North American Sales Manager in Data Center Technologies at Munters, one of the top suppliers of data center cooling systems in the world. At their plant in Daleville, which hopes to soon employ 1,000 workers, they make cooling systems from the ground up. “Data centers are a big part of our business,” Herwald said. And for good reason. With the advent of AI and other chip technologies, Data Centers are popping up everywhere. According to Cleanview, there are nearly 1,400 data centers in the U.S. with more than 2,800 planned. The site says there are 359 in Virginia with 459 in planning. “At its core, data centers produce a lot of heat,” explained Virginia Tech researcher Eric Sjostedt, who is searching for ways to make data centers less impactful to the communities where they are located. It’s getting rid of that heat that uses so much water, he explained. “When people say data centers use a lot of water, it’s all attributed to the cooling system,” Sjostedt said. When stacks of servers do their work – called “compute” they heat up. If they get too hot, they fail. Boiled down: conventional data center cooling uses large amounts of water evaporation to cool the systems. This is called evaporative technology. A 100-megawatt or medium-sized data center can use more than 2 million gallons of water per day. Eventually, for instance, in Google’s project in Daleville, it could go as high as 8 million. With drought conditions at Carvins Cove, one of the proposed water sources this year, dissenters claim that’s too much water. One of the reasons Munters is pivoting away from evaporative technologies. “When I look at our entire portfolio of equipment we’re building today, almost all of it is what’s called a waterless cooling technology. So, it’s not using evaporative technology to cool the data center,” Herwald said. Herwald showed us the massive systems Munters is now building. Unfortunately, there’s a catch – waterless systems present a different problem. “But I want to make this point really clear that the water question, if we’re only looking at the data center, is the wrong focus point,” Sjostedt said. If Data Centers move to waterless technology, they will require more energy – more electricity. “We can make all of our data centers air-cooled, so they don’t use a drop of water on the facility. We can absolutely do that. That’s an option. They’re gonna require more electricity to do so,” Sjostedt said. Sjostedt says it’s like kicking the can down the road. If the data center uses more energy, it may save water, but there are environmental impacts when the power is created. A problem Munters is trying to meet head-on with evolving technologies. “So you have to analyze the impact to the environment. Where is the electricity coming from? How am I being most responsible to the community? Either I’m going to consume water or I’m going to consume electricity. It’s one or the other,” Herwald said. That begs the question protestors have been asking all along. Do we need data centers? “Well, that’s a problem, right? Because our call right now is hosted by a data center. The texts that I’m getting right now are from a data center. My bank account is hosted by a data center,” replied Sjostedt. “Can our infrastructure sustain this given the change of climate and going up in our power generation and what’s needed for our society to keep on going? That’s the tough nut that I’m trying to figure out. And I don’t have an answer to it, but I know that problem exists,” he said. Both men interviewed for this story said data centers must be built in a place where either water or electricity is available, along with a population that requires connectivity to computing. Where those lines meet is where data centers will be built.

artigo.texto: A estimativa para a oferta pública inicial de ações (IPO) da Anthropic, protocolado na segunda-feira (26), revelou a dimensão dos gastos da companhia com chips de inteligência artificial e data centers. A empresa, que cresce rapidamente e já desembolsou mais de US$ 19 bilhões (R$ 101,36 bilhões) em infraestrutura de IA desde sua fundação, em 2021, já assinou contratos que somam mais de US$ 500 bilhões (R$ 2,67 trilhões) para os próximos 20 anos. Esses acordos incluem contratos com grandes empresas de computação em nuvem, como Amazon, Google e Microsoft, além das fabricantes de chips AMD, Broadcom e Nvidia. Há também contratos de capacidade computacional com a SpaceX, de Elon Musk, e uma série de operadoras de “neoclouds” e data centers, entre elas CoreWeave, Fluidstack — apoiada pelo Google —, Lambda — que tem apoio da Nvidia — e Nscale. Grande parte dessas parcerias já era de conhecimento público, mas, até agora, os valores dos contratos não haviam sido divulgados. Segundo a projeção, em junho, a Anthropic tinha compromissos de aproximadamente US$ 587 bilhões (R$ 3,13 trilhões) relacionados a chips e data centers até 2045. Nos quatro meses seguintes, a criadora do Claude assinou outros US$ 266 bilhões (R$ 1,42 trilhão) em contratos novos e revisados. Há ainda US$ 20 bilhões (R$ 106,69 bilhões) em capacidade computacional prevista da AMD e outros US$ 125 bilhões a US$ 150 bilhões (R$ 666,83 bilhões a R$ 800,19 bilhões) destinados à aquisição de mais chips desenvolvidos pelo Google. Isso significa que as obrigações da empresa podem chegar a aproximadamente US$ 1 trilhão (R$ 5,33 trilhões) até 2045 — o equivalente a 3% dos US$ 31,6 trilhões (R$ 168,57 trilhões) que a gigante de consultoria PwC estima que serão investidos na expansão global da infraestrutura de inteligência artificial até 2050. A OpenAI, principal rival da Anthropic, estaria planejando destinar US$ 750 bilhões (R$ 4 trilhões) à capacidade computacional até 2030. Números altos É um salto gigantesco em comparação com o que a Anthropic gastou em sua curta história. De janeiro de 2023 a junho de 2026, a companhia desembolsou US$ 19,2 bilhões (R$ 102,42 bilhões) em capacidade computacional e infraestrutura de IA, incluindo data centers, chips, equipamentos e softwares utilizados para gerenciar essas operações. No mesmo período, a empresa registrou US$ 21,3 bilhões (R$ 113,63 bilhões) em receitas. A maior parte desse faturamento, US$ 16,3 bilhões (R$ 86,95 bilhões), foi contabilizada apenas no primeiro semestre de 2026, uma alta de 1.300% na comparação anual, enquanto as despesas com computação e infraestrutura cresceram apenas 283%. A capacidade da Anthropic de continuar construindo e pagando por esses data centers e chips depende de seu crescimento de receita acompanhar o ritmo dos investimentos. Aproximadamente 80% do faturamento da companhia no primeiro semestre do ano veio de clientes que pagam de acordo com o consumo, ou seja, conforme a utilização dos serviços da empresa. O restante teve origem em assinaturas. Com a concorrência cada vez maior da OpenAI e de uma ampla variedade de modelos de pesos abertos mais baratos, pode se tornar difícil para a Anthropic manter seu ritmo acelerado de crescimento. “O futuro deles depende da capacidade de cobrar esses preços elevados por seu modelo mais recente”, afirma Stijn van Nieuwerburgh, economista da Columbia Business School. “Sempre haverá um próximo modelo de um concorrente que fará algo um pouco melhor. Isso fará com que esse negócio seja muito mais volátil.” Outro fator que torna a situação mais complexa é o fato de vários dos maiores contratos da Anthropic terem sido firmados com seus próprios investidores. “O financiamento circular está se tornando cada vez mais relevante”, afirma Chan Ahn, CEO e fundador da plataforma de mercados privados Tessera PE. “Há muitas participações interligadas. A probabilidade de empresas como Anthropic e OpenAI quebrarem é muito pequena, mas tudo depende do fato de elas continuarem crescendo.” Ampliando os horizontes A companhia possui um contrato de US$ 114,5 bilhões (R$ 610,81 bilhões) com o Google para serviços de computação em nuvem e chips; outro de US$ 110 bilhões (R$ 586,81 bilhões) com a Amazon para computação em nuvem; e um acordo de US$ 45 bilhões (R$ 240,06 bilhões) com a Microsoft para capacidade computacional e acesso aos sistemas da Nvidia. As três empresas possuem participações na Anthropic, embora nenhuma delas apareça na tabela de capitalização apresentada no formulário S-1. O maior contrato da Anthropic é um acordo de US$ 161 bilhões (R$ 858,87 bilhões) com a Broadcom para fornecimento de chips e infraestrutura. A fabricante de semicondutores também detém US$ 42 bilhões (R$ 224,05 bilhões) em notas conversíveis que podem ser transformadas em ações da Anthropic. Segundo o S-1, a companhia espera gastar mais de US$ 20 bilhões (R$ 106,69 bilhões) em chips da AMD, que concordou, em julho, em comprar até US$ 5 bilhões (R$ 26,67 bilhões) em ações ordinárias da Anthropic. A empresa também compra memória e armazenamento da Micron, Samsung e SK hynix, todas participantes da rodada de financiamento Série H realizada em maio, que avaliou a Anthropic em US$ 965 bilhões (R$ 5,15 trilhões). O S-1 não trouxe informações sobre o tamanho exato das participações dessas companhias na empresa. Outro contrato de grandes proporções é o acordo de US$ 120,5 bilhões (R$ 642,82 bilhões) para acessar chips GPU da Nvidia por meio da SpaceX, que acumulou esses processadores. Quando a empresa de Elon Musk entregar toda a capacidade contratada, o que está previsto para dezembro, o acordo custará à Anthropic US$ 3,1 bilhões (R$ 16,54 bilhões) por mês. O contrato ainda representa uma fonte de receita para a SpaceX: nos três primeiros meses de 2027, responderia por aproximadamente 25% do faturamento projetado da companhia para o primeiro trimestre. artigo.texto: How a lifelong Republican came to lead the data center battle in Ohio Candidates work to ease concerns as data centers become hot-button issue for Ohioans Stay up to date with our Politics newsletter, sent weekly. MT. ORAB, Ohio — The data center mystery in this rural exurb of Cincinnati has consumed Nick Owens. The lifelong Republican and self-described small-town attorney has spent countless hours trying to figure out what's going on with 1,000 acres of farmland and trees that property records show were sold to a data center developer in 2024 and 2025. In a few spots, the data center property runs right up against beautiful two-story homes. "This is the Ohio that people brag about. This is the Ohio people love. This is the small town charm," he says. "Living in the rural area, but getting the benefits of a nice, lovely neighborhood." Some of the most coordinated opposition to data centers anywhere in the country grew out of what happened in secrecy in this village of 4,300 people, a short drive up a country road from Owens' home. Nondisclosure agreements have stymied Owens' efforts to learn more. But along his quest, he crossed paths with another local attorney and a real estate agent who were equally alarmed. Together, they mobilized a network of volunteers in nearly all 88 counties in the state. They are Democrats, Republicans and Independents. They called themselves Conserve Ohio. "We all share the same ethos and the same passion for preserving our way of life, preserving the future of Ohio, frankly, from the hyperscale data center invasion," says Owens. "It's really beautiful." This fall, the group is behind ballot initiatives in 10 communities that would amend local charters to prohibit the construction of large-scale data centers — the kind used to power artificial intelligence. It's an effort that goes beyond the temporary pauses that hundreds of municipal and county governments have embraced. "All too often you hear from the politicians, 'Well, the community should have a say,'" says Owens. "We're going to find out in ten communities whether or not the communities want them." Meanwhile, the grassroots group is working on a more ambitious undertaking: a petition for an amendment to the state constitution that would ban large-scale data centers statewide. Their goal is to put that to Ohio's voters in 2027. Data centers bring economic benefits and angst It's been more than a decade since tech companies first came to Ohio, drawn by the state's inexpensive and abundant land, its energy infrastructure and its generous tax breaks. That combination paved the way for some of the fastest data center growth in the country. Now, despite the economic benefits — considerable tax revenue, money for schools, numerous construction jobs and a smaller number of permanent jobs — no one seems to want a computing campus in their backyard, especially one shrouded in secrecy. "Should the school have extra money or the local government have extra money so we have a constant hum and ridiculous amounts of emissions and pollution?" Owens says, pointing out that hyperscale data centers will require new power plants. "Our community is not for sale." Pressed to consider whether the state should forgo all opportunities, Owens says he'd entertain the idea of putting data centers on old industrial sites, where they'd be buffered from people. "If we're going to have data centers, those are the prime places," he says, while acknowledging that it'd be cheaper and easier for a developer to build on pristine farmland than on an old coal site. "I don't know if there are enough brownfield sites, but shouldn't we start with those first?" A hot-button election issue In recent months, candidates running for statewide office in Ohio have been trying to convince voters that they hear their concerns — even as they stop short of backing the kind of sweeping moratorium data center opponents are seeking. Until recently, data center projects weren't all that controversial, in part because they were smaller and weren't being built for AI. But as the issue has gained traction, it's become a hot topic in the midterms, including in the tight race to fill a U.S. Senate seat. Former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown has cast his opponent, the incumbent Republican Senator Jon Husted, as "the face of data centers." Brown has been reminding voters that as lieutenant governor, Husted welcomed tech companies to Ohio and championed their data center investments. Meanwhile, Husted has accused Brown of hypocrisy, pointing to Brown's past support for data centers. Husted has also introduced his own solution, pushing a bill in Congress aimed at getting data centers to pay for power grid upgrades and other costs associated with their massive energy use. Senate Democrats have blocked the bill, calling it toothless, prompting Husted to accuse the Democrats of not caring or helping. Unconvinced that politicians will help These political gestures have not persuaded Linda Moodie, an independent who's been volunteering with Conserve Ohio. She doesn't trust that any of the candidates running for statewide office "will do the right thing" if elected, which is to give the people a say in the data center buildout. "It's really something that I think a lot of us didn't see coming, and all of a sudden there's just an influx of them," she says. Between now and election day, she's seizing every opportunity to collect signatures to get the statewide ban on the ballot next year. On a recent evening, she set up a booth at the "Halloween on the Green" celebration in the Cincinnati suburb of Fairfield. She handed out candy to kids and clipboards with the petition to parents. Both were enthusiastically received. "The closer it hits to home, the more people that are going to want to do something," says Moodie. artigo.texto: Novas regulamentações para o registro de contas de crédito de carbono. O governo emitiu o Decreto nº 396/2026/ND-CP, que estipula claramente a autoridade, os procedimentos e os prazos para a concessão de contas de registro de créditos de carbono no Sistema Nacional de Registro. Em nome do Governo, o Vice-Primeiro-Ministro Ho Quoc Dung assinou o Decreto nº 396/2026/ND-CP, que altera e complementa diversos artigos do Decreto nº 06/2022/ND-CP, que regulamenta a redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa e a proteção da camada de ozono, o qual foi alterado e complementado pelos Decretos nº 119/2025/ND-CP, nº 83/2026/ND-CP e nº 112/2026/ND-CP. O Decreto 396/2026/ND-CP altera e complementa o inciso 2º do artigo 18º, relativo ao cadastro de contas no Sistema Nacional de Cadastro de Cotas de Emissão de Gases de Efeito Estufa e Créditos de Carbono, especificando o órgão responsável pela concessão de contas no Sistema Nacional de Cadastro para cada grupo de entidades. Especificamente, o Decreto estipula que, para as instalações que recebem cotas de emissão de gases de efeito estufa, para as agências e organizações participantes em programas e projetos registrados de acordo com os mecanismos especificados nos itens a e b da Cláusula 1, Artigo 20a deste Decreto, e para as agências e organizações participantes em projetos de carbono florestal com áreas florestais dentro dos limites administrativos de duas ou mais unidades administrativas de nível provincial , o Ministério da Agricultura e do Meio Ambiente concederá contas no Sistema Nacional de Registro e enviará informações para a instalação, agência ou organização. Você também pode gostar Para as agências e organizações que participam de projetos registrados no âmbito do mecanismo de troca e compensação de créditos de carbono, o Presidente do Comitê Popular da província que receber o pedido de registro do projeto concederá uma conta no Sistema Nacional de Registro e enviará as informações à organização após a aprovação do registro do projeto. Para as agências e organizações participantes em programas e projetos registrados de acordo com o mecanismo especificado no ponto c, cláusula 1, do artigo 20a deste Decreto, a agência ou organização deverá apresentar o dossiê de registro da conta em uma das seguintes formas: diretamente ou via correio ao Centro de Serviços da Administração Pública Provincial, no caso de um projeto registrado em uma unidade administrativa de nível provincial, ou ao Centro de Serviços da Administração Pública Provincial de uma das áreas de implementação do projeto, no caso de um projeto registrado em duas ou mais unidades administrativas de nível provincial, ou online no Portal Nacional de Serviços Públicos ou no Aplicativo Nacional de Identificação. No prazo de 5 dias úteis a partir da data de recebimento do dossiê de inscrição, o Presidente do Comitê Popular da província que o recebeu deverá conceder uma conta no Sistema Nacional de Registro e enviar as informações à agência ou organização; em caso de recusa da concessão da conta, os motivos deverão ser claramente indicados. A identificação e autenticação de organizações e indivíduos no acesso e utilização do Sistema Nacional de Registro são realizadas em conformidade com a lei sobre identificação e autenticação eletrônicas. Você também pode gostar O Decreto 396/2026/ND-CP acrescenta a Cláusula 10 após a Cláusula 9 do Artigo 20. Especificamente, os procedimentos para registro, ajuste e cancelamento de registro de projetos de carbono florestal; concessão de créditos de carbono florestal no âmbito do mecanismo; e troca e compensação de créditos de carbono nacionais serão aplicados de acordo com as normas do Decreto Governamental nº 180/2026/ND-CP, de 21 de maio de 2026, sobre serviços de sequestro e armazenamento de carbono em florestas. O Decreto 396/2026/ND-CP também altera e substitui alguns formulários do Anexo V e revoga a Cláusula 3 do Artigo 20a, juntamente com alguns formulários antigos. Os pedidos recebidos pelos ministérios competentes antes de 1º de agosto de 2026 continuarão a ser processados de acordo com os regulamentos vigentes na data de recebimento e não precisam ser reenviados. O Decreto entra em vigor em 12 de dezembro de 2026.

artigo.texto: Nano One Materials Corp. has provided an update on its strategic collaboration with Sumitomo Metal Mining Co. Ltd (SMM), highlighting continued progress in validating its One-Pot process for lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cathode materials. The partnership, supported through Natural Resources Canada (NRCan)-funded programmes, focuses on developing cost-effective LFP production technology as demand for lithium battery energy storage continues to grow. Since SMM’s strategic investment in Nano One in 2023, the companies have worked together on technical development and commercial opportunities for the One-Pot process. Positive results from validation work SMM has continued evaluating the technology through economic modelling, product testing and supplying One-Pot LFP samples to its customers. Feedback on the samples has been positive, while SMM’s economic assessment continues to indicate potential for a cost-effective manufacturing solution. Based on the modelling, Nano One estimates that conversion costs could be reduced by up to US$1 million annually for every 1,000 tonnes of production capacity. SMM is continuing to develop its existing LFP production capabilities and solid-phase processes, while assessing the One-Pot technology as an additional route to competitive supply. Munekazu Kawata, Managing Executive Officer and General Manager of SMM’s Battery Materials Division, said the process offered potential benefits from both production and commercial perspectives, with customer feedback supporting its ongoing evaluation. Progress towards commercial supply Nano One’s latest One-Pot LFP material has achieved a pressed density suitable for assessment by high-performance battery cell manufacturers, and samples are ready for customer evaluation. Discussions are underway with SMM’s existing cell manufacturing and automotive customers. Product qualification remains a multi-stage process that must be completed before commercial offtake can proceed. Denis Geoffroy, Chief Operating Officer of Nano One, said the positive customer response could strengthen the technology’s appeal to prospective customers, licensees and joint venture partners. Plans for Canadian production The companies are continuing to explore a large-scale LFP production facility in Canada. Progress towards the project remains subject to securing customer offtake agreements, financing and government funding. SMM has contributed technical expertise, testing and validation through NRCan initiatives, including a C$9.3 million Energy Innovation Program award and a C$3 million LFP supply chain initiative. artigo.texto: O Gaispi (Grupo de Acompanhamento da Implantação das Soluções para os Problemas de Interferência) aprovou propostas apresentadas pela EAF (Entidade Administradora da Faixa) que destinam R$ 1,66 bilhão a novas políticas públicas no país. Entre as iniciativas estão a distribuição de conversores de TV 3.0 a famílias de baixa renda e a implantação de um data center voltado ao processamento de dados e à execução de aplicações de inteligência artificial (IA) para o governo federal. Os recursos são provenientes do leilão de 5G e poderão beneficiar 910 mil famílias de baixa renda. A maior parte dos recursos, R$ 1,28 bilhão, será destinada à aquisição e à distribuição de conversores de TV 3.0 em regiões como São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro e Distrito Federal. A prioridade será para beneficiários do Bolsa Família inscritos no Cadastro Único (CadÚnico). O orçamento contempla: - aquisição dos equipamentos; - logística; - distribuição; - comunicação; - atendimento à população; - tecnologia; - demais despesas operacionais necessárias à execução do programa. A implementação deverá ocorrer em até 24 meses, de forma escalonada, com início pelo município de São Paulo, onde será realizado um projeto-piloto. Centro de dados A construção do data center receberá R$ 375 milhões. A estrutura será operada pela Telebras e terá como foco o processamento de dados e a oferta de soluções de inteligência artificial. O projeto prevê uma área de cerca de 5 mil metros quadrados, dividida em dois módulos. O primeiro será dedicado a aplicações de inteligência artificial e contará com 20 racks, seis servidores com um total de 48 GPUs e sistemas de armazenamento de alta capacidade. O segundo módulo será voltado a serviços tradicionais de tecnologia da informação (TI) e à colocalização de equipamentos. O investimento também contempla sistemas redundantes de energia e conectividade, além de soluções de resfriamento adequadas às operações de processamento de alto desempenho. O prazo estimado para a implantação do data center é de 12 meses. As medidas aprovadas pelo Gaispi ainda precisam passar pelo Conselho Diretor da Anatel para entrar em vigor.

artigo.texto: This town ain’t big enough for just one launch provider. On Monday evening, Cowboy Space pulled back the curtain on Big Iron—a launch vehicle whose upper stage is designed to remain in orbit as a megawatt-class data center. “What we want to do is put a lot of available power in orbit, in our case to power chips, to power AI data centers,” Cowboy Space COO and Chief Legal Officer Joseph Yaffe told Payload. “The most efficient and most effective way to do that is to build our own vehicle to get us into space.” Cowboy is also opening Big Iron to outside customers—who can fly payloads that need up to a megawatt of power—through a program dubbed Big Iron Express. “Launch capacity is at a premium right now, if available at all,” Yaffe said. But many of the alternatives—Big Iron included—have yet to fly, and government customers “want to see a completed rocket,” Yaffe said. Horsepower check: Big Iron is no lightweight. To move fast and keep costs down, the team turned to proven architectures, and designed for existing infrastructure. - The 86 m stainless-steel vehicle is sized to be transportable by road. - Each vehicle is designed to carry 15,000+ kg to sun-synchronous orbit. - Nine liquid-oxygen and methane “Clydesdale” engines will power the first stage—each providing 300,000 lbs of thrust. Cowboy tested part of the Clydesdale at NASA’s Stennis Space Center last week. A ~30-person team built and tested its combustion chamber in 90 days, and the company is “almost a year ahead of schedule,” Yaffe said. Rather than being discarded, the upper stage joins Cowboy’s constellation. Once deployed in dawn-dusk orbit, each sat will measure 132 m by 73 m and carry five racks of NVIDIA Vera Rubin GPUs. Two-trick pony: To make every kilogram sent to orbit count, many of Big Iron’s parts take on a second job once they’re in orbit. - The rocket’s skin becomes the data center’s radiator; - Ammonia propellant works a double shift as coolant; - Nitrogen that pressurizes the second stage also deploys the solar wings. “If you build a small satellite with GPUs on it, you’re going to have to put radiators on it,” Yaffe said. “And so you’re paying for that same metal twice to lift it into space.” Hold your horses: Cowboy got its first taste of orbit with Reason-1, a laser power beaming demo sat that launched Oct. 1 aboard SpaceX’s Transporter-18. Yaffe said the first beaming attempt will likely happen in the next few weeks, and testing so far has turned up “zero red flags.” Reason-2—slated for launch in 2027—will run GPUs in orbit for commercial and government customers, including a NOAA effort to process weather data in space. Cowboy is targeting Big Iron’s first flight in 2028. From there, it’s off to the races to scale Stampede, its planned constellation of up to 20,000 sats, pending FCC approval. “We just still have a lot of executing to do,” Yaffe said.

artigo.texto: Opinião Data centers e a fome por recursos Tao e Gao referem que um data centre hiperescalável típico pode utilizar 11 a 26 milhões de litros por dia, apenas para arrefecimento A economia digital está cada vez mais dependente dos data centres (ou centros de dados), infraestruturas altamente consumidoras de eletricidade e de outros recursos. Em setembro de 2026, segundo dados divulgados pela Forbes Portugal, os países europeus com mais data centres eram o Reino Unido (568), a Alemanha (533), a França (393) e a Espanha (219). Portugal apresentava 46. Os data centres, vitais para suportar a evolução da economia digital e, em particular, da Inteligência Artificial, são responsáveis por diversos impactes ambientais. Consumiram cerca de 1,5% da eletricidade mundial em 2024. Segundo a Agência Internacional de Energia, este consumo poderá mais do que duplicar até 2030. Dependendo do local onde são instalados e da origem da eletricidade que os alimenta, podem também contribuir para as emissões de gases com efeito de estufa. Têm ainda uma enorme pegada hídrica. Em determinadas regiões, até 57% da água utilizada para arrefecimento pode provir de fontes potáveis. Tao e Gao referem que um data centre hiperescalável típico pode utilizar 11 a 26 milhões de litros por dia, apenas para arrefecimento. Segundo Tao e Gao, existem várias medidas que devem ser consideradas. Em primeiro lugar, aumentar a utilização de fontes de energia renovável para alimentar os data centres. Em segundo lugar, devem ser priorizadas tecnologias de arrefecimento mais eficientes, que reduzam o consumo de água, bem como soluções para recuperar e reutilizar o calor residual. Em terceiro lugar, a informação sobre as emissões e outros impactes ambientais destas infraestruturas deve ser pública e transparente. Finalmente, a localização dos data centres deve considerar a capacidade a capacidade dos territórios em fornecer os recursos. A localização não pode ser determinada apenas pela disponibilidade de terrenos ou pela proximidade de infraestruturas digitais, tem de considerar o ambiente e os cidadãos.

artigo.texto: New alliances offer hope to battery swap sector By Cao Yingying | China Daily | Updated: 2026-10-26 09:24 As China's electric vehicle energy supply competition pivots toward ecosystem dominance, a string of major battery-swapping alliances has formed to address the sector's long-running hurdles of fragmented standards and hefty up-front infrastructure investment. BAIC and CATL signed an agreement on Thursday to deepen battery-swapping cooperation and build a unified battery swap ecosystem. According to the agreement, BAIC will roll out adapted models across its multiple brands to connect to CATL's EVOGO solutions. Earlier last week, Huawei-affiliated Yinwang Intelligent Technology signed a cooperation agreement with CATL and CATL's battery-swapping subsidiary CAES to codevelop a smart battery swap ecosystem. The alliance will link vehicle, station and cloud data, enabling EVs fitted with Huawei's Qiankun intelligent driving system to autonomously locate swap stations, drive into position, align and complete a 99-second battery swap before departing. Local media reports state the three partners plan to launch five swappable EVs by 2027. The first model will be by Epicland, a joint brand developed by Dongfeng and Huawei. Aistaland, a Huawei-GAC marque, also has swappable vehicles in its pipeline. As of Sept 30, CATL had built 2,520 EVOGO swap stations covering 200 cities across China's 31 provincial-level regions, more than doubling its network from December 2025. The battery provider targets 3,000 stations by year-end. Even so, vehicle development has lagged station expansion. CATL has released over 20 EVOGO-compatible models from partners including FAW, Changan, BAIC, Chery and GAC. Most carry price tags below 150,000 yuan ($22,470) and target commercial fleets, with low uptake among private buyers. The new partnerships are expected to speed up the rollout of battery-swappable EVs for private users. Tong Zongqi, general manager of the Open Service Platform at the China Electric Vehicle Charging Infrastructure Promotion Alliance, said battery manufacturers' push into swapping primarily aims to boost battery shipments and deepen ties with automakers. Combined with battery graduated sequential utilization and recycling, the business model closes the industrial value chain. For battery makers, swapping acts not merely as a sales channel but as a critical source of life-cycle battery operation data, Tong added. Nio, China's pioneer of consumer battery swapping, operated 4,186 swap stations and provided more than 120 million such services by mid-October. Its fifth-generation stations serve its Nio, Onvo and Firefly-branded cars. Since 2023, Nio has inked battery swap cooperation agreements with Changan, Geely, JAC, Chery, FAW and GAC. Yet these partners have not launched compatible vehicles to date; non-Nio vehicles on its network remain mostly fleet-focused. In late September, Nio and Geely signed a strategic deal covering charging and swapping, solidifying cross-shareholdings in their energy businesses. Geely Holding Chairman Li Shufu said last week at an industry conference that the tie-up avoids redundant infrastructure build-out. "There is no need for Geely and Nio to build separate systems, so we joined forces," Li said. The battery swap industry still faces fundamental headwinds: steep up-front capital expenditure, long payback cycles, cross-brand battery incompatibility and low adoption by private motorists. Batteries make up roughly 40 percent of an EV's total cost. Capacity degradation and poor residual values remain major deterrents for buyers. Battery as a Service, or BaaS, decouples battery costs from vehicle pricing and pools battery packs for shared use, easing consumer concerns over long-term battery performance decay. Ji Xuehong, director of the Automotive Industry Innovation Research Center at North China University of Technology, noted that business models like BaaS transfer battery ownership from consumers to operators, cutting up-front purchase costs. CATL Chairman Zeng Yuqun forecast China's future EV energy replenishment market will evolve into three parallel tracks: private home chargers, public fast chargers and battery swap stations.

artigo.texto: County Supes Approved Major Use Permit in September By Jacob Aere / kpbs / October 22, 2026 San Diego County and developers of a solar and battery storage project in East County are facing a lawsuit alleging the project’s environmental review was insufficient. The suit was filed in San Diego Superior Court last week. It focuses on the Starlight Solar project near the town of Boulevard. The county Board of Supervisors approved a major use permit for the development for last month. The 588-acre project, which includes a solar farm and a 868 megawatt-hour battery energy storage system, has faced community pushback. The suit, filed Oct. 15 by a group calling itself the Back Country Community Alliance for Responsible Development, was brought under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). “This is CEQA action brought under the California Environmental Quality Act. And what we’re alleging is that the Environmental Impact Report that was prepared and certified by the county was inadequate,” said Jamie Hall, the group’s attorney. The lawsuit seeks to suspend all activity on the project “pending full compliance with CEQA and with the requirements of law.” A major concern the suit raises is the potential for lithium-battery fires. “My client doesn’t believe the county adequately analyzed those impacts, they didn’t analyze the evacuation routes sufficiently, they didn’t assess whether there was enough water for this particular project,” Hall said. Boulevard residents previously told KPBS they are concerned about the proximity of the battery storage containers to homes and a school. Fires producing toxic gas have broken out at battery storage facilities in Otay Mesa and Escondido in recent years. “We don’t think we’ll have a fire and if we do we have enough safeguards in place,” said Jim Whalen, the Starlight Solar project’s land use consultant. Whalen went on to say that the lawsuit lacks merit. “I don’t think the lawsuit has any merit, number one. We will be addressing the allegations going forward. We’re going to try and see if we can settle,” he said. He pointed out that projects like Starlight Solar help meet state and county green-energy mandates. “The county has to approve renewable energy projects at scale, that’s a given. ‘Where do they go,’ is the only question. We think we’ve done the best job fitting a large project into an area with the least number of people being affected,” Whalen said. A county spokesperson would not comment, citing the pending litigation.

artigo.texto: OPINION| by Danny Bixby, Springfield In his first encyclical, or “letter to the faithful,” Pope Leo focused on an issue that’s been a hot topic in Springfield and across Missouri: how to protect our communities from the environmental, social, and economic harms caused by AI data centers. As a Christian, I find myself agreeing with the Pope. In fact, I think the concerns he expresses feel familiar to many of us, regardless of religion: damage to our environment; unchecked development controlled by a few powerful tech companies; exploitation, prioritizing profit over human dignity. His words were top of mind when I saw that our elected officials in Jefferson City are going “all in on nuclear power” to meet the extraordinary demand from new AI data centers – despite people in Springfield and across the state saying NO to rampant data center development. My common sense quickly kicked in – who’s going to pay to build all of these nuclear reactors? It’s not the tech billionaires developing these hyperscale data centers, or the corporations profiting from them. It’s us. That’s right – even though 68% of Missourians don’t want data centers in our communities and nearly 60% of Missourians worry about being able to afford utilities, Jefferson City politicians passed legislation this year clearing the way for data centers by letting power companies raise our utility bills to cover the cost of building these new plants. It doesn’t take much digging to uncover how we got here. A small handful of special interest megadonors has been buying influence in Jefferson City to get even richer at the expense of our water and energy, our jobs, and our way of life. Right here in Springfield, where voters will soon choose between Rep. Betsy Fogle and Rep. Melanie Stinnett to be our new state senator, all you have to do is follow the money to see where the candidates stand on the issue: Betsy Fogle voted against letting power companies charge families to build new nuclear power plants. Melanie Stinnett voted YES on the bill – YES to forcing us to pay for nuclear plants that “have to be built to provide the power that we need for the data centers” according to the bill’s sponsor. I added it up, and Stinnett has gotten over $1 million in campaign cash (through her campaign committee and the Heart of SGF PAC, which is aligned with her) – over 70% of it coming from corporations and special interests, including those that could profit from data center development. I’ve been fortunate enough to live in Springfield for 26 years. I’ve put down roots here. It’s where I met my wife; where we raised our four daughters; where I served as a pastor and started my own business. I want to spend the rest of my days waking up to a view of God’s green earth – not server farms. That’s why I’m voting for Betsy Fogle for state senate. I trust her to stand up to Big Tech and make sure our communities have a say when it comes to what gets built in our backyard and who gets the bill. Submit a letter to the editor.

artigo.texto: BloombergNEF forecasts energy storage additions to reach 188 GW/535 GWh in 2026 and 209 GW/638 GWh in 2027 It expects annual additions in India to exceed 6 GW in 2026, supported by tender-driven procurement Analysts highlight that rising solar penetration and supply-chain localization policies are reshaping deployment and battery manufacturing Global energy storage installations are set to reach a new record in 2026 with 188 GW/535 GWh, forecasts Bloomberg New Energy Finance (BloombergNEF). The market is expected to set another record in 2027, with annual additions reaching 209 GW and 638 GWh. In its latest energy storage market outlook, BNEF forecasts 2026 global additions to represent a 45% year-on-year (YoY) increase in GWs. Analysts attribute the expected growth to rising solar penetration, government policies promoting storage and growing demand for electricity. Deployment is now expanding beyond China and the US, as India, Australia, and several European markets accelerate battery adoption, they point out. China, the US, and Australia are expected to account for 62% of global additions in 2026. China’s energy storage market remains strong despite the withdrawal of a policy mandating storage for renewable projects. New measures, including output-firming requirements for standalone solar and wind projects and a 300 GW storage target by 2030, are supporting growth. The storage market grows in the US thanks to tax credits and on-site energy storage demand from data centers, while India’s tender-driven annual additions will likely exceed 6 GW of total installations this year, up from a 'few hundred megawatts' last year, according to BloombergNEF. Deployment is also spreading to new markets as countries seek to integrate more renewable energy, improve grid flexibility, and strengthen domestic battery supply chains. Several European countries are also expected to make larger contributions in 2026. Bulgaria, Romania, Poland, France, Greece, the Netherlands, and Ukraine are among the markets forecast to reach gigawatt-scale annual additions. In 2027, Spain, the UAE, Chile, and Japan are expected to accelerate deployment, supported by power market fundamentals, diversified revenue stacks, and utility-led procurement activity. The growing share of solar power in electricity generation is increasing the need for storage. Batteries can store surplus electricity when generation is high and release it when demand rises, or solar output falls. By the end of 2025, approximately 69 GW of energy storage power capacity, equivalent to 196 GWh of energy capacity, was paired with around 299 GW of solar capacity globally, according to the analysts. China accounts for a substantial share of solar-plus-storage installations. Solar curtailment and the decline in electricity prices during periods of high solar generation are among the factors encouraging storage deployment in markets such as the US, Australia, and Chile. However, the trend is spreading, with countries including India, Mexico, and the Philippines introducing regulatory or auction-linked requirements to promote battery integration with renewable energy projects. BloombergNEF expects renewable energy projects paired with storage to remain an important source of deployment growth in the coming years. The US has introduced tariffs and incentives to support domestic battery production, alongside restrictions affecting equipment and supply chains linked to China. The European Union and Japan are also addressing supply-chain security and cybersecurity concerns. These policies could make market access more difficult for some Chinese suppliers. In response, Chinese equipment manufacturers are increasingly exploring markets with fewer restrictions, including the Middle East, Latin America, and sub-Saharan Africa. India, South Korea, and Brazil have also introduced measures intended to encourage domestic production and the use of locally manufactured components, although their approaches are less stringent than those in the US, according to BNEF. In terms of technology, despite growing interest in alternative battery technologies, lithium iron phosphate (LFP) is expected to remain the primary battery chemistry for energy storage over the next decade. BNEF attributes its expected dominance to cost competitiveness, long cycle life, and an established supply chain. Sodium-ion batteries are also gaining attention amid rising prices for LFP materials. They offer advantages such as a lower risk of fire and the ability to operate across a wide temperature range, potentially reducing cooling requirements and auxiliary energy consumption. However, limited manufacturing scale and challenges in competing on cost remain barriers to wider adoption of sodium-ion and other non-lithium long-duration storage technologies. BNEF expects cumulative global energy storage capacity to grow approximately tenfold by 2036 compared with the end of 2025, reaching around 3 TW of power capacity and 11 TWh of energy capacity.

artigo.texto: New alliances offer hope to battery swap sector By Cao Yingying | China Daily | Updated: 2026-10-26 09:24 As China's electric vehicle energy supply competition pivots toward ecosystem dominance, a string of major battery-swapping alliances has formed to address the sector's long-running hurdles of fragmented standards and hefty up-front infrastructure investment. BAIC and CATL signed an agreement on Thursday to deepen battery-swapping cooperation and build a unified battery swap ecosystem. According to the agreement, BAIC will roll out adapted models across its multiple brands to connect to CATL's EVOGO solutions. Earlier last week, Huawei-affiliated Yinwang Intelligent Technology signed a cooperation agreement with CATL and CATL's battery-swapping subsidiary CAES to codevelop a smart battery swap ecosystem. The alliance will link vehicle, station and cloud data, enabling EVs fitted with Huawei's Qiankun intelligent driving system to autonomously locate swap stations, drive into position, align and complete a 99-second battery swap before departing. Local media reports state the three partners plan to launch five swappable EVs by 2027. The first model will be by Epicland, a joint brand developed by Dongfeng and Huawei. Aistaland, a Huawei-GAC marque, also has swappable vehicles in its pipeline. As of Sept 30, CATL had built 2,520 EVOGO swap stations covering 200 cities across China's 31 provincial-level regions, more than doubling its network from December 2025. The battery provider targets 3,000 stations by year-end. Even so, vehicle development has lagged station expansion. CATL has released over 20 EVOGO-compatible models from partners including FAW, Changan, BAIC, Chery and GAC. Most carry price tags below 150,000 yuan ($22,470) and target commercial fleets, with low uptake among private buyers. The new partnerships are expected to speed up the rollout of battery-swappable EVs for private users. Tong Zongqi, general manager of the Open Service Platform at the China Electric Vehicle Charging Infrastructure Promotion Alliance, said battery manufacturers' push into swapping primarily aims to boost battery shipments and deepen ties with automakers. Combined with battery graduated sequential utilization and recycling, the business model closes the industrial value chain. For battery makers, swapping acts not merely as a sales channel but as a critical source of life-cycle battery operation data, Tong added. Nio, China's pioneer of consumer battery swapping, operated 4,186 swap stations and provided more than 120 million such services by mid-October. Its fifth-generation stations serve its Nio, Onvo and Firefly-branded cars. Since 2023, Nio has inked battery swap cooperation agreements with Changan, Geely, JAC, Chery, FAW and GAC. Yet these partners have not launched compatible vehicles to date; non-Nio vehicles on its network remain mostly fleet-focused. In late September, Nio and Geely signed a strategic deal covering charging and swapping, solidifying cross-shareholdings in their energy businesses. Geely Holding Chairman Li Shufu said last week at an industry conference that the tie-up avoids redundant infrastructure build-out. "There is no need for Geely and Nio to build separate systems, so we joined forces," Li said. The battery swap industry still faces fundamental headwinds: steep up-front capital expenditure, long payback cycles, cross-brand battery incompatibility and low adoption by private motorists. Batteries make up roughly 40 percent of an EV's total cost. Capacity degradation and poor residual values remain major deterrents for buyers. Battery as a Service, or BaaS, decouples battery costs from vehicle pricing and pools battery packs for shared use, easing consumer concerns over long-term battery performance decay. Ji Xuehong, director of the Automotive Industry Innovation Research Center at North China University of Technology, noted that business models like BaaS transfer battery ownership from consumers to operators, cutting up-front purchase costs. CATL Chairman Zeng Yuqun forecast China's future EV energy replenishment market will evolve into three parallel tracks: private home chargers, public fast chargers and battery swap stations.

artigo.texto: New Mexico is known for its art. Data centers designed to train and deploy artificial intelligence are antithetical to that famed reputation, said Otis Caserta, a sophomore at New Mexico School for the Arts. “We are artists as a state and also artists in a desert,” he said. “And we are sitting here watching this government blindly build a data center we don’t need that will suck up all of the water that we need to drink and survive.” Caserta was one of about 200 NMSA students who walked out of class Tuesday and marched to the state Capitol to protest Project Jupiter, the massive data center being built in Doña Ana County. The students clutched signs — one read “every bad sci-fi movie starts like this,” another read “you can’t drink data” — and chanted all the way to the Governor’s Office. Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham was not there, staff told the students, but they were welcome to write letters to her. So 50 at a time — some in zombie makeup amid a lively school spirit week — poured into the office and sat on the floor with sheets of paper and pencils. The undead getups were a coincidence, said Phoebe Salazar, a junior who had fake blood pouring from her face. Tuesday was “Plants vs. Zombies Day.” “But I think there could be some sort of tie to this for sure,” Salazar added. In an email to The New Mexican, Governor’s Office spokesperson Michael Coleman wrote Lujan Grisham received the students’ letters and plans to read and consider them. The governor hopes the students stay informed and continue to participate in the political process, Coleman wrote. “Governor Lujan Grisham understands that young New Mexicans are frustrated with the American political system, and she shares their concerns about some of the issues raised during today’s protest,” he wrote. “The governor respects anyone’s right to assemble and protest peacefully, but she also believes it’s important to respect public property and spaces and not interfere with government employees who are simply doing their jobs.” Several students spoke to the age gap between themselves and many politicians — something they said makes it easier for those in power to skirt responsibility. “You, the adults, the ones supposed to be fighting for us — you may get the privilege of dying of old age, but our children will die from climate change,” Isabelle Taylor-Ault, a junior, shouted toward Lujan Grisham’s office. “You are elected by the people, for the people, and the people say stop.” Taylor-Ault was one of several organizers of the walkout, spreading the word on social media and catching the eye of statewide environmental groups. Volunteers walked with the students and helped block the street; they followed as the group walked downstairs and into a meeting of the state Legislature’s Water and Natural Resources Committee, where they continued to chant before they marched back to school. About a dozen New Mexico State Police cars remained parked outside of the Roundhouse at about 1:30 p.m. as the students left. The Santa Fe Police Department’s bike sergeant was present and checked in with an organizer, interim police Chief Ben Valdez wrote in a text message. NMSA Head of School Eric Crites said in a statement he received comments from Santa Fe police that students behaved respectfully during the walkout. Though the action was entirely student-organized and not sponsored by NMSA, the school “encourages our students to find their own voices and participate in society in peaceful and respectful way,” Crites said. The school’s attendance policy allows for one excused absence per school year for civic engagement, though parents or guardians must notify the attendance office to excuse their students under that policy. Those who left the school Tuesday without parental permission were marked unexcused, Crites said. A statewide affair The walkout was one of a few that took place Tuesday across New Mexico. A parallel event in Las Cruces was more muted. No students attended, but over a dozen protesters held signs and tote bags with phrases like “AI data centers fuera del desierto” and “Water for life. Not for data,” with an X over the Oracle logo — the main developer behind Project Jupiter. Tuesday morning’s event at the Plaza de Las Cruces came at the heels of a statewide convening in Las Cruces this weekend, where advocacy groups strategized how to campaign for bans on such projects ahead of January’s legislative session. Lennie Maldonado, a local advocate, at Tuesday’s protest criticized Doña Ana County commissioners’ lack of transparency about Project Jupiter. Maldonado mentioned the commissioners were again convening in closed session Tuesday morning to discuss the project’s industrial revenue bonds. When commissioners initially approved the $165 billion in bonds, they did so in closed session, prompting lawsuits over an alleged Open Meetings Act violation. “I want us all to encourage our county commissioners to hold public meetings before they have their vote, because we can remember last year, that was the biggest issue,” Maldonado said Tuesday. “They said, ‘We’re going to vote this day,’ and they were going to give the community zero time to give input or feedback ... and then they obviously ended up voting yes.” Esperanza Chairez, policy manager at Youth United for Climate Crisis Action, expressed disappointment in her remarks Tuesday that an environmental advocacy group’s attempt to halt progress on the data center’s state air quality permit hit a roadblock Monday. The permit’s public hearing will take place the week of Dec. 7 in Sunland Park. Chairez thanked the students organizing in Northern New Mexico in solidarity with Southern New Mexico. “As we know, Project Jupiter is within five miles of a high school, of an elementary school, of a middle school, of daycares,” Chairez said. “So young people are going to certainly be impacted if they are to successfully build their … gas-powered plant using fuel cell technology.” In Albuquerque, Universi
