artigo.texto: The U.S. government's new designation of helium gas as critical for artificial intelligence and data centers may spur drilling projects in Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas. "Helium is essential to producing the semiconductors and advanced technologies that power our economy. By designating helium as a critical material, we are taking another step toward securing our supply chains, creating American jobs, and ensuring the United States leads the world in energy and technological innovation," U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright announced Oct. 23. Reasons for the critical-material designation were outlined the same day in a four-page Federal Register notice. It stated that growing AI infrastructure in the United States will depend on the ability of the nation to produce semiconductors. "Helium's unique properties make it indispensable to semiconductor production, with no viable substitutes in many critical applications. The United States has significant domestic deposits of helium-rich natural gas to support growing industrial demand," the Department of Energy noted. What Is Helium? Helium is one of seven types of "Noble Gases" named as such because they don't have normally have chemical reactions with any other gas or substances. (Other types of these inert gases include helium, krypton, neon and radon.) "Noble gases are the least reactive elements in the periodic table, and they condense out of the air at very low temperatures. They are therefore extremely difficult to trap at temperatures above freezing," according to DOE. Helium (which is non-toxic and lighter than air) has no odor or color. A byproduct of extracting natural gas, helium has multiple high-tech uses including in use in quantum computing, air-to-air missile guidance systems, medical MRI machines, cardio-pulmonary resuscitation pumps for heart surgery, fiber-optic cables, blimps, deep sea diving and leak testing natural gas infrastructure. Domestic Helium The most recent U.S. Geological Survey assessment of helium stated that in 2025 there were 29 plants producing various types of helium domestically. In addition, Texas had three underground cavern storage sites for helium. "In 2025, six new helium operations (three in New Mexico and one each in Colorado, Kansas, and Montana) began producing helium in the United States. A helium storage cavern was brought online in Beaumont, TX, which was able to store excess helium production," stated a 2026 mineral commodity summary for helium. USGS estimated that last year's sales of Grade-A helium (99.997% helium or greater) and gaseous helium (above 98% helium) amounted to $970 million.

artigo.texto: At 7x24 Exchange, AI Data Center Growth Confronts New Realities of Power, Grid Reliability and Community Trust SAN ANTONIO, Texas — The data center industry's accelerating transition toward artificial intelligence is challenging some of its longest-standing assumptions about infrastructure design, operational reliability and relationships with the outside world. That was the overriding message Monday, October 26, as the 7x24 Exchange Fall 2026 Conference opened its technical program in San Antonio under the theme The Intersection of AI & Traditional Data Centers. Across a series of presentations spanning agentic AI, power system engineering, grid reliability and community engagement, speakers described an industry confronting challenges that extend well beyond higher rack densities and greater demand for electricity. AI workloads are changing how power must be delivered and managed. Large data center campuses are becoming consequential participants in grid operations rather than simply customers of electric utilities. And developers are finding that technical and economic arguments alone may no longer be enough to secure acceptance in communities where they intend to build. Opening the proceedings, 7x24 Exchange Chairman Bob Cassiliano identified community opposition as a challenge that has overtaken several of the industry's other longstanding concerns. "Last year it was artificial intelligence, sustainability, the labor shortage," Cassiliano said. "Although these challenges remain, they have been superseded by community opposition to data centers." Cassiliano pointed to mounting concerns over electricity prices, water consumption, noise, land use and property values, along with the increasingly political character of efforts to restrict development. He suggested that industry organizations develop a more coordinated strategy for engaging governors and senior state officials, complementing ongoing outreach to local communities. The opening also included an announcement that 7x24 Exchange would contribute $40,000 to American Red Cross disaster relief efforts supporting communities affected by wildfires, hurricanes and flooding across the United States. Agentic AI Raises New Questions for Infrastructure Design The morning keynote, delivered by AI futurist and former Google DeepMind executive Steve Brown, placed the industry's infrastructure expansion within a larger transition from conversational AI tools toward autonomous agents capable of executing complex work. "We're using data centers to turn energy into intelligence," Brown told attendees, describing the physical infrastructure required to support an increasingly AI-driven economy. Brown argued that growing demand for AI inference and autonomous agents could sustain the industry's expansion even as questions persist about the financial sustainability of massive infrastructure investments. "There may be a financial bubble, there may be a debt bubble, but I do not believe there is a demand bubble," he said. Of particular relevance to data center operators, Brown described how agentic computing introduces different workload characteristics from conventional chatbot interactions. Rather than responding to a single prompt, AI agents may execute repeated cycles of reasoning, tool use, database access and task completion over hours or days. Depending on their complexity, he suggested, agents could consume hundreds or thousands of times more tokens than conventional chatbot interactions. The implications extend to hardware architecture. Agentic applications move between GPU-intensive reasoning and CPU-based operations, increasing the importance of heterogeneous computing environments with both CPU/GPU and CPU-only infrastructure. Brown also emphasized persistent memory, low-latency interconnects and secure execution environments as requirements for increasingly autonomous systems. Those changes, he suggested, will demand new ways of evaluating AI infrastructure efficiency. Rather than emphasizing tokens generated per second, Brown proposed measuring useful tasks or economic outcomes relative to energy consumption. The shift, in his view, points toward a future in which data center productivity is judged less by raw computational output than by the useful work that computing delivers. Google and Cummins Examine the Electrical Consequences of AI Loads The next presentation moved from AI's computational requirements to the electrical systems needed to support them. In a joint session on AI load dynamics, Google power systems engineer Ashish Upreti and Cummins technical advisor Rich Scroggins detailed the challenges created by rapid, synchronized changes in power demand from AI computing equipment. Unlike conventional data center workloads, AI training can produce repeated swings between high-power computation and comparatively low-power states as processors complete calculations, exchange information and begin subsequent operations. These fluctuations can occur over milliseconds or seconds, creating distinct challenges for generation equipment, power electronics, UPS systems and electrical distribution infrastructure. The speakers outlined a layered approach to mitigating those fluctuations. Software-level controls can limit how quickly computing loads increase or decrease, although slowing workload transitions can affect computational efficiency. Supercapacitors can address extremely short-duration power spikes, while battery energy storage systems are better suited to absorbing fluctuations occurring over several seconds. The distinction matters because repetitive power swings can create operating conditions that conventional generator acceptance testing does not fully capture. Scroggins explained that a generator may successfully handle an individual load step but behave differently when similar changes occur repeatedly, particularly when the next transition arrives before the governor or voltage regulator has fully recovered. MAHOMET — A few weeks after public backlash led the village of Mahomet to end preliminary talks with a data-center developer, the village board is set to vote on a resolution calling on state lawmakers to protect the Mahomet Aquifer from data-center development. The board will vote tonight on whether to approve the resolution, which would authorize Mayor Jason Tompkins to sign and send identical letters on the subject to state Sen. Chapin Rose, R-Mahomet, and state Rep. Chris Miller, R-Hindsboro. “On behalf of the Village of Mahomet Board of Trustees, I write to express our support for efforts through legislation to protect the Mahomet Aquifer including the requirement of a closed-loop cooling system for data-center developments,” the proposed letter from Tompkins states. “We further urge the legislature to resolve this important issue during your fall veto session or during (the lame-duck) session in January.” The village of Mahomet announced on Sept. 28 that it was in talks with Clean Cloud Energy about a potential data-center project in “a rural area west of Champaign” that falls within Mahomet’s extraterritorial jurisdiction. One week later, the village announced the end of those discussions amid public opposition, including concerns about transparency and the potential impact on the aquifer. Documents released by the village on Sept. 28 following a Sept. 14 Freedom of Information Act request by Mahomet resident John Bambenek show that Clean Cloud Energy began talking with Mahomet officials about the project in December. The village entered into a nondisclosure agreement with the company in early 2026 but was released from the agreement on Sept. 16. Individuals who signed NDAs include Village Administrator Patrick Brown, Village Planner Abby Heckman and Economic Development Specialist Austin Shufflebarger. The village board discussed data centers during a study session last week, Tompkins said. “One of our trustees, Trustee (Bruce) Colravy, felt that it would be appropriate for us to acknowledge the work that Senator Rose is doing as far as for the protection of the aquifer,” Tompkins told The News-Gazette. “… That is something that I believe our entire board is very committed to. And it’s a very important resource, and so we were just lending support to Senator Rose in his efforts.” “I just feel like the NDA, the data center and there seemed to be some disregard, then, for how that might impact the aquifer — or at least perceived disregard,” said Colravy, who has a degree in natural resources and helped found the Upper Sangamon River Conservancy. “And so I wanted to do something to try to clear that up.” He doesn’t like the idea of data centers being located over sole-source aquifers but added that he’s not sure if banning this is legally an option. The proposed resolution states that the village supports legislation that would prevent data centers from using groundwater from the Mahomet Aquifer and require alternative cooling methods such as “reclaimed water, surface water, or closed-loop or air-cooled systems.” Andrew Rehn, director of climate policy at Prairie Rivers Network, said in a previous interview that closed-loop cooling systems for data centers do not consume as much water as evaporative cooling systems, though they do use more electricity. Colravy supports the requirement of closed-loop cooling systems but would like the language about reclaimed water and surface water to be removed from the resolution. “I think you can create some environmental problems with that as well,” he said. “As you may know, the Sangamon River, we put processed wastewater back into the river, but that water is not waste. It is used by wildlife until it gets to Decatur, ends up in their lake, then it’s used for recreation and it’s also their water source. So when you take from that, you’re also taking from downstream.” Tompkins acknowledged that the protection of the aquifer was a concern that the village heard from members of the public after announcing that it was in initial talks with Clean Cloud Energy. “Had the data center ever gotten to a point of an official proposal by a developer, we would’ve been very adamant about that, making sure it’s a closed-loop system and that all measures to protect the aquifer would be put in place,” he said. According to Prairie Rivers Network, the Mahomet Aquifer is the sole source of drinking water “for nearly 1 million people across 14 counties in Central Illinois.” Clean Cloud Energy previously said in a public statement that it would use “zero water” to cool the proposed project near Mahomet. “The coolant is an engineered solution that will be trucked on-site with a small amount of water that may be used during the initial fill,” company officials said. “The only potable water used would be for the needs of the employees in the building — sinks, bathrooms, and canteen — just like any other business or manufacturing facility.” “As a business, we only do closed-loop, air-chilled cooling that uses no water,” Clean Cloud Energy CEO Raj Keswani said in a previous interview. “Evaporative cooling is, in our view, not a responsible way to develop data centers.” However, community members remained concerned about the project’s potential impact. And despite the village’s decision to end talks with the company, Mahomet officials have still been criticized by some in regards to how the discussions were handled. “The last couple study sessions, there (have) been comments about the project,” Tompkins said. “Obviously, we have listened to those items. We have taken them very seriously. And we felt the letters to legislators was a good first step as far as acknowledging that we do recognize the importance of the aquifer. We also, in future study sessions, will be discussing NDAs, how they work and what policies we may have going forward on those.” Colravy said he was first told that the company had app

artigo.texto: Data centers are using more water than at any point in the internet era, and the question of why is the top trending technology story on October 27, 2026. WSLS and TechRadar both put the topic in front of readers this week, and the explanation starts with one fact of physics. Nearly all the electricity that powers server hardware ends up as heat, and someone has to remove it. According to Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, U.S. data centers directly consumed approximately 17.4 billion gallons of water in 2023, up from an estimated 5.6 billion gallons in 2014. Eric Sjostedt, a Virginia Tech researcher, summed up the core problem for WSLS on October 26: “At its core, data centers produce a lot of heat. It’s getting rid of that heat that uses so much water.” That sentence explains why data center water use keeps climbing even as chips get more efficient per calculation. More computing in a smaller space means more heat per rack, and the cheapest way to move heat outdoors is often to let water evaporate. This analysis walks through the mechanics, the numbers, the tradeoffs and the money. It also separates what the record confirms from what it does not. The AI build-out now underway echoes earlier infrastructure booms, a pattern we examined in our look at the AI infrastructure race and its old boom echoes, and water is one of the places where that history shows up first. No single facility, product or company drives today’s headlines, so this piece treats the story as an industry-wide trend. Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. Why Data Centers Use So Much Water: The 17.4 Billion Gallon Baseline The best anchor for any discussion of why data centers use so much water is the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimate. The lab puts direct U.S. consumption at roughly 17.4 billion gallons in 2023. That is water the facilities themselves take in and lose, mostly through evaporation in cooling systems. It does not include the water used to generate the electricity that runs the buildings, which is a separate and larger conversation we cover below. A year-over-year headline number hides how the use is distributed. Water consumption depends on how each site rejects heat outdoors, and that varies widely by design and climate. Facilities that lean on fans and outdoor air generally use less water but more electricity. Facilities that lean on evaporation generally do the opposite. LBNL’s figure is therefore a national blend of many different engineering choices rather than a per-building constant. The growth rate matters as much as the level. Going from 5.6 billion gallons in 2014 to 17.4 billion in 2023 means direct consumption rose roughly 3.1 times in nine years. The same arithmetic implies compound growth of about 13 percent a year over that span. Those two derived figures are our own calculations from the laboratory’s published endpoints, not numbers the lab reported, but they give readers a feel for the pace. Congress has taken notice of the topic. The Congressional Research Service published a primer titled Data Centers and Water: Frequently Asked Questions, which signals that lawmakers want a plain-language baseline before they write rules. Heat Is the Real Problem, Not Thirst Servers do not consume water the way a factory consumes a raw material. They consume electricity, and the electricity becomes heat. According to the LBNL reporting summarized in the research for this story, nearly all of the power drawn by IT equipment is converted to heat that must be removed to keep chips from overheating. Water enters the picture only because it is a very good way to carry that heat away. Matt Green, president of Brucker HVAC Solutions, told Network World why operators accept the water bill: “The reason why we evaporate water is because it’s a very effective way to cool.” The statement is blunt, and it captures the engineering logic. Evaporation moves a large amount of heat for each unit of water, so it keeps fan and compressor loads low. Green also drew a comparison with ordinary buildings. In the same Network World interview he said that office cooling uses a tolerable amount of water, but that data centers are “basically power plants in reverse,” and that the heat they generate demands substantially more water than a building of the same footprint would normally use. The comparison helps explain why a data center can look modest from the street and still dominate a local utility’s demand forecast. The heat load is also continuous. Offices empty out at night and homes cool down in winter. Servers run around the clock, and the AI hardware now filling new halls runs hot at all hours. Cooling plants therefore operate at high duty cycles, and any system that depends on evaporation pulls water every day of the year, with peaks in summer when outdoor air offers the least free cooling. How Evaporative Cooling Works and Why Operators Pick It In an evaporative system, warm water or refrigerant loops carry heat from the server floor to a cooling tower or similar device outside. There, a portion of the water evaporates and takes heat with it. The remaining water cools down and returns to the loop. The evaporated portion is gone, which is why engineers call it consumption rather than withdrawal. Operators must keep topping up the system with fresh supply. The attraction is energy efficiency. The research gathered for this story notes that evaporative cooling is generally more energy-efficient than air-cooled or waterless systems, though it consumes more water. In a business where electricity is among the largest operating costs, that tradeoff usually points toward evaporation unless local water is scarce or expensive. artigo.texto: The Hayward City Council is temporarily halting the development of data centers. On Oct. 20 the city council approved an urgency ordinance that activates a 45-day moratorium. This stops the approval of data centers and gives the city time to work on researching their impacts. One resident worried about the impacts of STACK, a data center that’s under construction. “I’m very concerned about the new data center that is coming into our community. So about a mile and a half away from my house. From the evidence that we have seen from previous data centers, I’m a little concerned for myself, for my environment, for my home, things from property value, when these data centers come in, from environmental safety concerns, obviously, from water usage, from electrical grid usage. These are all big concerns for us.” According to the urgency ordinance, water is used to cool off servers that use a huge amount of power. Data centers impact air quality and cause noises from the equipment, like diesel generators. The city said a developer confirmed they are interested in potentially building two data centers that would be 90 MW (megawatts) each on Arden Road and Corporate Avenue, a half mile away from the city’s four data centers. The city plans to take a closer look at how air quality, water use, noise and electricity would be impacted by data centers. One resident said he wants a stop to new data centers. “I believe that it is a detriment to our community and to our health. If they are gonna throw money at us, they need to subsidize our power, our water and our medical bills, because they are taking that from us. They are making it more expensive on our power and water, and it’s costing our health.” One resident believed data centers won’t negatively impact the community. “So I think facts matter, critical thought matters and I think the fact is that there is no evidence in California or in the Bay Area that data centers have caused any harm,” he said. “We have CEQA, we have local laws. Those studies have been completed, and they’ve been evaluated to demonstrate that most of the claims made this evening are inaccurate.” The council can choose to extend the moratorium to 10 months and 15 days, which requires a hearing and decision from the council. That hearing is tentatively set for Dec.1.

artigo.texto: Maritime emissions specialist EmissionLink has called for a dedicated proportion of EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) revenues to be invested in onboard carbon capture trials and supporting port infrastructure, warning that the technology risks remaining commercially unviable without targeted financial support. Philippos Ioulianou (pictured), Managing Director of EmissionLink, believes Europe has an opportunity to accelerate the development of maritime carbon capture by directing emissions trading revenues towards full-scale demonstrations that establish whether the technology can deliver verified emissions reductions at an economically sustainable cost. The call comes as the IMO moves to develop interim safety guidelines for onboard carbon capture systems. While welcoming the initiative, Mr Ioulianou argues that regulatory progress must be matched by investment in the infrastructure, emissions accounting mechanisms and commercial arrangements necessary to make the technology attractive to shipowners. "Developing safety guidelines is an important step, but regulation alone will not persuade shipowners to invest in carbon capture," said Mr Ioulianou. "Owners need a credible business case, backed by verified emissions savings, workable carbon disposal arrangements and a clear understanding of the financial benefits. "Europe is well positioned to lead this work. Allocating a proportion of EU ETS revenues to onboard trials and port reception infrastructure would help establish whether carbon capture can become a commercially viable decarbonisation solution for shipping." EmissionLink is advocating investment in demonstration projects that assess every stage of the carbon capture process, from onboard collection and storage to offloading, transportation and permanent storage or approved use. Such projects should operate against clearly defined performance criteria and generate independently verifiable emissions data that can inform regulatory development and future investment decisions. However, EmissionLink cautions that onboard carbon capture is unlikely to be a practical solution for every vessel. Ships operating on fixed and predictable routes offer the most promising early applications, as operators can plan carbon storage capacity and establish offloading arrangements at designated ports. For vessels trading on irregular routes or spot charters, the logistical challenges are considerably greater, particularly where carbon reception facilities and onward transportation arrangements are unavailable. Technical suitability will also depend on factors including vessel age, available space, additional power demand and remaining commercial life. Ship owners and charterers must also resolve contractual questions surrounding additional fuel consumption, offloading delays and the allocation of regulatory compliance benefits. "Installing carbon capture equipment introduces responsibilities that extend well beyond the initial investment," Mr Ioulianou explained. "Shipowners must consider the operational impact, the demands placed on crews and who ultimately bears the additional costs. These questions need answering before the technology can be adopted with confidence." A further concern is the need for greater clarity around emissions accounting and regulatory recognition. While the EU ETS recognises qualifying carbon capture and permanent geological storage or chemical binding, practical monitoring, reporting and verification arrangements for maritime carbon capture remain underdeveloped. Mr Ioulianou also warned that shipowners should not assume carbon capture benefits recognised under the EU ETS will automatically provide equivalent compliance advantages under FuelEU Maritime, which regulates the greenhouse gas intensity of energy used onboard ships rather than absolute emissions. "Capturing carbon is not necessarily the same as delivering a verified reduction in emissions," he said. "Shipowners need certainty over how those savings will be measured, independently verified and recognised under the relevant regulations. Without that clarity, it becomes extremely difficult to justify the capital and operating expenditure." EmissionLink believes the period during which the IMO develops its safety framework should be used to advance commercial trials, emissions verification procedures and port infrastructure in parallel.

artigo.texto: Next Upcoming Canary Live Bay Area By Canary Media Energy storage is taking off as the state moves to make development easier and more profitable, but the horizon isn’t all clear for the sector. Just outside Boston, a developer is getting set to build a 700-megawatt storage facility that is expected to dwarf every other battery project in New England. One town over, another energy company just closed on $850 million in financing to build a 250-MW battery. Down near the Rhode Island border, ground has been broken on a 200-MW storage facility that is expected to be up and running by the end of the year. These and roughly a half dozen other projects at various stages are taking advantage of policies Massachusetts has put in place to help reach its goal of getting 5 gigawatts of battery storage capacity online by 2030, with another 5 GW to follow by 2035. While several larger and generally sunnier states top the list for installed storage capacity — California boasts a whopping 23 GW — Massachusetts’ ambition and policies put it at the forefront of the push to get more batteries on the grid. Thirteen states have set procurement targets for battery storage, but Massachusetts’ total of 10 GW by 2035 is the highest. And its policy landscape is setting the state up for success, observers say. “Massachusetts is really a leader in this space,” said Erin Smith, energy and grid policy director for the Environmental League of Massachusetts. “We’re ahead of the pack as it relates to encouraging battery buildout.” Massachusetts has ambitious clean energy goals and some of the highest electricity prices in the country. Batteries, the state figures, can help with both. They can store energy when power is cheapest and cleanest — like on sunny days when solar farms are producing in abundance — then send it back onto the grid during times of heavier demand, cutting down on the need to generate pricier, dirtier power. Battery systems can also bolster resilience, reducing outages during increasingly extreme and erratic weather. “If we have storage on the system, we can deploy it at different times to manage our load,” said Elizabeth Mahony, commissioner of the state Department of Energy Resources. So for the past 11 years, Massachusetts has been working to encourage the development of large-scale batteries, beginning with the launch of the Energy Storage Initiative in 2015 under then-Gov. Charlie Baker (R). The state blew past its initial target of installing 1 GW of storage capacity by 2025, topping 1.6 GW. Progress has only accelerated since then, thanks to a trio of state policies making it easier and more profitable to locate batteries in the state. The Clean Peak Standard, which went into effect in 2020, is a first-in-the-country program that pays renewable energy facilities and energy storage owners to send power onto the grid during times of peak demand. It provides an additional revenue source that can make battery developments more financially viable. “Those credits are incredibly important to financing and developing these projects,” said Aaron Lang, a partner at Boston law firm Foley Hoag who counts several battery developers among his clients. New siting and permitting reforms that went into effect on July 1 are also making Massachusetts more attractive to storage developers by streamlining and speeding up the approval process, Lang said. The new rules give the state Energy Facilities Siting Board authority to approve large energy projects, including storage facilities with a capacity of 100 MW or higher, rather than making developers work with the disparate permitting processes of individual municipalities. Decisions must be made within 15 months of application. “It ensures we can bring more clean energy, including batteries, online sooner,” Smith said. The state has also undertaken a series of procurements aimed at securing large-scale storage capacity. In December 2025, Massachusetts selected four projects totaling 1.3 GW of capacity to move ahead to contract negotiations with the major utilities. A second solicitation received 35 bids before it closed earlier this month; selected projects are set to be announced in February. Together, these actions create a climate that storage developers can rely on, said Hans Detweiler, vice president of development for Jupiter Power, the company behind the 700-MW Trimount project just outside Boston, where construction is slated to begin next year. “Moving through permitting and state solicitations takes years, so developers need confidence that the policy framework will remain stable over that period,” he said. “The Healey administration has consistently supported a procurement process that brings cost-effective resources to the grid to reduce electricity costs for consumers.” Even with all the state’s efforts, however, barriers remain. Perhaps the most pressing is the cost of interconnecting major projects like these to the grid. In September, developers canceled plans for a 125-MW battery system in the town of Tewksbury, citing the unexpectedly high cost — $65 million — of the upgrades necessary to hook into the grid. And that number is on the low end. Grid operator Independent System Operator New England recently completed a study of likely interconnection costs for a number of proposed projects, most of which were battery developments sited in Massachusetts. Many of the estimates topped $200 million, “quite a bit higher than developers anticipated,” Smith said. “We have an older grid here in New England, and it genuinely does require some upgrade costs to accommodate the influx of batteries,” she said. “How to allocate grid upgrade costs is going to be a debate.” Many battery proposals are also running into ardent community opposition. artigo.texto: APsystems apresentará novos microinversores e soluções de armazenamento de energia na Expo Solar Colombia 2026 AGÊNCIA DE COMUNICAÇÃO Conteúdo de responsabilidade da empresa 26 de outubro de 2026 Os modelos QS2, DS3D de 2.200 W e QT2 de 480 V serão os destaques da exposição da empresa, juntamente com a APstorage e uma prévia de sua oferta de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS, Battery Energy Storage System). BOGOTÁ, Colômbia, 26 de outubro de 2026 /PRNewswire/ — A APsystems participará da ExpoSolar Colombia 2026, que será realizada de 28 a 30 de outubro, no centro de convenções CORFERIAS em Bogotá. No estande 58, localizado nos pavilhões 11 a 16, a empresa apresentará suas mais recentes inovações em microinversores e armazenamento de energia para aplicações residenciais, comerciais e industriais. Um dos principais destaques será o QS2 de 2.500 W, que possui quatro rastreadores de ponto de potência máxima (MPPT, Maximum Power Point Trackers) independentes para otimizar a saída de cada módulo em instalações residenciais e comerciais. A exposição também destacará o DS3D Boosted de 2.200 W e o QT2 de 1.800 W para redes trifásicas de 480 V, ampliando as opções para projetos com módulos de alta potência e diferentes requisitos de instalação. O armazenamento de energia será o foco principal do APstorage PCS ELS 11.4K, uma solução acoplada em corrente alternada que permite a integração do armazenamento em sistemas fotovoltaicos compatíveis. A exposição incluirá a bateria APbattery e o controlador híbrido AHS 6.3, juntamente com a série EZOG-LV, para proporcionar aos visitantes uma visão mais detalhada das diversas opções do portfólio residencial da APstorage. A APsystems também oferecerá uma prévia de sua divisão C&I Solutions, sua família de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) para aplicações comerciais e industriais. Soluções de energia de reserva, resposta à demanda e opções de escalabilidade serão o foco desta primeira análise das inovações futuras da marca. Os visitantes poderão obter mais informações sobre esta oferta durante a feira comercial. “Estamos prestes a apresentar uma pequena amostra das novidades da APsystems como parte de um importante marco global: a chegada de soluções voltadas para projetos de alta demanda e alta capacidade, expandindo o portfólio da empresa em diferentes segmentos para atender tanto ao setor comercial e industrial quanto a aplicações em escala de serviços públicos”, disse Alma Aldana, gerente de marketing para a América Latina (LATAM). A experiência no estande será complementada por demonstrações do APdesigner, atualizações sobre o EMA Manager e conteúdo sobre o APbot. Essas ferramentas auxiliam os profissionais do setor no desenvolvimento, monitoramento e acesso a informações sobre as soluções da marca. A agenda técnica contará com uma apresentação de Miguel Campos intitulada “A Nova Era do Armazenamento de Energia: “Soluções Escaláveis para Residências, Empresas e Aplicações Comerciais”, agendada para 28 de outubro às 17h00, na Sala de Conferências 9 do Hall 12. artigo.texto: Pakistan is reportedly planning a major investment in lithium-ion battery manufacturing, with military-owned Margalla Heavy Industries Limited (MHIL) said to have signed a $2.25 billion agreement with Chinese partners and local investors to establish a battery plant in Rawalpindi. The proposed facility is expected to have an annual production capacity exceeding 1,000 megawatts (MW), with initial output projected at 200–300 MW. However, the project’s production timeline depends on the government’s approval of a dedicated battery manufacturing policy. According to the reported plan, commercial production could begin within six to eight months after the policy receives government approval. Hamad Ali Mansoor, chief executive of the Engineering Development Board (EDB), reportedly said the factory building was ready, and machinery had been installed. The Chinese and Pakistani investors signed the agreement in July, although their identities have not been publicly disclosed. Battery Policy Approval Remains Key Hurdle The proposed investment comes as Pakistan seeks to reduce its dependence on imported batteries and expand domestic manufacturing for electric vehicles (EVs), solar power systems and large-scale electricity storage. The government’s National Lithium-Ion Battery Manufacturing Policy 2026–2031 aims to support local production, attract investment and develop an export-oriented battery industry. However, the policy was still awaiting approval in the latest reports. Approval of the policy is expected to be a key step towards starting commercial operations at the proposed plant. Read More: Pakistan Govt Borrows Net Rs. 373.97 Billion in a Week Battery Demand Could Reach 100,000 MW by 2030 The Engineering Development Board estimates that Pakistan’s demand for battery energy storage systems could reach 100,000 MW by June 2030 if economic growth reaches 5% or more. Demand could reach around 80,000 MW if growth remains below 3%. According to the reported estimates, meeting the projected demand could require four to five large battery manufacturing plants, each costing approximately $1 billion to $1.25 billion. Grid stabilisation alone could require 3,000–5,000 MW of battery storage capacity, highlighting the potential role of energy storage in supporting Pakistan’s electricity infrastructure. The proposed Rawalpindi facility is expected to manufacture lithium-ion batteries for applications including electric vehicles and energy storage systems. Domestic production could help reduce reliance on imported battery technology, create industrial employment and support Pakistan’s transition towards cleaner energy. However, the project’s final production schedule remains dependent on government approval of the battery manufacturing policy.

artigo.texto: Georgetown extends data center moratorium to June 2027 GEORGETOWN, Ky. — The Georgetown City Council voted Monday night to extend the city’s data center moratorium, pushing the expiration date to June 30, 2027. The vote passed unanimously. Unlike similar meetings around the commonwealth where data centers have been on the agenda, Monday night’s public comment portion did not include fiery calls for a moratorium extension. The extension is the second of its kind for a data center moratorium in Georgetown. Council cites lack of resources Councilwoman Karen Tingle Sames said the city cannot support a data center. “As I’ve said before and I’ll continue to say it, the city of Georgetown doesn’t have the resources to have a data center here in our community,” Tingle Sames said. City considers full ban Georgetown has also begun the process of drawing up legislation to completely ban hyperscale data centers throughout the city. Mayor Burney Jenkins acknowledged that might be difficult, as data centers are a legitimate business. He said the moratorium extension gives the city council, in collaboration with planning and zoning, more time to fine-tune restrictions if a ban is unsuccessful. “Yes, we may try to put out a ban, but we better have something else in place like some restrictions so then if the ban doesn’t go over, then we have these restrictions to where it makes it tough for any types of data center to come in,” Jenkins said. Mayoral candidate weighs in WKYT reached out to council member Kim Menke, who is also running for mayor of Georgetown. He expressed a similar sentiment, issuing the following statement: “Data centers should be evaluated like any other major industrial project. Before making long-term decisions, we need the tools and regulations to properly assess their size, infrastructure needs, benefits, and potential impacts. I support a moratorium that gives Georgetown time to better understand these projects and establish appropriate Planning & Zoning standards. Once we have that information, then we can make an informed decision about whether a data center is a good fit for our community.” Copyright 2026 WKYT. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Bulloch County data center committee asks for more time before moratorium expires A Bulloch County committee is seeking a 180-day extension of the current moratorium on new data center applications to complete zoning regulations. Bulloch County data center committee asks for more time before moratorium expires A Bulloch County committee is seeking a 180-day extension of the current moratorium on new data center applications to complete zoning regulations. A newly formed committee in Bulloch County is requesting an extension of the county's moratorium on new data center applications to allow more time to develop zoning regulations. The 15-member committee, tasked with reviewing proposed zoning rules and making recommendations to the Board of Commissioners, held its first meeting Monday night. The current moratorium is set to expire on December 31, but committee members are asking for an additional 180 days to finalize regulations before new applications can be submitted. The committee plans to meet twice a month and elected a chairman and vice chairman during the meeting. "We don't want the moratorium to expire until we have a complete set of ordinances so that when if somebody is interested in bringing a data center in, they know what the rules are and they know what the expectations are, and then through that process, the citizens know that we've done due diligence to make sure that things are fair for everyone," said Frank Davis, chairman of the Data Center Committee. David Bennett, chairman of the Bulloch County Commission, expressed his thoughts on the timeline. "I’m fine with all those things. You know, going into this, we knew that our moratorium is will end on the 31st of December. I knew realistically that this committee is not going to be able to provide us answers by then. I want them to provide us intelligent, well thought out, rational recommendations to the board of commissioners. I didn't feel like they'd be able to do that in three months," Bennett said. The committee will focus on four key areas: water, electricity, land use, and the application process. The chairman stated the goal is to complete the committee's work by the summer. The next meeting is scheduled for Monday.

artigo.texto: Close to three-quarters of Americans oppose artificial intelligence data centers in their local communities. Another two-thirds have broader fears about AI. That’s according to recent national polls. Opposition to new data centers and worries about AI eliminating jobs, or worse, come ahead of the midterm elections next month as big technology companies look to build new facilities to power machine learning models. A poll released Oct. 20 by polling firm IPSOS in a survey of U.S. voters for the Washington Post and ABC News shows: • 72% oppose new data centers in their local communities • 57% believe AI will be bad for society • 65% worry AI will eliminate jobs • 33% fear there is a high risk of AI resulting in human extinction. Another 32% believe there is a moderate risk. • 62% say AI could result in people losing their decision making capabilities. “When 72% of voters don’t want a data center down the street, that’s not a tech story anymore. It’s a kitchen-table story,” said Joseph Roberto Lopez, a Texas-based communications strategist and managing partner with The Prescient Group. Lopez said the AI data center issue has moved from Silicon Valley and Wall Street to Main Street and local communities throughout the country. “The fight moved from ‘jobs and investment’ to ‘my power bill, my water, my neighborhood.’ Once an issue gets that local, it stops being abstract and starts moving votes,” Lopez said. The wave of new data centers has also brought home wider fears about AI’s global impacts, including infrastructure, jobs and security. “In my view, a data center becomes the physical place where people can express concerns about a technology that otherwise feels abstract,” said Nick Khami, founder of call4me.com, an AI phone agent. Khami said there are security concerns about AI that need more examination and transparency. “Developers need to explain specific benefits and safeguard in terms people can evaluate,” Khami said. Sydney Gomez said AI is causing anxiety for some Americans. Gomez, a clinical training specialist with Thriveworks, said a recent survey by the national mental health provider shows more than one in five Americans (21%) say AI is causing anxiety for them. “Data centers make AI feel tangible. Instead of thinking about AI as something happening somewhere online, residents may see a proposed facility near their homes and begin asking what this technology will mean for their community, resources and future,” she said. “Those concerns can overlap with broader anxieties about job security, privacy, environmental impacts, lack of trust in government to regulate, losing control of what is happening in their communities, and how quickly technology is changing our lives,” Gomez continued. While there is bipartisan and across-the-board consternation about AI and data centers, Democrats and young people are the most concerned and most opposed. A late September survey by the Pew Research Center shows 81% of self-described liberals are opposed to new data centers in their communities. That compares to 58% of conservatives. Almost two-thirds (64%) of young adults, ages 18 to 29, in the Pew survey believe new data centers will be bad for the environment. Data center opponents frequently cite energy and water consumption as well as noise and land-use concerns in their pushes against the technology facilities. William Pirrone, a founding member and managing principal of Georgia-based Rubicon Professional Services and Rubicon Technical Services, said energy tops the list of local concerns. Pirrone and his firm are veterans in the data center and technology infrastructure space. “Primary objections about new data center builds typically center around whether the local electric grid and natural resources can withstand the additional demand,” Pirrone said. “Since electricity requires an enormous amount of additional energy, it’s often the center point of discussion.” Pirrone said power supplies outside of utilities’ power grids can help assuage community concerns about infrastructure strains and higher electricity bills. “Engineers are deploying various design strategies that include solar, battery energy storage, fuel cells and onsite power generation plants,” he said. Another September survey by the Associated Press, NORC Center for Public Affairs Research and University of Chicago shows 70% of Democrats want limits in data centers compared to 57% of Republicans. More than 360 U.S. jurisdictions have enacted pauses, restrictions or bans on new data center developments, according to Interconnected Capital LLC. That includes ones in Florida, Maryland, Wisconsin, Minnesota, North Carolina and Ohio. The AI data center wave is being pushed by some of the richest companies and richest billionaires in the world. That includes Amazon, Alphabet/Google, Meta/Facebook, NVIDIA and Microsoft. The majority of existing data centers globally are located in the U.S. The technology sector contends that new bigger data centers are needed to keep up with exponentially bigger computing needs to feed and fuel machine learning models. A hefty portion of U.S. economic activity is also currently tied into AI and the data centers to power machine learning, according to an analysis by the Columbia Business School. Trump warns if the U.S. does not embrace the AI wave, including data centers, it could see China challenge American technology hegemony. Trump wants AI data center users to offer financial dividends to communities where they are landing. “I have watched the process closely, and data centers that were highly unpopular in a certain area, have become extremely popular when a financial deal is struck. MAKE DEALS, and get them built!!! GREAT FOR THE U.S.A.,” Trump said in a Truth Social post Oct. 21. Some data center developers and users have been offering community benefits money to local communities that help with education funding childcare access and infrastructure improvements. artigo.texto: At Trump rallies, data centers take back seat to butts President’s comments on physiques keep making headlines The backsides of Ohio GOP Sen. Jon Husted, rapper Nicki Minaj, even former Rep. Mike Rogers. As the midterm campaign enters its home stretch, President Donald Trump has talked up what he claims are the benefits of increasingly unpopular data centers, at the same time that he has made headlines taking about the physiques of Husted and others. After being an outspoken proponent of the technology facilities for months, Trump has shifted to putting the onus on local jurisdictions to extract economic value. At a Saturday night rally in Perry, Ga., he said: “Tell them to pay you $10,000, $15,000, $20,000 for everybody that lives in the community — they’ll do it. You just got to ask.” At the same time, he continues to discuss the literal bodies politic: During a Friday rally in Florida, he credited 72-year-old Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., for having, “the body of a 30 year old.” At the Georgia weekend rally, the president focused on Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff, calling him “a guy that looked very much to me like Pee-Wee Herman.” There was plenty of time Tuesday night in Greenville, N.C., to make his pitch for data centers, which have become a big issue this election cycle. Trump set a new record for his second term, speaking for 1 hour and 51 minutes, besting his Feb. 24 State of the Union Address by 3 minutes and 14 seconds, according to Roll Call’s Factba.se. But Trump, a self-described data center true believer, didn’t bring up the sprawling, power-needy facilities. Instead, Trump waited a few hours after returning to the White House to make another plug for the power-hungry facilities that have angered voters. He walked back into the executive mansion around 11 p.m. Tuesday night. About two-and-a-half hours later, at 1:37 a.m. Wednesday, he told his supporters to “make deals” around them. “As the President of the United States, I have been watching Data Centers very closely, and have come to a very strong conclusion. New and large, in some cases gigantic, Data Centers are mandated by me to make their own electricity, and give or sell any excess back to the local community, or grid, and therefore there is electric price increase,” he wrote on his social media platform, Truth Social. “If companies want to make their Data Centers popular, pay the community, and/or individuals within the community, a ‘dividend,’” he wrote before giving technology companies some guidance. “MAKE DEALS, and get them built!!! GREAT FOR THE U.S.A.” Trump did make a passing mention of the facilities Wednesday night at a rally inside a livestock expo center in Clemson, S.C. — and the crowd reacted with silence. He said if the companies that own data centers begin paying local school systems, governments or residents, “all of a sudden you’re going to see data centers are going to be so popular.” But such comments get overshadowed by his other favored topics, according to transcripts compiled by Factba.se. Husted, for instance, was very much on his mind in eastern North Carolina Tuesday as he stumped for his hand-picked GOP Senate candidate, Michael Whatley. “I’m studying his body. I’ve never studied the body of a man before — it’s not my thing. Nothing wrong with it of course, nothing. I always precede by saying nothing wrong, but it’s never been my thing, to be honest with you, but I looked at his ass. And then I looked at his legs and … I said, ‘His ass is, it’s like it’s like a pile of muscle,’” the president said to laughter. “Then I looked at his legs, and I said, ‘Man, his feet are big.’ Then I looked at his shoulders. And I tapped him on the shoulder, and it actually hurt my hand — it was like a piece of steel. And I said, ‘This guy’s a monster.’ And Jon Gruden told me that he was a violent tackler,” he said, referring to the former NFL head coach who played with Husted in college. Trump spent nearly 10 minutes at a Sunday rally in Port Huron, Mich., saying the news media did not understand that he was joking about evaluating Husted. “I’ve been living with this whole thing about the ass,” he said. “And, believe me, it’s of no interest to me — except to say that Jon Husten is one hell of an athlete.” He told former Rep. Rogers, the GOP Senate nominee in Michigan, that he would say nice things about his rear end, too, if it would guarantee a GOP seat pick-up. As voters fret about the cost of everyday life, he also on Sunday brought up the derrière of entertainer Minaj, who was at the Michigan rally: “By the way, I looked at one hell of a beautiful ass before: Nicki Minaj. That’s hard to miss. Stand up. That’s hard to miss.” But he did not plug data centers. Vice President JD Vance, on the other hand, focused on Husted’s Senate voting record during a Wednesday rally in Cincinnati. “Don’t worry, I’m not gonna talk about Jon Husted’s ass. I’m not gonna do it,” the former Ohio senator quipped of his appointed successor. Trump has seemed fixated on Husted’s build since Gruden told him about the senator’s days as a defensive back before an Oct. 3 rally in Vandalia, Ohio. He did make a pitch for data centers at the Vandalia rally and one on Oct. 12 in Youngstown. But that was to boost Husted, who pushed for a vote on the “Ratepayer Protection Act” before the Senate broke for its campaign recess. That measure, which was not advanced by the Senate, would require state regulators to consider adopting standards to ensure large data centers pay for needed grid upgrades. The White House responded to an email asking for comment about Trump’s rally mentions of the centers by providing a link to the Wednesday social media post, and provided a list of such projects and their economic benefits. Natalie Baldassarre, national press secretary for the Republican National Committee, said in a Thursday statement that “Republicans put up legislation to protect Americans from increased costs associate

artigo.texto: What is a BESS? BESS is a battery electric storage system. As the name suggests, the system stores power for future use. This past April, TVA and Tenaska, one of the largest privately held energy companies in the United States, signed a long-term energy storage agreement for a 225-megawatt/900-megawatt hour storage project in East Tennessee. The Bobwhite Energy Storage project in Hawkins County will generate an estimated $300 million investment as well as annual tax revenue for the county. It will be located in the Hawkins County Industrial Park. This project will not only provide economic value but will benefit the entire region by providing energy to the electric grid during high demand (such as weather extremes) or high-rate periods. The battery energy storage system stores energy when there is excess and distributes it when needed. BESS is quite different in operation from crypto-mining and data centers. Crypto-mining and data centers require vast amounts of energy and water on a 24/7 basis. As stated above, BESS draws energy (charges) when there is excess, in periods of low demand. BESS distributes energy (discharges) when there is a need, resulting in lower costs to local utilities and electric cooperatives that supply power to consumers. Care NET has invited Tenaska to hold an informational meeting for the public on Monday, Nov. 9 at 6 p.m. at Holston Electric Cooperative, located at 1200 West Main Street in Rogersville. Tenaska staff will present information about the Bobwhite project and battery energy storage systems. After the presentation, there will be an opportunity for questions. Care NET is a local environmental group with members in four East Tennessee counties: Hawkins, Hancock, Greene, and Grainger. The public is encouraged to attend. For more information, contact Care NET at carenetsc@gmail.com.

artigo.texto: On October 24, 2026, CnEVPost reported that CATL had said on Weibo that the 60-kWh Nio Firefly pack uses its Qilin battery line. Firefly had announced the pack the day before, rating it for up to 560 km on China’s CLTC test cycle. What the Qilin report adds The Qilin identification links the Firefly’s larger battery option to a CATL product line. Firefly’s October 23 announcement covers the 60-kWh capacity and its claimed performance and battery design; the Qilin identification came in CnEVPost’s account of CATL’s statement on October 24. How the 42-kWh and 60-kWh packs compare CnEVPost reports that the 42-kWh standard pack is supplied by Sunwoda and uses LFP cells. It identifies the 60-kWh pack as a CATL Qilin battery with NCM cells. Firefly describes the larger pack’s chemistry as ternary lithium. The two configurations’ stated ranges use the China Light-Duty Vehicle Test Cycle, or CLTC. The long-range version’s stated CLTC figure is 140 km higher, about 33% above the 420-km rating. Both capacity and chemistry change between the versions, so the range figures do not isolate the effect of chemistry. CLTC is a standardized test-cycle rating, not a measure of distance in everyday driving. Firefly’s claims about performance and battery design Firefly says the 60-kWh pack keeps the 42-kWh model’s acceleration and energy-consumption performance while adding thermal-protection measures. The company also describes its battery design as having an all-aluminum grid structure, cross-shaped crash beams and water-and-electrical isolation. It says it conducted 14 safety assessments that exceeded national-standard requirements. For battery longevity, Firefly lists five technologies for the 60-kWh pack: low-lithium-loss anodes, passivated cathodes, biomimetic self-repairing electrolyte, electrode-sheet microstructure design and adaptive expansion-force management. These are the company’s descriptions of its design and assessments.

artigo.texto: Mercedes-Benz's decision to develop its own batteries in-house is already paying big dividends, after the German brand announced that it has developed a pioneering new battery chemistry that will herald cheaper, faster-to-charge batteries that offer 30 per cent more range. Joining the ranks of Tesla, Volkswagen, Ford and Toyota, as well as leading EV giant BYD, Mercedes only opened its substantial eCampus back in 2024 and it was scientists working at the new R&D hub who were behind the new manganese-rich battery tech. No timescale was revealed for when the new Lithium-Manganese-Oxide battery (LMO) or the even more energy-packed Lithium-Nickel-Manganese-Oxide (LNMO) unitwill be rolled out, but the new lithium iron phosphate (LFP)-replacing tech is expected to be introduced within the next two years, ahead of Benz's own solid-state batteries that will launch towards the end of this decade. Read more - 'We won't be left wanting': Solid-state battery-powered cars with a potential 1500km of range likely for Australia - Major battery breakthrough confirmed - The Australian electric car battery breakthrough: Aussie smarts commercialise new battery that could result in a big change for the EVs we drive such as the Tesla Model Y, BYD Seal and more New batteries are greener and more sustainable The new batteries were unwrapped at the premium German brand's 140 Years of Innovation celebrations, where Mercedes scientists said that as well as being superior to the current LFP batteries available in cars like the new Mercedes CLA, its new LMO/LNMO pave the way for a greener, more sustainable future. That's because the manganese-rich chemistries are less reliant on cobalt, with the LNMO completely free of the in-demand element. Cobalt remains problematic for the car industry, with more than three-quarters of it sourced from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) from mines that are known to use unsafe working conditions and environmentally damaging extraction practices. The challenge for Benz, explained the scientists and battery engineers, was to attempt to replicate the same high energy density of its current LFP battery technology without cobalt. New batteries to beat BYD's LFP cells First to launch in the "near future" is the LMO tech, which blends its chemistry with Nickel-Manganese-Cobalt (NMC) oxide to maintain its energy density, but the big gains will come later with the completely cobalt-free LNMO tech, which costs less to produce than equivalent LFP cells. Crucially, when scaled up to the same size and weight of the equivalent LFP batteries, which have been popularised by BYD, the new tech offers far faster charging and, at least 30 per cent more range. Capable of working with far higher voltages, the new LMO batteries are also said to be safer than existing cells. Mercedes engineers wouldn't be drawn on figures, but if applied to the current 58kWh LFP battery that powers the Mercedes CLA, the new battery will raise the range of the base model from 447km to more than 580km with higher charging rates, potentially above 400kW (+200kW) for a sub-10-minute 10 to 80 per cent top-up. The same power packs are also tolerant of fast DC charging, retaining as much as 80 per cent of their original capacity after more than 1500 charge cycles, in research carried out on non-Benz batteries. Full technical details have not been revealed on either the LMO or LNMO batteries, nor exact timings of when they will be rolled out, but it's thought both will be replacements for the current LFP chemistry, rather than the brand's flagship NMC cells. The latter will then be superseded by the firm's most advanced solid-state batteries that are currently being developed in partnership with US-based Factorial and Taiwan's ProLogium for an introduction around 2029. When questioned by CarsGuide, Mercedes insiders said if the German brand was beaten to market in the race to introduce solid-state batteries, or other more advanced chemistries, by the likes of China's CATL it would favour the off-the-shelf solution, so long as it offered the "best price for the customer". Originally, many analysts had written off LMO and LNMO batteries as 'transitional chemistries' but, the prolonged delay in introducing solid-state and the high costs and ethical issues concerning sourcing cobalt have now seen CATL and Japan's Toyota also investing heavily in manganese-rich alternatives that will rival Benz's tech. Opened back in 2024 as part of a €14 billion ($A22b) investment in R&D, the new eCampus is a 10,000-square-metre facility that consists of three labs that are designed to fast-track new battery innovation with the ultimate aim of slashing the cost of a high-voltage battery by 30 per cent in the near future. The facility, located within Benz's Stuttgart R&D hub, is one giant building that enables scientists to develop the chemistry, build prototype cells to torture-test, and then evolve the concept, before scaling it up for full mass production.

artigo.texto: da Agência iNFRA O Fase (Fórum das Associações do Setor Elétrico), em nome de 21 entidades, pediu ao presidente Lula prioridade na regulamentação do Redata, regime que prevê incentivos fiscais para data centers. Em carta enviada na sexta-feira (16), as associações alertam que a demora na publicação do decreto pode comprometer o uso dos benefícios tributários. A suspensão de PIS/Pasep, Cofins e IPI, que concentra a maior parte dos incentivos, vence em 31 de dezembro de 2026. Segundo dados mencionados da Receita Federal, o benefício é estimado em R$ 5,2 bilhões neste ano. As entidades pedem regras para adesão ao regime e definição dos equipamentos contemplados. A Brasscom projeta US$ 92 bilhões em investimentos em data centers no Brasil até 2031. A demanda energética dessas instalações deve passar de 0,3 GW médio em 2026 para 5,7 GW médios em 2030, quase um terço do crescimento previsto do consumo elétrico nacional no período. Entre as fontes que podem abastecer essas instalações, a Abren (Associação Brasileira de Energia de Resíduos), uma das signatárias da carta, destaca a recuperação energética de resíduos sólidos. A fonte é prevista na lei como opção de energia de baixa emissão para atender às exigências do Redata e tem a vantagem de gerar eletricidade continuamente, sem depender das condições climáticas. Biomassa, biogás e biometano também são citados. Segundo a Abren, as usinas de recuperação energética operam com fator de capacidade entre 92% e 95%, característica que pode atender à demanda contínua dos data centers. A entidade também defende o conceito Wastai (Waste to Data), que propõe integrar, em um mesmo complexo, uma usina de recuperação energética de resíduos e um data center, aproveitando o calor gerado no tratamento do lixo para auxiliar no resfriamento dos servidores. O Brasil gera cerca de 192 mil toneladas de resíduos sólidos urbanos por dia e ainda não possui usina comercial de recuperação energética em operação, segundo levantamento da Abren. A associação estima potencial de 3,3 GW em 28 regiões metropolitanas, com 441 MW em projetos. A primeira usina da América Latina, em Barueri (SP), com capacidade de 20 MW, tem previsão de início de operação em 2027. Na avaliação do Fase, a demora na regulamentação pode adiar contratos de energia e investimentos em geração, armazenamento e redes. A carta também aponta indefinições sobre pedidos de conexão em análise no ONS (Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico) e cita cortes de cerca de 20% da geração eólica e solar potencial desde 2025, sobretudo no Nordeste, como outro desafio para o aproveitamento da energia disponível.

artigo.texto: Missoula Co. leaders hold Q&A on data center study MISSOULA, Mont. — Missoula County leaders hosted a question-and-answer session about new data center construction. The meeting followed the county’s approval of a one-year moratorium and the recent release of an impact study. After adopting the moratorium, county leaders had to prove that an emergency order was necessary to comply with state law. Climate Action Program manager Svein Newman said the study supports the moratorium. “The study concludes that data centers can have very real impacts to health safety and the environment, and therefore the moratorium was an appropriate step to take,” Newman said. County officials took questions and recommendations from the public, including a Missoula resident with prior experience building data centers. “The reason that developers are interested in areas that have water is because it’s cheaper for them, it’s not better for us,” the resident said. “I would recommend the county look at a 100% ban on evaporative cooling.” Further action depends on what the Montana Legislature decides during its upcoming session. State lawmakers at the meeting said discussions are already taking shape. “Many, many of these concerns that you’re bringing up that Missoula County is dealing with right now is something that’s happening at the state level too," said State Rep. Bob Carter (D-Missoula). "We’re probably a year away from anything actually going into effect; that’s why we have to have local control being able to handle these things and being out in front of it." The Missoula County Consolidated Land Use Board will host a meeting at 6 p.m. on Nov. 4 at the Sophie Moiese Room of the County Courthouse, and the Board of County Commissioners will host a meeting on Nov. 12 at 2 p.m. at the same location. For more details about the study, see NBC Montana's previous coverage.

artigo.texto: Reduzir as emissões através de soluções de captura, utilização e armazenamento de CO₂. A tecnologia de captura, utilização e armazenamento de CO₂ (CCUS) é uma solução potencial para reduzir as emissões de gases de efeito estufa, especialmente para indústrias em que é difícil reduzir as emissões, como energia térmica, cimento, aço, petróleo e gás e produtos químicos. Este foi o tema central do workshop "Tecnologia para captura, utilização e armazenamento de CO₂: Soluções para promover emissões líquidas zero no Vietnã", organizado pelo jornal Agricultura e Meio Ambiente, pelo Departamento de Mudanças Climáticas ( Ministério da Agricultura e Meio Ambiente ) e pelo Instituto de Petróleo do Vietnã, na manhã de 27 de outubro, em Hanói. Segundo o vice-ministro da Agricultura e do Meio Ambiente, Le Trong Yen, os estudos iniciais sobre o armazenamento de CO₂ em alto-mar, as soluções para a utilização de CO₂ na produção de produtos químicos, combustíveis e materiais de construção, bem como a combinação da captura de CO₂ com a produção de hidrogênio, estão abrindo novas vias de cooperação. O Vietnã concentra as emissões de CO₂ nos setores industrial e energético, e possui potencial para armazenar CO₂ em diversas bacias sedimentares e em campos de petróleo e gás offshore em declínio. A formação de um mercado de carbono, o desenvolvimento do financiamento verde e o aprimoramento da legislação relacionada às atividades de petróleo e gás também fornecem uma base para a pesquisa e implementação de CCUS (Captura, Utilização e Armazenamento de Carbono) no futuro. Entretanto, o Dr. Nguyen Thanh Tung, Vice-Diretor do Instituto de Petróleo do Vietnã, acredita que a inclusão de regulamentações relacionadas à captura, utilização e armazenamento de carbono na Lei do Petróleo alterada é um importante passo adiante, criando uma base legal para que o Vietnã implemente projetos na prática. “Para o armazenamento de CO₂, o potencial geológico não se traduz automaticamente na viabilidade de um projeto comercial. Cada local de armazenamento precisa ser totalmente avaliado e verificado quanto à capacidade de armazenamento, possibilidade de preenchimento e integridade do armazenamento, garantindo também o monitoramento de segurança a longo prazo. Um projeto só pode ser implementado em escala comercial quando um modelo de negócios viável for estabelecido, com fluxos de receita suficientemente estáveis para compensar o investimento, os custos operacionais e os riscos para o investidor”, afirmou o Dr. Nguyen Thanh Tung. Você também pode gostar Em relação às informações sobre a direção da gestão das emissões de carbono rumo à meta de emissões líquidas zero no Vietnã, o Dr. Luong Quang Huy, Chefe do Departamento de Gestão de Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa e Proteção da Camada de Ozônio (Agência de Mudanças Climáticas), afirmou que, durante o período de 2021-2025, as regulamentações do marco legal para o inventário obrigatório de gases de efeito estufa foram basicamente concluídas; o projeto piloto de intercâmbio de carbono foi implementado; e um sistema nacional de medição, relato e verificação (MRV) que garante a transparência foi estabelecido. Durante o período de 2026 a 2030, o foco será acelerar a redução das emissões e aperfeiçoar a estrutura operacional da bolsa de créditos de carbono. O Vietnã iniciará oficialmente as operações da bolsa de créditos de carbono em 2028, visando atingir o pico de emissões e realizar uma reestruturação abrangente e sincronizada de todo o setor energético. Em relação à viabilidade da implementação de CCUS no Vietnã, o presidente e CEO da QIS Global, Le Van Nghi, observou que a eficiência econômica continua sendo um grande desafio, uma vez que os custos de captura, transporte, uso ou armazenamento de CO₂ precisam ser equilibrados com a receita proveniente de produtos que consomem CO₂ e com o valor econômico da redução de emissões. Portanto, o roteiro de desenvolvimento do CCUS precisa ser construído em etapas, adaptado às condições específicas de cada indústria e instalação industrial. Inicialmente, deve-se priorizar projetos de escala adequada, com fontes favoráveis de captura de CO₂, opções claras de produção ou armazenamento e capacidade de mobilizar recursos. Com base nesses projetos iniciais, o Vietnã pode desenvolver gradualmente polos industriais que compartilhem infraestrutura para coleta, transporte e armazenamento de CO₂, otimizando custos e criando oportunidades para a participação de mais empresas. A longo prazo, o desenvolvimento de CCUS precisa estar vinculado à formação de um ecossistema tecnológico que atenda à meta de emissões líquidas zero. Isso deve incluir cooperação internacional, juntamente com transferência de tecnologia, treinamento de recursos humanos e maior participação de empresas vietnamitas no projeto, fabricação, integração, teste, operação e segurança do sistema. Você também pode gostar Entretanto, Darshil Korde, Diretor Geral Adjunto e Chefe de Desenvolvimento de Negócios Sustentáveis da ISSPL Limited, afirmou que, globalmente , estruturas legais bem desenvolvidas estão criando sinais claros de demanda. Para lidar com a questão do capital, são necessárias instituições financeiras intermediárias para conectar fundos orçamentários, mercados internacionais de títulos, crédito comercial, capital privado e fluxo de caixa do mercado de créditos de carbono. No seminário, delegados, especialistas e empresas concentraram-se em discutir as condições necessárias para a implementação da tecnologia CCUS no Vietname; esclarecer as dificuldades que precisam de ser superadas e sugerir direções para a cooperação e implementação de projetos adequadas às condições nacionais.
