artigo.texto: A CPFL Energia recusou, nos últimos 12 meses, pedidos de conexão de data centers que somam cerca de 8 gigawatts, oito vezes a demanda dos centros de dados em operação hoje no Brasil, e o presidente da empresa diz que o problema é a falta de linhas de transmissão. O número foi dado por Gustavo Estrella, presidente da CPFL, num painel da 17ª edição do Brazil Windpower, em São Paulo, nesta terça-feira (27), segundo reportagem da CNN Brasil. “Eu neguei cerca de 8 GW de capacidade de conexão de data centers por dificuldade de conexão”, afirmou o executivo. Ele mesmo reconheceu que parte desses pedidos tem caráter especulativo. Os 8 GW equivalem a oito vezes o que o país levou 16 anos para montar Segundo Estrella, o Brasil precisou de cerca de 16 anos para chegar a 1 GW de demanda de data centers. Os pedidos recusados pela distribuidora somam oito vezes esse volume, acumulado em apenas um ano de solicitações. - BC vê dívidas problemáticas no maior nível desde 2012, mas considera bancos resilientes - Tesouro recompra R$ 31,6 bilhões em dois dias e cancela leilões após disparada dos juros - Mercado reduz previsão da Selic para 11,75% em 2027 e inflação para 5,19% em 2026, enquanto Banco Central aponta crescimento menor do PIB no Boletim Focus - Dólar chega a superar R$ 5,60 após vitória de Lula e coloca Petrobras diante de pressão sobre gasolina e diesel, enquanto economistas avaliam risco de aumento nos postos Ao jornal Valor Econômico, ele situou as recusas nos últimos 12 meses e repetiu que existe um desafio real: separar a demanda que vai sair do papel daquela que é só reserva de lugar. Mesmo com o desconto da especulação, o tamanho dos pedidos mostra a pressão sobre a rede. Um pedido de 200 MW já não é raro, disse Estrella. A área da CPFL concentra cerca de 70% do consumo desses centros no país A CPFL atende boa parte do interior de São Paulo, onde ficam polos como Campinas. Segundo Estrella, as áreas de concessão do grupo concentram cerca de 70% do consumo de eletricidade dos data centers brasileiros. Ao Valor, ele falou numa faixa entre 60% e 70%. Em qualquer dos dois números, a empresa é a porta de entrada de quase toda a indústria de dados que já opera no país. Por isso, a recusa de pedidos pela CPFL não é um problema local. Quando a rede dela trava, o investidor perde a região onde já estão os clientes, as fibras ópticas e os outros centros de dados. Campinas sozinha teria 350 MW pedidos, e dois projetos já passam disso Para dar a dimensão das novas cargas, o executivo citou uma demanda de aproximadamente 350 megawatts para Campinas. É a referência que ele usou para mostrar quanto a cidade teria de receber de uma vez. Dois empreendimentos de 200 MW cada, porte que segundo ele já não é raro nesse mercado, somariam 400 MW. Só esse par já passaria da referência apresentada para toda a cidade. Na prática, cada novo pedido dessa escala exige subestação, linha nova e reforço de transformação. Nada disso fica pronto no tempo que o investidor de data center costuma aceitar esperar. Uma obra de transmissão leva em média sete anos para ficar pronta Estrella disse que o principal gargalo não está nos fios das ruas, mas na transmissão, que leva grandes blocos de energia até os centros de consumo. A distribuição também tem limites, mas pesa menos. Segundo ele, o prazo médio entre identificar a necessidade de expandir a rede e ver a obra funcionando é de sete anos. A indústria de data centers, avaliou, não vai esperar todo esse tempo. Para quem quer abrir um data center em 2027, sete anos é tempo demais. O descompasso é o centro do problema. A energia existe, muitas vezes sobrando no Nordeste, mas falta o caminho para levá-la até o lugar onde o investidor quer construir. O segundo obstáculo citado é o imposto, que depende do Redata O executivo apontou a carga tributária como o outro freio. Ao Valor, disse que esse ponto deve ser tratado com a regulamentação do Redata, o regime especial de tributação para serviços de data center. Ele também defendeu algum regime especial para que essa indústria não deixe o país por causa do gargalo de rede. O receio é perder projetos para outros mercados que conseguem ligar a carga mais depressa. A disputa por incentivo já mobiliza o setor. Em outubro, 32 entidades pediram incentivos para data centers e colocaram o gás natural no centro do debate sobre como abastecer essas cargas. O consumo dos centros deve crescer 40% neste ano e 100% em 2027 Mesmo com as recusas, a expectativa é de alta. Segundo Estrella, o consumo de data centers deve crescer 40% em 2026 e 100% em 2027, ainda que numa velocidade menor do que a desejada. É esse o recado do título da entrevista ao Valor: a demanda está vindo, mas mais devagar que o projetado. O freio, para ele, está na rede e no imposto, não na falta de interessados. O plano decenal do governo já incorporou essa curva. O PDE 2036 põe os data centers em 30 TWh e prevê 31,9 mil quilômetros de linhas novas. A CPFL quer que o dono do data center ajude a pagar a obra Além de cobrar velocidade, o executivo defendeu que os interessados em instalar os centros participem do financiamento da infraestrutura construída para atendê-los. Para ele, essa demanda precisa assumir parte do esforço financeiro. A proposta mexe numa regra sensível. Hoje, boa parte do custo das redes é diluída na conta de todos os consumidores, e não paga só por quem provocou a necessidade da obra. A gente volta, então, à pergunta de sempre: quem paga a obra? Se o investidor bancar uma fatia, a linha pode sair antes. Se não bancar, o risco é o consumidor comum pagar por uma estrutura feita para um projeto que, no fim, pode nem sair. As chamadas Temporadas de Acesso, previstas na Pnast, a Política Nacional de Acesso ao Sistema de Transmissão, organizam os pedidos à Rede Básica. artigo.texto: Why data centers are sparking debate over energy and water As AI drives rapid growth, communities are weighing big tech’s promises against concerns about electricity, water use and long-term costs DAVENPORT, Iowa (KWQC) - Every time we use artificial intelligence, somewhere, a data center is helping make it possible. But as these facilities grow, so do concerns about their impact on the environment. Thousands of computers working around the clock, processing information we use every day. But all that computing power comes with a cost, and it is not just financial. Data centers accounted for nearly 5% of all electricity used in the United States in 2024, according to the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. By 2030, that could climb to nearly 12% under one projection. If that additional electricity comes from fossil fuels, it also means more carbon emissions. And the electricity has to get there, potentially requiring new power plants and transmission infrastructure. Electricity is only half the conversation. There is also water Most data centers that are being built today are trying to conserve water because they see the controversies happening around water and they want to be responsible developers, Jean Hardy, associate director of the Quello Center at Michigan State University, said. In 2023, American data centers consumed an estimated 17 billion gallons of water directly. That is roughly three times as much as in 2014. Why so much? Computers generate heat, and some data centers rely on evaporating water to keep them cool. That water is not destroyed. It returns to the atmosphere. But it is no longer immediately available to the community that supplied it. Even data centers that do not consume water for cooling can have a water footprint. That’s because generating the electricity they use can also require water, sometimes at power plants many miles away. Other concerns include wastewater from certain cooling systems, pollution from backup generators, and the environmental cost of manufacturing computer equipment. Not every data center operates the same way. In Clinton, QTS said its proposed facility would use a closed-loop cooling system that would not consume water for cooling once operational. It is one example of how technology can reduce some environmental impacts — but does not necessarily eliminate all of them. As communities weigh the benefits against the costs, the question is not simply whether data centers use resources. It is how much they use, where those resources come from, and whether their impacts can be reduced. Clinton city leaders are considering new zoning regulations for data centers, including standards addressing environmental concerns. The company exploring the proposed data center in Clinton said it would pay for its own energy infrastructure and use a cooling system designed to minimize water consumption. Copyright 2026 KWQC. artigo.texto: Evergy says new data centers will pay more for electricity WICHITA, Kan. (KWCH) - Evergy said new data centers will pay more for electricity. The company sent out an email in hopes of answering some questions that customers have. Kansas previously passed a law saying that utilities can’t subsidize what these large scale users, like data centers, need by charging residential and small commercial customers more. Evergy, the main private electric company in Kansas, went further. It says it’s charging big users premium rates per kilawatt and extra fees, which amounts to about 20% more than ordinary commercial rates. It said none of that extra goes to Evergy. “The 20% premium, that higher rate, none of that stays with us. That all goes back to our existing companies and helps put downward pressure on rates,” explained an Evergy employee. “So for example, if we raise rates 10%, that 20% is going to help make it a 6% or 7% increase instead of 10%.” It said that the company has said no to dozens of data centers that could not satisfy requirements like collateral. artigo.texto: AURORA, Colo. — Aurora City Council shut down an effort to reconsider a data center moratorium amid boos and cries from Aurora residents at Monday night's meeting. The motion to suspend council rules failed 6-5 just before midnight. Council members Rob Andrews, Françoise Bergen, Curtis Gardner, Stephanie Hancock and Angela Lawson voted no. Without the seven votes needed to move forward under current council rules, council members were unable to discuss the moratorium. It’s the latest setback in a long fight over the 900,000-square-foot Trident data center. The proposed site is just a stone’s throw from homes in Aurora. Residents waited hours to make their plea to city leaders Monday night. “This has turned into an amazing, colossal fiasco. So I think it’s time to start reflecting what went wrong here? How did this all happen?” Aurora resident Ray Czaplewski said. Public comment extended well into the early morning hours on Tuesday. “The council has been quick and smart to take steps on the residential front to mitigate the water supply concerns, especially around lawn watering,” southeast Aurora resident Nathan Lyon said. “So why would you negate all that progress without proper regulations on mass water users like data centers and fracking operations?” Denver City Council member Stacie Gilmore, an outspoken critic of the Trident site, which sits on Denver's border, also addressed Aurora city leaders late Monday night. "Everyone has a moratorium on them because we have zero laws… to regulate them," she told Aurora City Council members. "I think we’re going to just have to keep pushing forward and find a a way to get it away from our homes," homeowner Michael Llanos said. Watch our coverage ahead of the meeting below: Over the summer, city council rejected a six-month moratorium and the mayor was the tie-breaking vote. Now, the mayor is coming out in support of an indefinite moratorium. Denver7 asked the mayor about the change in position. "Before I felt that well, it's OK, we can go ahead, we we don't need a moratorium," Coffman said. "We'll just go ahead with the regulations. Then when I saw Trident, I thought wow, if I don't want to see any more of those and I don't want to see from the time that we begin debate, and by the time that we enact these regulations, I don't want to see more data center applications come through that are subject under current law, current regulations, which are inadequate." After Monday night's vote to discuss the indefinite moratorium did not pass, Coffman said he will be bringing back the same motion with the same resolution at the next regular city council meeting. artigo.texto: New Data Center Regulations Previewed at Community Meeting New provisions to regulate data centers in East Lansing, including limits on noise, building size and water usage, were previewed at a community meeting on Thursday, Oct. 22. Previously, the city established a multi-department workgroup to propose data center regulations that are not addressed by current ordinances. A moratorium on data centers took effect in March 2026 and runs until March 17, 2027 to give the group time to develop regulations. While new rules were previewed at the meeting Thursday, a final draft ordinance is not likely to be presented to the City Council until December or later. During the moratorium window, the workgroup has consulted experts, analyzed environmental data and reviewed other communities’ data center regulations. No formal applications have been submitted yet to build data centers in East Lansing, according to Principal Planner Landon Bartley, though the city has received “quite a few inquiries” before and during the moratorium period. “I think there’s interest here,” Bartley said. “We just haven’t gotten any real, formal interest around data centers.” Data centers are facilities that house IT infrastructure used to process, store and distribute digital data. They generally fall into three categories: micro, standard and hyperscale, though sizes are not universally standardized. Because rapid data center expansion raises environmental and infrastructure concerns, the workgroup suggested scale limits: under 10,000 gross square feet for micro centers, under 250,000 square feet for standard centers and under 500,000 square feet for hyperscale centers. For comparison, a city staff member noted that the Meijer on Lake Lansing Road is 221,000 square feet. Residents at the meeting expressed concern over the gargantuan scale of hyperscale facilities, calling them too big for the community. Resource consumption was a primary focus at the forum. Because many data centers require vast amounts of water for cooling, the workgroup plans to suggest prohibiting evaporative cooling systems that burn through a great amount of water. Bartley noted that East Lansing and Meridian Township collectively consume 11.6 million gallons of water per day, while a single hyperscale data center can demand millions of gallons daily. “If we had someone saying, ‘I’m going to [use] five million gallons a day,’ that’s a huge amount of water compared to our overall use,” Bartley said. Regarding power usage, the group is proposing to require facilities to draw energy from the Lansing Board of Water and Light, or BWL. In response to audience concerns about data centers driving up local electricity rates, Mayor Erik Altmann noted that East Lansing currently lacks representation or leverage on the BWL board since losing its non-voting seat. Noise regulations were also introduced to counter the continuous low-frequency hums and vibrations produced by facility machinery. The workgroup recommends requiring operators to run independent noise studies before construction, after construction and annually thereafter, with the city selecting the testing firm. To ensure no damage is caused, the recommendation sets limits on two frequencies: one that measures the audible noise the human ear hears (dBA) and another that measures low frequencies like bass (dBC). The limits are measured based on the noise picked up at adjacent property lines. For audible noise, the proposed daytime limit is similar to the noise of a coffee maker brewing (55 dBA). The nighttime limit is similar to a quiet in-room air conditioner (45 dBA). For daytime low frequency limits, the committee recommends setting a limit similar to a heavy HVAC hum (65 dBC). At night, the proposed limit is comparable to a large commercial air conditioning unit running 100 feet away (55 dBC). Finding physical space for these facilities presents a major hurdle. The workgroup proposes restricting data centers to the city’s two industrial zones: Manufacturing and Office Industrial Park. Together, these zones comprise just eight parcels totaling 15 to 20 acres, two of which belong to Michigan State University. “The industrial locations make the most sense,” Bartley said. “They are quite limited, so we would have to execute a rezoning in my opinion if … any data center … wanted to go bigger.” Due to the limited industrial space, an applicant would have to obtain a Special Use Permit to rezone land, Bartley said. This would add an additional level of public input to the process and require developers to receive approval for the rezoning request from the City Council. Bartley clarified that the workgroup is working on text amendments to update the zoning language itself, rather than altering the physical zoning map. To protect the city if data center companies fail or cease operations, the workgroup recommends requiring applicants to submit comprehensive decommissioning plans backed by financial assurance in the form of construction, landscaping and decommissioning bonds. Finally, addressing transparency concerns, specifically how other cities like Saline have utilized Non-Disclosure Agreements, or NDAs, to fast-track data center projects in secret, the workgroup is reviewing legal options. They hope to establish boundaries regarding NDAs between applicants and elected or appointed City of East Lansing officials, staff, or contractors, pending official confirmation of municipality rights from the city attorney. The earliest an ordinance draft could be introduced to the City Council is Nov. 17, though Bartley expects the process to extend into late December or early 2027. Once introduced, the ordinance must pass through mandatory public hearings with the Planning Commission and City Council before adoption.

artigo.texto: Data centers are popping up all over the world at stunning speed. But not everyone is rolling out the welcome mat. Countries have long housed power-hungry data centers—the facilities packed with computing infrastructure that underpins the internet as we know it. But their numbers have exploded amid the global artificial intelligence race, which requires massive computing power. That has led to the spread of even bigger data centers around the world, including the more controversial “hyperscale” facilities used by tech giants. Data centers are popping up all over the world at stunning speed. But not everyone is rolling out the welcome mat. Countries have long housed power-hungry data centers—the facilities packed with computing infrastructure that underpins the internet as we know it. But their numbers have exploded amid the global artificial intelligence race, which requires massive computing power. That has led to the spread of even bigger data centers around the world, including the more controversial “hyperscale” facilities used by tech giants. Last year, data centers consumed more electricity than all but 10 countries, according to a United Nations University report, with even more to come. If data centers were their own country, BloombergNEF forecasted that they are set to gobble up so much energy by 2035 that they could rank among the top 5 countries in terms of electricity use. While governments have courted data centers due to their potential economic benefits, many local communities have resisted their development over concerns about the impact on jobs, energy bills, water usage, and the environment. From Chile to Scotland to Australia, opposition to the massive facilities has erupted around the entire world. “It’s a complicated moment,” said Boris Gamazaychikov, co-founder of the Sustainable AI Group, a research firm that focuses on AI’s environmental impacts. “The space is really polarized.” As data centers proliferate, Foreign Policy looked at what their global footprint looks like right now and how it might evolve in the coming years. To grasp the full scale and scope of these facilities’ global footprint, it’s important to first establish that it’s only the beginning of the boom. The world is still in the early stages of deploying data centers and AI, and significant growth is expected, according to Ashish Sethia, the global head of commodities at BloombergNEF. Here is what we know: In 2024, data centers accounted for about 1.5 percent of global electricity consumption. But that share is set to more than double by 2030—which means that data centers would consume as much electricity as Japan does today, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA). For regions with big clusters of data centers, demand can be far more overwhelming. In some places, the facilities can account for as much as 25 or 30 percent of total electricity consumption—posing a big challenge for the local grid, said Siddharth Singh, an analyst at the IEA. “These data centers are coming up very, very quickly,” he said. About three quarters of the world’s data center capacity is concentrated in just three regions: the United States, China, and Western Europe, Singh said. The United States is the clear leader in the charge. With U.S. President Donald Trump’s ambitions of AI supremacy, more than 1,500 data centers are now in development, adding to the 3,000 that are already operational across the country. That expansion has been largely powered by natural gas: To secure more energy, and fast, many tech giants have turned away from the electric grid and instead resorted to building their own on-site natural gas plants. Yet the Trump administration’s push for a rapid data center buildout has faced fierce bipartisan backlash, and at least 15 states have weighed moratoriums. Trump has dismissed data center critics and said that they are playing into the interests of Beijing. Chinese President Xi Jinping “will take every data center that we don’t want,” Trump told reporters last month. “He would love to have every single one, because you know why? They’re smart.” China is indeed going all-in on data center construction in its bid for AI dominance, although it still lags behind the United States. Beijing’s operational data center computing capacity is still less than half of Washington’s, according to SemiAnalysis, a research firm. But Beijing has some key advantages in ensuring a swift expansion. Unlike the United States, public pushback is rare, and Chinese companies can build quickly. The country also has cheap land and abundant energy, with coal currently fueling the bulk of the country’s data center electricity supply, according to the IEA. The bigger constraints that Beijing faces are accessing advanced chips and the high-end IT equipment going into data centers, said Thomas Spencer, an analyst at the IEA. (U.S. export bans have limited Beijing’s access to powerful AI chips.) Western Europe, Japan, and South Korea also have sizable data center markets. But those booms have come with their own strains: Many of these advanced economies are grappling with stagnant electricity demand and older electricity networks, and community pushback has been forceful. Ireland, for example, developed so many data centers that they sucked up more energy than all the country’s urban homes combined—ultimately forcing the government to bar new data center construction. And across Europe, public backlash has delayed or canceled roughly $42 billion in data center investments. “There’s a combination of social pushback and infrastructural bottlenecks, which holds across developed markets as a sort of general trend,” Spencer said. With so much of the world’s data center capacity concentrated in just a handful of countries, emerging market economies are eager to attract data centers and see their own ecosystems grow. artigo.texto: Two clean energy companies, Vara Energia Ltd and HydroThermIA Inc. of Canada, have presented a technical and commercial framework to the Federal Government aimed at unlocking Nigeria’s estimated $3bn annual carbon finance potential. The proposal was presented during a technical session in Abuja with officials of the Mitigation Division of the Department of Climate Change at the Federal Ministry of Environment. In a statement issued by Vara Energia’s chief executive officer, Segun Aikulola, the companies said the framework was designed to support industrial decarbonisation, clean hydrogen production and the development of Nigeria’s carbon market. The initiative, according to the statement, aligns with the Federal Government’s climate commitments and the National Carbon Market Framework. The companies said the proposal builds on discussions at the National Green Growth Dialogue, organised by the Nigerian Economic Summit Group (NESG) in collaboration with the Federal Ministry of Budget and Economic Planning under the theme, “From Commitments to Green Growth”. They also cited the government’s climate governance structures and emissions-reduction commitments as opportunities for developing carbon finance and clean energy projects. Under the proposed framework, the companies plan to deploy containerised technologies at industrial sites to address emissions from hard-to-abate sectors, including oil and gas operations. The proposed systems would capture gas currently being flared and convert it into hydrogen and electricity, potentially reducing emissions while providing an alternative source of energy for industrial operations. The framework also includes modular wastewater treatment systems integrated with hydrogen production, which the companies said could help industrial facilities secure water supplies and access lower-emission energy on-site. Speaking on the proposal, Vara Energia’s executive director of commercial and business development, Ochonogor Uche Zoe, said the initiative could reduce industrial carbon emissions while creating alternative revenue opportunities for Nigeria. He also stressed the importance of local technical integration and domestic manufacturing, saying Nigerian engineers should play a leading role in developing the clean energy sector. The assistant director and head of the Mitigation Division at the Department of Climate Change, Dr Asmau Jibril, said the partnership aligned with the government’s climate objectives and the National Green Growth Dialogue. According to the companies, the proposed technologies could reduce operating costs for heavy industries and upstream oil and gas operators by lowering dependence on diesel and unreliable grid electricity. Vara Energia’s deputy chief executive officer, Victor Ntofon, said the initiative could attract foreign exchange through verified carbon credit revenues, create jobs and improve access to international climate finance, including green climate funds. The companies also projected that the development of domestic clean hydrogen production could position Nigeria to supply hydrogen and ammonia to regional and international markets. They called on the Presidency, the National Council on Climate Change and the Federal Ministry of Environment to support the proposed framework, while urging manufacturers and energy companies to explore participation in the initiative. The companies said they remained committed to supporting Nigeria’s industrial decarbonisation objectives through technology deployment, local capacity development and investment in cleaner energy systems. artigo.texto: CATL told investors it will start small-batch pilot production of solid-state cells in 2027, maintaining that its chemistry leads the industry, while its chairman warned the technology remains at readiness level 4 of 9. CATL will begin pilot production of solid-state batteries in 2027, the company told investors in a recent reply. The world’s largest EV battery manufacturer says it continues to invest in the technology and considers its approach industry-leading. The company expects initial penetration around 1% with energy density near 500 Wh/kg. CATL has assigned roughly 1,000 engineers to the project and produced 20 Ah sulfide samples. Pilot lines will start in 2027, though CATL describes the output as small batches because high demand will keep utilization rates elevated even as new capacity comes online. CATL first dismissed the solid-state push. CEO Robin Zeng pointed to a decade of research and urged adoption of sodium-ion and semi-solid cells instead. The company reversed course, setting the 2027 target and backing it with expanded engineering resources. In October 2025, CATL confirmed the 2027 window but warned that scale remains limited. Drones and humanoid robots will receive the cells before mass-market electric vehicles. Chief Scientist Wu Kai rated production readiness at 4 out of 9, predicting an 8 by 2027. At this year’s Summer Davos in Dalian, Chairman Zeng Yuqun said the technology has not advanced beyond level 4, where level 9 represents full mass production. He added that reliability, supply chains, and market acceptance matter as much as the chemistry itself. Rival startups are moving faster by skipping liquid electrolytes entirely. Eve Energy has started producing 10 Ah sulfide cells at 300 Wh/kg for drones and robots. Sunwoda offers a 400 Wh/kg polymer cell and a 520 Wh/kg prototype, also targeting 2027. Chery promises vehicles with 600 Wh/kg cells that same year, while Toyota aims to use the technology in premium Lexus models priced above liquid-electrolyte equivalents. China is drafting the world’s first regulatory framework for solid-state batteries. The initial standard separates hybrid cells containing about 5% liquid electrolyte and 95% solid electrolyte from true solid-state designs. CATL once rejected the hybrid solid-liquid approach as impractical but now embraces it as a bridge technology. Beijing’s five-year plan targets 2030 for initial mass-scale production of solid-state batteries in everyday electric vehicles. That timeline supports CATL’s cautious stance on widespread adoption. artigo.texto: Data center moratorium extended in city of Charlotte: What to know City council votes to extend moratorium for nearly 1 year CHARLOTTE, N.C. (WBTV) - City council members on Monday voted to extend the data center moratorium for the city of Charlotte for nearly one year. On Monday, Oct. 26, the Charlotte City Council voted to adopt a measure that extends the city’s data center moratorium until Oct. 18, 2027. In June this year, the city council approved a 150-day data center moratorium amid growing concerns nationwide about data centers’ impact on the environment, resources, and community. The initial 150-day data center moratorium for the city of Charlotte was slated to expire on Nov. 5, 2026. The moratorium’s end date has been pushed back nearly a year, however, following a unanimous vote at a council meeting on Monday. The language in the newly-adopted moratorium is similar to the previous moratorium, which temporarily pauses the acceptance, processing and approval of applications for new data center projects within city limits. The moratorium will give city leaders time to evaluate existing ordinances, consider new ordinances, and determine best practices related to data center development, according to the city. Under the initial moratorium that took effect on June 8, data center projects that had already been approved would not be impacted by the city’s moratorium. Communities across the United States have been outspoken against data centers over the past few years, and more potently over the past few months. Residents point to a variety of concerns about issues of polluted water, centers’ energy and water usage, noise pollution, and the possibility of chemical leaks. ---> Related: How data centers shift landscape of rural communities Action NC and local climate groups said earlier this year that U.S. communities have seen a strain on infrastructure and an impact on the quality of life due to data centers. Prior to the initial moratorium enactment in June, Action NC specifically pointed to the proposed Powerhouse Charlotte development, which would span five buildings across 122 acres. The site could use 300-400 megawatts of electricity -- enough power for about 300,000 homes -- according to advocates. Another proposed data center in east Charlotte drew concern from neighbors, who do not believe there are enough policies in place to address possible harms. “I hope the council would do the right thing and go at least another year because, as we found on the task force, there is an enormous, enormous amount of work that still needs to be done,” said Cristopher Scalise, who served on a city task force regarding data centers. “We’re not ready to move forward as a city on this issue.” ---> See more: Charlotte residents urge city to extend data center construction pause Data centers have been around for years, but are becoming more prevalent as companies look to expand and rely more on artificial intelligence. The Donald Trump administration maintains that the U.S. must keep its lead over China when it comes to AI advancement, and has frequently dismissed AI concerns. Opponents across the U.S. argue that there is not enough AI regulation, and that the technology could have serious impacts on jobs, infrastructure, the environment, and humanity. artigo.texto: Governo lança leilões com foco no armazenamento de energia Os municípios deverão colher 30% das receitas do leilão de armazenamento autónomo e 70% das receitas do leilão de capacidade sobrante. O Governo lançou novos leilões de capacidade com foco no armazenamento, informa o Ministério do Ambiente e Energia, através de um comunicado. Estão a concurso um total de 1.050 MVA, na sua maioria destinados à ligação de projetos de armazenamento autónomos. Escolha o ECO como fonte preferida no Google O pontapé de saída estava marcado para setembro, mas foi a 22 de outubro que, num despacho publicado em Diário da República e assinado pelo secretário de Estado da Energia, Jean Barroca (na foto), foram lançados os dois concursos anunciados pela ministra da tutela, Maria Graça Carvalho, no passado mês de maio, numa conferência do ECO/Capital Verde. Estão agora a leilão 300 megavolt-ampére (MVA) para centros eletroprodutores que utilizem fontes de energia renovável, associados a instalações de armazenamento na mesma localização. Estas instalações de armazenamento devem ter uma potência mínima correspondente a 20% da capacidade de injeção atribuída e capacidade de armazenamento suficiente para assegurar uma duração mínima de quatro horas à potência máxima de injeção. Em paralelo, abriu o concurso para atribuição de títulos de reserva de capacidade de injeção na rede destinados à instalação, construção, exploração e operação de instalações de armazenamento autónomo de eletricidade. O procedimento abrange uma capacidade máxima global de 750 MVA, distribuída por diferentes localizações. Estas instalações devem dispor de potência instalada correspondente a, pelo menos, 100% da capacidade de injeção e de carregamento atribuída, bem como assegurar uma duração mínima de armazenamento de quatro horas à potência máxima de injeção. Ambos os procedimentos vão decorrer através de leilão eletrónico, aberto a todos os interessados que preencham os requisitos definidos nas respetivas peças, compreendendo as fases de qualificação, licitação e atribuição. Estes procedimentos preveem que para os municípios fiquem reservadas 30% das receitas do leilão de armazenamento autónomo e 70% das receitas do leilão de capacidade sobrante, a que acrescem ainda as compensações anuais pagas pelos titulares dos projetos. “O claro reforço dos benefícios para as comunidades que acolhem estes projetos reconhece não só o seu contributo para o sucesso dos mesmos, como recompensa o seu apoio e envolvimento”, lê-se na mesma comunicação. De acordo com o Governo, estes são os primeiros procedimentos concorrenciais para atribuição de capacidade de ligação à rede lançados desde 2021. “Estes leilões dão um novo impulso ao armazenamento em Portugal e a uma transição energética que combina eletricidade mais acessível com a valorização das comunidades e do uso do solo”, afirma a ministra do Ambiente e Energia, citada no comunicado. A Estratégia Nacional de Armazenamento de Energia, recentemente submetida a consulta pública, aponta para que o país atinja três gigawatts de armazenamento em baterias até 2030. artigo.texto: Gaispi aprova proposta de data center de R$ 375 milhões para IA Projeto da EAF prevê infraestrutura para aplicações governamentais, com operação pela Telebras, e segue ao Conselho Diretor da Anatel. O Gaispi, grupo da Anatel presidido pelo conselheiro Edson Holanda e que supervisiona o cumprimento de obrigações do 5G, também aprovou nesta terça-feira, 27 de outubro, a proposta da Entidade Administradora da Faixa de 3,5 GHz (EAF) para implantar um data center preparado para aplicações de inteligência artificial, com orçamento estimado de R$ 375 milhões. O projeto será submetido ao Conselho Diretor da Anatel e prevê utilizar recursos remanescentes do leilão do 5G para atender órgãos e instituições federais. Segundo a proposta, a infraestrutura deverá permitir o processamento de dados sensíveis, o treinamento e a inferência de modelos de IA e a hospedagem de serviços governamentais críticos. O arranjo recomendado é de titularidade da União e operação pela Telebras, com implantação a cargo da EAF. O prazo pretendido para implantação é de 12 meses, condicionado à disponibilidade de energia, ao licenciamento e aos prazos de fabricação e integração dos equipamentos. Dois módulos e 48 GPUs O cenário de referência prevê terreno de aproximadamente 5 mil metros quadrados e dois módulos externos. O primeiro será dedicado à infraestrutura de IA; o segundo, à infraestrutura física para serviços tradicionais de tecnologia da informação e colocalização. O módulo de IA contempla 20 racks de 42U, seis servidores com um total de 48 GPUs, nove servidores CPU, armazenamento all-flash e armazenamento de objetos. Já o módulo tradicional comportaria até dez racks de colocalização, sem aquisição de servidores na etapa inicial. A arquitetura prevê alimentação elétrica redundante, geração de emergência, resfriamento líquido no módulo de IA e conectividade redundante. A estimativa de carga inicial é de 2 MW para o módulo de IA, sendo 1 MW comissionado e 1 MW de reserva. Telebras na operação O grupo técnico recomenda que o data center seja estruturado como infraestrutura pública vinculada aos serviços e sistemas governamentais, em modelo igual ao da Rede Privativa de Comunicação da Administração Pública Federal. Ou seja, a titularidade será da União e a operação ficará a cargo da Telebras. A atuação da EAF ficará restrita à implantação. A análise financeira considera R$ 3,69 bilhões sob responsabilidade da EAF no fechamento do segundo trimestre de 2026. Desse total, propõe reservar aproximadamente R$ 2 bilhões para concluir os projetos originais do edital, incluindo margem de segurança de 10%. Com essa reserva, a disponibilidade estimada para projetos adicionais seria de R$ 1,69 bilhão. O data center consumiria R$ 375 milhões, restando cerca de R$ 1,32 bilhão que vão para a distribuição de conversores de TV 3.0.

artigo.texto: Australian startup MP Space raised an AUD $23M ($16.1M) seed round to expand its satellite battery manufacturing capacity, and begin building other pieces of satellite power systems, the company announced on Monday. Blackbird VC led the round, which included additional participation from Seraphim Space, Systemiq Capital, Speedinvest, and MFV Partners. Meet MP: MP Space was cofounded in 2024 by two ex-Tesla engineers—CEO Jay Manley and CCO Sam Paterson—with the aim of manufacturing low-cost, high-performing power systems for space applications. Manley explained that the company is trying to provide a new option to satellite operators who currently only have two choices: buying batteries and power systems from an expensive, slow-moving supply chain, or building them in-house. “We’re kind of becoming this third option,” Manley told Payload. “I can sell this product…about a fifth to a third below the market average while still making a profit, which basically brings it in line—or below—the cost to develop [batteries] in-house.” The market seems to be responding well to the pitch. MP Space’s batteries launched for the first time last week with an undisclosed customer on SpaceX’s Bandwagon-5 mission, and already the company has orders to support 500+ spacecraft. To meet this demand, MP Space plans grow its manufacturing capacity and engineering team at its facility in Sydney, Australia. The goal, according to Manley, is to be able to produce “5,000 space widgets per year, by the end of next year.” Power training: MP Space will also use the new funds to grow its product line beyond small-sat batteries. The company aims to produce low-cost products for sat-power parts between the solar panels and the payload—including maximum power point trackers and chargers, power-conditioning and distribution units, and solar-array drive assemblies. The company is also looking ahead to products that can support larger, more power hungry satellites, since power demands are increasing as the industry prepares for SpaceX Starship to come online. Today, the company’s two batteries both weigh in at under 5 kg, but Manley told Payload power products for Starship will need to be ~10x bigger and more powerful. “We’re trying to go engineer a power backbone that would bring Starlink satellite-unit economics to everyone who’s not Starlink,” Manley said.

The Mayor and City Council moved to temporarily halt new data center proposals inside city limits after residents packed a City Council meeting Tuesday night to oppose a large project planned for the Bennett Ranch Industrial Complex. The proposed project from Weitz and Co. would have spanned 3.4 million square feet near West Fifth North Street, with four three-story buildings covering roughly 19.5 acres each. Mountain Home Mayor Rich Sykes said data centers are not a permitted nor conditional use in any zone within the city. Residents who spoke out at Tuesday night’s meeting urged the city to block such projects going forward. “I want to advocate for us to add data centers on the prohibited list so that this is not something that moves forward in the future,” Mountain Home resident, Aaron Summers said. “The whole data center project has many problems, these facilities have many problems which i think cannot be of benefit to our community,” Mountain Home resident, Rob Monastario added. Mayor Sykes said Weitz and Company has not submitted a formal land use application or building permit for the proposed data center.

artigo.texto: Funding data centers is drying up, electricity demand skyrockets Capital markets are closing out AI data centers while 15 GW of power is on the waiting list. What is realistic? Published on October 26, 2026 Team IO+ selects and features the most important news stories on innovation and technology, carefully curated by our editors. The Dutch data center sector is facing a double crisis: funding is drying up, while the waiting list for power connections is skyrocketing to 15 GW—enough to supply power to every household in the Netherlands. Grid operators warn that a third of these requests come from data centers, but in most cases these are not concrete plans, but rather reservations made to keep options open. The combination of closed capital markets, uncertain demand, and an overloaded power grid threatens to turn the AI boom into a bust. AI-driven growth hits a wall In recent years, demand for data centers has skyrocketed: neoclouds, which specialize in AI computing power, had already contracted 420 MW of colocation capacity in Europe in the first half of 2026—nearly five times as much as in the same period of 2025. Two-thirds of this growth is taking place in the Scandinavian region, where cheap, renewable energy is available and average temperatures are low. Yet this expansion is not without risks. Real estate advisor CBRE warns that the rapid growth is putting pressure on power grids and the availability of green energy. Despite strong demand for AI computing power, the market remains skeptical about the financial viability of these projects. Elon Musk recently emphasized that most of the more than 200 neo-cloud providers will not survive on their own. Capital markets are closing the door on high-risk projects By 2026, the financing market for data centers will be virtually closed to companies without solid, independent revenue streams outside of AI infrastructure. Musk and venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya point out the risks of debt financing and the need for better capital structures. Jensen Huang of Nvidia confirms this: the lack of working capital is the biggest bottleneck for neoclouds, while the scale of capital required exceeds current financing options. The AI infrastructure market is facing delays in project pipelines, which could lead to underutilization of expensive hardware by 2027. Analysts such as Dauvin Peterson of 22V Research do see momentum in demand for AI infrastructure through 2027, but emphasize the risks of insufficient capital. 15 GW on the waiting list: how realistic are these plans? In the Netherlands, 15 GW of power requests are on the waiting list, a third of which come from data centers. This capacity is enough to supply power to nearly all 8.5 million Dutch households. However, most of the demand is not for concrete plans but rather a strategic reservation. Stijn Grove of the Dutch Data Center Association explained to the NOS that companies are applying early and in large numbers to secure a spot in line, with wait times of about ten years. Grid operators such as Alliander emphasize that the waiting list of 15,500 applicants in 2026 says little about actual implementation. The government is being called upon to make tough decisions about where and how many data centers will be allowed to be built, with clear conditions regarding energy, the environment, and water usage. Financial risks and unclear demand forecasts The financing crisis in the data center sector threatens to lead to a harsh restructuring. Musk warns that of the more than 200 neo-clouds, only a few will survive. CoreWeave has approximately $50 billion in debt, Nscale has $24 billion in committed purchases, and Amsterdam-based Nebius has $10 billion in convertible debt. Gartner expects that more than 80% of neo-clouds will no longer operate independently by 2030. The market for used GPUs could come under pressure if financially weak neoclouds are forced to sell assets, which could trigger a negative chain reaction. In 2027, the sector faces a crucial test: project delays and insufficient revenue could lead to “stranded compute,” where expensive hardware fails to deliver a sufficient return on investment. Grid operators must anticipate uncertainty Grid operators in the Netherlands, such as Alliander and TenneT, face an impossible task: investing in grid expansion while actual demand remains unclear. The costs of grid expansion are estimated at over €200 billion through 2040, which will significantly increase household energy bills in the coming years. The government is being called upon to establish clear and uniform conditions for data centers, but ultimate control must remain at the regional level. State Secretaries Willemijn Aerdts and Jo-Annes de Bat acknowledge the need for better management of the scarcity of space and electricity, but no concrete policy has been established yet. Alliander advocates for more efficient electricity consumption by data centers, for example through the use of batteries or by supplying residual heat to homes.

artigo.texto: 23/10/2026 O Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES) credenciou o primeiro sistema de armazenamento de energia em baterias (SAE) que atende às exigências de conteúdo local do leilão de reserva de capacidade (LRCap) previsto para 2 de dezembro. A solução é da brasileira You.On, primeira empresa a concluir o processo de análise de um equipamento completo e obter o código Finame para o certame. O equipamento aprovado é o You.On MOD A 7MW, com potência de 7 MW e capacidade de armazenamento de 25 megawatts-hora (MWh). Segundo a descrição apresentada ao BNDES, a solução utiliza baterias de fosfato de ferro-lítio (LFP), conversores de potência e sistema de gerenciamento de energia (EMS), além de contar com tecnologia grid-forming, exigida para os equipamentos do leilão. O credenciamento é feito pelo Sistema de Credenciamento de Fornecedores Informatizado (CFI), plataforma do BNDES utilizada para cadastrar fornecedores e produtos submetidos às regras do Finame. O banco analisa separadamente a empresa e o equipamento: primeiro verifica se a companhia atende aos requisitos para atuar como fabricante ou empresa de engenharia e, depois, se o sistema cumpre as regras de nacionalização. Para o leilão com conteúdo local, o BNDES estabeleceu um índice mínimo inicial de nacionalização de 15%, que considera o valor agregado de componentes nacionais, mão de obra e serviços de engenharia e integração realizados no Brasil. O código Finame comprova que o sistema foi credenciado, mas não equivale à habilitação de um empreendimento para participar do leilão, que cabe à Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) aprovar ou não, e considera outros critérios, incluindo potência mínima de 30 MW e capacidade de operação durante quatro horas consecutivas. A comprovação do BNDES será obrigatória para os vencedores do primeiro leilão, mesmo que utilizem recursos próprios ou financiamento de outros bancos. Pelo cronograma divulgado, os empreendedores terão até 7 de maio de 2027 para apresentar o certificado de conformidade de credenciamento, exigido para a contratação. No início de outubro, a You.On anunciou um acordo vinculante com a chinesa HyperStrong para atuar conjuntamente nos leilões de baterias previstos para 2 e 4 de dezembro. Na ocasião, a empresa informou que já havia sido credenciada como fornecedora pelo BNDES e avançava no processo para obter o código CFI de seus equipamentos. A parceria reúne a tecnologia de armazenamento da HyperStrong e a atuação da You.On em engenharia, integração de sistemas, conteúdo local e prestação de serviços no Brasil. Financiamento pelo Fundo Clima Mesmo com o credenciamento, um eventual financiamento do investimento pelo BNDES, por meio de recursos do Fundo Clima, dependerá de comprovações adicionais sobre o cumprimento das regras de conteúdo local. O banco de fomento prevê financiamento para sistemas de armazenamento, packs de baterias, inversores e sistemas de gerenciamento de energia. A participação do BNDES pode chegar a 100% dos itens financiáveis para operações enquadradas nas rotas 2, 3 ou 4 do regulamento de credenciamento, que preveem diferentes níveis de nacionalização das próprias baterias. Para a rota 1, que permite cumprir as exigências de conteúdo local com outros componentes do sistema, como inversores e equipamentos de controle, o limite é de 80%, com complementação por outra operação de crédito. Nas operações diretas com empresas privadas, o custo financeiro do Fundo Clima é de 6,5% ao ano, acrescido da remuneração do BNDES, a partir de 1,3% ao ano. O financiamento tem prazo de até 16 anos, incluindo carência de até seis anos. O valor mínimo é de R$ 20 milhões, com limite de R$ 1 bilhão por grupo econômico a cada período de 12 meses. Em setembro, o BNDES estimou que o financiamento dos projetos dos leilões de baterias poderia demandar até R$ 34 bilhões em recursos de linhas incentivadas, volume ainda condicionado à definição do orçamento de 2027. O Fundo Clima é a principal fonte de crédito incentivado para os empreendimentos, em conjunto com o BNDES Mais Inovação, mas os investidores vão precisar combinar diferentes fontes de financiamento. Lista de fornecedoras cresce Além do primeiro sistema completo credenciado, a lista de fornecedoras reconhecidas pelo BNDES aumentou de sete para nove empresas desde setembro. As novas integrantes são a Canadian, classificada pelo banco como empresa de engenharia, e a SecPower, cadastrada como fabricante. Elas se juntam a BYD, Gotion, Moura, TBEA, Trina, WEG e You.On. O credenciamento como fornecedor é a primeira etapa do processo e permite que a empresa apresente seus equipamentos à análise do BNDES. Segundo o banco, essa fase representa aproximadamente 15% do percurso necessário para a obtenção do código Finame de um sistema completo. Para as empresas de engenharia, como You.On, Canadian, Gotion e TBEA, o BNDES exige a participação de um parceiro com capacidade industrial para comprovar o atendimento aos requisitos de fabricação. Outra atualização é a inclusão da Reivax na relação de empresas que tiveram validado pelo BNDES o desenvolvimento de software e firmware de sistemas de gerenciamento de energia (EMS). A companhia se junta à Moura e à Automa, que já constavam da lista em setembro. O EMS funciona como o centro de comando do sistema de armazenamento, coordenando quando as baterias devem carregar ou descarregar, em qual potência e como a operação será executada pelos demais equipamentos. O BNDES separa duas partes do EMS: o hardware, que corresponde aos equipamentos físicos de controle, e o desenvolvimento do software e do firmware, programa instalado nos controladores para executar as funções necessárias à operação. Fonte: MegaWhat

Leilões de armazenamento Na sequência da publicação dos Despachos n.º 12924-B/2026 e n.º 12924-C/2026, que determinaram a abertura dos procedimentos concorrenciais para a atribuição de títulos de reserva de capacidade de injeção na Rede Elétrica de Serviço Público (“RESP”), destinados a (i) instalações de armazenamento autónomo de eletricidade e (ii) instalações de armazenamento colocalizado, foram publicadas, no sítio oficial da Direção-Geral de Energia e Geologia (“DGEG”), as peças dos dois procedimentos. Para consultar o programa do procedimento e o caderno de encargos relativos ao armazenamento autónomo, clique aqui; para consultar as peças relativas ao armazenamento colocalizado, clique aqui. B. Despacho n.º 12991-A/2026: Procedimentos de controlo prévio aplicáveis às instalações de armazenamento Foi publicado o Despacho n.º 12991-A/2026, de 23 de outubro (“Despacho 12991-A/2026”), que estabelece os procedimentos aplicáveis à obtenção dos títulos de controlo prévio necessários ao desenvolvimento e à exploração de instalações de armazenamento de energia elétrica (i.e. licença de produção e a licença de exploração ou, registo prévio e certificado de exploração, consoante a potência instalada), nos termos do artigo 11.º do Decreto-Lei n.º 15/2022, de 14 de janeiro. O novo Despacho, que revoga o Despacho n.º 1859/2025, estabelece, entre outros aspetos: - os elementos que devem instruir o pedido de licenciamento de instalações de armazenamento autónomo e de instalações de armazenamento colocalizado (cfr. artigos 3.º e 4.º do Despacho 12991-A/2026); - os elementos necessários ao registo prévio de instalações de armazenamento (cfr. artigo 5.º do mesmo diploma); e - a tramitação aplicável aos respetivos pedidos (cfr. artigo 8.º). Em regra, os procedimentos em curso à data da entrada em vigor do novo Despacho continuam a reger-se pelas normas aplicáveis à data da apresentação dos respetivos pedidos (cfr. artigo 10.º, n.º 1, do Despacho n.º 12991-A/2026). Contudo, aplica-se um regime transitório específico aos procedimentos em curso relativos a pedidos de alteração de centros eletroprodutores de fonte solar fotovoltaica para instalações de armazenamento autónomo, apresentados ao abrigo do artigo 4.º do Despacho n.º 1859/2025. Nestes casos, a DGEG deve notificar os requerentes, no prazo de 30 dias a contar da entrada em vigor do Despacho n.º 12991-A/2026, para que possam optar por (i) adaptar os respetivos pedidos ao novo regime ou (ii) renunciar aos mesmos. O Despacho n.º 12991-A/2026 entrou em vigor no dia 24 de outubro de 2026. Para mais informações sobre o mesmo, poderá consultá-lo aqui.

artigo.texto: County Supes Approved Major Use Permit in September By Jacob Aere / kpbs / October 22, 2026 San Diego County and developers of a solar and battery storage project in East County are facing a lawsuit alleging the project’s environmental review was insufficient. The suit was filed in San Diego Superior Court last week. It focuses on the Starlight Solar project near the town of Boulevard. The county Board of Supervisors approved a major use permit for the development for last month. The 588-acre project, which includes a solar farm and a 868 megawatt-hour battery energy storage system, has faced community pushback. The suit, filed Oct. 15 by a group calling itself the Back Country Community Alliance for Responsible Development, was brought under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). “This is CEQA action brought under the California Environmental Quality Act. And what we’re alleging is that the Environmental Impact Report that was prepared and certified by the county was inadequate,” said Jamie Hall, the group’s attorney. The lawsuit seeks to suspend all activity on the project “pending full compliance with CEQA and with the requirements of law.” A major concern the suit raises is the potential for lithium-battery fires. “My client doesn’t believe the county adequately analyzed those impacts, they didn’t analyze the evacuation routes sufficiently, they didn’t assess whether there was enough water for this particular project,” Hall said. Boulevard residents previously told KPBS they are concerned about the proximity of the battery storage containers to homes and a school. Fires producing toxic gas have broken out at battery storage facilities in Otay Mesa and Escondido in recent years. “We don’t think we’ll have a fire and if we do we have enough safeguards in place,” said Jim Whalen, the Starlight Solar project’s land use consultant. Whalen went on to say that the lawsuit lacks merit. “I don’t think the lawsuit has any merit, number one. We will be addressing the allegations going forward. We’re going to try and see if we can settle,” he said. He pointed out that projects like Starlight Solar help meet state and county green-energy mandates. “The county has to approve renewable energy projects at scale, that’s a given. ‘Where do they go,’ is the only question. We think we’ve done the best job fitting a large project into an area with the least number of people being affected,” Whalen said. A county spokesperson would not comment, citing the pending litigation.

artigo.texto: Resumo - SpaceX firmou financiamento de cerca de US$ 40 bi com entidade ligada à Apollo - Operação prevê arrendamento de GPUs e equipamentos para centros de dados - De acordo com documento enviado à SEC, o acordo com força obrigatória foi firmado no dia 24 de outubro - Contratos de arrendamento devem começar no 1º semestre de 2027, em lotes - SpaceX teve lucro líquido de US$ 4,4 bi no 3º trimestre de 2026 - Receita subiu 161% no ano, para US$ 14,6 bilhões no período A SpaceX, de Elon Musk, assinou com uma entidade administrada pela Apollo Global Management um compromisso de financiamento próximo de US$ 40 bilhões. O objetivo é bancar a compra de equipamentos voltados a data centers. Revelado nesta segunda-feira (26) em documento enviado à SEC (órgão americano com papel semelhante ao da CVM), o acordo contempla o aluguel de GPUs (unidades de processamento gráfico) e de itens relacionados. O documento entregue ao órgão regulador aponta que esse compromisso vinculante passou a valer em 24 de outubro. Na estrutura montada, cabe à entidade vinculada à Apollo adquirir os itens e repassá-los à SpaceX via aluguel, enquanto a empresa quita parcelas a cada trimestre por perto de cinco anos. Como será a entrega dos equipamentos Os equipamentos serão repassados em lotes, e para cada lote existirá um contrato de arrendamento específico. Espera-se que tais acordos comecem a vigorar já no primeiro semestre de 2027, cada um com duração que oscila entre 60 e 63 meses. De acordo com a empresa, haverá antecipação dos pagamentos feitos a cada trimestre. Cada parcela, via de regra, equivale à vigésima parte do valor financiado em cada lote. A isso se acrescentam os juros incidentes sobre o saldo devedor, apurados por uma taxa anual fixa que ainda não foi definida, e também custos adicionais. Ao longo de todo o período dos contratos, o montante de principal quitado deve atingir aproximadamente US$ 40 bilhões, na projeção da SpaceX. Esse número deixa de fora os juros e demais despesas. A finalização do acordo é esperada pela empresa ainda neste ano de 2026, caso certas condições venham a ser atendidas. Movimento vem após balanço forte A novidade chega logo depois de um trimestre forte. Na semana passada, em seu segundo balanço desde a oferta pública inicial (IPO), a SpaceX reportou, no terceiro trimestre de 2026, US$ 4,4 bilhões de lucro líquido. O lucro ajustado por ação ficou em US$ 0,35, acima dos US$ 0,13 que analistas compilados pela FactSet esperavam. A receita, por sua vez, avançou 161% na comparação anual e alcançou US$ 14,6 bilhões, ante projeção de US$ 12,87 bilhões levantada pela FactSet. Entre os segmentos, o de conectividade (onde está o Starlink, serviço de internet por satélite) encerrou o período com 13,6 milhões de assinantes e receita de US$ 5,2 bilhões. Em Espaço, o faturamento foi de US$ 1,77 bilhão, enquanto Inteligência Artificial rendeu US$ 7,56 bilhões. O capex (gastos de capital), por sua vez, saltou de US$ 6,9 bilhões há um ano para US$ 19,6 bilhões no trimestre.

artigo.texto: Experimentos de longa duração no interior paulista indicam que a recuperação de pastagens degradadas pode elevar a produtividade e aumentar o armazenamento de carbono no solo. A intensificação moderada — com correção da acidez, fertilizantes e quantidade equilibrada de animais — apresentou bons resultados sem exigir tecnologias inacessíveis. A pesquisa também desenvolveu formas mais simples e baratas de medir o carbono retido, o que pode facilitar o acesso de produtores ao mercado de créditos de carbono. Os estudos integram o projeto temático “Entendendo sistemas intensificados e integrados de produção: do mundo quântico à agricultura de baixa emissão de carbono”, apoiado pela Fapesp e coordenado por Ladislau Martin Neto, pesquisador da Embrapa Instrumentação. Os pesquisadores compararam desde pastagens degradadas, sem adubação e com pastejo contínuo, até sistemas com diferentes níveis de intervenção, incluindo áreas irrigadas, com altas doses de nitrogênio e maior concentração de animais. Em uma área de intensificação moderada, o carbono armazenado no primeiro metro de solo subiu de 102 para 162 toneladas por hectare entre 2011 e 2020. O aumento médio foi de aproximadamente duas toneladas por hectare ao ano em relação à pastagem degradada. Segundo Martin Neto, análises indicaram que uma parcela importante do carbono adicional veio da própria forrageira cultivada no local. A pesquisadora Patrícia Perondi Anchão Oliveira, líder do experimento, ressaltou que o modelo combina capins adaptados ao clima brasileiro com gado de origem indiana, como o nelore. Após mais de duas décadas de manejo, a pastagem apresentou 148 toneladas de carbono por hectare na forma de matéria orgânica associada aos minerais do solo, ante 92 toneladas na área degradada. A pesquisa mostra que é possível recuperar solos já convertidos para a pecuária e ampliar sua capacidade de armazenar carbono sem avançar sobre a vegetação nativa. Os resultados foram publicados na revista Geoderma e apontam a possibilidade de remunerar produtores pelo carbono adicional, desde que seja possível comprovar quanto foi incorporado e permanece no solo. Para investigar essa permanência, a equipe analisou as interações entre matéria orgânica e minerais. Parte da matéria orgânica pode ser decomposta por microrganismos e liberar carbono como CO₂; outra parte se associa a argilas e óxidos de ferro e alumínio, o que dificulta sua decomposição. Os pesquisadores usaram a espectrometria de massa de íons secundários (NanoSIMS), na Universidade Técnica de Munique, na Alemanha, com apoio da Fapesp e durante estágio de Lucas Raimundo Bento. A técnica produz mapas químicos em escala nanométrica. As análises mostraram que as manchas de matéria orgânica cobriam, no máximo, cerca de 3% da superfície mineral observada na camada superficial. Para Martin Neto, isso indica que a entrada de compostos orgânicos e a atividade dos microrganismos são decisivas e que ainda há superfície mineral disponível para novas associações. O manejo também favorece a fertilidade: na camada de até 5 centímetros, a capacidade de troca catiônica da pastagem bem manejada foi aproximadamente 250% superior à da degradada. Outro estudo, publicado em Soil & Tillage Research, comparou combinações de adubação nitrogenada, irrigação e lotação animal.

artigo.texto: Meta recorre ao mercado para financiar expansão de data centers Meta planeja captar até US$ 95 bilhões com emissão de ações; NVIDIA, AMD e Broadcom avaliam participar da oferta. A Meta anunciou, nesta segunda-feira, um plano para captar até US$ 95 bilhões no mercado acionário norte-americano, com o objetivo de financiar a expansão de sua infraestrutura de IA. A operação prevê ofertas públicas de aproximadamente US$ 35 bilhões e um programa adicional de venda de ações de até US$ 60 bilhões, previsto para começar após o início das negociações de uma nova classe de papéis, no primeiro trimestre de 2027. O financiamento ocorre em um período de ampliação dos investimentos da companhia em data centers, equipamentos de processamento e capacidade computacional. Para 2026, a controladora do Facebook, Instagram e WhatsApp projeta despesas de capital entre US$ 135 bilhões e US$ 145 bilhões, incluindo pagamentos de principal de arrendamentos financeiros. A primeira etapa da captação será composta por US$ 22,5 bilhões em ações ordinárias Classe A e aproximadamente US$ 12,5 bilhões em certificados de depósito representativos de ações preferenciais obrigatoriamente conversíveis. As ofertas foram lançadas simultaneamente, mas a conclusão de uma não depende da realização da outra. No caso das ações ordinárias, a Meta pretende utilizar contratos de venda futura (forward sale agreements) com instituições financeiras. A companhia não receberá inicialmente os recursos dessa parcela, que serão transferidos conforme a liquidação dos contratos, prevista para ocorrer até novembro de 2027. Fabricantes de chips avaliam participar da oferta NVIDIA, AMD e Broadcom manifestaram interesse em adquirir, conjuntamente, até US$ 5 bilhões em ações ordinárias Classe A da Meta, nas mesmas condições oferecidas aos demais investidores. A manifestação, porém, não constitui compromisso vinculante. As três fabricantes poderão adquirir quantidades diferentes das inicialmente indicadas ou desistir de participar da operação. As empresas fornecem semicondutores e tecnologias utilizadas em infraestrutura de IA. O comunicado não vincula a eventual participação na oferta à assinatura de novos contratos comerciais. Investimentos em data centers pressionam fluxo de caixa A intenção de financiamento acompanha a ampliação da infraestrutura computacional da Meta. Segundo a companhia, sua rede de data centers próprios está presente em 23 estados norte-americanos, enquanto quatro complexos de processamento, denominados superclusters, estão em construção, cada um com capacidade superior a 1 gigawatt. A empresa também prevê praticamente dobrar sua capacidade total de infraestrutura em 2026, na comparação com o ano anterior. Os investimentos contemplam equipamentos de processamento, desenvolvimento de chips próprios e medidas para reduzir o custo operacional das cargas de trabalho de IA. Os resultados financeiros do terceiro trimestre mostram os efeitos dessa expansão sobre a geração de caixa. Entre julho e setembro, a Meta registrou fluxo de caixa livre negativo de US$ 2,12 bilhões, ante resultado positivo de US$ 10,63 bilhões no mesmo período de 2025. Apesar do indicador trimestral, a companhia manteve fluxo de caixa livre positivo de aproximadamente US$ 11,05 bilhões no acumulado dos nove primeiros meses de 2026. Já o caixa gerado pelas atividades operacionais, antes dos desembolsos de investimento, alcançou cerca de US$ 97 bilhões no período. Ao final de setembro, a Meta possuía US$ 82,45 bilhões em caixa, equivalentes de caixa e aplicações financeiras, enquanto sua dívida de longo prazo somava US$ 80,92 bilhões. O relatório trimestral apresentado à Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) também detalha compromissos financeiros associados à infraestrutura. Entre eles estão contratos não canceláveis de aproximadamente US$ 454,52 bilhões, abrangendo principalmente serviços de nuvem, servidores, equipamentos de rede e fornecimento de energia para data centers. O documento registra ainda US$ 355,73 bilhões em obrigações de arrendamento cujos períodos contratuais ainda não começaram. Esses compromissos incluem instalações de processamento, infraestrutura energética e espaços de colocation, com início previsto entre 2026 e 2036. Os valores representam obrigações futuras, não despesas integralmente realizadas. Nova classe de ações preservará controle de Zuckerberg A segunda etapa do plano de financiamento prevê a criação de um programa de venda de ações Classe C diretamente no mercado, conhecido como at-the-market (ATM), com valor potencial de até US$ 60 bilhões. A operação deverá ocorrer após o início das negociações desses papéis, previsto para o primeiro trimestre de 2027. A Meta ressalvou que ainda não firmou os acordos necessários para implementar o programa e que não há garantia sobre seu lançamento ou o volume efetivamente comercializado. A nova Classe C foi aprovada pelo conselho de administração em outubro, com vigência prevista para janeiro de 2027. Os papéis não terão direito a voto, permitindo à companhia captar recursos, remunerar empregados e realizar eventuais aquisições sem alterar o poder político dos atuais acionistas. A medida preserva a estrutura de controle liderada pelo fundador e CEO Mark Zuckerberg. A Meta pretende distribuir uma ação Classe C para cada ação Classe A ou Classe B existente, em operação com efeito equivalente a um desdobramento acionário de dois para um. A empresa informou que pretende financiar sua expansão por meio da combinação de geração operacional de caixa, emissão de dívida, parcerias estratégicas e recursos provenientes do mercado acionário.

artigo.texto: BYD has reached a major milestone in commercial vehicle production, rolling out its 150,000th new energy commercial vehicle at its manufacturing facility in Huai’an, Jiangsu province, China. The milestone vehicle is the Q3 battery-electric semi-truck, highlighting the automaker’s growing ambitions in heavy-duty electric transport. The achievement comes as BYD shifts more attention toward electric trucks, particularly vehicles designed for long-distance freight operations. While the Chinese automaker is widely known for its electric passenger cars and battery technology, its commercial vehicle business is becoming an increasingly important part of its expansion strategy. According to CNEVPost, the milestone vehicle left the production line on October 9, marking 18 years of development in BYD’s commercial new energy vehicle business. The BYD Q3 is designed for demanding heavy-duty transport applications, combining a large battery pack, powerful electric motors and fast-charging capability. The electric semi-truck features a commercial-vehicle version of BYD’s Blade Battery technology, using lithium iron phosphate (LFP) chemistry. Its battery capacity is reported at up to 600 kWh, while the dual-motor powertrain delivers a peak output of 600 kW, equivalent to approximately 805 horsepower. That level of power makes the Q3 a notable entry in the growing market for battery-electric heavy-duty trucks. The truck is also reported to support a gross combined vehicle weight of approximately 108,000 pounds, or around 49 metric tons. With a fully charged battery, its reported range reaches approximately 325 kilometers (202 miles), although actual range will depend on payload, road conditions, weather and driving patterns. For operators running demanding freight routes, charging speed can be just as important as battery capacity. The Q3 supports dual-gun DC fast charging, with a reported charging time of around 30 minutes to increase the battery’s state of charge from 20% to 80%. These specifications are intended to help electric trucks handle intensive commercial operations while reducing dependence on diesel fuel. BYD Commercial EV Sales Continue to Grow BYD’s production milestone arrives as its commercial new energy vehicle sales show strong growth in 2026. The company sold 6,848 commercial NEVs in September, an increase of 113.33% compared with the same month in 2025. Sales during the first nine months of 2026 reached 53,032 vehicles, up 28.46% year over year. The figures are particularly notable because BYD’s overall new energy vehicle sales moved in the opposite direction during the same period. The automaker sold approximately 3.13 million passenger and commercial new energy vehicles in the first nine months of 2026, down 3.94% from a year earlier. This contrast suggests that commercial vehicles are becoming an important growth area for BYD as it looks beyond the highly competitive passenger EV market. However, the 150,000-vehicle milestone represents cumulative commercial NEV production, not the number of trucks produced in 2026 alone. BYD’s commercial vehicle portfolio includes multiple vehicle types and powertrains, rather than exclusively heavy-duty battery-electric trucks. BYD’s commercial vehicle business began with electric city buses before gradually expanding into other applications. The company started truck research and development in 2012, building a portfolio that now covers urban delivery vehicles, light-duty trucks, cold-chain logistics vehicles and heavy-duty trucks. Its commercial lineup includes both battery-electric and hybrid models. In 2025, production of BYD’s T5 light-duty truck reached 10,000 units, while the T4 mini truck was introduced for international markets. The expansion reflects a broader effort to apply BYD’s battery, electric motor and electronic control technologies to commercial transportation. Rather than relying solely on passenger cars, the company is targeting sectors where electrification could help reduce fuel costs and emissions across large vehicle fleets. Heavy-duty trucks are a particularly important opportunity, although their adoption depends on factors such as purchase prices, charging infrastructure, battery capacity, vehicle utilization and the availability of suitable charging stops along freight routes. International Expansion Becomes a Bigger Priority BYD says its commercial vehicle business has expanded into more than 70 countries and regions. Trucks are increasingly central to its international growth plans as the company seeks opportunities beyond its established electric bus business. At IAA Transportation 2026 in Hanover, Germany, BYD presented an integrated zero-carbon logistics solution combining commercial vehicles with charging infrastructure, fleet management and maintenance services. The strategy goes beyond selling electric trucks. Commercial operators need dependable charging access, vehicle servicing and fleet-management systems to keep vehicles working efficiently and control operating costs. By combining vehicles with supporting services, BYD aims to offer fleet operators a more complete electrification package. This could become especially important for businesses managing multiple trucks across regional distribution networks and long-distance routes. International expansion will also require BYD to address local regulations, service coverage, charging standards and the specific operating requirements of different markets.

artigo.texto: Sioux County approves strict new rules for future data centers ORANGE CITY, Iowa (KTIV) — Leaders in Sioux County have approved changes to county ordinances that impact the future of data centers in the county. On Tuesday morning, the Sioux County Board of Supervisors voted 4-1 to approve the third and final reading of an amendment to County Ordinance One. The amendment adds strict regulations for data centers in unincorporated areas, including limiting the size of data centers and creating standards on where they can be built. It also addresses water usage, noise and light pollution, and requires a decommissioning plan in case a data center is abandoned after becoming obsolete. Officials note the vote was only on a change to the ordinance, and not on the creation of any data center. Want to get the latest news and weather from Siouxland’s News Source?
