artigo.texto: A Galaxy Digital Inc. (NASDAQ:GLXY) reportou um lucro líquido de US$ 323 milhões para o terceiro trimestre encerrado em 30 de setembro de 2026, em comparação com um prejuízo líquido de US$ 85 milhões no trimestre anterior, devido ao aumento da receita e dos lucros ajustados provenientes de suas operações de data center. A empresa de infraestrutura de ativos digitais e data centers registrou EBITDA ajustado de US$ 455 milhões e lucro bruto ajustado de US$ 569 milhões no trimestre. O lucro diluído por ação atingiu US$ 0,66, enquanto o lucro ajustado por ação totalizou US$ 0,83. A Galaxy também reportou crescimento em seu balanço patrimonial, expandiu seu portfólio de desenvolvimento de data centers e anunciou uma nova autorização de recompra de ações no valor de US$ 200 milhões, após a conclusão de um programa anterior de recompra. Galaxy Digital volta a apresentar lucro trimestral A Galaxy Digital reportou um lucro líquido de US$ 323 milhões no terceiro trimestre, revertendo o prejuízo líquido de US$ 85 milhões registrado no segundo trimestre de 2026. O EBITDA ajustado totalizou US$ 455 milhões, enquanto o lucro bruto ajustado atingiu US$ 569 milhões. A empresa reportou lucro diluído por ação de US$ 0,66 e lucro ajustado por ação de US$ 0,83. O total de ativos aumentou 51% em relação ao trimestre anterior, atingindo US$ 16,4 bilhões em 30 de setembro de 2026. O patrimônio líquido total era de US$ 3,0 bilhões ao final do período analisado. Os resultados trimestrais refletiram as contribuições dos negócios de data center e ativos digitais da Galaxy, juntamente com mudanças na posição financeira da empresa. O segmento de data centers reporta lucros ajustados mais altos O segmento de Data Centers da Galaxy registrou lucro bruto ajustado de US$ 79 milhões durante o terceiro trimestre, em comparação com US$ 20 milhões no trimestre anterior. O EBITDA ajustado do segmento aumentou para US$ 69 milhões, ante US$ 11 milhões no segundo trimestre. Os resultados incluíram o primeiro trimestre completo de receita associada ao arrendamento da Fase I do Helios I. Nos termos do acordo, a Galaxy forneceu 133 megawatts de carga crítica de tecnologia da informação para a CoreWeave. A contribuição desse arrendamento foi um fator no aumento do lucro bruto ajustado e do EBITDA ajustado reportado pelo segmento de Data Centers. Galaxy garante financiamento de US$ 3,5 bilhões para expansão do Helios A Galaxy concluiu uma oferta de US$ 3,5 bilhões em títulos seniores garantidos para financiar a construção da Fase II do projeto Helios I. A empresa prevê que as entregas dos data centers associados à segunda fase comecem no segundo trimestre de 2027. O financiamento apoia a próxima etapa de desenvolvimento do centro de dados Helios, após a entrega da capacidade na fase inicial. A Galaxy também informou que sua capacidade total de geração de energia bruta agora ultrapassa 5,7 gigawatts. O número de projetos em desenvolvimento representa a capacidade de desenvolvimento divulgada pela empresa e deve ser diferenciado da infraestrutura que já foi concluída ou colocada em operação. O segmento de ativos digitais registra um crescimento de 9% no lucro bruto ajustado O segmento de Ativos Digitais da Galaxy reportou um lucro bruto ajustado de US$ 71 milhões no terceiro trimestre. O valor representou um aumento de 9% em comparação com o trimestre anterior. O total combinado de ativos sob gestão e ativos em risco atingiu US$ 10,4 bilhões, um aumento de 46% em relação ao trimestre anterior. Os números refletiram o crescimento dos ativos gerenciados ou suportados por meio de atividades de staking nas operações de ativos digitais da Galaxy. A empresa também anunciou um acordo com o objetivo de expandir seus serviços de infraestrutura de ativos digitais institucionais. Galaxy firma acordo plurianual de ativos digitais com o BNY A Galaxy firmou um acordo plurianual com o BNY para desenvolver infraestrutura de ativos digitais para mercados institucionais. O acordo inclui suporte para serviços de staking por meio da plataforma de Custódia de Ativos Digitais do BNY. O acordo tem como objetivo apoiar o acesso institucional à infraestrutura de ativos digitais e serviços relacionados. A Galaxy não divulgou o valor financeiro do acordo no comunicado fornecido. A parceria faz parte das atividades comerciais de ativos digitais da empresa, juntamente com a gestão de ativos e as operações de staking. Reservas em dinheiro, stablecoins e títulos do Tesouro atingem US$ 4,9 bilhões A Galaxy reportou possuir, em 30 de setembro de 2026, um total de US$ 4,9 bilhões em reservas combinadas de dinheiro, stablecoins e títulos do Tesouro dos EUA. O valor se compara aos US$ 2,5 bilhões registrados no final do segundo trimestre. O aumento representou um crescimento de aproximadamente 96% em relação ao trimestre anterior. A empresa também reportou ativos totais de US$ 16,4 bilhões e patrimônio líquido total de US$ 3,0 bilhões ao final do trimestre. Esses números fornecem informações sobre a situação financeira da Galaxy, à medida que a empresa continua desenvolvendo suas operações de data center e seus negócios de ativos digitais. Galaxy conclui programa de recompra de ações de US$ 200 milhões A Galaxy informou ter recomprado aproximadamente 9,8 milhões de ações durante 2026, no âmbito de um programa de recompra de ações de US$ 200 milhões. A empresa concluiu esse programa em 15 de outubro de 2026. Após a sua conclusão, o conselho de administração da Galaxy autorizou um novo programa de recompra de ações no valor de 200 milhões de dólares em 26 de outubro de 2026. A nova autorização permite à empresa realizar recompras adicionais de ações, sujeitas às suas decisões de alocação de capital e às condições aplicáveis. O comunicado não especificou o cronograma nem o volume de recompras no âmbito do programa recém-autorizado. Quais são os próximos desenvolvimentos para a Galaxy Digital? artigo.texto: Nuclear power plants were engineered to do one thing exceptionally well: generate electricity at a steady rate, around the clock. That design philosophy made sense for decades, but it is increasingly at odds with a grid that now shares space with solar and wind resources whose output rises and falls with the weather and the time of day. Researchers at the University of Central Florida’s Center for Advanced Turbomachinery and Energy Research (CATER) argue that thermal energy storage, or TES, could be the key to reconciling the two. In a study published in the Journal of Energy Resources Technology, Part A: Sustainable and Renewable Energy, the CATER team paired thermodynamic modeling with an economic analysis of how nuclear plants could operate in a shifting energy market. The paper, titled “Molten Salt Reactor Dispatch Optimization via Thermal Energy Storage: Coupled Thermodynamic Modeling and Rolling-Horizon Economic Analysis,” examines how a molten salt reactor equipped with TES could be dispatched more flexibly than conventional nuclear plants allow. The research team included doctoral research assistants Augusto Delavald Marques and Abhilash Prasad, postdoctoral scholar Shinjan Ghosh, associate professor Erik Fernandez, alumnus Marcel Otto, and CATER director Jayanta Kapat. The core problem the researchers set out to address is a mismatch between reactor design and grid demand. “Nuclear power needs to be flexible while nuclear reactors operate at a steady pace because grid demand varies throughout the day,” Marques says. “This is a challenge for power plants because they must adjust quickly to meet grid demand.” Traditional nuclear plants are not built to cycle rapidly on and off. When demand drops, operators face an unattractive choice: deliberately ramp down output, which can place mechanical stress on equipment, or keep producing electricity that the grid does not currently need. Both options carry costs, and both become more frequent as weather-dependent renewables claim a larger share of generation. TES offers a third path. Instead of forcing the reactor itself to follow demand, a storage system can absorb excess heat produced by the reactor and regulate how much of that heat is delivered to the power conversion side of the plant. When electricity demand is low, heat accumulates in storage; when demand climbs, the stored thermal energy can be drawn down to run the plant’s generation equipment. The reactor keeps operating at the steady pace it was designed for, while the plant’s electrical output flexes to match the grid. The flexibility has a financial dimension as well. Electricity prices fluctuate through the day as supply and demand shift, and the researchers’ rolling-horizon economic analysis was designed to capture how dispatch decisions play out under those changing conditions. “By storing the energy when demand and prices are low and using it when demand and prices increase, it can increase the value of the electricity produced,” Ghosh says. In effect, TES lets a nuclear plant sell its output when it is worth the most rather than when the reactor happens to produce it. The study’s focus on molten salt reactors reflects where the researchers see the opportunity. “As renewable power generation grows, the need for flexibility in nuclear plants has become more important,” Marques says. “The deployment of next-generation nuclear reactors in the US over the next few years, such as molten salt reactors, is an opportunity to incorporate TES and improve the integration of nuclear and renewable energy on the same grid.” It is worth emphasizing what the study does and does not show. The findings come from coupled thermodynamic modeling and economic analysis, not from an operating plant, so the results represent model-based projections of how a TES-equipped molten salt reactor could be dispatched and how such dispatch might affect revenue. Real-world performance would depend on factors the models necessarily simplify. For a country investing in both advanced reactors and large volumes of solar and wind, the CATER team’s analysis suggests that the heat leaving a reactor does not have to become electricity at the exact moment it is produced. Stored as thermal energy and released on schedule, it could give nuclear power the dispatch flexibility that modern grids increasingly demand, without asking reactors to do something they were never designed to do. artigo.texto: Texas' rapidly expanding data-center industry could threaten decades of progress in reducing air pollution, according to new research examining the enormous amounts of electricity the state's AI boom may need. A recent assessment published by the Houston Advanced Research Center (HARC) modeled how different ways of meeting future data-center electricity demand could affect emissions of nitrogen oxides (NOx), volatile organic compounds (VOCs), sulfur dioxide, fine particulate matter (PM2.5) and carbon dioxide through 2031. The researchers found that the impact depends heavily on how the additional electricity is generated. Newsweek has contacted HARC for comment. The warning comes as data centers spread across Texas, with state records showing projects in Abilene, the Dallas-Fort Worth area, San Antonio, Austin and parts of West Texas. The Texas comptroller maintains registers of qualifying data centers and qualifying large data-center projects, including facilities associated with companies such as Google, Microsoft, Amazon and Oracle. The City of Abilene maintains a dedicated information page for data-center construction, including the Stargate project, while the City of Fort Worth reported in June that it already had four data centers comprising 10 buildings and about 3 million square feet, with additional projects proposed within the city and surrounding area. Pollution Could Reverse Years of Progress Texas has made substantial reductions in emissions over the past two decades. HARC found that between 2002 and 2024, NOx emissions from power generation declined by 67 percent, sulfur dioxide by 80 percent, VOCs by 37 percent, carbon dioxide by 52 percent and PM2.5 by 60 percent. But electricity demand from data centers could change that trajectory. Under HARC's scenario in which new data-center demand is supplied entirely by the Texas electricity grid, using the mixture of energy sources the grid is projected to have at that time, NOx emissions in 2031 would be 136 percent higher than HARC's projected no-data-center baseline, approaching volumes last recorded around 2004. VOC emissions would exceed their 2002 volume by 32 percent, while PM2.5 emissions would rise to about their 2006 level. Power sources make a pronounced difference. HARC found that nitrogen oxide emissions could be two to 10 times higher if data centers generate the additional power they need by burning fuel rather than relying on a combination of grid electricity, solar and wind. Even under the cleanest energy scenario studied, the research center found that data-center growth would still increase emissions because of the large amount of additional electricity the facilities require. Texas Data Center Demand Surges Separate figures from the state's electric-grid operator, Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), illustrate the scale of potential data center development. In August, Republican Governor Greg Abbott's office said ERCOT was considering more than 474 gigawatts of requests to connect to the grid and that about 90 percent were from data centers. Abbott ordered the Public Utility Commission of Texas and ERCOT to carry out an audit of data-center projects going through the interconnection process, including their electricity and water requirements and plans for on-site generation. The administration went further in September, when Abbott directed the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) to halt permits sought by data centers until the ERCOT audit was completed, citing concerns such as grid reliability and natural resources. Newsweek has contacted TCEQ for comment. HARC said Texas' future emissions depend on decisions now being made about power supply, concluding that the projected data-center build-out could produce impacts ranging from relatively marginal increases to a reversal of much of the progress made over the past two decades. artigo.texto: The Prince George’s County Council approved legislation Tuesday that removes development privileges previously granted to data centers in the county. The bill removes an exemption, which was approved in 2021, that allowed data center developers to bypass a process called a detailed site plan review. A detailed site plan review is a step in the county’s permitting process for larger projects that includes an in-depth review and a public hearing. District 1 council member Thomas Dernoga, council chair Krystal Oriadha and at-large council member Wala Blegay first introduced the legislation in January, The Diamondback previously reported. During Tuesday’s meeting, District 5 council member Shayla Adams-Stafford said the legislation was created to ensure that data center applications will no longer be able to bypass the site plan review, as the now-shuttered Landover Mall site did. County residents started to raise concerns about the proposed $5 billion data center project, which is located in Adams-Stafford’s district, after it went through the fast-tracked review process. The council approved the site plan exemption in 2021 to make it easier and cheaper for data centers to move forward in the county. Oriadha, who represents District 7, said in a September council meeting she felt the exemption blindsided the community. [Voters to weigh in on fate of at-large Prince George’s County Council seats] “It created a process that would allow for data centers not to come before the council, it would allow them to go straight to permitting,” Oriadha said. “I think it was done intentionally to allow for the Landover site to get where it was in the dark of night.” The council is currently under a two-year moratorium it approved in July for the review and approval of new data center applications. Tuesday’s legislation does not end the current moratorium, but the pause would expire automatically in July 2028 if the council fails to implement zoning regulations. The council established a data center task force in April 2025 to assess the potential community impacts and economic prospects of data centers in the county. The county also approved a 180-day moratorium on reviewing and approving new data center proposals in September 2025. During the Tuesday meeting, District 2 council member Wanika Fisher proposed an amendment to the legislation that would have required data center proposals to come before the council for approval before they can move forward. The council approved the bill without Fisher’s amendment in a 10-0-1 vote, from which Fisher abstained. Fisher argued that the measure would help the council have a more involved role in controlling data center development once the countywide moratorium on their development expires. [Joan’s House details services to Prince George’s County amid nonprofit funding controversy] Adams-Stafford, Blegay and Oriadha all said they did not want to approve the amendment because it would require an additional public hearing due to the significance of the legislative change. The necessary public hearing would significantly delay the bill’s approval because there is not another council meeting until December. “If we want to create a regulation bill around data centers, we have to follow what the task force advises us to do,” Adams-Stafford said during the meeting. “Convene the public, convene experts and put forward real legislation.” During the vote, Blegay told the council she felt the legislation was important to pass now given the county’s opposition to data center development. In a Tuesday statement to The Diamondback, Adams-Stafford stood by her decision, writing that she is glad the bill was approved without the amendment. She also wrote that she is confident that the approved legislation is the best way to meet the community’s concerns about data centers. Blegay, Oriadha and Dernoga did not respond to The Diamondback’s request for comment in time for publication. Fisher declined to comment. The County Council’s approval came during its last legislative session before the midterm elections on Nov. 3. Its next scheduled meeting is on Dec. 8 and will introduce the newly elected council. artigo.texto: FUZHOU, China, Oct. 26, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- SCUDPower will showcase custom electric motorcycle battery solutions developed around different vehicle requirements at the 83rd International Motorcycle Exhibition (EICMA 2026), held November 3-8 at Fiera Milano Rho. The exhibit will show how its R&D and custom battery development platform helps OEMs translate a vehicle’s load profile, operating environment, packaging limits and performance targets into a battery system engineered and validated for the application. Electric motorcycles used for city commuting, off-road riding and high-speed performance place different demands on range, discharge power, durability and protection. Rather than applying one standard pack across vehicle platforms, SCUDPower develops robust solutions around each program’s unique requirements. That development approach is reflected in two closely connected priorities: - Safety and reliability for real riding conditions. Pack protection, BMS controls and thermal management are developed and validated against the mechanical, electrical and thermal stresses expected in the intended operating environment. - Customization for each vehicle platform. Multiple cell chemistries, pack architectures and system configurations give OEMs more options as requirements evolve. The lineup also includes high-energy-density semi-solid-state battery packs designed to support the range and power needs of high-speed e-motorcycle programs. Backed by 30 years of experience, SCUDPower supports this work with a nearly 300-member R&D team covering BMS, electrical and mechanical design, firmware, algorithms, testing and engineering services. "Our engineers do not begin with a fixed pack design,” said Awen Chen, R&D Vice General Manager at SCUDPower. "We begin with the motorcycle-what it needs to deliver and what it must withstand-then work with the OEM to build and verify the right solution.” That engineering work is supported by more than 600 invention and utility-model patents, including nearly 70 related to thermal management and thermal-runaway prevention. A 2026 research collaboration with Tsinghua University extends that work into high-safety battery-pack design, thermal-runaway prevention, early warning and state-of-health estimation. SCUDPower welcomes EICMA attendees to Hall 18, Booth H96 to meet its engineering team, discuss vehicle requirements and explore a battery development path tailored to their platform. About SCUDPower SCUDPower is a custom battery pack manufacturer serving established equipment brands and hardware startups across light electric vehicles (LEVs), smart home, robotics, consumer technology, medical, UPS and BBU applications. Its capabilities span custom engineering, testing, manufacturing and global service, supporting customer programs from concept development through volume production. In the LEV sector, SCUDPower has received recognition from customers including Ninebot-Segway and NIU Technologies. Learn more about SCUDPower’s battery development capabilities at www.scudpower.net. artigo.texto: Vantage data center plan draws questions ahead of Oregon vote Vote on Issue 25 decides whether to block construction of data center OREGON, Ohio (WTVG) - Vantage Data Centers held an open house Sunday at Clay High School, giving residents a chance to ask questions about its proposed $1 billion data center ahead of a vote on the project next week. Resident group opposes project United Neighbors of Oregon, a resident-led group, has spent the past few months working to prevent construction of the data center off Corduroy and Wynn roads. “We didn’t come this far to only come this far,” said Laura Davis, a volunteer with United Neighbors of Oregon. “They’re spending monies, thousands, hundreds of thousands of dollars on this campaign to try and buy their way into Oregon. But I keep saying Oregon is not for sale,” Davis said. Davis said she is concerned about the wetlands and the people who live near the proposed site. Vantage addresses energy, water questions Misty Allen, vice president of public policy for North America at Vantage Data Centers, said residents have raised questions about the project. “People want to understand the, where’s the energy coming from? How will that affect their energy rates? What about water use? And how is the data center going to use water?” Allen said. Allen said Vantage will purchase its own power and cover the necessary infrastructure costs. “When it comes to water use, we’re not going to use any more water than, say, a typical medium commercial office building. And we use closed loop water for chilling of the data center,” Allen said. Allen said the facility would use 22,000 gallons of water a day, the same amount used by 65 homes. She said Vantage checked with the city’s water plant and was told it has the ability to service that need. Open house draws mixed reaction Davis said she remains unconvinced. “They had some people in there trying to convince other people that this is the right thing for Oregon. But we were in there telling people, this is not the right thing for Oregon,” Davis said. Davis said Allen and Vantage staff gave her one answer she liked. “If we win this vote, they will pull out,” Davis said. “Obviously we would have to have conversations with city council and the folks who have been working on this development. But certainly, if the community doesn’t want us here, we’ll have to seriously consider not being here,” Allen said. What’s on the ballot Davis said the ballot language is confusing residents. Voting yes on Issue 25 supports amending the city charter to prohibit construction of the data center. Voting no on the issue opposes blocking the construction. artigo.texto: Piedmont City Council voted Monday, Oct. 26, to advance plans for a second proposed data center as residents continued raising concerns about the developments. Council members approved an amended master design statement for Beltline Energy’s proposed 640-acre data center campus, which could include approximately 19 buildings. The council also voted to send the amended plan back to the Planning and Zoning Commission for further consideration. Council members requested a special meeting for Nov. 17 at 6 p.m. That decision does not give the developer final approval to begin construction. What about the Cloverleaf data center? The decision comes after the council approved an amended master design plan for a separate data center proposed by Cloverleaf Infrastructure on Oct. 22. MORE ON THE PROPOSAL: How a 4-1 City Council vote moved Piedmont’s data center plans forward That project covers approximately 633 acres and could include six data center buildings. Both developments are moving through the city’s approval process, but neither has received final construction approval. What are residents concerned about? During Monday’s meeting, residents voiced their opposition to the developments, raising concerns about noise, water consumption, infrastructure and the impact on nearby homes. WATCH THE FULL CITY COUNCIL MEETING HERE. Council members discussed additional requirements for Beltline’s proposal, including environmental studies, noise protections and landscaping. The council also postponed action on a proposed data center moratorium until November. What happens next for the proposed data centers? Both proposed data centers have additional steps in the city’s approval process. The next reported project-approval hearing for Cloverleaf Infrastructure is scheduled for Nov. 12, while Beltline Energy’s amended proposal is expected to return to the Planning and Zoning Commission for a special meeting on Nov. 17 at 6 p.m. Beltline’s proposal would then need to return to the City Council for further consideration. A date for a final council vote has not been confirmed. Residents will have additional opportunities to voice concerns as the projects move through the approval process. Neither project has received final construction approval.

artigo.texto: A data center under construction in South Brunswick is drawing environmental concerns from residents who said they only recently learned about the project, more than a year after local officials approved it. The New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection (NJDEP) is currently reviewing an application from Sentinel Data Centers to install several backup diesel generators at the former Princeton Nurseries property on Rt-1. The agency has opened a public comment period as part of its permitting process. Many residents said they didn't become aware of the project until the state began to seek public input on the generator permits. However, the proposed data center received approval from the South Brunswick Planning Board in May 2025. "It's only been in the last month, maybe a little bit longer than that that people have truly been aware of it and been able to raise their voices," said Kingston resident Karin Gillespie. "If there is an opportunity to impact the diesel generators and think about some kind of an alternative to that, that would be great." The property is situated on the border of several towns including South Brunswick, Kingston and Princeton. “This is about more than one data center. It is about the health of our families, the protection of our air and water and the long-term future of our communities,” said Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman. “Pollution does not stop at municipal borders. The impacts of this project will extend far beyond South Brunswick, threatening the health and quality of life of residents across the surrounding communities." Though the approval for the data center was granted by the South Brunswick Planning Board, Princeton Mayor Mark Freda and the city council released a statement at the beginning of October in opposition of the backup generators. "When running, these generators will undoubtedly send emissions across municipal boundaries, often negatively affecting air quality and public health in Princeton’s residential neighborhoods and at two of our elementary schools. We urge DEP to deny the air permit application for the center in its present form," the statement said. The two candidates running to replace Coleman in November are also speaking out on the data center and the potential impacts for nearby residents. Adam Hamawy, the Democratic candidate running to represent New Jersey's 12th district said in a statement, "Our communities deserve the right to decide their own future, not have it dictated by billionaires and corporate developers. The New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection has a responsibility to protect public health, and that starts with denying this air permit.” His Republican challenger, Gregg Mele, also spoke to News 12 about the planned data center. “Residents deserve a complete, independently reviewed accounting of generator emissions, noise, water demand, and electricity infrastructure costs—including all planned phases," Mele said. "Developers should pay the infrastructure costs they create, and protections for neighboring communities must be enforceable." While the current state review is focused on the backup generators, some residents continue to call for the entire project to be reconsidered. "Maybe we can do what so many other communities have done. Maybe we can get them to not have this data center," said South Brunswick resident Janice Gossman. "A lot of people say it's too late. We have to try." For some neighbors, the debate is personal. Michael Van Pelt, who lives down the road from the site of the data center, said he worries about how the facility could impact his family, including his son, who has autism. "My son is very sensitive to sound," Van Pelt said. "His special education program is magnificent. His teachers are wonderful and if he loses that, I don't know what we're going to do."

artigo.texto: The Federal Government has pledged support for Cross River State’s maiden Climate Transition Plan, expressing its readiness to help the state attract climate finance, access emerging carbon markets and develop investment projects that combine environmental conservation with economic growth. The commitment came from the National Council on Climate Change (NCCC) and the Federal Ministry of Environment at an inception workshop on the development of the plan, held at the State Library, Calabar. Director-General of the NCCC, Omotenioye Majekodunmi, said Cross River’s extensive tropical rainforests, biodiversity and other natural resources placed it in a strategic position to benefit from emerging opportunities in carbon trading, nature-based solutions and international climate financing. She stressed that Nigeria’s climate commitments could only translate into measurable results through effective implementation at state and community levels, where environmental protection must be accompanied by improved livelihoods and sustainable development. “Nigeria’s climate ambitions will ultimately be delivered at the state and community levels, where forests are protected, infrastructure is made more resilient, clean energy is deployed, and livelihoods are strengthened,” she said. “Cross River State has a particularly important role to play with its rich tropical rainforest, the biodiversity and significant natural capital. “The state has an opportunity to demonstrate that climate action, conservation and economic development can go hand in hand.” Majekodunmi explained that the greenhouse gas inventory, climate vulnerability and risk assessment, alongside other baseline studies being undertaken by the state, would provide the scientific evidence required to translate policy ambitions into practical interventions. According to her, credible environmental data and clearly defined projects would strengthen Cross River’s capacity to attract investors seeking measurable climate and development outcomes. “It will also position Cross River State to take advantage of the emerging opportunities in nature-based solutions, carbon markets and climate finance,” she said. “As Nigeria operationalises its national carbon market architecture and advances implementation of our NDC, we need new and strong state-level projects that are credible, investable and capable of delivering measurable results and ultimately improve incomes.” She assured the state government of the council’s commitment to ensuring that its transition plan aligns with national climate priorities and attracts the partnerships required for implementation. “The National Council on Climate Change stands ready to work with Cross River State to ensure alignment with national climate priorities and, importantly, to help translate this plan into implementation and investment,” Majekodunmi declared. Similarly, Director of the Department of Climate Change, Federal Ministry of Environment, Iniobong Abiola-Awe, described the initiative as another demonstration of Cross River’s leadership in environmental conservation and subnational climate governance. She said the state’s longstanding reputation as a major ecological destination, particularly its vast forest resources and biodiversity, made the transition plan an important framework for balancing conservation with development. “Cross River State has long been celebrated as Nigeria’s premier eco-destination and vital subnational vanguard for forest conservation. “By unveiling this important framework, Cross River State is once again proving its proactive leadership in subnational environmental governance,” she said. Abiola-Awe commended the state government for initiating baseline studies, explaining that reliable data would enable policymakers to establish realistic priorities, measure progress and develop interventions capable of delivering results. “We are highly encouraged to see that Cross River State is executing critical baseline studies, and these studies provide the precise empirical formula needed to translate plans to implementation,” she added. She assured the state of the ministry’s readiness to collaborate on relevant programmes. Governor Bassey Otu, represented by the Speaker of the Cross River State House of Assembly, Elvert Ayambem, said the transition plan would strengthen climate resilience, safeguard the state’s natural resources and create opportunities for sustainable economic growth under his administration’s People First agenda. He emphasised the need to protect the state’s ecological assets, including what he described as more than half of Nigeria’s remaining tropical rainforests, extensive mangrove ecosystems and rich biodiversity. Otu said the transition framework would provide a coordinated approach to addressing environmental vulnerabilities while ensuring that conservation efforts contribute meaningfully to economic development. Earlier, Director-General of the Cross River State Council on Climate Change, Edu Effiom, said the inception workshop marked the beginning of the technical process for developing the plan, including reviewing its preliminary draft and conducting baseline studies. She called on ministries, departments, agencies and local government councils to provide reliable sector-specific data and technical contributions to guide policy priorities, climate projections and implementation targets. Effiom stressed that climate action must go beyond policy declarations, insisting that environmental commitments should be integrated into government budgets and local development plans to ensure measurable results. The Federal Government’s intervention is expected to strengthen cooperation with Cross River in developing a climate transition framework capable of attracting investment while protecting the ecological resources on which many communities depend.

Designed to address the core challenges of commercial deployments—such as limited space, noise restrictions, and heavy power demands—the SigenCube introduces industry-leading energy density, ultra-quiet operation, and robust overload performance to the global market. Simplified Deployment: Big Energy Doesn't Need Big Space Deploying commercial energy storage no longer means sacrificing massive amounts of valuable real estate. The SigenCube boasts an exceptional energy density over 220kWh/m², dramatically shrinking spatial requirements. In a 4MWh project, traditional solutions typically require over 80m² of land, whereas the SigenCube requires only 54.5m², successfully saving over 30% in overall footprint. Beyond saving space, the system is engineered for maximum installation efficiency. It features a highly integrated, compact architecture that combines the Power Conversion System (PCS), high-voltage components, and distribution units into a single cabinet. To scale up multi-megawatt projects easily, the SigenCube incorporates a built-in Energy Management System (EMS) in each cabinet, supporting up to 100 units in parallel without the need for external data loggers, complete with automated failover to prevent single points of failure. Once on site, deployment is streamlined through factory pre-commissioning and quick app-based setup, allowing technicians to complete basic configurations and diagnostics in just 3 to 5 minutes. Peak Performance: Quiet Operation Meets Heavy-Duty Power While traditional commercial storage solutions are often notoriously noisy—frequently causing disruptions that make normal conversation difficult for people nearby—the SigenCube completely redefines the acoustic standard. It stands out as the quietest commercial energy storage system available, maintaining noise levels below 60 dB at one meter, which is comparable to the ambient noise of a normal conversation. This allows businesses to install the system smoothly near office buildings, commercial centers, and residential-adjacent areas. Despite its quiet and compact design, the SigenCube packs formidable power capabilities. It delivers a robust 150% peak power overload for 10 seconds, providing the critical surge support needed for heavy industrial machinery. Whether handling the sudden inrush currents of industrial air compressors, conveyor drive systems, or motor-driven centrifugal pumps, the system prevents tripping and handles load spikes effortlessly. To ensure this peak performance remains stable and efficient over time, the system features predictive smart thermal management that continuously monitors real-time cell conditions and day-ahead load forecasts to optimize cooling. By dynamically adjusting coolant temperatures before load changes occur, it cuts auxiliary power consumption by up to 20% while actively mitigating calendar aging to help extend battery life. All-Round Safety: Multi-Layered Protection from Pack to System Safety forms the foundation of the SigenCube, featuring strong protections spanning from the pack level up to the entire system. Within the battery pack, the system utilizes high-temperature fire-resistant isolation design and reinforced six-sided insulation, backed by a dense configuration of 40 NTC temperature sensors monitoring 64 cells per pack (0.625 NTC per cell, which is much denser than the industry average). Additional pack-level safeguards include pressure relief valves, electrical insulation sheets, crash frames, high-strength crossbeams, leakage detection and optional aerosol fire suppression available for select regions. At the system level, the SigenCube integrates top explosion vents, smoke and heat detectors, emergency fans, cabinet-level aerosol suppression, and a water firefighting interface, supported by 8 layers of overcurrent protection for complete peace of mind. Optimized O&M: Lower OPEX and Effortless Maintenance Commercial and industrial energy storage is never a short-term investment, minimizing long-term operational and maintenance burdens is essential for maximizing project returns. The SigenCube is engineered for long-term reliability with exceptionally low maintenance requirements. It uses a special sealed cooling loop that delivers a 10-year coolant life, significantly reducing scheduled replacements. Additionally, its pack-level active balancing delivers a strong 7A balancing current—keeping battery strings uniformly balanced over years of operation and eliminating the need for periodic on-site SOC calibration. Grid-Forming Resilience for Every Scenario Commercial and industrial facilities constantly face unpredictable grid fluctuations, weak infrastructure, and unexpected outages—making robust grid-forming resilience essential. Engineered with comprehensive grid-forming capabilities, the SigenCube leads with 0ms load-side disruption to keep critical industrial loads running without interruption. Beyond seamless switchover, the system delivers exceptional all-around grid support, including 100% three-phase imbalance handling under complex load conditions, robust fault ride-through during voltage sags and swells, and reliable MWh-level black start without external grid support. Furthermore, it incorporates advanced grid-stabilizing intelligence—featuring rapid reactive power response for voltage regulation, virtual inertia support to stabilize grid frequency, active power oscillation damping, and superior weak grid adaptation for stable, clean operation in high-impedance environments. artigo.texto: Samsung — o maior diferencial hoje para data centers que pagam mais por HBM não é só tecnologia, mas a previsibilidade da entrega: clientes premium estariam aceitando pagar até 25% a mais pela garantia de fornecimento e pelos ganhos de rendimento que a empresa vem reportando. Preço e comparação: quanto custa um HBM no mercado A cotação atribuída à Samsung para HBM aparece em $4,50 por unidade, frente a $4,00 para Micron e uma faixa de $3,60–$3,80 para SK hynix. Esse spread equivale a um prêmio de até 25% sobre o preço dos concorrentes. A diferença de preço ganha sentido quando se considera que a HBM4 da Samsung é mencionada como posicionada na faixa média-alta dos US$4, tornando-a até três vezes mais cara que a referência anterior de HBM3E em cotações comparativas. A Samsung tem uma cotação de $4,50 para HBM, contra $4,00 da Micron e $3,60–$3,80 da SK hynix, refletindo um prêmio ligado à capacidade de fornecer volumes estáveis e avanços na produção de HBM4. Vantagens industriais por trás do prêmio A capacidade da Samsung de aliar sua divisão de foundry e múltiplos nós avançados, como um 4nm maduro, tem sido apontada como fator que reduz defeitos e eleva a utilidade industrial, favorecendo yields superiores durante a produção de HBM4. Relatos de rendimento em torno de 80% para HBM4 e a possibilidade de conciliar recursos entre memória e chips não relacionados à memória são citados como razões práticas para a empresa manter preços mais altos, atraindo clientes sensíveis a risco de falta de oferta. O que você acha? Você considera justificável que data centers paguem um prêmio por garantia de fornecimento e yields mais altos? Para acompanhar mais, acesse nossa editoria. Perguntas Frequentes Por que a Samsung está cobrando até 25% a mais por HBM para data centers? A Samsung está cobrando até 25% a mais por HBM porque sua capacidade de produção e estabilidade de suprimento oferecem menos risco aos data centers, com cotações citadas em $4,50 frente a $4,00 da Micron e $3,60–$3,80 da SK hynix. Essa diferença reflete preferência por continuidade de entregas e rendimentos superiores. O que torna a HBM4 da Samsung mais cara que a HBM3E? A HBM4 da Samsung aparece posicionada na faixa média-alta dos US$4, o que a deixa cerca de três vezes mais cara que a referência de HBM3E citada. Essa precificação incorpora melhorias de rendimento (relatos de até 80%) e custos de processo em nós avançados, além da integração com sua foundry. Como essa diferença de preço afeta os data centers na prática? A diferença de preço impacta o custo total de servidores e aceleradores: data centers que priorizam disponibilidade e performance podem optar por pagar $4,50 por HBM para reduzir risco de falta, enquanto outros podem escolher fornecedores mais baratos, como Micron a $4,00, dependendo de capex e estratégia de suprimento. © Diário da Mídia · Conteúdo protegido por direitos autorais — reprodução ou cópia proibida sem autorização. artigo.texto: Morro Bay City Council plans to ban battery storage plants October 25, 2026 By KAREN VELIE After a more than four-year battle, the Morro Bay City Council is planning to pass an ordinance on Tuesday in an attempt to ban battery storage plants that provide power to the state’s electric grid. Vistra Energy, a Texas-based energy company, has plans to construct and operate a 600 megawatt battery storage facility on approximately 24 acres of a roughly 70-acre site. However, residents, concerned the facility would endanger the public while negatively impacting tourism and the fishing industry, have battled against the proposed project for years. Legislation passed in 2022 allows applicants to skip local approvals. However, it requires approvals from both the California Energy Commission and the Coastal Commission. So, even if the California Energy Commission green-lights the battery storage plant, it would still need approval from the California Coastal Commission, which has criticized the project. In an Aug. 2, 2024 letter regarding Vistra Energy’s proposed project, the Coastal Commission outlined serious issues about the location of the project. In summary, they stated that the future hazards of flooding and sea level rise and the impact on the environmentally sensitive habitat area are acute. In the 2024 election, Morro Bay, residents largely supported a measure requiring voter approval for changes to some zoning on the waterfront. Vistra Energy decided to seek state approval while bypassing the city’s consideration shortly before the November election. On Jan. 28, 2025, the Morro Bay City Council voted for an urgency ordinance to temporarily halt the proposed battery storage project. The urgency ordinance, which was extended once, is set to expire on Jan. 28, 2027. Even if the city council enacts an ordinance banning battery storage plants in the city, Vistra Energy could ask the state to override the ordinance and permit the project. However, a large amount of the funding for the battery storage facility is slated to be provided through the Inflation Reduction Act, which included $369 billion in subsidies for renewable energy. “The Inflation Reduction Act is anticipated to provide the opportunity to realize material benefits to Vistra with respect to its renewables and energy storage projects, as well as provide strong price support via the nuclear production tax credit for its nuclear facilities, including those acquired through the Energy Harbor transaction,” Vistra Energy said in a first quarter 2024 press release. However, the Trump administration and the Republican-led Congress have frozen, and rolled back major provisions of the Inflation Reduction Act. Without subsidies and tax credits, it is unlikely Vistra Energy will move forward with its plan for battery storage in Morro Bay. artigo.texto: Davidson County commissioners to consider 4-month moratorium on data center development Davidson County commissioners are holding a public hearing about a proposed four-month pause on data center development to address zoning and infrastructure concerns. Davidson County commissioners to consider 4-month moratorium on data center development Davidson County commissioners are holding a public hearing about a proposed four-month pause on data center development to address zoning and infrastructure concerns. Davidson County commissioners are considering a four-month moratorium on data center development to give leaders time to evaluate regulations and address concerns about infrastructure and environmental impact. In August, commissioners rejected a proposal for a six-month moratorium. The new six-page proposal outlines the reasons for the 4-month pause, citing concerns local and national about data centers’ electricity use, water supply issues, heat production and noise pollution. Get the latest news stories of interest by clicking here Keep up with the latest news and weather by downloading the WXII app here. The document also states that the county’s zoning ordinance "has no current means to regulate the siting, construction, and operation of data centers in a direct and meaningful way." It further explains that state law prevents commissioners from making certain sweeping changes to the zoning ordinance. The proposal outlines a plan for the moratorium. During the first two months, county leaders would consult experts about data centers, review the county’s land and utilities, and visit nearby data centers. In the final two months, they would consider potential zoning changes and possibly propose rules to regulate data center development. Watch: NOWCAST streaming newscasts Members of the public can share their thoughts on the proposed moratorium during a public hearing at the Davidson County Board of Commissioners meeting, which begins at 6 p.m. Monday. The meeting will be held in the meeting room on the fourth floor of the Davidson County Governmental Center on Greensboro Street in Lexington. artigo.texto: Vertiv Simplifies High-Density AI Infrastructure Deployment Across Data Center Environments The new Vertiv™ SmartIT platform is a pre-engineered AI infrastructure solution based on NVIDIA MGX™ and OCP ORV3 architecture The scalable solution supports deployment in existing enterprise facilities, new builds, commercial spaces, colocation and hyperscale environments without redesign COLUMBUS, Ohio , Oct. 26, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Vertiv Holdings Co. (NYSE: VRT), a global leader in critical digital infrastructure, today introduced the Vertiv™ SmartIT solution, a pre-engineered architecture designed to simplify high-density AI deployments for enterprises, research institutions and colocation providers across existing facilities and new data centers. Previously deployed with NVIDIA to support the NVIDIA DGX™ GB300, the highest-performing, largest-scale AI system available for enterprises, the Vertiv™ SmartIT solution integrates rack infrastructure, DC power conversion and distribution, direct-to-chip liquid cooling, in-rack cooling distribution and monitoring in a factory-validated design. By integrating and validating these systems before shipment, Vertiv™ SmartIT helps reduce on-site integration complexity and connects to facility power and cooling infrastructure. The solution is available now for AI deployments globally. "AI is fundamentally changing the demands placed on data center infrastructure, requiring closer coordination across power, cooling and IT systems to support increasingly complex workloads," said Scott Armul, Chief Product and Technology Officer at Vertiv. "Vertiv™ SmartIT reflects our approach to solving that challenge by bringing these disciplines together in a factory-validated architecture. By combining Vertiv's expertise across critical infrastructure, we're helping customers simplify deployment, build greater consistency into their AI environments and establish a foundation that can evolve alongside their computing needs." Vertiv™ SmartIT helps customers address key deployment challenges, including: - Deployment timelines compress: Factory validation replaces on-site integration, limiting the commissioning scope to facility connections. - Multi-vendor coordination is reduced: Customers benefit from a single order, one partner and one architecture spanning rack, power, cooling and monitoring. - Existing spaces become AI-ready: Brownfield enterprise facilities and Class A commercial buildings can support AI-class density without full reconstruction. - Scalability becomes repeatable: The same building block supports growth from single rack to multi-rack deployments, without redesign between phases. - Operational visibility increases: Integrated leak detection, automated response and continuous monitoring provide visibility from rack to site, with these capabilities built into the solution from day one rather than assembled from separate vendor tools. Vertiv™ SmartIT is a scalable, pre-engineered infrastructure platform for high-density AI deployments, supporting NVIDIA GB300 NVL72, NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72, NVIDIA DGX™ Rubin NVL8 and NVIDIA HGX™ Rubin NVL8 on NVIDIA MGX™ and Open Compute Project (OCP) ORV3 architectures. Designed to scale from a single rack to multi-rack deployments, it enables customers to deploy and expand AI infrastructure within a common architecture while integrating power, cooling, monitoring and controls. Built-in monitoring, leak detection and support for Redfish, SNMP and Modbus simplify operations, while Vertiv™ Global Services supports deployment, commissioning and lifecycle management. Vertiv SmartIT can be deployed as part of a broader Vertiv infrastructure architecture, with complementary solutions extending integration and management capabilities beyond the rack. Vertiv™ SmartRun extends integration across the row, while Vertiv™ rack power distribution units (rPDU) provide power distribution and monitoring. Vertiv™ Unify provides integrated monitoring, analytics and controls across power and thermal infrastructure, including leak detection and coordinated response control. Together, these solutions help customers scale from individual Vertiv™ SmartIT deployments to larger AI environments. Vertiv showcased a Vertiv™ SmartIT with a NVIDIA HGX™ Rubin NVL8 demo unit during NVIDIA GTC Berlin in October, demonstrating an integrated infrastructure architecture designed to support NVIDIA DGX Rubin NVL8 deployments, enabling customers to start at the right scale and expand within a common infrastructure architecture as AI demand grows. For more information about the Vertiv™ SmartIT and Vertiv's growing portfolio of power, cooling and IT infrastructure solutions and services, visit Vertiv.com. About Vertiv Holdings Co. (NYSE: VRT) brings together hardware, software, analytics and ongoing services to enable its customers' vital applications to run continuously, perform optimally and grow with their business needs. Vertiv solves the most important challenges facing today's data centers, communication networks and commercial and industrial facilities with a portfolio of power, cooling and IT infrastructure solutions and services that extends from the cloud to the edge of the network. The project was signed in July with a Chinese company he described as one of the “top-tier manufacturers,” of China along with a local private-sector investor. He did not name either party. The facility will produce lithium-ion cells with an annual capacity of more than 1,000MW. The first factory will initially produce 200-300MW before reaching full capacity. The plant is located at Heavy Industries Taxila in Rawalpindi district. MHIL manufactures defence equipment, including battle tanks, armoured vehicles, unmanned drones and protective gear, as well as compact battery energy storage systems, EV buses and two-wheelers. The general manager for digital media in MHIL, Muhammad Ameen, was not immediately available for comment. Automotive and Auto Parts Manufacturing Policy 2026-2031. The agreement follows the approval by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif of the Automotive and Auto Parts Manufacturing Policy 2026-2031. The policy awaits IMF approval over proposed tax incentives for the electric vehicle industry and their potential revenue implications. The EDB estimates that demand for battery energy storage systems (BESS) could reach 100,000MW by June 2030 if the economy grows by 5 percent or more. If GDP growth falls below 3 percent, demand is projected at up to 80,000MW. Mansoor said demand would come from households, commercial buildings, industry and electric vehicles, including two-wheelers, three-wheelers, cars, buses and trucks. Grid stabilization alone could require 3,000-5,000MW of battery storage. Meeting the projected demand would require four to five gigafactories, each costing around $1 billion to $1.25 billion. The government prepared a lithium battery manufacturing policy and submitted it to the Ministry of Industries in March. It awaits approval. The plan includes four major factories, three in the Lahore, Faisalabad and Rawalpindi divisions of Punjab and one in Karachi. Manufacturers would be required to export a specified percentage of production, though Mansoor declined to give the target before approval. He said the policy incorporates international safety and performance standards. Pakistan currently assembles around 3,000-4,000MW of batteries, along with parts such as motors, controllers and chargers. Mansoor said local manufacturing of all these parts will begin at 100 percent by next year.

artigo.texto: From Grid Constraint to AI Growth: Hitachi Vantara and Duraflow Transform Data Center Energy Management for Greater AI and Compute Capacity - Hitachi Vantara pilots one of the world's largest Phase Change Material installations in itsNetherlands data center, demonstrating how organizations can use up to 90% less electricity for thermal management - Implementation requires zero water for cooling, reducing the resources needed to support data center operations - This generates more computing capacity from existing power infrastructure, rather than diverting power to cooling ZALTBOMMEL, The Netherlands and SANTA CLARA, Calif., Oct. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- As artificial intelligence (AI) accelerates demand for computing power, data centers face a growing challenge: how to increase AI and compute capacity when access to additional electricity is increasingly constrained. Hitachi Vantara , the data storage, infrastructure and hybrid cloud management subsidiary of Hitachi Ltd. (TSE: 6501), is demonstrating a new approach to address this challenge by showing how data centers can effectively use their power for AI and compute capacity rather than power and cooling. At its data center in the Netherlands, Hitachi Vantara has deployed one of the world's largest operational Phase Change Material (PCM) installations, using technology developed by Dutch thermal energy company Duraflow. For more information about Hitachi Vantara's approach to AI, please visit: https://www.hitachivantara.com/solutions/ai-analytics Depending on the application, PCM technology can help reduce electricity consumption related to thermal management by up to 90%, while requiring no water for cooling. By reducing the energy needed to manage power and cooling, a greater share of available electrical capacity can be used for computing – an increasingly important consideration as organizations deploy more energy-intensive AI workloads. Tackling the energy challenge behind AI Every watt consumed by AI ultimately becomes heat and managing that heat requires as much as 40% of a data center's total energy needs. At the same time, as AI workloads continue to grow, the ability to convert available electricity into useful computing capacity will increasingly determine how quickly digital infrastructure can expand. This creates a growing challenge for data center operators seeking to increase computing capacity within constrained power infrastructure. In regions where grid congestion or limited access to additional electricity can constrain data center expansion, improving infrastructure efficiency can help organizations make more computing capacity available within their existing power connection. Hitachi Vantara faced this challenge as demand for high-density computing and AI infrastructure increased. Rather than assuming that more computing required a greater amount of power, the company explored ways to make its existing electrical capacity work harder. The resulting deployment of Duraflow's PCM technology provides a real-world proof point for this approach at an operational scale. Real-world performance: 240 kW of cooling with low electrical consumption The installed system provides a total cooling capacity of 240 kW across two 120 kW PCM units. According to operational monitoring data, the two units collectively consume just 5–8 kW of electricity, depending on operating conditions. For comparison, a conventional DX cooling system delivering the same 240 kW cooling capacity would require an estimated 60–80 kW of compressor power. These operational figures illustrate how PCM-based thermal management can significantly reduce the electricity required for cooling, freeing up more of the data center's available power capacity for computing. "This project started with a very practical challenge: how do we grow our computing capacity when access to additional electricity is limited," saidSimon Ninan, Senior Vice President of Business Strategy, Hitachi Vantara. "We realized that if we could dramatically reduce the amount of power required for thermal management, we could make more of our existing electrical capacity available for computing. By partnering with Duraflow, we are demonstrating how smarter energy management can become an important enabler of AI growth." The approach also supports Hitachi Vantara's broader commitment to operating more efficiently and sustainably, including its goal of becoming carbon neutral in Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions by FY2030. Building efficiency across the infrastructure stack The deployment is part of Hitachi Vantara's broader focus on helping organizations get more value from their infrastructure while managing the growing energy demands of digital workloads. That approach extends across the infrastructure stack. Hitachi Vantara's Virtual Storage Platform One (VSP One) Block includes a 4:1 Data Reduction Guarantee and features Dynamic Carbon Reduction technology, which reduces energy consumption by switching CPUs into eco-mode during periods of low activity. Its always-on compression capability allows the system to switch from inline data reduction to post processing, which further reduces energy consumption and helps reduce a CO2 footprint by as much as 40%. "Addressing the energy demands of AI isn't about optimizing one part of the business in isolation," said Courtney Hadden, Sustainability Director, Hitachi Digital. "It's about working in concert across the organization and with innovative ecosystem partners to find efficiencies at every stage – from the products we build, how we bring them to market, and everything in between. The answer cannot simply be to consume more power. We need to become smarter about how we use the power we already have." Click here to purchase a paywall bypass link for this article The town of Bloomfield has banned data centers, joining a number of Connecticut towns that have blocked or restricted the power-hungry facilities, and went a step further by also barring battery energy storage. The Town Plan and Zoning Commission approved the zoning amendments without any opposition at its meeting Thursday. The commission itself proposed the changes. The new rules prohibit data centers “as a principal use, accessory use, or component of a mixed use in every zoning district.” Planning Director Jonathan Colman said the rules target the large standalone facilities going up around the country. He said the town wrote the definition broadly on purpose. “They are often referred to by other names and titles, often to try and avoid the regulations that may be in place in the community,” Colman said. Colman said the town had already received one informal data center proposal, for the northwest part of town, that would now be barred. In June 2025, New York-based Atlas Capital Group made an informal presentation to the commission about a possible data center at 132 Griffin Road North. The project called for about 900,000 square feet of data center space and a 127,000-square-foot substation on a vacant 44-acre former tobacco field. Companies can still run servers for their own operations as an accessory use, town staff said. The amendments create a separate category for offices and engineering sites where computers serve on-site employees. Staff said that use differs from a data center, which relies on backup generators, chillers and cooling towers. The changes also eliminated a provision that let the commission approve uses not specifically allowed in a zone. Now, if a use isn’t listed, it isn’t permitted. The vote came two days after East Lyme’s zoning commission unanimously banned traditional and AI data centers, along with data center accessory uses. In 2021, Connecticut lawmakers created tax breaks to lure data centers, letting the state exempt projects of at least $200 million, or $50 million in certain economic development zones, from sales and property taxes for up to 30 years.

Pointing out that an expert consultant’s report had not yet been considered, the San Benito County Planning Commission voted Oct. 20 to postpone until Dec. 16 its consideration of proposed new battery energy storage system (BESS) rules. A draft BESS ordinance presented to the commission would have included amendments to the county’s zoning codes governing battery storage projects, such as Longroad Energy’s proposed Allium Solar project off Hwy 156. County Director of Planning and Building Abraham Prado presented the draft ordinance, which staff recommended the commission approve and forward to the San Benito County Board of Supervisors for approval. But the commissioners indicated they believed the draft ordinance wasn’t nearly ready for their review yet because expert consultant Mike Nicholas’ report on his review of the draft had not yet been considered by the ad hoc committee of interested parties. Nicholas, a retired Kern County fire captain who has worked with state officials on creating BESS project standards, agreed to review the draft ordinance and provide recommendations. However, Prado told the commission Nicholas’ recommendations had not been added to the agenda prior to the meeting. Prado then proceeded to give a lengthy review of the proposed ordinance, including changes made at the ad hoc committee’s behest. He said the staff recommended the commission approve the ordinance and forward it to the supervisors to adopt. Commissioner Robert Gibson was quick to comment, “The staff recommendation is a little off. The ad hoc requested more time to work on the ordinance. We did not want the Planning Commission to send this to the board because it’s half written. There’s a lot of changes that need to be made to make it a workable ordinance.” After a brief back and forth between commissioners about setback distances, better maps, and the need for community meetings, Chair Richard Way suggested, “Why don’t we continue this and send it back to the ad hoc committee for further review?” During public comment, ad hoc committee member Leslie Austin said she wanted the ad hoc review to continue before the ordinance goes before the supervisors. “We need an ordinance that protects people, the environment, wildlife, public funds with requirements that fit different project types that the county can actually administer and enforce,” Austin said, adding that she had been preparing a side-by-side review of the county’s language, research from government agencies and other jurisdictions along with suggested changes and questions needing county council review. “I began this work to contribute effectively to the ad hoc process and to support the community staff, commissioners, and supervisors in this critical work,” she said. “The document explains each recommendation, its supporting research, and questions about responsibilities and costs. But we also need to understand how the requirements work together, building on the county’s mapping. That means looking at realistic projects and locations and considering land use rules, electrical connections, safety costs, and oversight all together.” She suggested that the county bring affected residents, climate and environmental groups, and other key stakeholders together to compare options before deciding whether any protections should change. “The document is substantially drafted and I’m checking that its recommendations fit together and will deliver it no later than Oct. 28,” she said. “I ask you to please allow enough time afterwards for staff, council, commissioners and stakeholders to review it before the next hearing.” Long Road Energy spokesperson Laren Cypress agreed that the ordinance needs more work. “Some provisions in the current form cannot even be met by an applicant,” Cypress said. “The ordinance requires soil testing on neighboring land that an applicant has no legal right to enter, and it requires a geo-liner under the batteries that would result in rainwater pooling around energized equipment. artigo.texto: Vaisala, a global leader in measurement instruments and intelligence for critical environments, will showcase data center measurement and service solutions at DCD>Connect Virginia, November 3–4 at Lansdowne Resort & Spa in Leesburg, Virginia. At stand 58, Vaisala will feature two additions to its data center offering, Vaisala Indigo Supervisor and Vaisala Care for Data Centers, alongside the Origo product family. Together, these offerings help operators support cooling performance, energy efficiency, operational reliability and uptime. The Vaisala Indigo Supervisor is designed to simplify environmental monitoring as facilities expand. It enables up to 100 measurement points to be managed as a single system. The solution supports two independent daisy-chained probe networks with up to 50 probes per chain and integrates with building management systems through a single Modbus TCP connection. A local touchscreen provides dashboards, measurement visibility, alert management and calibration information. Web-based commissioning tools help teams deploy the system efficiently. Touchscreen-enabled probe replacement and CSV configuration export support maintenance and more consistent implementation across multiple sites. Indigo Supervisor is expected to be available in early 2027. Vaisala will also highlight Vaisala Care for Data Centers, a service portfolio that provides a structured approach to maintaining measurement performance throughout the lifecycle of a facility’s measurement systems. Designed for hyperscale, colocation and enterprise data centers, the portfolio includes Vaisala Care, Vaisala Care+ and Vaisala Commissioning Care. Available options include calibration services, expert support, replacement probe pools, service documentation, and commissioning-phase calibration and handover documentation. Subject to Vaisala approval, agreed verification scopes may also include selected third-party measurement devices. These services help operators manage calibration, verification and documentation needs across growing measurement networks. The Origo product family will also be on display. This modular platform of transmitters and compact probes supports HVAC measurement in data centers and other mission-critical facilities. Origo provides real-time measurement of temperature, relative humidity, carbon dioxide and dew point to support stable environmental conditions and efficient HVAC operation. Interchangeable probes allow teams to configure the platform for specific measurement requirements. Two probes can be combined in one transmitter to support multi-parameter monitoring while reducing device count. With ±0.1 °C temperature accuracy and ±1% RH humidity accuracy, Origo helps operators reduce unnecessary cooling while supporting the stable environmental control that critical spaces require. Visitors can meet with Vaisala at stand 58 during DCD>Connect Virginia to learn how its measurement instruments, monitoring architecture and lifecycle services help support the reliable and efficient operation of scalable, AI-ready data center infrastructure.

artigo.texto: Dive Brief: - Despite trade barriers and project cost inflation, the U.S. is set to deploy 30% more energy storage capacity over the next 10 years than expected just six months ago, BloombergNEF said Thursday. BNEF forecasts cumulative U.S. deployments of 213.9 GW by 2030 and 434.4 GW by 2036, BNEF senior energy storage analyst Isshu Kikuma told Utility Dive. - The latest edition of the energy consultancy’s semiannual energy storage outlook sees global deployments reaching 3,098 GW/11,106 GWh in 2036, roughly 10 times today’s levels. In the U.S., near-term drivers include favorable economics for colocated storage and renewables and data centers’ growing appetite for both behind-the-meter and front-of-meter capacity, BNEF said. - BNEF’s report landed amid signs of continued momentum for the U.S. energy storage industry. On Thursday, Google said it would expand by a factor of 10 the battery-supported virtual power plant it plans to deploy with Voltus in the PJM Interconnection, to more than 1 GW. The same day, the sodium-ion battery manufacturer Peak Energy said it closed $108 million in financing from General Motors and other backers as it works to deploy nearly 5 GWh of capacity by 2030. Dive Insight: Energy storage deployments have far outpaced solar capacity additions in recent years, with the global cumulative installed solar-to-storage ratio falling from 94:1 in 2016 to 7:1 in 2026, BNEF said Thursday. BNEF sees the capacity ratio stabilizing at 4:1 in 2030, and annual deployments remaining steady at 3:1 thereafter, as the energy storage industry matures. Much of the new solar and storage capacity is colocated. The United States had installed 20.7 GW/66.4 GWh of energy storage projects colocated with 41.3 GW of solar by the end of 2025, about 30% of total colocated solar-plus-storage capacity, according to BNEF. Some 4 GW of storage was colocated with solar in the U.S. in the first nine months of 2026, the group said. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which extended federal tax credit eligibility for energy storage through 2035 while sunsetting solar eligibility later this decade, will support a pipeline of 83.7 GW/166.1 GWh of energy storage to be paired with 149.2 GW of solar, BNEF said. The robust U.S. pipeline comes despite the Trump administration imposing trade barriers BNEF characterized as world-leading, including import restrictions on foreign-made power conversion systems and recent broad limits on imports of bulk power system equipment. The combined duty on stationary storage batteries imported from mainland China is 40.9%, according to BNEF. “The US has been making the most aggressive [protectionist] efforts by favoring the domestic battery storage industry while restricting the use of supply chains involving mainland China through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and other policy measures,” the report said. Though still a relatively small share of overall U.S. battery deployment, on-site data center energy storage is growing quickly, with 4.9 GW/7.4 GWh expected this year — up from 500 MW/1.4 GWh in 2025, BNEF said. The group sees on-site data center energy storage deployments reaching 6.3 GW/8.4GWh in 2027 and continuing through the decade thanks in part to large-scale deployments like the 2.6-GW battery array NextEra Energy plans to build alongside a 2-GW gas-fired power plant at a $100 billion proposed Brookfield Asset Management computing campus in Kentucky. Multiple battery suppliers have announced firm commitments from data center customers or utilities serving them this year, BNEF said. Fluence Energy inked a $300 million deal with a data center operator for behind-the-meter batteries earlier this year, while Canadian Solar subsidiary e-Storage said in March it would deliver 500 MW/2.5 GWh of energy storage to “a major U.S. utility” in 2027 to support data center grid infrastructure. Cumulative data center energy storage could reach 36 GW/66 GWh in 2036, much of it on grids overseen by the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, PJM and the Midcontinent Independent System Operator. Data centers in PJM are more likely to use energy storage for load shifting than behind-the-meter gas due to tighter restrictions on power plant emissions in the region, BNEF said. Though lithium-iron-phosphate will remain the dominant chemistry for new energy storage deployments over the next 10 years, sodium-ion alternatives will begin to eat into its market share, reaching 9% penetration by 2036, BNEF said. Sodium-ion batteries can be passively cooled, reducing parasitic energy load, and may be more durable than lithium batteries over a 20-year service life, proponents say. Led by Google, data center operators are experimenting with alternative chemistries that can discharge power for longer than lithium- or sodium-based batteries, including a proposed 10 MW/100 MWh zinc battery in West Virginia and a 300 MW/30 GWh iron-air battery in Minnesota. But those efforts are too early to include in deployment forecasts, BNEF said.
