artigo.texto: Interferry has warned that further delays to carbon pricing for road transport could undermine the competitiveness of European ferry services, potentially encouraging freight to shift from sea to road despite the EU’s transport decarbonization objectives. In a statement issued, the ferry industry association raised concerns over ongoing negotiations concerning the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS), arguing that differences in the timing of carbon pricing between maritime and road transport are creating an uneven competitive environment. According to Interferry, European ro-ro and ro-pax operators face an estimated €1 billion in annual ETS compliance costs, while road freight continues to benefit from delays to its separate emissions trading framework. Ferry operators face rising costs as road transport avoids ETS2 Since 2024, commercial passenger and cargo vessels of 5,000 GT and above calling at European ports have been included in the EU ETS, with the maritime sector’s obligations being phased in. In an exclusive interview with SAFETY4SEA, Mike Corrigan, CEO of Interferry, identified the difference in carbon pricing between maritime and road transport as the main reason behind the association’s call for an immediate halt to further phasing-in of the maritime EU ETS. The CEO had argued that the imbalance could undermine the EU’s environmental objectives by encouraging freight and passengers to move away from ferry services towards road transport. Interferry estimates that current compliance costs are equivalent to approximately €250 per tonne of diesel fuel for affected ferry operators. Meanwhile, the EU’s ETS2, has already been postponed from 2027 to 2028 and faces pressure from several EU member states for further delays. What is the EU ETS2? As part of the 2023 revisions of the ETS Directive, a new emissions trading system named ETS2 was created. Separate from the existing EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS), this new system will cover and address the CO2 emissions from fuel combustion in buildings, road transport and additional sectors (mainly small industry not covered by the existing EU ETS). Johan Roos, Director of Regulatory Affairs at Interferry, said: “The burdens and challenges of decarbonization cannot be borne by individual sectors alone, and all transport sectors must be treated equally.” Risk of freight shifting away from ferry services The central concern is that uneven carbon pricing could have consequences beyond the ferry industry’s operating costs. Ro-ro and ro-pax services often compete directly with road transport for freight movements, particularly on routes where customers can choose between transporting goods by ferry or using an alternative land connection. According to Interferry, higher compliance costs make ferry services less competitive and can encourage freight customers to favour road transport. The association also argues that competitive pressure limits operators’ ability to pass additional costs on to customers, potentially reducing the funds available for investments in cleaner vessels and technologies. Such a development could conflict with EU efforts to encourage greater use of short-sea shipping as part of transport decarbonization. However, the extent of any resulting shift from sea to road has not been quantified in the statement, and the environmental consequences would depend on the routes and transport alternatives involved. Interferry calls for equal carbon pricing and reinvestment To address the imbalance, Interferry is calling for changes to the structure and implementation of ETS2. Furthermore, The association proposes separating road transport from building emissions under the framework, allowing carbon pricing for road freight to proceed independently of concerns over household heating costs. Alternatively, it argues that carbon costs should be applied consistently across competing transport sectors. Interferry is also calling for all revenues generated through maritime ETS compliance to be reinvested in shipping’s decarbonization, particularly through support for: - Sustainable marine fuels produced within the EU. - Cleaner vessel technologies. - Onshore charging infrastructure for ferry operations. According to the association, redirecting ETS revenues towards these measures would help operators invest in reducing emissions while addressing the financial pressures arising from compliance. The broader concern is that carbon pricing designed to support decarbonization could produce unintended consequences if competing transport modes face substantially different obligations. For ferry operators, the issue is therefore not only the cost of EU ETS compliance, but whether the regulatory framework provides consistent incentives for freight transport across sea and road.

artigo.texto: Home › Energy Storage ›GoodWe Launches ESA 125 kW/251 kWh BESS at REI Expo 2026 GoodWe Launches ESA 125 kW/251 kWh BESS at REI Expo 2026 GoodWe has launched its ESA 125 kW/251 kWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) for C&I applications at the Renewable Energy India (REI) Expo 2026, alongside showcasing its comprehensive energy storage portfolio spanning residential, commercial, and utility-scale segments. October 26, 2026. By Mrinmoy Dey At the Renewable Energy India (REI) Expo 2026, GoodWe announced the launch of its ESA 125 kW/251 kWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS), expanding its portfolio of energy storage solutions for commercial and industrial (C&I) applications. The ESA Series is suited to a wide range of use cases, including factories, commercial complexes and other grid-connected or off-grid applications. It integrates the Power Conversion System (PCS), battery cells, Energy Management System (EMS) and Battery Management System (BMS) in a single cabinet, which simplifies installation, operation and maintenance while allowing flexible capacity expansion. The system scales from hundreds of kilowatt-hours to multi-megawatt-hours, supporting up to 15 units in parallel for a total capacity of up to 3.91 MWh in on-grid scenarios. At the expo, GoodWe also presented a full range of energy storage technologies, from residential systems to large-scale utility projects. In the utility-scale energy storage segment, the company showcased AC ESS 2MW/4MWh, which offers a one-stop integrated solution with in-house-developed battery, PCS, EMU and MVS components in a 20-foot containerised design that enables easier transportation and fast deployment. With 90.5 percent round-trip efficiency, a 7 percent increase in lifetime energy throughput and an AC/DC-separated architecture, it improves project returns while enhancing safety and simplifying maintenance, the company stated. It further added that the UT Series complements this offering for large renewable energy projects and grid-connected installations. GoodWe also showcased its residential hybrid energy storage portfolio, featuring the ES Uniq + Lynx A G3 and ET LV + Lynx A G4 solution. Designed to integrate solar power, battery storage, and intelligent energy management, these solutions highlighted the potential for greater energy independence, efficient solar utilisation, and reliable power supply for modern homes. In the C&I segment, the company showcased the GT Series string inverter, which is designed to enhance productivity and deliver high power density in C&I applications. With 8/10 MPPTs, a high input current of 21A per DC string and a maximum efficiency of 99 percent, it increases overall yield with high-power PV modules. It also supports string-level monitoring and an optional PID (Potential Induced Degradation) recovery function for better module performance. Type II surge protection on both the AC and DC sides protects the inverter against lightning, giving C&I PV projects added safety, reliability and a stronger return on investment. Aniket Sawant, Country Head, GoodWe India, said, “As GoodWe celebrates 10 years in India, we remain committed to driving the country’s clean energy transition through innovative and reliable solutions. The launch of our ESA 125 kW/261 kWh BESS at REI 2026 reflects our continued focus on delivering advanced energy storage solutions across residential, C&I and utility-scale segments.” If you want to cooperate with us and would like to reuse some of our content, please contact: contact@energetica-india.net.

artigo.texto: Bartow County data center: Neighbors raise water, land concerns KINGSTON, Ga. - Community members packed a local restaurant to question developers over a massive data center proposed on more than 500 acres of rural Bartow County land. Kingston data center proposal What we know: New York City-based Thor Equities wants to build a data center along State Route 293 about two miles east of town. Organizers had to move a town-hall-style meeting from Kingston City Hall to a nearby restaurant because of high resident turnout. The developer holds a 561-acre site but plans to build on only half of the property. Developers told neighbors the site will run on a closed-loop water system to reduce municipal water consumption. Bartow County land debate What they're saying: Thor Equities Executive Vice President Raj Vohra defended the economic impact of the project during the meeting. "We're really hoping to do it in a way that will add net benefits to the community through new tax dollars," Vohra said. "We believe the community and the schools in the area can greatly benefit from [the revenue]." Vohra said. Some neighbors supported the potential financial windfall for the small town of under 1,000 residents. Resident Jody Hardin attended to verify his personal research. "I think it's good for Kingston." Hardin said. "For the revenue and everything, because we do need the revenue for improvements and everything like that here." Other neighbors voiced concerns about development swallowing rural green space. Paul Muir lives down the road from the proposed site. He says that elected leaders haven't been transparent about the zoning process. "I love farming, agriculture, conservation work, and the more development that comes to Kingston and Bartow County, the more the natural resources get pushed away," Muir said. He added: "You have economics to make money, and the forest usually loses. So my concern is the forest, my farm." Community development concerns What we don't know: Thor Equities confirmed that no client has signed a contract to occupy the planned data center facility. It remains unclear exactly which technology or enterprise companies might eventually operate on the site. Construction timing is also pending final local authorizations. If the project clears all required government reviews, construction will still take between two and four years to begin. City council permit decision What's next: The Kingston Unified Zoning Board approved a recommendation for a special use permit Monday in a 2-1 vote. The full Kingston City Council ultimately needs to approve the special use permit. The council's next meeting is scheduled for Monday, Nov. 2 at 7 p.m. The Source: The information in this story was gathered from FOX 5 Atlanta reporter Hernan Gutierrez, who attended the developer town hall and interviewed residents and company officials, as well as local zoning board records.

artigo.texto: O desenvolvimento de uma infraestrutura digital sob controle nacional, a expansão de data centers, o fortalecimento da inteligência artificial (IA) desenvolvida por empresas brasileiras e a digitalização de serviços públicos estão entre as propostas para o período de 2027 a 2030 registradas no plano de governo de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva apresentado ao Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) para a eleição de 2026. CONTEÚDO RELACIONADO – Soberania digital expõe dependência externa e pressiona Brasil por política de cibersegurança Embora o documento indique diretrizes e iniciativas para o próximo mandato, nem todas vêm acompanhadas de cronogramas, orçamento específico ou metas quantitativas de execução. Vencedor no pleito de 2026, o documento possui traz capítulo dedicado à economia digital, o documento estabelece a soberania digital como diretriz e prevê o desenvolvimento de um ecossistema nacional de tecnologia, que abrange desde a cadeia de data centers até os serviços de computação em nuvem. O texto também propõe investimentos em infraestrutura computacional, pesquisa, hardware e software de alto desempenho, além de medidas para ampliar o uso da inteligência artificial na economia. Data centers e infraestrutura computacional soberana O plano prevê ampliar a capacidade brasileira de desenvolver, operar, regular e governar tecnologias estratégicas e infraestruturas críticas. A diretriz inclui a construção de um ecossistema nacional de tecnologia digital, com atenção à cadeia de data centers e aos serviços de nuvem, além do fortalecimento da inteligência artificial desenvolvida por empresas brasileiras. Para viabilizar essa estratégia, o documento propõe mobilizar investimentos, inovação, compras governamentais e parcerias entre empresas públicas e privadas, universidades e centros de pesquisa. Também prevê avançar em uma infraestrutura computacional soberana, com supercomputadores desenvolvidos e operados por instituições nacionais. A expansão dos data centers e das infraestruturas de IA deverá, segundo o plano, ser acompanhada de salvaguardas socioambientais obrigatórias. Entre os pontos mencionados estão a eficiência energética, a utilização progressiva de fontes 100% renováveis e a avaliação dos impactos sobre os sistemas elétrico e hídrico e sobre as populações locais. O documento também estabelece que a instalação de data centers no Brasil deverá prever contrapartidas relacionadas ao conteúdo local e à oferta de capacidade computacional para o mercado interno. As medidas estão associadas à proposta de fortalecer a autonomia do país em tecnologias estratégicas e ampliar a participação nacional nas cadeias digitais. O plano, porém, não detalha nesse trecho o volume de investimentos previsto nem estabelece um cronograma específico para a implantação da infraestrutura. Inteligência artificial e desenvolvimento de tecnologia nacional A inteligência artificial aparece como um dos eixos da política para a economia digital. O programa prevê acelerar sua adoção no setor produtivo, com foco em agronegócio, saúde e serviços financeiros, além de levar a transformação digital às pequenas empresas e à economia popular. O texto também propõe investir em instituições públicas de pesquisa e desenvolvimento que já trabalham com IA e na indústria nacional de hardware e software de alto desempenho. A intenção declarada é ampliar a capacidade brasileira de desenvolver tecnologias e fortalecer os diferentes elos da cadeia digital. Outra iniciativa prevista é desenvolver e manter modelos de linguagem em português e em outras línguas, orientados a problemas do país. Para isso, o documento propõe uma plataforma nacional de dados destinada ao treinamento e à avaliação desses modelos, além do estabelecimento de regras e infraestrutura para a economia de dados. A formação de profissionais também integra a estratégia. O plano prevê desenvolver talentos para consolidar um hub nacional de competências digitais, articulando polos de inovação, universidades, centros de pesquisa e setor produtivo. O documento não especifica, nesse conjunto de propostas, quantos profissionais deverão ser formados, qual será o investimento destinado às iniciativas ou quais indicadores serão utilizados para acompanhar sua execução. Digitalização da indústria e indústria 4.0 A transformação digital da indústria é outro eixo do programa. O plano propõe ampliar a produção nacional em cadeias de valor consideradas estratégicas, fortalecer a posição do Brasil nas tecnologias relacionadas à indústria 4.0 e aumentar a incorporação de tecnologia aos processos produtivos. Entre as diretrizes estão a internalização de tecnologias, a verticalização de cadeias de produção, a digitalização ampla e a renovação do parque de máquinas industriais. O documento prevê priorizar setores de média-alta e alta intensidade tecnológica. A proposta conecta a digitalização industrial à política de desenvolvimento produtivo e à ampliação da capacidade nacional de produzir equipamentos, sistemas e soluções tecnológicas. Para o setor de tecnologia digital, esse eixo abrange oportunidades relacionadas a hardware, software, pesquisa e desenvolvimento e integração de tecnologias aos processos industriais. O programa, entretanto, não apresenta metas específicas de adoção de tecnologias digitais por segmento industrial nem um calendário detalhado para a renovação do parque de máquinas. Serviços públicos digitais e uso de IA pelo governo Na administração pública, o plano prevê ampliar o compartilhamento de infraestrutura pública digital entre os diferentes níveis de governo. A proposta está relacionada à cooperação entre União, estados e municípios para enfrentar diferenças de capacidade na prestação de serviços à população. O documento também prevê investimentos no Portal da Transparência para transformá-lo em uma plataforma inteligente baseada em dados abertos e inteligência artificial. artigo.texto: Overview: For predominantly Black neighborhoods already confronting pollution concerns, Memphis' abbreviated data center moratorium offers limited breathing room. Residents and advocates say the council's decision falls short of protecting communities from the environmental costs of AI expansion. The fray over locating more AI data centers in Memphis reached a small break Oct. 20, after a long, contentious City Council meeting in which a proposed 18-month moratorium on data-center development or expansion failed and a much shorter 135-day pause passed. “The Memphis City Council failed the people of Memphis and the mid-South tonight,” state Rep. Justin J. Pearson, a Democrat from the area, told WREG after the five-hour meeting that drew more than 400 people. LEARN MORE: A Billion-Dollar Data-Center Tax Break Along the Civil Rights Trail “The four-and-a-half-month moratorium, passed with rushed, piecemeal guidelines, was not what the people wanted,” he said. What Went Wrong Pearson, who is running for Congress in a district Republicans gerrymandered into existence, currently represents Boxtown, the historically Black neighborhood founded by freedmen in 1863. For much of the past two years, Pearson and many of his constituents have lived beside Colossus, one of Elon Musk’s three hyperscale data centers. Each data center Musk has developed in the Memphis area is located in predominantly Black neighborhoods. Pearson has made the fight against data center development a key component of his campaign. Even before the Memphis City Council met last Tuesday for a third and final vote on a proposed moratorium, the question was who would be allowed in the City Council chambers. Earlier in October, activists on both sides packed the room for the expected final vote. When the council voted to delay the decision, the meeting plunged into chaos, with heated exchanges between council members and moratorium supporters in the crowd. The council decided to delay the final vote to Oct. 20. But Pearson and five other residents who attended that meeting later received letters banning them from the next two meetings. A federal judge partly overturned the ban just hours before the council convened on Oct. 20. The moratorium failed on a tie vote. Many blamed the result on the absence of Council member Yolanda Cooper-Sutton, who co-sponsored the moratorium in August with two colleagues but missed the meeting because of a family emergency. At times, she has been a vocal critic of SpaceXAI and was at the center of the conflict during the last council meeting when she voted to delay the third and final reading of the moratorium ordinance. After verbally sparring with activists — and some fellow council members — Cooper-Sutton was suspended from her duties on two committees for 30 days. However, she was still eligible to attend and participate in this week’s pivotal meeting. Moritorium Fails, Pause Succeeds Before the vote, the original proposal for a yearlong moratorium was amended to 18 months. A shorter, 135-day pause on data centers was then introduced during the council session and was approved on a 7-5 vote. While no one seemed happy with the final result, the pause offers a brief window to figure out how to regulate data centers, which critics say consume massive amounts of power and water and pollute neighborhoods that are already fighting for cleaner air. Council members who supported the original moratorium were also frustrated. RELATED: A Massive Data Center Helped Topple a Mayor. What’s Next? “We had hundreds of people packed in there who waited for hours, Council member Jerri Green told CNN. “They’ve been pushing for this for over a year. They’re the people who are being deeply impacted by these environmental hazards.” Green said that the City Council had failed the people of Memphis. During the 135-day ban, the city will study how data centers affect residents and the resources they demand. Recommendations are also to follow on where future data centers can be located and how such facilities will be defined.

artigo.texto: Greenvolt Group, through Greenvolt Power, has agreed to sell two standalone battery energy storage system (BESS) projects in Poland to A&R Investments. The projects are located in Ełk and Turośń Kościelna in north-eastern Poland, and have a total installed capacity of 400 MW/1,600 MWh. Both projects were completed in the third quarter of 2026 and have received the required permits for use. The transaction is expected to close by the end of 2026, subject to the fulfillment of the applicable conditions. Furthermore, both Ełk and Turośń have secured 17-year capacity market contracts starting in 2028. Under these contracts, each project will receive a fixed payment for making 85 per cent of its capacity available to the system. The projects are also covered by 10-year tolling agreements, under which the batteries will be optimised and their flexibility traded in the power markets. Earlier, in October 2026, Greenvolt Power raised € 284 million in project financing for its 253.1 MW wind project in Gurbănești, located east of Bucharest, Romania. The project is currently under construction and is expected to begin commercial operations by the end of 2027.

artigo.texto: Gov. Josh Shapiro says he’s reining in Pennsylvania’s data center development after previously promising to speed it up. His Aug. 18 executive order removed data centers from the state’s Permit Fast Track Program and put new conditions on how developers can move forward. It was a marked shift for a governor who had once celebrated the industry as an economic development win. As recently as June 2025, Shapiro was touting Amazon’s planned $20 billion investment in Pennsylvania cloud computing and AI campuses, promising jobs and new opportunities for local communities. The Fast Track permit program aimed to help accelerate that growth: Data centers accounted for more than half of the projects approved for expedited permitting. Data center development has since become a campaign issue. Shapiro, a Democrat, faces Republican Stacy Garrity in the Nov. 3 election. Public sentiment has shifted significantly since Fast Track launched in November 2024. Two-thirds of likely PA voters now oppose data center construction, according to an August poll conducted by The Philadelphia Inquirer, The New York Times and Siena University. Nearly 74% of Pennsylvanians would oppose an AI data center in their community. The nine projects formerly listed in Fast Track show a mixed record. State officials credited their assistance with speeding an Amazon permit review. At least two projects, however, received no state environmental permits during their time in the program, according to Technical.ly and NewsWorks Lab’s review. Fast Track’s stated goal was to give businesses in Pennsylvania clearer timelines and greater certainty of obtaining permits necessary for construction and operations. By March of this year, data centers accounted for more than half of the projects listed on its dashboard, the Pittsburgh Media Partnership reported. The program didn’t guarantee approval or let developers bypass environmental laws and required local approvals. It did assign project managers to help speed the process. “What Fast Track did was put a coordinator in the room to keep agencies moving,” Kate Cooper, a lawyer at Pittsburgh-based law firm Babst Calland, told Technical.ly and NewsWorks Lab. “But in terms of a data center project, getting a state permit decision faster doesn’t mean that a project got delivered faster.” For Amazon’s Falls Township project in Bucks County, the Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) processed an air permit in under four months, compared with the typical six-month review, PA Secretary Jessica Shirley boasted at an August 2025 event. Removing a data center from Fast Track doesn’t cancel its permits The nine data center projects are at different stages, from planning and permit reviews to construction. Their progress also depends on local decisions that Fast Track could not make for them. “One question I get a lot is: ‘Is removal from Fast Track like a revocation of permits?’ and that’s not the case,” said Cooper, of Babst Calland. “The difference is if they’re going to work with you before or after you get your local approval.” FAQ: Pennsylvania’s Permit Fast Track Program When did the Permit Fast Track Program launch? Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro launched the PA Permit Fast Track Program in November 2024 by signing Executive Order 2024-04. The initiative was designed to speed up state permitting and licensing decisions for major economic development and critical infrastructure proposals across the commonwealth. How does the Fast Track process work? The state coordinates interagency reviews and assigns dedicated project managers, but it does not waive regulatory requirements. The Governor’s Office of Transformation and Opportunity (OTO) convenes participating state agencies to identify required permits, establish milestones and resolve interagency disputes. Progress is monitored through a public online dashboard. The program expedites the state’s administrative review clock, but it does not guarantee permit approvals, override local zoning authority or accelerate physical construction and utility hookups. What projects qualify? Any public, private or public-private entity can apply for Fast Track consideration through OTO. The coordinating office evaluates applications based on project scale, capital investment, job creation, potential economic benefit and overall public impact. Which projects are currently on the Fast Track dashboard? At publication time, the state’s PA Permit Fast Track dashboard includes seven industrial and infrastructure developments: • The Bellwether District: A 1,300-acre innovation and logistics campus on the site of the former Philadelphia Energy Solutions refinery in South Philadelphia. • Project Tribeca: A planned $1 billion-plus Johnson & Johnson pharmaceutical manufacturing facility in Montgomery County. • PennSTART: A specialized highway safety and autonomous vehicle testing facility in Westmoreland County (completed). • URBN Nuuly Bucks County: A roughly 975,000-square-foot fulfillment and laundry facility for Urban Outfitters’ clothing rental brand. • CrossRoads East Business Park (Phase 2): An industrial and commercial logistics park in Luzerne County. • Martinsburg Community Digester: An agricultural anaerobic digester project in Blair County designed to convert manure into biogas (on hold). • Century Development Industrial Park: A manufacturing and distribution facility in Lackawanna County (on hold). Which data centers were removed from Fast Track? Gov. Shapiro removed all data centers from the program in August 2026, under Executive Order 2026-05, making them permanently ineligible for Fast Track processing. Past data center project pages now redirect, but they can be found on the Wayback Machine. artigo.texto: Lula cobra regulação de big techs e contrapartidas de data centers No discurso da vitória, presidente defende inteligência artificial brasileira e reserva de capacidade de data centers para o país. Em seu discurso feito ontem à noite, 25, após a confirmação da vitória pelo TSE nas eleições de 2026, o presidente reeleito Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defendeu a regulação das plataformas digitais, a atração de data centers com contrapartidas para o Brasil e o desenvolvimento de inteligência artificial nacional em seu discurso da vitória. Ao comentar a disputa eleitoral, acusou empresas de tecnologia de interferência no processo e afirmou que crimes cometidos no ambiente digital devem receber tratamento equivalente ao dos praticados fora dele. “Essa eleição foi uma eleição em que a gente teve que vencer a intromissão vinda de fora para dentro, através de plataformas digitais”, afirmou. Na sequência, disse que será necessário regulá-las. O presidente também criticou o poder econômico e a tributação dessas empresas: “Nós não podemos ter empresas monstruosas de grana, ganhando milhões e bilhões, não pagando nenhum imposto para esse país, e tentando direcionar o resultado eleitoral desse país”. Vale lembrar que as empresas instaladas no Brasil pagam tributos locais, como ISS e IOF por remessa de capitais. Redes sociais sob fiscalização A cobrança ocorre em meio a apurações sobre as práticas de moderação das redes sociais. Em 19 de outubro, conforme noticiou o Tele.Síntese, a Agência Nacional de Proteção de Dados (ANPD) notificou a Meta para explicar os critérios usados na suspensão de contas, remoção de conteúdos e restrição do alcance de publicações no Instagram e no Facebook. Denúncias com possível repercussão eleitoral foram encaminhadas ao Tribunal Superior Eleitoral. O Ministério Público Federal também instaurou procedimento sobre a moderação da Meta e do X, a partir de uma representação de organizações que reuniram mais de mil relatos de bloqueios, remoções e suspensões durante o período eleitoral. Essas iniciativas apuram as práticas das empresas; não constituem, por si, comprovação da interferência denunciada pelo presidente. A regulação defendida por Lula encontra um cenário de mudanças nas obrigações das plataformas. No julgamento sobre o artigo 19 do Marco Civil da Internet, o Supremo Tribunal Federal ampliou as hipóteses de responsabilização por conteúdos de terceiros sem necessidade de ordem judicial prévia. Data centers com capacidade para o Brasil Na frente de infraestrutura, Lula defendeu aproveitar o potencial brasileiro de energia renovável para atrair data centers e manter dados no país. “Vão ter que deixar uma parte do data center para informações brasileiras”, declarou. A exigência tem correspondência no Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata), elaborado pelo governo federal e sancionado em 15 de setembro após aprovação na Câmara e no Senado. As empresas habilitadas terão de destinar ao mercado interno pelo menos 10% do fornecimento efetivo de processamento, armazenamento e tratamento de dados instalado com os benefícios do programa. O regime prevê suspensão de tributos federais sobre aquisição de equipamentos e componentes e estabelece contrapartidas de pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação. Também exige atendimento da demanda contratual de eletricidade com fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão e fixa requisitos de eficiência hídrica. O setor aguarda a publicação da regulamentação vai que listar os equipamentos isentos na importação. Inteligência artificial brasileira Lula também falou de inteligência artificial. Associou a formação em matemática e engenharia ao desenvolvimento de tecnologia nacional. Disse que não quer depender de inteligência artificial “chinesa ou americana” e que pretende desenvolver uma alternativa brasileira. A declaração retoma objetivos do Plano Brasileiro de Inteligência Artificial (PBIA). Em 20 de agosto, o governo anunciou uma nova etapa do plano, com investimentos em supercomputação, desenvolvimento de chips em arquitetura aberta e criação da Nuvem Brasileira,. O projeto de nuvem prevê a participação do governo e do setor privado no desenvolvimento de infraestrutura e tecnologia nacionais para armazenamento e processamento de dados. A proposta é reduzir a dependência de provedores estrangeiros em componentes críticos, adotar padrões abertos e interoperáveis e estimular fornecedores brasileiros. O pacote também prevê um supercomputador estimado em R$ 1 bilhão, a ser instalado no Parque Tecnológico Augusto Severo, da Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Norte. A execução ficará sob responsabilidade do Laboratório Nacional de Computação Científica, com recursos do FNDCT e previsão de operação no final de 2027. Outra iniciativa anunciada foi o Centro Nacional de Transparência Algorítmica e IA Confiável, na UFMG, destinado a pesquisas e ferramentas para avaliação de segurança, riscos, transparência e vieses de sistemas de inteligência artificial.

artigo.texto: Data center de R$ 7,4 bilhões começa com 100 MW, e pelo número do Século Diário, 500 das 550 vagas são de obra, cargos que duram só enquanto a construção durar Baixo Guandu, no Noroeste do Espírito Santo, perto do Rio Doce, vai receber um data center de grande porte. Segundo o A Gazeta, o projeto custa R$ 7,4 bilhões e começa com 100 MW de capacidade. O complexo pode chegar a 1 GW se a demanda crescer. O projeto se chama Projeto Rubi e é da empresa capixaba Line Solution, segundo o Século Diário. O complexo ocupa cerca de 566 hectares. Inclui ainda condomínios logístico e industrial. A operação está prevista para 2031. Quem explica as etapas é o fundador e CEO da empresa, Mário Rodrigues. Quando as obras começam? Rodrigues diz que, em Baixo Guandu, a fase atual é de engenharia, licenças ambientais e aprovação de conexões de energia. Essas etapas levam de 24 a 36 meses. - Hyundai vai abrir 3.750 vagas em fábricas de carretas nos EUA, nos antigos terrenos da Caterpillar e da Lion Electric, e um terceiro turno sozinho somou 1.250 empregos ao plano - Fender manda aviso legal a 533 funcionários de fábrica em Corona, mas a empresa garante que a parada de fim de ano não tem demissão - Macaé tem 2,7 mil cursos gratuitos de qualificação, mas nenhum é de offshore: o ciclo desta vez tem só beleza e panificação, e as inscrições já fecharam - Porto-Ilha de Areia Branca: Intersal deu lancha no 1º turno, avisou que não daria no 2º, e a Justiça mandou levar 50 embarcados às urnas sob multa de R$ 5 mil por trabalhador impedido Antes das obras físicas, a intenção é fechar contratos de pré-locação de 20 anos, em dólar, com multinacionais de tecnologia. Quantas vagas, afinal? O número muda de uma reportagem para outra. O A Gazeta fala em 300 a 500 empregos diretos, na montagem e nas obras civis. O Século Diário e a Tribuna Online falam em até 550 vagas. Pela conta do Século Diário, 500 das 550 vagas (91%, conta nossa) são de obra. Esses empregos duram enquanto a construção durar. Na operação do data center, o A Gazeta projeta cerca de 10% do total, de 30 a 50 postos para técnicos e engenheiros de alta qualificação. Para quem busca empregos fixos em Baixo Guandu, o número é bem menor que o anunciado. Quanto a prefeitura ganha com o data center? Segundo o investidor, o faturamento anual previsto passa de R$ 1 bilhão. Com a alíquota de 5% do Imposto Sobre Serviços (ISS), isso deve render entre R$ 50 milhões e R$ 60 milhões por ano para a Prefeitura de Baixo Guandu, segundo o A Gazeta. A conta bate: 5% de R$ 1 bilhão são R$ 50 milhões. A Tribuna Online cita também incentivos fiscais e a formação de condomínios logístico e industrial integrados ao data center. A água do Rio Doce entra na conta? O prefeito Lastênio Cardoso (MDB) disse ao Século Diário que a água viria de uma represa no Rio Doce. A energia já está ao lado, na Usina Hidrelétrica de Mascarenhas. Merci Fardin coordena o Observatório Capixaba da Água e do Meio Ambiente. Ele questiona o uso de água do projeto. E cobra que o data center seja avaliado junto com os outros empreendimentos anunciados para a região. Data centers usam água para resfriar servidores, e é por isso que o consumo hídrico entra na discussão. O empresário afirma, ao A Gazeta, que o resfriamento roda em circuito fechado, com a água recirculando. Ele diz que a perda por evaporação do bloco de 100 MW equivale ao consumo de três casas populares com quatro moradoras cada. Segundo ele, a água doce da região dispensa dessalinização do mar, e a proximidade com o Rio Doce pesou na escolha do local. Até o data center passar pelas licenças ambientais e pela conexão de energia, o número final de vagas e o consumo de água seguem como estimativas do investidor.

artigo.texto: Residents vent frustration after Aurora data center vote, tell city council "You failed us" Boos erupted inside the Aurora City Council chambers Monday night after a controversial vote left data center opponents feeling unheard and uncertain about what comes next. A motion to suspend council rules and reopen discussion on a proposed data center moratorium failed 6-5, falling one vote short of the seven needed to move forward. As the result was announced, residents shouted "shame" from the audience after what many viewed as one of their last opportunities to slow the rapid expansion of data centers across the city. "I'm scared for the water, I'm scared for the pollution, I'm scared for my air, I'm scared for my quality of life," one teenage resident told the council. "That's why I'm so disappointed in this." The frustration continued throughout hours of public comment. "We needed this moratorium, and you all failed us, and you failed yourselves," Aurora resident Gary Zimmerman said. One speaker accused the council of ignoring residents' concerns, while another delivered one of the night's sharpest rebukes. "These data centers, as they go up, if they do, they will be a monument to your stupidity," the man said. The five council members who voted against the motion were Rob Andrews, Francoise Bergan, Curtis Gardner, Stephanie Hancock, and Angela Lawson, which prompted immediate reactions from the crowd. Residents repeatedly argued the city should pause approvals until more protections are in place addressing concerns about water use, noise, energy consumption and proximity to neighborhoods. Councilwoman Amy Wiles, who first proposed a moratorium this summer, said she understands residents' disappointment but believes there has been confusion about what council actually voted on Monday night. She explained the vote was not on the moratorium itself; rather, council was deciding whether to suspend its rules and bring the proposal back for discussion. "A lot of people feel very blindsided about the data centers popping up, and so they don't feel heard," Wiles said. "Which I understand, and I understand their disappointment." Wiles said she shares many of the concerns she's heard from residents over the past several months and believes the city must continue working toward regulations that balance economic development with neighborhood impacts. At the same time, she's uncertain whether another attempt to advance a moratorium would be successful. Any moratorium proposed would need seven votes to pass because the effort previously failed. "I just don't know that we would ever get the seven votes to pass it," Wiles said. "And I worry that it would continually sort of give the community a little bit of false hope that it might happen, and then it doesn't happen." Still, Wiles urged residents not to view Monday night's outcome as the end of the discussion. "I don't want them to be discouraged because this didn't pass," she said. "The work is continuing; it's not stopping." While the moratorium effort appears stalled for now, city leaders are still considering a number of potential regulations for future projects. During Monday's study session, council members discussed measures including increased separation requirements between data centers and residential neighborhoods. Those proposals move next to the Planning and Zoning Commission before returning to city council for consideration.

artigo.texto: A proposed battery energy storage system in western Goleta divided the city’s Planning Commission and residents on Monday night. The commissioners voted 2-1 to recommend that the Goleta City Council defer a decision on the Greenbark 30 Battery Energy Storage System project. They noted potential fire risks and neighborhood incompatibility, and said the project needs more analysis. Commissioner Rita Serotkin was absent, and Anne Miller recused herself, citing a possible conflict of interest because of the proximity of her home to the project site. Developing Vacant Land on Viajero Drive Scale Microgrids LLC proposes installing 36 Tesla Megapack 2 XL battery units on a 2.1-acre site at an unaddressed location on Viajero Drive, which could provide up to 30 megawatts of stored power. The project has been in the works for about two years, according to project staff. The proposed system is expected to enhance the existing grid by storing power during peak generation. That power could then be discharged during peak demand or emergencies, according to city planner Travis Lee. The site is near the Ellwood Generating Station, Ellwood Elementary School and Westmont of Santa Barbara, a senior-living residential community formerly known as Mariposa at Ellwood Shores. “I support battery storage systems,” Commissioner Jennifer Fullerton said, “but I cannot support one in this location.” She called for a full environmental impact report, saying she was left with unanswered questions and that the project was incompatible with the area. “The location was selected because it’s the ideal location for a battery storage project in this area,” said Nelson Gould, an Environmental Resources Management Inc. project consultant. The project could “tap into” the Ellwood Generating Station’s Southern California Edison interconnection point and thus not need new development or transmission lines, Gould added. The project also would require a General Plan amendment to change the site’s zoning to office institutional to make way for the project, according to Lee. The proposed battery storage facility, however, is not adequate to serve the entire South Coast, and the ability to use that energy during power shutoffs depends on the ability to create islands with certain portions of the grid, according to Peter Imhof, Goleta’s planning and environmental review director. The project could provide power for four hours, enough power to support up to 30,000 homes within the greater Goleta area, according to Gould. Commissioner Cary Penniman agreed with Fullerton and advocated for further review. “I would like to bring the public up to speed on this. I would like to get up to speed. It’s super fascinating,” he said. “Let’s just not rush into it.” Goleta plans to analyze land use within the city to determine which areas would be appropriate for utility-scale battery storage, according to Imhof. Planning Commission members and some residents wanted the city to complete that study before making a final decision. “That is a little bit of a different time horizon than this project,” Imhof said. “We didn’t feel like we could hold up this project in order to complete that comprehensive planning effort.” A study found potentially significant environmental impacts associated with the facility’s construction and operation, but mitigation measures could reduce the impacts, Lee said. Goleta already has another battery energy storage system at 6864 Cortona Drive that was approved about five years ago, according to Mary Chang, a supervising city senior planner. Commissioner Katie Maynard said denying a recommendation of approval for the project would mean the city held the two projects to different standards. “I wish that we did have that more comprehensive assessment, but we didn’t ask the other battery storage project to wait,” she said. Commissioners Penniman and Fullerton voted to defer the decision, and Maynard opposed. The vote also carried a recommendation to postpone a General Plan amendment, ordinance amendment and development plan. Goleta Residents Divided in Stances A group of Goleta residents also pushed for approval of the project, citing its community benefits of renewable energy and electrical grid resilience. “I believe the Greenbark project will make the area safer, not riskier, while providing economic benefits and helping keep the power on for really critical needs,” said Katie Davis, a Sierra Club volunteer and Goleta resident. She added that she toured the larger Cortona Drive battery storage facility and noted it was “very quiet” and “three times closer” to homes. More than 20 local organizations and groups, including the Santa Barbara Unified School District, the nonprofit Clean Coalition and Mariposa at Ellwood Shores, the former name of the nearby senior-living community, are listed in a joint letter supporting the project. The batteries proposed for the vacant site are the “exact same” as those on various Santa Barbara Unified School District campuses, said Craig Lewis, Clean Coalition’s founder and executive director. He added that a battery fire is comparable to a house fire, citing nonfatal risks to human life unless someone is “in the fire.” “This is not something where people with pitchforks should be out here, screaming about this,” Lewis said. He also pointed to the fact that the project garnered the support of the nearby retirement home. However, one senior-living facility resident said otherwise. Westmont of Santa Barbara resident Jo Ann Winter said residents and facility management discussed the project but did not hear that management was in support. She said the 67 disabled and senior residents who live at Westmont of Santa Barbara and the Ellwood Elementary School community could be exposed to “toxic fumes” if a fire were to break out. artigo.texto: Croatian company ENNA Solar has signed an agreement to acquire a solar power project with a battery energy storage system in Romania. The Medgidia project comprises a solar power plant with a planned installed capacity of 166 MWp and a battery energy storage system (BESS) with a capacity of 612 MWh. Subject to obtaining the required regulatory approvals, the project will further expand ENNA Group’s renewable energy project portfolio in the Romanian market, ENNA Solar, a member of ENNA Group, said. ENNA Solar has signed a share purchase agreement setting out the terms for the acquisition of a 100% equity stake in the Romanian special-purpose company CIC Grenn Energy Medgidia, which holds the rights to develop the photovoltaic plant and its associated BESS. The project covers 204 hectares of land Construction of the Medgidia project is scheduled to begin in the first quarter of 2027. The solar power plant is expected to enter commercial operation and begin supplying electricity to the grid in the first quarter of 2028, ENNA Group stressed. Expected annual electricity generation amounts to 265,932 MWh. The completion of the transaction and the transfer of the equity stake to ENNA Solar are subject to approval by the competent Romanian authority responsible for screening foreign direct investment (FDI), and approval from the relevant competition authorities in the applicable jurisdictions. The project is located in the Medgidia area, in Romania’s Constanța county, and covers approximately 204 hectares of land. Napast: The deal reaffirms our ambition to expand significantly into Central and Eastern European markets “Medgidia represents a significant step forward in the continued development of ENNA Group’s energy portfolio and the strengthening of our presence in the sizable Romanian market. It also reaffirms our ambition to expand significantly into Central and Eastern European markets, where we see further investment opportunities,” Boštjan Napast, President of the Management Board of ENNA Group, pointed out. He noted that the company is interested in renewable energy projects that are at an advanced stage of development or ready for construction. First major investment outside of Croatia The Medgidia acquisition builds on ENNA Group’s existing investments in Romania. ENNA Solar has already acquired the Mihăilești solar power project, with an installed capacity of 87.52 MWp, which is now at an advanced stage of construction. The project also includes a 140 MWh BESS, with commercial operation expected to begin in April 2027. Back in late December 2025 ENNA started the construction of this solar power plant. It is the company’s first major investment outside of Croatia. It also signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) on renewable energy projects in Azerbaijan. Wisconsin has a multi-billion dollar budget surplus, and voters surveyed by the most recent Marquette University Law School poll said some of the most important issues to them revolve around affordability, healthcare, taxes and data centers. WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” invited both candidates for governor to sit down for one-on-one interviews about their positions on voters’ top concerns. Understanding Wisconsin, Together. WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter. Republican Tom Tiffany’s campaign declined the invitation, citing his busy schedule of events. Democrat David Crowley joined WPR host Kate Archer Kent last Thursday to share his plans for the state if he’s elected governor. The following was minimally edited for clarity. Kate Archer Kent: We’re fielding questions from WPR listeners for candidates for governor, and one question that comes up a lot is about lowering everyday costs like groceries and gas. Wisconsin ended the last fiscal year with over $3 billion in surplus. What would you propose lawmakers do with that money? David Crowley: Well, the first thing we have to do is actually tackle the affordability crisis. No matter where you go in the state of Wisconsin, each community member lets you know that they can’t afford the groceries, how that has gone up, the diesel and the gas prices, as well as renting or owning a home. And so, first and foremost, we want to pass the minimum markup law, repealing that particular sales tax as it relates to gas. That’s 40 cents a gallon that each person is paying at the pump, and we want to make sure that we can lower those costs, not just at the pump, but that will help to lower costs also in our grocery stores because of the amount of gas and diesel that they are utilizing. It’s also about utilizing that surplus to buy down the property taxes. So many communities across Wisconsin have gone through referendum after referendum just to make sure that our schools have enough resources to make sure that our children have what they need to build upon that foundation of learning. Funding our public schools here in the state of Wisconsin would naturally ease the property tax pressures that many of our older adults are feeling while being on a fixed income. But we also have to tackle healthcare. So many people have seen their premiums double or seen their doctor’s office, their clinics and their hospitals close because a trillion dollars were cut from the Medicaid/Medicare program with the help of Congressman Tom Tiffany. So we need to make sure that we expand BadgerCare across this state, which will not only help those who are uninsured and underinsured, but this will help everybody who has insurance to help lower their costs and, more importantly, make sure that you can get access to care whenever and whenever you need it. Also for those who have families or those who want a family, we know that childcare is not just expensive; it’s not accessible. The more we can work with our childcare providers to provide the floor of funding that they need and make sure that we can provide a slot for every working family — that’s going to provide every working adult to enter into the workforce or make the best decision for them and their family to get ahead. KAK: One thing I didn’t hear on your list was whether you would put any part of the surplus to send tax refunds to residents. Gov. Tony Evers and lawmakers pushed that bipartisan deal earlier this year. Would you try for one again? DC: When it came down to that deal, if I was the governor, I absolutely would have signed it. But unfortunately, my opponent actually pushed back and convinced many of the Republicans not to vote for that deal. I know what’s important is that we work with our legislative leaders and the legislature in general to make sure that we can come up with a bipartisan deal that works for everyone. I am open to doing whatever we can to make sure that we’re providing relief for the hardworking Wisconsinites that can’t get ahead. KAK: Your position on data centers has shifted recently. Over the summer, you said Wisconsin should not repeal state data center incentives. More recently, you’ve said you would absolutely sign a repeal. What has changed? DC: I’ve always been open to reforming the sales tax exemptions that the data centers have been getting. If we were to get a bill that came to my desk, I absolutely would sign it. I believe in those reforms because we have seen not just billionaires but big tech companies who have already received $80 billion in tax breaks from the federal government — a bill that my opponent actually supported and voted for. People are struggling to put food on the table, struggling to afford their rent or to afford their mortgage, struggling to put gas into their tanks. We need to be providing relief for them, not for the billionaire tech companies who are steamrolling communities with these data centers. We have to make sure that if a community doesn’t want a data center, they shouldn’t be forced to have one. They need to have a seat at the table. On day one, the legislature and I are going to get right to work to make sure that we have those guardrails in place to protect our communities. KAK: Would those guardrails entail a pause, a statewide moratorium? DC: I think right now we are effectively in a de facto moratorium. I know that there was recently a lawsuit, and now we’re going to have our Department of Natural Resources conducting an environmental analysis about what these data centers can actually do to our environment, and so I believe that we should continue to have a pause while this process plays out. artigo.texto: Simplified: Hundreds of people filled Carnegie Town Hall for a more than three-hour public meeting on Tuesday night to talk about data centers and share concerns with elected officials from the Sioux Falls City Council and the Lincoln County Commission. But unlike the typical long line of public input – though that was still part of it – this meeting gave a full hour for public officials to chat in small groups with residents. Why it matters - Earlier this year, the Sioux Falls City Council voted unanimously to pave the way for a hyperscale data center in northeast Sioux Falls after four hours of public input – largely in opposition. - Since then, residents have turned up time and time again to speak out against data centers at public meetings, including a contentious joint city-county meeting in August at which point officials agreed to the public meeting held Tuesday night. - Tuesday's meeting was a unique format centered on civic engagement and listening to residents. Residents arranged themselves in groups of 10-15 people, and both councilors and commissioners moved from group to group listening and discussing unanswered questions on data centers, impacts on the community and what expertise officials should seek as they look to establish policy around these facilities. "It's very different to sit down one-on-one with people to talk compared to getting emails or hearing people at the dais," Councilor James Oppenheimer said, adding, "It’s a very clear message from the public that they are not in favor of having data centers in Sioux Falls." Tell me more Tuesday's meeting started with a presentation from Brent Van Aartsen, chief technology officer for Dakota State University, who spoke as a subject-matter expert on data centers. Van Aartsen outlined the types of data centers and the various ways in which they operate. - After that, planning officials from the city and county shared the existing zoning ordinances and where data centers might be permitted. Then – in a move atypical of local government – the meeting recessed for a full hour while officials spoke to small groups of residents to hear their specific questions and concerns. After that, councilors and commissioners shared their takeaways before opening up to another hour-plus of public input before recessing around 10:15 p.m. Takeaways from officials included acknowledging the overall agreement that people don't want hyperscale data centers in Sioux Falls. "It is so interesting in this country today, nobody gets along on anything except for data center opposition," Commissioner Joel Arends said. "The community is prioritizing quality fo life over the perceived or real benefits of a data center." Additionally, councilors and commissioners noted still-unanswered questions about how any rules they put into place now would impact the proposed Gemini data center in northeast Sioux Falls. What happens next? The Sioux Falls City Council has engaged its Regulatory Oversight Committee to look closer at potential ordinances related to data centers. That group's next meeting will be Nov. 9. Folks are also able to share feedback online. - Councilors also asked for feedback on whether the community would like to see more of these types of public meetings with space for residents to talk directly with elected officials.

artigo.texto: The AI boom has led to a gargantuan surge in energy demand across the country. Critics say this upswell in connections is enacting a stress test on America’s aging grid infrastructure. Worries abound that, in the short term, the energy crunch could lead to surging electrical bills and, in the long term, may eventually lead to outages or other technical problems. At TechCrunch Disrupt earlier this month, industry insiders tempered much of this criticism with optimism about how the flood of new energy connections could actually be opening the door for grid modernization. Apoorv Bhargava, founder and CEO of WeaveGrid, Tim Heidel, CEO of Veir, and Kristin Eberhard, VP of policy at Rewiring America, said that though the grid faces new challenges, there are also plenty of new opportunities as well. “It’s a very different electric grid, right?” said Bhargava. “We’re dealing with a ton of new variables, including renewable energy. We’re dealing with a ton of new load in the form of electric vehicles and data centers and heat pumps, and the ability to manage and orchestrate is fundamentally what utilities are now grappling with.” While all of those new connections are driving an ever larger amount of stress to the grid, Bhargava’s company hopes to provide the kind of load orchestration and management that helps utilities maximize the potential of the current system. WeaveGrid’s software can help organizations efficiently deploy energy while also optimizing connections to reduce utility payers’ bills, the founder said. Heidel, on the other hand, runs a company that is working to build out and expand the physical infrastructure of the grid, while also making it run much more efficiently. Veir sells superconductive power lines that promise to transfer energy at a much more efficient rate than traditional ones. Veir’s cables can carry power five times farther than traditional cables while also requiring 20 times less space, the company has said. Earlier this month the startup raised $110 million in a Series C funding round. “The scale of the investment in AI infrastructure is driving a tremendous amount of innovation,” said Heidel. “There’s a ton of new technologies that are coming off the shelves and starting to get to scale that, pulled together, can actually really make sure that data centers are the best community neighbors and citizens they can possibly be.” He added: “I think that we really need to look at ways that we can really adopt all of that as fast as possible to ease this next stage of growth.” Eberhard, whose organization advocates for household electrification, also said that while the surge in data center energy demand has spurred a new urgency to the modernization cause, it has also created an environment where industries are ready to try new things. “I feel like this era of AI and load growth is a very improv era,” Eberhard said. “There’s a lot of yes-and-ing going on. So yes, we need more transmission lines. Yes, we need more centralized power plants, and we also need to make sure that we’re taking advantage of all this other stuff that we had previously been leaving on the table when we didn’t have this urgency of the AI demand.”

artigo.texto: Hopkins County Fiscal Court hosts public session on data centers MADISONVILLE, Ky. (WFIE) - Data centers drew another packed house Monday, this time inside the Hopkins County Fiscal Courtroom, as county leaders opened the floor for public comment on the facilities and their potential impact on the community. It’s a scene that’s become familiar across the tri-state in recent months, as data centers tied to the artificial intelligence boom have become a hot-button issue in county after county — and Hopkins County is no exception. County leaders said the meeting was designed to give residents an opportunity to raise questions, thoughts or concerns about data centers before any new ordinances or other proceedings move forward. One of many to speak, Hopkins County resident Michael Howard, didn’t mince words about the technology behind the facilities. “Data centers are infrastructure for artificial intelligence. Artificial intelligence is the most dangerous technology that humankind has ever invented, bar none, including atomic power, including genetic engineering,” Howard said. Overflow From a Madisonville Meeting Monday’s meeting came just a week after the city of Madisonville hosted its own public comment session on a draft data center ordinance, and many of the same residents showed up again — some from Madisonville itself, even though Monday’s meeting was a county matter, not a city one. Several speakers used the opportunity to tie the issue directly to next week’s election, criticizing Madisonville’s city administration in the process. “Why in the world do we even want to consider a data center? The mayor stood up, I heard him on the radio, ‘I’m for data center.’ He stood up and said he was. So vote him out when the election comes up,” Hopkins County resident Billy McKinsey said, drawing applause from the crowd. “Vote him out.” Environmental and Quality-of-Life Concerns Beyond the political back-and-forth, many residents who spoke Monday raised concerns about the day-to-day impact data centers could have on the county — from water and electrical usage to noise pollution and the loss of farmland and other environmental effects. Several speakers also pushed back on the idea that the issue breaks down along party lines. “This isn’t a Republican or a Democrat issue. It’s a human issue. We are everyday young professionals, parents, grandparents who have started to research and understand this issue. And the more we learn, the more concerned we become,” Hopkins County resident Marie Moyer said. What’s Next Monday’s session was limited to public comment — no votes or formal decisions were made. But officials say the feedback collected will factor into future discussions, including any new ordinances Hopkins County may consider to regulate data centers going forward. The county’s meeting follows closely on the heels of Madisonville’s own effort to draft data center regulations. City officials there are considering an ordinance that would restrict data centers to General Industrial zoning districts, require them to sit at least 250 feet from homes, schools, churches and daycares, cap building height at 75 feet, limit nighttime noise to 50 decibels, and require developers — not other ratepayers — to cover the cost of utility upgrades needed to serve large facilities. That ordinance has not yet been adopted, and city officials have said it can still be revised ahead of any vote. Madisonville’s public comment period on its draft ordinance was limited to a combined 10 minutes, a restriction that frustrated many residents who felt it didn’t allow enough time for the number of people who showed up wanting to speak. With both a city ordinance and now county-level discussions underway, data centers are expected to remain a central issue in Hopkins County in the weeks ahead. Copyright 2026 WFIE. artigo.texto: By Ashley Murray States Newsroom SPRINGDALE, Pa. – Residents in a small southwestern Pennsylvania town are facing the prospect of a 47-acre data center facility on their doorstep. “Right here behind this fence is where they want to put up the data center, and as you can see, there’s houses right across the street, roughly 100 feet,” said lifelong Springdale borough resident Cathy Mager, stretching her arms to show the distance from the development site’s perimeter to a line of houses across Porter Street. “We don’t want it,” she told States Newsroom on Oct. 19. The scenario is playing out around the United States. Both Democratic and Republican candidates during the heated midterm election cycle have had to navigate deep voter resentment of the massive advanced computer server farm developments that will power artificial intelligence. “The issue has blown up over the last year,” said Darrell West, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution’s Center for Technology. “It wasn’t that long ago politicians were fighting to bring data centers to their communities. Now these facilities are completely controversial, and many people don’t want them in their neighborhood. So public opinion has changed very rapidly on this issue.” 53 Years with a Power Plant Mager is among a few dozen residents in Springdale, in northeastern Allegheny County, who formed the group Save Allegheny Valley Environment to protest the proposed data center development on the community’s riverfront site of a coal-fired power plant that went offline in 2022. “We’ve already lived for 53 years under that power plant,” said Vicki Wanamaker, 66, a lifelong Springdale resident who lives about a 10th of a mile from the fencing around the site. She’s worried now about the noise a data center would bring to the neighborhood, with its water coolers running and backup diesel generators on site, and whether she would experience electricity shortages. Springdale’s council voted 5-2 in December to approve a conditional use permit for the project by Dynamo DC, a company with a Springdale-based address that “builds AI data centers on environmentally remediated brownfield sites,” according to its website. Residents are now asking Allegheny County to stop further land use plans. Dynamo DC spokesperson Brian Regli said the developers will use “acoustical shielding” to keep noise well below ordinance levels. The hyperscale data center will recycle 500,000 gallons of water in a closed-loop system to cool the servers, he told States Newsroom during an interview in late October. The facility is planned to handle up to 240 megawatts, which it will pull from a regional electricity grid, Regli said. Dynamo DC has not yet identified which company or contractors will actually use the data center. The company plans for the data center to go online by 2029. Regli said the company is exploring “environmentally conscious” fuels for the diesel backup generators. The amount of backup power needed for the site will ultimately depend on how the data center is used. Some uses “may need a fraction of the backup power that we put forward,” he said. “But you know, if this is a critical facility, let’s say it is being used by the military – which I doubt that the center would become that, but let’s use that as an example – you’re going to want to have as robust of a backup infrastructure as you can,” Regli said. Amie Downs, of Caveat Communications, which is providing communications for Springdale, said the borough “was able to negotiate a number of other provisions that benefit the community and its taxpayers that relate to noise, lighting, traffic, landscaping and other requirements, imposing stricter standards than the borough’s ordinances otherwise required.” Thousands of Data Centers Planned Data centers are a linchpin of the modern internet, but the scale needed for advanced computing is new. There are 1,394 data centers already operating around the United States, and they carry a combined capacity of 64,764 megawatts. As of October, 2,841 more data centers are planned and would add 413,152 megawatts of additional capacity, according to the energy market firm Cleanview’s data center project tracker. “What we’re seeing now is huge facilities that are being built. These are data centers that occupy the size of several football fields,” said West, who also publishes the progressive organization’s TechTank and is a senior fellow on governance studies. “They require a lot of energy. Some of them require water as well. So the size of the data centers creates public anxiety and worry.” Sixty-three percent of American adults say they don’t want a data center built in their community, according to a late August poll published by YouGov and The Economist. A CNN poll conducted in mid-September found nearly two-thirds of registered voters surveyed said AI and data center development will be an extremely or very important factor in their vote this midterm election. The poll also found a partisan divide: Democrats are 26 percentage points more likely than Republicans to say they’re very concerned about data centers, according to the results. From Trump on Down The issue is permeating politics and races at the federal, state and local levels. President Donald Trump on Wednesday wrote on his Truth Social platform that data centers “are mandated by me to make their own electricity.” “If companies want to make their Data Centers popular, pay the community, and/or individuals within the community, a ‘dividend.’ … MAKE DEALS, and get them built!!!” he wrote. The statement is a pivot from his late August post, when he called opponents of data center developments “backwards and poor.” Resentment against the large-scale projects has become a dominant issue in hotly contested U.S. Senate races that will determine party control for the closely divided upper chamber. artigo.texto: Where Solid-State Micro-Cooling Fits in Data Centers Solid-state micro-cooling could help data centers reduce hotspots in SSDs and other subsystems that liquid cooling and system fans don't fully reach. Managing heat in AI infrastructure is getting more complicated as rising power density turns thermal design into a performance constraint. Liquid cooling is increasingly focused on high-power CPUs and GPUs, but not every heat-producing component in a server sits under a cold plate. SSDs, memory, retimers, and optical subsystems can still develop localized hotspots that affect throughput and reliability. That is the gap xMEMS says its solid-state micro-cooling technology is designed to address. The company has begun mass production of its XMC-2400 and XMC-4800 chips, which use a silicon-based design to move air without rotating blades or bearings. xMEMS says the products mark the first large-scale commercialization of solid-state active cooling for edge AI systems. “As AI infrastructure evolves, component-level cooling will become an increasingly important complement to traditional system-level thermal management,” Mike Housholder, vice president and general manager of the Thermal Management Business Unit at xMEMS, told Data Center Knowledge. Why Liquid Cooling Leaves Some Hotspots Untouched Cold plates remove heat from the surface they touch directly. In liquid-cooled servers, that can leave some subsystems with uneven thermal coverage. xMEMS sees enterprise SSDs as the clearest near-term example. Housholder said a cold plate attached to one side of an SSD can cool the controller and some NAND packages, while NAND on the opposite side may run hotter. That temperature gradient, he said, can contribute to thermal throttling and limit I/O performance during sustained workloads. “We see enterprise SSDs as the strongest near-term use case,” Housholder said. “As AI workloads drive faster storage and more sustained data transfers, thermal throttling can limit SSD performance.” The company argues that localized airflow inside the drive can reduce that imbalance. “Placing uCooling inside the SSD to cool the opposite-side NAND can reduce or remove this temperature gradient to maximize performance,” Housholder said. He added that similar thermal challenges are beginning to emerge in other dense AI infrastructure components. How Solid-State Micro-Cooling Works Unlike a conventional fan, solid-state active cooling uses a silicon chip to generate directed airflow. xMEMS builds its uCooling chips on a piezoMEMS semiconductor platform and says the all-silicon design can deliver high-pressure airflow through narrow micro-channels without the mechanical wear associated with small rotating fans. According to xMEMS, the XMC-2400 delivers up to 28 cubic centimeters of airflow per second at up to 1,300 Pa of back pressure and consumes about 150 milliwatts (mW). The XMC-4800, which the company is targeting for enterprise SSDs, delivers up to 48 cubic centimeters per second at up to 1,100 Pa and consumes about 240 mW. “At approximately the size of a thumbnail, the XMC-2400 can be embedded into highly constrained environments to deliver highly targeted airflow to heat-generating components where conventional approaches are difficult to implement or scale,” Housholder said. (Image: xMEMS) Why Micro-Cooling Is a Complement to Existing Cooling Systems The company is not positioning the technology as an alternative to rack- or server-level cooling. Housholder said its airflow is only a fraction of what a conventional system fan can provide, making it better suited to localized hotspots inside tightly packaged subsystems than to whole-system thermal management. “Solid-state active cooling is best viewed as a complementary technology that helps address localized hotspots within a broader cooling architecture, rather than a replacement for conventional cooling methods,” Housholder said. “Comparatively, uCooling’s airflow is a small fraction of that from a conventional system fan, but its ability to be embedded inside hard-to-reach subsystems brings value to the overall system thermal architecture.” In practice, that means the technology is more likely to arrive as part of another component than as a field-installed data center retrofit. xMEMS says uCooling can be mounted on flex or rigid PCBs and pre-assembled inside subsystems such as SSDs and laser modules, where airflow is difficult to deliver with chassis fans or cold plates alone. Where Solid-State Micro-Cooling Could Expand Next Longer term, xMEMS sees a path toward co-packaging thermal solutions that bring cooling closer to the processor package itself. For mainstream data center processors, however, Housholder said air-based micro-cooling may give way to liquid micro-channel designs because of the power density involved. He said air-based uCooling is likely to be more viable in edge AI systems, where thermal envelopes are lower and space constraints are tighter. “Given the power density of data center processors, liquid (not air) micro-channels in the co-packaging architecture may be the next step,” Housholder said. “There are likely applications in co-packaging at the edge that are more viable for our air-based uCooling.” The future of cooling is likely to incorporate a combination of technologies. “Longer term, we expect future thermal architectures to combine liquid cooling, passive thermal solutions and localized active cooling technologies working together to optimize overall system performance,” Housholder said.
