artigo.texto: Construction Of Military Data Center On Maui Alarms Residents The nearly $100 million facility would work in conjunction with seven proposed telescopes near the summit of Haleakalā. The lab and data center are expected to be completed early next year. The controversial telescopes that the military is seeking to build in a state conservation district atop Haleakalā would be remotely operated from a two-story, 56,000-square-foot laboratory and data center that is currently under construction in Kīhei. Federal officials from the U.S. Air Force and U.S. Space Force finalized plans to build the nearly $100 million facility at the Maui Research and Technology Park around the same time that they proposed adding up to seven telescopes to the military’s existing space surveillance complex on the volcano’s summit. But while the telescopes have drawn intense public backlash, the Kīhei project flew under the public’s radar for several years. Environmentalists, Native Hawaiian advocates and other Maui residents have in recent weeks called attention to the planned South Maui facility and criticized the military for failing to more explicitly disclose its connection to the new telescopes planned for Haleakalā’s 10,000-foot summit. By introducing the two projects separately, federal officials were able to circumvent questions about their relationship and cumulative environmental impact, according to Hina Kneubuhl, an organizer with Protect Haleakalā, a collective of Hawaiian cultural practitioners, environmentalists, community leaders and others working to protect culturally significant landscapes. “They segment these projects, and it’s so deceptive. All of us who don’t have time to do this, were trying to catch them while we’re catching all of these balls flying in the air,” Kneubuhl said during an Office of Hawaiian Affairs community listening session on Maui earlier this month. Because the telescopes would be built on state land that has been set aside for the federal government, the project cannot move forward until military officials have completed an extensive environmental impact statement and review process that requires opportunities for public feedback. The Kīhei facility — called the Secure Integration Support Laboratory, or SISL — is being built on private property that the federal government purchased in 2023, so officials were only required to complete an environmental assessment, a less rigorous process than required for an environmental impact statement. According to the 2022 draft assessment, Air Force officials concluded that no significant adverse effects would result from building the facility. “Where is the transparency regarding its water and electricity demands?” Lisa Yamada said during the OHA meeting last week. “Our families, farmers and communities are already struggling for these precious resources. Our ʻāina and wai should not be sacrificed for military expansion.” “Our younger generations are rising to protect our kūpuna, our culture and our ʻāina.” Construction of the South Maui facility began in late 2024 and is expected to be completed early next year, according to the government contract awarded to Hensel Phelps. The project was designed to consolidate all of the U.S. Space Force 15th Space Surveillance Squadron’s operations across Maui from four facilities into one. It will include a high-performance data center, laboratories, a remote telescope operations center, offices, a conference center, warehouse space and associated infrastructure, according to an April 2023 design document. The draft environmental assessment did not include detailed information about the project’s water consumption, but it projected that consolidating the military’s operations would result in reduced water and energy consumption by the Air Force on Maui over the life of the facility. There would be additional “short-term minor adverse effects on potable water use,” during the early stages of the project, according to the document. Water for the facility would be supplied from an existing Maui County reservoir at the eastern end of Lipoa Road, and the draft environmental assessment proposed adding a new half-million gallon storage tank to increase capacity. It would also include an emergency 2,500-kilowatt generator, as well as a 12,000-gallon tank and three 20,000-gallon tanks to store a two-week supply of diesel fuel capable of powering the entire building in the event of an electricity outage. Some residents have raised concerns about storing such large amounts of fuel in the wildfire-prone area, especially because federal officials have not yet finished cleaning up a 720-gallon diesel fuel spill caused by a lightning strike at the Maui Space Surveillance Complex on Haleakalā in January 2023. There are also heightened public concerns about military fuel storage tanks after the Navy’s underground oil storage facility at Red Hill on Oʻahu leaked in 2021, poisoning tap water for thousands of residents and service members in the area. Like existing military operations in South Maui, the new facility would be connected to and receive data from the Maui Space Surveillance Complex on the Haleakalā summit via fiber optic cable, according to the draft environmental impact statement for the planned telescopes. Despite years of pushback from residents, federal officials have maintained that the military needs to build new telescopes and improve its space surveillance capabilities on Maui to track and identify threats among satellites and other objects orbiting the Earth above the Pacific. In addition to concerns about the potential negative impact on cultural and environmental resources, many community members have expressed worry that the military could use new facilities on Maui for war-fighting efforts and that the island could soon become a target for foreign adversaries. artigo.texto: Texas' rapidly growing data center industry could reverse much of the state's progress on air quality by the end of the decade, according to a new report released Tuesday. The air emissions report published by the Houston Advanced Research Center revealed that the industry's impact on air quality depends heavily on how data centers are powered. The outlook is far worse if the facilities rely on natural gas plants. "What we are showcasing here is that there is a significant increase in different pollutant emissions that needs to be addressed because otherwise this could have strong implications for the population and environment," said Carlos Gamarra, vice president for energy, air and IT for HARC, whose team produced the air quality impact scenarios. Between 2002 and 2024, Texas sharply cut its major air pollutants -- particularly from transportation, industry and the power generation sectors -- even as the state's population grew by millions and its economy roughly doubled, according to the report, which used federal and state agencies' data on air emissions. At least 288 data center projects are planned across the state, according to a recent Texas Tribune analysis. The scale of the projected data center build-out means that the sector's future emissions trajectory now depends heavily on how electricity is supplied. According to the report's modeling, emissions could plausibly range from a marginal increase to a reversal of two decades of progress in reducing air emissions. By 2031, the report projects that statewide nitrogen oxide emissions could rise 35% -- even under a cleaner "net zero" scenario where data centers connect to the grid and deploy wind and solar on site. Under a different scenario where data centers choose traditional on-site natural-gas power sources, those emissions could increase nearly 400%. Such emissions can damage the human respiratory system with long-term exposure, causing chronic lung disease. "We need to treat data centers as the industrial facilities they are ... to hold them accountable to the same industrial and power generation emissions standards that produced Texas progress," Gamarra said. The report's researchers argue that it's not too late to stop this outcome. Instead of relying on the cheapest, fastest power options, Gamarra said, Texas lawmakers and industry leaders have the opportunity to shape the state's air quality by choosing cleaner choices like renewable and wind and implementing regulation that could help reduce the impact. HOW DO DATA CENTERS IMPACT AIR QUALITY? Data centers need electricity to keep their servers running. Those servers also need cooling systems to avoid overheating, and some of the most water-efficient technologies use the most electricity to operate. As AI computing chips get more powerful and run at hotter temperatures, the need for cooling increases -- and that means more energy. Data centers can get that electricity in a number of ways. Historically, the most common method has been connecting to the Texas power grid. But there's a wait to get connected. The Electric Reliability Council of Texas, the grid operator, in the last two years received over 500 requests to connect large electricity users, many of which are data centers, compared to two dozen such requests the year before that, according to state records from this summer. Proposed data centers in Texas range from five to 11,000 megawatts in planned capacity, which reflects the maximum power an individual facility could use in any given moment. The estimated electricity that large projects could need from the grid added up to 439 gigawatts -- which would equal roughly a third of all the power generation in America. Gov. Greg Abbott has temporarily halted new data centers from connecting to the state's power grid pending an audit examining each facility's power demand, water and cooling use, public financial assistance and community impacts. Data center developers and operators that can't wait for a grid connection look for alternatives. "The challenge right now is for these data centers when they try to connect to the grid, they have long timelines, like three to five years, and they cannot wait," Gamarra said. "So they start deploying their own on-site energy systems, and they don't always pick the cleanest version of on-site generation because of timelines." He also notes that cleaner, more renewable technologies cannot always provide continuous energy to the data centers. Operators that choose cleaner technologies pay a higher price. GOING BACK ON TEXAS AIR QUALITY PROGRESS Researchers modeled how four power supply scenarios could affect air pollutant levels over the next five years, based on projections of data center energy demand. The report studied a number of scenarios, comparing pollution from data centers connected to the grid versus combinations of on-site generation, including natural gas, solar and wind. Gamarra attributed Texas's declining emissions over the past two decades to changes in the electricity mix, especially the growth of wind and solar, pollution controls across power generation for industry and transportation, and the retirement of coal-fired generation. That progress could be reversed if natural gas plants are the primary power sources for data centers. Levels of nitrogen oxides would increase 136% by 2031 and approach the level they were at in 2004. Volatile organic compounds would exceed their 2002 level by 32%. Levels of particulate matter, microscopic particles that can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream, would increase to levels not seen since 2006. Some scientists call particulate matter the deadliest form of air pollution because it can trigger health problems such as asthma attacks, irregular heartbeat and respiratory diseases. artigo.texto: MELBOURNE, Australia, Oct. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Sungrow, a globally leading PV inverter and energy storage system provider, is partnering with ENGIE and Elecnor on the 150 MW / 300 MWh Hazelwood Battery Energy Storage System expansion (HBESS 2) in Victoria, Australia, with Sungrow Australia as the technology provider and Elecnor as the BOP Contractor. This project will feature 66 units of Sungrow's ST5015-UX battery energy storage system (BESS), part of the PowerTitan 2.0 series, alongside 33 units of SC6900UD-MV Power Conversion System (PCS) inverters and Sungrow's smart controller EMS3000. Designed for utility-scale applications, the PowerTitan 2.0 system offers several key advantages: - High energy density: Optimises energy storage capacity. - Liquid-cooled technology: Helps maintain stable operating temperatures and support system reliability. - Advanced battery management: Supports battery safety, performance monitoring and long-term operational reliability. - High-performance power conversion: Paired with the SC6900UD-MV PCS inverters, it supports efficient power conversion and responsive grid support for utility-scale applications. With commercial operations targeted for 2028, the Hazelwood BESS 2 project will add significant battery storage capacity to Victoria's energy infrastructure, reinforcing Hazelwood's role in providing flexible energy resources for Victoria and the National Electricity Market (NEM). By storing and delivering electricity when needed, the system will help balance supply and demand as Australia's energy landscape continues to evolve. Grid-forming technology will further enhance the project's capabilities, helping strengthen network performance as renewable generation increases. Key benefits include: - Grid stability: Supports voltage and frequency stability to help maintain reliable network operation. - Fast response: Enables rapid responses to changing grid conditions to support power system reliability. - Renewable integration: Helps accommodate higher levels of variable renewable generation. - Grid resilience: Provides advanced grid support capabilities to strengthen the network under changing operating conditions. The combination of energy storage and advanced grid-forming capabilities will contribute to a more resilient and reliable power system. "The Hazelwood BESS 2 represents an important step in advancing grid-forming energy storage in Australia. Through our collaboration with ENGIE, we aim to bring advanced energy storage technology to support grid stability and enable greater integration of renewable energy. We look forward to contributing our expertise and supporting the continued development of a more resilient energy system in Victoria," said Thomas Hou, Managing Director at Sungrow Australia.

PV inverter and energy storage system provider Sungrow is partnering with ENGIE and Elecnor on the 150 MW/300 MWh Hazelwood BESS expansion (HBESS 2) in Victoria, Australia, with Sungrow Australia as the technology provider and Elecnor as the BOP contractor. artigo.texto: Previously Published in The Messenger By Matt Meduri Perhaps one of the most salient topics in Suffolk over the last couple years has been that of Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) facilities. These facilities hold lithium batteries capable of harnessing energy and dispersing it to the grid in times of blackouts or grid strain due to high electricity usage, particularly during the summer months. The State has been keen to roll these facilities out, with proponents arguing they’re necessary for sustaining the grid while broader concerns are addressed. Opponents say the technology is too new and firefighting capabilities have not yet evolved to combat lithium fires. At present, there is no conventional method of extinguishing these fires. Letting them burn themselves out is the only option, and that process can take days or weeks depending on the size of the fire. A proposed site on Weeks Avenue in Manorville has caused Senators Anthony Palumbo (R-New Suffolk) and Dean Murray (R-East Patchogue) to urge Governor Kathy Hochul (D-Hamburg) to pause the plans on this facility. The proposed facility is a 150MW lithium-ion storage facility developed by Key Capture Energy (KCE) on a 4-acre portion of a 13-acre light industrial site. It’s adjacent to a LIPA switchyard. “When it comes to the question of safety at these BESS facilities, there are simply too many important questions that have yet to be answered and I’m not willing to move forward without those answers and gamble with the safety of my constituents,” said Senator Murray in a statement. “God forbid a fire does break out at this massive facility, our firefighters need more of a plan than “let it burn”, which is the state’s official policy for such fires.” Local officials have even more reason to call for the brakes on BESS facilities after a 5MW facility in Wainscott caught fire in 2023. Contamination of at least three wells has been linked to that fire. The County announced in early October that the developer of that facility, NextEra Energy, has suspended operations at two East End locations. “Following the battery energy storage system (BESS) fire in East Hampton and the subsequent contamination of the area’s drinking water, I believe it is prudent to pause further construction of battery storage facilities in Suffolk County,” said Senator Palumbo in a statement. “That pause should last until a thorough review is completed, and safety measures are strengthened to better protect the region’s drinking water and Long Islanders.” KCE is the same developer that pitched a 79MW facility in Hauppauge, which led to vocal opposition from the community, a Town Council-led ban on large-scale BESS facilities in the Town of Islip, and the ascension of the Hauppauge Fire Department to be a de facto regional leader on the issue. While KCE, based in Houston, Texas, is the developer behind the project, the State is involved in the project through funding and contracting. The New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA) chose the Manorville project, while Governor Hochul selected this site as one of eight BESS projects as part of her initiative to deploy 6,000MW of energy storage across the state by 2030. The Town of Brookhaven has no blanket moratorium on BESS facilities. KCE is also behind a 50MW, LIPA-contracted facility in Shoreham on the grounds of the former nuclear site. A large-scale, 110MW plant in Holtsville (Savion Energy) continues to face zoning issues, while a separate, 79MW plant is also proposed in Holtsville (Rhynland). Savion Energy is also exploring large-scale facilities in the Setauket-Port Jefferson Station area. Another 1.9MW facility in Patchogue, developed by Agilitas Energy, is slated to come online by the end of this year or early next year. A 100MW Medford facility has also been proposed by AES. Seven towns – Babylon, Huntington, Islip, Riverhead, Smithtown, Southampton, and Southold – have extended their moratoria on these facilities until large concerns have been addressed.

artigo.texto: What are data centers, and why are Arizona neighbors pushing back? PHOENIX (AZFamily) — The number of data centers in Arizona continues to grow, with more than 100 online and another 50-plus planned. As the facilities become more visible, opposition to them is also increasing. Neighbors turn out against projects From Glendale to Flagstaff, neighbors have turned out in force against proposed data centers. “People over profits,” one opponent said. In Flagstaff, one speaker said, “This type of land use is not comparable with our city.” In Ahwatukee, homeowners have come together, holding biweekly meetings as they continue to fight a planned data center near 48th Street and Chandler Boulevard. “We’re concerned that this is in the wrong place,” one homeowner said. “All of this is going to be affected on a daily basis.” What is a data center? Dr. Kevin Hamlen, a professor of computer science at the University of Texas at Dallas, described a data center as “a large warehouse or building or series of buildings that store computing infrastructure, servers, data storage areas.” Hamlen said the growing number of centers is mainly about efficiency. “As computing infrastructure grows there’s more of a cost, benefit reward for centralizing all of that storage and all of that computation,” he said. He noted the Zoom call we were on likely required a data center, since its servers record and process the call. Storage is only part of the function Hamlen said people often misunderstand data centers as simple storage warehouses. “So data storage is part of what they do. Most of them don’t simply store data,” he said. He said companies are assuming centralizing computing is more efficient, but there has not been enough research to confirm that. “We’re doing a lot of guessing right now, and I think that part of it is a bad idea,” Hamlen said. “We should have standards and rigorous studies.” Hamlen said the public is asking important questions and that more research needs to be done to help answer them. artigo.texto: O impacto da instalação de Data Centers no Brasil e a influência da Inteligência Artificial no setor elétrico são temas da Coniben 2026 O encontro reunirá investidores, especialistas do Brasil, Portugal e da Espanha num encontro que antecipa o futuro do setor elétrico no país. Clique aqui e escute a matéria Tema central nas discussões de empresários, governos e diretores de instituições que cuida do gerenciamento do setor elétrico em nível global a instalação de Data Centers move tanto interesses de investidores interessado retorno desse novo negócio, como de ambientalistas preocupados com o consumo água para a refrigeração de seus parque de máquinas. E ele esteve entre os temas tratados pelo presidente Lula no seu discurso de agradecimento pela vitória eleitoral deste domingo (25), quando prometeu dar condições para que o Brasil seja um grande destino desses capitais, destacando a função estratégica para a segurança nacional. Faz sentido. Apenas no recorte dos grandes data centers, por exemplo, o consumo projetado passaria de aproximadamente 3 TWh em 2026 para 30 TWh em 2036. E impactaria o crescimento do consumo nacional em 3% em 2036, e a demanda em cerca de 10% no decênio. O Brasil, de fato, tem vantagens importantes para receber esses investimentos: uma matriz elétrica predominantemente renovável, grande disponibilidade de recursos energéticos e uma extensa rede interligada. Além disso, o próprio Plano Decenal de Energia (PDE 2036) elaborado pela Empresa de Pesquisa Energética projeta que 88,8% da geração elétrica permanecerá renovável em 2036, com cerca de 65 GW adicionais de solar e eólica, incluindo geração distribuída. Entretanto, para o planejamento, a abordagem disso não passa apenas por quanto esses empreendimentos vão consumir. E para o presidente da EPE, Thiago Prado, localização, potência demandada, cronograma de implantação, perfil horário e exigência de confiabilidade são igualmente importantes. Um data center de grande porte conectado em um ponto com capacidade disponível produz um impacto muito diferente do que um que exija reforços significativos na rede. “Por isso, será necessário coordenar o crescimento dessas cargas com geração, transmissão e novas soluções de flexibilidade, como, por exemplo, resposta à demanda, autoprodução e armazenamento de forma isolada ou combinada”, adverte o executivo. Ele chama a atenção para outro aspecto: a forma de planejar e operar também se transforma. Se antes cenários de perda da maior central geradora ou da maior máquina são considerados nos estudos de confiabilidade, o desligamento de grandes cargas também deverá ser objeto de estudo, antevendo os seus efeitos e perturbações no sistema elétrico. “O desafio não é apenas produzir energia suficiente para os data centers; é garantir energia, potência, rede e confiabilidade no lugar e no momento em que essas novas cargas surgirem e passarem a operar continuamente na rede”, diz Thiago Prado. Sua análise está em linha com a Assessora Executiva da Diretoria de Planejamento do Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS), Sumara Ticom, ao revelar que o ONS vê a chegada dos data centers como parte de um movimento mais amplo, que a Agência Internacional de Energia chama de “Era da Eletricidade”, em que o consumo de eletricidade cresce bem mais rápido que o consumo total de energia. No Brasil, desta Sumara Ticom, esse movimento já é concreto. Lembrando que, com a abertura da primeira Temporada de Acesso, em junho de 2026, o ONS havia recebido 144 pedidos de conexão de data centers à rede de transmissão, que somam 17,5 GW de demanda. Cerca de 8 GW desse total, viabilizados ainda no modelo anterior de acesso, já têm contrato assinado ou viabilidade de conexão confirmada. Empreendimentos de grande porte e impactantes Mas não basta querer. O principal desafio é de tempo e de lugar, afinal um data center pode ser construído em dois ou três anos, enquanto linhas de transmissão e reforços de rede exigem prazos bem maiores. Além disso, esses empreendimentos tendem a se concentrar em poucos pontos da rede, com demandas de centenas de megawatts. “Sem planejamento, o consumo pode crescer mais rápido que a infraestrutura capaz de atendê-lo, criando gargalos de conexão”, adverte. Para Sumara Ticom, as ações necessárias seguem quatro frentes: A primeira é a expansão da rede. A EPE, responsável pelo planejamento da expansão da transmissão, vem incorporando aos seus estudos as regiões que concentram os maiores pedidos de conexão e indicando os reforços e as novas instalações necessários para atendê-las, em estreita articulação com o ONS. A segunda frente é a conexão planejada, com o objetivo de reduzir o descompasso entre o prazo de implantação das cargas e o da rede. A rede deve chegar aonde as cargas pretendem se instalar e as cargas também precisam ser orientadas para onde a rede já pode recebê-las, o que exige transparência sobre a capacidade disponível em cada ponto, destaca a analista. A terceira, da lista dela, é a definição de requisitos técnicos que assegurem o bom desempenho dessas cargas diante de distúrbios na rede e, finalmente, a quarta é a discussão de modalidades de conexão flexível, “que permitam à carga se conectar mais rapidamente sem transferir riscos aos demais consumidores”. Tudo muito bom, tudo muito bem, mas, como o órgão de planejamento de médio e longo prazo, o que a EPE define como as premissas para o suporte técnico que esse novo cliente exige? O presidente da EPE avalia que a primeira premissa é justamente que não podemos tratar grandes cargas apenas como um acréscimo agregado de consumo. O planejamento precisa saber onde a carga pretende se conectar, qual sua potência, quando entrará em operação, qual seu perfil de consumo e quais são seus requisitos de continuidade e qualidade do fornecimento. artigo.texto: RES secures its first battery energy storage consent in Northern Ireland Mid and East Antrim Borough Council's Planning Committee approves RES's Ballyross project near Larne. According to the company, the site lies close to an existing substation and has limited visibility from local properties. British renewable energy developer RES announces that it has secured its first consent for a battery energy storage system (BESS) in Northern Ireland. Mid and East Antrim Borough Council's Planning Committee approved the Ballyross project. According to the company, the site is located on land approximately 2 kilometres south-west of Gleno and 8.5 kilometres south-west of Larne. Elsewhere in Europe, battery storage is also changing hands, with Greenvolt selling two projects in Poland to A&R Investments. A site close to the Ballyvallagh substation RES says Ballyross is located near the existing Ballyvallagh substation. According to the company, this proximity would support the efficient operation of the system while minimising the need for additional grid infrastructure. In the United Kingdom, storage questions also affect other sectors, as Cadent says UK CO2 storage rules effectively exclude biomethane producers. The company stresses that constraints on Northern Ireland's electricity system are increasing. In its view, clean, low-cost electricity can therefore be prevented from reaching consumers. Storage projects such as Ballyross would make better use of this electricity by storing it when generation is high and releasing it when demand rises. Landscaping and statements from RES The approved scheme includes a landscaping package that RES describes as substantial. New native-species planting is intended to help the development blend into the surrounding landscape. It is also meant to create wildlife corridors and pollinator-friendly habitat. Peter Deeney, Senior Development Project Manager at RES, says the company has contributed to Northern Ireland's energy future and economic growth since the early 1990s from its office in Larne. He describes securing consent for Ballyross, RES's first battery energy storage project to be consented in Northern Ireland, as an important milestone. According to him, battery storage is becoming increasingly important as Northern Ireland continues its transition to a low-carbon energy system. Mr Deeney adds that the site was selected in part because it has limited visibility from local properties. He says the new planting will further reduce that visibility. He thanks the local residents and stakeholders who engaged during consultation, whose feedback, he says, helped inform the landscaping plan and shape the project's final design. artigo.texto: Jason Padgett is convinced mathematics can reduce the need for data centers. Data centers are facilities that house computer systems, servers and related IT infrastructure to store, process and distribute large amounts of data. Padgett, a Carmel resident, was diagnosed with acquired savant syndrome after suffering a traumatic brain injury during a mugging in Tacoma, Wash. The aftermath allowed him to develop exceptional math and geometric visualization, which he applied to come up with his data center theory. It all comes down to black holes. “Black holes actually store data, and then they project what’s called probability waves, which are like waves in the ocean,” Padgett said. “When a bunch of waves overlap, they make a new wave inside a black hole.” Those waves create patterns, which he said can be linked through a process that looks like connecting the dots. Padgett said brains – and AI – process data in a similar way. “In the model I have been developing, many possible quantum paths interfere, some cancel out, and the strongest coherent path becomes the route to the readable result,” he said. “I began asking whether a computer could copy that basic idea: eliminate what does not fit early and follow the most efficient path to the answer.” He said finding ways for AI to process information in fewer steps could make a big difference. “Fewer unnecessary calculations can mean less work for computer chips,” he said. “At large scale, less work could mean less electricity, less heat to remove and less water needed for cooling. We believe we have an early proof of concept showing that some internal AI work can be reused and some repeated computation can be skipped. But this is still early, and the next step is much bigger than one person.” Padgett said a team is needed. “That means software engineers, AI and machine-learning specialists, mathematicians, physicists, hardware and data-center experts, researchers, business leaders, investors and people who know how to turn an early technical idea into something that can be tested at real scale,” he said. Padgett primarily works independently, but he has spoken at Science of Consciousness conference organized by Dr. Stuart Hameroff, an anesthesiologist and quantum consciousness theorist and researcher at the University of Arizona.

artigo.texto: The projects, located in Güeñes, Barakaldo and Lezama, will provide a combined power capacity of 55 MW and storage capacity of 220 MWh. The portfolio is, to date, the largest standalone battery storage portfolio in Spain to reach financial close. As technical advisor, DNV provided an independent assessment of the project design, technology selection, contracts and key technical risks, together with recommendations to mitigate those risks and support the financing process. Spain’s electricity system is expected to require substantial growth in energy storage capacity as the share of variable renewable generation increases. Battery energy storage systems can help balance differences between electricity production and demand, support grid stability and provide additional flexibility to the power system. The projects form part of Return Energy’s wider pipeline in the Basque Country, which exceeds 1,400 MWh of energy storage capacity and 352.6 MW of power capacity. “Energy storage is becoming an increasingly important part of Spain’s power system as renewable generation grows” said Brice Le Gallo, Brice Le Gallo, Vice-president and regional director for Southern Europe, MEA & LATAM, Energy Systems at DNV. “DNV’s Energy Transition Outlook for Spain shows that a more electrified, renewables-based energy system will require substantially more storage to provide flexibility and support grid stability. Projects reaching financial close are an important part of moving energy storage development from planning into deployment. Our role is to provide an independent view of the technology, design and technical risks so that the parties involved can make investment decisions with greater confidence.” Spain’s National Energy and Climate Plan foresees a substantial expansion of storage capacity by 2030: 22.5 GW, including 12.5 related to BESS. With deployment still at an early stage, projects now reaching financing and construction will help determine how quickly storage can scale alongside renewable generation. artigo.texto: Geraldo Campos Jr., Marisa Wanzeller e Lais Carregosa, da Agência iNFRA A área técnica da ANEEL (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica) sugeriu abrir espaço no edital do leilão de baterias para eventuais mudanças no modelo de custeio da contratação. Atualmente, a legislação prevê que as despesas sejam divididas entre os geradores de energia. No entanto, há um projeto de lei no Congresso (PL 3.716/2026) que inclui os consumidores na conta. Segundo fontes, essa proposta deve contar com o apoio do governo para viabilizar o certame em dezembro deste ano. Conforme proposta das notas técnicas disponibilizadas na segunda-feira (26), para os certames de conteúdo nacional e geral, o edital pode ser alterado para atribuir o pagamento dos encargos a “usuários de reserva de capacidade” no lugar de “agentes de geração de energia elétrica”, como estava na proposição original. Agentes consultados pela Agência iNFRA viram a mudança como positiva por permitir que a legislação seja alterada a qualquer tempo sem impactar a segurança do contrato. Fabio Lima, diretor-executivo da Absae (Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia), ressaltou que a entidade vinha pedindo o ajuste para evitar especificações no edital e contrato. “A ideia é que o contrato deve se referir ao usuário de reserva de capacidade, na forma da lei, podendo a lei a qualquer tempo ser alternada – sendo que não cabe a qualquer um de nós prever ou definir eventuais mudanças. E o usuário continuará sendo responsável pelo custeio, seja ele quem for nos termos da lei e da regulação”, disse Lima, que explicou ainda que todos os contratos regulados estão submetidos a mudanças da lei e da regulação. O diretor de Novos Negócios da Abeeólica (Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias), Marcello Cabral, diz que a alteração seria uma “boa vontade” da reguladora, para evitar a necessidade de futuras mudanças no edital caso o PL 3.716 seja aprovado no Congresso. “Apesar de a ANEEL ter criado uma mudança na referência que ela fazia aos agentes de geração, para usuários de reserva de capacidade, ela não está mudando a base pagante”, ressalta. O tema está pautado para reunião extraordinária de diretoria, convocada para esta terça-feira (27), a partir das 16h. Paralelamente à mudança de entendimento na ANEEL, fontes da Esplanada ouvidas pela reportagem afirmam que, passada a eleição, o governo deve ajudar na tramitação do PL das baterias. O projeto ainda não tem relator definido e já teve urgência aprovada. Baterias em usinas A área técnica também sugere a retirada da vedação para que usinas com contratos no ambiente regulado possam participar do certame, ofertando potência com baterias associadas aos seus empreendimentos. No entanto, o edital deve determinar que os contratos regulados não sejam prejudicados. Segundo os documentos, os agentes argumentaram que a proposta original da ANEEL era restritiva e que a medição individualizada e a independência operativa das baterias seriam suficientes para assegurar o cumprimento dos contratos regulados. A área técnica pondera que as usinas associadas às baterias compartilham o uso da rede, o que poderia afetar o ambiente regulado. Mas acata as sugestões da consulta, deixando a análise para cada caso. “Contudo, os contratos regulados dos agentes de geração e armazenamento têm prazos distintos, podendo levar a situações nas quais a sobreposição temporal de tais contratos seja pequena”, disse. Marcello Cabral, da Abeeólica, aponta que esse compartilhamento de rede, na verdade, otimiza o uso das conexões e pode tornar o leilão mais competitivo. Ele explica que, na associação com um gerador, as baterias podem contratar até cerca de 30% a menos de Must (Montante de Uso do Sistema de Transmissão). Assim, caso uma bateria com capacidade de até 30 MW (megawatts) se associe a uma usina de 100 MW, ela poderá contratar um montante de 100 MW para despacho, exemplificou o executivo. Garantia financeira Outra mudança que pode aumentar a competitividade do leilão é a redução da garantia financeira exigida dos participantes, conforme apontaram agentes ouvidos pela Agência iNFRA. Os documentos sugerem reduzir o aporte de R$ 9,8 milhões/MW para R$ 6 milhões/MW. As contribuições em consulta pública apontaram que o valor inicial baseava-se em premissas desatualizadas de custos de implantação de sistemas de baterias. Segundo os agentes, as referências mais recentes indicam custos de implantação de sistemas de armazenamento em baterias. Inadimplência As notas técnicas também mudam o trecho sobre o risco de eventual inadimplência do recebimento do encargo – seja qual for a base pagadora. A versão inicial, na abertura da consulta, previa que o risco total pela falta do pagamento recairia sobre o agente. Agora, o agente ficaria com o “risco de insuficiência momentânea” de recursos na conta setorial, o que posteriormente seria regularizado com repasse do fundo de garantia atrelado à conta, pela CCEE (Câmara de Comercialização de Energia). Fabio Lima, da Absae, explica que o risco de não pagamento é baixo, uma vez que se trata de uma obrigação de os usuários pagarem encargos que lhes forem legalmente atribuídos. Assim, deixar de pagar gera penalizações, como possibilidade de desligamento da CCEE. Com o ajuste feito pela ANEEL, o agente acabaria recebendo de qualquer forma, seja por uma fonte ou outra. “Quem paga a bateria não é cada usuário, mas sim essa conta para a qual todos os usuários contribuem. E essa conta tem um fundo para inadimplência. Então, para o agente não ter a sua remuneração, teria que ser uma inadimplência massiva que ultrapasse a inadimplência média prevista”, explicou Lima, que destacou ainda que a lógica é a mesma de outras contas setoriais. artigo.texto: Mário Nazzari Westrup* e Mariana Palandi** A interação entre o novo sistema de tributação sobre o consumo e o mercado regulado de carbono revela uma discussão que vai além da incidência tributária Enquanto empresas se preparam para a implementação da reforma tributária, outra transformação estrutural avança quase em silêncio: o desenvolvimento do mercado regulado de carbono brasileiro. À primeira vista, parecem ser agendas independentes, mas não são. Em poucos anos, ambas passarão a influenciar as mesmas decisões de investimento, precificação, competitividade e alocação de capital das empresas brasileiras. É nesse ponto de encontro que surge uma discussão ainda pouco explorada. Quando se fala em mercado de carbono, o debate costuma começar pela incidência da CBS (Contribuição sobre Bens e Serviços) e do IBS (Imposto sobre Bens e Serviços) sobre a negociação de créditos de carbono. Porém, antes de discutir a tributação de um ativo ambiental específico, vale perguntar como um sistema concebido para tributar de forma neutra deve se relacionar com instrumentos regulatórios criados pelo próprio Estado para alterar incentivos econômicos. A neutralidade é um dos pilares econômicos da reforma tributária. A lógica de um IVA (Imposto sobre Valor Agregado) consiste em reduzir interferências sobre as decisões dos agentes econômicos, permitindo que empresas invistam, produzam e concorram sem distorções provocadas pela tributação. Quanto mais neutro o sistema, maior tende a ser sua eficiência econômica. Essa foi uma das promessas da reforma brasileira. Entretanto, a própria reforma reconhece que esse princípio é limitado – o IS (Imposto Seletivo) é prova disso. Em determinadas situações, o Estado opta por utilizar a tributação não para arrecadar mais, mas para modificar comportamentos, elevando o custo de atividades associadas a externalidades negativas. Quando o mercado não produz sozinho o resultado social desejado, a neutralidade deixa de ser um objetivo absoluto. O próprio texto constitucional e a legislação complementar instituíram regimes diferenciados e tratamentos específicos, evidenciando que a busca por neutralidade convive, legitimamente, com outros objetivos de política pública. O mercado regulado de carbono nasce da mesma lógica econômica, embora utilize um instrumento diferente. Em vez de aumentar o custo de determinadas atividades, cria incentivos para que a redução das emissões adquira valor econômico. Trata-se de uma solução baseada em preços e negociação, capaz de permitir que o próprio mercado reaja às alternativas para descarbonizar a economia. Nesse sentido, tanto o Imposto Seletivo quanto o mercado de carbono procuram enfrentar a mesma falha de mercado: a ausência de um preço adequado para os impactos ambientais das emissões. Sob perspectivas distintas, ambos alteram os preços relativos da economia: enquanto a reforma tributária procura eliminar distorções tributárias, o mercado regulado atribui um preço às emissões de carbono. Em ambos os casos, o objetivo final é melhorar a alocação de recursos e orientar decisões econômicas mais eficientes. No entanto, o que acontece quando um mesmo investimento recebe um incentivo para reduzir emissões, mas simultaneamente sofre um aumento de custo decorrente da tributação? Se ambos os instrumentos pretendem orientar as decisões privadas, é desejável que transmitam sinais econômicos coerentes. Caso contrário, parte do incentivo criado por uma política pública poderá ser neutralizada pela outra. A experiência internacional mostra que não existe uma solução única para essa interação, mesmo entre países que adotam diferentes versões do imposto sobre valor agregado. Em Singapura, desde 2022, a emissão, transferência ou venda de créditos de carbono não é considerada fornecimento de bens ou serviços para fins do GST (Goods and Services Tax), ficando fora de sua incidência. No Reino Unido, desde setembro de 2024 determinadas negociações de créditos voluntários passaram a estar sujeitas ao VAT (Value Added Tax), após o amadurecimento do mercado secundário. Já o Canadá adotou uma terceira solução: preservou a incidência do GST/HST (Goods and Services Tax/Harmonized Sales Tax) sobre negociações de permissões de emissão no mercado secundário, mas atribuiu ao adquirente a responsabilidade pelo recolhimento. Os diferentes modelos revelam que a questão não se resume à escolha entre tributar ou não tributar – o desafio está em definir como a tributação se integra ao desenho e aos objetivos do mercado ambiental. A diversidade dessas experiências não conduz automaticamente à conclusão de que créditos de carbono devam ser excluídos da incidência da CBS e do IBS. A reflexão é outra. Se a própria reforma tributária admite relativizar a neutralidade quando o objetivo é corrigir externalidades, parece legítimo discutir como essa lógica deve dialogar com um mercado regulado criado exatamente para alcançar a mesma finalidade por meio de um mecanismo distinto. Mais do que definir a incidência tributária sobre esses ativos, será importante evitar que instrumentos concebidos para induzir a descarbonização acabem emitindo sinais econômicos contraditórios aos agentes privados, reduzindo a efetividade das políticas públicas. Para as empresas, o desenho dessa interação poderá influenciar decisões de investimento, estratégias de descarbonização, precificação de ativos ambientais, estruturação de projetos e até a atratividade econômica de determinadas tecnologias. artigo.texto: Sumitomo Corp. is studying how battery energy storage systems operate alongside electricity trading in Leicester, England, to prepare for expanding the technology across Japan. The Japanese trading house gained operational insights from a site storing enough power for 160,000 homes for two hours. Sumitomo studies UK battery storage model as Japan eyes wider adoption Japanese trading house Sumitomo Corp. is studying how battery energy storage systems operate alongside electricity markets in Leicester, England. The project offers lessons the company will apply as it pushes for wider deployment of the technology across Japan. A facility outside Leicester houses 30 shipping containers packed with batteries and inverters. Together, the units can store enough energy to power 160,000 homes for two hours. The site demonstrates what large-scale battery storage looks like in practice. Sumitomo gained insight into how the system functions as part of an electricity grid and how that relationship shapes trading activity. The company is learning how stored energy flows back into the market and how pricing signals drive demand for storage operations. Japan has been accelerating its own battery storage ambitions. The country's power sector faces growing pressure to integrate renewable energy sources while maintaining grid reliability. Battery systems offer a way to store surplus generation and release it when demand peaks, smoothing supply without relying on gas-fired backup plants. Sumitomo's move reflects broader momentum in Japan toward commercializing battery storage at scale. Trading companies have been positioning themselves as operators of the technology, leveraging their existing networks and relationships with utilities and industrial customers. The Leicester project gives them a concrete reference point for planning similar deployments domestically. The company did not immediately disclose specific timelines or investment figures for its domestic plans. Industry observers expect Sumitomo to use the Leicester experience to shape proposals for utilities and large industrial consumers who want storage assets on their sites. The East Midlands facility represents one of several battery storage projects being developed by UK firms as the country navigates its own energy transition. Japan's experience operating such systems at commercial scale could prove instructive as the technology moves from demonstration to widespread adoption. Sumitomo's exploration of the Leicester site underscores how international knowledge transfer is becoming a practical tool for energy companies seeking to accelerate deployment in markets where regulatory frameworks and market structures still are being defined. For Japan, the lesson is straightforward: build the capability, study the operations, then scale. Sources: Nikkei Asia reporting, Oct. 26, 2026 Source:asia.nikkei.com

artigo.texto: By Devyn Lyon, FOX23 News TULSA, Okla. — Oklahoma regulators have moved a hearing on OG&E’s proposed rules for large electricity users to January, extending a case that could help determine how the costs of powering data centers are divided and whether other customers could be left paying more. The hearing, previously scheduled for November 3, is now set for January 12, 2027. The central question for households and small businesses is straightforward: as large customers connect to the electric grid, who pays for the power plants, lines and other equipment needed to serve them? OG&E filed the case to seek approval of a proposed “large-load tariff.” A tariff establishes the rates, and service requirements customers must follow. In this case, OG&E wants special payment requirements for very large electricity users, including data centers. Google is participating in the proceeding and advocating for changes to how those customers can obtain power. In emailed responses to FOX23, OG&E said its proposal is intended to protect existing customers from costs associated with bringing large users onto the grid. “Current customers should never pay for the impact of bringing large-load customers onto the electric grid,” the company said. Simply put, OG&E wants large customers to make financial commitments, so the utility’s other customers are not left covering costs if a project uses less electricity than expected cuts back or closes. The company said its proposal would require large customers to: - Pay for infrastructure built to serve them - Sign long-term, binding contracts - Pay substantial minimum bills, even if they use less power than expected - Pay fees if they reduce their commitments of leave early - Provide financial security to back up those obligations OG&E also argues those customers should contribute toward the costs of its existing power plants. There are proposed requirements, regulators must determine what rules to approve. Google wants large customers to have the option to buy electricity from independent generators while continuing to use OG&E’s grid to receive it. Google argues that approach could reduce the need for OG&E to build expensive new power plants. OG&E argues those arrangements could leave large customers paying less toward its existing plants while continuing to depend on the utility’s system. The company also says it must maintain reliable service when a customer’s outside power source is unavailable. Its concern is that costs could fall to other customers if the large user does not adequately pay for that backup. Buying electricity from another supplier would still involve using power lines and other grid infrastructure. The dispute is over which costs those customers would remain responsible for, and whether state law permits the arrangements being proposed. The hearing delay itself does not approve a rate of increase or decide how those costs will be divided. The potential impact comes from the rules regulators ultimately adopt. If large customers do not cover the costs assigned to serving them, other customers could face pressure to cover more. But, if outside power purchases reduce the need for costly new utility construction, that could also affect future costs. Those competing arguments are part of what the commission must evaluate. Neither side’s position establishes what will happen to an individual customer’s bill. OG&E said other parties’ proposals raised legal questions that should be addressed before the commission hears the evidence. The company said it wants those parties to explain what law allows large customers to buy electricity from third-party generators while relying on OG&E’s grid. OG&E said the additional time would allow those arguments to be considered before the hearing. FOX23 also asked whether the requested date was connected to Commissioner Todd Hiett’s term ending January 11, one day before the rescheduled hearing. The company said it was not, saying its request was driven by proposals introduced by parties. The proceeding is Oklahoma Corporation Commission Case No. PUD2026-000046. Customers can search for that number in the commission’s Electronic Case Filing system to review filings, testimony, and orders. The commission’s October 21 scheduling order is available here. The January hearing is the next opportunity to examine the proposals and evidence. Moving that hearing does not resolve the underlying dispute over who should pay.

artigo.texto: Geminus has been selected by AFWERX for a SBIR Phase I contract focused on physics-informed AI for microgrid and battery optimisation to address the challenges in the Department of the Air Force (DAF) The award extends a platform already running across large-scale energy infrastructure into battery storage and grid management as a wave of new demand hits the grid. The Air Force Research Laboratory and AFWERX have partnered to streamline the Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) and Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) process by accelerating the small business experience through faster proposal to award timelines, changing the pool of potential applicants by expanding opportunities to small business and eliminating bureaucratic overhead by implementing process improvement changes in contract execution. The DAF began offering the Open Topic SBIR/STTR programme in 2018, which expanded the range of innovations the DAF funded and now, Geminus will begin creating and providing innovative capabilities that will strengthen the national defence of the United States. Geminus is the AI orchestration layer for intelligent twins. Digital twins were bespoke projects that were built by hand, calibrated once, and were often out of date the moment the real system changed. Geminus can make digital twins repeatable, reliable, and rapid, grounded in physics, aware of their own certainty, and fast enough to optimise live operations, even on systems that age and change. Greg Fallon, CEO of Geminus, said, “Every digital twin used to be a bespoke project, so most industrial systems never got one. We made intelligent twins repeatable, reliable, and fast enough to act on in real time. Storage is where the grid’s biggest problem gets solved or gets stuck.” For the Air Force, Geminus is set to build and intelligent twin of a forward-deployed microgrid: diesel generators, lithium-ion batteries, and shifting mission loads. It hopes to achieve longer battery life, consume less fuel, and deliver reliable power where it is mission critical, with Phase I opening the door to a follow-on pilot. The views expressed are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the official policy or position of the Department of the Air Force, the Department of War, or the U.S. government.

artigo.texto: Em 23 de outubro de 2026, Stargate Argentina ainda não tinha contrato definitivo, segundo a Bloomberg Línea. A publicação informou que a OpenAI poderia comprar capacidade computacional do projeto, desde que a Sur Energy desenvolvesse a infraestrutura e o fornecimento de energia necessários. Quem desenvolveria o projeto e quem poderia comprar capacidade No anúncio de 14 de outubro de 2025, a OpenAI informou que havia assinado uma carta de intenção com a Sur Energy para explorar o projeto. A empresa argentina lideraria o desenvolvimento e formaria um consórcio com uma desenvolvedora de infraestrutura em nuvem. A OpenAI se apresentou como potencial compradora da capacidade computacional, ou seja, do poder de processamento que o centro de dados viesse a oferecer. A Bloomberg Línea relatou em outubro de 2026 que uma eventual compra da OpenAI dependeria do desenvolvimento da infraestrutura e da energia pela Sur Energy. Assim, o papel anunciado para a OpenAI era o de possível cliente, não o de líder do projeto. Qual era a escala prevista Em outubro de 2025, a Data Center Dynamics noticiou uma capacidade total de até 500 MW e investimento previsto de até US$ 25 bilhões. A primeira etapa, de 100 MW, tinha como meta 2027. Esses números faziam parte da proposta relatada naquele ano. O que se sabia sobre o andamento A Bloomberg Línea informou em 23 de outubro de 2026 que ainda não havia contrato definitivo. Emiliano Kargieman, cofundador da Sur Energy, disse que a seleção do local havia avançado para a região de Confluencia, na província de Neuquén. Segundo a Bloomberg Línea, Kargieman também afirmou que a Sur Energy tinha acordos de fornecimento de energia com a Central Puerto e a Genneia, além de um acordo com a Fluidstack, empresa de infraestrutura computacional. Ele disse que o contrato definitivo seria o passo que permitiria iniciar a construção.

artigo.texto: A cidade de São Paulo está próxima da mediana no ranking de custos de regiões globais para construção de data centers elaborado pela Turner & Townsend, empresa global de gestão de projetos. O estudo aponta que São Paulo ocupa a 30ª posição, com um custo por watt de US$ 11,66, que representa R$ 62,12 por watt. Com isso, a capital paulista é uma alternativa competitiva em comparação com polos consolidados, como o Vale do Silício, nos Estados Unidos, onde o custo é de US$ 15,01 por watt (cerca de R$ 76,55 por watt), e o norte da Virgínia, também nos Estados Unidos, com US$ 11,80 por watt (cerca de R$ 60,18 por watt). A capital fluminense, por sua vez, tem um custo mais alto, de US$ 12,59 por watt (R$ 67,05). Segundo a Turner & Townsend, isso reflete a expansão da capacidade do Rio de Janeiro e a sua atratividade para novos investimentos. “A posição de São Paulo e do Rio de Janeiro no índice global reforça o Brasil como o principal polo de infraestrutura de data centers da América do Sul. Uma matriz energética diversificada, a crescente demanda por capacidade de computação em nuvem e a expansão da inteligência artificial mantêm o país atrativo para grandes investidores e empresas globais de hiperescala, conhecidas como hyperscalers”, analisa Henrique Cicchetto, diretor de Real Estate da Turner & Townsend no Brasil. No contexto do relatório, o indicador “custo por watt” (US$/W) corresponde ao custo médio de construção por watt de capacidade elétrica de um data center. Com isso, é possível comparar o custo de construção dessas instalações em diferentes localidades, independentemente do tamanho. O indicador não se refere ao custo da eletricidade consumida pelo data center, mas ao custo de construção da infraestrutura para cada watt de capacidade instalada. artigo.texto: Redata atrai investidores, mas não acelera obras de data centers Pesquisa do GRI mostra que apenas 4% apontam antecipação de projetos como principal efeito do incentivo O governo conseguiu aumentar a atratividade do Brasil para investimentos em data centers com a aprovação do Redata, mas ainda está longe de resolver um dos principais problemas enfrentados pelo setor: a demora para colocar os empreendimentos em operação. Um levantamento do GRI Institute mostra que apenas 4,08% dos participantes da pesquisa apontaram a antecipação dos cronogramas de projetos como o principal efeito esperado do novo regime de incentivos fiscais. O resultado evidencia uma distância entre a redução dos custos de investimento e a capacidade de acelerar a instalação dos centros de processamento de dados no país. A pesquisa, realizada em setembro durante um encontro do GRI que reuniu 239 participantes, entre executivos, investidores, financiadores e representantes do setor público, revela um contraste. Enquanto 53,06% apontaram o aumento da competitividade internacional do Brasil como principal efeito do Redata, a expectativa de antecipação dos empreendimentos ficou restrita a uma pequena parcela das respostas. O estudo captou as expectativas dos participantes no dia da sanção da lei, e não os resultados efetivos do programa. O obstáculo está principalmente na infraestrutura. Embora o Brasil tenha uma matriz elétrica predominantemente renovável e disponibilidade de energia para atrair grandes investimentos, a conexão dos empreendimentos à rede de transmissão esbarra em limitações de capacidade, obras de expansão e procedimentos regulatórios. Segundo o GRI, os prazos necessários para viabilizar essa infraestrutura podem ser incompatíveis com a velocidade de implantação exigida pelas empresas de tecnologia, sobretudo diante do avanço da inteligência artificial. A importância desse gargalo aparece em outro resultado do levantamento. A disponibilidade de infraestrutura de apoio, incluindo energia, conectividade e transporte, passou de 43,40% das menções em 2025 para 72,92% em 2026, tornando-se o principal fator apontado como capaz de impulsionar investimentos. Superou até mesmo a demanda por inteligência artificial, mencionada por 66,67% dos participantes. Já a proporção de respostas indicando apetite alto ou muito alto por investimentos no setor subiu de 76% para 83,78% no mesmo período. As limitações também dificultam uma das ambições do governo: distribuir os investimentos para além dos mercados tradicionais do Sul e Sudeste. Apesar dos incentivos diferenciados previstos para o Norte, Nordeste e Centro-Oeste, apenas 4,08% apontaram o redirecionamento regional dos projetos como principal efeito esperado do Redata. A escolha da localização continua condicionada à disponibilidade de infraestrutura elétrica, à conectividade e à proximidade dos principais centros consumidores. Sancionado em setembro, o Redata prevê benefícios tributários federais para a aquisição e importação de equipamentos destinados aos centros de processamento de dados, mas sua implementação ainda depende de regulamentação. O setor também cobra avanços na desoneração do ICMS, que exige articulação entre os estados. O diagnóstico do GRI indica que a política tributária pode ajudar o Brasil a conquistar investimentos, mas transformar esse interesse em projetos operacionais exigirá resolver obstáculos que os incentivos fiscais, isoladamente, não conseguem eliminar.

artigo.texto: BYD’s upcoming flagship EV will be its largest and most luxurious electric sedan yet, potentially debuting two firsts for the company: Rolls-Royce-style coach doors and solid-state batteries. BYD will unveil its new flagship electric sedan in the UAE BYD is better known for its low-cost electric cars, like the Seagull, a little hatchback that sells for under $10,000 in China. The Chinese auto giant has greatly expanded its portfolio over the past few months and years. BYD now offers everything from entry-level EVs to three-row flagship SUVs, pickup trucks, electric supercars, and just about everything in between. BYD has three sub-brands: Denza, FangChengBao, and Yangwang. It also has two main families under the BYD brand: the Dynasty and Ocean series. Yangwang sits at the top of BYD’s brand hierarchy and showcases its latest breakthrough technologies. Previously, Yangwang vehicles debuted on BYD’s quad-motor e4 platform, delivering a whopping 1,300 horsepower and featuring its DiSus-X intelligent body control system, which enables the vehicle to “dance,” jump, and drive on three wheels. For its next model, BYD is pushing further into the elite segment to take on ultra-luxury brands like Rolls-Royce, Bentley, and Mercedes-Maybach. Yangwang general manager Hu Xiaoqing revealed several images of its new executive sedan testing last month. Although it was disguised, it appeared to be about the same shape and size as the Mercedes-Benz Maybach S-Class or Rolls-Royce Phantom. Local reports indicate it will be around 5,500 mm (216″) long. HU confirmed for the first time last week that the global launch of the new flagship sedan will take place in the UAE, not in BYD’s home market of China. BYD has not yet revealed a specific launch date, but the Yangwang sedan could make its first appearance as early as next week. According to CarNewsChina, citing “sources familiar with the project,” BYD is aiming to reveal the new flagship model in Dubai, UAE, around November 5. Zheng Yu, Yangwang’s executive general manager, said the new model will feature “unprecedented disruptive technology,” but didn’t reveal specifics. Although details are still limited, the ultra-luxury sedan was shown at BYD’s Flash Charging station, suggesting it will support megawatt flash charging. It also features rear-hinged coach doors, a first for BYD. The flagship EV will reportedly be the first to feature BYD’s solid-state batteries. BYD executive vice president Stella Li said during an interview with Carwow.es last month that the company’s first vehicle to use solid-state batteries will debut in 2027. Li said BYD is “in the leading position” in solid-state battery technology and its commercialization, and the company plans to prove it next year. BYD’s battery unit, FinDreams, plans to begin production of sulfide-based all-solid-state batteries in 2027. It will initially be produced in limited batches, then scale to mass production closer to the end of the decade. Top comment by ModernMarvalFan BYD should get a different name (not Yangwang) if it wants its flagship product to sell outside of China. While BYD has yet to confirm it, introducing the new battery tech in a flagship model would make sense. The executive sedan is expected to debut around November 5. Prices are rumored to start in the 2 million yuan range, or about $300,000. Yangwang’s current electric sedan, the U7, starts at 658,000 yuan ($98,000). The brand also sells the U8 (and U8L), a plug-in hybrid luxury off-road SUV, and the U9, a fully electric super-coupe. The extended U8L is Yangwang’s highest-priced mass-produced vehicle, starting at 1.45 million yuan ($217,000).

artigo.texto: Data center construction to require many more workers SCOTT TRUXELL/independent editor Original estimates had approximately 1,500 construction workers needed to build Van Wert’s $10 billion QTS data center but those figures have been revised. The number is now larger – a lot larger. During Sunday’s “Commissioner’s Corner/Mayor’s Conference” program on radio stations 99.7FM WKSD and 1220AM/104.3FM, Van Wert Area Economic Development Director Brent Stevens said Stevens said ground was recently broken on Phase I of the project, which will include four buildings at the Mega Site on Van Wert’s east side. “Each building is roughly 650,000 square feet apiece and they’re all being built at once, so that has shifted their numbers up quite a bit,” Stevens said. “There’s going to be a couple of hundred people on this massive ground excavation over the next six months, then they’ll start to go vertical. For the first 12 months, we’re going to be in that 2,000 (construction worker) range, then all the subcontracters are coming in.” That when the number of construction workers is expected to climb to as many as 5,500 per day. “5,500 people in town per day, I would say after March of 2028,” he stated. With several thousand workers coming to the area, the question is – where will they stay? “I’ve been in the process of going to everybody that can facilitate new housing and going ‘we need to work on getting this done,” Stevens stated on the show. “We’ve been talking about housing for the last year and a half or two years, it’s just sinking in to everybody. I’m talking with several different developers – I’ve been talking to developers in Fort Wayne about building over there as well.” “Of the 5,550 that are going to come here, how many are actually going to be moving to Van Wert because we need to prepare the schools too,” he added. Stevens did say some of the workers will be local. As far as rest of the workers and where they will come from, Stevens quipped it’s like a “traveling road show” “They’ll go to this data center and build it,” he said. “They have these certain groups that will fly in, do all the things they need to do but for example, for this particular project, the head Suffolk guy (Suffolk Construction Company, the contractor in charge), is actually moving to Van Wert and will be here for 6-7 years.” The topic of an adequate number of local restuarants and bars was also discussed during the program and he mentioned the old Marsh hotel could and other storefronts downtown could be put to use, along with available space in the Towne Center Blvd area. Stevens mentioned that for every job that’s created at the data center, 3.5 ancillary jobs follow. “Even our surrounding communities – Ohio City, Convoy – people are looking at doing things over there because of this particular project,” Stevens said. Stevens noted that a temporary off-ramp will be built of off U.S. 30 directly into the construction site and a 6,000 spot parking lot. As far as dollars to the local community, Stevens stated QTS is going to take “zero incentives.” “None,” he said. “They’re going to give back to the community in an unbelievable fashion and I’m hoping we’ll be able to announce that (soon).” Stevens said there have been ongoing discussions about how to manage the money coming into the community and how to do things in a fiscally responsible way. “What we have decided in talking with the commissioners and the mayor, is there’s going to be funding coming in that will be city money and funding coming in that will be county money,” he explained. “We will create two boards – a board for the city and a board for the county.” The full program can be heard below. artigo.texto: A cellulose separator infused with bikitaite zeolite improved the high-rate performance of laboratory lithium-metal battery cells equipped with an NCM90 cathode, outperforming a conventional polyethylene separator at faster discharge rates while also producing smoother, more uniform lithium deposition at the lithium-metal anode. Researchers led by Professor Sun-Yul Ryou at Hanbat National University in South Korea reported that the composite separator, called CBT, raised NCM90 cathode capacity from 115 to 163 mAh g⁻¹ at 4C, an improvement of approximately 42%. In separate Li||NCM90 cells, CBT supported approximately 60% capacity retention after around 2,500 cycles under 2C charging and 4C discharging, although the release did not report a corresponding long-term cycling comparison with the polyethylene-separator cells. These results provide laboratory evidence that modifying the separator can influence ion transport and performance at both electrodes without changing the underlying cathode and anode chemistry. Lithium-metal batteries are being investigated for next-generation energy storage because lithium metal offers a very high theoretical capacity and could produce high energy density when paired with a high-nickel cathode such as NCM90. Rapid charging and discharging, however, create challenges on both sides of the cell. At the lithium-metal anode, uneven lithium-ion transport can lead to non-uniform lithium deposition and the formation of needle-like dendrites. These structures may damage the solid electrolyte interphase, continuously consume active lithium and electrolyte, and, in severe cases, penetrate the separator and cause an internal short circuit. Separators have consequently been investigated as a way to regulate lithium deposition and improve interfacial stability, while this study reports an additional effect on high-rate cathode performance. To address the transport problem, Ryou’s team developed the CBT separator from porous cellulose infused with bikitaite zeolite. The cellulose provides a porous supporting structure, while the zeolite contributes ion-transport properties and interconnected pathways for lithium-ion movement through the separator. The resulting architecture was intended to distribute lithium ions more rapidly and uniformly across the cell, reducing polarization and facilitating electrochemical reactions under demanding high-rate conditions. Unlike approaches focused solely on adding a new cathode or anode composition, the CBT design retains the NCM90 cathode and lithium-metal anode used in the reported cells and modifies the component positioned between them. The separator’s measured transport properties were an ionic conductivity of 3.45 × 10⁻³ S cm⁻¹ and a lithium-ion transference number of 0.742. In the researchers’ description, these characteristics enabled rapid and more uniform lithium-ion transport through the separator. The effect was linked to reduced polarization and improved electrode reactions, particularly as the discharge rate increased. Ryou said the study showed that battery performance can be improved not only through new electrode materials but also through separator engineering. He emphasized that the modified separator’s influence extended beyond the lithium-metal anode and significantly improved the high-rate performance of the NCM90 cathode. The cathode comparison showed little separation between the separator types at the lowest reported rate. At 1C, cells using either CBT or conventional polyethylene separators delivered approximately 197 mAh g⁻¹. At 2C, capacity was 187 mAh g⁻¹ with CBT and 165 mAh g⁻¹ with polyethylene. The difference widened at 4C: the NCM90 cathode delivered 163 mAh g⁻¹ with CBT compared with 115 mAh g⁻¹ with the conventional separator. The resulting 48 mAh g⁻¹ difference corresponded to an improvement of approximately 42% at that rate. These measurements concern laboratory cells and the reported cathode-specific capacity; the release does not provide a broader comparison across commercial formats or a full range of electrode loadings and operating conditions. Real-time observations of lithium deposition showed that CBT did more than improve the cathode response. Cells equipped with the modified separator displayed no visible dendrite growth during the reported deposition observations. Lithium instead formed a smoother, more compact layer, and it was removed more uniformly during stripping. The findings indicate that the separator’s transport behavior was associated with more even lithium handling at the anode interface. The observation of no visible dendrite growth applies to the conditions examined in the study and does not establish that dendrites are absent under every possible cycling, temperature, current-density or manufacturing condition. The reported electrochemical testing also covered demanding cycling and temperature conditions. Li||NCM90 cells using CBT and operated at 2C charge and 4C discharge retained approximately 60% of their capacity after around 2,500 cycles. At −25 °C, the cells retained approximately 68.9% of their initial capacity after 150 cycles. In a separate assessment, the CBT separator maintained its structural integrity at 200 °C. These results demonstrate performance under the specified laboratory protocols. The university release does not provide every detail of the thermal test or a head-to-head long-term cycling result for CBT and polyethylene, so it would be premature to conclude from the supplied evidence that the modified separator offers superior long-term stability across all tested conditions. Samsung SDI Samsung SDI signs 1 GWh US battery storage deal Cells and modules built in Indiana Delivery set before end of 2026 Stock video by Mumtaz Niazi via Pexels Oct 26, 2026 Samsung SDI Signs 1 GWh NCA Storage Supply Deal with Alpha Omega Power Samsung SDI has agreed to supply 1 GWh of nickel cobalt aluminum battery storage to a single customer in the United States, according to ESS News. The manufacturer will produce all cells and modules for the agreement domestically, with the cells and modules to be built at its StarPlus Energy plant in Kokomo, Indiana. The customer is Alpha Omega Power, a utility and independent power producer. Under the deal, Samsung SDI is expected to deliver its Samsung Battery Box 1.7 containerized energy storage to projects scheduled to begin construction in 2027, spanning the Western Electricity Coordinating Council and Electric Reliability Council of Texas energy markets. Delivery is expected before the end of 2026. The agreement reflects a notable commitment to NCA chemistry in a global storage market where cells based on lithium iron phosphate chemistry continue to hold the lead. It also arrives as the US government considers further restrictions on imported power equipment. Samsung SDI reports that the SBB 1.7 uses a high-nickel NCA chemistry and offers 17% higher energy density than its predecessor, the SBB 1.5, while keeping the same 20-foot footprint. The manufacturer also emphasizes fire safety in the design, noting that the system incorporates its proprietary Enhanced Direct Injection technology, which injects fire-extinguishing agents directly into individual battery modules. With the latest contract, Samsung SDI has now been engaged to supply a total of 1.5 GWh of energy storage to Alpha Omega Power, following an earlier supply agreement signed in 2025. Fabrice Hudry, president of ESS at Samsung SDI America, indicated in a press release that the company's differentiated technology and US production capabilities will support its continued expansion in the North American energy storage market. Paul Choi, chief executive of Alpha Omega Power, commented that American-made storage from Samsung SDI will play an important role in the company's continued growth and that the second agreement strengthens its domestic supply chain for next-generation energy infrastructure.
