EU Carbon Market EU plan favors bioLNG and e-fuels over waste biodiesel SMAP funds 110M allowances from 2028 Waste-based biodiesel gets no support Stock video by Wolfgang Weiser via Pexels Oct 26, 2026 EU Carbon Market Proposal Would Reshape Marine Fuel Economics Unevenly Europe's carbon market may soon begin compensating shipowners for fuel switching, yet the assistance available is anything but uniform. In July, the European Commission put forward a revision of the EU Emissions Trading System that would set aside as many as 110 million allowances from 2028 through 2040 for a new Sustainable Maritime Alternative Propulsion mechanism, designed to bridge part of the cost difference between fossil marine fuels and sustainable substitutes. Rystad Energy's analysis indicates that, taken together with the EU ETS itself and the FuelEU Maritime regulation, the proposal would alter the cost hierarchy of marine fuels across Europe. BioLNG and renewable e-fuels are positioned to benefit most, whereas biodiesel derived from used cooking oil and animal fats, among the most commonly used marine biofuels today, receives no support. Timing and Compliance Pressure Timing is significant. Starting in 2026, shipping firms must surrender ETS allowances covering 100% of their verified in-scope emissions, which now include methane and nitrous oxide, while FuelEU Maritime mandates a progressively stricter reduction in the greenhouse-gas intensity of onboard energy use. Both frameworks depend on the sustainability criteria of the EU's revised Renewable Energy Directive. For shipowners, charterers and fuel suppliers, the central question is which fuel pathway the combined rules favor. How the Subsidy Would Work SMAP would bridge 55% of the remaining price gap to fossil fuel for biogas and advanced biofuels, and 90% for renewable fuels of non-biological origin such as e-ammonia and e-methanol, with an extra 10 percentage points when the feedstock originates in the EU. Since support scales with the size of the gap, the costliest fuels receive the most per tonne, and EU-made e-ammonia could have its entire remaining premium covered. Support is cut in half for voyages entering or leaving the EU, and fuels generally must be produced within the EU or in a country with a linked carbon market. Cost Rankings on Intra-EU Routes Combined, the three instruments push several alternative fuels below the cost of very low sulfur fuel oil on intra-EU voyages. At third-quarter 2026 prices, bioLNG costs more than double that of VLSFO before any incentives, yet it ends up at roughly half the cost of VLSFO once FuelEU credits and the proposed subsidy are factored in. Most of that advantage stems from FuelEU Maritime, and bioLNG would already undercut VLSFO without SMAP. Since bioLNG is a drop-in fuel for liquefied natural gas engines, this reinforces the business case for LNG dual-fuel ships trading in Europe. Renewable fuels of non-biological origin receive the most generous treatment of all and, on paper, EU-produced e-ammonia could become the cheapest fuel on intra-EU routes, although very few vessels can burn ammonia today and EU output remains limited. Waste-Based Biofuels Left Out The most obvious losers are liquid biofuels made from waste oils and fats. Used cooking oil and category 1 and 2 animal fats satisfy every EU sustainability test and earn full credit under both the ETS and FuelEU Maritime, but SMAP covers only advanced biofuels made from feedstocks listed in Annex IX Part A of the revised Renewable Energy Directive. Biogas, in contrast, appears eligible irrespective of feedstock. The exclusion matters given the structure of Europe's biodiesel industry. By 2030, crops and waste lipids such as used cooking oil and other waste fats and oils are projected to make up about 96% of the region's biodiesel and renewable diesel production capacity, leaving only around 2% clearly eligible for support. Aviation's sustainable fuel mandate draws on the same waste lipids, meaning shipping is unlikely to secure much eligible liquid biofuel. artigo.texto: The debate over data centers has found its way into Los Angeles County’s election season, where for months, even the mention of data center in public forums in some local cities has drawn keen attention in the run-up to November. In cities such as Alhambra and Monterey Park, the local fate of centers — the giant warehouses, built to power the nation’s artificial intelligence boom, and their kin, battery energy storage systems (BESS) — has manifested itself in ballot measures and candidate talking points, as towns debate whether such hubs should be built. In most cases, the centers don’t exist at all, and in a handful they’ve been proposed. But in L.A. County, like the rest of the nation, they’ve often become a symbol of pushback in a nation grappling with high costs and the relentless drive of technology companies seeking to build an AI infrastructure. Case in point: Alhambra. In July, the City Council voted to place Measure DB on the Nov. 3 ballot, giving residents the chance to codify an existing city ban that has been an ordinance in the city. “While a Data Center ban already exists by ordinance, this measure lets Alhambra voters decide whether to make that ban permanent and subject to voter approval to change” City Manager City Manager Jessica Binnquist said back in September announcement, after the council approved the ballot measure. Many residents had reportedly emailed the city about wanting data center protections, leading to the June 22 ordinance. And, like many cities, the action for the ban came amid a broader discussion on responsible development and long-term investments in schools, infrastructure, public spaces and environmental safety. If the proposed Alhambra measure sounds familiar, it’s because neighboring Monterey Park has become the impetus for voter action on data centers after its voters approved a pioneering ban in June. The momentum has carried over, becoming a template for this November’s ballot action on the centers, proponents said. In Monterey Park, developer HMC StratCap had proposed a center before a months-long grassroots campaign and various city ordinances brought the project to a halt, first with a city council moratorium and then a vote of the people. In the wake of the win, an array of local community organizers and leaders involved in supporting the measure are running for office this November, not just in Monterey Park but in neighboring cities. - Also see: In Monterey Park, 2 candidates vie for a seat in aftermath of trailblazing data center ban In Monterey Park and Alhambra, the anti-data center movement led Steven Kung and Amy J. Wong – organizers from No Data Center Monterey Park and SGV Progressive Action – to run for their respective city council seats. Leveraging their Monterey Park success, Wong and others from SGV Progressive Action have advocated for other cities to follow suit: promote a voter-ballot based ban, which is harder to overturn than a council ordinance banning the facilities city-wide. Beyond advocating for ordinances in Montebello, El Monte and Baldwin Park, Wong’s advocacy could lead to Alhambra being the second city in the county to ban data centers city-wide through public vote with its Measure DB. Wong, who is running against Ron Sahu for an Alhambra seat, co-founded SGV Progressive Action, helped establish Monterey Park’s data center ballot initiative and campaigned for the same action in other San Gabriel Valley cities, including Alhambra. It’s become part of her pitch as she battles it out with Sahu over quality-of-life and development issues. Sahu also supports the ban. It’s not just them. Leslie Garcia, an air quality instrument specialist with the South Coast Air Quality Management District running for West Covina City Council District 2, became involved with the No Data Center San Gabriel Valley coalition, which has fueled her run for office. “I started becoming more involved with the No Data Center coalition, and as we’re continuing to do our work against the City of Industry, that’s when people who were running for positions in Covina started to speak up about the battery energy storage system,” Garcia said. In June, the Covina Planning Commission rejected energy developer RWE’s controversial Covina Reliability Project, a BESS facility, citing several inconsistencies in the project. And, in September, West Covina Council unanimously approved a resolution opposing large-scale data centers and BESS facilities from being built in the city. Locally, many see BESS facilities — which harness electrical energy — as a precursor to data centers. In February, the City of Industry’s City Council unanimously approved energy utility developer AYPA Power’s application to begin developing the Marici Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) Facility along Gale Avenue. The project’s approval followed previous concerns at a Jan. 27 planning commission meeting that the proposed facility would lead to a future data center, which AYPA and the city have denied. Stefanie Leilua decided to run for council in Walnut because “when one city gets an approval, it’s gonna affect two to three cities, no matter what, because of how we’re lined up.” “Look at the La Verne fire that happened,” pointing to the Metropolitan Water District BESS fire that led to a four-day evacuation in late September. The fire involved two 250-kilowatt battery units housed in an indoor-outdoor facility to support a 2-megawatt solar farm. By comparison, the City of Industry’s Marici BESS facility is to be approximately 400 megawatts. “It wasn’t even as big, but everybody had to end up staying indoors because of the chemical pollution that was coming out of the battery center,” Leilua said. Garcia noted the nexus between local cities. “I went to go help them out since they’re our sister city,” Garcia continued. “In the San Gabriel Valley, this feels like the first time we have a really large progressive movement united by the fact that we don’t want data centers … If we get

artigo.texto: Defiance voters to decide charter amendment limiting data center size Citizen-led proposal on the November ballot does not ban data centers outright TOLEDO, Ohio (WTVG) - Defiance voters will decide in November on a citizen-led charter amendment that places limits on the size of data centers in the city. The proposed amendment does not ban data centers outright. People on both sides of the debate want a bright future for the community, but they differ on how to get there. What the amendment would do Sonya Mavis, a local business owner, is one of the people behind the amendment. “We collected nearly 500 signatures, when we only needed 235ish,” Mavis said. “It’s just banning data centers that are over 25 megawatts within city limits,” Mavis said. Residents’ concerns Mavis said residents she spoke with voiced concerns about increased water and energy bills, along with noise. “Because of that frequency, that vibration, the hum that comes off of data centers, they don’t want that in their community,” Mavis said. Mavis said her group is not against technology. She said she agrees data centers are needed, but their size needs to be regulated. “We don’t need a data center at 400 megawatts that can power Portland, Oregon,” Mavis said. Property owner opposes amendment A local business owner is looking to bring industrial development to his 340-acre property. Bryan Keller, CEO of Keller Logistics, said the property has natural gas, some power to get started and is already zoned industrial. “I think the highest and best use for this would be a data center,” Keller said. Keller said he is against the charter amendment. He listed potential revenue to the city near the top of his reasons. “They’re writing significant checks to the schools, they’re putting money into community development,” Keller said. His land has been annexed into the city of Defiance. “We don’t have an end user yet,” Keller said. The reporter asked the city whether it has received proposals from any developers. The city said it could not comment on any proposed development that may have legal implications. How to vote A “yes” vote is for the restriction, meaning the voter is against large-scale data centers. A “no” vote means the voter would like to allow large-scale data centers. Temporary ban in effect The Defiance City Council passed a temporary ban on data centers. The moratorium went into effect in September and will stay in place for six months. Council said it needed the time to study the impact a facility would have on the community. Statement from the city A city spokesperson released the following statement to 13 Action News: “The City recognizes the public interest in data center development and its potential impact on our community. Any proposed development is subject to the City’s applicable laws, zoning regulations, and established review and approval processes. The City’s role is to evaluate development proposals in accordance with applicable law and the City’s adopted regulations, while considering relevant land-use, infrastructure, public safety, and community welfare issues. Because certain matters involving proposed development may have legal implications, the City will not comment on specific proposals or related legal issues at this time. The City will continue to follow the appropriate legal and municipal processes as these matters are considered.” Latest Local News | First Alert Weather | Crime | National | 13abc Originals Copyright 2026 WTVG. artigo.texto: O HSBC Vietnam anunciou a conclusão bem-sucedida de seu primeiro empréstimo verde sindicado internacional, no valor de US$ 105 milhões, para a Northern Power Corporation (EVNNPC). Os recursos do empréstimo serão utilizados para investir em sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) a serem instalados em subestações de 110 kV existentes na região norte. Um empréstimo verde de 105 milhões de dólares foi destinado a investimentos em infraestrutura de armazenamento de energia elétrica no norte do Vietnã. O HSBC atuou como único organizador principal, subscritor e estruturador de carteira de pedidos; único coordenador de transações verdes; e agente de empréstimo na transação de empréstimo verde sindicado de US$ 105 milhões, com prazo de 8 anos, da Northern Power Corporation. Nesta transação, o HSBC atua como único coordenador líder, subscritor e estruturador de carteira de pedidos, único coordenador da transação verde e agente de empréstimo. Com um prazo total de 8 anos, desde o primeiro desembolso até a data de vencimento final, o empréstimo é considerado uma transação de longo prazo no mercado internacional de empréstimos sindicados do Vietnã, dada a escassez de precedentes para transações semelhantes. O empréstimo recebeu um número significativamente maior de solicitações do que o valor inicialmente oferecido, atraindo 15 financiadores da China, Coreia do Sul, Taiwan e Tailândia . A conclusão bem-sucedida desta transação demonstra a forte confiança das instituições financeiras internacionais na EVNNPC e reafirma a importância estratégica dos sistemas de armazenamento de energia em larga escala na transição energética do Vietnã. O programa BESS da EVNNPC deverá ser implementado em 70 subestações existentes, contribuindo para a melhoria da estabilidade e confiabilidade da rede elétrica, atendendo à crescente demanda de carga e minimizando o risco de sobrecarga e falhas na rede. O projeto também apoia a concretização do Plano de Desenvolvimento Energético VIII revisado e o objetivo de desenvolver um sistema de armazenamento de energia em conformidade com o plano diretor nacional de energia. Tim Evans, CEO do HSBC Vietnam, declarou: “O HSBC tem orgulho de ser parceiro da EVNNPC em seu primeiro empréstimo sindicado internacional em dólares americanos e em seu plano de investimento em infraestrutura de armazenamento de energia em baterias. Esta transação histórica combina soluções de financiamento verde personalizadas para a EVNNPC com infraestrutura essencial para aprimorar a resiliência da rede e apoiar o Vietnã em sua jornada rumo a um sistema de energia mais flexível e sustentável. A forte resposta dos credores reflete a confiança do mercado na EVNNPC e a importância deste programa.” Esta transação fortalece a relação entre o HSBC e a EVNNPC, após as duas partes terem concluído diversos empréstimos bilaterais de longo prazo no mercado interno. A captação bem-sucedida de recursos no mercado internacional abre oportunidades para a EVNNPC diversificar suas fontes de financiamento, ao mesmo tempo que reafirma a posição do HSBC como um parceiro confiável para atender às diversas necessidades de captação de recursos das empresas vietnamitas. Ao estruturar o empréstimo de acordo com os padrões de empréstimos verdes, em consonância com os Princípios de Empréstimos Verdes, o HSBC trabalhou em estreita colaboração com a EVNNPC para garantir que o financiamento estivesse alinhado com os benefícios ambientais do programa BESS. A transação demonstra que soluções de financiamento sustentáveis, adaptadas a necessidades específicas, podem contribuir para a mobilização de capital para infraestrutura energética crítica. Esta transação está alinhada com a diretriz do Banco Central do Vietnã de incentivar o aumento de empréstimos sindicados para projetos de grande escala. Ao mesmo tempo, o empréstimo demonstra o compromisso do HSBC em apoiar as empresas nacionais em sua jornada rumo ao crescimento, diversificando as fontes de financiamento e promovendo investimentos para uma economia mais sustentável e resiliente.

artigo.texto: Bloomfield's zoning rules prohibit data centers and battery energy storage facilities in every zoning district, affecting an informal proposal for a nearly 1-million-square-foot facility that had been floated for the town's northwest corner. The new rules bar data centers as a principal use, an accessory use, or as part of a mixed-use development in every zone townwide, and they also prohibit battery energy storage facilities outright, according to Hartford Business Journal. The vote comes more than a year after New York-based Atlas Capital Group made an informal presentation to the town in June 2025 for a data center at 132 Griffin Road North, on a vacant 44-acre former tobacco field. The project as described to Hartford Business Journal would have included roughly 900,000 square feet of data-center space and a 127,000-square-foot substation, though a separate description on the town's own civic-alerts page characterized the conceptual plan as a 1-million-square-foot facility — the two accounts differ on the exact scale of what was pitched. Scope of the Zoning Change The prohibition applies across Bloomfield's zoning districts. The rules apply to data centers as a principal or accessory use, as well as projects that would combine them with other uses. The amendments also prohibit battery energy storage facilities. Part of a Wider Connecticut Pushback Bloomfield isn't alone. Days earlier, East Lyme's zoning commission voted unanimously to prohibit both traditional and AI data centers, along with their accessory uses, with that ban taking effect Oct. 24, as WFSB reported. Unlike the temporary moratoriums many towns have adopted, East Lyme's ban is intended to be permanent, though the underlying zoning regulations could still be changed later if officials choose. That town's commission pointed to concerns about strain on the water supply, noise from the facilities, and impacts on nearby residents. The resistance is showing up at the state level too. Connecticut currently has no large-scale AI data centers operating within its borders, according to a report from CT Public, yet critics have already zeroed in on the industry's heavy water and electricity use, warning it could drive up utility rates for residents who live nearby. State Senate Majority Leader Bob Duff has said he intends to introduce legislation creating a statewide moratorium on AI data centers when the legislature convenes next year, telling the outlet, “We need to have new legislation in the state of Connecticut that puts a moratorium on AI data centers across the state of Connecticut.” In Groton, a proposed AI data center drew resident opposition over fears about local electric rates. Tax Breaks Still on the Books The regulatory crackdown comes even as older state incentives remain in place to lure data-center investment. Connecticut lawmakers created tax breaks in 2021 aimed at attracting such projects. Qualifying developments investing at least $200 million — or $50 million in certain designated economic-development zones — may receive sales and property tax exemptions. For now, Bloomfield has decided those potential tax benefits aren't worth the tradeoff. With the amendments in place, any future data-center pitch — however it's labeled — would have to clear a zoning code that no longer leaves room for it anywhere in town.

artigo.texto: Dozens gather to discuss concerns on Google data center in Fort Wayne FORT WAYNE, Ind. (WPTA) - With Fort Wayne’s growing data center presence, Protect Allen County held a community gathering Sunday afternoon for residents to voice their opinions. About 50 people packed inside a home near the Google data center on Adams Road. Organizers said the goal was to build a coalition for those who are worried about the negative impacts, whether they relate to air quality or energy costs, and show concerned citizens how they can advocate for each other. The resident of the home everyone was gathered at, Barry Dibble, said traffic spiked near his house. “I want them to check their politicians out to see how they would feel about it. Without their support, this means nothing. Our politicians need to support us and to support what’s going on and stop this nonsense.” He added that he hopes Sunday’s gathering pushes more people to talk to local officials. Protect Allen County plans to hold more community gatherings going forward. View all previous coverage here. artigo.texto: Evergy says data centers won’t raise your rates. Here’s how that works KANSAS CITY, Mo. (KCTV) - Evergy customers received an email Monday about the company’s approach to data centers — including extra fees and other measures the company says are designed to protect ordinary customers from paying more. But there’s more to the story than what’s on that page. The debate over data centers has already played out locally. In Independence, the city council approved tax incentives for the Nebius data center project. Voters later ousted two council members and recalled another over their support for the incentives. In Gardner, developer Beale Infrastructure withdrew its application for a proposed data center in May after hundreds of residents packed a city council meeting to oppose it. The city said it would not offer incentives for the project. Neither Independence nor Gardner is served by Evergy. Both cities have public, city-run electric utilities. State regulators — the Missouri Public Service Commission and the Kansas Corporation Commission — only have authority over investor-owned utilities like Evergy, Ameren and Liberty Utilities. Public, city-run utilities and electric cooperatives fall outside their jurisdiction. That means the new rules don’t apply to customers of public utilities like Independence Power & Light, regardless of what rules Evergy follows. Not just data centers The rules Evergy outlined in its email apply to what the company calls “large load customers” — not data centers specifically. Under the new tariffs, any customer with a peak electric demand of more than 75 megawatts qualifies, whether that’s a data center, a large manufacturing plant or a logistics and distribution center. For comparison, the city of Independence has said the Nebius data center will require more than 800 megawatts once fully operational — more than 10 times the threshold that triggers the new rules. The rules apply to new customers starting service above that threshold, as well as existing customers that expand their electric use by 75 megawatts or more. According to Evergy and documents filed with state regulators, large load customers must, among other things: - Pay higher electric rates than other large commercial and industrial customers. - Pay 100% of the costs for any infrastructure — like substations or transmission lines — built solely to serve them. - Agree to a minimum monthly bill, even in months when they use less electricity than expected. - Provide collateral, equal to two years of their minimum monthly bills, to protect other customers if a project is delayed, downsized or abandoned. - Sign long-term contracts of at least 12 years, with the option of an additional five-year phase-in period, for a potential commitment of up to 17 years. Customers who try to leave early face exit fees and additional penalties for shorter notice. Kansas Corporation Commission staff estimated in testimony that large load customers will pay 7% to 10% more than Evergy’s existing industrial customers under the new rate plan. Rules already in place Evergy’s email went out Monday, but the rules behind it have been in place for months. The Kansas Corporation Commission approved the new rate plan on Nov. 6, 2025, as part of a unanimous settlement. The agreement was negotiated by Evergy along with the Citizens’ Utility Ratepayer Board, the Kansas Industrial Consumers Group, environmental groups including the Sierra Club and the Natural Resources Defense Council, the Data Center Coalition, Google and several Kansas school districts. In Missouri, state lawmakers passed Senate Bill 4 in 2025, requiring the Public Service Commission to adopt rates ensuring large load customers pay their share of costs without shifting those costs to residential and small-business customers. Evergy’s Missouri tariffs took effect in March. Ameren Missouri’s took effect in January. The two states took different paths to get there: Missouri’s Legislature required regulators to act, while in Kansas, Evergy itself proposed the rate plan and sought regulators’ approval. KCTV5 is working to line up an interview with Evergy. We’ve also reached out to Independence and other public utilities in the area to find out whether they’re considering any similar city-wide rules of their own. The Independence City Council recently passed new restrictions on future data center development, including setback requirements and a cap on generator testing hours, though the rules don’t apply retroactively to the Nebius project, which broke ground in May. Independence’s contract with Nebius requires the data center’s power to come from a new, privately funded power plant. Copyright 2026 KCTV. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: The San Diego City Council votes Tuesday on Mayor Todd Gloria’s proposed temporary ban on large data centers. The vote would put an emergency ordinance into place and pause for 45 days all pending applications for data centers, buying the city time (the City Council can renew the ban with consecutive votes for up to 20 months) to come up with regulations for how data centers might fit within city zoning. Gloria’s team had apparently already been working on a temporary ban for weeks, we reported in the Politics Report. They’d been waiting for input from the city attorney’s office. Then earlier this month, I broke the news that Manchester Financial Group was exploring the possibility of building a 400-megawatt data center on the U.S. Navy property near the Midway District. That added a lot of pressure to get the proposed ban on the books. Even if the ban passes, the city can’t really do much to stop a data center from being built at 4301 Pacific Highway. City councilmembers already acknowledged that. “Because NAVWAR is federal land, the moratorium can’t stop that project,” reads a press release from Councilmember Sean Elo-Rivera’s office. It turns out very little can stop data centers from popping up on federal property. A big reason for that is Donald Trump. Trump has ordered the Secretary of Defense to proactively identify sites on military installations that could house data centers. On July 23, 2025, he also signed Executive Order 14318, fast-tracking data centers larger than 100 megawatts through permitting processes under the Clean Air Act, the Clean Water Act and the Toxic Substances Control Act. Data centers that are funded with mostly private dollars would mostly be excluded from environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act, or NEPA, as well. NEPA is a landmark environmental law passed in 1970 requiring federal agencies to assess environmental impacts before making major decisions on permits, land management and constructing highways or publicly owned facilities. “This administration has watered down NEPA to where it’s pretty meaningless these days,” said Debbie Sivas, who teaches environmental law at Stanford University. “I don’t think people realize how much they’ve tried to neuter the laws because it’s going on in real time.” She said the Trump Administration’s opinion on what kinds of projects are subject to NEPA is “extremely narrow.” Each federal agency was allowed to adopt their own way of regulating under NEPA and, to her surprise, their interim guidelines went into effect right away. Manchester is currently negotiating with the Navy on what kind of redevelopment project might take place on the NAVWAR site. Manchester is supposed build the Navy a new command center and, in exchange, be allowed to redevelop the rest of the land. The final project will absolutely include some housing, Manchester officials have said, maybe as much as thousands of units. It also could include hotels, restaurants and other commercial uses. The Navy started the NEPA process for the project back in 2020 and released a draft environmental impact statement in 2021. Such a step allows the public to comment on their proposed plans, for which the Navy received over 650 letters and 1,000 comments. Under NEPA, the government is supposed to respond to each one. Sivas said when those sweeping changes to NEPA were announced, government officials said they wouldn’t apply retroactively to projects that were already in the middle of the process. That means, in theory, the old regulations should apply to the NAVWAR project. Sergio Hernandez, a spokesperson on behalf of the U.S. Navy, told me the agency expects to publish a revised draft environmental impact statement in 2027. A new Politico poll showed at least half of Americans oppose data centers being built within three miles of their home and Americans on both sides of the aisle are more likely to back candidates that oppose them. The topic has captured the public’s attention in political races and debates across the country as the Nov. 3 midterm elections draw nearer. Hundreds of cities have placed bans on data centers and that’s partly why developers appear keen to turn to federal land to build them. In January, the Department of Defense solicited competitive bids from developers interested in leasing land from the U.S. Army to develop commercial data centers at Fort Hood and Fort Bliss in Texas, Fort Bragg in California, and Dugway Proving Ground in Utah. Sivas likened what’s going on with data center development to how the Trump Administration is building detention centers on federal land to house people migrating into the United States. “They’re trying to get onto federal property to get a shield from local opposition,” Sivas said. artigo.texto: Banestes contrata Prod do Espírito Santo para data center Data center da prod do Espírito Santo passou por um retrofit pra conquistar contas como a da instituição financeira. O Banestes assinou contrato com o Instituto de Tecnologia da Informação e Comunicação do Estado do Espírito Santo (Prodest) para hospedar dados do banco em regime de colocation no Data Center do Estado, em Vitória. O acordo foi firmado por cinco anos e exige disponibilidade de quase 100% das informações do banco estatal capixaba. A contratação garante ao Banestes acesso a uma infraestrutura que inclui sistemas de detecção e combate a incêndio, climatização de alta performance e proteção contra fumaça, água, vandalismo e roubos. O Data Center também opera sem interrupção mesmo diante de falhas no fornecimento de energia, graças à redundância elétrica composta por subestação, geradores, transformadores e nobreaks. O Prodest realizou o retrofit do Data Center do Estado antes da assinatura do contrato. A atualização substituiu equipamentos responsáveis pelo funcionamento e pela disponibilidade contínua da estrutura por versões mais modernas, elevando o nível de segurança da operação. O diretor-geral do Prodest, Marcelo Cornélio, afirma que a adesão do Banestes valida o investimento feito na infraestrutura. “O retrofit foi uma atualização necessária para garantir que os dados das instituições públicas permaneçam seguros e sempre disponíveis. Com equipamentos mais modernos, ganhamos em confiabilidade e em eficiência energética. A decisão do Banestes de armazenar suas informações em nossa estrutura confirma a qualidade do nosso trabalho e reforça a importância de investir de forma contínua no fortalecimento da infraestrutura tecnológica do Estado”, completa Cornélio. Os valores do contrato não foram revelados.

artigo.texto: Europe’s carbon market is getting more room to manoeuvre as the EU agrees to raise the threshold for scrapping surplus permits. That should give industry flexibility while keeping a lid on oversupply and price swings. The Council of the EU and the European Parliament have reached a provisional deal to change how the EU’s carbon market handles surplus emissions permits. The mechanism for cancelling excess permits will stay in place. But the threshold will rise from 400 million to 700 million. The new threshold will take effect once the deal is formally adopted. The European Commission had originally proposed scrapping the cancellation mechanism altogether. Higher threshold, bigger buffer Negotiators instead settled on a compromise that preserves a safeguard against oversupply while leaving more room to respond to future market swings. “In response to European leaders’ call for accelerated action, we reached a balanced outcome on the Market Stability Reserve that provides European industry with immediate flexibility, while ensuring price stability and protecting the integrity of the EU carbon market,” said Darragh O’Brien, Ireland’s Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment. He described the deal as part of the EU’s ‘One Europe, One Market’ roadmap. The Mmarket Stability Reserve (MSR) helps balance supply and demand in the EU emissions trading system (ETS). When too many permits circulate, it removes some from the market. Under the rules, it can also release permits when needed. The mechanism aims to limit imbalances caused by a surplus or shortage of allowances. Three billion permits off the market Since the cancellation mechanism began in 2023, it has removed more than three billion permits from the market. This helped tackle the historic oversupply that had built up in the ETS. Negotiators say the higher threshold will strengthen the market’s long-term stability and provide a larger buffer against future fluctuations. The change could also matter after the mid-2030s, when the ETS emissions cap will continue to fall and the market could face tighter supply. A broader review of the ETS is still under way. It will also consider gradually lowering the cancellation threshold to ensure a consistent approach across the system. The current deal is a standalone change intended to help address high and volatile energy prices, rather than a full reform of the carbon market. The provisional agreement must now be confirmed by the Council and Parliament before both institutions formally adopt it.

artigo.texto: DeSoto County Commission fails to approve 237-acre rezoning for data center project near Arcadia More than 100 people attended a DeSoto County Commission meeting Tuesday evening to oppose a proposed data center project near Arcadia, urging commissioners to reject the plan due to concerns about its impact on the community. The DeSoto County Board of County Commissioners denied the first of two additional rezoning applications for the DCIP Group's proposed 825-acre data center project. On Tuesday, commissioners' vote to approve the application failed in a 2-2 tie on the nearly 238-acre rezoning request, which could delay the proposed development. Commissioners heard presentations from county and developer experts, plus public comment, in the more-than-six-hour meeting ending after midnight Wednesday. The project, located on East Roan Street just outside of Arcadia, involves rezoning a nearly 238-acre site and a separate 554-acre site of agricultural land. On Wednesday, commissioners are expected to consider a different, larger rezoning request for the additional 554 acres by Swisher Properties. Back in March, commissioners approved the first 34 acres of the site, which was previously a power plant. However, the two additional applications for the project have alarmed residents. "Please don't tell me that those 55+ citizens won't be affected by a data center 500 feet from their homes," said Eloise Johnson, an Arcadia resident, in a previous meeting. Former DeSoto County Commissioner John Johnson shared his concerns in August, saying, "I think the place where they want to put it is not a good place. I think the impact on too many people is too great." The DCIP Group, the developer behind the project, stated that only 10.9% of the property—roughly 100 acres—is planned for data center buildings. They say approximately 75 percent of the property will remain open land, adding that landscape buffers and setbacks will be expanded to 200 to 500 feet from surrounding neighbors. The DCIP Group has also said that existing wetlands and floodplains will continue to be preserved and protected. However, earlier this month, the planning commission raised unresolved issues, including water use, wastewater, traffic, noise, wetlands, and whether the project fits the county's long-term growth plan. The county's own report indicated that the project could affect nearby living conditions because it would operate 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, with potential noise, lighting, and visual impacts. "We just don't know what's going to happen, you know, with the water consumption, with the noise pollution," said Jennifer, an Arcadia resident. "There's so many what-ifs. And we just don't feel that this is a good thing for this town, in this county." The debate over the DCIP project is not over. On Wednesday, commissioners are expected to consider a larger rezoning request for an additional 554 acres by Swisher Properties. artigo.texto: Resumo - WEG teve lucro líquido de R$ 1,67 bilhão no 3º trimestre de 2026, alta de 0,9% - Vendas no exterior chegaram a 62,5% do faturamento, maior nível da história - América do Norte respondeu por US$ 722,8 milhões, 31% a mais que em 2025 - Margem bruta caiu de 33,6% para 32,9% e derrubou a ação (WEGE3) - Papel acumulou queda de 10,96% na semana, a pior do Ibovespa - Em 31 de dezembro, João Paulo Gualberto da Silva se despede do comando da vice-presidência de Energia A WEG, multinacional de Santa Catarina apelidada de ‘fábrica de bilionários’, teve lucro líquido de R$ 1,67 bilhão entre julho e setembro de 2026. O resultado ficou 0,9% acima do que a empresa havia obtido no mesmo intervalo de 2025, montante que equivale a mais de R$ 18 milhões por dia, ou cerca de R$ 750 mil a cada hora ao longo dos 92 dias do terceiro trimestre. Mesmo com esse desempenho, os investidores ficaram decepcionados com o balanço, que veio a público na quarta-feira (21). Na semana, nenhuma ação caiu tanto no Ibovespa quanto a WEGE3. O motivo tem menos a ver com o valor do lucro e mais com a margem que resta em cada item comercializado. Na mesma data, uma mudança que já estava prevista para a vice-presidência de Energia foi anunciada pela empresa. Essa área responde por parte dos negócios de crescimento mais acelerado dentro da WEG. Entre julho e setembro, a receita líquida alcançou R$ 10,86 bilhões, crescimento de 5,7% frente a um ano atrás, algo próximo de R$ 118 milhões faturados por dia. Já o Ebitda, medida do que a operação gera sem considerar juros, tributos e depreciação, teve avanço de 3,1%, somando R$ 2,35 bilhões. No quesito rentabilidade do capital aplicado, o índice ficou em 33,2%, o que significa 0,8 ponto percentual acima do verificado no mesmo período do ano passado. Exportações da WEG são impulsionadas por EUA Fora das fronteiras nacionais ficou o ponto alto: nunca a WEG havia visto as exportações atingirem 62,5% da sua receita. Quem puxou essa escalada foi, principalmente, a América do Norte. Por lá, as vendas somaram US$ 722,8 milhões no trimestre, alta de 31% ante o mesmo intervalo do ano anterior, o equivalente a 54,7% de tudo que a companhia comercializa para fora do Brasil. No mesmo período de 2025, tal fração ficava em 47,9%. Dois fatores explicam esse desempenho. De um lado, a entrega de transformadores para a rede elétrica dos Estados Unidos, que passa por modernização. De outro, os geradores da Marathon, marca sob a qual o grupo opera em território norte-americano, empregados para assegurar energia de reserva nos data centers, enormes galpões repletos de servidores sobre os quais se apoiam a internet e a inteligência artificial. Ainda assim, o ganho convertido em reais ficou abaixo do potencial. Na comparação entre os dois trimestres, a cotação média da moeda americana caiu de R$ 5,45 para R$ 5,14. Já que os resultados obtidos fora do país são transformados pela WEG em moeda nacional, o peso de cada dólar no balanço diminuiu. Assim, enquanto em dólares as exportações cresceram 14,8%, em reais o aumento foi de apenas 8,3%. Custo de produção e margem de lucro O ponto que mais pesou nas preocupações do mercado foi a rentabilidade. Depois de descontar o custo de produção, a fatia que sobra para a empresa, medida pela margem bruta, caiu de 33,6% para 32,9%. Traduzindo: a cada R$ 100 vendidos, a companhia reteve R$ 32,90, ante R$ 33,60 um ano atrás. A WEG atribui a queda desse número a três causas: o encarecimento do cobre, insumo essencial na fabricação de motores e transformadores; as taxas cobradas pelos Estados Unidos sobre importações; e os gastos maiores com pessoal, ligados à ampliação de fábricas que começou neste ano. Dentro do custo dos produtos, os salários saltaram de 19,2% para 20,3%, porque os funcionários são admitidos antes de as novas linhas chegarem à capacidade total. Com isso, a margem Ebitda caiu de 22,2% a 21,6%. Reação do mercado e queda das ações Segundo compilação da LSEG (London Stock Exchange Group), os analistas projetavam lucro de R$ 1,71 bilhão e Ebitda de R$ 2,40 bilhões. Os números ficaram um pouco aquém dessas estimativas, e investidores esperavam ainda que a margem recuasse menos. As ações caíram até 4,6% na quarta-feira pela manhã, chegando a R$ 46,53 cada. No intervalo de 19 a 23 de outubro, o papel somou perda de 10,96%, o maior recuo dentro do Ibovespa. Já o índice ficou praticamente de lado no período, recuando apenas 0,17%. Mudança na vice-presidência de Energia da WEG Na mesma divulgação do balanço, a empresa anunciou que João Paulo Gualberto da Silva, com 37 anos de trajetória na companhia, se despedirá da vice-presidência de Energia no dia 31 de dezembro. Graduado em engenharia elétrica pela Udesc, ele atuou na área comercial (com passagem pelos Estados Unidos) e esteve à frente da frente de novas energias, dedicada à eólica e à solar. O substituto será Paulo Leonardo da Silva Sinoti, atual diretor de Soluções em Energia & Serviços, que acumula mais de 30 anos na companhia. Ele toma posse em 1º de janeiro de 2027. Referendada pelo Conselho de Administração, a indicação se insere no plano de sucessão da empresa. Essa mudança acontece enquanto o setor de energia se expande. Encarregado dos transformadores e geradores que dão base ao crescimento nos EUA, o ramo que reúne distribuição, transmissão e geração teve suas exportações crescerem 24,1% no trimestre, quando comparado ao mesmo período de 2025. A história e o legado da ‘fábrica de bilionários’ A WEG nasceu em Jaraguá do Sul (SC), em 16 de setembro de 1961, tendo a fabricação de motores elétricos como atividade inicial. A sigla foi formada juntando as primeiras letras dos nomes de seus fundadores: Werner Ricardo Voigt, Eggon João da Silva e Geraldo Werninghaus. Atualmente, está entre as maiores fabricantes de equipamentos elétricos do planeta. Seu catálogo vai de motores, geradores, transformadores, painéis e sistemas de automação a soluções de energia, carregadores para veículos elétricos e tintas

artigo.texto: NIOSH Warns of Lead Exposure Risks in Battery Industry A new NIOSH bulletin highlights elevated blood lead levels among battery manufacturing and recycling workers, along with workplace conditions that can increase exposure. Workers in lead-acid battery manufacturing and recycling continue to face some of the highest occupational lead exposure risks in the United States, according to a new bulletin from the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH). Published Oct. 26 during National Lead Poisoning Prevention Week, the bulletin reviews surveillance data and workplace investigations that identify persistent hazards from airborne lead dust, contaminated surfaces, inadequate ventilation, and insufficient respiratory protection. Data from NIOSH's Adult Blood Lead Epidemiology and Surveillance (ABLES) program show that nearly 90% of adults with known lead exposure were exposed at work. In 2022, 60% of workers with blood lead levels of 25 micrograms per deciliter or higher were employed in manufacturing. More than 70% of those manufacturing workers were employed in battery manufacturing. The U.S. Census Bureau estimated that approximately 51,000 people worked in battery manufacturing in 2024, including workers involved in lead-acid battery production and recycling. Workplace Investigations Identify Exposure Hazards NIOSH highlighted findings from two previous workplace health hazard evaluations involving a battery manufacturing facility and an automotive battery recycling operation. At the manufacturing facility, investigators found that air contaminated with lead dust was entering locker rooms, offices and the cafeteria. Workers also carried lead contamination on their clothing, footwear and skin into areas intended to remain clean. Investigators identified additional concerns involving dry sweeping, inconsistent respirator use, improper respirator fit and inadequate maintenance practices. At the recycling facility, investigators detected lead contamination on most sampled work surfaces. Investigators also found inadequate local exhaust ventilation in areas with elevated airborne lead concentrations. Among workers interviewed at the recycling facility, 85% reported at least one symptom potentially associated with excessive lead exposure. Investigators also detected lead on workers' skin after showering, raising concerns about the effectiveness of decontamination procedures. Prevention Remains a Priority NIOSH emphasized that occupational lead exposure is preventable through effective engineering controls, workplace hygiene practices and appropriate personal protective equipment. Recommended measures include controlling airborne lead dust through local exhaust ventilation, using high-efficiency particulate air vacuums or wet cleaning methods instead of dry sweeping, and maintaining effective respiratory protection programs. Employers should also establish procedures to prevent lead contamination from spreading into break rooms, locker rooms and other clean areas. Contaminated clothing, footwear and personal belongings can carry lead dust into workers' homes, potentially exposing family members. NIOSH said continued demand for lead-acid batteries keeps workplace exposure prevention a priority for manufacturers and recycling operations.

artigo.texto: The debate over data centers has found its way into Los Angeles County’s election season, where for months, even the mention of data center in public forums in some local cities has drawn keen attention in the run-up to November. In cities such as Alhambra and Monterey Park, the local fate of centers — the giant warehouses, built to power the nation’s artificial intelligence boom, and their kin, battery energy storage systems (BESS) — has manifested itself in ballot measures and candidate talking points, as towns debate whether such hubs should be built. In most cases, the centers don’t exist at all, and in a handful they’ve been proposed. But in L.A. County, like the rest of the nation, they’ve often become a symbol of pushback in a nation grappling with high costs and the relentless drive of technology companies seeking to build an AI infrastructure. Case in point: Alhambra. In July, the City Council voted to place Measure DB on the Nov. 3 ballot, giving residents the chance to codify an existing city ban that has been an ordinance in the city. “While a Data Center ban already exists by ordinance, this measure lets Alhambra voters decide whether to make that ban permanent and subject to voter approval to change” City Manager City Manager Jessica Binnquist said back in September announcement, after the council approved the ballot measure. Many residents had reportedly emailed the city about wanting data center protections, leading to the June 22 ordinance. And, like many cities, the action for the ban came amid a broader discussion on responsible development and long-term investments in schools, infrastructure, public spaces and environmental safety. If the proposed Alhambra measure sounds familiar, it’s because neighboring Monterey Park has become the impetus for voter action on data centers after its voters approved a pioneering ban in June. The momentum has carried over, becoming a template for this November’s ballot action on the centers, proponents said. In Monterey Park, developer HMC StratCap had proposed a center before a months-long grassroots campaign and various city ordinances brought the project to a halt, first with a city council moratorium and then a vote of the people. In the wake of the win, an array of local community organizers and leaders involved in supporting the measure are running for office this November, not just in Monterey Park but in neighboring cities. - Also see: In Monterey Park, 2 candidates vie for a seat in aftermath of trailblazing data center ban In Monterey Park and Alhambra, the anti-data center movement led Steven Kung and Amy J. Wong – organizers from No Data Center Monterey Park and SGV Progressive Action – to run for their respective city council seats. Leveraging their Monterey Park success, Wong and others from SGV Progressive Action have advocated for other cities to follow suit: promote a voter-ballot based ban, which is harder to overturn than a council ordinance banning the facilities city-wide. Beyond advocating for ordinances in Montebello, El Monte and Baldwin Park, Wong’s advocacy could lead to Alhambra being the second city in the county to ban data centers city-wide through public vote with its Measure DB. Wong, who is running against Ron Sahu for an Alhambra seat, co-founded SGV Progressive Action, helped establish Monterey Park’s data center ballot initiative and campaigned for the same action in other San Gabriel Valley cities, including Alhambra. It’s become part of her pitch as she battles it out with Sahu over quality-of-life and development issues. Sahu also supports the ban. It’s not just them. artigo.texto: Bateria Gen6 da BMW ganha prêmio de inovação em tecnologia na China Tecnologia Gen6 equipa a linha Neue Klasse com arquitetura de 800 volts, carregamento bidirecional e ganho de até 30% em autonomia e velocidade de recarga O Grupo BMW foi reconhecido com o prêmio "Tecnologia Inovadora Global de Veículos de Nova Energia" durante o Congresso Mundial de Veículos de Nova Energia de 2026, realizado na China. A honraria premiou as inovações da sexta geração (Gen6) de baterias de alta tensão da montadora alemã, que se tornou a única fabricante automotiva estrangeira a receber a distinção no evento. A tecnologia serve como base técnica para a linha Neue Klasse, nova família de veículos 100% elétricos da marca alemã. A transição da quinta para a sexta geração da arquitetura eDrive envolveu o registro de mais de 500 registros de patente pelo grupo automotivo. "Ele confirma nossa abordagem de longo prazo, que combina inovação tecnológica com os mais altos padrões de qualidade e segurança. Com a Neue Klasse, estamos estabelecendo novos padrões nessa área", afirmou Jochen Goller, membro do Conselho de Administração da BMW AG. Células cilíndricas e arquitetura de 800 V Desenvolvida sobre uma arquitetura elétrica de 800 volts, a bateria Gen6 adota células cilíndricas com cátodo de alto teor de níquel e invólucro estrutural de aço. O conjunto elimina a necessidade de módulos intermediários — conceito conhecido como cell-to-pack —, permitindo que as células sejam integradas diretamente à carcaça do equipamento para elevar a densidade energética no mesmo espaço de instalação. Segundo dados da fabricante, o formato garante um ganho de densidade de energia superior a 20% em comparação à geração anterior, proporcionando um incremento de até 30% na autonomia do veículo e na velocidade de recarga. O sistema também foi projetado para permitir carregamento bidirecional (fornecendo energia da bateria de volta à rede ou a outros dispositivos) e suporte a infraestruturas de recarga de 400 V e 800 V. O gerenciamento do fluxo de energia e dos dados da bateria é realizado pela unidade de controle Energy Master, sistema com hardware e software desenvolvidos internamente pela própria BMW e instalado diretamente no conjunto da bateria de alta tensão. Produção global e estratégia industrial A revelação do prêmio ocorre em paralelo à consolidação da rede global de produção do componente. A BMW deu início à fabricação em série das baterias Gen6 no complexo de Shenyang, na China, que se somou às unidades de Debrecen (Hungria) e Irlbach-Straßkirchen (Alemanha). As fábricas de Woodruff (Estados Unidos) e San Luis Potosí (México) estão programadas para iniciar a montagem em série da tecnologia nas próximas etapas de expansão da rede. A estratégia industrial da montadora prevê a instalação das unidades de montagem de baterias próximas às linhas de produção dos veículos elétricos (conceito "local for local"), visando reduzir distâncias de transporte, mitigar gargalos de suprimento e padronizar o controle de qualidade por meio de inteligência artificial e inspeções automatizadas em tempo real.

artigo.texto: EU Carbon Market Proposal Would Reshape Marine Fuel Economics Unevenly Europe’s carbon market may soon begin compensating shipowners for fuel switching, yet the assistance available is anything but uniform. In July, the European Commission put forward a revision of the EU Emissions Trading System that would set aside as many as 110 million allowances from 2028 through 2040 for a new Sustainable Maritime Alternative Propulsion mechanism, designed to bridge part of the cost difference between fossil marine fuels and sustainable substitutes. Read also: IMO Approves New Safety Guidelines for Ammonia as Marine Fuel Rystad Energy’s analysis indicates that, taken together with the EU ETS itself and the FuelEU Maritime regulation, the proposal would alter the cost hierarchy of marine fuels across Europe. BioLNG and renewable e-fuels are positioned to benefit most, whereas biodiesel derived from used cooking oil and animal fats, among the most commonly used marine biofuels today, receives no support. Timing and Compliance Pressure Timing is significant. Starting in 2026, shipping firms must surrender ETS allowances covering 100% of their verified in-scope emissions, which now include methane and nitrous oxide, while FuelEU Maritime mandates a progressively stricter reduction in the greenhouse-gas intensity of onboard energy use. Both frameworks depend on the sustainability criteria of the EU’s revised Renewable Energy Directive. For shipowners, charterers and fuel suppliers, the central question is which fuel pathway the combined rules favor. How the Subsidy Would Work SMAP would bridge 55% of the remaining price gap to fossil fuel for biogas and advanced biofuels, and 90% for renewable fuels of non-biological origin such as e-ammonia and e-methanol, with an extra 10 percentage points when the feedstock originates in the EU. Since support scales with the size of the gap, the costliest fuels receive the most per tonne, and EU-made e-ammonia could have its entire remaining premium covered. Support is cut in half for voyages entering or leaving the EU, and fuels generally must be produced within the EU or in a country with a linked carbon market. Cost Rankings on Intra-EU Routes Combined, the three instruments push several alternative fuels below the cost of very low sulfur fuel oil on intra-EU voyages. At third-quarter 2026 prices, bioLNG costs more than double that of VLSFO before any incentives, yet it ends up at roughly half the cost of VLSFO once FuelEU credits and the proposed subsidy are factored in. Most of that advantage stems from FuelEU Maritime, and bioLNG would already undercut VLSFO without SMAP. Since bioLNG is a drop-in fuel for liquefied natural gas engines, this reinforces the business case for LNG dual-fuel ships trading in Europe. Renewable fuels of non-biological origin receive the most generous treatment of all and, on paper, EU-produced e-ammonia could become the cheapest fuel on intra-EU routes, although very few vessels can burn ammonia today and EU output remains limited. Waste-Based Biofuels Left Out The most obvious losers are liquid biofuels made from waste oils and fats. Used cooking oil and category 1 and 2 animal fats satisfy every EU sustainability test and earn full credit under both the ETS and FuelEU Maritime, but SMAP covers only advanced biofuels made from feedstocks listed in Annex IX Part A of the revised Renewable Energy Directive. Biogas, in contrast, appears eligible irrespective of feedstock. The exclusion matters given the structure of Europe’s biodiesel industry. By 2030, crops and waste lipids such as used cooking oil and other waste fats and oils are projected to make up about 96% of the region’s biodiesel and renewable diesel production capacity, leaving only around 2% clearly eligible for support. Aviation’s sustainable fuel mandate draws on the same waste lipids, meaning shipping is unlikely to secure much eligible liquid biofuel.

In Toledo, Ohio, around 20 miles north of the 280-acre site where Meta is currently building a data center despite pushback from local residents, former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-OH) spoke to supporters about what he called the “crypto/data center crowd” vowing to spend $30 million against his campaign to win back a Senate seat. “You know why? Because they know I’m going to take them on,” he told the crowd before launching into a story about his recent visit to the nearby data center construction site. “Once they’re built,” he said, “your electric rates are going up. Your electric rates go up and you have no say in it.” The $30 million announcement came late last month from the crypto industry’s super PAC Fairshake, backed by the likes of Andreessen Horowitz, Coinbase, and Ripple Labs. Now, the spending has reached over $55 million. It’s all part of a Machiavellian revenge plot, after Senate Democrats voted down an industry priority despite threats from crypto’s political arm. Brown wasn’t part of that vote, thanks to his 2024 defeat, which Fairshake took credit for after dropping $40 million in that race. Still, he’s found himself a target once again. The crypto industry hopes to prevent Brown from returning to the Senate, where he would be likely to play a significant role in overseeing digital asset regulation. His role as chair of the Senate Banking Committee and his vocal criticism of crypto originally made him a target in 2024. If they can make an example yet again out of the same candidate, the industry hopes they can hold onto some of their dwindling influence in Washington. Brown’s opponent, Sen. Jon Husted (R-OH), is already struggling to shake off his association with data center interests. “More than any other thing in this race, data centers are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck,” warned the National Republican Senatorial Committee in a leaked August memo. In an election already inundated with spending from outside groups, the money from a powerful Silicon Valley industry like crypto may only help Brown hammer home his campaign’s message of Husted as the corporate-friendly “face of data centers.” Nearly $14 million has been spent on ad spots with that attack on Husted, a message that is all the more salient with the crypto industry—or the “crypto/data center crowd,” as Brown would say—spending a small fortune to get Husted re-elected. “In Washington, crypto and Big Tech and AI, those fights are abstract, but in Ohio, they really turn into these data mining centers, data centers, electric bills, local infrastructure,” professor Henrik Schatzinger, who studies campaign finance and the role of interest groups in American politics at Ripon College, told the Prospect. “For many voters, the power of Big Tech tells a story that I think runs through the country, which is that the system is rigged, the system favors those with resources, including Silicon Valley and the Big Tech interests.” BROWN ISN’T WASTING A SECOND lingering on his old criticisms of crypto, instead using the spending to speak to the concerns of Ohio residents and tell a story of his opponent’s support from billionaire interests. “This money does tell you exactly who’s looking out for the billionaires and the corporations, giving them out-of-control tax breaks to bring their data centers to Ohio. It’s Jon Husted, that’s why they want to buy him this Senate seat,” he said in a video released shortly after Fairshake’s announcement. The nationwide anger directed toward data centers is particularly potent in Ohio, as a recent Prospect story shows. Developers have made the state a focal point of the massive build-out thanks to its generally cheaper energy, tax incentives, and lax permitting. So far, there are about 270 total data centers in the state, both currently operational and planned. Meanwhile, residents are pushing back; the state will be home to 21 of the 41 total local data center–related measures on ballots across the country on November 3. Recent polling from Bowling Green State University found that 75 percent of likely Ohio voters opposed data center construction in their community and 63 percent opposed construction across the state more generally. “This is a state with massive agricultural output. This is a state with massive manufacturing output. It’s the number two auto manufacturing state in the nation. And that’s Ohio’s image of Ohio,” said professor David Niven, who teaches political science at the University of Cincinnati. “The data center explosion really set off a skepticism about an economy that left Ohioans out and exploited Ohio.” Brown has homed in on the skepticism described by Niven, employing data centers in his message about fighting billionaires and corporate interests to make Ohio more affordable. He’s accused Husted of being beholden to data center interests, pointing to his track record of supporting tax breaks to incentivize development in Ohio as lieutenant governor and the $630,000 Husted took in from data center–linked donors over the years. In a Hail Mary attempt from Senate Republicans to reform his image, Husted sponsored the Ratepayer Protection Act, which would do nothing more than make state utility regulators consider rules requiring companies to pay for the extra electricity use caused by their data centers. The Company has resumed repurchasing shares under its existing share repurchase program, reflecting its continued belief that its shares are significantly undervalued relative to its balance sheet and that repurchasing shares at current levels represents an attractive allocation of capital. Going forward, the Company intends to repurchase shares opportunistically while maintaining sufficient cash to fund its current commitments and capitalize on future AI infrastructure opportunities. “Our focus remains on allocating capital to create shareholder value, balancing accretive repurchases with investments that can generate meaningful cash flow,” said Ryan Lane, Co-Chief Executive Officer of Empery Digital. Hunt Properties continues to pursue attractive lease terms for the partnership. The Company employs a bitcoin treasury strategy and is strategically expanding into AI infrastructure and data center investments, partnering with operators that have decades of real-estate and energy infrastructure development experience to capture growth at the intersection of digital assets and next-generation compute. Empery Digital is committed to transparency, efficiency, and accountability, applying rigorous decision-making to drive sustainable, long-term shareholder value. artigo.texto: A weekly roundup of public health news Data center boom puts pressure on US water supplies Data centers, which are multiplying across the U.S., are often built where water supplies are already strained, new research finds. About 21% of the nation’s 3,600 data centers are located in areas where demand for water exceeds the supply for at least one month annually, according to a study in the October issue of Environmental Science & Technology. Climate change could increase that share to 35% in coming decades, researchers estimated. The U.S. accounts for nearly 40% of the world’s data centers, with another 1,500 facilities in the works. That expansion could put additional pressure on local water supplies, particularly in communities where communities, farmers and businesses already compete for limited resources. More than half of U.S. data centers are located in areas where public water supplies account for the largest share of water consumption. Another 20% are in areas where agricultural irrigation is the largest water use. Data centers house thousands of heat-generating computer systems that are cooled using water. Unlike electricity, water generally must come from nearby sources, making data centers particularly vulnerable to local droughts and seasonal shortages. While most data centers in the eastern U.S. are located in areas with adequate water supplies, facilities in parts of the West and South face shortages for four to eight months annually, researchers said. Coal miners in high-dust jobs face outsized black lung risk Black lung disease continues to threaten U.S. coal miners, with workers in Appalachia facing particularly high risks, new federal research finds. Despite decades of regulations designed to protect miners, cases of coal workers’ pneumoconiosis, also known as black lung disease, continue to impact the workforce, according to an Oct. 20 study in Frontiers in Public Health. Underground dust may be playing a major role. Researchers from the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health examined 1991-2024 data collected through a U.S. coal worker health surveillance program, finding mining workers in dusty jobs are more at risk for the deadly disease. Continuous miner operators — workers who rip materials such as coal and stone from mine faces — and roof bolters — who reinforce and secure mine shafts and tunnels — were much more likely to develop black lung disease and progressive massive fibrosis, the disease’s severe, late-stage form, the study found. Both jobs involve heavy machinery that cuts or drills through coal and rock, releasing fine dust that workers can inhale deep into their lungs. The dust often contains coal particles and crystalline silica, which can cause permanent lung damage. Continuous miner operators had nearly twice the prevalence of black lung disease and three times the prevalence of progressive massive fibrosis compared with miners without those jobs. Roof bolters also faced elevated risks. The disparities were particularly severe in Central Appalachia, including Kentucky, Virginia and West Virginia. More than 8% of miners there had black lung disease, compared with less than 2% elsewhere in the U.S. Even after accounting for years of work, Appalachian miners had nearly four times the prevalence of black lung disease and 10 times the prevalence of its most severe form, researchers found. The region’s thinner coal seams often require miners to cut through more silica-containing rock, increasing exposure to dangerous dust. More PFAS may lurk in US drinking water than known Contamination of U.S. drinking water with “forever chemicals” could be much worse than reported. New research published Oct. 23 in Cell Reports Sustainability estimates levels of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, also known as PFAS, could be twice as high as current monitoring shows. Researchers examined 1.8 million PFAS measurements that were shared with the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency by public water systems, finding that standard reporting practices can overlook substantial amounts of the chemicals. At issue is the practice of excluding PFAS concentrations from calculations if they fall below certain levels. As a result, reporting may capture only 44% of the average concentration of 25 PFAS in community water systems, the study estimated. For six PFAS covered by federal drinking water standards, concentrations modeled by researchers were twice as high as those calculated using conventional reporting methods. The gap was larger for water systems relying on surface water than those using groundwater. PFAS are used in consumer and industrial products and have been linked to cancer, liver damage and other health issues. The chemicals persist in the environment and can accumulate in the human body, hence the name “forever chemicals.” World on course to blow past climate safety limits New estimates of increasing global temperatures paint a bleaker-than-expected picture for human health. The world is on track to warm by 2.8 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels this century if current climate policies continue, according to an Oct. 21 report from the U.N. Environment Program. The estimate is higher than last year’s projections and far above international goals for limiting climate change. The additional warming threatens to intensify deadly heat waves, flooding, wildfires and droughts, exposing millions more people to dangerous conditions and significantly increasing risks to health. Even if countries fulfill all their current commitments to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, global temperatures are projected to rise by 2.6 degrees Celsius, the report found. Meeting additional long-term targets would still leave warming increases at about 2.1 degrees. The 2015 Paris Agreement, approved by about 200 nations, set a goal of keeping warming increases below 2 degrees Celsius, while pursuing a more protective limit of 1.5 degrees. artigo.texto: South African commercial and industrial businesses are rethinking how they manage their energy costs. Instead of relying on solar panels alone, more companies are combining on-site solar PV, battery storage under a capable control system, and wheeled renewable energy from wind and solar farms. Wheeling lets a business buy energy generated elsewhere and have it credited to its facility through the existing grid. The goal is simple: lower the cost of every kilowatt-hour the facility consumes, with the added assurance that operations keep running when the grid fails. For years, the main concern for engineers and plant managers was keeping the lights on during load shedding or grid faults. That conversation has moved on. Now the bigger question is how to combine on-site solar with external renewable energy to get meaningful cost savings, not just backup power. Rooftops run out of space before demand runs out Most facilities that install solar panels quickly hit a ceiling. Even a factory or warehouse that covers its entire roof and all its available land with panels usually can't generate enough energy to meet its total annual electricity consumption. Solar might cover demand around midday, but across a full year, on-site solar rarely offsets more than about 30% of a facility's total electricity use, depending on the load profile. This is where wheeling comes in. Wheeling allows a business to buy renewable electricity from a wind or solar farm elsewhere in the country. It is a contractual and metering arrangement: the generator feeds energy into the grid, and that energy is credited against the facility's consumption, net of wheeling charges. It largely removes the rooftop constraint, although wheeling is currently most straightforward on the Eskom network and in a growing number of wheeling-ready municipalities. Wind is a particularly useful partner for solar in this setup. Wind farms often generate at night and during other times when solar isn't producing, which fills the gaps in a facility's renewable supply. Wind is not optional in this picture: it is what carries a facility's renewable offset past the solar ceiling. As a general example, a mix of roughly one-third solar and two-thirds wind typically gives a more stable renewable supply across the year than solar-heavy combinations, and can lift renewable electricity use from around 30% to as much as 80%. Batteries keep everything running smoothly Battery storage is what ties this all together. When on-site solar and grid supply, including wheeled energy, both feed a facility, the Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) control system manages the interaction between them. It does more than switch between sources: it optimises behind-the-meter solar consumption and shifts energy use across time-of-use tariff periods, which compounds the savings that wheeling already delivers. The BESS needs to be sized correctly for the job: the inverter should be rated to carry the facility's full electrical load the instant the grid drops out, and the battery should hold enough energy to supply roughly two hours of the facility's load during peak tariff periods. During the load-shedding years, sizing a battery for essential loads only was common in homes and small commercial sites, but large operations needed full business continuity and never really had that option. Today, with the grid more stable, most large commercial and industrial battery systems in South Africa are justified primarily on time-of-use arbitrage, with backup as the built-in insurance. A battery is a significant capital investment with a finite cycle life, which is exactly why the business case has to be built on daily tariff savings rather than on the occasional outage. Wheeled energy can also make charging the battery cheaper, but this depends heavily on how the wheeling power purchase agreement (PPA) is priced. Where the PPA is structured at a discount to the Eskom wholesale tariff across all tariff periods, every kilowatt-hour used to charge the BESS costs less than it otherwise would, which improves the economics of time-of-use arbitrage even further. A flat-rate PPA, by contrast, can end up more expensive than the wholesale tariff during off-peak periods, which is exactly when a battery is typically charged. The pricing structure of the wheeling agreement is therefore not a side issue: it determines whether wheeled energy strengthens or weakens the battery business case. The bigger picture Solar was never going to solve the problem on its own, and the problem is no longer just keeping the lights on. It is the cost of every kilowatt-hour a facility consumes. For South African businesses serious about cutting that cost, the real opportunity lies in combining what they can generate on site with what they can bring in from elsewhere, and using a well-controlled battery system to make it all work together. Henri van Eetveldt, Head of Business Development at EXSA. **The views expressed do not necessarily reflect the views of the National Media Group.
