artigo.texto: FORT WAYNE — The seemingly never-ending requests by the Google Data Center, 5801 Adams Center Road, for more generators and more land compelled the Protect Allen County Coalition (PACC) to act. On Oct. 25, PACC hosted a backyard community gathering near the giant data center. The official nonviolent and peaceful event was titled: “Not at Our Expense: Residents Fight for Clean Air, Protection of Local Lands, and Economic Stability.” Organizers shared Google updates, and residents shared their concerns. “Today’s community gathering is in direct response to Google’s new permit application for 228 additional diesel generators that they’d like on site,” Danielle Doepke, PACC organizer, said. Additionally, the destruction of wetlands also concerned the group. “We also have evidence of illegal destruction of wetlands violating an Endangered Species Act," Doepke said. PACC also had ongoing concerns about Google communications, transparency, and respect for the neighborhood. “We’ve had three years of very little communication and transparency from Google as well as from our local and state representatives,” Doepke said. “We’re hoping to get together with neighbors and the people who have been most directly impacted by Google’s presence in Allen County. We want to hear from them about what their experience has been,” she said. Organizers set up several tables and asked attendees to share their concerns and needs. The tables included one that was set up for residents to share what they wanted Google and various municipal representatives to know about their concerns. For example, Doepke cited both a data center moratorium and a local review commission that could have addressed resident concerns if both of the resolutions had not been recently shot down by a majority of Fort Wayne City Council members. Still another table was set up to recruit volunteers to help organizers moving forward on data center issues and other concerns. “There’s been an announcement of a potential nuclear facility coming to New Haven. And (talk of) an AEP transmission line. There is a lot coming at us all at once. So, that is a part of the reason we are here today. We want to stay connected and be able to talk about what is happening around us,” Doepke said. Back-to-back Neighbors The backyard chosen to host the gathering was a 1-acre property that backs up to the Google Data Center. A chain-link fence put up by the homeowner years ago and a new split rail fence installed by Google are all that separate the two properties. According to several neighbors living with the Google Data Center in your backyard is challenging. For example, currently, two giant red cranes on the data center campus dominate the sky-blue view. The high cranes contrast with the underground burrows that groundhogs and moles are carving throughout once inviting neighboring green lawns. According to homeowners Sue and Barry Dibble, the nearby construction and other land-use disruptions force moles and groundhogs into their backyard and other neighboring yards. The animals then create many underground tunnels that cause the grassy surface to become soft, squishy, and difficult to walk on safely. Both the homeowners and the event organizers cautioned attendees to be very careful and not to walk alone toward the fences separating the properties due to the unstable ground. To stay or to go Meanwhile, concerns about the environment and air pollution are top of mind for many. Some residents wonder about selling their respective properties while others dig their heels in and are determined to stay. For example, when asked what her most pressing concern was, homeowner Sue Dibble had a list of concerns. “I would say the air pollution, the noise, and the traffic. And I am not selling my house. So, I am really worried about them trying to take it,” she said. “My dad built this house in the 1950s,” she said. “It’s a homestead,” her husband, Barry Dibble, said. Likewise, a nearby neighbor is also concerned about the environment and what to do with her home. “My biggest concern is the environment. I have asthma and I am sure a lot of other people have health issues where the air quality is really going to make a big impact,” Amanda Scheitlin said. “I would love to move because I can’t imagine living with this for the rest of my life. I could see myself moving, but I do not have plans to move at this time,” she said. Respect and responsibility The community gathering highlighted the residents' desire that the nearby AI industry make environmentally responsible decisions and be a good neighbor. Scheitlin, who lives within a mile of the data center, said she wishes it would have been built somewhere else. “But now that they’re here, they should take responsibility for the environmental impact that they’re causing,” Scheitlin said. “They should have thought this through and did all the safeguards for the impact that it was going to make on the people and the animals. On our environment, and our wetlands,” she said. Meanwhile, Sue Dibble is looking for respect. “I want them to start paying respect to the people that live out here. I mean, it’s horrible. They pull out in front of you … the traffic is horrible. The dump trucks coming up and down constantly, the dirt is flying everywhere, and you normally can’t leave your windows open,” she said. Residents struggle with lights and noise Besides the cranes, and a risky trek across the lawn, three lights shine in the bedroom windows at night, Sue Dibble said. Additionally, she and others said they hear the humming during the week and on Saturdays. “I don’t know what it is. It comes all night long. It’s just a humming. I don’t know what’s causing it,” Scheitlin said. And then there’s the trucks According to Barry Dibble, truck traffic around his home is more than a little challenging. He shared several encounters. artigo.texto: BRAZORIA COUNTY, Texas (KTRK) -- A potential data center in Brazoria County is raising concerns among residents, who told ABC13 they're being left in the dark. Landowners in Damon said they noticed a company buying more than 400 acres along the Brazos River, which is when they started asking questions. On Sunday, residents held a community meeting to discuss what they've found out so far. "We got to fight. We got to stop it before it gets here," one resident said. They told ABC13 that the county district attorney's office held a meeting earlier this month and showed them a map of seven parcels of land that included solar panels and batteries. Residents said that infrastructure pointed toward the potential for a data center. "That means a data center which could have gas turbines, and that means 24 hours, seven days a week, 365 days a year, noise, lights, vibration," Christine Clark, a concerned citizen, said. Experts previously told ABC13 that Texas counties have few tools to stop these developments, particularly in unincorporated areas, where regulations and permitting hurdles are limited. SEE ALSO: Permits related to data centers issued after Abbott's halt directive, advocacy groups found Residents said they're concerned about what a potential project like this could mean for a place they say is rich in both wildlife and history. "It concerns the dignity of our ancestors, the preservation of Black family heritage, and our rights to continue caring for our land that has sustained our family for generations," one community member said. Residents said the company buying the land is CleanSpark. In January, CleanSpark announced an agreement to acquire up to 447 acres of land in Brazoria County that was "positioning the Company to develop a large-scale data center project." In its press release, CleanSpark called itself America's Bitcoin Miner, a market-leading data center developer. ABC13 reached out to the company for more information and is awaiting a response. This comes as data centers continue to expand across Texas. ABC13's data team found that, as of February, 429 data centers were in the state. They found 293 were already operating, and the rest are planned or under construction. Brazoria County residents hope the place they call home won't join that growing list. "We're not giving up," Clark said

artigo.texto: Retiree Eileen Castle hasn't been able to enjoy her backyard since a data center moved in next door in Lowell, Massachusetts, bringing noise, fumes, dust and water mist. But a few streets away, contractor Louis Haas is grateful to Markley, the company running the facility, for redeveloping an abandoned site he says was rife with drug use. Dubbed "the Dungeon" by some locals for the imposing black silhouette it casts over a residential neighborhood of this old milling city, those opposing views encapsulate how data centers are polarizing communities across the United States. Republican-governed states, with their looser regulations, host most of the country's current AI build-out. But in liberal-leaning New England, some feel betrayed by their elected representatives, while others fear being left behind if the industry is curbed. - 'Nothing but noise' - Over the din of construction behind a spiked fence, Castle, 82, told AFP her great-great-grandparents bought the property. But since the data center moved into a disused pasta factory a decade ago, "We have had nothing but noise. We have dust, dirt. We have all kinds of mist" from the adjoining cooling towers, which she fears could carry Legionnaires' disease. Noxious fumes made a long interview outdoors impossible, and she lamented that her grandchildren can no longer swim in her small pool. "I think every once in a while that maybe I should sell my house," she says, but adds her property value has plummeted. "The Markley Group serves more than 600 clients in Massachusetts and connects the digital infrastructure that powers our economy, our schools, and the everyday needs of our community," Markley Group CEO Jeff Markley said in a statement to AFP. The company said its backup diesel generators run only for five minute tests each week and, thanks to abatement efforts, produce "about 44 decibels of sound, quieter than a soft conversation three feet away." It said it tests its water twice a year for Legionnaires', and has planted 2,000 trees. In 2015, the city council gave Markley a 20-year property and personal property tax break estimated at $77 million, the Lowell Sun newspaper reported at the time. Enthusiasm has since cooled. In March, the council unanimously passed a 360-day moratorium on construction and expansion of commercial data centers, though Markley's 352,000-square-foot site was grandfathered in. Residents represented by the Conservation Law Foundation (CLF) and others have sued to challenge its expansion, which included increasing the number of generators to 27, and won a temporary injunction in August. CLF attorney Adam Reynolds told AFP that it is the "compounding effect of pollution that's really significant" in a historically industrial area. - Community divisions - Markley has supporters. Haas, 50, who supplies coffee to a major tech company, said the boom had been good to contractors like him. "I'm a big liberal, I'm a Democrat. But I'm also pro-jobs and pro-economy," he told AFP. Markley said it employs more than 100 full-time staff in Lowell, a third of them local. On top of that, over 100 unionized trades workers work on campus. Another backer, Sarah Bibeau, a 43-year-old single mother of two who works in the defense sector, told AFP the company had been "kind and considerate," fixing roads and offering favors ranging from yard work to free Red Sox tickets. Detractors include Jake Fortes, a 44-year-old travel agent who founded the group "Honest Future for Lowell" and whose property sits on the fence line. "We're getting steamrolled by this company. So some of us have taken it to task," Fortes told AFP. Like Castle, he feels let down by Democrats, including state Governor Maura Healey -- who signed a sales tax break for data centers into law but then paused new applications this year, a reversal that illustrates the party's dilemma. Luz Marte, a 38-year-old lab technician, bought her house a year ago, without realizing the site was a data center. "It sounds very loud, like an airplane is going to take off," she told AFP as her three-year-old son played. Her home insurer recently moved to triple her premium, which she believes is linked to Markley buying a building even closer to her property. "This is a home I bought for my son, to grow up, feel alive, and have a future," she said. "Now I'm doubting that idea."

artigo.texto: Brasil precisará de energia nuclear para data centers, diz setor Presidente da Associação de Atividades Nucleares defende que fonte é a melhor forma de assegurar fornecimento nos centros de processamento O Brasil não conseguirá absorver toda a demanda energética de data centers que deve chegar ao país nas próximas décadas sem considerar a geração de energia nuclear, afirma Celso Cunha, presidente da Abdan (Associação Brasileira para o Desenvolvimento de Atividades Nucleares). Em entrevista ao Poder360, o executivo disse que a energia nuclear “explodiu” no mundo inteiro, sobretudo por causa das aplicações em data centers, e é reconhecida como a melhor forma de assegurar o fornecimento ininterrupto de energia elétrica nos centros de processamento de dados. Executivos e representantes dos setores de infraestrutura digital e de energia elétrica vêm defendendo nos últimos meses que o Brasil tem capacidade de se tornar o principal destino de data centers na América Latina diante de um cenário de investimentos globais em inteligência artificial, computação em nuvem e capacidade computacional. Estimativas da Moody’s falam em um mercado que pode movimentar até US$ 3 trilhões no país nos próximos 5 anos. Na disputa por investimentos estrangeiros crescentes no segmento, o Brasil larga na frente dos seus vizinhos sul-americanos por causa da matriz predominantemente renovável e do potencial para combinar diferentes fontes de energia. Porém, é consenso no setor elétrico que a elevada demanda por energia desses empreendimentos ainda é um obstáculo a ser superado. Data centers são intensivos em consumo energético e precisam operar 24 horas por dia, 7 dias por semana. Demandam, portanto, energia contínua, confiável e a preços competitivos. “Alguns milissegundos sem energia em um data center custam mais caro do que uma usina nuclear inteira”, diz Cunha. Segundo o dirigente da Abdan, a geração nuclear oferece todas as características necessárias para abastecer os centros de processamento de dados: é firme, ou seja, consegue gerar energia de forma ininterrupta, e mais limpa do que renováveis como eólica e solar, as principais fontes usadas por data centers. Assista à entrevista de Celso Cunha ao Poder360 (27min): “O Brasil tem um potencial enorme para atrair data centers e se fala em até 70 gigawatts até 2050, mas é humanamente impossível atender uma demanda dessa sem considerar a energia nuclear. O mundo todo está usando”, disse durante participação no Poder Entrevista, o programa de entrevistas do Poder360. O Brasil fechou o 1º semestre com cerca de 706 MW (megawatts) de capacidade instalada em data centers. “É tanta energia que se precisa que nós vamos precisar de todas as fontes. Não vai ser só do gás ou só do nuclear. Se nós quisermos atender aos data centers, nós vamos precisar usar toda a nossa criatividade, nossa capacidade”, diz o executivo. Para Cunha, a introdução da energia nuclear nos data centers passa pela utilização dos SMRs (Pequenos Reatores Modulares, na sigla em inglês), uma das tecnologias em ascensão no setor. São equipamentos com potência típica de 50 MW a 300 MW por unidade, bem menores que as usinas nucleares tradicionais. A principal vantagem dessa tecnologia é a fabricação modular. Os reatores são construídos em série dentro de fábricas e montados no local de operação, o que reduz custos e prazos de instalação. “Você pode comprar como se fossem geladeiras. Ele já sai certificado e você compra o 1º, o 2º, o 3º e vai colocando em paralelo no data center. Ele não entra todo de uma vez, você pode botar esses SMRs de forma fracionada, de acordo com a necessidade do cliente do projeto”, diz Cunha. NUCLEAR NO REDATA O setor de energia nuclear, segundo o presidente da Abdan, tem interesse em atender projetos que venham a ser habilitados pelo Redata (Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter), lei recém-sancionada pelo governo federal que institui benefícios fiscais para instalação de data centers no Brasil. O texto aprovado pelo Congresso e promulgado pelo governo ainda tem uma série de pontos pendentes de regulamentação, como a definição das fontes de energia que serão exigidas para empreendimentos interessados nos incentivos do programa. O projeto original estabelecia que só data centers abastecidos por energia 100% limpa poderiam receber os incentivos fiscais, mas uma alteração no Senado incluiu também fontes “consideradas de baixa emissão”. Como mostrou o Poder360, a mudança abriu espaço para o uso de gás natural, defendido pela indústria e pelo Ministério de Minas e Energia. Segundo Cunha, a discussão atualmente em curso sobre o gás natural não preocupa. A avaliação do executivo é que o texto considera o uso de energia nuclear, apesar de não citá-la diretamente. Uma portaria ministerial com a definição das fontes permitidas deve ser publicada nas próximas semanas.

artigo.texto: Governor Josh Stein wants North Carolina to enact new rules requiring data centers to pay more for their electricity. He recommends the Utilities Commission should instate ‘large load’ tariffs on the companies that run data centers. Stein argues it's because they pull so much electricity. Some critics say their heavy power usage could raise bills for everyone else but that the large-load tariffs, if approved, could offset that. Other WRAL Top Stories WRAL asked the governor why North Carolina is behind other states who are receiving clean energy, for example, from their deals with tech companies that operate data centers. Stein said North Carolina does not have the framework in place to require the companies to provide the state those benefits. There is a proposed deal, between the tech companies building data centers and Duke Energy which provides most of North Carolina's electricity, that's currently before the state Utilities Commission for final approval. Stein indicated it's a step in the right direction but doesn't go far enough. He's urging the Utilities Commission to push for less industry-friendly rules, although he has little power to force such a change. The governor used to control the Utilities Commission, but after Stein was elected in 2024 the Republican-led state legislature stripped him of that power and gave Republican political appointees a majority on the commission. "There is no reason why the largest, wealthiest companies in the history of the world cannot be required to pay for the energy generation and transmission costs that they put onto the system. Let's create a world where regular North Carolinians actually benefit and not be harmed from these data centers," Stein said in a press conference in Raleigh. Other states have worked out contracts that require these tech companies to provide something in return for building and operating there. "For example, in Minnesota, Google agreed to pay for nearly 2,000 megawatts of wind, solar, and battery storage that will both power the data centers and strengthen the energy grid for all Minnesotans. In Indiana, Amazon is providing 960 megawatts of clean energy. In Ohio, Meta is paying for 1,200 megawatts of nuclear energy. North Carolina should be receiving these same kinds of commitments, but right now we're getting none of them," Stein said. Earlier this year, Duke reached an agreement with data centers that does include some protections. "Protections like making data center contracts use a public template, guaranteeing that long-term contracts have minimum purchase protections, requiring large energy users to reduce power when the grid is strained at the beginning of their contract. It only lasts for the first five years, but it's better than nothing, ensuring that data centers pay up front for the necessary improvements to the grids that are required, like substations and transmission lines. But there is still so much work to do, the governor said. WRAL reached out to Duke Energy for response to the governor's call for more benefits and protections to be placed in the current settlement. "Powering the demands of a growing state at the lowest possible cost requires balanced, diverse energy sources and is at the heart of the Carolinas Resource Plan and our recent settlement on a large load tariff. We look forward to continuing to work with Governor Stein, the North Carolina Utilities Commission, and other engaged partners on clean energy programs that can benefit all customers,”said Bill Norton with Duke Energy. In May, Duke Energy announced it was joining Amazon, Google, Microsoft and Nucor in signing onto agreements in North and South Carolina to accelerate clean energy options in response to growing demand. "In this new era of large-scale energy demand, Duke Energy is committed to working with our regulators and customers to find innovative and responsible ways to satisfy the growing need for more and cleaner energy. With the help of companies like Amazon, Google, Microsoft and Nucor, we can accelerate our service of large customer needs and the transition to cleaner energy, while reducing financial risks and supporting economic development in our communities," said Lon Huber with Duke Energy. However, Governor Stein wants the Utilities Commission to go beyond the agreed-upon settlement with Duke Energy that proposes large load tariffs on data centers to also require the companies provide clean energy. "One other very important protection that the large load tariff gets at, but doesn't fully encompass, is a separate rate class ... We have residential, we have commercial, we have industrial, but really these data centers exist as a separate category because of the sheer amount of energy," said Attorney General Jeff Jackson. Jackson's office used to have more sway over the Utilities Commission as well but, like with Stein, state lawmakers took away some of the attorney general's authority after Jackson won election in 2024. Jackson said rate agreements need to be made, and then communicated to residents so they are not under the impression they have to pay for data center improvements. The current deal lays out data centers will have to pay for upgrades like transmission lines, Jackson said. But, it is not clear who will foot the bill for other improvements, to the grid for example. Jackson said the proposed agreement would require large power users to cover certain grid upgrades, including transmission lines But he said it is not clear who will foot the bill for other improvements – like power plants for example. The Utilities Commission is finalizing its settlement and both leaders say they want to see changes before it’s all said and done.

artigo.texto: EnerSys To Acquire Ultralife, Expanding Differentiated Battery Technologies and Accelerating Growth in Defense Market - Accelerates EnerSys ’ growth in mission-critical defense applications particularly high growth drone and counter drone systems - Expands advanced, differentiated battery technologies with U.S .-based manufacturing - Increases manufacturing capacity for specialized FEOC-compliant batteries - Supports multiple avenues for value creation, including extending EnerSys’ capabilities into new applications within core markets, accelerating growth in existing high-growth areas, and realizing significant cost synergies READING, Pa.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 27, 2026-- EnerSys(NYSE: ENS), a global leader in stored energy solutions for industrial, infrastructure, and defense applications, today announced that it has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire Ultralife (NASDAQ:ULBI) for $16.00 per share in cash, representing a 166% premium to Ultralife’s unaffected closing share price on October 26, 2026. The transaction represents an enterprise value of approximately $320 million. EnerSys expects to realize $15 million to $20 million in annual run-rate cost synergies within the first 18 months, reflecting the unique benefits of combining Ultralife with EnerSys. Ultralife is a leading provider of rechargeable and non-rechargeable batteries, battery systems, and related accessories for military communications and other specialized applications. The company serves government, defense, and commercial customers globally and generated $191 million in revenue in fiscal 2025. Headquartered in Newark, New York, Ultralife employs more than 700 people, with principal operations across the U.S., Canada, U.K., and China. “This acquisition is a compelling strategic fit for EnerSys and directly advances our strategy to build a broader, more differentiated defense power platform,” said Shawn O'Connell, President and Chief Executive Officer of EnerSys. “Building on the success of our recent acquisitions, Ultralife expands our portfolio of advanced, reliable, high-performance power solutions. Together, we will be better positioned to support the U.S. Department of War (DoW) and allied forces with leading-edge, cost-effective technologies for the increasingly electrified battlefield of the future. We know the Ultralife business and its team well, and are confident that our shared commitment to engineering, problem solving, and customer focus will create a strong cultural fit. We look forward to combining our strengths to accelerate growth, enhance performance, and deliver greater value to our customers and shareholders.” Mark Matthews, Chief Technology Officer and President, Precision Power Solutions, added, “Ultralife complements our multi-chemistry expertise and our liquid reserve technologies with an impressive patent portfolio and strong, longstanding customer relationships. Ultralife’s products offer exceptional capabilities such as very high energy density, long shelf life, low self-discharge, useful pulse power, and cold-weather performance, which are ideally suited to the growing defense mission profiles of today and tomorrow.” “Combining with EnerSys is an exciting next step that will allow us to unlock value and growth opportunities for both companies, while delivering substantial and certain cash value to Ultralife shareholders,” said Michael Manna, President and Chief Executive Officer of Ultralife. “This transaction is a testament to the hard work and dedication of our entire organization, and now offers even greater opportunities for our valued employees. We look forward to partnering with the EnerSys team with the combined scale, resources, and shared vision to accelerate innovation and better serve our global customer base.” Acquisition Expected to Offer Compelling Strategic and Financial Benefits - Expands EnerSys’ advanced defense power technology portfolio with the addition of Ultralife’s differentiated multi-chemistry capabilities, purpose-built advanced manufacturing capacity with existing security and environmental permits, and operational expertise to scale production of EnerSys’ proprietary liquid reserve battery technology. - Increases scale and broadens exposure to the large and rapidly growing defense market with capabilities across mission-critical applications in munitions, soldier power, drones, counter drones, and autonomous systems accelerating EnerSys’ focused growth strategy. - Deepens customer relationships by creating a broader, Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC)-compliant product portfolio for U.S . DoW and allied customers. - Supports an attractive financial profile. The transaction is expected to be accretive to adjusted diluted earnings per share within approximately 18 months after closing, excluding transaction and integration costs and other non-recurring items. Transaction Details and Timing The transaction will be funded through cash on hand. The transaction has been unanimously approved by the Boards of Directors of both companies. Under the terms of the merger agreement, EnerSys, through a subsidiary, will commence a tender offer to acquire all of the outstanding shares of Ultralife common stock at a price of $16.00 per share in cash at closing, representing a total enterprise value of approximately $320 million. The transaction is subject to customary closing conditions, including the tender of at least a majority of the outstanding shares of Ultralife’s common stock and receipt of applicable regulatory approvals, and is expected to close in the first quarter of calendar year 2027. artigo.texto: TN candidates for governor explain how they’d handle data centers if elected A recent Beacon Center poll shows most Tennesseans oppose tax incentives for data centers. What This Story Is About - Four Tennessee candidates — Lauren Pinkston, David Hatley, Marsha Blackburn and Jerri Green — outlined differing positions on how the state should regulate its roughly 60 operational data centers and 15 to 20 proposed facilities. Why It Matters - A new Beacon Center poll found 61% of Tennesseans oppose tax incentives for data centers, and candidates differ on whether to pause development, let local communities decide, or impose new regulations and rate structures. What Happens Next - Candidates including Pinkston, Hatley and Green have called for moratoriums at the state or local level while rules on noise, environmental impact, water use and utility costs are developed. For Context - Tennessee data centers include the xAI facility in Memphis and the DC Blox facility proposed near the Nashville Zoo. Catch Up - Green is already sponsoring a Memphis moratorium resolution on data centers, and Pinkston says she was the first candidate to call for a statewide moratorium. NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV) - Tennessee has about 60 operational data centers, with 15 to 20 more proposed, and candidates in this election have different views on how the state should handle their future. A new Beacon Center poll found 61% of Tennesseans oppose tax incentives to bring data centers to the state. Pinkston calls for statewide moratorium Independent candidate Lauren Pinkston said she was the first candidate to call for a statewide moratorium on data centers. “I was the first candidate to call for a statewide moratorium [on] data centers because the state has not offered good guidance to local governments on how we make sure that the working class is not paying for the development that these data centers require,” Pinkston said. Pinkston said companies, not taxpayers, should cover the infrastructure data centers need. “If you’re coming to Tennessee, regardless of your infrastructure, that you are paying for the infrastructure that you are forcing to be developed. So the roads, the schools, the water, you pay for that. Growth has to pay for growth,” Pinkston said. Pinkston said the state needs to define allowable noise levels in decibels and the environmental and drinking water impacts of data centers. “What are the impacts of the environment and the drinking water? All of those things need to be clearly defined so that local communities have better guidance. And we need to have a moratorium across the state until those things are decided upon,” Pinkston said. Pinkston said she would not want a data center in her neighborhood or built on farmland. “In my neighborhood? Absolutely not. And taking up farmland? Absolutely not,” Pinkston said. She pointed to the former Saturn plant, now a GM facility, near her home south of Spring Hill, which she said was required to be built half underground with its above-ground portion painted blue to blend with the sky and is now hidden behind cornfields. “Those are really innovative solutions that keep the community happy while also adding good economic growth to the community as well,” Pinkston said. Pinkston said she is interested in building data centers underground, saying they run about 17 degrees cooler and that the heat they emit could be captured to fuel greenhouses, growing products for the local market. Hatley wants pause on new deals Independent candidate David Hatley also wants to pause new data center deals. “You know, they scare me,” Hatley said. Hatley pointed to the Blue Oval and Starbucks deals in Tennessee as examples of agreements he said are not always good for the state. “I see my opponents saying we’re going to pay for Starbucks with a payroll tax that doesn’t even exist. You know, so that’s what we get in government. We get guys that get to the front of the line, influence the people. And these deals happen that aren’t always good for Tennessee,” Hatley said. Hatley said data centers could have economic advantages, but the state needs to pause. “I think we need to stop right now and pause because... we don’t want to wake up in 10 years and have this economic boom in the first few years and then pay for it later,” Hatley said. Hatley said governors elsewhere are calling for moratoriums, and companies are increasingly offering to pay property taxes and electricity costs. He questioned how Tennessee got into the current situation. “We’ve given 20-year tax abatements to Google and now all of a sudden everyone’s against it. We should have never let these in the first place come into town,” Hatley said. When asked about concerns in Memphis over the xAI data center, including water pollution, electricity use and effects on lower-income neighborhoods, Hatley said he would place more regulations on existing data centers. “Even if they want to come in and pay our property taxes, they want to come in and pay electricity, why are they doing that? Asking yourself, we need to be making sure that these things aren’t harmful to our environment. That’s more important than anything else outside of economics,” Hatley said. “The state has to have some guardrails. We have to guide these local municipalities into how to handle these data centers and ultimately let them vote,” Hatley said. Hatley said local communities should be able to vote on whether a data center makes fiscal sense, while the state sets guidelines applied equally to new and existing data centers. Communities are going to decide if they want them or not,” Blackburn said. artigo.texto: Located on land approximately 2 kilometres south-west of Gleno and 8.5 kilometres south-west of Larne, Ballyross is strategically positioned close to the existing Ballyvallagh substation. This will support the efficient operation of the system while minimising the need for additional grid infrastructure. As constraints on Northern Ireland's electricity system increase, clean, low-cost electricity capable of powering homes and businesses can sometimes be prevented from reaching consumers. Battery energy storage projects such as Ballyross can help make better use of this electricity by storing it when generation is high and releasing it when demand rises. By adding flexibility and supporting grid stability, Ballyross will help create a more efficient and resilient electricity system. “From our office in Larne, RES has been proud to contribute to Northern Ireland’s energy future and economic growth since the early 1990s” said Peter Deeney, Senior Development Project Manager at RES. “Securing consent for Ballyross, our first battery energy storage project to be consented in Northern Ireland, is an important milestone as we continue transforming the way energy is generated, stored and supplied. Battery storage is becoming increasingly important as Northern Ireland continues its transition to a low-carbon energy system. Projects such as Ballyross can help make the electricity network more flexible and resilient, so that more renewable energy can be stored and used when it is needed most.” The approved scheme also includes a substantial landscaping package. New native-species planting will help the development blend into the surrounding landscape while creating wildlife corridors and pollinator-friendly habitat that deliver additional biodiversity benefits. “Alongside its strategic location close to Ballyvallagh substation, the site was selected because it has limited visibility from local properties” added Mr Deeney. “The new planting will further reduce visibility while providing valuable resources for a wide range of flora and fauna. We would particularly like to thank the local residents and stakeholders who engaged with us throughout the development of Ballyross. The feedback shared during consultation helped inform our landscaping plan and shape the project’s final design.” Construction of the BESS is expected to take around 20 months. artigo.texto: In the battleground state of Pennsylvania, data centers have become a kitchen-table issue. This September, nearly two-thirds of likely Pennsylvania voters told The New York Times they either strongly or somewhat oppose the construction of data centers to support artificial intelligence. For Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, who is seeking reelection in November, the subject has become unavoidable. After proudly announcing Amazon’s $20 billion data center investment in the Commonwealth in June 2025, the governor signed an executive order in August restricting further data center development across the state and requiring local approval for new installations. The reversal, according to his press release, was informed by “many residents who have expressed their concerns to him directly, and to many more who have shared feedback.” Neither political party has “really figured out how to respond to the challenge” of rising voter discontent over the issue, according to Matthew Levendusky, a professor of political science and communications. Levendusky expects the pressure to keep building into the 2028 presidential race. “Data center construction has become a bipartisan issue,” Parrish Bergquist, an assistant professor of political science, said. Any electoral effect, she added, might be “an anti-incumbent effect rather than a partisan effect.” “This is why you see Shapiro coming out against them, because if people are mad about these things, they will vote against whatever incumbent they view as being responsible for building them,” Bergquist added. “At the city council, town council level, I think that could have implications on both parties.” Bergquist thinks the debate over data center construction is largely driven by concerns from residents. “People don’t like the disruption associated with construction, or they don’t like noise or disruption to their sense of place,” she said in an interview. “People are like, ‘this isn’t a thing that's going to benefit us,’” Bergquist said. “Why does it need to be built here?” RELATED: Penn Democrats hosts Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro ahead of Election Day New Penn center aims to tackle AI-backed cybersecurity threats Levendusky — who is also the Stephen and Mary Baran Chair of the Institutions of Democracy division — said that media coverage of data centers and AI as a whole has generally “been framed in a way that generates a sense of grievance.” On one hand, he explained, voters are told the rise of AI will reduce the value of higher education, eliminate white-collar jobs, and might even wipe out humanity. The data centers that power that very technology, he continued, “raise utility bills, pollute, and reduce the quality of life for neighbors.” “Who benefits?” Levendusky continued. “Mostly a few large companies and their billionaire founders. So, you have highly concentrated benefits and much more broadly dispersed costs — a recipe for people to feel aggrieved.” John Quigley, a senior fellow at the Kleinman Center for Energy Policy, said that while corporations have made “promises about the economic benefits of data centers,” those claims “don’t withstand scrutiny.” While data centers create temporary jobs during construction, he said they “hardly employ anybody” once fully operational. According to Levendusky, companies need to “figure out how to structure the benefits of these centers” so that they “outweigh the costs for communities.” State Sen. Anthony Williams (D-8), whose district includes parts of Penn, said he has heard pronounced concerns from constituents regarding larger data centers. Despite that public opposition, he said the facilities did “meet a need that the public may have.” “There’s a lot of ads and literature that’s been generated about who supports a data center, who does not, what data centers would do to a community,” Williams explained. “The actual substantive portion related to policy and bills – I don’t think we’ve spent much time on that at all.” Instead, Williams said that on a statewide level, discussions of data centers and AI were more “political fodder” than substantive policymaking conversations. These concerns could be amplified by a lack of regulation, according to Quigley, who explained that, so far, the data centers proposed in Pennsylvania largely rely on diesel backup generation. “A data center could be running several hundred generators, which, even with the best available technology, are going to be releasing significant amounts of NOx and particulate matter pollution, to say nothing of carbon dioxide pollution,” Quigley said. If inhaled, NOx, or nitrogen oxides, can cause respiratory harm — and even lead to the development of asthma. Professor of Earth and Environmental Sciences Michael Mann wrote in a statement that data centers are “massive sinks of energy and water” that “produce substantial waste and pollution.” Mann, who is also the director of the Penn Center for Science, Sustainability, and the Media, said the environmental impact of data centers had previously been mitigated by using renewable energy. The Trump administration, though, has moved to have data centers run on natural gas, which Mann argued adds to “carbon emissions when we need to be rapidly decreasing them.” According to Bergquist, there has not been a concurrent push for the development of renewable energy sources to support the centers. “We have to figure out how to be able to build clean and renewable energy capacity and distribution in ways that are just and fair and not environmentally detrimental, but that don’t delay things for longer than they need to be delayed,” she explained. Despite rising calls for a pause on construction, Pennsylvania does not currently have a data center moratorium. Philadelphia already houses eight data centers, though none are the hyperscale developments needed for AI. artigo.texto: Lebanon Lebanon Launches National Carbon Market Roadmap with UN Support Lebanese Environment Minister Tamara Al-Zein launched a national roadmap for the carbon market, backed by the UNDP and Climate Promise initiative, aiming to finance climate projects and reduce emissions. Environment Minister Tamara Al-Zein emphasized "the state's responsibility in opening opportunities for scientific advancement, planning, and cooperation among its institutions," stressing that "Lebanon cannot afford to waste more opportunities or subject its citizens' interests to political tug-of-war." She considered that "the seriousness of work is measured by providing financing conditions and implementing projects," clarifying that "this approach directly guides the Ministry of Environment in preparing a national roadmap for the carbon market, allowing for the assessment of financing opportunities for climate projects and building the necessary foundations to benefit from them." Al-Zein affirmed that "political disagreement does not exempt anyone from the responsibility of agreeing on sound management of public utilities." She stated: "Waste and energy files must not remain hostage to disagreements while Lebanese people pay the cost of stagnation with their health and livelihoods." She noted that "this initiative has an economic dimension related to Lebanon's need to expand sources of financing for its projects and attract investment in sectors capable of reducing emissions." She pointed out that "developing this path may enable mobilizing additional resources to implement environmental and climate priorities, linking international commitments with tangible economic opportunities." Al-Zein's remarks came after she launched the process of preparing the national roadmap for the carbon market, supported by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) in Lebanon and the "Climate Promise" initiative, based on Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. To this end, Al-Zein chaired a technical working meeting attended by the Ministry of Environment team, the international expert on Article 6 of the Paris Agreement Dr. Axel Michaelowa, and the head of the National Solid Waste Management Authority. The discussion focused on opportunities for developing projects in the waste sector eligible to participate in international carbon markets, and the challenges facing them. Al-Zein explained that "the roadmap aims to assess the potential of converting emission reductions into financing and investment opportunities, including the possibility of selling carbon credits according to internationally accepted standards." She indicated that "potential revenues from these credits could constitute an additional resource for eligible projects, contributing to supporting their financing, enhancing their economic viability, and sustainability." She considered that "the importance of this path lies in making available economic value for achieved emission reductions, alongside their environmental benefit, which may enhance the attractiveness of investment in sustainable projects." She saw that "starting with the waste sector allows linking the handling of a daily crisis with opportunities for financing solutions and ensuring their sustainability." She noted that "improving the management of this sector and developing projects that reduce its emissions provide a basis for studying the possibility of benefiting from carbon financing to support them." Al-Zein affirmed that "the role of the Ministry of Environment goes beyond addressing existing damages to exploring economic and financial opportunities for climate action, and establishing scientific and institutional foundations to benefit from them," stressing that "clarity of rules and procedures constitutes a fundamental element in building the trust of funders and investors in projects that can be developed." She revealed that "consultations will expand to other sectors, particularly energy, in cooperation with the Ministries of Energy and Water and Finance, and specialized teams within the Ministry of Environment," clarifying that "the work will include identifying sectoral potentials, technical and financial requirements, and regulatory frameworks necessary for participation." She pointed out that "results of emission calculations and trajectory assessments indicate that Lebanon is moving in the right direction regarding its climate commitments, enabling the exploration of opportunities to benefit from carbon market mechanisms." She noted that "progress in reducing emissions does not automatically mean the availability of sellable credits," explaining that "benefiting requires project accreditation and proving, measuring, and verifying the reductions they achieve with integrity according to international rules, while preventing double counting and ensuring consistency with Lebanon's obligations under the Paris Agreement." Minister Al-Zein concluded that "the value of any climate financing is measured by what it enables in terms of actual projects that protect the environment and improve people's lives, and by what it adds in terms of capacity to finance solutions and ensure their sustainability," affirming that "the goal is to build a path that combines environmental impact, economic viability, and public interest."

artigo.texto: On Sept. 8, Massachusetts Governor Maura Healey issued an executive order requiring data centers in the state to receive local approval. The order also requires data centers to pay their own energy costs and establishes guardrails for environmental protection. In a September press conference, Healey claimed that data centers in other states — particularly Texas, Arizona and Virginia — have caused an array of issues. These include increased utility bills, environmental damage and public health risks, all while consuming large amounts of nonrenewable energy. “They consume massive amounts of energy, and that drives up utility bills, which truly no one can afford,” Healey said in the press conference. According to Healey, if left unchecked, data centers could consume more energy than is available on the grid. She argues that Massachusetts data centers should provide their own clean energy if they can; otherwise, they should pay ratepayers for the energy they consume until they have their own energy supply. The executive order creates a Ratepayer Protection Fund that will consist of fees paid by data centers that fail to provide their own clean energy. The fund will be returned to residents in an effort to offset costs associated with the data centers’ energy demand, and the exact mechanism of returns will be through the regulatory process. In the past, the Healey administration has returned Alternative Compliance Payments to ratepayers through bill offsets or direct credit bills. The order also explains that any project that exceeds 25 megawatts is subject to the administration’s siting and permitting reforms, which include community engagement and environmental protection. The reforms include the requirement of a Cumulative Impact Analysis. However, the guidelines outlined in Healey’s executive order could still leave ratepayers footing the bill. Barbara Kates-Garnick, a professor of practice in energy policy at the Fletcher School at Tufts University, explained that even if data centers pay their fair share of energy costs, utility rates could still increase. “Even though [the data centers are] paying quote-unquote ‘their fair share,’ they're going to require a lot of power, and we all pay for transmission in our rates,” she said. “So I definitely believe that that will be a place where prices will be higher for the customer, even though in theory that's something we’re trying to avoid.” Even so, Kates-Garnick recognized the challenge of balancing the state’s technology ambition with affordability and clean energy goals. “I think that’s important to the governor, too, and she was very careful in this to make sure that she stated the importance of technology while she’s still trying to protect the local customer and keep the costs down,” Kates-Garnick said. “It’s technology, affordability and clean energy all coming together. It’s a challenge.” Amid the AI arms race, Kates-Garnick noted the importance of making sure that technological development does not come at the expense of the local communities significantly impacted by the construction of data centers. “It’s really important that the community have a say and local control over the siting of the data center because it may use the resources of the community,” she said. The order also requires the Office of Environmental Justice and Equity to review the community benefit agreements under its established standards and guidelines. Audrey Hufnagel, an executive board member of the Tufts Climate Action Club, raised concerns about how data centers could contribute to environmental inequality. She stated that data centers “have a disproportionate impact on communities that are already suffering the worst effects of climate change.” Many critics like Hufnagel are concerned about whether communities have enough influence to prevent data center construction from being concentrated in lower-income and environmentally vulnerable areas. According to Hufnagel, it is often difficult for communities with fewer resources to organize and prevent the development of data centers, leaving them more vulnerable to its effects. Healey has made clear her intent to regulate the effects of data center construction and operation on local communities and the environment, all while keeping the state a hub for innovation. “[Tech companies] will not roll into a community, build a massive facility, dirty our water and leave ratepayers holding the bag,” Healey said. “If a company wants to do business here, they need to do it right, and they need to do it with community support.”

artigo.texto: Nevada regulators review NV Energy 2026 plan as data centers drive demand LAS VEGAS (KSNV) — Nevada regulators are reviewing NV Energy’s long-term plan for meeting electricity demand as the state draws growing interest from power-hungry data centers and other large customers. The Public Utilities Commission is going over NV Energy’s 2026 Integrated Resource Plan this week in Carson City. Regulators are also considering a proposed “Large Load Electric Service Agreement,” aimed at ensuring reliable service and financial protections as Nevada becomes more appealing to new large-load customers such as data centers. RCG Economics, which does local economic forecasting and analysis, reports Nevada’s data center boom is outpacing the power grid. The firm says 39 data center projects interested in Nevada have requested nearly three times the amount of power generated by NV Energy during peak hours last year. NV Energy is building a framework intended to prevent potential growth from leading to cost shifts for existing customers. Sean Dalesandro, the developer proposing the Manse Technology Campus in Nye County, said data center developers are required to cover major infrastructure upgrades tied to their projects. “What can data center developers do? Well, what they have to do is pay for all the upgrades required for their project, and because data center projects are large loads, those costs can be substantial,” Dalesandro said. Dalesandro said adding large loads can require reinforcing major parts of the transmission system. “There’s all this equipment that goes into the transmission system, transmission lines, substations, and transformers and switching yards. All of that has to be reinforced if you add a large load to it,” he said. NV Energy said its guiding principle is that “growth should pay for growth.” The utility said that as Nevada continues to attract new businesses and large energy users, including data centers, “we believe the customers driving significant new demand should bear the costs associated with serving that demand, while existing residential and business customers should be protected from those costs.” Dalesandro said requiring developers to pay for upgrades can also strengthen the grid for others. “They have to be paid for by the developer, and that enhances the bulk electric system so that all of the residential and other users on the grid benefit,” he said. Beyond power costs and infrastructure, experts say Nevada’s climate and connectivity help make it a premium location for data centers. Greg Moody, an associate professor of information systems at UNLV, said data centers are expensive to build and operators want to protect that investment. “We have lots of fantastic stuff,” Moody said. Moody said Nevada avoids many severe weather risks seen elsewhere. “But we don’t get big tornadoes, we don’t get large floods, we do not get hurricanes, risk of lightning storms, ice storms, all that fun stuff that hits all different parts of the country; we simply don’t have,” he said. Moody also said Nevada provides humidity-free air conditioning, adding that “75% of the year it is 72 degrees or cooler.” He said another major advantage is internet backbone access through Las Vegas. “Almost every single major ISP backbone provider goes through Las Vegas, and so as a result, if you build a data center right next to essentially what would be the spine of the nervous system, you get a lot better access speed, and speed is very important when you’re dealing with large quantities of data,” Moody said. Electricity prices are also a key factor NV Energy wants to protect as demand grows. According to Electricity Cost Comparison.com, Nevada pays less than 13 cents per kilowatt hour, with an average power bill of $110 a month. By comparison, the site lists Texas at about 16 cents per kilowatt hour, California at almost 30 cents, and Hawaii at 47 cents per kilowatt hour, with an average power bill of $407 a month. The Integrated Resource Plan and the Large Load Electric Service Agreement are expected to receive approval from the Public Utilities Commission, with possible language changes. Nevada’s lower tax rates compared with neighboring states and significant tax abatements also add to the state’s appeal for data center developers. Qualified developers can receive a sales tax reduction on equipment and building materials for new projects.

artigo.texto: O Google derrubou cerca de 400 mil árvores no norte da Finlândia para abrir espaço a dois data centers, os enormes galpões de computadores que sustentam serviços de internet e de inteligência artificial. Segundo reportagem do jornal britânico The Guardian, o desmatamento começou sem as avaliações de impacto ambiental exigidas por lei. No início de outubro, a autoridade ambiental do país mandou suspender as obras e o caso provocou uma onda de revolta entre os finlandeses. Os projetos ficam em Muhos e na vila de Otanmäki, a cerca de 100 quilômetros de distância. Os dois fazem parte de um investimento de € 13 bilhões (cerca de R$ 72,38 bilhões) do Google em infraestrutura de IA, o maior do tipo na história do país. O tamanho do desmatamento Em Muhos, o Google desmatou 330 hectares de floresta, uma área de 3 quilômetros de comprimento por 2 de largura, na qual havia cerca de 250 mil árvores. Segundo o Guardian, a empresa removeu até a camada superficial do solo e deixou no lugar um grande lamaçal, a 400 metros do rio Oulujoki. A ecologista Mari Annala, da Associação Finlandesa para a Conservação da Natureza (SLL), estima que outras 150 mil árvores foram derrubadas em Otanmäki. Moradores relatam que a água dos riachos próximos ficou marrom. Como o corte foi irregular, a madeira não pode ser vendida às serrarias. Por que o data center do Google foi suspenso Em 6 de outubro, a Autoridade Finlandesa de Licenciamento e Supervisão (LVV) enviou cartas ao Google e ordenou a interrupção temporária das obras nos dois locais. O motivo: a empresa não concluiu as avaliações de impacto ambiental antes de desmatar. O diretor do Google na Finlândia, Antti Järvinen, pediu desculpas, mas afirmou que a empresa agiu "com base no melhor entendimento que tínhamos da legislação na época". Em nota, o Google disse que parou os trabalhos, que vai cumprir todas as exigências e que pretende replantar árvores em 130 hectares em Muhos. Ambientalistas consideram a área pequena demais diante do estrago. "Pura arrogância" A reação foi forte. "Nunca ouvi falar de nenhuma empresa que tenha feito algo assim na Finlândia", disse ao Guardian Hanna Halmeenpää, presidente do conselho da SLL. "Eles compraram uma vasta área de terra e simplesmente começaram a desmatá-la. É pura arrogância e é inacreditável." Mais de 93 mil pessoas assinaram uma petição que pede regras mais rígidas para data centers e uma taxa para compensar as comunidades afetadas. O primeiro-ministro Petteri Orpo, que havia chamado a atração de investimentos de "prioridade máxima", classificou o caso como "um banho de água fria". Lobos na vila e medo de virar alvo Em Otanmäki, antiga vila mineira, moradores dizem sentir o impacto no dia a dia. "Tivemos lobos entrando na aldeia porque todos os animais selvagens saíram da floresta", contou Anni Ranta, de 53 anos, cuja família vive no local há gerações. Ela também teme o barulho das obras e que o data center transforme a vila em alvo da Rússia, país com quem a Finlândia divide uma longa fronteira. O biólogo Vesa Hyyryläinen, da SLL, afirma que pica-paus que faziam ninhos na floresta foram expulsos. Por que as big techs querem a Finlândia O país virou destino preferido para data center s, com 145 projetos em diferentes fases de planejamento. O clima frio ajuda a resfriar os computadores e reduz o gasto com energia, uma das maiores despesas desse tipo de instalação. A estabilidade política, a terra disponível e a energia renovável também pesam. A corrida da inteligência artificial acelerou essa procura. Treinar e rodar sistemas como o Gemini, do Google, exige milhares de computadores ligados o tempo todo e cada novo data center consome tanta energia quanto uma cidade pequena. Quem ganha com os data centers Parte dos moradores apoia os projetos pelos empregos e impostos locais, mas há quem questione o benefício para o país. "Na verdade, para a Finlândia, não há benefícios", afirmou Jussi Kangasharju, chefe do departamento de ciência da computação da Universidade de Helsinque. "São empresas internacionais que atendem clientes internacionais. A Finlândia arrecada muito pouco imposto corporativo." O Ministério do Meio Ambiente diz acompanhar o setor e estar pronto para propor mudanças na lei. O tema deve pesar nas eleições finlandesas de abril de 2027.

artigo.texto: O Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) ampliou de zero para até 50 MW a margem disponível para conexão de novos sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias no barramento de 69 kV da subestação Milagres, no Ceará. A mudança está na primeira revisão da nota técnica sobre a capacidade remanescente do Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN) para os leilões de baterias de dezembro, divulgada nesta segunda-feira, 26 de outubro. A alteração ocorreu após a Axia Energia, responsável pela instalação, corrigir as informações encaminhadas à Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) sobre a disponibilidade física para novas conexões no local. Na versão original, publicada em 30 de setembro, o barramento havia sido classificado como sem disponibilidade física, o que levou o ONS a considerar margem nula para novos empreendimentos. Em ofício de 19 de outubro, a transmissora retificou a informação, reconhecendo a existência de espaço para novas conexões. Com a atualização, o ONS passou a considerar uma margem de até 50 MW no barramento, na subárea e na área correspondente, conforme a tabela de conclusões da nota técnica. A revisão também corrigiu a capacidade de interrupção de curto-circuito de um disjuntor da subestação Milagres, em 230 kV, de 40 kA para 50 kA. Segundo o operador, a alteração não modificou os resultados das análises de curto-circuito, porque a restrição permanece associada a outro disjuntor, cuja capacidade é de 40 kA. O documento também recebeu correções em tabelas, classificações de barramentos e referências internas, sem outras alterações nas margens de capacidade remanescente. Os estudos do ONS identificam a capacidade disponível para conexão dos projetos que disputarão os dois leilões de baterias, previstos para 2 e 4 de dezembro. O primeiro será destinado a equipamentos com conteúdo nacional, enquanto o segundo permitirá a participação de sistemas de armazenamento independentemente dessa exigência.

artigo.texto: Aurora City Council to vote on data center moratorium following community pushback Aurora's mayor made his opinion on pausing the data center discussion clear in writing. The answer is a resounding "no," Mayor Mike Coffman said, responding to a developer's letter to the city council. Vantage said it will evaluate locating the Trident data center on sites farther from residential neighborhoods if the city council agrees to a 90-day pause on any efforts to enact new legislative requirements on development. Mayor Coffman said, "We need to move forward 'NOW' with new guidelines that protect residential areas so that we don't have another Trident situation." The co-presidents of Join Unite, a nonprofit formed just weeks ago to oppose the Trident data center, hope the third time's the charm to finally put firm rules in place around data centers. "We are cautiously hopeful that that actually is what's happening behind the scenes. But we're dealing with billionaires and huge corporations," said Makayla Llanos, one of the organization's leaders. Monday, city council will decide whether to implement a data center moratorium. That follows the city council's rejection of a six-month moratorium earlier this year, with Coffman casting the tie-breaking vote to kill it. After an uproar from the community in mid-October, the council unanimously voted to approve the first reading of an ordinance keeping data centers from being built in areas zoned "mixed-use office/ institutional" near schools, homes and assisted living facilities. City leaders will vote on an indefinite moratorium on new applications. "I hope the city does not agree to those terms, and I hope the city stands up for themselves and for us," said Tara Miller, one of the leaders of Join Unite. A new moratorium would not stop Vantage from moving forward with the Trident data center because it's already been approved. Any moratorium proposed would need seven votes to pass because the effort previously failed and likely wouldn't go into effect until February.

artigo.texto: Trending Champion and Warren township officials plan a public meeting Nov. 4 to discuss what needs to be on the books to handle a data center if one were to locate in either township. Champion Trustee Chairman Doug Emerine said to date, the Champion zoning department has not been approached by anyone about a data center. He said the township zoning board is working on guidelines and has been reviewing what Hubbard Township and other communities have done. Emerine said one property that has been discussed is the former Copperweld Steel property off state Route 45 that straddles both townships. He said the 360-acre site has one-third of the land in Champion and two-thirds in Warren Township. Emerine said of the available properties in Champion, that one would be the one to locate a data center on, and the zoning department needs to be prepared. “Right now we need to get as much information as we can on data centers. I am not sure what Warren Township officials want to do, but we need to get together and discuss this,” Emerine said. He said if a data center or any other large business were to express interest in locating in Champion, there would be public meetings to keep residents informed. “No matter what, there will be a data center located somewhere in Trumbull County,” Emerine said. Warren Township Trustee Ed Anthony said he agrees with Emerine that the Copperweld property would be the one where a data center would possibly locate. “It is prime property because of the available land and being by the river, which would provide water, but we have not received any inquiries,” Anthony said. He said the property does have many cleanup issues and there is litigation still on the property. Anthony said the township’s zoning board has been reviewing what to include in the zoning codes. Anthony said a joint meeting is being planned for 6 p.m. Nov. 4 at the Champion administration building. Also, Champion officials approved providing between $6,000 and $7,000 for the road department to do drainage upgrade work this year on Marshall Road. Emerine said the money will cover the costs for materials and supplies needed for the work. In another matter, Vanessa Teuscher found a bulletin and a service schedule from Dec. 1, 1985, when the township cemetery chapel was dedicated. She had the two items framed and they will be placed inside the chapel.

artigo.texto: A weaker ETS puts €90 billion in green investment at risk The review of the European Union's Emissions Trading System, or ETS, is now underway to bring the mechanism in line with the EU's new climate target: a 90% cut in net greenhouse emission by 2040 compared with 1990 levels. Yet that goal appears far off today. The ETS has helped decarbonize the power sector, but the EU urgently needs to drive investments in hard-to-abate sectors, where fossil fuels still dominate. Europe's carbon market is the very foundation of its climate policy. By putting a price on carbon dioxide, the cap-and-trade system gives industries a steady incentive to invest in alternative production methods, be competitive and reduce emissions. The ETS also generates large revenues that can fund climate and clean energy projects. A proven tool The carbon market cannot transform industry on its own. The right enabling conditions, whether in energy, infrastructure or markets for clean materials and products, are critical. But it is an essential industrial policy, and not a new one. For two decades, it has guided capital across many sectors. Following the price signal, companies are spending tens of billions of euros to switch to low-carbon or even net-zero processes. Where is new money going? Increasingly, into decarbonization. In 2025, large European companies put €313 billion into Taxonomy-aligned activities, and those with credible transition plans added a further €182 billion, according to the latest Report on Monitoring Capital Flows to Sustainable Investments, published by the Platform on Sustainable Finance, an advisory body to the European Commission. Clean power, green steel and net-zero cement: The future is already taking shaped. Mixed signals Despite the carbon market's positive economic and environmental impact, proposals now under negotiation threaten to derail the business models of companies that underpin Europe's long-term competitiveness and jobs. The Commission has tried to navigate pressures from industries and countries still heavily reliant on expensive and polluting fossil fuels while maintaining momentum toward the green transition. The aim is to avoid penalizing front-runners that have already invested in decarbonization. Nonetheless, the proposal includes several technical but far-reaching changes. It lowers the linear reduction factor, the annual rate at which the emissions cap shrinks. It also adds free allowances and creates a role for unproven international credits and carbon removals. On top of this, the European Parliament's draft report would weaken the market even further, potentially injecting more uncertainty into the outlook for the carbon price. A €90 billion shortfall According to a new study by Strategic Perspectives and Veyt, the Commission's proposal would blow a gigantic financial hole in Europe's climate plans. Industries covered by the ETS would spend €90 billion less on decarbonization technologies by 2040 than under current law, a drop of more than a quarter. In absolute terms, the Netherlands would be hit hardest, with its total halving to less than €20 billion. Germany would lose €15 billion and Italy €12.5 billion. The further softening proposed in Parliament's draft report could widen the gap even more. Recent reports by businesses and investors identify predictable price signals and policy coherence as key factors in their decisions. Europe will require hundreds of billions of euros a year, most of it from businesses and investors willing to commit capital at scale. In energy-intensive sectors such as steel, projects must be planned at least 10 to 15 years ahead. The jury is in: Diluting the ETS rewards high-emitting competitors and in the end punishes front-runners. A stable and robust carbon price is non-negotiable for European industrial leadership. Europe needs an agreement on an effective system that drives investment in industry. https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBM.resumo: O Banestes, banco estatal do Espírito Santo, contratou o Instituto de Tecnologia da Informação e Comunicação do Estado (Prodest) para hospedar seus dados no Data Center do Estado, em Vitória. O contrato tem duração de cinco anos e prevê a operação em regime de colocation, modalidade em que a organização utiliza espaço físico e infraestrutura de terceiros para instalar seus próprios equipamentos. O acordo estabelece a necessidade de manter as informações do banco com disponibilidade próxima de 100%. Para atender a esse requisito, o data center conta com sistemas de detecção e combate a incêndios, proteção contra fumaça, água, vandalismo e roubos, além de climatização para manter as condições de funcionamento dos servidores. A infraestrutura também dispõe de redundância no fornecimento de energia, com subestação, geradores, transformadores e nobreaks, recursos destinados a manter a operação durante interrupções no abastecimento elétrico. Modernização da infraestrutura de TI O Prodest realizou um retrofit do Data Center do Estado para atualizar equipamentos e melhorar a disponibilidade dos serviços de tecnologia da informação e comunicação prestados aos órgãos públicos. Segundo a autarquia, a modernização elevou o nível de segurança operacional e reduziu em aproximadamente 20% o consumo de energia da estrutura. Para o diretor-geral do Prodest, Marcelo Cornélio, a contratação pelo Banestes reforça a importância dos investimentos contínuos na infraestrutura tecnológica estadual. A atualização dos equipamentos, segundo ele, contribui para a confiabilidade dos sistemas e a eficiência energética. A contratação incorpora a infraestrutura estadual à estratégia de hospedagem de dados do banco, com foco na continuidade operacional e na proteção das informações.

artigo.texto: REDATA já é lei: Incentivos para data centers exigem planejamento antes da regulamentação Sociedades e fornecedores devem avaliar a habilitação, as contrapartidas operacionais e os efeitos da transição de PIS/Cofins para a CBS em 2027. terça-feira, 27 de outubro de 2026 Atualizado às 15:29 A lei 15.504/26 instituiu o REDATA - Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter, destinado a incentivar projetos de instalação, modernização e ampliação de centros de processamento de dados no Brasil. O regime pode reduzir significativamente o custo tributário associado à aquisição e à importação de equipamentos de tecnologia da informação e comunicação. Sua utilização efetiva, entretanto, ainda depende de regulamentação e do cumprimento de contrapartidas operacionais, ambientais e de investimento. Além disso, embora o REDATA tenha prazo legal de cinco anos, parte relevante dos benefícios previstos - relacionada a PIS/Pasep, Cofins e IPI - produzirá efeitos, de acordo com a legislação atualmente vigente, somente até 31 de dezembro de 2026. A ausência de previsão equivalente para a CBS representa um ponto de atenção para projetos com investimentos programados a partir de 2027. Quem poderá aderir ao REDATA Poderá ser habilitada ao regime a pessoa jurídica que implemente, no território nacional, projeto de instalação, modernização ou ampliação de serviços de data center. A lei considera serviços de data center aqueles prestados por meio de infraestrutura e recursos computacionais dedicados ao armazenamento, processamento e gestão de dados e aplicações digitais, incluindo: (i) computação em nuvem; (ii) processamento de alto desempenho; (iii) treinamento e inferência de modelos de inteligência artificial; e (iv) outros serviços correlatos a serem definidos pelo Poder Executivo de acordo com a Nomenclatura Brasileira de Serviços (NBS). Também poderá ser coabilitada a pessoa jurídica que industrialize, diretamente ou por encomenda, produtos de tecnologia da informação e comunicação destinados ao ativo imobilizado de beneficiário habilitado ao REDATA. O regime, portanto, não se limita aos operadores de data centers. Fabricantes e fornecedores que integrem a cadeia de implantação dos projetos também poderão ser alcançados, desde que atendidos os requisitos legais e regulamentares. A adesão dependerá de regularidade perante os tributos federais, inexistência de registro no Cadin - Cadastro Informativo de Créditos não Quitados do Setor Público Federal e habilitação ou coabilitação perante a Receita Federal. As pessoas jurídicas optantes pelo Simples Nacional não poderão aderir ao regime. A definição da estrutura societária, operacional e contratual do projeto assume relevância desde as fases iniciais de planejamento. A identificação da entidade que solicitará a habilitação, bem como das sociedades responsáveis pela aquisição ou importação dos equipamentos, poderá influenciar diretamente o acesso aos benefícios do regime, motivo pelo qual esses aspectos devem ser avaliados antes da implementação das operações. Benefícios tributários do REDATA O REDATA prevê a suspensão dos seguintes tributos federais incidentes sobre componentes eletrônicos e produtos de tecnologia da informação e comunicação destinados ao ativo imobilizado de operador de data center habilitado: As importações beneficiadas também poderão ser realizadas por conta e ordem de terceiro. No caso do imposto de importação, a suspensão ficará restrita aos produtos sem produção nacional equivalente. Tanto os equipamentos elegíveis quanto os critérios aplicáveis à verificação da produção nacional ainda deverão ser definidos pelo Poder Executivo. A definição de produção nacional equivalente poderá representar um dos aspectos mais relevantes da futura regulamentação. Em experiências anteriores envolvendo regimes aduaneiros e incentivos à importação, discussões sobre equivalência frequentemente envolveram especificações técnicas, capacidade produtiva, disponibilidade comercial e nível tecnológico dos equipamentos fabricados no país. Para projetos que dependam da importação de servidores, semicondutores, GPUs, equipamentos de conectividade ou infraestrutura destinada à inteligência artificial, a definição desses critérios poderá impactar diretamente a extensão dos benefícios relacionados ao Imposto de Importação. Os tributos não são definitivamente afastados no momento da aquisição ou da importação. Inicialmente, ocorre a suspensão de seu pagamento. Para a pessoa jurídica habilitada, a conversão da suspensão em alíquota zero dependerá da incorporação do bem ao ativo imobilizado e do cumprimento das contrapartidas previstas na legislação. No caso dos fornecedores coabilitados, a conversão ocorrerá após a conclusão da operação de venda e a entrega do produto industrializado à pessoa jurídica habilitada ao REDATA. Os bens adquiridos ou importados com suspensão tributária poderão ser alienados antes da conversão do benefício em alíquota zero. Nessa hipótese, a pessoa jurídica habilitada ou coabilitada deverá recolher os tributos suspensos, acrescidos de juros e multa de mora, além dos tributos normalmente incidentes sobre a operação de venda. Aspectos contratuais que merecem atenção A utilização do REDATA tende a exigir disciplina contratual específica entre operadores, fabricantes, fornecedores e eventuais importadores por conta e ordem. Recomenda-se que os contratos tratem expressamente: - Da manutenção da habilitação e da coabilitação; - Da comprovação da elegibilidade dos bens; - Da destinação dos equipamentos ao ativo imobilizado; - Da documentação necessária para fruição dos benefícios; - De alterações de escopo dos projetos; - Da responsabilidade pelo recolhimento dos tributos suspensos, juros e multas em caso de descumprimento das condições legais. Principais contrapartidas para manutenção dos benefícios O acesso ao REDATA depende do cumprimento de contrapartidas relacionadas ao mercado interno, sustentabilidade, energia renovável ou de baixa
