artigo.texto: The Oklahoma City Council approved rezoning for a proposed data center project Tuesday, allowing plans to move forward under specific conditions. The project, proposed by Beltline Energies, would be located near Interstate 40 and Frisco Road. The council’s approval includes special conditions addressing water usage, electricity and noise. Mayor David Holt said the company’s application was submitted before Oklahoma City’s moratorium on data center projects took effect. He emphasized that the council’s decision should not be viewed as a precedent for future developments. “I do not think that means that Oklahoma City is open for business for data centers. I think this is kind of a stand-alone vote that should not send a signal that Oklahoma City is open for this type of project. It merely is a reflection of a very unique set of circumstances,” Holt said. The city said additional agreements must be finalized before construction can begin.

artigo.texto: Senator Susan Collins and her Democratic challenger Troy Jackson have both embraced calls for guardrails on data centers ahead of the Maine Senate race, as polling finds that Maine voters are skeptical of their construction in the Pine Tree State. The midterm elections have been defined by the debate over artificial intelligence (AI) powered data centers, as a growing number of Americans—and Mainers—say they do not want to see them built in their communities. Collins has generally walked a fine line on data centers, voting for the Ratepayer Protection Act and calling for more local control over the issue. Meanwhile, Jackson has been highly critical of data center developers and has called for the state to implement a moratorium on their construction. The issue could be impactful in the race, which is one of a handful of toss-ups that could determine whether Democrats or Republicans control the Senate after the midterms. Proponents of data centers believe they are an important economic lifeline for communities that have the potential to create jobs. Critics, however, have raised numerous issues with data centers, including their impact on the environment, water usage, their potential to drive up electricity bills and noise pollution. In Maine, a state with a culture that values conservation, several municipalities have implemented moratoriums on data centers, as they are “very unpopular” in the state, Mark Brewer, professor of political science at the University of Maine in Orono, told Newsweek. “An exception might be old mill towns that have lost their mill but still have much of the infrastructure in place,” he added. The data center debate was on display during a viral moment in the final debate between the two candidates when a data center protester briefly disrupted while Collins was speaking. Collins said the protester was “obviously one of Troy’s supporters,” to which Jackson responded, “Oh, shut up. I don’t even know that kid.” During an October 13 debate, Collins said that the two candidates are “not that far apart on this particular issue” during a discussion about data centers. Here is a look at where the two candidates stand on the matter. Susan Collins Position on Data Centers Collins touted her support for the Ratepayer Protection Act, which required states to consider establishing standards for when data centers and other large electricity users connect to the grid, during the debate. “I voted and cosponsored a bill that the Senate considered just last month to put guardrails and encourage states to adopt guardrails on the construction of data centers. That included making sure that they have no impact on electric rates, very important for a state like Maine with the fourth highest electric rates in the country due to Troy’s policies,” she said. The senator said she believes the issue is decided locally. “There may be a former mill site, as Governor [Janet] Mills has said, where a data center would work out all right because there is a source of power and water, but in many other places, they would not work well,” she said. A spokesperson for Collins pointed to her statement about the Ratepayer Protection Act when reached by Newsweek. “Maine families and small businesses are already paying some of the highest electricity costs in the nation,” Collins said. “The bipartisan Ratepayer Protection Act ensures that they will not pay an even steeper bill by directing state utility regulators to consider standards that would make high-volume users like AI data centers offset their own costs. Mainers should not have to pay the bill for data centers’ power generation, transmission lines, and energy infrastructure.” Newsweek’s AI scorecard rates Collins as “Leans AI Skeptic.” Troy Jackson's Position on Data Centers Jackson has been much more critical of data centers. During the October 13 debate, Jackson said data centers have the ability to “create some jobs,” but that data centers being built in Maine cannot increase electricity rates or hurt the state’s water quality. “I want to make sure that we know what the data is. How they are using it, and there has to be real parameters, real guidelines to how we’re going to do this,” Jackson said. “I’m not really supportive of data centers, but I understand they’re maybe something that we have to deal with.” Jackson said data centers must be slowed down so people can better understand their development. “I am very much in favor of making sure the federal government or the state of Maine puts guardrails on these things because I don’t want the billionaires, again, writing the rules and making our communities worse off than they are right now,” he said. While campaigning for governor earlier this year, Jackson criticized Mills for vetoing a moratorium on data center development in the state. “Once again, we’re seeing power and influence coming into this state and ruining things for us Mainers. We needed a pause on this because it takes our power. It takes our water. There’s health effects. We need regulations because we don’t know what they’re doing without data, our information. We don’t know all the health effects to our kids,” he said. Newsweek reached out to Jackson's campaign via email. How Maine Voters View Data Centers Data centers are unpopular in Maine, according to polls. Only 29 percent of Mainers support the construction of data centers in the U.S., compared to 66 percent of whom oppose their development, according to a poll from The New York Times and Siena University of 619 voters from September 15 to 22. Forty-one percent of respondents said they believed Jackson would do a better job on data centers, compared to 39 percent who said they trusted Collins more on the issue, according to the poll, which had a margin of error of plus or minus 5.4 percentage points. artigo.texto: The Aurora City Council did not pass a moratorium on data centers for the second time on Monday night. For the indefinite moratorium to go to a re-vote, it would have needed two-thirds of the councilmembers to vote “yes.” Alison Coombs, Ruben Medina, Alli Jackson, Amy Wiles, Gianina Horton and Mayor Mike Coffman voted in support. Recommended Stories Curtis Gardner, Rob Andrews, Stephanie Hancock, Francoise Bergan and Angela Lawson voted in opposition. It was the second time the council had voted on a data center moratorium, with the first being in an Aug. 10 meeting. It was shot down with opposition from Coffman, Andrews, Bergan, Gardner, Hancock and Lawson. According to council rules, it requires a two-thirds vote to bring back a resolution that was previously voted down. Coffman changed his vote Monday, saying voted against the first moratorium because it had a fixed time frame of six months, whereas the new moratorium would be indefinite. If the moratorium had passed, the city would have halted on accepting development applications for new or expanded data centers. “There is considerable interest and concern among residents within the city that Data Centers have the potential to create an unmanageable burden on critical energy and water resources,” the resolution read. After Monday night’s vote, the mayor said he would bring the matter forward again. During Monday night’s study session before the regular meeting, the council moved forward with zoning changes that would require data centers to be at least 750 feet away from residentially zoned districts. If the regulations pass at a future regular council meeting, data centers would be outright banned within 750 feet of residential zones, up for conditional approval from the council between 750 feet and a half mile and use-by-right a half mile or farther from residential zones. “Our current regulations are really ill-equipped,” Coffman said Monday, adding that a third of Aurora is undeveloped. Councilmember Gardner countered that while there is a lot of undeveloped land in Aurora, not all of it has the power infrastructure to support a data center. Last week, Vantage Data Centers officially agreed to seek alternative sites for the Trident Data Center. Company officials also asked the council to pause on any new data center rules until then. “The answer is a resounding ‘NO,’” Mayor Coffman wrote in a Facebook post Thursday in response to the request, saying the city needs to move forward “now” with data center regulations. Trident Data Center is the latest project by Vantage, which has 30 data centers in 12 countries. The company submitted the application for Trident to the city on Aug. 25, 2025. As currently proposed, the data center would stand two stories and 1.5 million square feet on 108 acres of land, according to public documents submitted by the developer through the city’s development portal. The current proposal puts the data center at the northwest corner of the intersection of E-470 and East 48th Avenue. Those plans have already been through two formal city reviews, and a third is already underway, a city spokesperson told The Denver Gazette. Some residents of surrounding Green Valley Ranch communities, including The Reserve, a 55-plus area, oppose the data center, saying they worry about negative health impacts, declining home values and utility use. Vantage representatives have countered that they take measures to mitigate impacts to surrounding communities, saying their goal is to be a “responsible neighbor and steward of local resources.” Broadly speaking, supporters argue that data centers bring jobs and investment to local communities, as well as new tax revenues and that actions like moratoriums drive away businesses and ultimately hurt the economy. Supporters also insist that cultivating and growing data centers in America has positive repercussions for national security — that, in this technological race, the U.S. should not concede dominance to countries like China. Critics raise worries about energy, arguing that large data centers should pay for their electricity. They also point to water use, noting that much of the West is in a prolonged drought and data centers could exacerbate the situation. Others say data centers bring noise and other forms of pollution, as well as reduce property values and therefore should be built away from residential or urban centers. Meanwhile, a political split is emerging in how cities and counties deal with data centers. The Colorado jurisdictions that recently approved data center construction are conservative-leaning, while cities calling for or imposing moratoriums are more progressive.

artigo.texto: Retiree Eileen Castle hasn't been able to enjoy her backyard since a data center moved in next door in Lowell, Massachusetts, bringing noise, fumes, dust and water mist. But a few streets away, contractor Louis Haas is grateful to Markley, the company running the facility, for redeveloping an abandoned site he says was rife with drug use. Dubbed "the Dungeon" by some locals for the imposing black silhouette it casts over a residential neighborhood of this old milling city, those opposing views encapsulate how data centers are polarizing communities across the United States. Republican-governed states, with their looser regulations, host most of the country's current AI build-out. But in liberal-leaning New England, some feel betrayed by their elected representatives, while others fear being left behind if the industry is curbed. Over the din of construction behind a spiked fence, Castle, 82, told Agence France-Presse (AFP) her great-great-grandparents bought the property. But since the data center moved into a disused pasta factory a decade ago, "We have had nothing but noise. We have dust, dirt. We have all kinds of mist" from the adjoining cooling towers, which she fears could carry Legionnaires' disease. Noxious fumes made a long interview outdoors impossible, and she lamented that her grandchildren can no longer swim in her small pool. "I think every once in a while that maybe I should sell my house," she says, but adds her property value has plummeted. "The Markley Group serves more than 600 clients in Massachusetts and connects the digital infrastructure that powers our economy, our schools, and the everyday needs of our community," Markley Group CEO Jeff Markley said in a statement to AFP. The company said its backup diesel generators run only for five-minute tests each week and, thanks to abatement efforts, produce "about 44 decibels of sound, quieter than a soft conversation three feet away." It said it tests its water twice a year for Legionnaires' disease and has planted 2,000 trees. In 2015, the city council gave Markley a 20-year property and personal property tax break estimated at $77 million, the Lowell Sun newspaper reported at the time. Enthusiasm has since cooled. In March, the council unanimously passed a 360-day moratorium on construction and expansion of commercial data centers, though Markley's 352,000-square-foot (32,700-square-meter) site was grandfathered in. Residents represented by the Conservation Law Foundation (CLF) and others have sued to challenge its expansion, which included increasing the number of generators to 27, and won a temporary injunction in August. CLF attorney Adam Reynolds told AFP that it is the "compounding effect of pollution that's really significant" in a historically industrial area. Markley has supporters. Haas, 50, who supplies coffee to a major tech company, said the boom had been good to contractors like him. "I'm a big liberal, I'm a Democrat. But I'm also pro-jobs and pro-economy," he told AFP. Markley said it employs more than 100 full-time staff in Lowell, a third of them local. On top of that, over 100 unionized trades workers work on campus. Another backer, Sarah Bibeau, a 43-year-old single mother of two who works in the defense sector, told AFP the company had been "kind and considerate," fixing roads and offering favors ranging from yard work to free Red Sox tickets. Detractors include Jake Fortes, a 44-year-old travel agent who founded the group "Honest Future for Lowell" and whose property sits on the fence line. "We're getting steamrolled by this company. So some of us have taken it to task," Fortes told AFP. Like Castle, he feels let down by Democrats, including state Gov. Maura Healey, who signed a sales tax break for data centers into law but then paused new applications this year, a reversal that illustrates the party's dilemma. Luz Marte, a 38-year-old lab technician, bought her house a year ago, without realizing the site was a data center. "It sounds very loud, like an airplane is going to take off," she told AFP as her 3-year-old son played. Her home insurer recently moved to triple her premium, which she believes is linked to Markley buying a building even closer to her property. "This is a home I bought for my son, to grow up, feel alive, and have a future," she said. "Now I'm doubting that idea."

artigo.texto: Article Summary - ComEd data shows that the cost of connecting 30 data centers to the utility’s grid will cost upwards of $3 billion. Some of the spending has already been completed, with the rest of the investments to be made by 2031. - The data center developers have paid $721 million in deposits for the infrastructure needed to connect to the grid. Utility watchdogs warn that Illinois households and small businesses could end up footing the bill for the gap. - ComEd disputes the advocates’ conclusion, saying it has been proactive in protecting customers from data center costs, including by securing $1.1 billion in credit that can be collected if the projects do not materialize as planned. This summary was written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story. CHICAGO — Data centers have been the focus of growing debate across the U.S., facing a push for regulation that would require operators to pay for the energy and water resources they use, among other proposals. But beyond paying to generate new energy, consumer advocates warn that the costs of infrastructure to connect data centers to ComEd’s grid will be paid in part by households and small businesses in northern Illinois — something the utility disputes. Records filed by ComEd in an ongoing regulatory matter show that new infrastructure and system upgrades needed to connect 30 data centers to the grid will cost $3.1 billion. Some of those projects are already connected, with the rest expected to come online by 2031. Developers of those data centers have paid $721 million in advance deposits, just under 25% of the total cost, an amount that consumer groups including the Citizens Utility Board and Environmental Law & Policy Center say could leave a potential shortfall of $2 billion to be spread across regular customers’ bills. “Ordinary households should not foot the bill to provide power to data centers,” said Nick Wallace, a senior associate attorney with the environmental law center. “ComEd and the (Illinois Commerce) Commission can protect ratepayers and the grid by requiring data centers to pay for 100% of their power supply and infrastructure investments.” ComEd contends that the consumer groups’ analysis overlooks $1.1 billion secured by lines of credit that guarantee rate payments from the data centers for 10 years. Electricity delivery The $3.1 billion in costs comes from two components of the electricity delivery system: transmission and distribution. Both include using poles and wires to move electricity from one place to another, but at different stages in the process. Transmission lines carry high-voltage electricity long distances along highways and across state lines from power plants to local substations where it can be reduced into lower-voltage electricity. Distribution lines then carry that electricity to the homes and businesses that use it. The data center connection costs are split roughly equally, with $1.6 billion expected in transmission costs and $1.5 million in distribution costs. The transmission costs for several individual projects each exceed $100 million, with one project alone expected to cost $289 million and another expected to cost $269 million. Max Leichtman, ComEd’s director of economic and workforce development, said only the distribution costs are an appropriate apples-to-apples comparison for the $721 million in deposits. Some of those projects won’t come online until 2030 or 2031 and are in early stages of development, so the full cost of equipment needed has not been calculated, he added. “The deposits that today stand at $721 million may continue to increase as these projects move forward and become more mature and more well-defined,” Leichtman said. “That doesn’t mean that’s all we’ll ever collect.” Leichtman said any remaining distribution costs would not be spread among all customers, but rather between similar types of customers in the large-user rate class. Consumer advocates, though, say the data center developers cannot be taken at their word to pay the bills. “These data centers are some of the wealthiest corporations in the world,” CUB spokesperson Jim Chilsen told reporters. “They always say, ‘Trust us, we’re going to pay our energy bills,’ but Illinois customers can’t afford to take big tech’s word for it.” Reducing speculation Hyperscale data centers’ requests for energy usage are often understood to be largely speculative. The massive projects — often operated by multibillion-dollar tech companies looking to compete in the race for artificial intelligence — sometimes place duplicate requests with different utilities, meaning some do not come to fruition. The projects have also faced growing opposition from local communities in recent years, causing many to withdraw. ComEd, in cooperation with Illinois and federal regulators, has sought to weed out speculative requests that drive up energy demand prices by requiring deposits for large customers and requiring them to sign long-term contracts known as transmission security agreements, or TSAs, that require customers to provide a line of credit guaranteeing payment of transmission rates for 10 years, even if the project does not materialize. Regulators approved ComEd’s TSA requirement in 2025, meaning that projects after that point have them in place. Of the total $1.6 billion in planned transmission costs, ComEd has $1.1 billion protected through transmission security agreements. Nineteen of the 30 projects pre-date the TSA requirement. Implementing the TSAs has also resulted in “substantial attrition” of data center requests in ComEd’s queue, Leichtman said. Payments now or later Like many of the utility watchdogs, ComEd also endorses the idea that large-load customers like data centers should be directly allocated the cost of their projects. The electric utility has proposed a new approach in which it would directly assign rates to individual data centers based on their costs rather than assigning costs within groups

artigo.texto: ACME Solar Holdings Limited has commissioned an additional 17.91 MW/74.323 MWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) component for its Firm and Dispatchable Renewable Energy (FDRE) project in Rajasthan. The new installation was commissioned on October 23, 2026, with its commercial operation date scheduled for October 25, 2026. The project is being developed through ACME Sigma Urja Private Limited, a wholly owned subsidiary of ACME Solar Holdings Limited. It is located in Village Neemri, Tehsil Rawatbhata, in the Chittorgarh district of Rajasthan. The BESS installation forms part of the project’s planned total discharge capacity of 250 MW/1,069 MWh. With this latest commissioning, ACME Solar Holdings has increased its cumulative commissioned battery energy storage capacity to 71.640 MW/297.292 MWh. The development represents further progress in implementing the energy storage component of its FDRE project. Battery energy storage systems play an important role in supporting renewable energy integration by storing electricity and making it available when required. These systems can help address the variability of solar and wind power generation by enabling electricity generated during periods of high renewable output to be used during periods of lower generation or increased demand. For FDRE projects, energy storage is particularly important because it helps developers deliver electricity according to scheduled requirements. Combining renewable energy generation with battery storage can improve the flexibility and reliability of power supply while supporting the integration of clean energy into the electricity grid. The commissioning of the additional BESS capacity brings ACME Solar Holdings closer to completing the planned storage capacity associated with the project. The company has now commissioned a cumulative 71.640 MW/297.292 MWh of battery storage capacity against the project’s total planned discharge capacity of 250 MW/1,069 MWh. The remaining capacity is expected to be commissioned in phases as project implementation progresses. The expansion of its commissioned storage portfolio reflects the company’s continued efforts to develop renewable energy projects supported by energy storage infrastructure. As India increases its renewable energy capacity, battery storage is expected to become increasingly important in managing fluctuations in generation, improving grid flexibility, and supporting the delivery of reliable electricity. artigo.texto: CPFL negou conexão a 8 GW de data centers por gargalos na rede elétrica Volume equivale a oito vezes a demanda atual do setor no Brasil, mas inclui pedidos especulativos; CEO defende que empreendedores participem do financiamento das redes Gargalos na infraestrutura elétrica, principalmente na transmissão, levaram a CPFL Energia a negar pedidos de conexão de data centers que somam cerca de 8 gigawatts (GW), afirmou o CEO da companhia, Gustavo Estrella, durante a 17ª edição do Brazil Windpower, em São Paulo. Segundo o executivo, o volume equivale a oito vezes a demanda dos centros de dados atualmente em operação no Brasil. Estrella reconheceu, porém, que uma parte das solicitações tem caráter especulativo, mas ajuda a dimensionar a procura por conexão à rede e a preocupação do setor diante da perda de oportunidades. “Eu neguei cerca de 8 GW de capacidade de conexão de data centers por dificuldade de conexão”, afirmou o executivo. Segundo Estrella, o Brasil levou aproximadamente 16 anos para desenvolver uma demanda de cerca de 1 GW nesse mercado. A escala dos novos pedidos pressiona uma infraestrutura cuja expansão exige prazos superiores aos que os investidores em centros de dados estão dispostos a esperar. Ele apontou dois obstáculos ao desenvolvimento dessa indústria: a carga tributária e a conexão ao sistema elétrico. Embora existam limitações nas redes de distribuição, afirmou que o principal gargalo está na transmissão, responsável por transportar grandes blocos de energia até os centros de consumo. A localização dos empreendimentos acrescenta uma dificuldade. Segundo ele, os data centers precisam estar onde sua instalação faça sentido econômico, o que exige compatibilizar a disponibilidade da rede com as necessidades dos projetos. A existência de oferta de energia no país, assim, precisa ser acompanhada de capacidade para entregá-la nos locais escolhidos pelos investidores. De acordo com Estrella, as áreas de concessão da CPFL concentram cerca de 70% do consumo de eletricidade dos data centers brasileiros. Para ilustrar a dimensão das novas cargas, o executivo citou uma demanda de aproximadamente 350 megawatts (MW) para Campinas. Dois empreendimentos de 200 MW cada — porte que, segundo ele, já não é raro nesse mercado — somariam 400 MW, superando a referência apresentada para a cidade. O problema também envolve o calendário das obras. Estrella citou um prazo médio de sete anos para desenvolver a infraestrutura necessária e avaliou que a indústria de data centers não esperará todo esse tempo para colocar seus projetos em operação. A perspectiva é que a demanda aumente ainda mais. Segundo Estrella, o consumo de data centers será de 40% em 2026. Para 2027 será de 100%, mas em uma velocidade menor do que poderia acontecer. Além de cobrar maior velocidade, o executivo defendeu que os interessados em instalar os centros de dados participem do financiamento da infraestrutura construída para atendê-los. Na avaliação dele, essa demanda precisa assumir parte do esforço financeiro para viabilizar sua conexão. A presença de solicitações especulativas, reconhecida pelo próprio executivo, torna relevante distinguir intenções de investimento de projetos com perspectiva concreta de implantação antes de dimensionar as obras. A Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) ressalta que a concretização dos empreendimentos depende de fatores como infraestrutura elétrica e de telecomunicações, viabilidade econômica e atendimento às exigências de garantias para conexão. O planejamento do acesso à transmissão passa por mudanças. As chamadas Temporadas de Acesso defionidas no Pnast ((Política Nacional de Acesso ao Sistema de Transmissão) organizam a apresentação e a análise dos pedidos à Rede Básica, com processos competitivos quando há disputa pela capacidade disponível.

artigo.texto: Trump says tech companies should pay Georgians thousands to host data centers ATLANTA, Ga. (WRDW/WAGT) - President Donald Trump said local communities should have approval power over booming data center projects and receive significant financial benefits from tech companies to offset their impact. Trump said in an exclusive one-on-one interview Saturday backstage in Perry that developers have the resources to support host towns. The rapid spread of energy-intensive data centers has become a flashpoint across Georgia, sparking voter pushback over rising electric bills and straining regional power grids. Republican gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson previously broke with Trump on the issue, insisting local city and county leaders must have veto power over where campuses are built. Trump said he agrees with Jackson on local approval, arguing the solution to neighborhood resistance is simple: tech companies need to open their checkbooks. “I agree with that. No, I agree with that. And I think locals should be paid a lot of money for data centers,” Trump said. “When a data center goes in, I’ve seen it, people are very unhappy. All of a sudden, a data center decides to pay a community in the form of taxes, in the form of whatever — and all of a sudden, the same people love what they’re doing.” Trump acknowledged the global race for artificial intelligence, noting China is aggressively building competing infrastructure. He insisted tech giants have the capital to compensate local families directly. “We have to have them because you know who likes them? China,” Trump said. “China wants data centers, and they’re building them rapidly, and we’re beating China. But the data centers, they have money. They can pay local communities a lot.” Speaking before thousands in Houston County, Trump urged Georgia communities to demand substantial cash payouts. “And as far as data centers, we don’t want to get controversial,” Trump told the crowd. “The community that they’re being built in, they’re great. They give you a lot of money and everything. Ask for a lot of money. Tell them to pay you $10,000, $15,000, $20,000 for everybody that lives in the community. They’ll do it. You just gotta ask.” Trump cited an example in Louisiana where he claimed developer payouts flipped neighborhood opposition into support. “I saw one case in Louisiana where they were really fighting ... and then the company, I think it was Meta, they agreed to pay everybody $10,000,” Trump said. “And they went from, ‘we will not have it,’ to ‘do you have any more you want to bring?’ I’m telling you, just pay. Pay the people. Give them the money. They have so much money.” Trump then turned to Jackson on stage to address their policy alignment. “Do you agree with that, Rick? They’ll be very happy,” Trump said as Jackson looked on. “Rick’s a little bit tentative on that one. But no, they’ll be very happy.” The rally also served as the backdrop for major economic news. Backstage, Trump revealed to Atlanta News First that Audi plans to build its first U.S. manufacturing facility roughly 20 minutes from Perry. Gov. Brian Kemp later confirmed the German automaker will invest $4 billion in the Middle Georgia Megasite in Peach County, creating an estimated 4,500 jobs. U.S. Rep. Mike Collins, R-Ga., who is running for U.S. Senate, added that federal funding will ensure the Port of Brunswick is fully dredged to handle automotive exports from the new plant. Trump also addressed the U.S. Department of Justice’s notification that it is sending federal election monitors to six Democratic-majority Georgia counties, including Fulton, DeKalb and Gwinnett. Facing criticism from local election boards that the federal presence could intimidate voters, Trump defended the deployment. “They want to watch. You know, in Fulton County, you know that disaster,” Trump said. “They’re not going to do anything other than watch ... we want to all have honest elections.” On stage, Trump repeatedly targeted Democratic opponents, calling U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff a “radical-left extremist” and criticizing former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms over crime rates. Jackson echoed the sentiment, telling voters that “bad mayors don’t make good governors.” Trump suggested that if Jackson and Collins win, he would respond to calls to send the National Guard into Atlanta, which he labeled a “dangerous hellhole.” The Perry stop marked Trump’s second Georgia rally in recent weeks, aimed at energizing rural voters as early voting continues across the state. artigo.texto: Notícias O que a energia nuclear pode oferecer aos data centers O crescimento da inteligência artificial, da computação em nuvem e dos serviços digitais amplia a demanda por energia elétrica. Nesse cenário, a energia nuclear pode contribuir para o abastecimento de data centers, oferecendo geração contínua e baixa emissão de carbono. A possibilidade de integrar pequenos reatores modulares (SMRs, na sigla em inglês) e microrreatores a sistemas que combinam diferentes fontes de energia foi apresentada pela superintendente do IPEN, Isolda Costa, em evento realizado no Instituto de Engenharia, em São Paulo. Os SMRs podem atingir até 300 megawatts elétricos (MWe) por módulo, enquanto os microrreatores geralmente têm potência de até 10 MWe, conforme referências da Agência Internacional de Energia Atômica (AIEA). Essas tecnologias ampliam as possibilidades de fornecimento de energia em diferentes escalas, inclusive para instalações menores ou em locais com limitações de acesso à rede elétrica. A implantação dessas soluções exige avaliar fatores como demanda energética, custos, prazos, segurança, licenciamento, combustível, disponibilidade de água para resfriamento e gestão de rejeitos. A integração com fontes renováveis e sistemas de armazenamento também pode fazer parte do planejamento. A contribuição do IPEN O IPEN pode contribuir para o avanço de estudos sobre a aplicação da energia nuclear em data centers no Brasil, com pesquisas em materiais e formação de competências técnicas. Entre as possibilidades estão o fornecimento de energia nuclear pela rede elétrica, o planejamento de polos digitais associados a projetos de pequenos reatores e a avaliação de microrreatores para demandas localizadas. A viabilidade de cada alternativa depende de estudos técnicos e econômicos, além da disponibilidade de infraestrutura e de profissionais qualificados. A energia nuclear pode ampliar as opções para atender ao crescimento da infraestrutura digital com fornecimento firme e baixa emissão de carbono. O desafio é identificar as aplicações adequadas e demonstrar sua viabilidade para as necessidades brasileiras. Sem energia, não existe nuvem. A infraestrutura que construímos hoje precisa sustentar o mundo digital das próximas décadas.

artigo.texto: Power Brookfield Boosts Global Role in Batteries, Data Centers Industrial Info Resources is tracking more than $80 billion worth of active and proposed projects worldwide from Brookfield and its subsidiaries Released Tuesday, October 27, 2026 Reports related to this article: Written by Will Ploch, Assistant Editor-in-Chief for IIR News Intelligence (Sugar Land, Texas) Summary Two major acquisitions announced this year by Brookfield point to where the company is building out its presence, both in North America and globally: the battery-storage and data center markets, with the latter finding a new foothold in the Middle East. Charging Up the Battery Sector Brookfield Corporation, the parent company of Brookfield Asset Management Limited and Brookfield Renewable Partners, is broadening its role in the battery-storage and data center markets through its recent acquisitions of Aypa Power and Oaktree Capital Management, respectively. Industrial Info Resources is tracking more than $80 billion worth of active and proposed projects worldwide from Brookfield and its subsidiaries, including more than $28 billion worth focused on renewables, as well as more than $11 billion worth from Aypa. According to Industrial Info Resources data, Brookfield Renewable already is party to about $18.5 billion worth of battery energy-storage system (BESS) projects in development; the addition of Aypa, the largest stand-alone battery-storage developer in North America, will take that number to nearly $30 billion. Aypa's ongoing projects include two Canadian stand-alone BESS units that started construction over the summer: a unit in Elora, Ontario, which is designed to hold up to 211 megawatts (MW), and the Hedley unit in Jarvis, Ontario, which is designed to hold up to 200 MW. Both units will utilize lithium-ion containers and are set to wrap in the second quarter of 2027. The primary customer for both projects is Ontario's Independent Electricity System Operator (IESO). Industrial Info Resources offers more information on these units in its Global Market Intelligence (GMI) Power Plant and Project databases, where readers can find details--including construction schedules, investment values and necessary equipment--in reports for the Elora and Jarvis projects. Brookfield Renewable's own projects in this field include the Star Dairy Solar Plant in Paris, Texas, which comprises 149 MW of generation from photovoltaic (PV) panels and a 205-MW BESS unit. The project, which is managed by X-Elio North America Incorporated, which Brookfield acquired in 2023, is set to begin construction early next year. Subscribers can learn more from a plant profile and a detailed project report. Aypa currently is owned by The Blackstone Group, which announced earlier this year it would sell its subsidiary to Brookfield for an enterprise value of about $7 billion. For more information on this deal and Blackstone's own fortunes, see October 23, 2026, article - Blackstone Upbeat on Long-Term Outlook for U.S. Data Centers. By the Numbers - More than $80 billion: Total value of active and proposed projects worldwide from Brookfield and its subsidiaries - More than $11 billion: Total value of active and proposed projects across North America from Aypa - About $7 billion: Enterprise value of Brookfield's acquisition of Aypa from Blackstone Eyeing a Global Role Brookfield's expansions go beyond the power-generation market. The company recently acquired the remaining 26% stake in Oaktree, giving it full ownership of a firm that can provide it with a broader slate of global financing and credit solutions. The deal also establishes the U.S. as Brookfield's biggest market, accounting for nearly half of its total revenue. The Oaktree acquisition already is bearing fruit: Brookfield is in the process of opening a new office in Doha, Qatar, bolstered by its strengthened global credit platform. Brookfield already manages roughly US$20 billion of assets within the six-nation Gulf Cooperation Council, according to the company. That amount could be doubled through Brookfield's emerging partnership with Qai, a subsidiary of Qatar Investment Authority that focuses on AI infrastructure projects in Qatar and abroad. The Qatar deal complements Brookfield's increasing global approach to the data center market. One of its portfolio companies, DCI Data Centers, is preparing to expand of its Eastern Creek Data Center in New South Wales, Australia, to improve cloud data services in the region. The facility already handles 11 MW of load, and the expansions will bring it up to 64 MW. Subscribers can learn more from a plant profile and project report. The Industrial Info Resources GMI Project and Plant databases offer a full list of detailed reports for projects mentioned in this article, and a full list of related plant profiles. Industrial Info Resources also offers a full list of reports for active and proposed projects from Brookfield worldwide. Key Takeaways - Brookfield is broadening its role in the battery-storage and data center markets through two recent acquisitions. - Aypa's BESS projects include two Canadian stand-alone BESS units that started construction over the summer. - Brookfield's acquisition of Oaktree complements its increasing global approach to the data center market. artigo.texto: ENNA Solar, part of ENNA Group, has signed an agreement to acquire the Medgidia project, located in Constanța County, in Romania. The Medgidia project comprises 166 MWp solar plant with a 612 MWh battery energy storage system. The acquisition involves ENNA Solar acquiring a 100 per cent equity stake in CIC GREEN ENERGY MEDGIDIA S.R.L., holding the rights to develop the project. Furthermore, the project will be developed on approximately 204 hectares of land. Construction is scheduled to begin in the first quarter of 2027, while commercial operations are expected to start in the first quarter of 2028. Additionally, the project is expected to generate 265,932 MWh of electricity annually. The completion of the acquisition is subject to approval from the relevant Romanian foreign direct investment screening authority and competition authorities in the applicable jurisdictions. The Medgidia project will add to ENNA Group’s existing investments in Romania, including the 87.52 MWp Mihăilești solar project, which is under advanced construction.

artigo.texto: As rack densities climb toward 1 MW and beyond, traditional low-voltage alternating current (AC) architecture is being pushed into territory it wasn't originally designed to handle. A primary reason the industry is increasingly looking toward 800 VDC to support the next generation of high-density compute. But the bigger question isn't whether direct current (DC) can power these new racks. It's where the conversion to DC should happen and how much of the traditional power architecture is still necessary. Sidecars offer a bridge to 800 VDC One near-term answer is the sidecar, a power-conversion unit positioned next to the compute rack. Sidecars give operators a practical way to introduce 800 VDC racks into facilities built around existing low-voltage AC distribution. Rather than redesigning the facility, operators can convert AC power to DC beside the rack. That makes sidecars an important bridge between today's infrastructure and emerging DC compute. But much of the existing electrical architecture remains in place. Power still moves through transformers and low-voltage UPS infrastructure before another conversion takes place near the rack. Each stage introduces losses and nearly all of that lost energy ultimately turns into heat, putting more pressure on the cooling system to remove it. SMA's white paper models the difference. In the architecture studied, delivering 1 MW through a traditional AC system with rack-level conversion results in approximately 80 kW of power loss per megawatt delivered to the rack. Converting medium-voltage AC to 800 VDC outside the building and distributing DC directly reduces that loss to approximately 20 kW. At data center scale, the difference becomes more than significant. Moving power infrastructure outside Efficiency is only part of the equation. Data center operators are also under pressure to maximize one of their most valuable resources: white space. A native DC architecture takes a different approach. Instead of generating 800 VDC beside the rack, conversion from medium-voltage AC to DC happens once, outside the data center building. Native 800 VDC is then distributed throughout the facility. Much of the supporting electrical infrastructure can move outside as well, including power-conversion equipment, switchgear and energy storage. Inside, the architecture becomes more simplified: compute, cooling and DC busway. There are fewer conversion stages, fewer pieces of electrical equipment and more room for compute. Rethinking redundancy and energy storage Any new data center architecture still must meet demanding resilience requirements. DC creates new options. A rack can be supplied by two independent DC paths, each capable of carrying the full load. During normal operation, both can remain active and share the load. Unlike AC sources, DC sources don't have phases that must be synchronized. With the appropriate protection architecture, both sources can continuously supply the rack, potentially eliminating the need for a traditional transfer event. Sharing the load between two paths also reduces current on each path, helping lower electrical losses without sacrificing redundancy. Moving energy storage outside the building can expand its role. Instead of primarily waiting to provide backup power, storage integrated into an external DC power system can help smooth large power swings from AI workloads, provide ride-through during grid disturbances and control how quickly a facility returns to full power following an event. Depending on the system and market, storage could also support other grid services. Designing power around compute Sidecars have an important role as data centers begin adopting 800 VDC. They provide a practical way to deploy new compute infrastructure without rebuilding existing electrical systems. But the longer-term opportunity is bigger than changing the voltage delivered to the rack. Moving conversion outside the building and distributing native DC can reduce conversion stages and electrical losses, free up valuable space for compute, simplify redundancy and give energy storage a more active role. For an industry racing to add enormous amounts of computing capacity, those aren't incremental changes. They represent an opportunity to rethink data center power architecture from the grid to the rack.

artigo.texto: Georgia leaders call on EPA to curb diesel generator emissions at data centers U.S. Sen. Raphael Warnock and U.S. Rep. Hank Johnson called on the Environmental Protection Agency to immediately begin regulating the emissions of diesel generators that many data center operators are using for backup power and during peak times of electricity demand, arguing that the pollution poses significant harm to surrounding communities. In a letter dated Oct. 22, the Georgia Democratic leaders criticized the EPA for failing to oversee the generators, hundreds of which are being used at data center sites in Georgia alone. Even if the generators operate within state emission standards, their collective nitric oxide emissions would more than double that of Georgia Power’s two large coal-fired power plants, they wrote. artigo.texto: A CPFL Energia negou, nos últimos 12 meses, pedidos de conexão de data centers que somam cerca de 8 gigawatts (GW), segundo o CEO da companhia, Gustavo Estrella. O motivo são gargalos na infraestrutura elétrica brasileira, principalmente na rede de transmissão de energia. O volume negado equivale a oito vezes a demanda atual dos centros de dados em operação no país. Estrella falou durante a 17ª edição do Brazil Windpower, evento de energia eólica em São Paulo. "Eu neguei cerca de 8 GW de capacidade de conexão de data centers por dificuldade de conexão", afirmou o executivo. Parte dos pedidos, reconheceu, tem caráter especulativo. Segundo Estrella, o Brasil levou cerca de 16 anos para desenvolver uma demanda de 1 GW nesse mercado. Os novos pedidos pressionam uma infraestrutura cuja expansão leva mais tempo do que os investidores topam esperar. O prazo médio para desenvolver a infraestrutura de transmissão necessária é de sete anos, segundo o executivo. As áreas de concessão da CPFL concentram cerca de 70% do consumo de eletricidade dos data centers brasileiros. Para dimensionar as novas cargas, Estrella citou uma demanda de cerca de 350 megawatts (MW) para Campinas. Dois empreendimentos de 200 MW cada, porte já comum no mercado, somariam 400 MW, superando essa referência. O que trava a conexão Estrella aponta dois obstáculos ao crescimento dos data centers no Brasil: a carga tributária e a conexão ao sistema elétrico. Entre os dois, disse, o principal gargalo está na transmissão, responsável por levar grandes blocos de energia aos centros de consumo. Publicidade A primeira barreira deve ser endereçada pela regulamentação do Redata, o regime especial de tributação que o Congresso já começou a aprovar. A segunda é a própria velocidade da rede, tema que já colocava a energia como o teste decisivo para os data centers no país. Nem todo projeto emperra: em junho, a Voltalia assegurou conexão de 322 MW à rede elétrica para data centers no Ceará, mostrando que o gargalo varia por região e depende da disponibilidade local de linhas de transmissão.

artigo.texto: O Governo emitiu o Decreto nº 396/2026/ND-CP, que altera e complementa diversos artigos do Decreto nº 06/2022/ND-CP, o qual regulamenta a redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa e a proteção da camada de ozônio, tendo este sido alterado e complementado pelos Decretos nº 119/2025/ND-CP, nº 83/2026/ND-CP e nº 112/2026/ND-CP. O Decreto 396/2026/ND-CP altera e complementa o inciso 2º do artigo 18º, relativo ao cadastro de contas no Sistema Nacional de Cadastro de Cotas de Emissão de Gases de Efeito Estufa e Créditos de Carbono, especificando o órgão responsável pela concessão de contas no Sistema Nacional de Cadastro para cada grupo de entidades. Especificamente, o Decreto estipula que, para as instalações que recebem cotas de emissão de gases de efeito estufa, para as agências e organizações participantes em programas e projetos registrados de acordo com os mecanismos especificados nos itens a e b da Cláusula 1, Artigo 20a deste Decreto, e para as agências e organizações participantes em projetos de carbono florestal com áreas florestais dentro dos limites administrativos de duas ou mais unidades administrativas de nível provincial , o Ministério da Agricultura e do Meio Ambiente concederá contas no Sistema Nacional de Registro e enviará informações para a instalação, agência ou organização. Para as agências e organizações que participam de projetos registrados no âmbito do mecanismo de troca e compensação de créditos de carbono, o Presidente do Comitê Popular da província que receber o pedido de registro do projeto concederá uma conta no Sistema Nacional de Registro e enviará as informações à organização após a aprovação do registro do projeto; Para as agências e organizações participantes em programas e projetos registrados de acordo com o mecanismo especificado no ponto c, cláusula 1, do artigo 20a deste Decreto, a agência ou organização deverá apresentar o dossiê de registro da conta em uma das seguintes formas: diretamente ou via correio ao Centro de Serviços da Administração Pública Provincial, no caso de um projeto registrado em uma unidade administrativa de nível provincial, ou ao Centro de Serviços da Administração Pública Provincial de uma das áreas de implementação do projeto, no caso de um projeto registrado em duas ou mais unidades administrativas de nível provincial, ou online no Portal Nacional de Serviços Públicos ou no Aplicativo Nacional de Identificação. No prazo de 5 dias úteis a partir da data de recebimento do dossiê de inscrição, o Presidente do Comitê Popular da província que o recebeu deverá conceder uma conta no Sistema Nacional de Registro e enviar as informações à agência ou organização; em caso de recusa da concessão da conta, os motivos deverão ser claramente indicados. A identificação e autenticação de organizações e indivíduos no acesso e utilização do Sistema Nacional de Registro são realizadas em conformidade com a lei sobre identificação e autenticação eletrônicas. O Decreto 396/2026/ND-CP acrescenta a Cláusula 10 após a Cláusula 9 do Artigo 20. Especificamente, os procedimentos para registro, ajuste e cancelamento de registro de projetos de carbono florestal; concessão de créditos de carbono florestal no âmbito do mecanismo; e troca e compensação de créditos de carbono nacionais serão aplicados de acordo com as normas do Decreto Governamental nº 180/2025/ND-CP, de 21 de maio de 2026, sobre serviços de sequestro e armazenamento de carbono em florestas. O Decreto 396/2026/ND-CP também altera e substitui alguns formulários do Anexo V e revoga a Cláusula 3 do Artigo 20a, juntamente com alguns formulários antigos. Os pedidos recebidos pelo ministério competente antes de 1º de agosto de 2026 continuarão a ser processados de acordo com as normas vigentes na data de recebimento e não precisam ser reenviados. O decreto entrará em vigor a partir de 12 de dezembro de 2026.

artigo.texto: O Gaispi, grupo que coordena os projetos a seerem implantados pela EAF com os recursos do leilão de 5G, aprovou nesta terça, 27, dois projetos adicionais, que receberão investimentos de cerca de R$ 1,7 bilhão. Trata-se dos projetos de aquisição e distribuição de kits de recepção de TV 3.0 (a um custo estimado de R$ 1,3 bilhão) e um projeto de implementação de um data center soberano para uso do governo em projetos de Inteligência Artificial (a um custo de R$ 375 milhões). Confira aqui a análise técnica dos projetos. As duas propostas ainda precisam passar pelo crivo do conselho diretor da Anatel, mas o Gaispi conclçuiu, com base nas estimativas feitas pela EAF, que há caixa para uso imediato e é possível o início da execução, mesmo que os atuais projetos em desenvolvimento pela EAF não estejam concluídos. Os recursos da EAF vieram da venda do espectro de 3,5 GHz para as operadoras de telecomunicações, que não participaram da decisão. TV digital O projeto à TV 3.0 foi apresentado pelo setor de radodifusão no ano passado, conforme antecipou este noticiário, e prevê a distribuição de conversores que permitam a recepção dos sinais de TV aberta no novo padrão por domicílios de famílias em situação de vulnerabilidade socioeconômica, com foco nos beneficiários do Programa Bolsa Família nos municípios de São Paulo e Rio de Janeiro e no Distrito Federal. O estudo da EAF estimou em 910 mil famílias beneficiadas para o modelo de custos, o que permite concluir que cada conversor a ser distribuído terá um custo aproximado de R$ 1,4 mil (já incluindo os gastos com a logística e comunicação). A distribuição se dará de maneira faseada e em 24 meses. Data center Já o projeto para a construção do data center prevê a estrutura em um terreno de 5 mil metros quadrados, "com módulo de IA previsto para 20 racks de 42U, rede de alta velocidade, seis servidores GPU com 48 GPUs, nove servidores CPU, armazenamento all-flash e object storage. O módulo tradicional comportaria até dez racks de colocalização, sem aquisição de servidores na etapa inicial. A arquitetura prevê alimentação elétrica redundante, distribuição A/B, geração de emergência em configuração 2N, climatização compatível com alta densidade e resfriamento líquido no módulo de IA, conectividade redundante de 2 x 100 Gb e monitoramento contínunio".

artigo.texto: Data centers – O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), reeleito neste domingo (25), afirmou que pretende atrair data centers para o Brasil e desenvolver uma inteligência artificial brasileira durante seu quarto mandato. A estratégia prevê aproveitar o potencial de geração de energia renovável do país para atrair empresas de tecnologia, ampliar a infraestrutura de processamento de dados e reduzir a dependência de soluções estrangeiras. LEIA: Missão Rede Bee ao Vale do Silício para profissionais de TI tem data marcada; participe! Energia renovável para atrair data centers Durante o discurso, Lula destacou a capacidade energética brasileira como diferencial para receber centros de dados, estruturas fundamentais para serviços de computação em nuvem e sistemas de inteligência artificial. “Temos que aproveitar o potencial energético de um país que talvez seja o que tenha mais capacidade de energia renovável para trazer os datacenters necessários para acumular dados no Brasil.” O plano de governo prevê contrapartidas para empresas que instalarem data centers no país, incluindo capacidade computacional destinada ao mercado brasileiro. Também estabelece investimentos em supercomputadores nacionais e expansão dos serviços de nuvem. A instalação dessas estruturas deverá considerar eficiência energética, uso progressivo de fontes 100% renováveis e impactos sobre o abastecimento de água, o sistema elétrico e as comunidades locais. Governo prevê desenvolvimento de IA brasileira Outra proposta é desenvolver sistemas nacionais de inteligência artificial para diminuir a dependência de tecnologias dos Estados Unidos e da China. Para isso, o presidente defendeu ampliar o ensino de disciplinas ligadas à ciência e à tecnologia. “Queremos ensinar mais matemática, mais engenharia porque não quero ficar dependendo de inteligência artificial chinesa e americana. Quero criar uma brasileira”, afirmou. O plano prevê modelos de linguagem em português e em outras línguas, além de uma plataforma nacional de dados para treinamento e avaliação desses sistemas. Também propõe fortalecer instituições públicas de pesquisa, incentivar empresas brasileiras de hardware e software de alto desempenho e aproximar universidades e setor produtivo. Entre as áreas que poderão receber aplicações de IA estão o agronegócio, a saúde e os serviços financeiros. Regulamentação das big techs Lula também defendeu regulamentar as grandes empresas de tecnologia, relacionando a proposta à influência das plataformas digitais durante o processo eleitoral. “Vamos ter que regulá-las. Não é possível que a gente não tenha consciência de que um crime no mundo digital tem que ser tratado igual a um crime da vida real”, declarou. O presidente criticou empresas que, segundo ele, lucram no país sem pagar impostos e tentam influenciar os resultados eleitorais. artigo.texto: Eólicas miram data centers para ampliar demanda em meio a cortes de geração Dirigentes defendem novas usinas e reforços na transmissão; compensação financeira por restrições passadas mantém em aberto o desafio de aproveitar a energia disponível O setor eólico brasileiro aposta na chegada de data centers para impulsionar investimentos e destravar a demanda, enquanto parques já instalados enfrentam restrições para produzir energia. A aparente contradição foi tratada na 17ª edição do Brazil Windpower, em São Paulo, que expôs o desafio dessa estratégia: coordenar a expansão das usinas, das redes e do consumo para que novos empreendimentos encontrem espaço em um sistema que já precisa limitar a geração. A presidente executiva da Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica (Abeeólica), Elbia Gannoum, afirmou que o curtailment, como são conhecidos os cortes de geração, permanece sem solução operacional, apesar do avanço na regulamentação das compensações às empresas. A Portaria Normativa nº 140, publicada pelo Ministério de Minas e Energia em julho, tem alcance delimitado. Ela disciplina a compensação por cortes ocorridos entre setembro de 2023 e novembro de 2025, classificados como decorrentes de confiabilidade elétrica ou indisponibilidade externa. A adesão exige a assinatura de um termo de compromisso que inclui a renúncia a disputas sobre compensações por restrições ocorridas até a data estabelecida. O tratamento dessas perdas, entretanto, deixa em aberto as condições físicas que levam às restrições. Segundo o ONS (Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico), os cortes são uma medida técnica necessária para preservar a segurança do sistema quando a geração disponível não pode ser integralmente aproveitada. A produção eólica e solar varia ao longo do tempo e nem sempre coincide com os momentos de maior consumo. Essa distinção limita o alcance de uma solução centrada apenas na construção de linhas. Em diagnóstico sobre o curtailment, o ONS aponta que, mesmo com a eliminação de restrições de transmissão, podem continuar ocorrendo cortes quando a oferta supera a demanda em determinados horários. A expansão das redes resolve parte do problema; o equilíbrio entre produção e consumo exige outras respostas. É nesse contexto que os data centers aparecem na agenda da indústria. Elbia defendeu atenção à infraestrutura de transmissão necessária para receber essas novas cargas e aproveitar o interesse de grandes consumidores pelo Brasil. A dirigente também apontou a retomada da indústria eólica nacional como uma das prioridades do setor. João Galamba, assessor sênior do Conselho Global de Energia Eólica (GWEC), defendeu que a instalação de data centers seja acompanhada de nova geração limpa. Na avaliação dele, o desafio brasileiro está na capacidade de entregar essa energia, o que passa pela infraestrutura das redes e pelo enfrentamento do curtailment. A proposta abre uma frente de negócios para geradores e fabricantes, mas seu efeito sobre os cortes depende de como os projetos forem implantados. À luz do diagnóstico do ONS, o aumento do consumo pode ajudar a absorver excedentes; a construção simultânea de novas usinas exige avaliar onde e quando essa energia será produzida e consumida. O anúncio de uma nova carga, isoladamente, não permite medir o alívio que ela proporcionará às restrições existentes. A distribuição dos impactos dos cortes também continua em discussão regulatória. Em outubro, a Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) aprovou regras para organizar a ordem das restrições e compartilhar seus efeitos entre diferentes fontes. A aplicação definitiva foi prevista para 18 meses após a publicação da resolução, com uma etapa anterior de simulação dos resultados. No horizonte internacional, Elbia citou o objetivo de elevar a eletrificação do consumo mundial de energia a 35% até 2035. A meta integra a campanha Electrify Now, liderada pela Global Renewables Alliance com apoio do GWEC, e busca ampliar o uso de eletricidade em transportes, processos industriais e outras atividades hoje atendidas por combustíveis fósseis. Trata-se de uma agenda defendida pelas organizações, cuja concretização depende de decisões de governos, empresas e consumidores. Entre os fabricantes, Roberto Veiga, vice-presidente da Goldwind no Brasil, apresentou o investimento em capacidade industrial em Camaçari, na Bahia, como demonstração do interesse da companhia pelo mercado brasileiro e pelo fortalecimento da cadeia nacional. A produção local também tem uma função comercial. Ao anunciar a aquisição da fábrica da GE em Camaçari, em 2024, a Goldwind destacou que o atendimento aos critérios de nacionalização do BNDES facilitaria o acesso dos clientes ao financiamento de longo prazo para a compra dos equipamentos.

artigo.texto: Data center ou centro de distribuição de dados é um espaço projetado para abrigar diversos computadores, chamados de servidores, com funções variadas, como processamento, armazenamento e distribuição de dados. Sevidores são dispositivos em uma rede, responsáveis por gerenciar recursos de rede, com a capacidade de armazenar arquivos e aplicativos que são fornecidos a vários usuários ou dispositivos de uma vez só. Felipe Pameira, Desenvolvedor Web do Brasil Escola, explica que a principal função do data center é "garantir que informações, sistemas e serviços digitais estejam disponíveis, sejam processados com eficiência e possam ser acessados de maneira segura pelos usuários". Leia também: Folha divulga Ranking Universitário 2026 Tópicos desta notícia - 1 - Quem são os usuários de um data center? - 2 - Data centers no Brasil - 3 - Importância de data centers Quem são os usuários de um data center? Os data centers, atualmente, são utilizados de forma direta ou indireta por qualquer pessoa que utilize internet ou serviços digitais. "Por exemplo, quando uma pessoa acessa um aplicativo no celular dela, a empresa dona do aplicativo precisa ter um data center ou alugar data centers para que a informação daquele aplicativo seja carregada no celular do usuário", explica o desenvolvedor. Os usuários, mesmo sem esse conhecimento, recebem informações enviadas de um data center. Já bancos, hospitais, universidades, indústrias, empresas de comércio eletrônico, operadoras de telecomunicações, redes sociais, órgãos públicos e grandes plataformas de tecnologia utilizam os recursos do data center de forma direta para distribuir seus serviços. Data centers no Brasil Atualmente, o mercado brasileiro de data center está com ocupação de 96% dos data centers, de forma que novos clientes terão somente 4% disponíveis, estimado para manter assim até 2030, mesmo com a criação de novos projetos. A expectativa é que o mercado de data center no Brasil deva dobrar até 2030, atraindo investimentos bilionários, devido à demanda de novos centros. Segundo o Relatório de Mercado Data Center Brasil, realizado pela JLL, o estoque de data center cresceu mais de seis vezes desde 2012. Sendo a região de São Paulo, Barueri e Campinas a com a maior quantidade de datas ceters no país. Com o investimento em novas estruturas, é esperado que novos centros de processamento de dados surjam como alternativa; um deles é o de Fortaleza. Importância de data centers Felipe explica que os data centers se tornaram uma das infraestruturas mais importantes da economia digital, já que sustentam o funcionamento de algumas empresas e instituições, além de viabilizar o desenvolvimento de novas tecnologias. O desenvolvedor divide a importância dos data centers em três frentes: tecnológica, econômica e ambiental. A instalação de novos centros de processamento de dados atrai investimentos expressivos, movimenta a área da construção civil e sustenta o funcionamento de sistemas de informações disponíveis. Apesar disso, no quesito ambiental, essas construções enfrentam desafios significativos, como o consumo de água para o resfriamento dos servidores em funcionamento e o alto gasto de energia elétrica, tanto para alimentar os equipamentos quanto para manter a temperatura adequada. "Por isso, a expansão do setor exige planejamento para evitar pressões excessivas sobre a infraestrutura energética e os recursos hídricos das regiões onde essas instalações são construídas. Nesse contexto, cresce a busca por data centers mais eficientes, com equipamentos que realizam mais processamento utilizando menos energia, sistemas avançados de refrigeração e maior participação de fontes renováveis no fornecimento elétrico", afirma. artigo.texto: Moms in Western Henrico lead opposition to proposed Goochland data centers HENRICO, Va. (WWBT) - A group of mothers in Henrico are working to inform neighbors about proposed data center developments planned across the county line in Goochland. The women live in Henrico, near the Goochland County line. They are opposing data center campuses that could be built a few miles from their homes. “I feel like it’s just way too close to too many families,” Courtney Dare said. Last November, Goochland county officials approved it’s Technology Overlay District, an area zoned specifically for data center development. A pre-application was recently filed to build the Tuckahoe Tech Park, a nearly 900-acre data center campus along Route 6/Patterson Avenue. It would sit in a part of the Tech Overlay District known as ‘TOD West.’ That means it needs a conditional use permit to be built and would have to go through a public approval process. Back in the summer, when early plans were filed for the tech park, 12 On Your Side spoke with homeowners in the Mosaic at West Creek neighborhood in Goochland, who also live close to proposed Tuckahoe Tech Park. Regulatory filings by Dominion Energy to the SCC show developers have expressed interest in a few other data center projects that could be built by-right in the TOD. It includes a 1,000 acre campus within miles of where these moms live. One of the moms involved, Jennifer Butner, said her top concern is the back-up diesel generators used at these facilities. “They will have hundreds of generators that frankly the county will properly have very little control over when they are run,” Butner said. “And those generators are going to be within a mile of my children’s elementary school and my neighborhood and they’re going to be breathing in toxic fumes.” In addition to air quality concerns, the group said it is worried about noise, light pollution and the impact on home values. “There’s really been a lack of awareness in Henrico even though a lot of Henrico residents are going to be directly impacted,” Dare said. The group held a meeting last week to inform people about the proposals. Hundreds of neighbors attended, including elected officials from both Henrico and Goochland. A Goochland County spokesperson provided the following statement to 12 On Your Side when asked about the meeting: “We welcome the feedback and perspectives of all residents and interested stakeholders, including our neighbors in Henrico, on the important issues impacting Goochland County.” The group said it plans to continue its efforts, including attending the upcoming meetings with county officials in both Goochland and Henrico. “I personally think that it just needs to all slow down and I think the best way to do that is a moratorium. If that’s not possible, I want my state assembly members to put more of a restriction on where these data centers can be located,” Butner said. “We want to do whatever we can to protect our kids,” Robertson said. Goochland County is currently facing a lawsuit over the Tech Overlay District. Per the county’s website, there was a hearing on October 20 in Goochland County Circuit Court over the county’s request to dismiss the lawsuit. A ruling on the hearing has not been made yet. The Goochland Board of Supervisors also approved a motion on September 1 to re-examine what’s included in the TOD. It’s unclear how that review will affect projects proposed for the area. artigo.texto: The European Commission's new legislative package "Fit for 55" still needs to be approved by the EU member states and the European Parliament, but its main goals are already known and cover many key areas of the European Union's policy and economy. This is stated in an article by Iryna Stavchuk, Deputy Minister of Environmental Protection and Natural Resources of Ukraine. As is known, in July the European Commission published the "Fit for 55" legislative package aimed at revising the EU's current climate and energy targets for 2030. The package strengthens eight existing pieces of legislation and proposes five new initiatives across a range of policy areas and economic sectors: climate, energy and fuels, transport, buildings, land use and forestry, which will help achieve the set goal in the most effective way. Revision of the EU Emissions Trading System "Experience in recent years has shown that emissions trading is an effective and cost-efficient mechanism for reducing emissions, and the revenues it raises by auctioning emission allowances can be used by countries to support the transition to cleaner production and stimulate innovation," Stavchuk stressed. As noted, the "Fit for 55" package includes a proposal to lower the overall emissions cap further and increase the annual rate of reduction by gradually cutting the number of CO2 emission allowances (including free ones) granted to companies under the EU ETS. This should lead to a higher price per tonne of emissions and thus encourage companies to reduce emissions. It is also proposed to phase out free emission allowances for steel companies and sectors covered by CBAM, as well as for airlines, while including maritime shipping in the system from 2023. The argument is that a single ship produces as much carbon emissions as 8,000 cars a day. In addition, the EU intends to create a separate new emissions trading system for road transport and buildings heating and to start applying it from 2026. Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) One of the new proposals in the document is the creation of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), which will set a price on imports of a limited number of polluting goods based on the carbon emissions generated during their production. "This measure is aimed at protecting European businesses from environmental dumping and preventing "carbon leakage" in situations where European companies want to relocate outside the EU to avoid paying for CO2 emissions. The mechanism is also intended to encourage industry outside the EU and to encourage the EU's international partners to take steps in the same direction," the Deputy Minister emphasised. She noted that CBAM will operate in addition to the European Emissions Trading System, but instead of allowances, special CBAM certificates will be introduced, which importers will buy in the EU according to the volume of emissions generated in the production of their goods. Certificate prices will be calculated on the basis of the average auction price of EU ETS allowances. CBAM will initially apply to imports of fertilisers, electricity, cement and metallurgical products (iron, steel, aluminium) and will take into account only direct emissions from production. As noted, these are the sectors with the highest CO2 emissions and high trade intensity, which creates a risk of "carbon leakage" to other countries. CBAM applies to companies from all non-EU countries, except those that participate in the European Emissions Trading System or have a national ETS linked to the EU one. This applies to members of the European Economic Area and Switzerland. At the same time, it is noted that Ukraine can count on special conditions, namely an exemption from CBAM in the energy sector. "The preamble of the document notes that as soon as third countries are closely integrated into the EU electricity market through market coupling, technical solutions should be found to ensure the application of CBAM to electricity exported from such countries into the customs territory of the Union. If no technical solutions can be found, third countries with market coupling should benefit from a temporary exemption from CBAM until 2030 at the latest, only for electricity exports, provided certain conditions are met. However, these third countries must develop a roadmap and commit to introducing a carbon pricing mechanism with a price equivalent to the EU ETS, and must commit to achieving carbon neutrality by 2050, so as to align it with Union legislation on the environment, climate, competition and energy. This exemption should be withdrawn at any time if there are grounds to believe that the country concerned is not fulfilling its commitments or has not adopted an ETS equivalent to the EU ETS by 2030," Stavchuk said. Changes in the transport sector As noted, the EU wants to ban the registration of new petrol and hybrid cars in the EU from 2035. It also plans to tighten CO2 emission standards for cars and vans, which will accelerate the transition to zero-emission mobility. From 2030, average emissions of new cars must fall by 55%, and by 100% from 2035, compared to 2021 levels. As a result, all new cars registered as of 2035 will be zero-emission. Under the revised Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation, the EU plans to ensure the necessary roll-out of interoperable and user-friendly infrastructure for charging and refuelling clean vehicles across the entire EU, keeping pace with market developments and guaranteeing that rural and remote areas are covered too. This is because consumers are increasingly buying electric vehicles. That is why it is proposed to build charging stations for electric vehicles every 60 kilometres along the EU's main motorways, and hydrogen refuelling stations every 150 kilometres. artigo.texto: Evergy executive answers questions about data centers after email to customers LEE’S SUMMIT, Mo. (KCTV) - Evergy says it has turned down data centers that couldn’t meet its requirements for large electricity customers. The company sent an email to customers on Monday about its rules for data centers. KCTV5 asked local data center opponents for their follow-up questions that the email did not address in detail, then took those questions to Chuck Caisley, Evergy’s chief consumer officer. Caisley said the email was sent to dispel misunderstanding that has developed as concerns about data centers have grown locally and nationally. “There’s a lot of information floating around online, but a lot of it isn’t accurate,” Caisley said. “It’s from different parts of the country and just projected here. We wanted to answer some of the key questions we knew our customers had.” Questions for Evergy Evergy says it can’t simply refuse to serve data centers, unless those needs would jeopardize what other customers need. “We’re not an advocate for or against data centers,” Caisley said. “That’s not our job. Our job is to protect our existing customers and make sure that if data centers come to our area, they don’t jeopardize our reliability and they don’t negatively impact rates.” He frequently used the term “existing customers” but later clarified that he means all customers, current or future, who do not fit into the special “large load” category of large data centers. Asked whether Evergy has said no to anyone, Caisley said yes. “We’ve probably said no to dozens of data centers that just couldn’t meet the requirements that we’ve set out,” Caisley said. Asked what happens if other customers need more power during peak periods or due to growth in other sectors, Caisley said: “We can turn down or turn off to make sure that there’s still enough generation for our existing customers.” The rules apply to new facilities using 75 megawatts or more, and to existing customers who expand by that much. Asked if there are any other facilities in Evergy’s service area that require that amount of energy, he said not yet. “Panasonic is getting close, but no, right now data centers are an exclusive club over 75 megawatts,” Caisley said. Rates, collateral and who is covered Caisley said large load customers pay a premium over other large customers. He described how that money is used. “That money is put together in a pool and used to reduce future rate increases for our other customers,” Caisley said. In testimony at an Oct. 8, 2025, Kansas Corporation Commission hearing, KCC staff witness Justin Grady estimated large load customers would pay 7% to 10% more than existing industrial customers. The estimate is cited in the commission’s Nov. 6, 2025, order approving the Evergy plan. Caisley described the premium another way. He said large load customers pay about 20% more than other “similarly situated customers.” Additionally, large load customers pay for equipment built just to serve them. Their contracts also include early exit penalties and collateral. Asked what happens if the business goes bankrupt, Caisley emphasized that customers must post collateral in one of several forms. “They have to post either a letter of credit or cash or in some cases we have a parental company guarantee if they’re a big enough company,” Caisley said, citing parent companies like Meta or Google in some cases. Some of the rules stem from Missouri Senate Bill 4, passed in 2025. It requires the Missouri Public Service Commission to adopt large load rates that reflect those customers’ share of costs and keep other customers from paying unjust or unreasonable costs. The law applies to the investor-owned utilities the commission regulates. The Kansas rules came through a different process. Evergy applied to the Kansas Corporation Commission in February 2025 for approval of a Large Load Power Service rate plan. The commission approved a unanimous settlement on Nov. 6, 2025. The KCC says it does not regulate municipal utilities or electric cooperatives. Caisley said Evergy’s large load customer rules have been in place for months. He said every hyperscale data center in Evergy’s service area has to follow the rules because all of those data centers came about after the rules went into effect. Copyright 2026 KCTV.
