artigo.texto: US Signal buys Hillsboro data center for $20M amid city moratorium Published 4:29 pm Tuesday, October 27, 2026 As Hillsboro remains under a moratorium on data center development and just approved its first phase of permanent restrictions, a national digital infrastructure company has purchased an existing facility in the city for $20 million. US Signal announced the acquisition Tuesday, Oct. 27, of a 63,000-square-foot data center in an industrial park at 3295 N.E. 83rd Ave. The facility has approximately 14,000 square feet of data hall space and 4.5 megawatts of power on site, according to the company. Washington County property records show US Signal purchased the property from Madrona Joes LLC and Watumull GI Joe’s LLC in a transaction recorded Oct. 14. In a release, the company said the facility offers opportunities to “expand capacity,” although it remains unclear whether that would involve physically expanding the building, increasing its electrical capacity or making greater use of the existing space. It is also unclear whether any potential expansion would be subject to the city’s moratorium or newly adopted regulations. What are Hillsboro’s restrictions? The Hillsboro City Council approved a 120-day moratorium July 27, temporarily halting new and expanded data center development while city officials worked on permanent changes to the city’s development code. The moratorium is scheduled to expire Nov. 24, although the council could extend it for an additional six months. On Oct. 20, councilors unanimously adopted the first phase of those permanent regulations, limiting new standalone data centers to the city’s Industrial Park and Industrial Sanctuary zones and capping the amount of land they can occupy. Washington County property records classify the 5.08-acre property as Industrial Park land, although its specific zoning designation under Hillsboro’s development code has not been confirmed by city officials. The new rules also require public hearings for proposed standalone data centers, establish a temporary 1,000-foot buffer between new data centers and schools and place additional limits on smaller accessory data centers operated by businesses. The regulations are scheduled to take effect Nov. 19, five days before the current moratorium expires. Neither the company nor the city immediately responded to requests for comment Tuesday. “Hillsboro gives us a way to grow in a market where available capacity is extremely limited,” John White, US Signal’s chief operating officer, said in a release. “We’re bringing an existing facility into our network and building on the approach we’ve taken in other communities: data centers sized for the markets they serve, with the connectivity and services customers need to grow.” According to US Signal, Hillsboro’s data center market had an estimated vacancy rate of just 0.2% during the first half of 2026. The acquisition marks US Signal’s first owned data center in the Portland metro area, adding to its existing Oregon presence in Bend and a nationwide network of 17 data centers. The company said the Hillsboro facility creates opportunities to expand its colocation services, which provide space and infrastructure for customers to house computing equipment, connect the site to its fiber network and deploy additional cloud infrastructure in the Pacific Northwest. The acquisition is part of a broader expansion effort supported by US Signal’s owner, Igneo Infrastructure Partners, an international infrastructure investment firm. Meanwhile, city officials are preparing a second phase of data center regulations, expected to address building heights, buffers, environmental protections and other development standards during winter and spring 2027.

artigo.texto: CATL advances 20 Ah solid-state battery cells ahead of 2027 trial production CATL has advanced its all-solid-state battery development from a 10 Ah-class validation platform to 20 Ah sample trials, according to Y-Auto. It targets small-batch production in 2027, with large-scale manufacturing planned around 2030. The company provided an update on October 27 in response to investor questions on the Shenzhen Stock Exchange’s Hudongyi platform. Its development team has more than 1,000 people, and the programme targets an energy density of about 500 Wh/kg. CATL has not confirmed that figure as a production-cell specification or disclosed expected trial output, automotive customers or a vehicle launch date tied to these cells. What CATL’s solid-state cells still need to prove Energy density is only one measure of battery performance. Durability, manufacturing yield, cost, safety and performance under real operating conditions will also determine whether the cells are suitable for production vehicles. Chairman Robin Zeng previously rated CATL’s solid-state battery technology at Level 4 on a nine-level readiness scale. The assessment provides context for the development still required, but the more consequential test is whether the company can manufacture reliable cells at commercially viable cost. Sulfide cells face interface and durability hurdles. Sulfide electrolytes conduct lithium ions effectively, but maintaining stable contact between solid components remains a challenge. Electrodes expand and contract during charging and discharging, which can disrupt those interfaces. Cell design must manage contact pressure and interface resistance to maintain performance. Sulfide materials also require protection from moisture because reactions can release hydrogen sulfide (H₂S), a toxic gas. Material handling and manufacturing conditions therefore remain important considerations for commercial production. The 500 Wh/kg goal also raises questions about electrode design. Such high cell-level energy density can involve higher-capacity anode architectures, including lithium-metal or anode-less designs. For example, Samsung SDI has described an anode-less approach for its all-solid-state batteries. CATL has not disclosed the anode configuration used in the cells covered by its latest update. CATL, Toyota and Samsung SDI have different targets CATL is targeting small-batch production in 2027. Toyota and Idemitsu aim to commercialise sulfide-based all-solid-state batteries for battery-electric vehicles between 2027 and 2028, while Samsung SDI has targeted mass production in the second half of 2027. These milestones are not directly equivalent. Samsung SDI has also identified humanoid robots as a potential early application for its technology while continuing development for electric vehicles. These timelines do not mean the companies’ products will reach the market at the same time, in comparable volumes, or with equivalent performance. How all-solid-state batteries differ from semi-solid designs All-solid-state batteries use a solid electrolyte rather than relying on a liquid electrolyte within the cell. Semi-solid and hybrid designs retain some liquid electrolyte, although terminology and configurations vary by manufacturer. Progress with a semi-solid design does not, by itself, show that a company has overcome the interface, durability, and manufacturing challenges of an all-solid-state cell. For CATL, the central challenge is turning its current development work into repeatable, cost-competitive production.

artigo.texto: Marsh Advances Carbon Market Integrity Through Innovative Risk Management Solution for Carbon Project Developer Invert Press Release Date 10-27-2026 Invert and Marsh's 5-year partnership produced the first reversal insurance policy, replacing buffer pools to unlock capital and scale carbon markets. OTTAWA, ONTARIO, CANADA, October 27, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ -- Invert Inc. (“Invert”), a leading carbon reduction and removal company, and Marsh, a global leader in insurance broking and risk advising, announce the successful placement of the first reversal insurance policy under Verra’s durability pilot. This landmark achievement is the culmination of more than five years of Invert and its broker, Marsh, pursuing specialized risk management solutions for the rapidly evolving carbon markets, with a dedicated focus on buffer pool replacement. Marsh successfully brokered the transaction, placing the policy with Oka, with underwriting by CarbonPool, whose innovative product offering finally delivered the exact solution required to bring this long-term vision to life. As carbon markets mature and transition toward compliance-grade standards, robust and regulated risk transfer mechanisms have become essential for scaling project finance. Over the past five years, Invert, acting as a carbon project developer and investor, has engaged Marsh to help procure and design insurance products specifically suited to the complex needs of project developers. These bespoke solutions (ranging from non-delivery coverage and buffer pool replacement insurance to parametric and alternative risk transfer products) are designed to unlock better project economics and provide greater certainty for offtakers and buyers. Ultimately, utilizing these tailored financial tools improves Invert's working capital, enabling the company to fund new initiatives, optimize existing projects, and maximize its positive environmental impact. This newly placed policy, structured by CarbonPool and underwritten by Oka, provides critical protection against the risk of reversal, which is the chance that carbon previously credited as stored is unexpectedly re-released into the atmosphere. Historically, developers managed this risk by contributing a large portion of their credits to a buffer pool, a requirement that ties up valuable inventory that cannot be sold or financed. By participating in Verra's durability pilot and substituting the traditional buffer pool contribution with regulated insurance, Invert transfers the reversal risk directly to an insurer. This allows the company to make a significantly greater proportion of its issued credits immediately available for sale, optimizing cash flows and investor returns while ensuring a robust financial mechanism remains in place. "Our work with Marsh isn't just about derisking Invert’s portfolio; it's about building the financial infrastructure the entire carbon market desperately needs," said Andre Fernandez, CEO of Invert Inc. "Because of our deep involvement in designing these mechanisms, we act as an introducer for Marsh, serving as a vital bridge, introducing our peers and clients to Marsh's specialized capabilities. Whether you are a developer looking to unlock working capital or a buyer seeking certainty, we are working with Marsh to solve the carbon markets risk transfer challenges." Hema Mistry, UK CEO, Financial and Professional Liability, Marsh Risk, said: “This landmark placement demonstrates how insurance can play a practical role in helping carbon projects manage reversal risk in a more capital efficient way. This is an important part of the wider evolution of how carbon markets are managing permanence risk, with insurance solutions emerging to support the growth and integrity of high-quality carbon projects.” This evolving financial infrastructure demonstrates tangible market benefits beyond the project developer. Crucially, this approach provides buyers with the institutional credibility required for corporate balance sheets, signaling a new standard of financial rigor in carbon credit procurement. Invert remains committed to advancing the financial maturity and capital efficiency of the carbon market, continuing to pursue solutions with industry leaders like Marsh to ensure that high-quality, nature-based carbon projects are bankable, investable, and scalable. About Marsh. Marsh (NYSE: MRSH) is a global leader in risk, reinsurance and capital, people and investments, and management consulting, advising clients in 130 countries. With annual revenue of $27 billion and more than 95,000 colleagues, Marsh helps build the confidence to thrive through the power of perspective. For more information, visit marsh.com or follow us on LinkedIn and X. About Invert. Invert is an award-winning carbon reduction and removal company committed to empowering organizations to take bold climate action. With a mission to drive global goals for decarbonization, Invert is dedicated to making a measurable impact on our planet’s future through carbon project origination and financing and sourcing high-integrity carbon credits for businesses. artigo.texto: Portugal está a reforçar a sua posição como mercado emergente de Data Centers na Europa, impulsionado pelo crescimento da procura associada à inteligência artificial (IA), pela forte conectividade internacional e pela expansão de projetos de grande escala. De acordo com o mais recente Data Centers Iberian Region Snapshot, elaborado pela Colliers, empresa global e diversificada de serviços profissionais e de gestão de investimentos, especializada em Imobiliário Comercial, Engenharia e Gestão de Investimento, Lisboa dispõe atualmente de 25 MW IT de capacidade operacional, mas apresenta um pipeline de desenvolvimento de aproximadamente 1.389 MW IT. Cerca de 91% da capacidade assegurada deverá estar operacional antes de 2030. Apesar de não terem sido identificados novos projetos ou aumentos de capacidade operacional em Lisboa durante o período analisado (abril a setembro de 2026), o mercado mantém uma dinâmica de desenvolvimento significativa. A Colliers destaca que a combinação entre uma base operacional ainda reduzida e um pipeline de grande dimensão coloca Portugal numa posição forte para captar uma nova vaga de procura por infraestrutura digital. “O mercado de centros de dados em Portugal ainda é pequeno quando comparado com o de outros países com maior tradição neste setor (FLAP-D). No entanto, apesar de contar com menos projetos, Portugal tem três projetos que já são, ou virão a ser, muito relevantes em termos de dimensão: o Start Campus, em Sines, o Merlin, em Lisboa, e o Covilhã DC (Asterion). Em conjunto, estes projetos representam um pipeline de desenvolvimento muito significativo”, diz José María Guilleuma, managing director de Data Centers da Colliers, ao Jornal Económico. “Portugal já conseguiu atrair grandes projetos de Inteligência Artificial, mas falta-lhe transformar Lisboa numa localização atrativa para os grandes operadores de hiperescala, à semelhança do que acontece em Barcelona”, acrescenta o responsável. A crescente relevância da inteligência artificial está a alterar os requisitos dos operadores e utilizadores de Data Centers, aumentando a necessidade de capacidade energética, conectividade e instalações preparadas para cargas computacionais de elevada densidade. Neste contexto, a construção do Lisbon AI Campus da Merlin Edged está em curso. A primeira fase prevê 80 MW IT, distribuídos por duas instalações de 40 MW, com entrega prevista para o quarto trimestre de 2027. Está ainda prevista uma capacidade adicional de 100 MW IT em três edifícios, elevando a capacidade planeada do campus para 180 MW IT. Para além desta capacidade, a Merlin Edged prevê desenvolver até mais 1.120 MW IT no seu pipeline futuro, incluindo 200 MW IT em Vila Franca de Xira e outros 920 MW IT numa localização ainda não divulgada. Sines ganha importância estratégica na corrida à IA Fora da região de Lisboa, o projeto de Sines assume uma relevância crescente na estratégia nacional de infraestrutura digital. Segundo a Colliers, a Start Campus, em parceria com a Nscale e a Microsoft, ampliou o seu projeto para implementar mais de 66.000 GPUs NVIDIA Rubin a partir do final de 2027, complementando as mais de 12.600 GPUs NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra previstas para o SIN01. A Start Campus mantém autorização para uma capacidade total de 1,2 GW, reforçando Sines como uma das localizações europeias com maior potencial para infraestrutura de IA de grande escala. Também fora de Lisboa, a entrada da NxN no mercado português, através da aquisição de um Data Center operacional de 1 MW IT em Évora, evidencia a expansão gradual do mercado para outros pontos do território. A atratividade de Lisboa enquanto localização para Data Centers é suportada pela sua forte conectividade internacional, nomeadamente pela rede de cabos submarinos e pela infraestrutura de fibra ótica. O mercado beneficia ainda de um enquadramento regulatório considerado favorável e de uma crescente valorização das infraestruturas digitais como setor estratégico. “Portugal é uma geografia ideal, graças à sua localização estratégica voltada para o Atlântico. É verdade que o novo enquadramento regulatório em Espanha poderá beneficiar Portugal, ao posicioná-lo como uma boa alternativa para a diversificação europeia dos países nórdicos. No entanto, Portugal já beneficia de previsibilidade regulatória, e o seu modelo e estrutura da rede elétrica estão alinhados com as orientações da União Europeia”, conclui José María Guilleuma. artigo.texto: Aneel aprova editais de leilões de baterias e conta fica com geradores Agência mantém obrigação de custeio para geradores, enquanto agentes do setor articulam no Congresso mudança na legislação A Aneel (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica) aprovou nesta 3ª feira (27.out.2026) os editais dos 2 primeiros leilões de reserva de capacidade para contratação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias. A agência manteve os geradores de energia elétrica como responsáveis pelos custos da contratação, conforme determina a Lei nº 15.269 de 2025. Os certames estão marcados para 2 e 4 de dezembro –um deles exige um mínimo de conteúdo nacional, o outro admite equipamentos importados. Durante o processo de consulta pública, agentes do setor elétrico propuseram à agência reguladora uma redação mais genérica. Queriam que a expressão “agentes de geração”, fosse substituída por “usuários de reserva de capacidade”. A ideia era acomodar eventuais mudanças na legislação. A Aneel acolheu parcialmente a sugestão no edital, mas manteve a referência explícita aos geradores na definição dos responsáveis pelo pagamento no contrato. A decisão se dá enquanto o Congresso discute uma mudança na lei para retirar dos geradores a obrigação exclusiva de custear as baterias. Em 13 de outubro, a Câmara aprovou o regime de urgência do PL (Projeto de Lei) 3.716 de 2026, apresentado pelo deputado Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania-SP). A proposta revoga o trecho da lei de 2025 e estabelece a aplicação da regra geral de divisão de custo. Caso seja aprovada antes da realização do leilão, o edital precisaria ser alterado, pois as despesas passariam a ser divididas entre os usuários finais do SIN (Sistema Interligado Nacional), incluindo consumidores. PONTOS-CHAVE Apesar da recusa quanto às regras de custeio, a agência acabou aceitando parte das contribuições do setor privado. Eis alguns pontos chave do edital: - exigências patrimoniais – a Aneel flexibilizou as regras para permitir consórcios entre empresas de um mesmo grupo econômico. Para evitar a contagem duplicada de recursos financeiros, determinou que o patrimônio líquido exigido seja comprovado exclusivamente pela controladora, sem somar o patrimônio das subsidiárias controladas; - baterias colocalizadas – a agência manteve a proibição de participação de sistemas de armazenamento colocalizados em usinas geradoras, apesar dos pedidos de flexibilização. A justificativa é que esses sistemas dependem operacionalmente da usina à qual estão vinculados, o que poderia comprometer o atendimento integral aos comandos de carga e descarga do ONS (Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico). - participação de transmissoras – a Aneel autorizou a participação de concessionárias de transmissão nos certames. A possibilidade foi analisada a partir de consulta da Taesa. Segundo parecer da Procuradoria Federal junto à agência, as transmissoras também poderão atuar por meio de subsidiárias ou sociedades de propósito específico, mediante autorização regulatória e separação contábil e financeira das atividades.

artigo.texto: Building the Future, a new pro-data center super PAC, is spending more than $1.5 million to back Kansas state Sen. Ty Masterson, a Republican, in the state’s battle for governor, a person familiar with the spending said Monday in details first shared with NBC News. Building the Future is an offshoot of the pro-AI super PAC Leading the Future, backed by AI heavyweights and arguably the leading super PAC promoting industry interests in the midterm elections. Earlier Monday, The New York Times reported that Building the Future is also set to spend about $1.5 million in advertising to boost GOP Sen. Darline Graham in the South Carolina Senate race. In August, Build American AI, a nonprofit that is also in the Leading the Future network, announced a multimillion-dollar ad campaign in Kansas, Ohio and Wisconsin seeking to boost preferred policies to govern data center growth. At the time, it announced the formation of the political group, Building the Future. The group said in August it would back candidates who support “responsible policies that strengthen and protect communities, preserve water resources, and prevent rate hikes on electricity bills, while ensuring American leadership in AI and creating good-paying jobs for American workers.” Opposition to data center development has been intensifying for months, with the sprawling structures needed to power the AI boom becoming a key issue for voters across the country. Kansas is one of the only Democratic-controlled governorships that Republicans have a shot at flipping this fall. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report lists the race as leaning Republican. The state also features a competitive Senate contest between Republican Sen. Roger Marshall and Democratic pastor Adam Hamilton. In a statement Monday, Holscher called Masterson a “stooge for Big Tech” who wants “to put a data center on every corner and in every cornfield.” FOR SUBSCRIBERSBenjamin Netanyahu battles for political survival FOR SUBSCRIBERS6 key takeaways from Anthropic’s IPO filing FOR SUBSCRIBERSBenjamin Netanyahu battles for political survival FOR SUBSCRIBERS6 key takeaways from Anthropic’s IPO filing “It’s also why he’s going to give them tax breaks while everyday Kansans’ costs go up,” she added. “These billionaire CEOs know that I won’t do their bidding, and that’s why they’re spending millions to beat me. But I’ll keep fighting for guardrails on data centers, and I’ll always put Kansans first.” Masterson did not immediately provide comment for this article. Data centers have been a hot issue in both Kansas and South Carolina, as well as other states across the country. In Kansas, Masterson has opposed moratoriums and defended a 2025 law he voted for that provided sales tax exemption for data center investments. Holscher voted for that law, too, but has since called for a statewide moratorium on the developments. In South Carolina, Graham has framed the investments as necessary for national security while expressing support for local control over their construction. Annie Andrews, Graham’s Democratic opponent, has called for a moratorium on new projects and labeled Graham as “Data Center Darline.”

artigo.texto: Rockford advances proposed regulations for potential future data centers Draft rules would address water use, electricity demand, noise, pollution and infrastructure impacts ROCKFORD, Ill. (Rockford News First) - Rockford officials approved moving proposed data center regulations to the city’s Zoning Board of Appeals for a public hearing Monday night, advancing an effort to establish permanent rules for the large computer facilities. The proposal follows a temporary moratorium approved by the City Council in August. That moratorium paused the processing and final approval of new data center applications while city staff reviewed how the facilities could affect Rockford. The vote does not represent final approval of the regulations. Instead, it moves the draft rules to the next step in the city’s zoning process, where the Zoning Board of Appeals will hold a public hearing and consider the proposed amendments. Data centers are large facilities that house computer servers used for cloud computing, artificial intelligence, online services and data storage. They can require significant amounts of electricity, water and cooling equipment. City staff recommended treating data centers as their own land-use category rather than as a general type of high-technology facility under Rockford’s existing zoning ordinance. The proposed regulations would require new data centers and significant expansions to receive performance-based approval. Eligible sites would be limited to appropriate industrial areas with adequate infrastructure. Developers also would need to provide detailed evaluations of a project’s potential effects on electrical service, water supply, wastewater, transportation, stormwater and emergency response. The draft rules call for closed-loop or other resource-conserving cooling systems designed to produce nearly no wastewater discharge from heat exchange equipment. Water use was a major focus of the city’s review. Rockford’s water system serves about 52,000 customers and produces an average of approximately 16.5 million gallons per day, with a systemwide production capacity of about 60 million gallons per day. City officials noted that available systemwide capacity does not necessarily mean every location can handle the demand of a large industrial facility. Proposed data centers would be reviewed based on factors including average and peak water use, seasonal demand, fire-flow needs, required water-main improvements and potential effects on existing customers. The regulations also would require professional noise studies addressing normal operations, peak cooling conditions, backup-generator testing and, when appropriate, low-frequency noise. Noise levels would have to comply with Illinois Pollution Control Board standards. Backup generators would be subject to state and federal air-permitting requirements. Developers would have to provide proof of the required permits before receiving a certificate of occupancy. Other proposed requirements include enhanced setbacks and landscaping near homes, schools and parks; limits on lighting near less-intensive zoning districts; stormwater and flood-control reviews; and fire and life-safety plans addressing generators, fuel systems, batteries, hazardous materials and emergency access. Developers would be responsible for paying for required public infrastructure improvements, such as water mains, streets, traffic signals and storm sewers. The proposal also would require confirmation that ComEd or another applicable utility could reasonably provide the necessary electrical service. City staff said data centers could provide construction jobs, capital investment and additional property, utility and sales tax revenue. However, the facilities generally are expected to create fewer permanent jobs than traditional manufacturing facilities of a similar size. The proposed rules also would require each new data center to submit a decommissioning plan explaining how unused servers, cooling systems, batteries, electrical equipment and hazardous materials would be removed or handled if the facility closes. The draft regulations now move to the Zoning Board of Appeals for public input and review before returning through the city’s approval process. Copyright 2026 Rockford News First. artigo.texto: Xpanner Launches X1 Piling R6 Automated Pile Driving System for Solar and BESS Sites Xpanner has introduced the X1 Piling R6, a fully automated pile driving system aimed at utility-scale solar and battery energy storage sites, according to Solar Power World. The construction automation company said the system combines its automation stack with the Everstar R6 crawler base machine. Under the workflow described by the company, operators upload a pile plan, move the machine to the relevant row and press a single button. The X1 then travels to each pile, aligns and hammers it, and holds it plumb while the operator supervises remotely. The company said the machine uses high-precision GNSS antennas and receivers, precision sensors and an Xpanner-developed automation controller to reach each pile position and drive to the required location and elevation. Xpanner said conventional pile driving depends on a two-person crew plus separate survey, marking and preparation work, while the X1 consolidates those steps into one automated cycle run by a single operator who does not stand next to the mast. The automation stack is carried over from the company's PD10 platform, which Xpanner said has been deployed on more than 67 U.S. jobsites with more than 10 of the country's top engineering, procurement and construction firms. On the R6 base machine, the company said the X1 delivers a 45% faster cycle time than the prior generation. Henri Lee, co-founder and chief executive of Xpanner, said solar and BESS builders are under pressure to bring new power online for the grid and for data centers and cannot find enough skilled crews. He said the X1 allows one operator to drive each pile plumb with a single touch, keeps people away from the mast and logs each pile as it is installed, extending automation that EPCs already use on the PD10 to a more powerful and versatile machine. The system connects to Xpanner Connect, the company's web-based project dashboard. Project teams can load the pile schedule and coordinates, assign machines and set up a site in minutes, according to Xpanner. As the X1 works, it records each pile's position, depth and plumb and posts the data to a live project map, replacing manual counts, phone calls, spreadsheets and end-of-day reports. Managers can also monitor machine state, cycle counts and alerts across the fleet without visiting a site. The X1 Piling R6 launches commercially on Oct. 26, 2026, through the Xpanner subscription. A single agreement covers the machine, the X1 automation kit, Xpanner Connect and Xpanner On-Site Support, with service delivered directly by Xpanner from demonstration and site validation through training, operation and maintenance. During site validation, Xpanner reviews each customer's pile schedule to confirm reveal heights and embedment. Xpanner said future capabilities for the X1 Piling R6 will include screw driving and pre-drilling. - 1. artigo.texto: Seu navegador não oferece leitura em voz alta. A concentração de grandes estruturas de tecnologia na Região Metropolitana de São Paulo não é coincidência. Nas últimas duas décadas, o estado se consolidou como o principal polo de processamento e armazenamento de dados do país, atraindo investimentos bilionários de operadoras de telecomunicações, provedores de nuvem e empresas especializadas em colocation. Esse movimento ajuda a explicar por que tantas companhias, mesmo de outros estados, escolhem hospedar seus sistemas críticos na capital paulista ou em cidades do entorno. Escolha o Por Dentro de Minas como sua fonte de notícias no Google Novo recurso permite definir quais portais você quer ver. Receba conteúdo de quem você já confia. Concentração econômica e demanda corporativa O primeiro fator é simples: São Paulo é o maior centro econômico do Brasil. A região reúne sedes de bancos, seguradoras, indústrias, varejistas, startups e empresas de serviços que dependem intensamente de tecnologia. Quanto maior o volume de negócios, maior a demanda por processamento de dados, baixa latência e alta disponibilidade. Em vez de dispersar a infraestrutura por diferentes estados, muitos provedores preferem estar próximos de onde se concentra a maior parte dos clientes corporativos. Essa proximidade reduz tempo de resposta entre servidores e usuários finais, algo decisivo para operações financeiras, comércio eletrônico, plataformas de streaming e serviços em nuvem. Para uma corretora de valores, por exemplo, milissegundos podem fazer diferença em negociações de alta frequência. Já para um grande varejista digital, o atraso em consultas de estoque ou meios de pagamento pode significar carrinhos abandonados e perda de receita. Outro ponto é a presença de equipes técnicas e executivas na própria cidade. Quando as áreas de tecnologia e negócios estão baseadas em São Paulo, torna-se mais simples negociar contratos, acompanhar projetos de migração e realizar visitas de auditoria aos data centers. Essa dinâmica reforça um círculo em que a demanda local justifica novos investimentos em infraestrutura, que por sua vez atraem mais empresas. Infraestrutura de telecomunicações e rotas internacionais Além da força econômica, o estado conta com uma infraestrutura de telecomunicações mais robusta que a média nacional. A capital é um grande ponto de interconexão entre operadoras, provedores de internet e redes corporativas. Diversos backbones de fibra óptica se cruzam na região, permitindo redundância de rotas e maior capacidade de tráfego. Isso é fundamental para data centers que precisam garantir conectividade estável e de alta velocidade, mesmo diante de falhas em um dos caminhos. São Paulo também se beneficia da ligação com cabos submarinos que chegam ao litoral brasileiro. Embora os pontos de desembarque estejam em outros estados, como Rio de Janeiro e Ceará, grande parte do tráfego internacional de dados acaba passando por rotas que convergem para a Região Sudeste. Para provedores globais de computação em nuvem, isso facilita a integração entre suas estruturas no Brasil e data centers em outros continentes. A existência de pontos de troca de tráfego (IXPs) relevantes na capital contribui ainda mais. Nesses ambientes, diferentes redes se conectam diretamente, reduzindo o caminho entre provedores de conteúdo, operadoras e empresas. O resultado é menor latência e melhor desempenho para aplicações críticas. Não por acaso, muitos projetos de expansão de infraestrutura de internet consideram São Paulo como ponto de partida. Energia elétrica, riscos e desafios de infraestrutura Data centers consomem grandes volumes de energia e exigem fornecimento estável. A Região Metropolitana de São Paulo, apesar de enfrentar desafios típicos de grandes centros urbanos, oferece uma malha elétrica relativamente mais robusta que a de áreas menos desenvolvidas. Empreendimentos de grande porte costumam contar com múltiplos alimentadores, subestações dedicadas e sistemas de redundância com geradores e bancos de baterias. Ainda assim, a concentração de consumo traz desafios. A necessidade de garantir disponibilidade próxima de 100% leva os operadores a investir em projetos complexos de engenharia, com caminhos independentes de energia e refrigeração. A busca por certificações internacionais de confiabilidade, como Tier III e Tier IV, faz com que as instalações em São Paulo adotem padrões rigorosos de projeto e manutenção. Há também a questão do espaço físico. Terrenos em áreas centrais são caros e escassos, empurrando muitos projetos para regiões periféricas ou cidades vizinhas, como Barueri, Santana de Parnaíba, Osasco e Campinas. Nesses locais, é possível construir estruturas maiores, com salas técnicas modulares e áreas reservadas para futuras expansões. A proximidade com rodovias e aeroportos facilita a logística de equipamentos e o deslocamento de equipes técnicas. Clima de negócios, mão de obra e ecossistema tecnológico Outro diferencial está no ambiente de negócios. São Paulo concentra escritórios de fornecedores de hardware, software, serviços de nuvem e consultorias especializadas em infraestrutura. Esse ecossistema reduz o tempo de resposta para manutenção, atualizações e suporte, fatores essenciais em ambientes que não podem parar. A disponibilidade de mão de obra qualificada também pesa. Universidades, escolas técnicas e programas de formação em tecnologia abastecem o mercado com profissionais de redes, segurança da informação, engenharia elétrica e ciência de dados. Para operadores de grandes data centers, conseguir montar e manter equipes especializadas é tão importante quanto ter bons equipamentos. A presença de hubs de inovação, parques tecnológicos e comunidades de startups cria um ambiente em que novas soluções são testadas com rapidez. artigo.texto: As word spread about NAVWAR being considered as a potential site for a data center, the community immediately responded. A group rallied last week calling for those plans to be scrapped. Stream San Diego News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC 7. Others, like Francisco Martinez, are open to the idea of data centers coming to San Diego. “People don’t want the things too close to the neighborhood, but on the other hand, it’s the present and the future and we need all of that to develop the next step forward in many things,” Martinez said. District 9 Councilmember Sean Elo-Rivera, has been a vocal critic of the possibility of the U.S. Navy’s cybersecurity hub becoming what would be the largest data center in California. “The conversation that is happening in NAVWAR is a flashing red light, and we need to think about this as a threat and it can happen in San Diego and one that we need to get ahead of,” Councilmember Elo-Rivera said. Local He worries the project would impact San Diegans' energy costs and plans for affordable housing. Martinez thinks if the land is available, developers should be able to move forward. “If it’s a land that is open and has no use for anything else, they can put a bid. It’s fair,” Martinez said. The redevelopment plans extend beyond a data center. Ted Elridge, the project’s CEO, told NBC 7 that they are also exploring a medical center, a university and defense campus, along with a life sciences facility. Elridge also confirmed there have been early talks with energy providers but said there have been no negotiations or agreements. Since NAVWAR is federal property, Elo-Rivera is calling on congress to take the project off the table. This week, San Diego City Council is set to vote on a temporary moratorium on new data centers and the expansion of existing ones. “What we don’t want is a rush to submit permits and get projects going before rules are in place,” Elo-Rivera said. If approved, the initial moratorium would last 45 days, and the city council could vote to extend it once it expires. The moratorium would buy city leaders time while they work to establish regulations with clear guardrails for developers wishing to bring data centers to San Diego. Elo-Rivera said they have submitted a policy proposal and need to start drafting the law. He said they want to ensure the draft has no loopholes before it becomes permanent. Martinez hopes they’re able to reach an agreement that satisfies everyone while moving San Diego forward. “It’s a balance between new technology and new needs, and what people want around their neighborhoods,” Martinez said. Mayor Todd Gloria has signed an executive order to freeze any data center construction, marking what advocates described as a first step addressing concerns about the project. Poway was the first city in the county to ban data centers, earlier this month, citing air quality, noise and water-use concerns, as well as a lack of local long-term job creation because much of a data center is automated.

artigo.texto: SAMSUNG SDI has signed a 1 gigawatt-hour (GWh) energy storage system (ESS) supply agreement with Alpha Omega Power (AOP), a US-based utility-scale battery storage developer and independent power producer. The agreement was announced by SAMSUNG SDI, which will supply the systems through its Michigan-based subsidiary, SAMSUNG SDI America (SDIA). Including an initial contract signed late last year, the two agreements bring the total contracted supply to 1.5 GWh. Alpha Omega Power plans to deploy the battery storage systems in large-scale power projects designed to support grid reliability and meet growing electricity demand across the United States. Construction of the projects is scheduled to begin next year in the Western Electricity Coordinating Council (WECC) and Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) power markets. Under the latest agreement, SAMSUNG SDI will supply its Samsung Battery Box (SBB) 1.7, an integrated energy storage solution featuring nickel cobalt aluminum (NCA) battery technology. All battery cells and modules for the contracted systems will be manufactured at the StarPlus Energy (SPE) facility in Kokomo, Indiana. Deliveries are scheduled to be completed by the end of this year. The SBB 1.7 system uses high-nickel NCA chemistry to improve energy density and storage performance. According to the company, the system provides 17% higher energy density than its predecessor, SBB 1.5, while maintaining the same 20-foot footprint. This design allows the system to deliver greater storage capacity without increasing its physical dimensions. The solution also incorporates artificial intelligence-powered algorithms designed to detect anomalies at an early stage and predict battery life. SAMSUNG SDI has designed the system for 25 years of continuous use, highlighting its focus on durability and long-term performance in utility-scale energy storage applications. Safety is another key feature of the SBB 1.7. The system has obtained certifications and meets safety standards, including NFPA 855, which covers the installation of stationary energy storage systems, and UL 9540, a safety standard for energy storage systems. It also incorporates the company’s proprietary Enhanced Direct Injection (EDI) technology, which delivers fire-extinguishing agents directly into individual battery modules to strengthen fire protection. SAMSUNG SDI said it has secured several ESS supply agreements with US energy companies this year and is in discussions with other local customers. The company expects additional orders as demand for large-scale battery storage continues to develop. Industry analysts have attributed the company’s recent contract wins partly to its prismatic battery technology, known as PrismStack. SAMSUNG SDI stated that it is currently the only non-Chinese supplier of prismatic ESS batteries in North America, with its technology offering durability and fire-safety advantages compared with pouch-type batteries. Alpha Omega Power CEO Paul Choi said the agreement would support the company’s growth and strengthen the domestic supply chain for future energy infrastructure. Fabrice Hudry, President of the ESS division at SAMSUNG SDI America, said the partnership would help address grid reliability challenges and expand the company’s presence in the North American energy storage market. artigo.texto: Advocates raise concerns over Nevada data center expansion, cite water and energy use Opponents point to fossil fuels and water cooling, while industry coalition touts closed-loop systems and renewables. RENO, Nev. (KOLO) - Advocates against data center expansion in Nevada came together on Monday to express concerns with continued construction in the state. Debra Hendrickson, climate advocate for the NV Chapter of American Academy of Pediatrics, questioned the approach: “If you agree that AI, that this is a worthwhile goal, why are you pursuing it in ways that are so destructive to the state and to the world?” Josh Dini, of the Walker River Paiute Tribe, cited water concerns around the Monarch Data Center in Lyon County: “It’s on private land. And our concern is the water.” Hendrickson also tied the issue to climate change: “We’re one of the fastest warming places in the country. And pumping all our goals for reducing our greenhouse gases to address the threat of climate change, which manifested itself this summer in wildfires at the north end of town that caused tens of thousands of people to evacuate. And across the west, we’re seeing this massive increase in wildfires.” The use of fossil fuels to power data centers was among the top concerns raised. Bri Schmidt, Nevada Conservation League, advocated for using existing rooftop solar to support the grid instead of new methane gas plants: “Instead, we’re spending millions on new methane gas plants in the proposed plan... when we have solar, we get over 300 days of sunshine in Nevada. There’s other options... These are solar panels that are already installed in our homes that people already have that could be helping to meet demand.” Tray Abney of the Nevada Data Center Coalition addressed renewable energy, pointing to Greenlink Energy’s plan to connect north and south grids: “Greenlink is Energy’s plan to connect the power grids north and south.” he explained. “These lines will go through a lot of areas where you can build renewables. You can do solar. You can do wind. You can do geothermal.” On water use, Abney said newer centers use closed-loop technology: “The new ones that are being built in Nevada, water is not an issue. I toured one the other day... that’s a completely closed-loop system... water and glycol that cools off their systems... If you can picture your car, you don’t ever have to add water to your car unless there’s some kind of a problem... That stays in there for pretty much the life cycle of the building.” He acknowledged older centers built 10 or 20 years ago use different technology. Copyright 2026 KOLO. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: The San Diego City Council Tuesday unanimously backed a 45-day moratorium on the permitting, approval and development of data centers within city limits. The vote was prompted last week after a local developer floated the idea of building one near Old Town in the Naval Information Warfare Systems Command site, known as NAVWAR. Mayor Todd Gloria immediately issued and signed an executive order to temporarily pause data center development in San Diego until the city can develop regulations. Stream San Diego News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC 7. "San Diego is a city of innovation, and I want us to continue leading in the technologies and jobs of the future," Gloria said. "But we cannot allow a rapidly expanding industry to get ahead of the rules needed to protect our residents. Data centers can place significant demands on our water supply, electricity grid and limited land, with consequences for utility bills, housing opportunities and neighborhoods." Dozens of San Diegans spoke at Tuesday's council meeting, including speakers dressed as Elmo from "Sesame Street" and Lord Farquaad from "Shrek," nearly unanimously opposed to the development of data centers in the city. "San Diegans were clear, unambiguous and passionate about why data centers don't belong in San Diego," Council President Joe LaCava said. Tuesday's action puts the pause on the development of data centers for 45 days while city staff develop a framework on how to proceed with such facilities, if at all, in the future. The moratorium could be extended for nearly two years if the council chooses to. City staff would have a deadline of 180 days to bring forward preliminary recommendations to the mayor and council. It would be guided by a Data Center Stakeholder Working Group, including representatives with expertise in fields ranging from technology, utilities, water, land use, housing and community advocacy, according to a statement from the mayor's office. The plan is to officially amend the city's land development code next year. Councilman Sean Elo-Rivera tacked on amendments to the moratorium intended to guide the creation of a framework, including: - Council notification of any proposed centers within seven days - No costs from data centers imposed upon city residents - Project labor agreements needing to use union labor during construction, clean, renewable energy only - A minimum distance from schools, parks and child care centers, among others The idea of a 400-megawatt data center by the San Diego-based Manchester Financial Group was being considered for the NAVWAR location. It would include enough energy to power around 300,000 homes annually and would be the largest in the state of California. Local "The costs dramatically outweigh any benefits in the current environment," Councilman Raul Campillo said. Ted Eldredge, president and CEO of that company, said the data center was one of several ideas and that nothing had been finalized. "Manchester Financial Group's priority for the Old Town Campus redevelopment is delivering modern facilities for NAVWAR, and we remain committed to working with the Navy and other community stakeholders to do so throughout this process," he wrote in a statement. "Several other project elements are being considered such as retail, commercial, industrial and hospitality uses. The possibilities of a medical center, university campus, defense industry campus, data center and life science facility are also being explored." This 70-acre, Navy-owned site has been the subject of redevelopment speculation for several years, including as a mixed-use site that could include affordable house as well as military housing. Since NAVWAR is federally owned, a city moratorium is more of a symbolic measure for that specific site, but several council members said the fight would continue. "The people asking the hardest questions and fighting the hardest are the ones who will live with it," said Elo-Rivera, referring to dozens of young people speaking at Tuesday's meeting. "The future does not belong to billionaires. Donald Trump wants data centers on federal land so he can dodge communities like ours." Trump has ordered Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to find military property that could be used to house data centers. "San Diego needs more affordable housing, not more computer servers," Councilman Stephen Whitburn said. "Federal ownership does not mean San Diegans should be shut out of decisions which will impact us for generations to come." One of Elo-Rivera's amendments was to get Gloria's government affairs team to lobby lawmakers to take the issue up in Congress. "Working families and young people are being priced out of the city, struggling to afford rent, and wondering whether they can ever buy a home in San Diego," Council President Pro Tem Kent Lee said. "That includes countless service members who call San Diego home. NAVWAR should maximize its potential as a transit-oriented development with a vibrant residential neighborhood. The city should utilize the extent of our land use authority to regulate data centers and to protect the quality of life for all San Diegans."

artigo.texto: A empresa sul-coreana LS Eco Energy planeja investir aproximadamente 65 bilhões de won (US$ 49 milhões) por meio de sua subsidiária no Vietnã para construir uma linha de produção de supercapacitores destinados a centros de dados de inteligência artificial ( IA ). A empresa pretende iniciar a produção e o fornecimento em massa de supercapacitores a partir de abril de 2027, visando uma receita anual de 150 bilhões de won com este produto até 2030. De acordo com um comunicado de imprensa da LS Cable & System, datado de 26 de outubro, a subsidiária da LS Eco Energy no Vietnã, a LSCV, lançará um projeto de fabricação de supercapacitores para atender à crescente demanda de encomendas da LS Materials, uma subsidiária do mesmo grupo. A LS Eco Energy planeja fabricar produtos utilizando um modelo OEM, empregando tecnologia da LS Materials. Os supercapacitores são dispositivos de armazenamento de energia capazes de carga e descarga rápidas, ajudando a compensar as quedas instantâneas de energia em sistemas de geração de energia de células a combustível de hidrogênio. A demanda por esses dispositivos deve aumentar à medida que o investimento em data centers de IA e sistemas de fornecimento de energia relacionados se expande. Em 13 de outubro, a LS Materials assinou um contrato para fornecer supercapacitores no valor aproximado de US$ 51,5 milhões a um fabricante americano de células a combustível de hidrogênio. A empresa está negociando contratos adicionais este ano. A expansão da capacidade produtiva no Vietnã ajudará a LS Materials a diversificar sua base de fornecedores e a criar uma nova fonte de receita para a LS Eco Energy. Segundo a empresa, a LSCV pode utilizar o espaço ocioso da fábrica existente para construir uma nova linha de produção, reduzindo assim os custos iniciais de investimento. Os custos relativamente baixos de mão de obra e de serviços públicos no Vietnã também devem contribuir para a competitividade de preços. A LS Eco Energy afirmou que considerará investimentos adicionais dependendo do volume de pedidos. O projeto representa um passo rumo à expansão das operações da LS Eco Energy, do setor de fios e cabos elétricos para produtos de alto valor agregado que atendem à infraestrutura de data centers com inteligência artificial. Contudo, a meta de receita para 2030 ainda depende do progresso da implementação, da demanda de mercado e da capacidade de expansão dos pedidos.

artigo.texto: After a long discussion on data centers during the joint subcommittee on tax policy Monday morning, it appears tension remains between Senate Finance Chair Louise Lucas, D-Portsmouth, and House Appropriations Chair Luke Torian, D-Fairfax, after a hard-fought budget negotiation process earlier this year. “You know, I just want to reiterate my desire for us to have a third meeting,” Lucas said at the end of the meeting. “We’ve only had two meetings, and I’m not satisfied that we’ve been given enough information for us to make any substantial recommendations on tax policy.” Lucas and Senate Democrats were adamant that they wanted to end the sales tax incentive for data centers in Virginia earlier this year when legislators were negotiating Virginia’s new two-year budget. The House and Gov. Abigail Spanberger did not want to renege on the commonwealth’s commitment to the tax incentive, which is set to run until 2035. Ultimately, the incentive stayed, but a new tax on energy consumption was included, which is expected to generate $600 million annually. The negotiations were tense at times in public, with Lucas publicly calling out Spanberger and House Speaker Don Scott, D-Portsmouth, for supporting keeping the incentive. But since then, there has been no public animosity between the two chambers as Lucas deals with her own legal troubles and faces multiple federal indictments. However, on Monday, the tension resurfaced in Lucas’ closing comments at the meeting. She brought up an alleged poll Torian is conducting to gauge House members’ interest in holding another subcommittee meeting to discuss taxes on data centers. “I don’t know if you’ve gotten that poll done yet, but I know the members of the Senate… We’d like to see a third meeting, and we’d like to see it somewhere in the community, especially the communities that are impacted by data centers,” she said. “So, if the House colleagues do not see the importance of this work, I feel compelled to give the people what they want and work on this issue in our committee, including having a meeting on data centers.” Torian then responded to Lucas, who was seated directly to his right, before delivering his closing statement for the meeting. “Let me share with you that there will be a meeting, perhaps maybe a couple of meetings, and I’m not in a position to articulate to the public how that will proceed because I believe you and I had a conversation a couple days ago, and we’re supposed to be meeting after this meeting, so we can talk,” Torian said. “But I’d still like to have those meetings fast,” Lucas responded. Torian began to say something, but Lucas interrupted and said, “We’ll talk.” “Okay,” Torian responded. Torian and Lucas did not respond to a question asking for clarification from Virginia Scope after the meeting.

artigo.texto: Russian ministry recommends underground data centers following Ukrainian drone strikes Russia's Digital Development Ministry has proposed building data centers underground, camouflaged from the air, and fitted with drone defenses, Russian state-controlled media Kommersant said on Oct. 25, following several Ukrainian drone attacks on data centers. Guidelines for existing, planned, and under-construction facilities outline the protection standards for three tiers of data centers, including whether sites are placed above ground or underground, according to Kommersant. The top tier includes strategic sites whose loss could disrupt key state functions for an hour or more; the second tier includes sites supporting regionally or economically important systems, where outages could last four hours or more; and the final tier covers corporate data centers whose damage would not have wider consequences for the state, Kommersant said. Existing data centers should be protected by reducing their visibility from the air and by deploying layered defenses, including reinforced structures, electronic warfare measures, and drone defense systems. The announcement came after Ukrainian drones struck three Yandex data centers, a Sberbank facility under construction, and a data center belonging to social media giant VK between Oct. 8 and Oct. 18. Russia's centralized digital infrastructure leaves Moscow facing two challenges: inflicting comparable damage on Ukraine and protecting its own data centers from further strikes. Serhiy Petrenko, former head of Yandex Ukraine, estimated that around 80% of Russia's data centers are concentrated in Moscow and the surrounding region — within reach of Ukrainian long-range drones. The consequences of Ukraine's strikes on Russian data centers could extend far beyond disrupted banking and online services, potentially setting back the country's AI development and affecting military technology. On Oct. 16, Kemerovo Oblast governor Ilya Seredyuk proposed housing data centers inside depleted open-pit mines and quarries, given their natural protection from aerial bombardment.

artigo.texto: A SpaceX (NASDAQ: SPACE) celebrou um compromisso vinculante de financiamento de até US$ 40 bilhões com uma entidade estruturada e gerida pela Apollo Global Management. A operação destina-se à aquisição e arrendamento comercial (sale-leaseback de infraestrutura) de unidades de processamento gráfico (GPUs) e equipamentos avançados para centros de processamento de dados (data centers), segundo documento protocolado nesta segunda-feira (26) junto à Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). A assinatura do compromisso ocorreu no sábado, 24 de outubro, e prevê a compra direta dos chips e equipamentos de IA pela Apollo, que os alugará de volta à SpaceX mediante pagamentos trimestrais ao longo de aproximadamente cinco anos. Estrutura Operacional e Cronograma Financeiro - Entrega em Lotes: A infraestrutura de chips será entregue em fases, com os contratos individuais de arrendamento iniciando-se no primeiro semestre de 2027. Cada contrato individual terá maturidade de 5 anos a 5 anos e 3 meses. - Dinâmica de Pagamentos: As parcelas trimestrais serão efetuadas antecipadamente, compostas pela amortização do principal (equivalente a $1/20$ do custo financiado por lote) somada a juros com taxa anual fixa cobrada sobre o saldo devedor restante (cuja taxa de juros definitiva será fixada no fechamento de cada contrato). - Volume do Principal: O total amortizado de principal alcançará cerca de US$ 40 bilhões, excluindo juros e despesas acessórias. A SpaceX prevê concluir a formalização final dos termos até o encerramento de 2026. Desempenho Financeiro do 3T26 e Expansão em IA A operação de financiamento de infraestrutura vem no encalço de um balanço trimestral robusto, o segundo apresentado pela empresa espacial desde a sua oferta pública inicial (IPO) no início de 2026: - Lucro Líquido: Atingiu US$ 4,4 bilhões no 3T26. O lucro por ação (LPA) ajustado ficou em US$ 0,35, superando a estimativa de consenso do mercado (US$ 0,13 apurado pela FactSet). - Receita Líquida: A receita total disparou 161% no comparativo anual, alcançando US$ 14,6 bilhões (frente a consensos de US$ 12,87 bilhões). - Divisão por Segmentos: - Inteligência Artificial (IA): Gerou US$ 7,56 bilhões no trimestre. - Conectividade (Starlink): Faturou US$ 5,2 bilhões, impulsionada pela marca de 13,6 milhões de assinantes ativos. - Lançamentos e Sistemas Espaciais: Somou US$ 1,77 bilhão. Os investimentos em capital (capex) escalaram para US$ 19,6 bilhões no trimestre (ante US$ 6,9 bilhões no 3T25), refletindo a corrida acelerada por capacidade computacional e constelações de satélites de última geração.

artigo.texto: Charlotte City Council votes unanimously to extend data center moratorium CHARLOTTE, N.C. – Charlotte City Council voted unanimously on Monday to extend its moratorium on new data centers until October 18, 2027. The decision pauses new facility approvals to give city planners time to study the environmental impacts, high power consumption, and immense water demands these facilities require. Following that vote, District Four councilmember Renee Johnson issued a stark warning to council members, noting that 5.5 million square feet of “hyperscale” data developments are already actively under construction near residential backyards. Johnson stressed that because these projects were previously approved, they will completely bypass the city’s upcoming safety and zoning restrictions unless aggressive legal options are pursued. She says, “So I need to sound the alarm. We have two hyperscale developments. It’s actually 5.5 million square footage of data centers that are under, currently under construction that will not be subject to these provisions.” The city’s specialized task force will continue reviewing distance and noise impacts over the next 11 months, to determine how existing facilities can be forced to comply with local noise ordinances.

artigo.texto: Here's why data center campaign contributions to Nevada politics are rising Political contributions from companies with a data center footprint in Nevada are on the rise ahead of a legislative session where the industry is likely to face unprecedented scrutiny, a Nevada Independent analysis found. In May, Jessica Roy, the wife of Switch founder Rob Roy, gave $1 million to a PAC supporting Gov. Joe Lombardo (R). From July through September, companies with an existing or planned data center donated more than $100,000 to candidates and groups, the highest quarterly total in eight years (excluding the $1 million donation from Roy). More than 65 percent of this money went to Democrats. It's a notable development in donations from the industry, which has given about $17 million in donations to candidates and groups across the past two decades. More than 80 percent of this total came through Switch's efforts to pass an energy ballot initiative during the 2016 and 2018 election cycles. There was also a spike in the mid-2010s as Switch, a company at the center of Nevada's data center industry, eyed a lucrative tax break package. The data suggests that although these companies have shown a willingness to spend in Nevada politics, its presence remains nascent. With the issues around data centers showing no sign of going away, that appears to be changing. Ken Miller, a UNLV political science professor, said that data centers haven't had as much of a reason to consistently donate to Nevada officials and PACs. "A lot of times some industries need to keep up a high level of maintenance of donation because they need to ensure that regulations on them don't change or they don't move against the competing industry," he said. "Those are the types of reasons why you maintain very high levels of political spending and that that hasn't been the case for data centers until now." With its proximity to Silicon Valley and business-friendly tax policies, Nevada has emerged as a hotbed for data centers. So far, there are more than 80 data centers operating, under construction or planned in the Silver State, according to a tracker from More Than Just Parks, a group focused on protecting public lands. The Indy's analysis included any company with a planned or built data center in Nevada, as well as people tied to those companies. At the same time, the nature of Nevada's data center industry makes it difficult to directly link political donations to companies' data center activities. Outside of Switch, many of the most prominent political donors with a data center footprint are large tech companies. Many of these donations could relate to the company's operations outside of data centers. "Google, Microsoft, Verizon, these are all groups that have a variety of interests across different sorts of regulatory environments," Miller said. "They could really be anything." Switch's donations More than 90 percent of the political donations come from Switch, which has massive data center campuses in Las Vegas and the Tahoe-Reno Industrial Center. The company's donations took off in the 2010s as it successfully sought to bring a data center tax break package to Nevada and supported a failed ballot initiative to end the state's energy monopoly. Switch has long supported members of both parties, with a slight lean for Democrats, who have long controlled the Legislature, except for the notable 2015 session when Republicans controlled both chambers and when the data center tax break bill passed. Up until this year, the company had donated about $840,000 to Democratic candidates and groups, compared with about $710,000 to Republicans, The Indy's analysis found. But the tides turned this year with Jessica Roy's $1 million donation to the pro-Lombardo PAC. Lombardo had previously not received any money from Switch as governor or gubernatorial candidate. He did receive $10,000 in 2018 from Stella Roy, Rob Roy's then-wife, while serving as Clark County Sheriff, and the company also gave Lombardo $1,000 in 2016. By contrast, the company gave about $130,000 to former Gov. Steve Sisolak's (D) gubernatorial campaigns and associated groups. Attorney General Aaron Ford (D), the Democratic nominee for governor, has pounced on the $1 million donation to Lombardo's PAC. Ford, who co-sponsored the data center tax break bill, has received about $35,000 from Switch over the years, but the most recent contribution was in 2021. Data centers have emerged as a prominent issue in the governor's race. Ford has pledged pausing the tax break program and banning water-intensive cooling technology statewide. Meanwhile, Lombardo has supported data centers — calling it the state's new "gold rush" — but has also curtailed the data center tax break program, requiring companies to cover their own power costs and ending relief on a tax that supports local schools. In a statement, Prerna Jagadeesh, a spokesperson for Ford's campaign, said that Ford "has a plan to rein in data centers" and accused Lombardo of catering "to the data center interests propping up his campaign." Switch did not respond to a request for comment about its spending habits. However, Missy Young, a senior fellow at the company, said during an IndyFest panel last week that "economic considerations" drive the company's political spending. As an example, she thinks Ford's pledge to end the state's "right to work" law could "potentially negatively affect economic development and growth." The money Switch gives to Nevada candidates pales in comparison to what it spent on the energy ballot initiative in 2016 and 2018. Following years of tensions with NV Energy, Switch left the energy utility and eventually threw its support behind a ballot question that would have required the state to adopt a competitive electric market. Altogether, the company poured more than $12.6 million to support the ballot question, topped off with a $10 million infusion of cash into a group behind the ballot question in 2018

artigo.texto: Rushin submits alternative data center plan as Pulaski County considers permitting rules LITTLE ROCK, Ark. (KATV) — Discussions around data center regulation remain a major talking point in the race for Pulaski County judge. Republican nominee Michael Rushin laid out his framework for data centers in the county as a proposed ordinance around data centers is on tomorrow night's Pulaski County quorum court agenda. The county's JPs will have a chance to override a veto that would regulate data centers in Pulaski County, and Rushin weighed in on the subject Monday afternoon in Little Rock. "I want to let everyone know that it is our firm belief that no local government is sophisticated enough to know what is right, what the right measure or balance is in terms of regulation or conversation might be at this point," Rushin stated in front of media on Monday. Rushin states that he has submitted his own plan for addressing data centers to the quorum court, one that he says will help avoid costly lawsuits. "Protecting the interests of Pulaski County residents, rate and taxpayers, without going to court should not be difficult, and with the plan I have submitted to the quorum court, it will not be." In September, Pulaski County judge Barry Hyde vetoed an ordinance that would establish new permitting processes for data centers in the county, including the AVAIO data center that is set to be built near Wrightsville. Rushin says it was the right move at the right time. "I thanked him for his veto, I thought it was a very wise decision, because he is trying to keep us out of a court of law, he understands what's at stake. My opponent only knows litigation, that's what he's done for his career." The ordinance was backed by Wendell Griffen, the Democratic nominee for Pulaski County judge. He defeated Barry Hyde in the March 3rd primaries and now faces Rushin in November's general election. Channel 7 News spoke to Griffen earlier this month about his stance on data center regulation, and he addressed Hyde's veto and what could happen after. "It only takes 9 JPs to override the veto--when that happens, that law will be effective immediately." Rushin believes that if this ordinance is overridden by the quorum court, it could clash with his framework if he were to be elected. "It would create a pretty big headache," says Rushin. "I still think that if it does become into law, it just creates too much of an opportunity for us to end up in litigation that would be for years and years and years." Rushin believes that any money or resources spent towards hypothetical litigation would be better spent on fixing county roads and infrastructure. Tuesday night's quorum court meeting will decide whether or not the county's Justices of Peace will override Hyde's veto on the ordinance. It will be the final determination on whether the ordinance that regulates data centers will pass.

artigo.texto: Polaris awards battery storage contract, advances $60 million Punta Lima project By THE STAR STAFF Canadian renewable energy company Polaris Renewable Energy Inc. has recently awarded a key supply contract to Trina Energy Storage Solutions for its planned battery energy storage project at Punta Lima in Naguabo, marking a major step forward in the island’s ongoing efforts to strengthen grid reliability through utility-scale energy storage. The company announced last week that it has executed an agreement with Trina Storage to provide battery energy storage systems (BESS) for the Punta Lima project, which is being developed under Puerto Rico’s Accelerated Storage Addition Program (ASAP by its acronym in Spanish). The program was created to accelerate deployment of large-scale battery systems alongside existing generation facilities to improve grid resilience and reliability. The contract award allows the project to move from the planning and contractual phase into equipment procurement and implementation, Polaris said. The Punta Lima facility will consist of a 35.7-megawatt (MW) battery storage system with eight hours of duration. Under the terms of its agreement with the Puerto Rico Electric Power Authority (PREPA), the system will provide 71.4 MW of storage capability through two four-hour energy delivery blocks. Polaris estimates total project costs will range between $55 million and $60 million, including the battery system, medium-voltage transformer, fees and balance-of-plant infrastructure. The company said it plans to fund the investment with cash on hand. Once operational, the project is expected to contribute some $12.5 million in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization, or EBITDA, during its first year of operation. The development is one of several storage projects being advanced under ASAP, which seeks to add battery capacity to Puerto Rico’s power system following years of reliability challenges, storm-related disruptions and generation shortfalls. Polaris’ U.S. subsidiary, Polaris Power US Inc., secured its place in the program earlier this year when it executed a battery energy storage standard offer agreement with PREPA on June 5. Under that agreement, the company will receive monthly fixed and performance-based payments for providing energy storage services, including capacity and grid support. Deliveries of battery containers from Trina Storage are scheduled for March and April 2027, with commercial operations currently expected to begin during the third quarter of 2027. The agreement has a 20-year term beginning on the project’s commercial operation date. “The execution of the supply contract with Trina Storage is a significant milestone in advancing our investment in Punta Lima, moving the project from its contractual framework into equipment procurement and implementation,” Polaris CEO Marc Murnaghan said in a statement. “This investment reflects our confidence in Puerto Rico’s long-term energy transition and our commitment to delivering critical storage capacity that will enhance grid reliability and resilience.” Trina Storage, a global utility-scale energy storage provider, has some 30 gigawatt-hours of battery storage projects either commissioned or under execution worldwide, including over six gigawatt-hours in Latin America and the Caribbean, according to the company. Toronto-based Polaris Renewable Energy operates a portfolio of renewable energy assets across Latin America and the Caribbean, including geothermal, hydroelectric, solar and wind facilities. The Punta Lima project represents a growing trend toward deploying long-duration battery storage resources in Puerto Rico, where regulators and policymakers have increasingly emphasized energy storage as a critical component of the island’s transition to a more resilient and renewable electric grid.

artigo.texto: SALEM TWP. — Supervisors paved the way for a potential $43 million community benefit agreement that includes a $12 million “micro-hospital” with their votes Tuesday to nearly triple the size of the township’s data center overlay district. Supervisor John Fogg and Chairman Rick Talanca voted to approve two ordinances to amend the township zoning map at a regular meeting that immediately followed a public hearing on the expansion issue. Supervisor Steven Fraind abstained from the vote because the house in which his mother resides and transferred into his name several years ago is part of a $1.2 billion land sale necessary for the establishment of 4,466-acre data center campus in the township. Jack Sordoni, principal of the 4-3 Consulting Group that negotiated that land deal, touted the hospital as one of the benefits the community would see with the establishment of a third data center campus in the township during a slide presentation that was part of his testimony at the public hearing. The supervisors also approved further expanding the data center district by 185 additional acres to accommodate a fourth data center campus as requested by Moores 109 LLC. Sordoni said 4-3 is proposing a “stabilize-and-transfer” micro-hospital with a full emergency department open 24 hours a day, seven days a week, on 42 acres along U.S. Route 11 (Salem Twp. Boulevard) at the intersection with Stone Church Road. The facility would be a welcome addition to the community, given that Berwick Hospital Center closed in 2022. The next-closest hospital to the township is Geisinger Bloomsburg Hospital, which Google Maps puts at a 22- to 40-minute drive, depending on where in the township the drive begins. Thirteen members of the public spoke about the Proposed data center district expansions, with eight supporting them and five opposed. The data center developers will have to come before the board of supervisors for approvals of land development plans and they will need state approvals, as well. Check back for an updated story with more details from the hearings and supervisors meeting.
