artigo.texto: CATL's Buyback Arithmetic Meets the Margin Test Published on 10/25/2026 at 15:01 | Editorial boerse-global.de CATL shares jumped 7.8% on Friday, snapping a seven-session losing streak as Chinese equities, automakers and battery names rallied together. Reuters linked the broader advance to a burst of trading in exchange-traded funds favoured by state-linked investors, while media reports tied CATL's move to share buybacks. No single catalyst has been confirmed for the gain. The scale of the rebound matters less than what comes next. The real question for investors is whether CATL can convert its formidable revenue growth back into convincing profit — a buyback supports that case but cannot substitute for operational proof. A Buyback With a Cancellation Clause The company's repurchase programme carries an unusual detail: the bought-back shares are to be cancelled, with registered capital reduced accordingly. That resolution covers a announced plan, not a completed buyback. Separately, a mandatory disclosure documents a specific purchase on 19 October, when CATL bought back A-shares for RMB 49,993,616.4. That transaction has already been executed and should not be conflated with the planned total volume. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying CATL? CATL also put real money behind its stock during the recent slump. On Wednesday it repurchased 3.4886 million A-shares for close to RMB 800 million, according to a filing published Thursday. In Hong Kong, the stock recovered alongside the wider market and a raft of auto names, ending seven consecutive days of losses. Revenue Surges, Profit Lags Tuesday's quarterly report laid bare the tension at the heart of the investment case. Third-quarter 2026 revenue reached RMB 165.221 billion, up 58.6% year on year. Net profit attributable to shareholders came in at RMB 21.246 billion, a gain of 14.54%. Reuters reported that analysts had expected profit growth of 41.2%. The disappointment was therefore not a decline in earnings but a sharply missed pace of expansion — and it was this shortfall, according to Reuters, that triggered the severe sell-off after the numbers. The cash picture adds another cautionary note. Operating cash flow for the first nine months of 2026 fell 23.60% compared with the prior year, meaning the inflow from day-to-day business shrank even as quarterly profit rose. JPMorgan downgraded CATL to "Neutral" on Wednesday, with media reports citing concerns about fading profitability in China's electric-vehicle industry. The broker's price target was cut to HK$500 from HK$725, reflecting a faster-than-expected deterioration in battery-sector margins. Swap Orders Offer a Counterweight Against that backdrop, CATL's battery-swapping business provides the most tangible offset. The company said Tuesday it had secured orders for swap products covering 13,000 vehicles, naming logistics clients SF Holding and China Postal Express & Logistics among the buyers. Such orders give the expansion a firmer footing than product announcements alone. CATL also plans to build out its battery-swap network for heavy trucks. Should those orders translate into profitable business and the network pull in further demand, they could counterbalance competitive pressure. The standardized swap blocks unveiled Tuesday were presented with fewer components and lower costs. According to the company, component count drops 52% versus existing products, while costs are set to come in 15% lower. Those figures describe product-level advantages; they do not yet prove a corresponding improvement in group profit. In the bull case, however, such cost savings would make additional volume more economically attractive — a more meaningful driver for valuation than the number of new product variants. CATL at a turning point? This analysis reveals what investors need to know now. Competition Could Cap the Upside The bear case is equally concrete. Reuters identified fierce competition in the battery market and cooling Chinese car sales as the backdrop to the weaker profit growth. Either could prevent large revenue gains from producing a comparable lift in earnings. Buybacks do nothing to solve that operational problem. They change neither the competitive landscape nor the earnings quality of new orders, and a larger swap network does not automatically guarantee attractive margins. If CATL is forced to pass cost advantages on to customers, volumes could rise without profit growth accelerating enough to satisfy the market. Until CATL can back its revenue growth with firm orders and lower product costs, an operational basis for recovery remains intact. It would become far more convincing if those gains showed up in profit. Should the weaker earnings momentum instead become entrenched, Friday's advance would look like little more than a technical bounce after the losses. The next tangible test is execution: turning the secured swap-product orders into revenue and expanding the truck-swap network as planned. Progress there could shore up the growth story; a re-rating would require it to be economically convincing as well. Orders, cost cuts and buybacks demonstrate what the company can do — but the missed profit expectations show that growth alone is not enough. Profitability must supply the next piece of evidence. artigo.texto: Finance first, batteries twice: what India's DISCOMs will discuss at DUM 2026 India Smart Grid Forum's 10th Distribution Utility Meet runs October 27-28, 2026 in Jaipur, with senior officials from 40+ power distribution companies expected. The first session covers distributor finances and capital market readiness. Two of the seven sessions name battery storage. This story was produced through MarketScale. See how Energy teams put it to work with Customer Stories & Case Studies. Key takeaways Two of DUM 2026's seven sessions name battery storage, and finance and capital-market readiness is listed first: India's distributors are putting the hardware and the money on the same two-day program. ISGF’s event page records 688 participants and 45-plus DISCOMs at the 2025 Mumbai edition, a baseline suppliers can use when judging whether DUM reaches DISCOM decision-makers. Free workspace Turn your Energy expertise into content. Record interviews, organize footage, and write with AI on a free trial of the MarketScale platform for qualifying companies. No demo required, no credit card. The first session at India's 10th Distribution Utility Meet is about money: DISCOM financial transformation and capital market readiness. Two of the seven sessions on the program name battery storage outright. Senior officials from 40+ DISCOMs across India are expected at the two-day event in Jaipur, which opens on October 27. The 10th Distribution Utility Meet will take place on 27-28 October 2026 in Jaipur, Rajasthan, with India Smart Grid Forum (ISGF) as organizer. According to ISGF, the host utilities are all three of Rajasthan's distribution companies, or DISCOMs: Jaipur Vidyut Vitran Nigam (JVVNL), Jodhpur Vidyut Vitran Nigam (JdVVNL) and Ajmer Vidyut Vitran Nigam (AVVNL). The event is supported by the Ministry of Power, NITI Aayog, Rajasthan's energy department, the Central Electricity Authority (CEA) and the All India DISCOMs Association (AIDA). Taken together, the agenda suggests what is on distributors' desks: paying for upgrades, storage on local grids and large new loads. That could make it useful to anyone who sells into Indian distribution networks or plans for them. The meet's theme, according to trade outlet Exhibition Showcase, is "Collaborative Growth." Seven sessions, two on batteries Over two days, the meet will hold seven thematic sessions: - DISCOMs financial transformation and capital market readiness - Scaling digital intelligence and advanced smart meter data analytics - How renewables can help handle new and emerging loads while keeping supply reliable and power quality high - CEA standards for solar PV and BESS, along with flexibility solutions for distribution networks - Climate resilience and securing the physical assets of DISCOMs - India Energy Stack, data exchange framework, cyber security and data privacy for digital grids - BESS applications in power distribution: select case studies Storage turns up twice. It sits beside distribution-network flexibility and the CEA's standards for solar PV and battery energy storage systems (BESS), then gets a session built entirely on case studies. Renewables get a third slot, framed around new and emerging loads and keeping supply reliable and power quality steady. Session 2 is Scaling Digital Intelligence and Advanced Smart Meter Data Analytics, which suggests a focus on using meter data. Finance leads the running order, ahead of every technology topic on the list. Exhibition Showcase likewise expects the conference to cover utility performance and the financial sustainability of DISCOMs alongside grid modernisation and digitalisation. For a supplier, that ordering suggests the conversation about any upgrade may start with how it gets paid for. In the announcement, ISGF president Reji Kumar Pillai tied these themes together. He said utilities are moving "from turnaround to transformation" as their networks take on smart meters, distributed renewables and storage, along with large new loads like AI data centres and EVs. That change, he said, gives peer learning among DISCOM leaders more value. Read beside a first session on capital market readiness, Pillai's "transformation" framing suggests finance is still part of the job, not a chapter that closed with the turnaround. The technology on his list, from smart meters to storage, maps directly onto sessions 2, 4 and 7. For suppliers selling solar PV equipment, battery systems or meter-data software into Indian distribution networks, sessions 2, 4, 6 and 7 could be the most relevant. Session 2 is the meter-data slot. Session 4 covers the CEA standards. Session 6 covers the India Energy Stack (IES), the data exchange framework, cyber security and data privacy for digital grids, topics that could shape how DISCOMs choose digital grid products. India Smart Grid Forum describes itself as a think-tank on energy transition, electric mobility and grid modernization. It was set up in 2011 as a public-private partnership initiative of the Government of India and is registered as a not-for-profit society in New Delhi. It has run DUM since 2017 around the objective of "Experience Sharing and Learning from Each Other." Who fills the hall in Jaipur ISGF expects more than 500 participants this year, including senior officials from 40+ DISCOMs and more than 100 speakers from utilities, regulators, policy bodies, research groups and technology providers. The 9th edition, which took place in Mumbai on 04-05 November 2025, is the obvious baseline. ISGF's event page records it this way. artigo.texto: African governments are developing policies to manage waste from solar panels, batteries and other clean tech equipment as installations surge, with officials warning the energy transition could create a new environmental problem unless it is accompanied by investment in recycling and reuse. Many African households and businesses are increasingly turning away from unreliable grid power or deciding not to wait for access, and are installing more solar panels and battery storage. Data from energy think-tank Ember, published in August, projects that the continent will install a record 17 gigawatts (GW) of solar capacity in 2026 - equal to around 100,000 solar panels every day. This would mark the third consecutive year of record growth, following increases of 51% in 2025 and 25% in 2024. While generally a welcome sign of progress towards a cleaner energy mix, this trend could also create a headache for African officials. Anselm Marungu, Namibia’s deputy minister of environment, forestry and tourism, believes rules should be put in place to ensure that valuable materials can be recovered from discarded solar panels, batteries and inverters at the end of their useful life. artigo.texto: A data center is often discussed as a digital asset. Itâs also a physical one: a major site that depends on power, electrical equipment, and a connection to the grid. That matters as UK Chancellor John Healey prepares to deliver his first budget on Oct. 28, with the government planning to give mayors a larger share of business rates from April 2027. The case for devolution is clear. Places that attract investment should share in its benefits. But the way that investment is taxed will shape where projects go, what infrastructure gets built, and whether promised capacity can be delivered. Business rates are a recurring property tax, calculated by applying a multiplier to a propertyâs rateable value. For data centers, valuation can include plant and machinery as well as the building. Most pay the higher multiplier for the most valuable properties. This yearâs revaluation increased rateable values at prime sites in London and Slough by between a quarter and a half. If local mayors retain more of the resulting revenue, a data center can become a substantial continuing addition to a regionâs tax base. That creates a direct incentive to attract projects and potentially offer rate relief to win them. Devolving business rates therefore can become a form of tax competition: regions forgoing revenue today in the hope of collecting more tomorrow. The danger is that while tax policy can influence a developerâs choice of location, it canât create the power needed to operate the site. A tax break can bring a project to the table but not deliver a grid connection. The US offers a stark warning. States spent a decade using sales-tax exemptions to attract data centers and, this year, lawmakers in two dozen states tried to repeal or reduce them after costs exceeded forecasts. In Virginia, the cost reached about 16 times the original estimate. Tax relief can lower a developerâs bill, but if a site canât get power, the public bears the cost without securing the investment or capacity the incentive was meant to support. The UK budget should set a clear test for business-rate relief. Whether offered by local councils or mayors, it should be conditional on grid readiness â a firm connection date or capacity reserved in an AI growth zone. Relief should be linked to delivery milestones, with a review or clawback if a project fails to proceed on time. The tax benefit should follow progress on the ground, not simply a developerâs choice of location. A national framework would help avoid regions competing through increasingly generous packages. It should define connection readiness and delivery milestones, and require government to publish the expected and actual cost of relief. Business-rate discounts and capital allowances need to be assessed separately. A rate discount reduces local receipts while it applies; a capital allowance changes when a company can deduct qualifying investment from taxable profits. The budget should use capital allowances to support the grid infrastructure developers are starting to fund themselves. In AI growth zones, developers may be able to build their own substations and high-voltage lines where that gets them connected sooner. These assets can add capacity the network would otherwise need to fund and help ease constraints beyond a single data center site. Qualifying special-rate expenditure generally can now receive a 50% first-year allowance, with the remaining balance written down at 6% on a declining balance basis. A qualifying main-rate plant can receive a 100% first-year allowance. Electrical equipment around data centers may fall into either category, depending on its classification and use. The chancellor should consider extending a 100% first-year allowance to qualifying private substations and connection assets. Bringing tax relief forward would improve project cash flow and reduce the tax penalty on developers who invest in infrastructure that adds network capacity. It wouldnât be a cash grant; its fiscal cost would depend on the qualifying investment and the timing of deductions. Eligibility should depend on an assetâs contribution to connection, not simply its location inside a data center site. Power equipment is another constraint. Switchgear, transformers, and protection equipment can take months or years to arrive because manufacturers are fully booked. A targeted allowance or credit for investment in UK production capacity could support data centers, housing, transport, and other electrification projects. It should reward additional capacity, with clear eligibility and a measurable fiscal cost. These proposals should be judged on whether they change the location, timing, or scale of investment enough to justify the revenue forgone. Relief that only changes the timing of a project that was already proceeding may have little additional effect. Fiscal discipline and infrastructure delivery should be considered together. A data centerâs value is measured in megawatts. Tax policy should follow the power, not the location. Get the balance wrong, and regions may compete for projects the grid canât serve. Get it right, and tax relief can steer investment to available power, encourage developers to add capacity and help build the supply chain that Britainâs wider electrification depends on. artigo.texto: Principais Conclusões - Elon Musk disse no sábado que espera ver muito poder de computação ocioso em data centers parcialmente concluídos. - Esse risco recai sobre as neoclouds como CoreWeave e Nebius, que compraram GPUs antes dos prédios para operá-las, e o CEO da NVIDIA diz que a escassez de capital já está desacelerando suas construções. - A CoreWeave pagou $1,2 bilhão de juros líquidos em 2025 contra uma perda operacional de $46 milhões, portanto não tem lucro para absorver um local paralisado. - O relatório da CoreWeave de 12 de novembro mostrará se sua potência ativa está alcançando os 4,2 gigawatts que contratou. CoreWeave (CRWV) perdeu mais de um terço de seu valor em outubro, conforme seus títulos caíram devido a temores sobre a dívida. Agora, Elon Musk deu aos acionistas mais um motivo para se preocupar. O cofundador da Hyperbolic, Yuchen Jin, publicou no X o que ouviu de um "amigo de neolab" que garantiu capacidade de GPU antecipadamente: "Os preços de aluguel de H100/B200/B300 desde então subiram 2–3x. Podemos simplesmente revender o poder de computação e imprimir dinheiro." A resposta de Musk no sábado: "Acho que vamos ver muito poder de computação ocioso em data centers parcialmente concluídos." Isso é um problema para quem comprou os chips antes do prédio estar pronto. Uma GPU em um local pela metade não gera receita, enquanto a dívida que a pagou continua custando juros. Esse risco está com as neoclouds como CoreWeave e Nebius (NBIS), que compraram capacidade antes dos prédios para operá-la. O TIKR acompanha 42 analistas da CoreWeave. Quantos dizem "Comprar"? Veja a distribuição completa das recomendações de Compra, Manter e Venda para a CoreWeave, junto com as estimativas de receita e lucro de Wall Street, tudo em um só lugar. Mais de 500.000 investidores usam o TIKR para pesquisar ações como esta. Veja as Recomendações dos Analistas para a CoreWeave Cada peça precisa aparecer Musk explicou o porquê em outra resposta no mesmo dia. Ele estava respondendo a uma publicação que listava o que limita a energia para data centers: terreno, licenças, acesso à rede, transformadores e quadros de distribuição, até mesmo grandes tornos para usinar eixos. "Se faltar qualquer coisa, por mais trivial que pareça, o poder de computação não funciona", escreveu ele. Alguns desses chips já estão esperando. No episódio de sexta-feira do podcast Moonshots de Peter Diamandis, o fundador da Link Ventures, Dave Blundin, disse que "há 15 gigawatts de chips ociosos porque não conseguem encontrar data centers que tenham resfriamento líquido." (Ele ainda acha que os chips serão o maior gargalo assim que a próxima onda de construção for concluída.) A conta de juros da CoreWeave não espera A CoreWeave tomou muito empréstimo para construir sua frota de GPUs da NVIDIA (NVDA). Sua dívida total no TIKR, que inclui obrigações de arrendamento, foi de $2 bilhões no final de 2023 para $29,8 bilhões no final de 2025… …e atingiu $51,6 bilhões até 30 de junho de 2026, incluindo $16,5 bilhões em arrendamentos. O negócio não gera receita suficiente para cobrir os juros dessa dívida. Em 2025, a CoreWeave pagou $1,2 bilhão de juros líquidos contra uma perda operacional de $46 milhões. A lacuna cresceu desde então. Os juros foram de $640 milhões apenas no segundo trimestre de 2026, contra uma perda operacional de $49 milhões, e a administração prevê de $860 milhões a $940 milhões para o terceiro trimestre. Locais inacabados já estão custando dinheiro. A CoreWeave capitalizou $176 milhões em juros sobre capacidade ainda em construção no primeiro semestre de 2026. E atrasos já a prejudicaram antes: em novembro de 2025, atrasos de um desenvolvedor de data center a forçaram a reduzir sua previsão de receita para 2025. Pagar pelo restante também está ficando mais difícil. O CEO da NVIDIA, Jensen Huang, disse à CNBC na semana passada que uma "escassez de capital" está prejudicando as construções das neoclouds. A Nebius também está gastando rápido A CoreWeave não é a única neocloud construindo antecipadamente. Os gastos de capital da Nebius foram de $82,9 milhões em 2023 para $808 milhões em 2024 e $4,07 bilhões em 2025. Nenhum desses gastos gera receita até que os locais para os quais estão indo tenham energia e resfriamento. Preços mais altos só pagam em chips conectados Os preços de aluguel estão ajudando o poder de computação que está em operação. A CoreWeave aumentou os preços cerca de 25% em todos os tipos de GPU em julho, e o amigo de Jin coloca os aluguéis de H100, B200 e B300 com alta de 2x a 3x. Mas um preço mais alto não paga nada em uma GPU que está esperando por um transformador. Em 21 de outubro, uma publicação no X chamou a demanda da SpaceX por poder de computação de otimista para as neoclouds. Musk respondeu: "Somente se conseguirem colocar seu poder de computação online e confiável, o que é extremamente difícil de fazer em escala." Os analistas não esperam que a receita operacional da CoreWeave cubra seus juros até 2028, quando o consenso projeta um EBIT de $8,8 bilhões contra $7,7 bilhões em juros. Um local paralisado só empurra isso mais para frente. A conclusão Musk está certo de que algum poder de computação ficará ocioso. A CoreWeave, com uma conta de juros maior que sua receita operacional, é quem carrega esse risco. Seus clientes tinham comprometido $104,2 bilhões de backlog até 30 de junho. Mas ela tinha apenas 1,5 gigawatt de potência ativa naquela época, contra 4,2 gigawatts contratados até 11 de agosto, e seu primeiro local de construção própria só entra em operação no final deste ano. A maior parte dessa lacuna depende de outras empresas concluírem seus prédios no prazo. Minha opinião: eu esperaria por provas de que a potência ativa da CoreWeave está alcançando seus contratos antes de comprar a ação. Claro, o relatório do terceiro trimestre de 12 de novembro poderia fornecer essa prova. A administração prevê uma receita operacional ajustada de $200 milhões a $260 milhões contra essa conta de jur

artigo.texto: Columbia County chair candidates discuss data centers, growth, traffic at library forum COLUMBIA COUNTY, Ga. (WRDW/WAGT) - Democrat Cambrey Wood and Republican Alison Couch addressed data centers, traffic and growth in front of a room of voters as they run to lead Columbia County for the next four years. A forum at the Columbia County Library brought the candidates together to discuss the big issues facing the county. Both candidates said Columbia County should slow residential growth. Both said public safety is their top budget priority. Couch has served as Appling Harlem’s commissioner while the county voted to bring a 3,000-acre data center to that area and developed the data center zoning ordinance. She said the county did it for property tax relief for citizens. Couch said she voted for the White Oak data center because it is in an industrial park. Augusta airport targets holiday parking, hangar completion while TSA checkpoint timeline Airport Executive Director Herbert Judon said much of the work remains on track for holiday travel. She said she voted against the project in Pumpkin Center, which is across the street from a neighborhood. “I do not see the need for any more data centers in Columbia County,” Couch said. “The goal was property tax relief and that will be achieved with the funding from the data centers that we currently have. I worked diligently on the data center ordinances to provide guardrails for our citizens and protect them.” Wood has been critical of the project. Wood said the tax relief deal still gives data centers a tax break and that the community is not getting enough in return. “I think that $40 million a year is a pretty short-sighted and low payoff solution when you’re leaving 2 plus billion dollars on the table over the next 25 years that could have been used to offset costs for other things like capital improvement projects or road projects or safety upgrades or law enforcement equipment,” Wood said. Traffic was also a topic of discussion. Wood brought up rural, underdeveloped roads that need to be redeveloped. Couch said the area near the Interstate 20 Grovetown exit is where she has heard the most concern. She said the county is putting a lot of work into that area now. Wood advocated for a zoning overhaul to spread development into rural parts of the county while keeping their character. “I would definitely support an overhaul of our existing planning, zoning, and development ordinances, targeting specific areas within the county as appropriate for increasing density, which would allow us to then plan our growth out into the more rural areas of the county and maintain the county character that we have in the various areas,” Wood said. Halloween candy prices vary across Augusta stores Bag prices range from under $9 to about $30 at Kroger, Walmart, Target and Costco as Halloween falls on a Saturday. Couch said bringing business is important but that expanding county services into areas of growth is the top priority. “An important part of growth also is to be able to provide services for the residents that are joining our community,” Couch said. “So responsible growth means providing sheriff’s department, providing fire services, providing quality of life projects and providing traffic infrastructure.” District 1 candidates Michael Jordan and Alex Griffin also answered questions about how they would lead in the seat Connie Melear is termed out of. Griffin said he’d like to see work put into the stretch of Washington Road around Bobby Jones Expressway to redevelop aging infrastructure. Jordan said the growth in Columbia County is good, but he wants to ensure the County can afford that growth. Copyright 2026 WRDW/WAGT. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: SpaceX firma acordo de US$ 40 bilhões para financiar equipamentos de data centers A SpaceX, de Elon Musk, firmou um compromisso de financiamento de cerca de US$ 40 bilhões com uma entidade administrada pela Apollo Global Management para adquirir equipamentos destinados a centros de dados (data centers). Segundo documento enviado nesta segunda-feira, 26, à Securities and Exchanges Commission (SEC, a CVM dos EUA), a operação prevê o arrendamento de unidades de processamento gráfico (GPUs) e equipamentos relacionados. O compromisso vinculante foi assinado em 24 de outubro e estabelece que a entidade ligada à Apollo comprará os equipamentos e os alugará à SpaceX, que realizará pagamentos trimestrais ao longo de aproximadamente cinco anos. Os equipamentos serão entregues em lotes, com contratos individuais de arrendamento previstos para começar no primeiro semestre de 2027. Cada contrato terá duração de cinco anos a cinco anos e três meses. Segundo a companhia, os pagamentos trimestrais serão feitos antecipadamente e incluirão, em geral, um vigésimo do custo financiado de cada lote, além de juros calculados a uma taxa anual fixa sobre o saldo devedor e despesas adicionais. A taxa de juros ainda será definida. A SpaceX estima que os pagamentos de principal totalizem aproximadamente US$ 40 bilhões durante a vigência dos contratos, sem incluir juros e outros custos. A empresa espera concluir a formalização do acordo antes do fim de 2026, mediante o cumprimento de determinadas condições. Investimento em data center após balanço forte Na última semana, a SpaceX registrou um lucro líquido de US$ 4,4 bilhões no terceiro trimestre de 2026, em seu segundo relatório de lucros após a Oferta Pública Inicial (IPO, na sigla em inglês). O resultado ajustado por ação da SpaceX foi de US$ 0,35, acima das projeções de analistas compiladas pela FactSet, que projetavam lucro de US$ 0,13. A receita da empresa, por sua vez, subiu 161% na comparação anual, para US$ 14,6 bilhões, ante a estimativa de US$ 12,87 bilhões apurada pela FactSet junto a analistas. O segmento de conectividade, que consiste no serviço de internet via satélite Starlink, registrou 13,6 milhões de inscritos no terceiro trimestre deste ano e obteve receita de US$ 5,2 bilhões. Já os setores de Espaço e Inteligência Artificial (IA) registraram receita de US$ 1,77 bilhão e US$ 7,56 bilhões, respectivamente. Os gastos de capital (capex) atingiram US$ 19,6 bilhões no trimestre, um aumento em relação aos US$ 6,9 bilhões registrados no mesmo período do ano anterior.

artigo.texto: Aberta a consulta pública para a primeira metodologia de carbono azul Metodologia pretende mobilizar investimento privado para recuperar e conservar pradarias marinhas em Portugal continental A primeira metodologia de carbono azul do Mercado Voluntário de Carbono (MVC) português está em consulta pública até 22 de novembro. A proposta “Restauro e Conservação de Pradarias Marinhas em Portugal Continental” pretende mobilizar investimento privado para financiar projetos de recuperação e conservação destes ecossistemas através da venda de créditos de carbono. “Queremos que o Mercado Voluntário de Carbono seja também um instrumento para financiar a recuperação da natureza”, afirmou a Ministra do Ambiente e Energia, Maria da Graça Carvalho, acrescentando que a metodologia valoriza o papel do carbono azul e os ecossistemas marinhos na ação climática. A proposta de metodologia permite alargar o mercado aos ecossistemas marinhos e prevê a atribuição de “Créditos de Carbono +” a projetos que demonstrem benefícios adicionais para a biodiversidade e património natural. A metodologia foi proposta pela ANA – Aeroportos de Portugal, S.A., com o apoio de entidades científicas, e analisada pela Comissão Técnica de Acompanhamento do Mercado Voluntário de Carbono. Os interessados podem apresentar contributos para a versão final no portal Participa. Leia na íntegra o comunicado: “Carbono Azul chega ao Mercado Voluntário para impulsionar recuperação de pradarias marinhas”.

artigo.texto: A Motorola lançou hoje (27) o Moto G47 Power, versão com melhorias na bateria do modelo que estreou no primeiro semestre, prometendo autonomia superior a 78 horas com uma carga graças ao tanque de energia de 7.000 mAh. A novidade chega primeiro ao mercado europeu, mas com preço acima do especulado anteriormente. O mais recente integrante da série Moto G também tem, entre os destaques, a câmera de 108 MP liderando o conjunto fotográfico com abertura f/1,7 e zoom de 3x sem perda de qualidade da imagem, segundo a fabricante. A certificação IP64 é outro atrativo, oferecendo resistência contra água e poeira. Quanto custa o Moto G47 Power? Com ficha técnica semelhante à do Moto G47 convencional, o lançamento possui tela LCD de 6,67 polegadas com resolução HD (1604 x 720 pixels) e taxa de atualização de 120 Hz. O chip também é o mesmo MediaTek Dimensity 6300, acompanhado de 4 GB de RAM expansível até 12 GB por meio da função RAM Boost. - Ele tem 128 GB de armazenamento interno, com possibilidade de expansão via cartão microSD de até 1 TB; - Voltando à parte de câmeras, há o sensor macro de 2 MP junto à lente de 108 MP na traseira, enquanto a câmera de selfie tem 8 MP; - Alto-falantes estéreo com Dolby Atmos, 5G, NFC, Bluetooth 5.4, porta USB-C, entrada P2 para fone e proteção de tela Corning Gorilla Glass 7i também estão presentes; - Carregamento rápido de 30W e carregamento reverso de 6W são outros destaques do modelo que vem com Android 16 instalado de fábrica. Já à venda em alguns países europeus, o Moto G47 Power custa entre 309 e 369 euros, dependendo do mercado, o que dá entre R$ 1.836 e R$ 2.193 pela cotação do dia, sem considerar impostos e taxas. Ele pode ser encontrado nas cores azul, preto e capri. Os valores ficaram acima do que havia sido especulado por informantes, recentemente, como observa o site PhoneArena. Por enquanto, o novo intermediário da Motorola não tem previsão de lançamento no Brasil. Trabalhando em novidades para a sua linha de dobráveis, a empresa estaria preparando a estreia do Razr Flex. Saiba mais sobre o dispositivo nesta matéria. Com informações de PhoneArena.

artigo.texto: An inside look of the massive data center tearing a Wisconsin community apart In Port Washington, Wisconsin, there's a data center being built that's as big as 500 football fields. Residents aren't sure if it could save their community or destroy it. SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST: Back here in Wisconsin, I've been driving through the state this week. And just north of Milwaukee, you quickly enter farm country - cornfields, rolling hills, barns and grain silos. Then suddenly, next to a highway, you get a visual shock. And - oh, Henry, is this the data center on the left? HENRY LARSON, BYLINE: It's huge. PFEIFFER: There's something massive under construction over there. It's a hyper-scale data center in Port Washington, Wisconsin. I went there with NPR producer Henry Larson, and we could barely find words for how colossal this project is. This skyline of cranes and... It stretches along 2 miles of highway. It covers 2 1/2 million square feet of former farmland. LARSON: It goes literally to the horizon. PFEIFFER: This emerging data center complex has torn up the land and torn up this community. It's a local story playing out nationally as artificial intelligence companies race to build data centers to power their AI and many people increasingly say we don't want these here. (SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING) UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #1: Will you acknowledge the mental health impacts of the residents living closest to the data center? Will you offer support to people who have endured the most? PFEIFFER: Port Washington's gargantuan project has led to angry protests, multiple lawsuits and opponents arrested for civil disobedience. Supporters say data centers will keep the United States competitive and could bring great wealth to places where they're built. But many residents feel frightened and helpless as they watch this rapid change, like 67-year-old Amanda Mueller. She relocated to Port Washington five years ago. AMANDA MUELLER: This was my last move. I feel like an elephant looking for a place to die in life, and I found utopia. It was so perfect. PFEIFFER: She bought a four-bedroom ranch house within walking distance of a beautiful, undeveloped stretch of beach on Lake Michigan. (SOUNDBITE OF FOOTSTEPS ON GRASS) PFEIFFER: Is this all your yard you see here, all this? MUELLER: Yeah. I own... PFEIFFER: Wow. MUELLER: ...Three acres. PFEIFFER: All the way to that fringe of... MUELLER: Yeah. PFEIFFER: ...Pine trees. MUELLER: Oh, all the way through there. PFEIFFER: Wow. MUELLER: This is the perfect retirement home. I mean... PFEIFFER: Look at this view you have. But her view is different this year. You can glimpse cranes in the distance. Port Washington's data center is being built about a half mile from her house. When did you get a hint that something was about to dramatically change in your neighborhood? MUELLER: I'm going to say two years ago. The farmer right next to me just sold a lot of his farmland. And then someone else said, yeah, another farmer's selling. And it's like, wait - it's all consolidated. PFEIFFER: Were you feeling some combination of kind of dread, dismay? MUELLER: I put my house up for sale. PFEIFFER: Literally? MUELLER: Yeah. PFEIFFER: But she says she got just one offer that eventually fell apart. She believes the buyer got spooked by the data center. Mueller is infuriated with the mayor and city council for approving this project. She's now one of Port Washington's leading crusaders against it, pushing back with litigation and asking for moratoriums and environmental reviews and more voter input. MUELLER: There should be a buffer zone around data centers, and it should be within at least a mile of a data center, you should not have residents living anywhere near it. There has to be guardrails. PFEIFFER: Port Washington Mayor Ted Neitzke says adequate guardrails have been put in place. There may be no bigger champion for this project than the mayor. (SOUNDBITE OF CAR DOOR CLOSING) TED NEITZKE: I don't know where you want me to start, but - so I'm 55. So I've lived here, went to high school here, married my wife, who's from here, our kids went to school here. PFEIFFER: He drives us around Port Washington, recalling when it was a declining industrial city that didn't yet have a cute touristy downtown. He thinks people against the data center have it all wrong, just like they were wrong about a popular brewery now located near the city's pretty marina. NEITZKE: So this is one of the new developments. This is where we'll go for beer and cheese curds. But this building here was very controversial. People lost their jobs on their council because this was a parking lot, and nobody wanted to lose the parking lot. Change is something that does not come easy to small Midwestern towns. PFEIFFER: In Port Washington, being mayor is a part-time job. It pays an annual stipend of $7,500. But the role gave Neitzke the power to help approve this $15 billion data center project. He envisions thousands of local jobs, beautification and infrastructure projects and a gusher of new tax revenue. NEITZKE: One of the things I did was I flew out to Loudoun County, Virginia, and I went and visited all the data centers... PFEIFFER: One of the epicenters... NEITZKE: Yeah. PFEIFFER: ...Of data centers. NEITZKE: I mean, I don't know if you can find more in the United States. And as I drove around, I really could not understand - what are people so mad about? Because when you're in that area, and you're driving around, they're just large boxes filled with computers. PFEIFFER: But you really can't imagine what people would be mad about? artigo.texto: Watson Farley & Williams (WFW) has advised BNP Paribas Asset Management, Santander, Banco Sabadell, and Banco Cooperativo Español, acting as lenders, on the €222 million financing of a portfolio of hybrid solar photovoltaic (PV) and battery energy storage system (BESS) projects in Spain owned by BRUC Alter Energías Renovables, S.A., a joint venture owned by BRUC and Alter Enersun. The financing combines the financing of an operational 208 MW PV portfolio with the financing for the construction of 118 MW/472 MWh of co-located BESS capacity across four projects in Extremadura and Andalucía, Spain. This creates an integrated renewable generation and storage portfolio designed to optimise the management and distribution of renewable electricity. The transaction forms part of BRUC and Alter Enersun’s strategy to further integrate renewable generation and energy storage, reinforcing the growing role of hybrid renewable projects in Spain’s energy transition. The addition of battery storage capacity enables the storage of the electricity generated by the PV plants and facilitate its dispatch according to system requirements, providing greater flexibility to renewable generation. BRUC is a leading independent renewable energy platform in the Iberian market, with a diversified portfolio of renewable generation assets. Alter Enersun is a leading Iberian renewable energy company with PV installations across Spain, Portugal, and Italy. The WFW Madrid Energy team that advised the lenders was led by Finance Partner, José María Anarte, supported by Senior Associate, Antón Ramil, and Associate, Sara Estradera. José María commented: “This transaction highlights the growing convergence of renewable generation and energy storage in Spain’s energy market. The financing of a portfolio combining operating PV assets and large scale battery storage reflects the increasing sophistication of the country’s renewable energy sector and the evolution of financing structures required to support it. We are delighted to have advised the lenders on a landmark transaction at the forefront of this trend, an area in which WFW continues to play a leading role.” For more news and technical articles from the global renewable industry, read the latest issue of Energy Global magazine. artigo.texto: POTTERVILLE — U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett is pushing legislation to increase transparency around data center projects and protect local control over their development, alongside health insurance reforms and limits on presidential war powers as he seeks a second term. The Livingston Post and its partner, Michigan Firsthand, caught up with the Republican congressman as he went door-to-door in the Potterville neighborhood near the first home he bought after returning from an Iraq deployment. In the wide-ranging interview, Barrett — who faces Democratic challenger William Lawrence in the Nov. 3 election for Michigan’s 7th Congressional District — also discussed inflation, artificial intelligence, Israel, education and public safety. (You can watch the full discussions with Barrett and Lawrence on YouTube, and read our companion interview with Lawrence here.) Acknowledging the high stakes – the race is the nation’s costliest House race for advertising according to WKAR and AdImpact – Barrett said he is feeling “optimistic.” “I’ve been in tough political campaigns before, and I know what it feels like to be in a close race,” he said. Local control of data centers Barrett said data center decisions should rest with local townships, villages and cities, and that residents should have the right to examine proposals before agreements are signed. On Aug. 20, Barrett introduced legislation to protect state and local authority over data center siting. On Sept. 24, he joined Maryland Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin in co-sponsoring Ohio Democratic Rep. Greg Landsman’s No Secrets for Data Centers Act, which would make covered nondisclosure agreements unenforceable. “I don’t want to do a ban on the development of AI or a ban on data centers entirely,” Barrett said, saying he was concerned about rising electricity costs, water consumption, noise and what communities would do with large facilities if technological changes ever made them obsolete. “What I want to make sure is that any data center project is done with the consent of the residents who live there.” Barrett said some communities may conclude a proposal meets their needs, while others may reject it. He argued that transparency requirements would not undermine the United States’ ability to compete in artificial intelligence, saying “if we’re going to do this, we’re going to do it with transparency and in the right way that addresses the concerns that people have.” Keeping humans in control of AI The 22-year Army veteran, who served in Iraq, Guantanamo Bay and South Korea, also supports pursuing an international agreement governing artificial intelligence and autonomous weapons. “I think every country should agree that having fully autonomous lethal weapons is dangerous in so many different ways,” he said. Barrett joined Democratic Reps. Don Beyer of Virginia and Sara Jacobs of California in introducing the Human Authority over Autonomous Weapons Act, which would require meaningful human oversight of intentionally lethal strikes by autonomous or AI-enabled weapons used by the U.S. military. He said the possibility that terrorist groups could obtain such weapons should give countries a common interest in negotiating limits. “I can’t say with certainty that they would, but I can say that I believe that it’s the appropriate thing to do,” he said. Health care reform and private insurance On health care, Barrett called for substantial changes to the healthcare system, including requiring insurers to spend more of their premium revenue on patient care, and expanding access to tax-exempt health savings accounts. “So I agree that the healthcare system in the country is broken, and we need substantial, radical reform,” he said. “I’ve actually introduced legislation that would increase what’s called the medical loss ratio.” His Care Over Profits Act would require insurers to spend at least 85% of premium revenue on medical care and quality improvement. Barrett said he also wants broader access to health savings accounts and expanded eligible expenses, including healthy food, gym memberships and fitness equipment. He argued that allowing workers and employers to contribute to accounts that follow people between jobs would give families more control over their coverage and encourage preventive care. “These big health insurance companies have gotten by on raising premiums and not increasing quality of care,” he said. Barrett rejected the Medicare for All approach, arguing that eliminating the commercial insurance market could undermine medical innovation and reduce the revenue hospitals and physicians rely on. “Today, the Medicare system works because we have a robust commercial insurance program as well,” he said. He said providers depend on a mix of patients with commercial insurance, Medicare and Medicaid, and warned that moving everyone to government payment rates could affect services. Iran, affordability and congressional authority In between conversations with voters, Barrett said people frequently have concerns about gasoline and diesel prices, and the effects on groceries, deliveries and agriculture. He blamed today’s inflationary environment on spending during the Biden administration, and acknowledged the Iran war is helping drive fuel-price increases. Ending the conflict, he said, would help stabilize costs. In April, Barrett introduced the bipartisan Prevent Endless Wars Act with Democratic Rep. Jared Golden of Maine, a measure that would deny expedited congressional consideration to military-force authorizations lasting more than five years or lacking an expiration date. “Our Constitution makes it clear that only Congress can decide to send our men and women into combat or not,” he said. Barrett described Iran as a serious threat but said that does not make prolonged military intervention the only response. “I don’t believe that we should be doing nation building or sending boots on the ground or the other things that got us into these prolonged wars in

artigo.texto: Long before much of Maryland knew what a data center was, Frederick County looked like it could be the industry’s next hub. A Washington, D.C. exurb of rolling farmland, Frederick sits just across the Potomac River from Northern Virginia’s “Data Center Alley” and boasts fiber-optic connection to the industry capital. When County Executive Jessica Fitzwater was elected four years ago, she promised policies and regulations to make Frederick “a national leader” in responsible data center development. Today, Frederick is home to Maryland’s only large-scale data center development, and its leaders are learning the hard way about the hazards of navigating the charged and changing politics of the industry, which critics decry for devouring energy, water and land. The divide over data centers has all but consumed Frederick politics. Fitzwater, a Democrat, faces a surprisingly strong challenge from the former Frederick Mayor Jeff Holtzinger, and the race has turned into a reckoning over her handling of the industry. Over two weeks last month, Fitzwater touted — then spiked — a $110 million agreement with the county’s lead data center developer, and she has extended the county’s data center moratorium from the end of this year to next summer. Next week’s election could help shape the county’s — and Maryland’s — longer-term approach to data centers. While most of the state lives under a data center freeze, the outcome in Frederick will be an early test of just how resilient the state’s grassroots backlash will be. Read More A secret courtship Four years ago, developers broke ground on a sprawling campus at the site of an old aluminum smelting plant outside Adamstown, a quaint village in southern Frederick. Known today as Quantum Maryland, the data center complex spans hundreds of acres and draws busloads of construction workers a day. County leaders once flirted with an even bigger vision. In 2019, Frederick officials entered a nondisclosure agreement with Amazon. The county then held closed-door meetings for close to a year with the company on a proposal they called “Project Holiday,” which would have set aside three areas of southern Frederick County for a $30 billion venture with as many as 15 data centers. The extent of these exchanges is public because the Sugarloaf Alliance, a group dedicated to preserving Frederick’s rural character, successfully sued over access to the records. “Everybody [was] looking at us like we’re wearing tinfoil hats,” Steve Black, a southern Frederick farmer and president of the alliance, said about the early days of his anti-data center advocacy. Black said he knows many loyal Democrats who are torn over whether to support Fitzwater in the general election. At the time of Project Holiday, Fitzwater served on the County Council and was briefed on the Amazon talks months after they happened. She was elected county executive in 2022 and is quick to point out that her administration hasn’t approved any new data centers. Instead, she appointed a task force to study the industry and has imposed a series of moratoriums, the latest of which expires in July 2027. Nevertheless, Fitzwater has drawn the ire of the county’s anti-data center coalition in part because of zoning changes enacted by the county council. The changes, similar to a proposal introduced by Fitzwater, expanded a designated data center zone from roughly 1,600 acres to 2,600, including several hundred acres of farmland. In an August interview, Fitzwater said her job is to ensure the industry is strictly regulated and brings benefits to her constituents. Frederick has collected more than $55 million in property and land transfer taxes from the Quantum campus, and industry boosters say the project could eventually net over $200 million annually for the county. For some neighbors near the Quantum campus, the upside is hard to see. Where Hope Green once looked out over mountains and deer from her yard, she now sees a hulking warehouse and stacks of diesel generators. She says construction on the Quantum site has tarnished her well water, and Maryland environmental regulators have cited developers there for repeated discharges into a local creek and other violations. A spokesperson for the site’s master developer, Catellus Development Corporation, declined to comment on environmental issues but said in a statement that the company remains committed to the project. “For years, we have operated in good faith through the County’s legally established land-use process,” a Quantum Maryland spokesperson said. Born and raised on an Adamstown farm, Green had hoped to spend her retirement in her house. Now she insists the county or developer should buy her and her neighbors out of their homes. “What’s left of my family is here. My church is here. My friends are here,” she said. But “if I want to have peace of mind for the rest of my life, I have to leave.” A political landmine Last month, Frederick County officials announced a proposal they said would squeeze the local data center industry for a transformative infusion of cash. The agreement with Catellus, valued at $110 million, would pay for renovations to an elementary school near the county’s sole data center campus; a new community recreation building; a jobs-training facility; and protections for farmland. It would also freeze parts of the county’s rezoning and bar changes to noise and environmental regulations for at least eight years. Fitzwater called the agreement “unprecedented” and touted it as among the largest commitments of its kind in the country. But instead of plaudits, the county’s anti-data center faction condemned the package for provisions that threatened to lock in some of the project’s most controversial aspects. The announcement inflamed a debate that had dominated the primary contests in June. artigo.texto: BYD announced on October 26 that blind orders are now open for the second-generation Seal 07. The car was first unveiled by the regulatory filings on August 7th. Design and dimensions The new model continues the “Ocean Aesthetics” 2.0 design language and shares its overall styling with the Seal 08. The front features a wave-shaped split headlight arrangement and a closed grille. A LiDAR unit on the roof suggests the car may come with BYD’s God’s Eye B advanced driver-assistance system. Six exterior colors are offered: Pala Green, Aurora Pink, Sea Mist Purple, Liuguang Silver, Snow White and Obsidian Black. The car measures 5,080 mm long, 1,960 mm wide and 1,495 mm high, with a 2,960 mm wheelbase that BYD says expands cabin space. Its rear uses a full-width taillight design derived from the Seal 08. Interior Inside, the Seal 07 adopts BYD’s latest design language. It keeps a large floating central display and a digital instrument cluster, and adds a new three-spoke steering wheel. The center console trim and air vent shapes have also been revised. Wireless phone charging and two cup holders remain in the front center console. Three interior color schemes are available: Yunxi White, Phantom Grey and Ningye Purple. The car also features a 20-speaker audio system. Seating includes zero-gravity front seats with massage, ventilation and heating functions. The rear has a large sofa-style bench. The 2,960 mm wheelbase is said to improve passenger space. Storage includes a 618-liter trunk and a 160-liter front trunk, described as the largest in its class. The Seal 07 will be offered in two powertrain options. The plug-in hybrid uses a 1.5T turbocharged engine rated at 115 kW and a drive motor rated at 160 kW (215 hp). It has a 38 kWh battery pack and a WLTC electric range of 245 km. The battery-electric version uses a drive motor with a peak output of 300 kW (402 hp), offers up to 718 km of WLTP range. Both versions will feature BYD’s second-generation Blade Battery, flash charging and DiSus-M suspension.

artigo.texto: Oregon residents debate Issue 25 during council meeting one week before vote on data center Supporters and opponents speak out ahead of vote on $1 billion data center OREGON, Ohio (WTVG) - Oregon residents voiced their opinions on a potential $1 billion data center one week before they vote on the issue. Residents say the language of Issue 25 is confusing. A yes vote supports a ban on a data center with a demand or peak load of 25 megawatts or greater. A no vote opposes that ban. Supporters cite financial benefits Ben Pfeiffer, a science teacher at Clay High School who has taught in the community for 28 years, said passing any kind of levy would be difficult given current economic conditions. “I think that we can agree that given the economic times we’re in, passing any kind of levy would be difficult. It doesn’t have to be this way,” Pfeiffer said. Pfeiffer said the data center could help avoid future financial strain on the school district. “Over 15 years, this commercial project is estimated to bring more than $100 million to Oregon City Schools. That includes $10 million in milestone payments over the next three to four years, and $7 million every year through a pilot agreement,” Pfeiffer said. Pfeiffer said the district would need to put forth an operating levy in 2028 unless the data center moves forward. He said the financial forecast has determined this revenue would offset the operating deficit and avoid a levy request for eight to 10 years. Melissa Mummert, an intervention specialist at Clay High School, also said the data center is necessary. “Our children are doing their part every day. Now we must do ours. We need to build an educational future defined by opportunity rather than program cuts and inspiration rather than reduced services,” Mummert said. Opponents raise concerns Those arguments did not sway several people in the audience who support Issue 25. Laura Davis, a volunteer with United Neighbors of Oregon, compared the district’s planning strategy to an unreliable financial gamble. “This planning strategy is like buying a car and hoping to make the payments when you win the lottery. There does not seem to be a plan B if the data center does not happen,” Davis said. Mary Crowley, who opposes the data center, cited concerns about artificial intelligence and data security. “We don’t want a data center. We don’t want unregulated AI. We don’t want surveillance technology. We don’t want our data being stolen and used against us. We don’t want our resources exhausted,” Crowley said. Those who spoke at the meeting are urging Oregon residents to research data centers before casting their vote. artigo.texto: Regulating data centers in San Antonio has boiled down to one choice. Should data centers be approved on a case-by-case basis or can they be built by-right, whenever they meet a set of pre-determined city standards? On Tuesday, the City of San Antonio’s Zoning Commission recommended a plan for regulating data centers. It gives San Antonio City Council, which will make a final decision next week, a fourth option for regulations after three were presented last week. All four use by-right, case-by-case or a combination of those approval processes. There are some clear starting points for any data center land-use policy in San Antonio. Data centers will only be built in industrial, commercial or manufacturing zones. They will also not be allowed over the Edwards Aquifer Recharge Zone. These rules are only for land use — regulations regarding power or water use would fall under CPS Energy and the San Antonio Water System’s authority. The city’s Development Services Department presented two initial options for data center rules. The by-right option allows data centers to be approved automatically once they meet a list of city requirements. The case-by-case policy would require each data center project in the city to be plead its own case in front of City Council. Mayor Gina Ortiz Jones presented a third option last week, giving developers a list of citywide standards that developers could meet before they earn approval from City Council on a case-by-case basis. On Tuesday, the city’s Zoning Commission put forward its own recommendation. The committee of council member-appointed residents, which makes recommendations on land-use to City Council, outlined a policy that allows by-right data centers in some parts of the city , but not in others. San Antonio City Council will decide what the new rules will be at an Oct. 29 A session. The newest proposal On Tuesday, the Zoning Commission put forward its proposal for regulations. The commission’s policy proposal would allow by-right development in industrial areas, specifically the general, heavy, mixed and mixed heavy industrial districts, while there would be specific use authorization in business park, light industrial and general commercial zones. To build data centers by-right, developers would have to leave 350 feet of separation between data centers and residential or neighborhood buildings and have a 100-foot setback from their own property line. The rules also require downward-facing lighting, to prevent light pollution. The Zoning Commission also considered data centers that were already built; San Antonio currently has at least 19 data centers, according to the Texas Tribune. Sparrow said many previously built data centers would be non-conforming with new rules. They would be allowed to keep operating, he said, but they would not be able to expand or conduct extensive repairs unless they come into line with new policies. Commissioner John Bustamante recommended including an exemption for older data centers under the new rules, allowing them to finish expansions or phased construction. It was approved as part of the Zoning Commission’s recommendation. The Zoning Commission does not enact policies. Its recommendation will go to City Council members, who will consider it when making their decision. The first two options Councilman Ric Galvan (D6) got the ball rolling on data center regulations almost a year ago, when he submitted a request in October 2025 to start the policymaking process. Data centers have multiplied across Texas as larger facilities look to serve artificial intelligence needs. Galvan’s district has been a hotspot for their development within city limits. Staff from the city’s Development Services Department had four public meetings between May and September, where they discussed potential policies with stakeholders. “If you wanted to participate, you were invited,” said Logan Sparrow, assistant director at the DSD. “Not going to lie, a lot of those folks were from the [data center development] industry, but we certainly tried our best to include as many people as we could.” Developers have pushed for a set of clear requirements for construction. They see those rules as more stable, making investment and construction more dependable. That’s why they want by-right development, one of the first policies proposed by DSD. Developers could build a data center if they own the land and meet city requirements, which would include being 500 feet away from residential, school, hospital, day care and assisted living properties and a landscape buffer onsite. City officials are referring to this as Option 1. “Anytime we want to attract investment, there has to be consistency and predictability. They want to know the rules of the game,” said Stephanie Reyes, president of the Real Estate Council of San Antonio, who spoke in favor of by-right development on Tuesday. DSD staff also proposed case-by-case evaluations of data centers. That would require what’s known as a specific use authorization for each proposed data center. That means every data center would go in front of the Zoning Commission and City Council, which would lay out specific requirements for each data center. City officials are referring to this as Option 2. “It’s so important for you all to recommend to City Council this specific use authorization because it would give the public the opportunity to ask these questions and to give feedback and to share their concerns,” said Deedee Belmares, Clean Energy advocate for advocacy group Public Citizen. Public Citizen monitors data centers and informs residents about their development in San Antonio and across the state. On Wednesday, Belmares advocated for case-by-case evaluations of data centers, speaking out against DSD’s by-right proposal and the Zoning Commission’s latest recommendation. The Mayor’s proposal During an Oct. 14 City Council meeting, Jones shared what she called a combination of by-right and case-by-case processe

artigo.texto: RWE completes sale of shares in Five Estuaries Offshore Wind Farm 09.10.2026 RWE and Borussia Dortmund officially commissioned the new battery storage system at SIGNAL IDUNA PARK today during the Bundesliga home match against Eintracht Frankfurt. This marks the completion of the two partners’ joint energy concept for the stadium. Following the installation of the photovoltaic system on the roof of the BVB FanWelt and the completion of the world’s most powerful photovoltaic system on a stadium roof, the battery storage system has also become operational. The battery storage system has a capacity of 3.7 megawatts and can supply this output for just over an hour. The photovoltaic system, which was commissioned in December 2025, comprises 11,132 solar modules and has a capacity of more than 5 megawatts (MWp). By linking the battery to the new PV system, the electricity generated can be used even when the sun is not shining. With the new photovoltaic system, BVB can meet up to 45 per cent of SIGNAL IDUNA PARK’s electricity requirements. Dr Markus Krebber, Chief Executive of RWE AG: “With the commissioning of the battery storage system, the entire system comprising the photovoltaic plant and the battery at SIGNAL IDUNA PARK is now fully operational. Linking the two systems makes it possible to use the solar power generated on site even more flexibly, even when the sun isn’t shining. The experts from BVB and RWE have breathed life and energy into our partnership through this project. It provides a solid foundation for further joint developments.” Carsten Cramer, Chairman of the Executive Board of Borussia Dortmund: “SIGNAL IDUNA PARK is not only our iconic home, but also a central element of our holistic decarbonisation strategy. With the battery storage system, we are collaborating with RWE to complete a forward-looking energy concept that makes our solar power even more usable. We are delighted that our stadium will thus continue to stand for resource-efficient and innovative action in the future.” As a “Premium Partner” and a key part of the “BVB Empowers” initiative, RWE will continue to support BVB in optimising the energy management of SIGNAL IDUNA PARK as part of the six-year partnership. The aim is to further increase the stadium’s contribution to security of supply, energy efficiency, and decarbonisation. Images for media use (image rights: BVB) are available in the media library. Further information on the project can be found at: www.rwe.com/bvb

artigo.texto: - Data centers have become a topic of intense debate in Michigan as tech giants rush to build the computing facilities - A Bridge Michigan panel explored the tension between Michigan’s economic goals and the environmental realities of data centers - The discussion caps Bridge Listens, a yearlong experiment in reader-led journalism Michigan lawmakers are under intense pressure to regulate data centers more strictly as public opposition to the computing facilities becomes too strong to ignore. That’s a key takeaway from speakers on an expert panel at the inaugural Bridge Michigan Issues Summit at Marygrove Conservancy, titled “Innovation Collision: Balancing High-Tech Ambitions with Energy and Water Realities.” The half-day Issues Summit featured expert speakers on some of the most pressing issues facing Michigan ahead of the November election, from education outcomes to healthcare costs and housing affordability. The event capped Bridge Listens, the news organization’s yearlong focus on top issues identified by more than 6,400 Bridge readers in survey responses. Environmental topics including data centers ranked high on readers’ list of concerns. In response, Bridge has spent much of the year digging into Michigan’s data center debate, including reporting on candidates’ policy stances, documenting the public pushback and exploring Michigan’s strategy to absorb the facilities’ massive energy and water demand. More than 375 people attended the Issues Summit in Detroit, virtually or at a watch party at Alpena Community College. During the data center discussion, audience members heard from: - Brenda Stumbo, Ypsilanti Township supervisor - Michelle Martinez, director of the University of Michigan Tishman Center for Social Justice and the Environment - Erik E. Nordman, director of Michigan State University’s Institute of Public Utilities - Jeff Guilfoyle, senior strategist at Public Sector Consultants All agreed that intense pushback against data centers has begun to reshape Michigan’s policy landscape just two years after lawmakers first passed tax breaks meant to lure data center developers to the state. By exempting qualifying data centers from sales and use taxes, lawmakers “opened the floodgates” to development with little input from residents, said Martinez. It left many feeling “blindsided by the scope, the speed and the lack of channels to have a voice in the decision-making,” she said. The panelists offered differing perspectives about how the industry may shape the state, with some expressing concerns about negative environmental and quality-of-life consequences from data center development while others argued Michigan stands to reap meaningful returns from the multi-billion-dollar investments. In Saline Township, for example, annual property tax revenue from Oracle and OpenAI’s forthcoming Stargate data center will boost local tax revenue from a few hundred thousand annually to more than $10 million annually, said Guilfoyle, who has studied the potential economic benefits of data center development. “That’s a significant increase and that money is a driver in the community,” Guilfoyle said. The facility is also expected to employ 450 people permanently on-site while supporting thousands of temporary construction jobs. The promised benefits so far haven’t won over many Michigan residents, nearly two-thirds of whom oppose the building of data centers in the state, according to recent polling. Ypsilanti Township Supervisor Brenda Stumbo is familiar with that pushback, which she blames in part on lawmakers welcoming the industry to Michigan without consulting voters or local public officials who’d be left to negotiate the details with some of the world’s wealthiest companies. “It was rushed,” Stumbo said of Michigan’s process, “and we know as individuals, in our personal lives and professional lives, when you rush something, it doesn’t really go well.” Data center developers have since fanned out across Michigan looking for land and available energy. A single 1-gigawatt facility demands as much power as a large US city, prompting questions about how Michgian utilities can absorb the spiking demand without raising rates on residential customers. “It’s the million-dollar question,” said Nordman. And so far, the answer is unclear. In some areas, increased demand from data centers has helped tamp down on residential rates by adding a new customer to split the cost of maintaining poles, wires and power plants, Nordman noted. But in others, data center demand has outstripped existing capacity on the grid, creating a mismatch between energy supply and demand that has driven rates up. Michigan should be insulated from at least some of that rate shock, he said, because state policy prohibits utilities from forcing other customers to shoulder the cost of investments needed to serve data centers. Asked whether Michigan utilities can absorb data centers’ skyrocketing energy demand while still meeting Michigan’s mandate to transition to 100% clean energy by 2040, Nordman was less optimistic. “It will be challenging,” he said. “Very, very difficult. Because, when we put these laws in place, we had relatively flat demand growth … now we have to work twice as hard.” Even if Michigan utilities manage to meet the 2040 deadline, Martinez noted, data center demand in other states is likely to lead to new investments in fossil fuel infrastructure that drives climate change. “In Texas, they have a 424 GW backlog for data centers alone,” Martinez said. “The air that comes from Texas does not stay in Texas.” Watch the entire Issues Summit here:

artigo.texto: A specific kind of development has been assigned new Washington County zoning requirements: battery energy storage facilities. The county’s board of supervisors voted unanimously last week to put special permits in place for projects involving large industrial installations that store and distribute power to the electric grid. The regulations apply to storage facilities that have a capacity greater than 600 kilowatts per hour and, with the approval of a permit, they can be built only in light and heavy industrial zones. With the ordinance in place, the supervisors will have to vote to approve any battery energy storage projects. Lightshift Energy, an Arlington-based energy storage developer, has expressed interest in building one in Washington County, according to county officials. The projects would likely only be built in places near electrical substations, said Stephen Richardson, the county’s planning commission coordinator. “They don’t want to be very far away because you lose all your efficiency,” Richardson said. “You lose your current the longer the line is.” Combined with the new zoning restrictions, the only viable places would likely be in industrial parks, he said. There are three Appalachian Power substations around Abingdon: the Hillman Highway Substation, South Abingdon Substation and Arrowhead Substation. The power company also operates a major facility at Highlands Business Park near Glade Spring. Data centers have begun using energy storage systems to act as a buffer for voltage spikes and reduce reliance on diesel generators, and utility companies have begun to install them too. Earlier this spring, the Salem-based Blue Ridge Power Agency announced it was pairing with Lightshift to deploy energy storage installments across five sites in the region. In addition to the projects in Salem, Lightshift is also seeking federal approval for an energy storage installation at Highlands Business Park. The company is leasing a parcel there for $10,000 annually until it gets the proper permits, and then it plans to buy the property, County Administrator Jason Berry said by phone. It should be beneficial for anyone using the grid, Berry said, since the facility would be able to stabilize it and prevent blackouts. Appalachian Power uses the lines the facility would attach to, and its parent company, American Electric Power, also feeds power through those lines to multiple other states, he said. Lightshift declined to comment on the Washington County project. Once the company buys the property, the board of supervisors would have to vote to approve the development plans now that the stricter zoning regulations are in place. Though battery energy storage facilities require no onsite jobs, it would bring in more business property tax revenue for the county, Berry said. “For us, it’s more of a tax generator than a job generator,” he said. Other than Lightshift, there has been no other interest in battery energy storage projects in Washington County, Berry said.
