artigo.texto: A Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) aprovou nesta terça-feira, 27 de outubro, os editais dos dois leilões de baterias com redução de cerca de 39% nas garantias financeiras e flexibilização das condições de participação, mas manteve exigências para comprovar a capacidade financeira dos concorrentes. Durante a deliberação, a diretoria também indicou que uma eventual mudança na lei que atribui aos geradores o custeio da contratação exigirá nova avaliação da agência sobre os efeitos nos contratos. Aprovados por unanimidade, os editais estabelecem preços-teto de R$ 1,76 milhão por MW ao ano para o leilão de 2 de dezembro, voltado a sistemas com conteúdo nacional, e de R$ 1,58 milhão por MW ao ano para o certame de 4 de dezembro, sem essa exigência. Os valores foram definidos pelo Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME) e informados à agência na segunda-feira, 26 de outubro. Os contratos terão duração de 15 anos, com início de suprimento em 1º de agosto de 2028. As mudanças aprovadas após as consultas públicas incluem a possibilidade de formação de consórcios entre empresas do mesmo grupo econômico e a retirada de restrições à associação de baterias com usinas que possuem contratos regulados. A Aneel preservou, porém, mecanismos para evitar a dupla contagem do patrimônio líquido, verificar compromissos financeiros assumidos nos dois leilões e identificar investidores sujeitos a impedimentos de contratar. Flexibilização das regras Ao apresentar seu voto, o diretor-relator, Gentil Nogueira, destacou que as alterações permitiram reduzir restrições à participação sem dispensar a comprovação da capacidade dos empreendedores. Um dos exemplos é a formação de consórcios entre empresas do mesmo grupo econômico, proibida na minuta original para evitar a dupla contagem do patrimônio líquido. A solução aprovada permite a participação conjunta, mas determina que a comprovação patrimonial das empresas relacionadas seja feita exclusivamente pela controladora, sem somar o patrimônio das controladas. Sociedades coligadas continuam sujeitas à comprovação individual. A Aneel também decidiu verificar cumulativamente os compromissos financeiros assumidos nos dois leilões e ajustou as exigências de identificação dos cotistas de fundos de investimento em participações (FIPs). O relator modificou a proposta das áreas técnicas para considerar a participação econômica indireta de cada cotista no empreendimento, exigindo a identificação dos investidores cuja participação seja superior a 5%, considerando toda a cadeia societária. As garantias financeiras foram reduzidas após a atualização do investimento de referência de R$ 9,8 milhões para R$ 6 milhões por MW, com base nos parâmetros do Plano Decenal de Expansão de Energia (PDE) 2035. A garantia de proposta passou de R$ 98 mil para R$ 60 mil por MW, enquanto a garantia de fiel cumprimento e o patrimônio líquido mínimo caíram de R$ 980 mil para R$ 600 mil por MW. A diretoria também retirou a proibição de participação de baterias associadas a usinas com contratos regulados, desde que a associação não prejudique o atendimento dos compromissos da geradora. Permanecem vedados os sistemas colocalizados abrangidos pela outorga da própria usina e as associações que restrinjam o despacho das baterias pelo ONS. As concessionárias de transmissão poderão participar dos certames como agentes de armazenamento, respeitadas as obrigações previstas nos contratos de concessão, inclusive quanto à necessidade de autorização prévia da Aneel para outras atividades, quando aplicável. Durante a reunião, a Taesa pediu esclarecimentos sobre a participação sem autorização prévia e sem reversão de receitas à modicidade tarifária. Gentil afirmou que as condições dependerão da estrutura de cada empreendimento. Outra flexibilização permite a reposição e ampliação de equipamentos ao longo dos 15 anos de contrato, sem exigir que todos os componentes incorporados posteriormente sejam novos. No leilão nacional, contudo, deverá ser mantido o atendimento aos requisitos de conteúdo nacional considerados no credenciamento pelo Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES). Custeio e riscos contratuais A possibilidade de mudança na legislação sobre o rateio do Encargo de Reserva de Capacidade (Ercap) foi um dos pontos discutidos durante a aprovação dos editais. A Lei 15.269/2025 estabeleceu que os custos da contratação de baterias sejam rateados apenas entre os geradores de energia elétrica, regra que é objeto de propostas de alteração no Congresso Nacional. Durante as consultas públicas, associações de geração e armazenamento pediram referências genéricas aos responsáveis pelo encargo, para permitir a adaptação dos contratos a futuras alterações legislativas. A Aneel acolheu parcialmente as contribuições, substituindo no edital referências diretas aos geradores pela expressão “usuário de reserva de capacidade”. No entanto, manteve no contrato a definição desses usuários como os geradores abrangidos pela legislação. Durante a leitura do voto, Gentil explicou que a referência ao dispositivo legal é necessária para diferenciar o custeio das baterias da regra geral de pagamento da reserva de capacidade. Segundo ele, mesmo com uma redação mais genérica, uma eventual mudança legislativa exigiria nova análise da Aneel sobre seus efeitos nos contratos. “Qualquer texto que fosse aqui colocado, ele invariavelmente traria discussão aqui para a Aneel sobre os efeitos sobre esse contrato”, afirmou. O diretor-geral da agência, Sandoval Feitosa, também defendeu a manutenção das referências à legislação vigente. “Se houver alguma alteração legislativa, que é própria da dinâmica legislativa, nós vamos recepcionar aqui e faremos com a maior agilidade e eficiência possível”, disse. artigo.texto: SHAKOPEE, Minn. (Oct. 27, 2026) -- Xcel Energy advanced its battery storage strategy Monday with the arrival of battery units at its Blue Lake site, a significant construction achievement that supports the company's efforts to build a more flexible, resilient energy system for customers across Minnesota. The Blue Lake project is part of a broader plan to diversify the resources that power Minnesota while maintaining the reliable service customers depend on and keeping bills as low as possible. Together with two planned projects in Becker, Minnesota, Xcel Energy expects to operate more than 735 megawatts of battery energy storage in Minnesota by the end of 2027, creating the largest battery portfolio in the Upper Midwest. "For more than a century, energy companies have generated electricity when customers need it and delivered it almost immediately. Battery storage changes what's possible. It allows us to store energy and dispatch it when it's needed most, giving us a powerful new tool to maintain reliability, support growing energy needs and make the most of the diverse resources that power our system," said Bria Shea, president of Xcel Energy–Minnesota, North Dakota and South Dakota. Battery storage helps strengthen grid reliability by storing energy when it is available and dispatching it back to the grid when customer demand is higher. The evolution of energy storage systems over the years means they can be deployed more broadly at existing energy sites such as Blue Lake, allowing Xcel Energy to leverage existing infrastructure while integrating new technologies. The Blue Lake batteries will store energy generated across Xcel Energy's Upper Midwest system, including energy from wind, solar, nuclear and natural gas resources. The 135.5-megawatt battery energy storage facility will include 132 battery units capable of storing energy and delivering electricity for up to four hours, enough energy to power approximately 125,000 homes when demand is highest. "The Blue Lake project demonstrates how battery storage is becoming an increasingly important part of grid operations," said Justin Meagher, Xcel Energy battery storage project manager. "These systems can respond quickly to changing conditions, store energy when it's available and provide electricity when customer demand is high. That flexibility helps us operate the electric system more efficiently while continuing to deliver reliable service to customers." The Blue Lake Battery Energy Storage System is expected to begin serving customers in 2027. # # # About Xcel Energy Xcel Energy (NASDAQ: XEL) is a leading energy provider, dedicated to serving millions of customers with excellence. We make energy work better for customers, helping them thrive every day. That means always raising the bar — delivering better service and providing more reliable, resilient and sustainable energy. Headquartered in Minneapolis, we work every day to generate and distribute electricity and gas to customers across eight states: Minnesota, Colorado, Wisconsin, Michigan, North Dakota, South Dakota, New Mexico and Texas. For more information, visit xcelenergy.com or follow us on X and Facebook.

artigo.texto: Sungrow is partnering with ENGIE and Elecnor to advance the 150 MW / 300 MWh Hazelwood Battery Energy Storage System expansion (HBESS 2) in Victoria, Australia. The project will use Sungrow’s advanced battery storage and grid-forming technology to support electricity network stability and enable greater integration of renewable energy. Commercial operations are targeted for 2028. Under the project, Sungrow Australia will serve as the technology provider, while Elecnor will undertake the balance of plant (BOP) contracting work. The expansion will add significant battery storage capacity to Victoria’s energy infrastructure and strengthen the role of large-scale energy storage in Australia’s National Electricity Market (NEM). The Hazelwood BESS 2 project will feature 66 units of Sungrow’s ST5015-UX battery energy storage system, part of its PowerTitan 2.0 series. The installation will also include 33 SC6900UD-MV medium-voltage power conversion system (PCS) inverters and the company’s EMS3000 smart controller. These components are designed to support efficient energy storage, power conversion and system management in utility-scale applications. The PowerTitan 2.0 system incorporates high energy density to optimise storage capacity and liquid-cooled technology to maintain stable operating temperatures. Its battery management capabilities are designed to monitor performance, support battery safety and improve long-term operational reliability. The associated PCS inverters will facilitate power conversion and provide responsive support for electricity grid operations. Grid-forming technology is another important feature of the project. It is designed to help maintain voltage and frequency stability as the share of renewable energy in the electricity network increases. The technology can respond rapidly to changing grid conditions, supporting reliable operation during fluctuations in electricity supply and demand. The integration of grid-forming capabilities with battery storage is expected to help accommodate higher levels of variable renewable generation. It can also provide advanced network support under changing operating conditions, contributing to a more resilient electricity system. As Australia continues to transition towards renewable energy, large-scale battery storage is becoming increasingly important for managing fluctuations in generation from solar and wind power. Battery systems can store electricity when supply is available and deliver it when required, helping balance the electricity network and improve the flexibility of the power system. Thomas Hou, Managing Director at Sungrow Australia, said the Hazelwood BESS 2 project represents an important step in advancing grid-forming energy storage in Australia. He said the collaboration with ENGIE aims to deploy advanced storage technology to support grid stability and greater renewable energy integration. The project highlights the growing role of battery energy storage systems in Australia’s evolving energy infrastructure. By combining utility-scale storage with grid-forming technology, Hazelwood BESS 2 is expected to support Victoria’s electricity network as renewable generation expands. Keystone FlexBase is building a technology center in Laufenburg, Aargau. At its heart is a battery that will one day help stabilize the power grid. But from the perspective of FlexBase CEO Marcel Aumer, this can only be the beginning. When the Keystone-SDA news agency visited FlexBase in mid-September, the large construction site in Laufenburg was characterized above all by a massive excavation pit and numerous cranes. In the future, a building 218 meters long, 80 meters wide, 25 meters deep, and 30 meters high will stand there, as Aumer explained. To blend into the landscape, the concrete structure will be clad with a blue photovoltaic system, as Aumer explained. This complements the often-blue skies of the Fricktal region. The system will be one of the largest PV facade installations in Europe and will have “a capacity of at least two megawatts.” However, according to Aumer, the PV system is out of proportion to the battery storage system being installed. Plans at the time called for 108 vanadium redox flow batteries (VRFB) with a maximum capacity of 1.2 gigawatts by 2029—equivalent to that of the Leibstadt nuclear power plant. According to FlexBase, the planned storage capacity of 2.1 gigawatt-hours corresponds to the electricity needs of 170,000 households over a 24-hour period. Unlike a lithium-ion battery, the VRFB model planned for Laufenburg is neither flammable nor explosive, as Aumer noted. The tanks are mostly filled with water, which also simplifies disposal. Furthermore, the vanadium dissolved in the water—which is used as an electrolyte—is reusable. There is virtually no degradation, and the service life of redox flow batteries is longer than that of lithium-ion storage systems, for which the disposal problem remains unresolved. The largest facility of its kind to date is located in China and began operations at the start of the year, as Rongke Power announced at the time. According to the company’s figures, its capacity and output amount to one gigawatt-hour and 200 megawatts—significantly less than what is planned for Laufenburg. From Aumer’s perspective, this is the technology for a sustainable future, and it is gaining ground worldwide. “I have clear goals in mind,” said Aumer. “The peaks caused by renewable energy need to be smoothed out.” This refers both to short-term fluctuations and to storing excess capacity during the day and releasing it at night when capacity is insufficient. “But we still have a long, long way to go before we can ensure a 24-hour, 356-day power supply from renewable energy sources,” Aumer said. He cited Europe as an example. In its Electrification Action Plan published in July, the European Commission cited a need for 200 gigawatts of storage capacity by 2030 and as much as 500 gigawatts by 2040. According to Aumer, the demand for power and capacity is enormous. “Our project is large, but our 1.2 gigawatts of power and 2.1 gigawatt-hours of capacity are just a drop in the bucket,” Aumer noted. However, he added, batteries cannot simply be connected to the grid at will. The grids are aging, and there is a lack of connection capacity. Expansion is difficult—partly due to objections. “It’s the only place to build something on this scale. There’s no other place like it,” Aumer said of the site. That’s because the Laufenburg star connects the Swiss power grid to the European grid—here, more than 41 cross-border lines provide access to the European electricity market. “I don’t have that anywhere else,” said Aumer. Aumer knows the location very well. Over the past ten years, he has been coming and going from the Stern in Laufenburg for work. He developed the idea for the project over the course of several years, drawing on his experience. When the property in Laufenburg went up for sale in 2023, he “knew within a second: This is it.” When it comes to finances, Aumer is keeping a low profile. He said the total costs would range from 2.5 to 5 billion Swiss francs. The money comes from private funds—but he does not want to publicly disclose his investors. The CEO revealed that he is the majority shareholder of FlexBase. However, he isn't doing it for the money—his passion project can only be realized in this location and in this way, as a campus that covers a wide range of subject areas. These include, for example, an AI data center above the Batterie and space for startups.

artigo.texto: Economic leaders announce plan for possible data center in Delhi Township: Here’s what you need to know Possible data center site planned at Holt Economic Opportunity Park LANSING, Mich. (News 10) - The Lansing Economic Area Partnership and Lighthouse Sustainability want to build a data center on 423 acres off College Road that was set aside for future economic development in 2003. The site is known as the Holt Economic Opportunity Park. It is west of US-127 and south of Holt Road. The two organizations announced the effort Tuesday. What LEAP and Lighthouse are proposing According to the announcement, a strategic plan “will define what a data center project should look like before an application is filed.” The framework is “intended to change how those larger projects work” and will “begin with the community, establish expectations and propose projects that can meet rigorous environmental standards and provide meaningful community investment.” Bob Trezise, president and CEO of LEAP, said the announcement describes a process and not a project. “What we actually announced today is a process, not a project,” Trezise said. “We are basically flipping the script on how to introduce a major economic development project. We want to do community engagement first.” The pitch includes a fully funded residential solar and battery program estimated to cut participating homeowners’ energy costs by 50%. It also includes a required community benefits agreement and a separate $20 million community investment fund. “It’s kind of a Goldilocks. It’s not a big thousand acre site in a farm field. It’s not in an urban area. It’s in an industrial area. And we also believe that the data center itself is going to be very unique in being a clean, green data center,” Trezise said. In a press release, Trezise said: “Delhi Township had a vision for the property before we sought a development partner. We chose Lighthouse because they bring deep renewable energy expertise and a commitment to making development work for the people who live here. That combination matters. Smart growth means attracting investment that strengthens our economy while protecting the natural resources and way of life that make this community home.” No application filed, no end user named No formal application has been filed, and no end user has been identified. Delhi Township has had a moratorium on data center reviews since April. Township Manager Tracy Miller said the board approved a 12-month moratorium. LEAP and Lighthouse said they will “respect that moratorium and focus on community engagement strategy.” The engagement process gives residents time to examine studies, question the project team and provide input before the township is asked to consider future development. Trezise said community input will be the ultimate decision maker. “It’s definitely up to the community. Delhi Township has a moratorium in place. We welcome that. It provides great space to have a non-pressure conversation,” Trezise said. A community engagement webinar is scheduled for Tuesday at 6:30 p.m. Delhi Township responds Miller released a statement Tuesday afternoon: “Delhi Township is committed to being a great place for residents to live, work and raise a family. As the state and federal government have continued to consider rules and regulations for data centers, and they have continued to be a significant issue for those communities currently considering proposals, our Township Board approved a 12-month moratorium on data centers last April,” Miller said. “The Township is learning about the LEAP/Lighthouse Sustainability announcement at the same time as members of the media. Township Board members have not received any kind of land use application or proposal from a data center developer. There is no data center proposal being considered or discussed. Board members have not communicated with a data center developer and they have not, and will not, sign any non-disclosure agreements,” Miller said. “To be very clear, this topic has not been discussed at Township Board meetings. The Township and its staff are not involved in this. The LEAP/Lighthouse effort is independent from the Delhi Township Board, Planning Commission or administration and the Township was not at all aware of this announcement before receiving a press release on Tuesday,” Miller said. Neighbors push back Neighbors who back up to the land, including Nicole Blumhart, disagree with the description of the area as industrial. “This is a residential community with 112 homes, and it’s not industrial whatsoever,” said Blumhart, who lives next to the proposed site. “You don’t hear anything. I cannot imagine living here with a 24-7 hum. It would be a living nightmare.” “I really hope that they hear our concerns,” Blumhart said. This is a developing story. artigo.texto: Columbus data centers could pay more under proposed rate hike for high-usage customers COLUMBUS, Ohio (WSYX) — Columbus Water and Power reached its October 26 deadline to submit a proposed rate structure for high-usage customers. The proposal comes as utility costs remain a concern for Columbus residents and city leaders look for ways to ensure large customers cover the costs of the utilities being used. Columbus Councilman Christopher Wyche, chair of the Public Utilities & Sustainability Committee, said the city wants to identify customers whose water demand regularly puts additional strain on the system. “I think we want to have that flexibility to one, have conversations with customers who may face the surcharge, but two, as we are having those discussions, to find those who are peaking and surcharging on a regular basis, that they are in this methodology,” Wyche said during a Public Utilities & Sustainability Committee meeting on October 21. How would the new rates work? Columbus Water and Power Deputy Director Jon Lee said the proposed structure includes a high-demand surcharge for about 400 commercial customers whose water usage spikes above typical levels. “The purpose of the rate is straightforward. It is to more fairly recover the additional system capacity costs created by commercial customers whose water demand rises significantly above their normal usage,” Lee said. Lee said the utility must maintain enough capacity to meet periods of unusually high demand, including the treatment, pumping, storage and distribution needed to deliver water. “When a customer has unusually high peaks, we still have to maintain the treatment, pumping, storage and distribution capacity necessary to serve that peak,” Lee said. “The proposed surcharge will cover those additional costs.” Under the proposal, commercial customers using at least 100 hundred cubic feet (CCF) of water per month and meeting a peak-demand factor of 2.0 times their typical usage would qualify for the high-demand surcharge. One CCF equals 748 gallons, meaning 100 CCF is equivalent to 74,800 gallons per month. That number is roughly 15 times the average water usage of a single-family home. The proposed high-demand surcharge is $1.62 per CCF. According to Lee, about 426 customers would qualify under the current model, generating an estimated $6 million in revenue. “Based on our current modeling, approximately 426 customers would qualify with those parameters. Customers creating higher system capacity requirements should bear an appropriate share of those costs,” Lee said. The proposal focuses on water usage and infrastructure costs. It does not establish whether data centers or other large customers would face higher electricity rates under a separate structure. What could it mean for residents? City leaders say the goal is to keep customers with unusually high water and energy demand from shifting the additional costs onto the average homeowner. “We should be careful not to spread those extra costs onto households and businesses already relying on the system,” said Emmanuel Remy, vice-chair of the Public Utilities & Sustainability Committee. However, the proposed surcharge does not guarantee lower household utility bills or prevent future rate increases. The city has not indicated that residents would see immediate savings if the proposal is approved. The Water & Power Dept. also recommended changing its water capacity fees so new customers help pay for planned infrastructure projects, including the Home Road water treatment plant, rather than shifting those costs onto existing ratepayers. Customers who do not meet the proposed high-demand criteria would not be subject to this particular surcharge. If approved, the new charges are expected to begin in late 2027 or early 2028. What's next? Water revenue would shift some costs away from residential and small business customers, making their standard water rates about 1.6% lower than usual. While that would only slightly offset Columbus’ planned 18% water rate increase in 2027, it could help limit future increases as data centers and other high-demand users grow. Columbus Water and Power confirmed Monday that it submitted its rate recommendations to City Council. The department declined an interview before the council's public hearing on the proposal. The public hearing is scheduled for Thursday, November 12. The legislation is then expected to go before City Council for a first reading on November 16 and second reading on November 23. The proposal will need to move through the council process before the new rates can take effect.

artigo.texto: Emergent technologies raise concerns about natural resources, exploitation and education in Montana From mining to timber to tourism, Montana’s natural resources have been the bedrock of economic opportunity and industrial extraction for more than a century. Now that data center developers have descended on the Treasure State, some local tribes are outlawing these projects to safeguard sovereignty, land and water. There’s a lot to like about Montana for companies seeking to site data centers, according to energy industry veteran Bob Morris with Montana Technological University. Reliable, affordable electricity, he said, is a draw for data center builders — and Montana boasts the seventh-lowest electricity rates in the country. Plus, he said, the northern climate makes for economical cooling of the machinery used in these facilities. “We’ve got great infrastructure,” he added. “We’ve got a good fiber-optic network. We’ve got good highways, good rail transport, and then there’s us. Montana’s got a great workforce, hardworking and a thriving business environment.” The attraction doesn’t necessarily go both ways between potential developers and the communities in their crosshairs. In 2026, the Fort Peck Tribes and the Northern Cheyenne Tribal Council both made official policies to keep data centers out. Leaders for both groups said they wanted to avoid risks to their natural environment, and the long history of outside exploitation didn’t endear the developers to Native community members. But technological developments like AI will still be a part of Montana’s digital landscape, no matter where the infrastructure to power them ends up being built. Some Indigenous technology leaders from across the region have advocated for tribes to embrace AI so community members avoid being left out of a major trend shaping education and career possibilities. Software engineer Michael Running Wolf from Birney, Montana, on the Northern Cheyenne Indian Reservation, travels North America promoting AI use as an avenue to address pressing Native community needs. His work with a team of “Indigenous technologists” from the Crow Tribe and the Little Shell Chippewa in Montana focuses on language revitalization using AI. He cautions against the impulse to turn away from innovative technologies altogether. Similarly, Caitlin Bordeaux, a director at the computer science group Indigitize, is a Sicangu Lakota educator who works across Montana and South Dakota engaging Indigenous communities in culturally relevant digital education. Indigitize helps expand computer science opportunities for underserved students in Indian Country, rooted in the hope that emerging technologies can support Native priorities rather than exacerbating existing disparities. Ready for the future Access issues for high-tech tools disproportionately hinder small, rural schools, according to Montana Digital Academy Executive Director Jason Neiffer. To level the playing field, the academy’s new Frontier Learning Lab offers resources for Montana teachers to navigate AI and other digital tools while sharing insights and best practices for implementation. Neiffer told Buffalo’s Fire he understands the hesitations around joining the AI bandwagon, and he hopes the lab can inform thoughtful approaches to adoption. “Education has to prepare students for the world in which they’re going to live,” Neiffer said. Grant funding for the Frontier Learning Lab came from the nonprofit aiEDU, which equips teachers with an understanding of AI readiness and AI literacy so they can effectively support students and families encountering new technology on the ground. The organization’s national programs lead, Connor Mulvaney, lives in Polson on the Flathead Reservation, where he’s collaborated with the local community to boost knowledge around using AI and deploying it responsibly. “I think we need to be informed decisionmakers,” he told Buffalo’s Fire. He said his goal with aiEDU in Montana is to give individual communities the foundations for determining their own preferred approaches to new technology. Since AI is hardly a singular, static piece of new technology, Mulvaney added, the decisions being made today will likely need to be revisited and built upon as these concepts evolve over time. It’s important, he said, to make sure Indigenous communities have what they need to navigate current conversations and prepare for what might come next. And research by the Montana Afterschool Alliance, another grantee supported by aiEDU, demonstrates the important role young people have to play in guiding and informing these discussions. In 2025, the alliance piloted community conversations in parts of Montana that rarely see themselves considered the vanguard of change and innovation. The team deliberately began their work with convenings in Harlem on the Fort Belknap Reservation, Poplar on the Fort Peck Reservation and in the Flathead Reservation communities of Pablo and Ronan. The alliance focused heavily on incorporating input from younger community members into these conversations, revealing noteworthy ways Indigenous youth are interacting with AI. “Through our conversations we heard the sentiment that unlike prior technology rollouts, generative AI was already in use from within communities,” Heather Jameson from the afterschool alliance told Buffalo’s Fire. “And in many cases youth are outpacing adults in adoption.” The findings in the alliance’s landscape review from these sessions showed Montana Native youth have a healthy skepticism of AI and they recognize its limitations for providing factually accurate answers to specific questions. They’re highly exposed to AI-generated multimedia via social channels, less versed in using large language model chatbots, and good at identifying AI content in ways that often far surpass their elders’ ability to recognize such media. artigo.texto: Kern CASA program electrifies first home with new appliances, solar and battery storage BAKERSFIELD, Calif. (KBAK/KBFX) — For one Kern County homeowner, a new set of home upgrades means more than new appliances. Maria Perez’s home is the first to be fully retrofitted through the Kern CASA Project, a program that helps qualifying families make energy and health-related improvements at no cost. Perez, who has asthma and lives on a fixed income, received a series of upgrades including an electric HVAC system, water heater, stove and dryer. Her home was also weatherized and equipped with solar panels and battery storage. Project Manager Brianda Castro said the work is designed to reduce the home’s reliance on gas while also addressing indoor air quality. “Simply just switching gas appliances to electric appliances and making sure that we remove any fossil fuel footprint with gas combustion from the home,” Castro said. Perez had previously received asthma-related services through the Central California Asthma Collaborative. Castro said that connection helped make her a strong fit for the project, which is also focused on reducing pollutants inside the home. “So, when you eliminate the use of gas in the home it eliminates those pollutants and so therefore it creates a healthier just air quality within the home,” Castro said. The cost of making those changes can be a major hurdle for families, Castro said, particularly for lower-income households that may not be able to afford newer appliances or larger home upgrades on their own. “And then lastly these appliances are also newer which means that they are not very affordable for the regular low-income household. the beauty about the programs that we offer to residents in low-income communities is that it has no cost to the homeowner,” Castro said. Perez said the improvements are especially meaningful because managing her asthma while living on a fixed income has often meant prioritizing household expenses over her own health needs. The first completed home is expected to be one of several. Castro said the project plans to complete upgrades at another 18 homes. The funding also included a workforce development component. Twenty Kern County residents were trained in skills related to home retrofits, and Castro said some have since worked on homes included in the project. Although applications for this round of Kern CASA funding are closed, Castro said her team continues to connect families with other programs that may help them qualify for similar home improvements.

artigo.texto: WUXI, China, Oct. 28, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Solid-state batteries are at a critical stage of transition from pilot production to large-scale manufacturing. To address key challenges in densification and solid-solid interface contact, Lead Intelligent has developed a horizontal warm isostatic pressing machine that delivers uniform three-dimensional pressure of up to 600 MPa across a wide temperature range from room temperature (RT) to 150°C. The machine achieves temperature control accuracy of ±2°C and pressure control accuracy of ±2%. Integrating automatic loading and unloading with precise, coordinated temperature and pressure control, the machine can increase cell density to over 95%, accelerating the industrialization of solid-state batteries. As solid-state batteries move toward mass production, two major challenges remain: high impedance caused by insufficient solid-solid interface contact, and the limitations of conventional unidirectional pressing, including uneven density and pronounced edge effects. Based on Pascal's principle, isostatic pressing applies isotropic pressurization within a sealed chamber to achieve multidimensional material compaction and densification. It is a key processing route for addressing solid-solid interface contact challenges in solid-state batteries. For the practical requirements of large-scale solid-state battery manufacturing, warm isostatic pressing offers an effective balance between densification performance, production efficiency, and manufacturing cost, making it a highly cost-effective option for mass production. As construction of solid-state battery capacity accelerates, warm isostatic pressing machines are becoming core incremental machines for battery manufacturers' next-generation solid-state production lines. Core Technology: Precise Temperature-Pressure Coordination for High-Precision Process Control Building on its R&D system, Lead Intelligent's horizontal warm isostatic pressing machine overcomes the "black box" limitations of traditional warm isostatic pressing process by enabling real-time monitoring of temperature and pressure inside the chamber. The machine upgrades from conventional unidirectional pressing to precise temperature-pressure coordination to promote closer contact between electrodes and electrolytes, making it well suited for solid-state battery mass production. - Pressure system: It delivers uniform three-dimensional pressure of up to 600 MPa, with pressure control accuracy ≤±2%. Automatic pressure compensation and emergency depressurization functions keep pressure fluctuations within ±2% during a 30-minute pressure holding period, ensuring process stability and repeatability. - Temperature system: The working temperatures can reach up to 150°C, and can be adjusted within a wide operating range from room temperature (RT) to 150°C, with temperature control accuracy of ±2°C. The initial heating time to 150°C takes no more than three hours, balancing process adaptability with mass production cycle-time requirements. - Chamber specifications: The working chamber inner diameter is ≥400 mm, the effective length is ≥4,000 mm, and the volume is around 500 L. It accommodates batch processing of workpieces in various sizes and meets the capacity requirements of GWh-scale production lines. Designed for Mass Production: Comprehensive Optimization for Large-Scale Manufacturing For GWh-scale manufacturing, warm isostatic pressing machines must do more than meet core process specifications. They shall also coordinate with whole line cycle time, logistics systems, and upstream and downstream processes. To meet these requirements, Lead Intelligent has optimized machine structure, automatic operation, and safety systems in parallel. Horizontal Design for Continuous Production Lines The horizontal working chamber and automatic loading and unloading design significantly reduce factory height requirements while seamlessly integrating with automatic logistics systems to meet the needs of continuous production and material transfer between upstream and downstream processes, adapting to takt-based operation on large-scale production lines. Electrodes and solid electrolytes can be stacked and assembled before being loaded into the chamber for pressing and densification, simplifying process flow. Full-process Automation to Minimize Manual Intervention The machine enables unmanned operation throughout cell pretreatment and material box circulation. It integrates four key functions: cell hot air preheating, cold air drying and cooling, automatic fixture loading and unloading, and material box automatic circulation. The machine covers the entire workflow including loading, pretreatment, isostatic pressing and unloading, minimizing manual intervention and improving production efficiency and process consistency within each batch. Multi-Layered Safety Controls for Reliable Operation The machine incorporates a comprehensive multi-layered safety assurance system. At the foundational level, the machine is equipped with dual pressure and temperature monitoring for the chamber, together with pipeline pressure-relief ports to safeguard machine operation. In addition, an innovative triple deformation monitoring system provides real-time monitoring to enhance operational safety and maintain process precision. As a world-leading provider of intelligent manufacturing solutions for the new energy industry, Lead Intelligent has completed the full-process layout for solid-state battery manufacturing, covering key stages including dry electrode processing, high-precision stacking, warm isostatic pressing, and formation and grading. The company has the capacity for batch delivery of GWh-level solid-state battery whole line solutions. artigo.texto: Wall Street's fastest traders are building data centers and backing chip startups to stay ahead in AI High-frequency traders like Jane Street and Hudson River Trading are now racing each other for AI computing power. The biggest firms are spending billions on cloud contracts, startups, and their own data centers, Bloomberg reports. Part of the reason is that they increasingly rely on machine learning to predict market moves. One executive estimates that compute spending is now ten to twenty times higher than it was before ChatGPT launched. XTX Markets is building a data center in Finland, and Jane Street runs one in Texas with more than 4,000 Nvidia GPUs. Hudson River spends $1 billion a year on AI, according to AI chief Iain Dunning, and signed a multiyear deal with CoreWeave. Jane Street went a different route. It invested $1 billion directly in CoreWeave and committed $6 billion to its computing services. Jane Street also led a funding round for chip startup Etched and became the first customer for its AI chip, which is supposed to deliver more performance by running at a lower voltage. According to Bloomberg, the industry sees rising costs and fast-aging chips as real risks. Executives like Jan Boomaars, CEO of Amsterdam-based high-frequency trader Optiver, still think doing nothing is more dangerous. artigo.texto: Siga o Times Brasil - Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC no Setor elétrico defende novas regras para baterias e aponta economia de R$ 1,6 bilhão por ano Publicado 26/10/2026 • 18:01 | Atualizado há 2 dias BREAKING NEWS: Polícia Federal faz buscas em endereços ligados a Flávio Bolsonaro Oracle integra ChatGPT e Codex a seus aplicativos e amplia linha de chips para computação em nuvem S&P 500 fecha em alta pela segunda sessão consecutiva, impulsionado por ações de chips e queda do petróleo IPO da Anthropic pode ser “ficção especulativa” ou um “momento histórico” Boeing reduz prejuízo no terceiro trimestre com alta nas vendas de defesa, mas foco segue na produção do 737 Max Nvidia investe US$ 3 bilhões na Meta após big tech anunciar plano de captar US$ 95 bilhões para infraestrutura de IA KEY POINTS Foto: Canva Associações do setor elétrico defendem a equiparação dos sistemas de armazenamento de energia por baterias às demais soluções de capacidade no regime de custeio da Reserva de Capacidade. Em manifesto conjunto, as entidades questionam a atribuição dos custos dessas tecnologias exclusivamente aos geradores, enquanto os encargos relacionados às demais soluções são distribuídos entre os usuários finais conforme os parâmetros previstos em lei. Segundo as associações, o modelo atual cria uma divergência entre o caráter sistêmico dos serviços prestados, a distribuição dos benefícios e a responsabilidade pelo pagamento. As entidades argumentam que os sistemas de armazenamento podem contribuir para reduzir outros encargos dos consumidores ao otimizar a operação do parque gerador, considerando diferentes fontes de energia. Um estudo da VOLT Robotics aponta que os sistemas de armazenamento de energia por baterias, conhecidos como BESS (Battery Energy Storage System), podem reduzir a variação do Preço de Liquidação das Diferenças (PLD), diminuir o acionamento de usinas termelétricas e gerar uma economia superior a R$ 1,6 bilhão por ano para os consumidores. O manifesto também questiona os efeitos do modelo de custeio sobre os preços da energia. De acordo com as entidades, a atribuição do encargo aos geradores não impede o repasse dos valores aos consumidores finais, inclusive com a incorporação de tributos e despesas administrativas adicionais. Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. Siga o Times | CNBC No ambiente de contratação regulado, as associações afirmam que a Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) já reconheceu a necessidade de incorporar o custo integralmente e de forma automática às tarifas. No mercado livre, o repasse poderá ocorrer por meio de renegociações ou reajustes de preços. Já na autoprodução de energia, o encargo poderá integrar os custos de bens e serviços, com possíveis efeitos sobre a competitividade da indústria brasileira e repercussões para os consumidores. As entidades também avaliam que o modelo elimina o sinal econômico necessário ao ajuste da demanda. Por isso, defendem regras equivalentes para os sistemas de armazenamento por baterias e as demais soluções de capacidade, incluindo alternativas relacionadas à potência e à flexibilidade. Na avaliação das associações, a equiparação permitiria aos consumidores acesso à tecnologia mais eficiente para cada cenário, favorecendo a redução do custo final da energia e aumentando a transparência na distribuição dos encargos. Entre as medidas defendidas está a aprovação do Projeto de Lei (PL) 3716/2025. Segundo o manifesto, a iniciativa contribuiria para ampliar a segurança jurídica e regulatória e criar condições para o desenvolvimento sustentável do mercado brasileiro de armazenamento de energia por baterias. Assinam o documento a Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias (ABEEólica), a Associação Brasileira dos Investidores em Autoprodução de Energia (ABIAPE), a Associação Brasileira da Indústria do Hidrogênio Verde (ABIHV), a Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia (ABSAE), a Associação Brasileira de Energia Solar Fotovoltaica (ABSOLAR) e a Associação Brasileira dos Produtores Independentes de Energia Elétrica (APINE). 🔷 Canal 562 ClaroTV+ | Canal 562 Sky | Canal 592 Vivo | Canal 187 Oi | Operadoras regionais 🔷 TV SINAL ABERTO: parabólicas canal 562 🔷 ONLINE: www.timesbrasil.com.br | YouTube 🔷 FAST Channels: Samsung TV Plus, LG Channels, TCL Channels, Pluto TV, Roku, Zapping | Novos Streamings

artigo.texto: KARACHI: Pakistan’s military-owned Margalla Heavy Industries Limited (MHIL) has signed an agreement with Chinese partners and local investors to set up a $2.25 billion lithium-ion battery manufacturing plant in Rawalpindi, an official said on Monday, with production expected to begin within months of the government approving a policy for the sector, reports Arab News. The development comes as the South Asian country seeks to reduce its reliance on imported energy technologies and develop local manufacturing capacity amid growing demand for energy storage, electric vehicles and renewable energy. Lithium-ion batteries are central to storing electricity generated by solar and wind power and powering electric mobility, making domestic production a potential avenue for reducing import costs and attracting foreign investment. The gigafactory’s feasibility studies have been completed and the project is awaiting approval before it could start manufacturing, according to Hamad Ali Mansoor, CEO of the Engineering Development Board (EDB), an apex government body entrusted to strengthen the engineering base in Pakistan. “The building is ready, the machines are installed, so after the policy comes, the production will start within six to eight months,” Mansoor told Arab News, adding that Islamabad was working with Chinese and local stakeholders to invest in the multibillion-dollar project. “They are investing $2.25 billion in Pakistan.”Located at Heavy Industries Taxila in Rawalpindi district, MHIL manufactures defence equipment, including battle tanks, armoured vehicles, unmanned drones, protective gear, compact battery energy storage system and EV buses and two-wheelers. Arab News reached out to MHIL’s general manager for digital media, Muhammad Ameen, but he was not immediately available for comment.The development comes days after Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif approved the Automotive and Auto Parts Manufacturing Policy 2026-2031, which awaits IMF approval over proposed tax incentives for Pakistan’s Electric Vehicles industry and their potential revenue implications. After the new EV-based auto policy takes effect, EDB estimates that Pakistan’s demand for battery energy storage systems (BESS) could reach as much as to 100,000 megawatts (MW) by June 2030. Building a local plant to manufacture lithium-ion batteries would be crucial for the cash-strapped country, which aims to shift its petrol-powered vehicles to EVs to save billions of dollars it spends every year to import fuel. Mansoor said the battery gigafactory project was signed in July with a Chinese company he described as one of the “top-tier manufacturers in China” alongside a local private-sector investor. He would not name the Chinese and local investors now. “They are manufacturing lithium-ion cells,” he said, adding that the facility would produce lithium-ion cells having a capacity of more than 1,000MW annually.EDB has estimated that grid stabilization alone could require 3,000-5,000MW of battery storage and that meeting the projected demand would require four to five gigafactories, each costing around $1 billion to $1.25 billion. “In our industry, we will have up to 100,000 megawatts of battery energy storage systems. This is a very large capacity. For this, we need four to five gigafactories,” the EDB CEO said.The first factory will initially produce around 200-300 MW before reaching its planned capacity of 1,000 megawatts, according to Mansoor. “If our economy grows by 5.0 per cent or more than 5.0 per cent of GDP (gross domestic product), then by June 2030, our demand will be up to 100,000MW,” he said.“And if our GDP grows by less than 3 percent, then our demand will be up to 80,000MW.” Mansoor said the demand would come from households, commercial buildings, industry and electric vehicles, including two-wheelers, three-wheelers, cars, buses and trucks.The government has prepared a lithium battery manufacturing policy that was submitted to the Ministry of Industries in March and is awaiting approval, according to the official. The plan includes four major factories, three in Punjab’s Lahore, Faisalabad and Rawalpindi divisions and one in southern city of Karachi, aimed at building domestic capacity for batteries used in electric vehicles and energy storage. The policy would require manufacturers to export a specified percentage of production, although Mansoor declined to provide the target before the policy’s approval.“We will manufacture it in Pakistan and export it,” he said, adding that the policy incorporates international safety and performance standards. Pakistan currently assembles around 3,000-4,000MW of batteries as well as parts like motors, controllers and chargers, but needs to move toward domestic manufacturing to avoid costly imports, according to Mansoor.“All these parts we [will] start manufacturing 100 per cent in Pakistan by next year,” he added.

artigo.texto: O mercado de carbono na encruzilhada da reforma tributária Falta de definição sobre a natureza jurídica dos créditos de carbono abre lacuna para interpretações diversas e incerteza sobre incidência dos novos tributos Atualizado A regulamentação da reforma tributária acabou criando uma contradição relevante para o mercado brasileiro de carbono. Ao instituir o Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões (SBCE), a Lei nº 15.042/2024 buscou conferir tratamento tributário favorecido aos créditos de carbono, afastando a incidência de PIS e Cofins para estimular o desenvolvimento desse mercado estratégico. Entretanto, a disciplina do IBS e da CBS, introduzida pela Lei Complementar nº 214/2025, não reproduziu essa diretriz nem definiu expressamente a natureza jurídica desses ativos para fins de incidência dos novos tributos. A lacuna abre espaço para interpretações divergentes – se os créditos de carbono constituem ativo financeiro, valor mobiliário ou direito sujeito à tributação sobre o consumo – e cria um ambiente de insegurança jurídica justamente em um setor que depende de previsibilidade para viabilizar investimentos de longo prazo. Em determinadas interpretações, a carga tributária incidente sobre essas operações poderá alcançar cerca de 30%, comprometendo a competitividade do mercado brasileiro. A raiz desse impasse decorre da assimetria conceitual estabelecida pelo próprio arcabouço normativo. O artigo 14 da Lei nº 15.042/2024 estipula que os ativos do SBCE e os créditos de carbono configuram valores mobiliários apenas quando negociados nos mercados financeiro e de capitais sob regulação da CVM, enquanto o artigo 53 da mesma lei os qualifica como frutos civis nas iniciativas florestais. Em contrapartida, a Lei Complementar nº 214/2025 restringiu a não incidência de IBS e CBS aos títulos e valores mobiliários (artigo 6º, inciso VII), sujeitando a negociação de direitos e bens imateriais à regra geral do imposto sobre o consumo (artigo 4º). As alienações diretas de balcão – que concentram o mercado voluntário 2 ficam, assim, desprovidas de proteção tributária expressa. Com o término da desoneração do PIS e da Cofins em 2027, tais operações migrarão para uma alíquota padrão estimada entre 27% e 30%. Essa indefinição afeta toda a cadeia do mercado de carbono, alcançando empresas desenvolvedoras de projetos, produtores rurais, instituições financeiras, plataformas de negociação e companhias que utilizam créditos de carbono para cumprir metas de descarbonização. Além do aumento potencial da carga tributária, a ausência de regras claras tende a exigir revisões contratuais, provisões tributárias e reavaliações de investimentos até que haja posicionamento do legislador ou da Administração Tributária. A nosso ver, essa situação contraria os princípios da segurança jurídica, da neutralidade e da coerência normativa que orientaram a reforma tributária. Espera-se, portanto, que a regulamentação complementar ou eventuais ajustes legislativos esclareçam o tratamento tributário desses ativos, preservando a finalidade do SBCE e assegurando um ambiente regulatório compatível com a expansão do mercado de carbono no Brasil. O cenário é ainda mais sensível na aposentadoria ou cancelamento dos créditos pelas empresas compradoras. Sem a garantia de creditamento pleno no modelo não cumulativo, a tributação converte-se em custo à descarbonização. Cabe ao Comitê Gestor do IBS e à Receita Federal editar normas integradas que harmonizem o sistema fiscal com os princípios constitucionais de proteção ambiental inseridos pela Emenda Constitucional nº 132/2023. Sobre a autora Fernanda Rizzo é sócia da área Tributária & Aduaneira do escritório de advocacia Vieira Rezende.

artigo.texto: Democratic congressional nominee William Lawrence is calling for a federal moratorium on new data centers until regulations give communities greater control over development, saying opposition to the projects is bringing together voters across party lines. In a wide-ranging interview with Michigan Firsthand for The Livingston Post, Lawrence also outlined a gradual expansion of Medicare that could retain a role for private insurance, proposed a national infrastructure bank to finance housing, and endorsed legislation restricting transfers of offensive weapons to Israel. He also discussed his association with political streamer Hasan Piker, and his relationship with U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. Lawrence faces Republican incumbent U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett in the Nov. 3 election for Michigan’s 7th Congressional District, which includes all of Livingston County. Advertising spending in the district has exceeded $61 million this election cycle, making it the nation’s costliest House race for advertising, according to WKAR and AdImpact data, as Democrats hope to wrest control of the U.S. House and Senate away from Republicans. Watch the full discussion with Lawrence on Michigan Firsthand, the YouTube podcast produced in partnership with The Livingston Post, by clicking here. Read our companion interview with Barrett in The Livingston Post and watch the full discussion on Michigan Firsthand here. A pause on data centers The Lansing resident and community organizer who defeated the former U.S. Ambassador Bridget Brink and former Navy SEAL Matt Maasdam for the Democratic nomination argues that communities should not have to accept the projects to secure a prosperous future, particularly when the technology they support could displace workers. “We need to slow this down,” Lawrence said, calling for federal rules that would help communities “determine their own future rather than having it pushed onto us from above.” He described concerns over data centers as a bipartisan issue that surfaced in his meetings in Howell Township, Lyon Township, Mason and elsewhere with residents who shared concerns about electricity bills, water use and property values. “Unfortunately, there’s also been a lot of bipartisan support from the top down for supporting the interests of the big tech companies and data center developers,” he said. “I think people deserve to have a good future and a prosperous economy without just having to accept this deal that’s being pushed to us from Silicon Valley with no opportunity for local communities to determine their own futures.” Lawrence also acknowledged the state’s role in attracting data center developers through incentives such as tax breaks, and he criticized Gov. Gretchen Whitmer and state lawmakers for their handling of data center development. “I’ve been clear that I disagree with how the governor and the Michigan legislature has handled this issue,” he said. “And I think it really demonstrates that, again, this is an area where people from the grassroots have a lot in common: Democrat, independent and Republican.” Earlier this year, Attorney General Dana Nessel, in a previous interview with Michigan Firsthand for The Livingston Post, said that she thinks the Governor sold the legislature a “bill of goods.” A gradual expansion of Medicare On health care, Lawrence described Medicare for All as a goal reached through successive changes rather than an immediate replacement of the existing system. “It’s gonna be a step-by-step process,” he said. His proposed steps include lowering Medicare’s eligibility age to 55 or 50, adding dental, vision and hearing benefits and expanding coverage for long-term care. He also said reversing Medicaid cuts would be an immediate priority. Asked whether he still sees a role for private insurance, Lawrence said a public plan could provide baseline coverage while people purchase additional benefits. “I think that we can continue to have private insurance in some form,” he said. But he did not give a firm guarantee that people could keep their current insurance. Asked directly, he began with “most likely” before saying the answer would depend on the plan’s details and the transition. “What I’m clear on is that we need to have universal guaranteed coverage,” he said. Housing and tenant protections On housing, Lawrence proposed stronger tenant protections, including legal representation in eviction proceedings, alongside efforts to make construction and financing less expensive. He said he would co-sponsor existing legislation to establish a “national infrastructure bank,” with lending directed toward housing, water systems and transportation. “Now we can have a national infrastructure bank that still delivers profit to its investors and has a public purpose and can be targeted towards investments like housing,” he said. Lawrence said the goal should include housing affordable to middle-income residents as well as people with lower incomes, with opportunities for both renters and prospective homeowners. Tariffs and rising costs Lawrence also criticized President Donald Trump’s tariff policies, arguing that unpredictable changes make it harder for businesses to invest and families to plan. “You know, tariffs can be okay if it’s part of a consistent trade and industrial strategy,” he said. “But what the president is doing is he’s seemingly waking up in the morning and then just deciding what he wants the tariff rate to be – 55% or 40% or 25% or 5%, depending on his mood, or depending on the last of his advisors who happen to have his ear. That creates completely erratic business conditions.” Lawrence said Michigan families were paying an average of $5,000 more over the past year because of tariffs. The National Taxpayers Union Foundation estimated $23 billion in executive tariff costs on imports into Michigan from January 2025 through June 2026. That’s equivalent to $5,619 per household when divided by the state’s household count. Foreign policy

artigo.texto: CATL secures major Australian battery deal as sodium-ion technology draws industry interest Chinese energy giant CATL will supply a major 400MW Victorian battery project, expanding its Australian footprint while unveiling new sodium-ion technology. Chinese energy storage giant CATL has been selected to supply a major 400-megawatt battery project in Victoria, marking a significant expansion of its footprint in Australia’s National Electricity Market while unveiling new sodium-ion technology tailored for extreme heat. Strategic Grid Integration The Baranduda Electrical Energy Reserve, a 400-megawatt facility with 1.86 gigawatt-hours of storage, is being developed by Birdwood Energy near Wodonga. The project sits adjacent to the existing Victoria-New South Wales electricity interconnector, positioning it as a critical node for grid stability during peak demand periods. The State Electricity Commission, a publicly owned entity revived by the Carroll Labor government, recently injected $43 million to acquire a minority stake in the development. This investment finalizes the capital stack required for construction and represents the first public-private partnership between the state government and a superannuation fund, specifically Aware Super, to deliver a renewable energy asset. Birdwood Energy managing director Alex Marriott-Smith confirmed that CATL was chosen following a rigorous procurement process evaluating cost, technical capability, and deliverability. The selection underscores CATL’s dominance in utility-scale storage, leveraging its global manufacturing scale to secure large-scale contracts in competitive markets. Sodium-Ion Alternative At the All Energy Australia conference in Melbourne, CATL showcased its new utility-scale Tener+ system, which the company claims reduces the required physical footprint by 35 per cent compared to legacy models. More significantly, the company highlighted its Tener Sodium battery, a modular grid-scale system utilizing sodium-ion chemistry rather than traditional lithium iron phosphate. Sodium-ion technology has emerged as a vital alternative amid persistent supply chain constraints and geopolitical tensions surrounding lithium and cobalt extraction. CATL asserts that its sodium-ion modules are specifically engineered for Australia’s harsh climate, maintaining operational integrity at temperatures up to 55 degrees Celsius. Zane Zhou, general manager of CATL Australia and New Zealand, noted that the sodium-ion offering has generated substantial interest across the National Electricity Market and the off-grid mining sector. Mining operators are increasingly seeking to electrify heavy machinery and reduce diesel consumption, requiring robust storage solutions that can withstand remote, high-temperature environments. Market and Policy Implications The Baranduda project claims the longest storage duration in Victoria at 4.65 hours, allowing it to absorb excess daytime solar generation and dispatch power during the evening peak. This duration is essential for managing the rapid influx of rooftop solar and the scheduled retirement of legacy coal-fired power stations. Industry analysts note that while lithium-ion remains the standard for grid storage, sodium-ion technology offers a lower total installation cost and eliminates reliance on critical minerals that face export restrictions. The commercial validation of sodium-ion at Baranduda could accelerate its adoption across the Asia-Pacific region. The Victorian government’s revival of the State Electricity Commission was explicitly designed to intervene in a market where private capital has occasionally hesitated to underwrite long-duration storage projects. By taking a minority stake, the SEC de-risks the investment for private partners like Aware Super, bridging the gap between ambitious climate targets and the actual deployment of firming capacity. Unlike lithium-ion batteries, which rely on expensive and geographically concentrated minerals, sodium-ion cells utilize abundant, low-cost materials. This structural advantage insulates developers from the volatile price swings that have periodically disrupted the global battery supply chain over the past three years. Furthermore, the thermal stability of sodium-ion chemistry reduces the need for energy-intensive liquid cooling systems. In outback mining operations and regional grid nodes, where ambient temperatures regularly exceed 40 degrees Celsius, the ability to operate safely at 55 degrees Celsius without derating capacity provides a distinct engineering advantage. The integration of the Baranduda facility into the National Electricity Market will also test the regulatory frameworks governing long-duration storage. Current market mechanisms were primarily designed around two-hour discharge cycles, and operators are lobbying for updated capacity value metrics that properly remunerate four-hour and six-hour systems for their extended grid-support capabilities. As Australia accelerates its transition away from coal, the deployment of diverse storage chemistries is viewed as a critical hedge against technological lock-in. Grid operators require a heterogeneous mix of assets to manage frequency, voltage, and seasonal energy shifting, ensuring that the failure or degradation of one technology class does not compromise overall system security. Construction timelines and final grid connection dates for the Baranduda reserve are expected to be finalized following the completion of remaining environmental and planning approvals. The project’s successful deployment will serve as a primary benchmark for the viability of alternative battery chemistries in Australia’s transitioning energy grid. How did this story land? artigo.texto: Australian installers will get a closer look at Solis’ expanding battery storage range at All Energy Australia 2026. The company will showcase three SolisStorage products: EverCore C&I ESS, FlexCore-OD, and FlexAIO. Together, they cover integrated commercial storage, modular outdoor batteries, and all-in-one home energy storage. Visitors can explore the range at Stand JJ143, Melbourne Convention and Exhibition Centre, on 28 and 29 October. For retailers, installers, and engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) providers, the display offers an opportunity to discuss practical project requirements. These include system configuration, installation planning, inverter compatibility, and matching storage to customer needs. Solis will also host an on-site product launch during the exhibition, giving visitors another reason to stop by. Quick summary - Commercial storage: EverCore integrates battery storage, power conversion, and energy management, while FlexCore-OD offers modular outdoor battery storage. - Residential storage: FlexAIO combines an all-in-one approach with a modular, stackable design and plug-and-play connections. - Visit Solis: Explore the products and discuss upcoming installations at Stand JJ143 on 28 and 29 October. EverCore brings an integrated approach to commercial storage Commercial battery projects can involve very different operating requirements. A business managing daytime demand may need a different configuration from one with substantial evening consumption. The SolisStorage EverCore C&I ESS brings battery storage, power conversion, and energy management functions together in an integrated solution. For installers and EPCs, that makes it a product to investigate when considering an integrated approach to commercial and industrial storage. At the exhibition, Solis will discuss how EverCore may support energy cost management and greater energy flexibility. The team will also address application requirements, system design, and project planning. These conversations can help installers assess whether the solution suits a customer’s operating needs. The useful starting point is the project itself: how the business consumes electricity, its storage objectives, and its installation constraints. Bringing those details to the stand can help move discussions beyond product features and towards a suitable system configuration. FlexCore-OD offers modular outdoor battery storage Solis will also showcase SolisStorage FlexCore-OD, an outdoor battery storage solution for commercial and industrial applications. Its modular, stackable architecture offers another approach for projects with different capacity and site requirements. FlexCore-OD features a plug-and-play design and IP66 protection, supporting its intended use in outdoor installations. For installers, the exhibition provides an opportunity to examine the product and discuss how its modular design works in practice. Visitors can also explore compatible inverter solutions and ask how different configurations accommodate site conditions and customer energy requirements. That compatibility discussion matters. Selecting a battery involves understanding how the complete system will operate, including its inverter and control arrangements. EverCore and FlexCore-OD give commercial installers two approaches to compare: integrated energy storage and modular outdoor battery storage. The right fit will depend on the application, configuration requirements, and conditions at the installation site. Get FREE Quotes for a Solis system FlexAIO puts residential installation in focus For residential installers, SolisStorage FlexAIO combines an all-in-one home energy storage approach with a modular, stackable design. Its plug-and-play connections aim to simplify installation, while the modular format provides flexibility when planning around household energy requirements. Visitors can examine FlexAIO at the stand and discuss configuration options, installation workflows, and home energy management. These are useful conversations for retailers building proposals and installers planning how equipment will fit within a customer’s property. Household consumption, available installation space, and the intended role of the battery all influence system selection. The exhibition offers an opportunity to work through those considerations directly with the Solis team. The residential display will also feature SolisStorage IntelliHome, SolisStorage FlexHome, and compatible Solis inverters. These include the Solis S6-EA1P6K and Solis S7-EH1P10K, providing further opportunities to discuss residential system configurations. Bring your next project to the conversation A product display becomes more useful when you can connect it to an actual installation. Solis is encouraging installers and partners to bring project questions to the stand. These might cover storage capacity for business premises or configuration options for a home battery installation. For commercial projects, useful discussion points include system sizing, inverter compatibility, site layout, and energy management requirements. For residential projects, installers can explore configuration options, installation processes, and how the system will address household energy needs. Visitors should also clarify product availability, applicable certifications, warranty terms, and technical documentation before progressing a customer proposal. Those details help turn an exhibition conversation into a practical next step. Visit Solis at All Energy Australia 2026 Solis’ display brings commercial and residential storage together, allowing installers to explore several system approaches in one visit. Whether your next project involves business energy storage or a household battery, bring your questions and make the conversation count. - Dates: 28 and 29 October 2026 - Venue: Melbourne Convention and Exhibition Centre - Stand: JJ143 - Featured products: SolisStorage EverCore C&I ESS, FlexCore-OD

artigo.texto: Plataformas Broadcast Soluções de Dados e Conteúdos Soluções de Tecnologia 27 de outubro de 2026, às 18:34 A Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) aprovou nesta terça-feira, 27, os editais dos leilões para a inédita contratação de baterias, que irão contribuir para a segurança do Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN). Para o certame com conteúdo local, o preço-teto foi fixado em R$ 1.760.000,00/MW ao ano, enquanto o certame sem a restrição terá preço-teto de R$ 1.580.000,00/MW ao ano. O relator é o diretor Gentil Nogueira. Conforme lei de 2025, os sistemas de armazenamento de energia, na forma de baterias, terão custos de contratação rateados apenas entre os geradores de energia. Isso gerou críticas do setor, e um dos argumentos é a falta de tratamento isonômico. No início de outubro, a Câmara dos Deputados aprovou o requerimento de urgência do projeto de lei que abre margem para o custo da contratação de baterias ser arcado pelos usuários finais de energia elétrica do Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN), incluídos os consumidores. A votação do mérito do texto (PL 3716/2026) deve ocorrer em breve. Tendo em vista eventual mudança, o Diretor-Geral da Aneel, Sandoval Feitosa, reforçou que eventual mudança legislativa será recepcionada “com a maior agilidade possível”. Nos processos de hoje, a Aneel faz um ajuste de redação para substituir a expressão “gerador de energia” por “usuário de reserva de capacidade”, tanto no edital quanto no Contrato de Reserva de Capacidade na forma de Potência (CRCAP). A nova redação permite melhor adequação à proposta de regulamentação do rateio dos custos dos Leilões de Reserva de Capacidade na forma de Potência (LRCAPs) de baterias. A norma está em discussão na consulta pública, com prazo de contribuição até 6 de novembro. O titular do empreendimento fará jus à receita fixa (em R$/ano), a ser paga em 12 parcelas mensais. Em geral, os contratos terão 15 anos de duração, com início de suprimento em 1º de agosto de 2028. A área técnica da Aneel propôs uma mudança nos editais dos leilões para a contratação de baterias, que pode levar à inclusão dos consumidores no rateio do custo de contratação. Os certames estão previstos para 2 e 4 de dezembro. As baterias serão contratadas na modalidade de “reserva de capacidade”. Em geral, os custos administrativos e financeiros e os encargos tributários precisam ser rateados entre todos os usuários finais de energia elétrica do SIN, incluídos os consumidores. A exceção, contudo, foi dada aos sistemas de armazenamento de energia. Daí a alegação de falta de isonomia. Contato: renan.monteiro@broadcast.com.br Veja também

artigo.texto: The 350 MW/1.4 GWh Albatross BESS in Germany has reached financial close, which GIGA Storage, a Netherlands-based energy storage company, completed on 23 October 2026. Seven international banks, among which are ABN AMRO, ING and SMBC, are providing the debt of €260 million (~ $290.85 million). The plant is to be built near Neuenkirchen in Lower Saxony, Germany, and it will be the first project that GIGA Storage has in the country. CATL will be responsible for the engineering, construction and maintenance of the plant, and the construction is to start in early 2027. The plant will be connected directly to the 380 kV Merzen substation of Amprion, and it is expected to begin operation in early 2029. That financing has taken the storage capacity that GIGA Storage has under construction in the Netherlands, Belgium and Germany to approximately 1.4 GW/5.6 GWh. artigo.texto: O Motorola Edge 70 Neo deve ser o novo lançamento da Motorola para as próximas semanas ou meses. Um novo vazamento revela algumas especificações desse aparelho, como sua bateria massiva de 7.000 mAh e até mesmo o visual do produto, que não é muito diferente do restante da linha. Segundo o vazamento, o novo Edge 70 Neo deve entregar uma tela de 6,78 polegadas na resolução 1.5K com taxa de atualização de 144 Hz, além da proteção Gorilla Glass 7i. Mas o que realmente chama a atenção é essa bateria com capacidade de 7.000 mAh, que possivelmente será compatível com recarga de 45W. No segmento interno, a fabricante deve inserir o chip Snapdragon 7s Gen 3, introduzido ao mercado em 2024 para celulares intermediários. Para memória RAM, há uma expectativa para versões de 6 GB ou 8 GB, que é o padrão nesse tipo de produto. No armazenamento é bem provável que o Motorola Edge 70 Neo seja vendido com 128 GB e 256 GB. Em relação ao conjunto de câmeras, a região traseira desse smartphone deve entregar um sensor primário Sony Lytia Y710 de 50 MP, com abertura de f/1.8. Ele se juntará a uma câmera macro de 2 MP e um sensor de luz 3 em 1. Já na câmera frontal, utilizada para as selfies, a resolução é de 32 MP, sugere o rumor. Motorola já confirmou o celular sem querer Em agosto, um funcionário da Motorola acidentalmente revelou esse smartphone ao publicar sobre testes do Android 17 Beta em um fórum da Lenovo. Tanto na postagem do fórum quanto no formulário de inscrição para os testes, o nome do Motorola Edge 70 Neo foi repetido algumas vezes. A fabricante já lançou os modelos Edge 70 padrão, Edge 70 Max, Edge 70 Pro, Edge 70 Pro+, Edge 70 Fusion, Edge 70 Fusion+ e anunciou o super Signature 27 recentemente. Historicamente, essa linha da Motorola possui um modelo Neo, mas neste ano isso ainda não aconteceu. Havia a esperança que esse Edge 70 Neo fosse lançado em setembro ou ainda em outubro, mas parece que esse produto ficará cozinhando no forno por mais algumas semanas. Vale notar que os vazamentos são rumores e é necessário aguardar pela revelação oficial da Motorola. Por falar na Motorola, a empresa lançou o novo Moto G47 Power com uma bateria gigantesca e uma câmera bem parruda de 108 MP.
