artigo.texto: Energy storage development plan for Green Belt between Busby and Thorntonhall Plans for an 86-acre long-duration energy storage development on Green Belt land between Busby and Thorntonhall are moving forward again. The proposed Busby Long Duration Energy Storage project would cover 34.9 hectares of land at Meikle Dripps Farm, roughly equivalent to 54 football pitches, close to Waterfoot Road. It would have a capacity of up to 150MW and store 1,200MWh of electricity, enough to operate at its maximum output for eight hours. Correspondence received by the Jackton, Thorntonhall and Busby Alliance LDES Action Group indicates that developers are now preparing to hold a statutory pre-application consultation before submitting the full plans. Consultants Cavendish Consulting have told campaigners that residents will be given an opportunity to see and comment on the proposals before an application for consent is lodged. No date has yet been announced for the consultation. The Scottish Government’s Energy Consents Unit continues to list Busby LDES as a “Pre Application” project. The live record names Apatura Project 22 Ltd as the applicant and confirms that no full Section 36 application has yet reached the determination stage. Documents already submitted as part of environmental screening give a clearer picture of the potential scale of the development. The site extends across six agricultural fields approximately 100 metres west of Thorntonhall and 250 metres south of Busby. The nearest residential property is immediately beside its southern boundary. The developer’s original screening submission modelled a development of up to 3,510 battery blocks. It considered container units around 2.6 metres high, with one potential configuration allowing them to be double-stacked. The accompanying landscape assessment said that could result in structures around 5.2 metres high, although the final design and technology had not been fixed at that stage. Frontier Power Energy Holdings acquired the rights to the Busby project and a separate 200MW scheme at Ayr from Apatura on 26 May 2026. Apatura said it would retain an active role in progressing both developments. Frontier now says Busby is expected to use long-duration batteries supplied by US manufacturer Eos Energy Enterprises, including its Z3 zinc-based technology, rather than conventional lithium-ion batteries. The company has also confirmed that Busby has received a Gate 2 notification through the National Energy System Operator’s reformed grid connection process. Gate 2 means a project has met NESO’s tests for readiness and can secure a place in the reformed connections queue, with a confirmed connection point and date. It is separate from planning permission and does not amount to approval for the development to be built. The Green Belt location is likely to remain one of the main issues when the full application is considered. The developer’s own landscape assessment says the Green Belt in this location helps maintain separation between East Kilbride, Busby and Clarkston, Thorntonhall and Waterfoot. It also acknowledges that developing the site would increase the urban influence on the landscape and result in an “unavoidable loss of openness” that would conflict with its Green Belt designation. South Lanarkshire Council reached a similarly conclusion during environmental screening. Its assessment said the project would be out of scale with the existing environment, describing it as a medium-scale development being introduced into a semi-rural area. Scottish Ministers subsequently determined that the development did not need to be accompanied by a full Environmental Impact Assessment. A future application is still expected to include detailed assessments covering aspects including landscape and visual impact, noise, ecology, flooding and drainage. Construction itself was estimated in the screening documents to take around 12 to 18 months, including work on the access, underground cables, fencing and landscaping. The transport assessment anticipates construction traffic using Waterfoot Road and Peel Road, including HGVs, light goods vehicles and “a small number of abnormal loads”. A public Core Path connecting Thorntonhall and Busby also crosses the site. The developer has proposed retaining and upgrading the route, although South Lanarkshire’s environmental screening states that the surroundings of sections of the path would be altered. The scheme has attracted sustained opposition in Busby, Thorntonhall and Jackton. Campaigners argue that energy storage infrastructure of this scale is inappropriate for agricultural Green Belt land separating established communities and have raised concerns about landscape change, construction traffic and noise. A Change.org petition opposing the Busby LDES development has now attracted 2,962 verified signatures. The petition states: “The BESS/LDES Local Action Group and the Jackton and Thorntonhall Community Council (JTCC) are fighting back against this development because of the dangers it poses - from fire risks and noise, to environmental damage and traffic. “While we acknowledge the importance of energy infrastructure, we believe this location is completely inappropriate and that safer, more suitable alternative locations should be considered.” The action group is also due to meet Scottish Labour South Scotland MSP Joe Fagan later this month as it prepares for the expected public consultation.

artigo.texto: With public distaste for data centers in Connecticut on the rise, residents in several communities are pushing for new restrictions even as the company looking to build one in Cromwell is stepping up its public relations effort. East Lyme’s zoning board last week unanimously prohibited any data centers from being built there, making the town at least the seventh in Connecticut to impose tougher rules. Morris, Trumbull, New Haven, Waterford, West Haven and Groton have all either banned new data centers altogether or imposed temporary moratoriums against them. Even so, Trumbull appears to be on track for the massive expansion of an existing data center. The $200 million cogNovum project would enlarge a former Nasdaq center in the town’s Merritt Boulevard office park. So despite the town’s newly enacted two-year moratorium against new centers, zoning officials are treating cogNovum as an expansion — and immune to the ban. A band of Trumbull residents this week tried to get their zoning board to adopt a new regulation adding expansions to the temporary ban, but were turned back. “We wanted a one-year moratorium against expansion of existing data centers,” opponent Richard White told WICC radio interviewer Melissa Sheketoff on her Melissa in the Morning program Thursday. “They voted against us 5-0.” In mid-summer, First Selectman Vicki Tesoro told residents that the project isn’t like the mega-centers that are proposed around the country. Developers want to put up a 10-gigawatt facility on more than 2,500 acres in Piketon, Ohio, for instance, and Meta and Blue Owl Capital are looking to build a 5-gigawatt center totalling 4 million square feet in northeastern Louisiana. “This is a renovation of a decades-old, existing data center — not the new construction of a hyperscale AI facility,” Tesoro told residents in late July. “Four main concerns rise to the top of my conversations with residents: electricity, noise, water, and expansion of the building’s footprint,” Tesoro said. “When it comes to these four things, I told the applicant directly: no increase in electrical draw beyond existing site capacity, no increase in noise, no increase in water use, no expansion of the building’s footprint. They have agreed to all four.” But the Trumbull AI Data Center Watch, an organization of opponents, is still fighting. Similarly, a group organizing against a potential 100-megawatt data center in Beacon Falls is connecting with local data center opponents in several communities, and recently started selling coffee cups, T-shirts and more to promote its message “Happy to not be on the map.” First Selectman Gerard Smith got blowback from opponents when he said the center would “put Beacon Falls on the map in a big way.” Meanwhile, a commercial real estate firm promoting plans for a data center in Cromwell said residents there haven’t heard enough about the proposal’s upside. The Algonquin gas pipeline runs through the Cromwell property and along with on-site fuel cells means the operation would be powered without taking anything from the electrical grid, according to Jay Morris of O,R&L Commercial, the real estate broker for landowner Gardner Nurseries. Although no formal application has been filed with the town, developers have signaled they want to put up a 1.2 million-square-foot, 300-megawatt data center on part of a 160-acre site off Geer Street. “This site is zoned for Industrial, and if this opportunity goes away it could be developed for manufacturing and distribution uses that could have much more building density, truck traffic and noise, and likely not seek to preserve open farmland,” Morris wrote in a letter to The Courant. “The developer has been meeting informally with local residents and has designed the preliminary layout to be set back far from the road and houses,” Morris wrote, saying the project would use only about a third of the acreage and leave the rest as open space. “Many of the national data centers are enormous, many 10x or more what is being discussed in Cromwell,” he wrote. A data center would add no burden to schools or other town services, wouldn’t require substantial water supplies, would generate no traffic after construction and would provide “substantial” local tax revenue, he wrote. “I believe if the public understood the benefits of this use in this location vs any other type of industrial development, they would welcome this opportunity,” according to his letter. Late Friday afternoon, however, Mayor James Demetriades posted a detailed zoning proposal from resident Juan Duque aimed at curbing data centers in Cromwell. It would set safety standards along with maximum limits on noise and vibrations; the Planning and Zoning Commission is scheduled to hear the proposed regulations Dec. 3. Of special relevance to the Geer Street project, the regulations would establish a cap of 100,000 square feet and require at least a mile buffer from any school. The Geer site is across the street from the town’s Woodside Intermediate School.

artigo.texto: In the first six months of 2026, Australia saw more clean energy generation capacity reach financial close and more large-scale battery storage capacity switched on than during the whole of 2025, according to the country’s latest biannual investment report. According to the Clean Energy Council (CEC)’s latest report, nine utility-scale batteries, worth $4.3 billion and representing 2.3 GW / 7.1 GWh of storage capacity, were switched on during the period. With these additions, the country surpassed the 2 GW / 5.1 GWh of battery storage capacity added during 2025. The report, Large-scale renewable generation and storage (January–June 2026), found that 12 generation projects, totalling 2.6 GW of new capacity, reached a final investment decision (FID) in H1 2026. This exceeded the 2.3 GW recorded across the whole of 2025, with solar farms and hybrid solar-and-battery projects leading the additions. Five generation projects, totalling 1.4 GW of new capacity and worth more than $2.8 billion, were commissioned during the first half of the year. These included the 756 MW first stage of Victoria’s Golden Plains Wind Farm, which is expected to generate enough electricity to power more than 400,000 homes. Renewable Investment Sustains Despite Economic Pressure Australia’s renewable energy investment performed strongly despite a challenging economic environment, strengthening the country’s energy security and helping deliver a more reliable and affordable electricity system. Clean Energy Council (CEC)' CEC Chief Executive Jackie Trad said the results demonstrate the resilience and growth of the clean energy industry despite significant headwinds. “Australian sun and wind cannot be cut off by conflict overseas. Each new solar, wind and battery investment helps make Australia more energy independent and economically resilient, shielding Australians from global fossil fuel price shocks and supply disruptions,” she said. “An increase in renewable generation and storage is already putting downward pressure on power prices, with wholesale electricity prices averaging $74 per megawatt-hour in the June quarter, down nearly 50 per cent on the same period in 2025.” Trad also said Australian-made clean energy would deliver more affordable and reliable electricity for households and businesses, alongside tens of thousands of jobs and billions of dollars in investment and economic activity, particularly in regional Australia. Queensland Leads in Clean Energy Investment Queensland led the nation in clean energy investment, accounting for $9.6 billion and 4.5 GW of projects that were either at financial close or under construction. New South Wales, meanwhile, had the largest battery storage pipeline, at 4.3 GW / 11.2 GWh. “Queensland is leading the nation in clean energy investment, showing what can be achieved when world-class renewable energy resources are matched with investor confidence,” Trad said. “But the story is bigger than any one state or territory; across Australia, investors are backing the technologies they know will power our economic future and strengthen our energy security. “With $32.5 billion worth of generation and storage projects now under construction or at financial close, maintaining this momentum will require predictable approvals, timely transmission and long-term revenue certainty to help more projects, including onshore wind, progress into operation. “Australian-made clean energy will not only deliver more affordable, reliable electricity for households and businesses, but also tens of thousands of jobs and billions of dollars in investment and economic activity, particularly in regional Australia,” she said.

artigo.texto: New BESS in Portugal will be required to form the grid and to supply synthetic inertia, under an ordinance that the Portuguese Government, a Portugal-based national government, has issued. The requirement applies in full to plants of 45 MW or more, and also to those that are connected at 110 kV or above. Plants of 10 MW to 45 MW will have to form the grid as well, but on terms that the grid operator is yet to set. Every plant that is covered must keep an energy reserve, so that it can answer frequency swings between 47.0 Hz and 52.5 Hz. The ordinance also requires every plant of 500 kW or more to switch automatically from charging to discharging when the frequency falls. It came into force on 23 October 2026, and it applies to the connection requests that have been filed since that day. Portugal makes grid forming mandatory for BESS of 45 MW or more An ordinance of the Portuguese Government has made grid forming and synthetic inertia mandatory for every BESS of 45 MW or more that seeks a connection in Portugal. artigo.texto: SALT LAKE CITY, Utah — It currently takes around four gigawatts of energy to power the entire state of Utah each year, but two planned data centers could more than quadruple that consumption. One in Millard County is working toward an energy capacity of more than 10 megawatts, while another in Box Elder County is targeting nine megawatts. And more are coming. But as Utah faces an energy deficit caused by increasing demand and decreasing supply, "there's not enough power in Utah to provide these data centers what they need,” notes Shon Hiatt, a University of Southern California professor who has studied Utah’s data center landscape. “Especially at this scale.” That's why many data centers under development in the state are now opting to bring their own energy. The move to what's sometimes referred to as “behind the meter” or “off-the-grid" energy comes after the Utah Legislature approved a new law last year that created an alternative process to provide power to large-load customers. "If they can't get it from the utility, Utah — with that law that just passed this session — basically says, ‘Oh, well then we'll give you permission to build your own power, bring your own,’” Hiatt said in an interview. His research for the Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute found that seven data centers currently under construction will use nearly three times as much energy as all the ones that currently exist in the state combined. More than half of that energy will be “behind the meter.” Celebrity investor Kevin O’Leary’s controversial Stratos project in Box Elder County, for example, would tap directly into a natural gas pipeline near the Great Salt Lake called the Ruby Pipeline. Creekstone Energy, which is building what’s been billed as the “world’s largest data center” in Delta, plans to tap the Kern River Gas Pipeline and will also bring its own solar energy. While state law has greased the wheels, the “bring your own energy” movement also comes amid growing concerns nationally about how data centers could impact prices for ratepayers around the country. President Donald Trump called on hyperscale data centers in March to “build, bring, or buy” all their needed energy and to pay “the full cost of their energy and infrastructure, no matter what.” Abe Silverman, an assistant research scholar at Johns Hopkins University who focuses on energy markets and data centers, said there is "bipartisan" consensus that "data centers need to pay their own way.” “Grandma should not be subsidizing Google’s electric bill,” he said. The state hasn’t seen cost increases from data centers yet, according to Michele Beck, director of the Utah Office of Consumer Services. She told FOX 13 News that she believes Utah laws will continue to protect ratepayers from electricity rate spikes moving forward (though natural gas is a more complicated picture). “What SB132 has done is create pathways so that the data centers themselves can be responsible for procuring their power,” she said in an interview. “And then that helps to keep the shifts away from the regular customers.” But Olivia Douglas — a Bountiful resident who recently moved back to Utah from the northern Virginia area known as “Data Center Alley” — is skeptical the state will be able to mitigate the environmental and cost impacts of hyperscale data centers. "You can’t create energy out of thin air,” she said in an interview. “You can’t create water out of thin air. It has to come from somewhere. And then who’s paying for it?” WATCH: Hiatt, with USC, explains why data centers would rather not bring their own energy 'A geographically specific picture’ When Douglas and her family first moved to Prince William County, Virginia — a “beautiful area” with lots of trees — she had no idea there were data centers there. But as more came into the area, she started feeling their impacts. The construction boom increased traffic, she said, and the community began to feel “more industrial by the day.” Douglas, who recently moved back to Utah in part over concerns about quality of life and rising costs, also blames data centers for spikes in her monthly electricity bill. "Over the course of, I want to say, like five years, energy prices rose 30%,” she estimated. “Even within the last couple of months, I still am in contact with neighbors and they’re seeing even more increases — jumping $100, $200 a month in their energy bills.” Prince William County is home to at least 41 data centers, with 70 more on the way, according to the U.S. Data Center Map. (Research from the Kem C. Gardner Institute found, by comparison, that there are currently 48 operational data centers in the entire state of Utah.) While it can be difficult at times to parse the impact of data centers on energy prices, Silverman said there’s “pretty clear evidence” that they have contributed to rising costs in some regions, including in Virginia. But “it is very much a geographically specific picture,” he added. A Bloomberg analysis published last year found electricity rates spiked as much as 267% per month compared to the previous five years in areas near “significant data center activity.” But the Data Center Coalition, a group that represents the industry, points to reports showing rising energy costs are instead a product of inflation, grid modernization, natural gas volatility and other dynamics. Hiatt’s research found minimal data center impacts on energy prices in the United States between 2019 and 2025, though he stresses “that was looking backwards.” “Moving forward, though, I think we are at a risk,” he added. Experts agree the picture is particularly complex when it comes to questions about how data centers could impact the price of natural gas, a traded commodity that also heats homes. “I think the natural gas side will be trickier because so much of it is federally regulated or subject to market forces,” said Beck, with the Utah Office of Consumer Services, which advocates on behalf of ratepayers. artigo.texto: General Motors Co. in Detroit says it’s considering allowing battery technology startups to use its new, 500,000-square-foot battery development center in Warren when the facility opens in December. According to reports, Kurt Kelty, GM’s vice president of battery and sustainability, says the automaker has held internal discussions about potentially opening the new facility to startups interested in learning battery cell manufacturing processes. This could provide smaller companies with access to capabilities that would otherwise require substantial capital investment. Despite these reported internal discussions, GM insists no decision has been made. The new, $145 million battery prototype facility is located at GM’s Global Technical Center in Warren. It’s designed to accelerate the development of next-generation battery technologies, including lithium manganese-rich (LMR) and sodium-ion chemistries. GM has announced a partnership with Peak Energy, a California-based energy storage system manufacturer, to develop and deploy sodium-ion cell batteries for stationary grid applications. Meanwhile, LMR battery technology has been tapped as a “big step” for GM’s proposed all-electric vehicle portfolio.

artigo.texto: Bondada Engineering Secures 20 MW/120 MWh VRFB BESS Order 27 Oct 2026 2 Min Read CW Team Share Bondada Engineering has received a Letter of Intent from Gujarat Industries Power Company for an engineering, procurement and construction package for a 20 MW/120 MWh Vanadium Redox Flow Battery Energy Storage System at GIPCL’s 165 MW natural gas power plant complex in Vadodara, Gujarat. The award also includes operations and maintenance services for 10 years. The project is scheduled for completion within 18 months of receipt of the notice of award. GIPCL is a domestic entity, and the disclosure stated that the contract does not involve any interest of Bondada Engineering’s promoter, promoter group or group companies. It also does not fall under related-party transactions. The order marks Bondada Engineering’s expansion into advanced energy storage technologies and complements its renewable energy engineering, procurement and construction portfolio. The company described the project as India’s largest grid-scale Vanadium Redox Flow Battery Energy Storage System project, positioning it in the long-duration energy storage segment. The company’s disclosure highlighted the growth potential of India’s energy storage market as renewable energy capacity expands and the need for grid stability increases. The Government of India has set a target of deploying approximately 236 GWh of battery energy storage systems by 2030, compared with current installed capacity of around 9.3 GWh. Bondada Engineering said the project would strengthen its position in the battery energy storage system sector and support its participation in India’s clean energy ecosystem. The company is expected to undertake the EPC scope and subsequent operations and maintenance obligations under the award from Gujarat Industries Power Company. artigo.texto: Dados do Banco Central mostram avanço de 9,2% em relação ao acumulado de agosto de 2025, enquanto energia renovável, mineração, petróleo e infraestrutura digital aparecem entre as áreas associadas ao interesse estrangeiro no país. O investimento direto no país chegou a US$ 86,6 bilhões no acumulado de 12 meses até agosto, com recursos ligados a atividades que vão de energia e mineração à infraestrutura digital. O resultado ficou acima dos US$ 79,3 bilhões registrados no mesmo recorte um ano antes. A série do Banco Central do Brasil mostra que o volume correspondia a 3,39% do Produto Interno Bruto e representa crescimento de aproximadamente 9,2% na comparação anual. Somente em agosto, os ingressos líquidos alcançaram US$ 7,4 bilhões. - Brasil reúne uma combinação difícil de ignorar: 90% da produção mundial de nióbio, segunda maior reserva conhecida de terras raras e uma agenda com os Estados Unidos que envolve tarifas, investimento e abastecimento industrial - Brasil tem um amortecedor entre dólar e inflação: estoques antigos, contratos fechados, concorrência e margens fazem a alta cambial atravessar importações e indústria antes de alcançar os preços pagos pelo consumidor - 88,0 nas expectativas contra 81,4 na situação atual: confiança melhora em outubro, mas a distância entre futuro e presente cresce enquanto o indicador financeiro das famílias recua ao menor nível desde janeiro - Brasil entra na reta decisiva de um tributo estimado em R$ 636 bilhões: TCU julga nesta quarta o cálculo da CBS, ainda sigiloso, antes de o Senado definir a alíquota para 2027 O resultado mensal reuniu US$ 9,3 bilhões em participação no capital, dos quais US$ 5,7 bilhões corresponderam a lucros reinvestidos. Houve, ao mesmo tempo, saídas líquidas de US$ 1,9 bilhão nas operações entre empresas relacionadas. O que entra no investimento direto O indicador não representa apenas dinheiro aplicado na construção de fábricas, parques de geração ou centros de dados. Ele reúne diferentes relações financeiras entre investidores estrangeiros e empresas instaladas no Brasil, incluindo aportes de capital, reinvestimento de lucros e operações entre companhias relacionadas. Por isso, os US$ 86,6 bilhões não equivalem ao valor de novas obras iniciadas no período. A própria composição de agosto mostra que parte relevante do fluxo veio de lucros reinvestidos por companhias que já operam no país. A dimensão internacional do movimento foi destacada pela agência EFE, que classificou o acumulado como recorde. A reportagem informou ainda que o Brasil havia sido, em 2025, o terceiro maior destino mundial de investimento estrangeiro, atrás de Estados Unidos e China, com base em dados da OCDE. A EFE também citou levantamento da Conferência das Nações Unidas sobre Comércio e Desenvolvimento segundo o qual o Brasil recebeu 43% dos fluxos destinados à América Latina. Entre os setores associados ao capital estrangeiro aparecem energia renovável, mineração, centros de dados, indústria farmacêutica e madeira. A presença de atividades diferentes no mesmo recorte não permite concluir que os recursos tenham sido distribuídos de maneira uniforme. O valor agregado do Banco Central também não identifica, por si só, quanto cada um desses segmentos recebeu no período. Renováveis, minerais, petróleo e centros de dados Na área de energia, a composição da matriz elétrica brasileira aparece entre os fatores destacados pela agência. A reportagem informa que 88% da eletricidade do país vem de fontes renováveis, com participação da geração hidrelétrica e presença de fontes como eólica e solar. Essa característica também aparece relacionada à infraestrutura digital porque centros de dados exigem fornecimento elevado e contínuo de eletricidade. Cada empreendimento, porém, permanece sujeito a condições próprias de custo, disponibilidade de infraestrutura, licenciamento e cronograma antes de chegar à operação. O interesse em atividades ligadas à transição energética convive com investimentos em setores tradicionais. A EFE aponta minerais críticos e terras raras entre as áreas acompanhadas por investidores estrangeiros e registra, paralelamente, projetos vinculados à indústria de petróleo. O recorte reúne, portanto, atividades com características diferentes: geração renovável, recursos minerais estratégicos, óleo e gás e infraestrutura necessária aos centros de dados. A presença desses setores no mesmo fluxo não significa que todos estejam no mesmo estágio de implantação. Um anúncio empresarial, uma intenção de investimento, um aporte financeiro e a entrada em operação de um empreendimento representam momentos distintos. Essa diferença impede que o volume registrado como investimento direto seja tratado automaticamente como obra executada, contratação realizada ou nova capacidade produtiva já disponível. A referência temporal também limita interpretações políticas sobre o dado. A série utilizada pela EFE termina em agosto e, portanto, não representa uma reação à eleição de domingo (25) nem permite relacionar o fluxo registrado pelo Banco Central a acontecimentos ocorridos depois do período medido. Para avaliar o efeito do capital estrangeiro sobre a economia local, será necessário observar quais projetos avançam para etapas como construção, contratação, compra de equipamentos e início da produção. Os próximos dados mensais do Banco Central também indicarão se o volume acumulado mantém a trajetória observada até agosto.

artigo.texto: Italy continued to expand its solar and energy storage fleet in the third quarter of 2026, with 1.742 GW of new photovoltaic capacity connected, up 37% from the 1.269 GW installed in the same period of 2025 and 5% higher than in the previous quarter. In the first nine months of the year, the country added 4.834 GW of new solar capacity through 147,632 new installations, according to calculations by ITALIA SOLARE based on Terna’s Gaudì data, updated to September 30. By that date, Italy had 2,314,113 photovoltaic installations connected to the grid, with a total installed capacity of 48.347 GW. The number of new connections also increased during the third quarter, rising from 38,660 in the second quarter to 58,459 between July and September, an increase of 34%. Utility-scale solar drives new installations Growth in the Italian solar market is increasingly being driven by larger projects and commercial and industrial installations. Between January and September, the utility-scale segment, covering plants of at least 1 MW, added 2.241 GW through 473 new connections, accounting for 46% of all new photovoltaic capacity installed in Italy during the period. The commercial and industrial segment, covering installations between 20 kW and 1 MW, added another 1.697 GW through 11,905 new projects, equivalent to 35% of newly connected capacity. The residential market, comprising systems of up to 20 kW, added 897 MW through 135,254 new connections, representing 19% of the new capacity. In the third quarter alone, utility-scale projects added 858 MW, compared with 457 MW in the same quarter of 2025. Of this volume, 394 MW came from projects between 1 MW and 10 MW, while another 464 MW came from installations above 10 MW. The C&I segment reached 543 MW, up from 500 MW a year earlier, while residential additions increased from 312 MW to 341 MW. Paolo Rocco Viscontini, president of ITALIA SOLARE, said the third-quarter figures confirm continued growth in the Italian solar market, with large-scale projects playing an increasingly important role and the commercial and industrial segment maintaining a positive trajectory. The association nevertheless said the residential market remains an area to monitor after contracting in the first half of 2026 compared with the previous year. Sicily leads new solar capacity additions At regional level, Sicily ranked first for newly connected photovoltaic capacity in the first nine months of 2026, with 686 MW, followed by Lombardy with 644 MW, Piedmont with 498 MW, Veneto with 463 MW, Emilia-Romagna with 443 MW and Lazio with 432 MW. The composition of growth varied significantly by region. Of the 686 MW added in Sicily, 476 MW came from installations larger than 10 MW, reflecting the strong contribution of utility-scale projects. In Lombardy, by contrast, the commercial and industrial segment accounted for a significant share of new capacity, with 405 MW, while large-scale installations were largely absent. By number of new installations, Lombardy ranked first with 22,999 connections, followed by Veneto with 18,099, Emilia-Romagna with 13,405 and Sicily with 11,653. Italy approaches 20 GWh of energy storage The expansion of solar capacity is being accompanied by further growth in electrochemical energy storage. As of September 30, Italy had 984,829 connected storage systems, with a total capacity of 19.983 GWh and a combined power rating of 8.338 GW. Of this capacity, 12.552 GWh was associated with photovoltaic installations, while 7.368 GWh came from stand-alone storage systems. A further 57 MWh was linked to thermal power plants and 6 MWh to wind installations. During the first nine months of 2026, Italy connected 98,197 new storage systems, adding 1.953 GWh of capacity and 907 MW of power. Almost all new installations by unit count were batteries associated with photovoltaic systems: 98,186 units, representing 1.486 GWh of capacity and 773 MW of power. By contrast, just 11 new stand-alone storage systems added a combined 467 MWh of capacity and 134 MW of power, highlighting the significantly larger average size of these projects. Solar-linked storage capacity rises despite fewer installations During the third quarter, storage systems associated with photovoltaic installations added 480 MWh of new capacity, 252 MW of power and 31,039 new units. Compared with the third quarter of 2025, newly connected storage capacity increased by 15%, from 417 MWh to 480 MWh, even as the number of installations declined from 32,697 to 31,039. The figures also show a change in the size profile of newly installed batteries. Storage systems associated with photovoltaic installations of up to 6 kW added 242 MWh during the third quarter, compared with 129 MWh in the previous quarter. By contrast, systems associated with photovoltaic installations between 6 kW and 20 kW fell from 229 MWh to 105 MWh, while storage linked to installations above 20 kW added a combined 133 MWh. Across the first nine months of the year, storage systems associated with photovoltaic installations of up to 6 kW added 481 MWh, those linked to systems between 6 kW and 20 kW added 596 MWh, and those associated with installations above 20 kW added a total of 409 MWh. Lombardy also leads distributed storage Lombardy also recorded the highest amount of new storage capacity associated with photovoltaic systems between January and September, with 206 MWh, followed by Emilia-Romagna with 155 MWh, Veneto with 146 MWh and Sicily with 144 MWh. The region also ranked first by number of new systems, with 14,672 installations, ahead of Veneto, Emilia-Romagna and Sicily. On a cumulative basis, Lombardy now has 164,950 storage systems associated with photovoltaic installations, representing 2.095 GWh of capacity. It is followed by Veneto with 1.562 GWh and Emilia-Romagna with 1.154 GWh. artigo.texto: [Digital Today reporter Jinju Hong] Chinese electric vehicle maker BYD is expected to unveil an ultra-luxury electric sedan in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) in early November. The new flagship model from BYD's top-end brand Yangwang could adopt unconventional technologies, including a solid-state battery and rear-hinged coach doors. The expected price is about $300,000 (about 400 million won), raising attention on whether BYD can move beyond mass-market EVs into the ultra-luxury segment. Electrek, an EV outlet, reported on Oct. 26 that Yangwang chose the UAE, rather than China, for the global unveiling of its new flagship sedan. While the exact date has not been announced, Chinese auto outlet CarNewsChina cited a project source as saying it could be unveiled in Dubai around Nov. 5. The new car is expected to be a symbolic model for BYD's premium-car strategy. Yangwang is a sub-brand at the top of BYD's brand structure and has sought differentiation with high-performance EV technology and body control systems. Its signature technologies, the four-motor-based e4 platform and the Disus-X body control system, enable various movements such as rotating in place, moving the body and driving with only some wheels. The new sedan is also expected to stand apart from existing BYD models in size and design. Yangwang General Manager Hu Xiaoqing (후 샤오칭) last month released photos of a test vehicle during a trial drive. Details are hard to confirm due to camouflage, but assessments say its proportions recall ultra-luxury sedans such as the Mercedes-Benz Maybach S-Class or Rolls-Royce Phantom. Locally, the overall length is estimated to reach about 5,500 mm. A key technical difference being discussed is the possible use of a solid-state battery. Yangwang Executive General Manager Zheng Yu (정위) said the new car would apply "unprecedented disruptive technology", but did not disclose detailed specifications. BYD has also not officially confirmed whether a solid-state battery will be used. Even so, BYD's battery development timeline is drawing attention to the outlook. Stella Li, BYD's executive vice president, said in an interview with Cawawe Eswa last month that BYD's first solid-state battery vehicle is scheduled to come out in 2027. She stressed that BYD holds a leading position in solid-state battery technology and commercialisation and indicated it would prove that next year. BYD's battery affiliate FinDreams plans to begin producing sulfide-based solid-state batteries in 2027. It plans to focus on small-volume production initially and expand mass production as it gets closer to the 2030s. That has led to speculation that the new flagship sedan could showcase solid-state battery technology, but whether it is actually fitted must be confirmed through an official announcement. Charging performance is also in focus. After the test vehicle was spotted at BYD's flash charging station, speculation emerged that it could support megawatt-class ultra-fast charging. Specific performance, including charging output and charging time, has not been disclosed. It is also not yet confirmed whether rear-hinged coach doors will be applied to the mass-produced model. The price is expected to be set far above Yangwang's existing lineup. Locally, there is an outlook that the new car's starting price could be in the 2 million yuan range, or about $300,000. Yangwang's all-electric sedan U7 is sold from 658,000 yuan, and its lineup also includes the plug-in hybrid luxury off-roader U8 and U8L and the all-electric super coupe U9. The U8L starts at 1.45 million yuan. If the new sedan is priced as expected, it would enter a price bracket higher than existing Yangwang models. This can be interpreted as an attempt by BYD to win recognition for its technology and brand value in the ultra-luxury car market beyond being a mass-market EV maker built on price competitiveness. Key specifications, including a solid-state battery, megawatt-class charging and coach doors, have not yet been confirmed. If the unveiling takes place in early November, the actual battery technology, performance and price are expected to be key benchmarks for gauging BYD's ultra-luxury EV strategy.

artigo.texto: What Six Months of Fluid Data Says About Aluminum in Liquid Cooling We have two sets of charts from our liquid cooling test. One is from June, the other from December. Same loop, same coolant, six months and more than 4,000 hours apart. Put them side by side and you cannot tell which is which. That would be unremarkable in an all-copper system. This loop had an aluminum heat exchanger sharing coolant with copper cold plates and stainless steel plumbing, the mixed-metal combination the industry has spent a decade avoiding. Conventional caution says the June charts and the December charts should look different. They don't. Here is what we built, why we built it, and what operators should take from it. Why test aluminum at all Liquid cooling inherited its materials. Copper went into cold plates, and stainless steel and brass went into manifolds, piping, and fittings. Each was a sound choice when it was made. At AI scale, the bundle is getting heavy, scarce, and expensive. A coolant distribution unit can weigh one to two tons, and an AI rack is approaching four to five thousand pounds. Copper is being pulled in several directions at once by grid buildout, electrification, and transportation, which means our industry is now competing for tonnage with the power grid it depends on. Aluminum eases all three pressures. It is roughly one-third the density of copper, more abundant, less expensive, and easier to extrude into the geometries modern heat exchangers call for. What has kept it out of the wetted path is galvanic corrosion. Put aluminum and copper in the same water-based coolant without adequate protection and the aluminum gives up material to the fluid. For equipment expected to run for years untouched, few engineers wanted to take that risk on faith. So we tested it. What we built Working with Valvoline, we built a test bench at their research facility in Ashland, Kentucky, modeled on the wetted path of a liquid-to-air CDU serving direct-to-chip loads. An aluminum microchannel heat exchanger fed five copper cold plates in parallel through stainless steel tubing and EPDM hoses. The coolant was Valvoline's PG25 Advanced, a propylene glycol formulation with an inhibitor package tuned for data center loops. Heat pads put one to two kilowatts on each cold plate. The loop moved 20 liters per minute in total, split unevenly across the five cold plates at roughly four to five liters per minute each. We left that imbalance in place on purpose, because real deployments are rarely balanced perfectly, and controlled the plates to a common temperature target instead. The test ran continuously from June through December 2025, 4,362 hours in total, and we pulled 28 fluid samples along the way. What the fluid told us We tracked the loop the way an operator would, through the fluid. Twenty-eight samples drawn over six months were analyzed for dissolved metals, coolant chemistry, and inhibitor levels, because the fluid is where corrosion leaves its record. We had not cut open the heat exchanger or cold plates before publication, and that is a fair limitation to name. But if aluminum were leaving the heat exchanger, the fluid would have shown it as a steady climb in dissolved aluminum. That climb never came. For most of the test, aluminum, copper, and iron (our proxy for the stainless steel) read at or near zero. During one stretch, between roughly 1,030 and 1,867 hours, all three rose briefly, with aluminum peaking at 1.08 ppm and copper and iron at about a tenth of that, then fell back and stayed low. Two things about that stretch matter. Every reading stayed well under the 2 ppm limit the OCP PG25 base specification sets for fresh fluid. And the three metals moved together. Galvanic corrosion would look different. Dissolved aluminum would climb on its own and keep building over time, while the copper stayed protected. Nothing in the data shows that pattern. The rest of the chemistry held as well. pH stayed around 8, and reserve alkalinity stayed between 0.8 and 1.0. Specific gravity and freeze point were flat, so the glycol ratio did not drift. The organic acid inhibitors finished essentially where they started, and the copper-protecting azoles declined slowly and predictably, on a trend that projects useful protection well beyond the test window. Thermal conductivity and heat capacity matched their initial values, and the cold plates showed no thermal drift. What operators should take from it The lesson is not to swap your copper for aluminum. For now, copper remains the standard at the cold plate, where heat flux is highest and its conductivity earns its cost. Our focus was the CDU side of the loop. The same cost, weight, and supply pressures apply at the chip, though. We expect cold plate designers and chip makers to run their own analysis on whether aluminum makes sense there too. The lesson is that aluminum belongs where its strengths matter and its weakness can be managed. The heat exchanger has always been the toughest place to justify aluminum in the wetted path, and with the right chemistry it now has data behind it. That makes the coolant a design decision rather than a commodity line item. If you are evaluating mixed-metal equipment, a few practices follow: - Specify the fluid with the hardware. Ask which inhibitor package the loop was qualified with, and keep that chemistry in service. - Sample on a schedule. Dissolved metals, pH, and reserve alkalinity are inexpensive to track and tell you early whether protection is holding. - Watch the inhibitors, not just the metals. Inhibitor depletion shows up before metal loss does. - Use the OCP PG25 specification as your yardstick. It gives buyers and suppliers a shared reference for what healthy fluid looks like. None of this is exotic. Automotive cooling systems have run aluminum, copper, brass, and iron in one inhibited coolant for decades, at higher temperatures and with drivers who rarely check. artigo.texto: Data centers are a hot-button issue for Ohioans as midterms near Candidates work to ease concerns as data centers become hot-button issue for Ohioans In Ohio, many people are displeased with the state's rapid buildout of data centers. It's a hot-button issue in the midterms, as political candidates from both parties try to ease voter concerns. MICHEL MARTIN, HOST: Back here in the U.S., Ohio has seen some of the fastest data center growth in the country and some of the fiercest backlash. NPR's Andrea Hsu reports on how the hot-button issue cuts across party lines. UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #1: Can you say, trick or treat? ANDREA HSU, BYLINE: Halloween has come early in the Cincinnati suburb of Fairfield. Pint-sized pirates and princesses weave their way through booths set up by local businesses and churches and other groups. UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #1: You get a prize, and you get a piece of candy. HSU: At this booth, there's something for the grown-ups too. LINDA MOODIE: Do you have any interest in signing a petition while you're here? UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #2: What is it for? MOODIE: To ban large-scale data centers in the state. HSU: That's Linda Moodie with Conserve Ohio. The all-volunteer group has been working to stop the development of huge data centers - the kind used to power AI. They're behind ballot initiatives in 10 communities this fall, and they're still collecting signatures for a statewide ban they hope to get on the ballot in 2027. It's an effort many are happy to back. UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #2: Yeah. Yeah, yeah, yeah. MOODIE: Awesome. Are you a registered voter? HSU: More than a decade ago, tech companies came to Ohio, drawn by the state's inexpensive and abundant land, its energy infrastructure and its generous tax breaks. Like many parents in this crowd, Kyler Osterberger is now worried about the impact the data center boom is having. KYLER OSTERBERGER: Just, like, the resources, electricity, rising costs. HSU: Others fear the pollution new power plants will bring. Linda Moodie is wary about data centers further enabling AI. MOODIE: We don't necessarily trust that the government's going do the right thing. HSU: Whoever gets elected? MOODIE: Yeah. Absolutely. HSU: Data centers have figured prominently in the tight race for a U.S. Senate seat in Ohio. Both candidates are calling for greater accountability, but neither has gone as far as to back a moratorium. The Democrat, former Senator Sherrod Brown, has cast his opponent, current Republican Senator Jon Husted, as the face of data centers. Back when Husted was lieutenant governor, he did champion investments in them. Now Brown's running ads featuring disgruntled Ohioans. (SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING) UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #3: Even today Husted wants to build more data centers. UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #4: No matter how much water they use. UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #3: Or how much they cost. HSU: For his part, Husted has called Brown hypocritical, pointing to his past support for data centers. And Husted's has been pushing a bill in Washington aimed at getting data centers to pay for things like upgrades to the power grid. (SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING) JON HUSTED: The Ratepayer Protection Act rests on a principle every American understands - pay your own way. HSU: But to Nick Owens, the problem goes far beyond who's footing the bill. Owens is one of the founders of that grassroots group, Conserve Ohio. I meet him in the village of Mount Orab, an hour east of Cincinnati. We drive through a neighborhood of beautiful homes on big, grassy lots. NICK OWENS: This is the Ohio that people brag about. This is the Ohio people love. HSU: At the end of a block, there's a huge field - part of 1,000 acres that have been sold to a data center developer. There's corn right here, so this is farmland. OWENS: Yeah. I mean, literally, we are feet from the data center property and where you will have the constant hum, noise, pollution, whatever - I mean, literally from these people's backyards, front yards. You know, people don't deserve to live this way. HSU: He says, why not build data centers on old industrial sites instead? OWENS: If we're going to have data centers, those are the prime places. HSU: Owens is an attorney and a lifelong Republican, a former Trump delegate. He won't say how he's voting this fall. But he says the data center issue, along with $6 diesel, is dampening enthusiasm for Republicans. He didn't appreciate Trump's warning that communities that oppose data centers will lose out. OWENS: When, you know, the president says, well, you'll just be poor and backwards, no. I want our regular way of life. HSU: Construction at the site hasn't begun yet. It's not clear when it will. Owen says, because of nondisclosure agreements, people who live here know nothing. For now, all you hear is birds. Andrea Hsu, NPR News in Mount Orab, Ohio. (SOUNDBITE OF SONG, "OHIO! artigo.texto: The Ełk and Turośń Kościelna battery projects in north-eastern Poland are to be sold to A&R Investments by Greenvolt, a Portugal-based renewable energy group. The two stand-alone projects hold 1.6 GWh between them, and each has 200 MW of power and 800 MWh of storage capacity. Both were completed in the third quarter of 2026, and each of them can discharge at full power for about four hours. Each project also holds a 17-year capacity market contract, under which it is to receive a fixed payment from 2028 for keeping 85% of its rated capacity available. A 10-year tolling agreement covers both projects, and under it their flexibility is to be traded in the power markets. The transaction is expected to close by the end of 2026. For Greenvolt, the sale forms part of an asset rotation strategy, which foresees the sale of approximately 70-80% of the projects that it develops internally. Greenvolt to sell 1.6 GWh of BESS in Poland to A&R Investments A&R Investments is to buy the two battery projects that Greenvolt Power has completed in north-eastern Poland, and each of them holds a 17-year capacity market contract. artigo.texto: Sungrow and ENGIE Advance Australia’s Energy Transition with Grid-Forming Technology at Hazelwood 2 BESS By PR Newswire MELBOURNE, Australia, Oct. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Sungrow, a globally leading PV inverter and energy storage system provider, is partnering with ENGIE and Elecnor on the 150 MW / 300 MWh Hazelwood Battery Energy Storage System expansion (HBESS 2) in Victoria, Australia, with Sungrow Australia as the technology provider and Elecnor as the BOP Contractor. This project will feature 66 units of Sungrow’s ST5015-UX battery energy storage system (BESS), part of the PowerTitan 2.0 series, alongside 33 units of SC6900UD-MV Power Conversion System (PCS) inverters and Sungrow’s smart controller EMS3000. Designed for utility-scale applications, the PowerTitan 2.0 system offers several key advantages: - High energy density: Optimises energy storage capacity. - Liquid-cooled technology: Helps maintain stable operating temperatures and support system reliability. - Advanced battery management: Supports battery safety, performance monitoring and long-term operational reliability. - High-performance power conversion: Paired with the SC6900UD-MV PCS inverters, it supports efficient power conversion and responsive grid support for utility-scale applications. With commercial operations targeted for 2028, the Hazelwood BESS 2 project will add significant battery storage capacity to Victoria’s energy infrastructure, reinforcing Hazelwood’s role in providing flexible energy resources for Victoria and the National Electricity Market (NEM). By storing and delivering electricity when needed, the system will help balance supply and demand as Australia’s energy landscape continues to evolve. Grid-forming technology will further enhance the project’s capabilities, helping strengthen network performance as renewable generation increases. Key benefits include: - Grid stability: Supports voltage and frequency stability to help maintain reliable network operation. - Fast response: Enables rapid responses to changing grid conditions to support power system reliability. - Renewable integration: Helps accommodate higher levels of variable renewable generation. - Grid resilience: Provides advanced grid support capabilities to strengthen the network under changing operating conditions. The combination of energy storage and advanced grid-forming capabilities will contribute to a more resilient and reliable power system. “The Hazelwood BESS 2 represents an important step in advancing grid-forming energy storage in Australia. Through our collaboration with ENGIE, we aim to bring advanced energy storage technology to support grid stability and enable greater integration of renewable energy. We look forward to contributing our expertise and supporting the continued development of a more resilient energy system in Victoria,” said Thomas Hou, Managing Director at Sungrow Australia. The commencement of Hazelwood BESS 2 reflects the continued development of large-scale battery storage in Australia and the role of Sungrow’s technology in delivering infrastructure to support the evolving energy system. artigo.texto: Microtek Unveils BESS Solutions for Energy Management and Cost Optimisation at REI Expo 2026 Microtek highlighted its high-voltage lithium battery pack and i-BESS 125kW/261kWh system at REI Expo 2026, designed to support peak shaving, microgrid integration and electricity cost management. October 26, 2026. By News Bureau Microtek showcased its integrated solar, energy storage and power management portfolio at Renewable Energy India (REI) Expo 2026, from October 22 to 24 in Greater Noida. Led by its ‘Har Ghar Bijli Ghar’ vision, the company introduced its new Battery Energy Storage System (BESS), highlighting its focus on making reliable energy solutions accessible to households and businesses. With nearly four decades of power management experience, Microtek’s portfolio spans: power generation, distribution, conditioning and storage. The showcase products included home inverters, UPS systems, batteries, electrical wires, solar panels, solar inverters and lithium batteries. This breadth underpins its holistic approach, connecting solar generation with power distribution, protection and storage within one portfolio. Microtek’s new High-Voltage Lithium Battery Pack and BESS range was a key highlight at the EXPO, showcasing the i-BESS 125kW/261kWh system. These intelligent energy storage solutions are designed to support peak shaving, microgrid integration and electricity cost optimisation. This marks Microtek’s entry into the high-voltage energy storage segment. Commenting on the participation, N.K Aggarwal, Founder and Chairman of Microtek International, said, “Our vision of ‘Har Ghar Bijli Ghar’ reflects our ambition to help households generate and manage their own electricity. Our portfolio across generation, distribution, conditioning and storage builds on nearly four decades of experience in keeping power reliable. Through our BESS and lithium-based solutions, we are strengthening our capabilities to serve India’s changing energy needs.” Microtek’s reach is supported by over 1 lakh plus dealers across India. The company expects to more than double revenue in FY 2026–27 to INR 5,000 crore, with an ambition to reach INR 10,000 crore within two years. At REI Expo, Microtek connected with channel partners and industry experts to showcase its solar and energy storage solutions. The exhibition will also provide a platform to discuss new business opportunities, expand its distribution network and build partnerships to make its solutions more widely available for homes and businesses. please contact: contact@energetica-india.net.

artigo.texto: Em julho deste ano, o historiador Greg Pirio compareceu à Junta de Supervisores do condado de Loudoun, na Virgínia (EUA), para dizer uma coisa simples: não há mais pássaros na vizinhança. O som os expulsou. Pirio mora em Sterling, a cerca de 140 metros do campus VA2 da Vantage Data Centers. Loudoun fica a 40 quilômetros de Washington e reúne a maior concentração de data centers do mundo. O galpão vizinho a Pirio funciona com usina própria a gás e dezenas de geradores a diesel; desde o início de 2025, ele e os vizinhos relatam um apito agudo e contínuo das turbinas, dores de cabeça, noites mal dormidas, olhos irritados e gosto de diesel ao sair de casa. O caso vem sendo documentado pela imprensa norte-americana desde o primeiro semestre. A primavera que zumbe A frase de Pirio remete a um livro de 1962. Rachel Carson abriu “Silent Spring”, a “Primavera Silenciosa”, com uma fábula: uma cidade no coração dos Estados Unidos onde, certa primavera, os pássaros simplesmente não voltaram, e as manhãs, antes cheias de canto, amanheceram mudas. O veneno que os calou era invisível, agia devagar e vinha de uma indústria que negava o nexo. A fábula era um aviso, e o aviso mudou o direito ambiental do século 20. Em Loudoun, os pássaros também se foram, mas a primavera não ficou silenciosa. Ficou ruidosa. O que os expulsou não foi um agente químico que ninguém via, e sim um zumbido que todos ouvem, dia e noite, vindo de um galpão que se apresenta ao mundo como “nuvem”. A inversão é instrutiva: a poluição digital, como a denominei no livro, é invisível por projeto, escondida atrás de uma metáfora que sugere leveza; o dano que ela produz, porém, chega pelo ouvido, pelo olho irritado e pelo gosto de diesel na boca. O que se repete de Carson a Loudoun é o padrão, não o agente: dano difuso, de instalação lenta, sentido primeiro por quem mora perto e negado por quem lucra longe. Carson escreveu para que a primavera seguinte não fosse muda. O recado de Loudoun é que a primavera já chegou zumbindo, e que ainda há tempo de regulamentar antes que ela chegue aqui. O galpão de Sterling foi construído por direito de uso (“by right”), em área zoneada como industrial; a usina própria, com oito turbinas a gás, não foi mencionada na reunião pública de 2022, segundo os moradores. A empresa diz que as turbinas são solução provisória, até que a rede elétrica tenha capacidade, e anunciou medidas de isolamento acústico. Há aqui um dado jurídico que interessa mais do que a cena. Nos Estados Unidos, a localização desses empreendimentos é decidida sobretudo no plano local, com base no zoneamento, e a reação política costuma vir depois do dano: na Virgínia, projetos de moratória já se acumulam para a sessão legislativa de janeiro, e o tema entrou na campanha das eleições de meio de mandato de 3 de novembro. Diante disso, a pergunta que se impõe é: e se o galpão fosse brasileiro? Sustento que o Direito brasileiro oferece duas formas de enxergar o problema, ambas em vigor e nenhuma delas escrita para a inteligência artificial. Duas lentes para um só galpão A primeira lente é civil. O artigo 1.277 do Código Civil assegura ao proprietário ou possuidor de um prédio o direito de fazer cessar as interferências prejudiciais à segurança, ao sossego e à saúde dos que o habitam, provocadas pela utilização de propriedade vizinha. O parágrafo único manda considerar a natureza da utilização, a localização do prédio, as normas que distribuem as edificações em zonas e os limites ordinários de tolerância dos moradores da vizinhança. Cada uma das interferências relatadas em Loudoun já nasce qualificada por esse dispositivo. O ruído contínuo atinge, de início, o sossego e, quando impede o sono, a saúde. A fumaça dos geradores a diesel atinge a saúde e, nos episódios de acionamento em bloco, a segurança. Nenhuma dessas interferências depende de culpa do operador: o direito de vizinhança não indaga se o vizinho agiu bem, mas se o uso ultrapassou o que o confinante está obrigado a suportar. O morador de Sterling, se estivesse no Brasil, teria ação própria contra o vizinho que o adoece, com fundamento nos artigos 1.277 a 1.279 do Código Civil. É o problema do que tenho chamado de vizinho algorítmico: a nuvem tem endereço, o endereço tem confinantes, e os confinantes têm os remédios de sempre. Registre-se, porém, o limite do instrumento. A ação de vizinhança protege quem mora ao lado. Ela não alcança a bacia hidrográfica que abastece o resfriamento, a rede elétrica sobrecarregada, o território convertido em galpões nem as gerações que ainda não nasceram. Para isso existe a segunda lente. A lente ambiental: a lei de 1981 A Lei nº 6.938, de 31 de agosto de 1981, instituiu a Política Nacional do Meio Ambiente. Foi recepcionada pela Constituição de 1988, que no artigo 225 assegura a todos o direito ao meio ambiente ecologicamente equilibrado, bem de uso comum do povo, e impõe ao poder público e à coletividade o dever de defendê-lo e preservá-lo para as presentes e futuras gerações. O artigo 170, inciso VI, fez da defesa do meio ambiente princípio da ordem econômica. O artigo 3º, inciso III, da lei define poluição como a degradação da qualidade ambiental resultante de atividades que, direta ou indiretamente, prejudiquem a saúde, a segurança e o bem-estar da população, criem condições adversas às atividades sociais e econômicas, afetem desfavoravelmente a biota ou as condições estéticas ou sanitárias do meio ambiente, ou lancem matérias ou energias em desacordo com os padrões ambientais estabelecidos. O inciso IV define poluidor como a pessoa física ou jurídica, de direito público ou privado, responsável, direta ou indiretamente, por atividade causadora de degradação ambiental. Note-se que o vocabulário é o mesmo do Código Civil: saúde, segurança, bem-estar. O que o vizinho sofre dentro de casa, a coletividade sofre no território. artigo.texto: Baixo Guandu, no Noroeste do Espírito Santo, vai ganhar nos próximos anos um data center voltado para abrigar e executar sistemas de inteligência artificial (IA). O investimento contempla a instação de um sistema modular com capacidade de computacional 100 Megawatts (MW) e está estimado em R$ 7,4 bilhões. O novo data center capixaba foi projetado para processar e armazenar volumes massivos de dados de clientes internacionais e gigantes mundiais de tecnologia. "O nosso data center é uma estrutura voltada para inteligência artificial. Não é um projeto para atender apenas ao mercado local. Nossa intenção é processar e armazenar dados globais de clientes do mundo inteiro", destaca o empresário Mário Rodrigues, que integra o projeto com um grupo de investidores capixabas, em parceria com empresas e fundos de investimento. O projeto, segundo Rodrigues, está atualmente na fase de desenvolvimento de engenharia, obtenção de licenças ambientais e aprovação de conexões de energia — processo regulatório do setor que leva de 24 a 36 meses. O terreno onde será o complexo tem 11,3 milhões de metros quadrados e fica a nove quilômetros da cidade. O empresário acrescenta que, paralelamente, o grupo vai realizar roadshows internacionais visando fechar contratos de pré-locação de longo prazo, com previsão de 20 anos e em dólar com multinacionais de tecnologia. A intenção é garantir a ocupação total da estrutura antes do início das obras físicas. A capacidade inicial de 100 MW de poder computacional do data center equivale ao consumo de processamento de 15 a 20 milhões de pessoas assistindo simultaneamente a vídeos em resolução 4K em serviços de streaming como a Netflix. A estrutura é modular e tem potencial para expandir no futuro para até 1 Gigawatt (GW), conforme o crescimento da demanda por IA. O que é um data center? Um data center, ou centro de dados, em português, é uma instalação física ou prédio projetado para abrigar uma infraestrutura de TI — como servidores, sistemas de armazenamento e equipamentos de rede — que processa, guarda e distribui grandes volumes de dados. A estrutura é a base física por trás de tudo o que usamos na internet, como redes sociais, serviços de streaming, bancos digitais, aplicativos de entrega e a computação em nuvem. A instalação do complexo de tecnologia no Noroeste capixaba se deu por fatores como localização e acesso a água e energia. O complexo vai ficar próximo da Usina Hidrelétrica de Mascarenhas (a maior geradora de eletricidade do Espírito Santo) e da subestação local. Além disso, três redes de distribuição de alta tensão ligadas ao Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN) cortam a propriedade, com sinalização positiva do órgão regulador sobre a capacidade de tráfego livre. Também pesa a favor a passagem da linha férrea Vitória-Minas, com cabo de fibra óptica que conecta a Região Metropolitana de Belo Horizonte ao cabo submarino internacional em Vitória, a apenas 1,5 metro dos dormentes. "O que um data center demanda? Energia, infraestrutura elétrica e fibra óptica. Nós temos a maior usina do Estado ao lado, redes de alta tensão livres e a fibra óptica que acompanha a ferrovia. É um cenário completamente diferenciado", afirma Mário. A proximidade com o Rio Doce também foi um dos motivos para a instalação do local. O sistema dos data centers precisa de resfriamento. O empresário afirma que isso ser um sistema em circuito fechado, que faz a água recircular continuamente. “A perda mensal por evaporação para o bloco de 100 MW equivale ao consumo de apenas três casas populares com quatro moradoras cada. Além disso, a presença de água doce na região elimina a necessidade de aportes em dessalinização do mar”, pontuou. A previsão é que a instalação do empreendimento crie entre 300 e 500 empregos diretos na montagem e obras civis. Na fase de operação, a projeção é ter cerca de 10% desse contingente de forma direta, porém formada por técnicos e engenheiros de alta qualificação e remuneração elevada. Na avaliação do investidor, isso vai injetar capital no comércio, na rede hoteleira, em restaurantes e em prestadores de serviços locais. Na arrecadação pública, ele estima que, com o faturamento anual do data center previsto em mais de R$ 1 bilhão, a alíquota de 5% do Imposto Sobre Serviços (ISS) direcionará entre R$ 50 milhões e R$ 60 milhões por ano diretamente para o caixa da Prefeitura de Baixo Guandu.

artigo.texto: Coordenador da organização cobra análise dos impactos acumulados na região A empresa capixaba Line Solution anunciou a instalação de um data center com investimento previsto de R$ 7,4 bilhões em Baixo Guandu, no noroeste do Estado. O prefeito Lastênio Cardoso (MDB), que reassume o cargo nesta terça-feira (27) após afastamento determinado pela Justiça Eleitoral, afirmou que a água necessária ao empreendimento viria de uma represa no Rio Doce. Ele disse ter articulado a apresentação do projeto ao governo estadual, mas não soube informar se foram apresentados estudos de impacto ambiental. A expectativa de transformar o município com a instalação de um data center contrasta com as preocupações sobre a pressão adicional nos recursos hídricos da região. Enquanto o prefeito Lastênio Cardoso fala em geração de empregos e no aumento da arrecadação municipal, Merci Fardin, coordenador do Observatório Capixaba da Água e do Meio Ambiente, aponta a necessidade de avaliar os impactos do empreendimento em conjunto com os de outros projetos previstos para a região. O Projeto Rubi, apresentado ao Executivo pela Line Solution, prevê a implantação de um data center voltado ao processamento de dados e à inteligência artificial, além de condomínios logístico e industrial. O complexo ocupará uma área de aproximadamente 566 hectares, e a previsão divulgada pela empresa é iniciar as operações em 2031. O projeto ainda está nas fases de desenvolvimento, licenciamento e captação de recursos. O prefeito Lastênio Cardoso afirmou que o município reúne condições estratégicas para receber a estrutura, especialmente pela disponibilidade de água e energia. “O data center precisa de muita água e a água que nós temos aqui é a represa, no Rio Doce. Precisa de energia e já tem a energia ali do lado”, disse, em referência à Usina Hidrelétrica de Mascarenhas, localizada no Rio Doce, em Baixo Guandu. A usina foi vendida pela portuguesa EDP à VH GSEO UK Holdings Limited, subsidiária da gestora britânica de investimentos Victory Hill, em uma operação concluída em dezembro de 2022. O prefeito relatou que participou da articulação política para apresentar o projeto ao governo estadual, incluindo reuniões com secretários, o ex-governador Renato Casagrande e o vice e atual governador Ricardo Ferraço (MDB). Segundo ele, essa etapa já foi cumprida, e o avanço agora depende do empreendedor e do grupo responsável pela implantação. “Eu apenas fiz a minha parte pra ajudar politicamente”, afirmou. Questionado sobre a apresentação de estudos de impacto ambiental, Lastênio direcionou a pergunta ao empresário Mário Rodrigues, fundador e CEO da Line Solution, alegando que ele poderia fornecer informações mais precisas sobre essa etapa. Apesar de não detalhar o estágio dos estudos ambientais, o prefeito demonstrou confiança nos efeitos econômicos do empreendimento. “Eu acho que isso acontecendo transforma o nosso município, entendeu? É outro patamar, em termos de porte, em termos de emprego”, afirmou, comparando a expectativa em torno do data center à transformação que atribui à construção e à inauguração da Usina Hidrelétrica de Mascarenhas, em 1974. “Esse data center, pra nós, vai ser 100 vezes mais do que aquilo”, afirmou. A empresa estima a criação de até 550 vagas de trabalho, sendo 500 durante as obras e 50 na operação. Também projeta uma arrecadação anual de R$ 50 milhões a R$ 60 milhões em Imposto Sobre Serviços (ISS), considerando uma alíquota de 5% sobre a receita bruta. Os valores são projeções apresentadas pela própria companhia, e não receitas ou empregos já concretizados. Para Merci Fardin, a discussão que trata da instalação do complexo não pode se limitar à disponibilidade de recursos naturais nas proximidades do terreno. É necessário considerar a pressão acrescentada por diferentes empreendimentos e seus efeitos conjuntos sobre a água e as atividades econômicas existentes. O coordenador da organização chamou atenção para o risco de novos projetos serem avaliados isoladamente, sem que se considere o conjunto das intervenções previstas para a região. “Se você coloca mais um projeto, tem uma tendência de aumento do uso dos recursos hídricos, contando com os outros projetos que estão anunciados ali”, observou. Ele ressalta que o planejamento precisa levar em conta os efeitos acumulados sobre os recursos naturais provocados na expansão de diferentes atividades econômicas no Norte do Estado e defendeu que a análise do data center considere os demais empreendimentos que poderão disputar recursos e demandar infraestrutura. A preocupação é relevante diante das características do Projeto Rubi. De acordo com as informações divulgadas pela Line Solution, o data center terá capacidade computacional inicial de 100 megawatts (MW). A estrutura vai ser voltada ao processamento de grandes volumes de dados, atividade que exige fornecimento contínuo de energia e sistemas de controle térmico para manter os equipamentos em funcionamento. Apesar de empresa afirmar que utilizará um sistema fechado de resfriamento, com reutilização contínua da água e reposição mensal estimada em volume equivalente ao consumo de três casas populares, essa projeção precisa ser analisada à luz dos dados técnicos do projeto, incluindo a fonte de abastecimento, a demanda efetiva e as condições de disponibilidade hídrica do território. Ainda não há, nas informações divulgadas sobre o empreendimento, detalhamento suficiente para confirmar qual manancial vai ser utilizado para abastecer o complexo, qual volume será solicitado ou se já foi protocolado pedido de outorga para captação de água. A identificação da fonte é essencial para determinar quais órgãos são responsáveis pela autorização de uso. O Rio Doce é um curso d’água de domínio federal, enquanto a competência sobre outros mananciais depende do enquadramento de cada corpo hídrico. artigo.texto: Years after the pandemic-era supply chain crisis has faded for much of the economy, data center developers are still battling equipment shortages and long, unpredictable lead times, a bottleneck that threatens to delay projects amid an artificial intelligence data center arms race. Equipment shortages persist as a major source of delays and uncertainty in an industry where developers are already struggling to keep pace with unprecedented demand. And delays can be costly, with hyperscalers and other tenants writing substantial penalties into contracts for missed delivery dates. The supply chain pinch is still being felt across nearly every part of the development process, from natural gas turbines and transformers to cooling systems and basic construction materials, industry insiders said at Bisnow’s Data Center Investment Conference and Expo: Central in Dallas this month. Sophisticated developers are finding ways to navigate many of these constraints, panelists said, but even then there are trade-offs. Strategies like stockpiling equipment or ordering long-lead items before designs are finalized require significant upfront capital and can raise project costs. And while some panelists expressed frustration that shortages tracing back to the pandemic nearly seven years ago have persisted for data centers long after easing in other industries, there is broad recognition that the procurement landscape isn’t returning to normal as long as the sector continues on its stratospheric growth trajectory. “There were discussions about how long Covid would impact us, and I don't know if we're ever going to go back to pre-Covid,” said Sam Caddell, CyrusOne’s senior director for facilities engineering and operations systems. “There are still impacts on lead times — from raw materials all the way down.” The most significant lead times are for equipment involved in getting power to data center project sites, panelists said. Gas turbines can take a decade or more to be delivered, a bottleneck that is currently contributing to yearslong timelines for grid connections and limiting developers’ ability to pursue on-site and behind-the-meter power as an alternative to utility interconnection queues. Transformer shortages are felt even more broadly, with panelists citing lead times of up to three years for equipment required on virtually every large-scale project. Similarly, backup generators can take more than a year to procure. The supply chain pinch extends well beyond power infrastructure. Chillers and other cooling system components routinely carry lead times of 12 to 18 months, panelists said, as do switchgear, uninterruptible power supply, or UPS, systems and other critical electrical and networking equipment integral to data center operations. Manufacturers said they simply can’t keep up with the flood of demand, even as they scramble to scale up production. “We're about to bring on a brand-new chiller factory. We'll have four chiller factories that can supply this market, and even then it's not enough,” said Dara Sanii, a director at cooling equipment provider Carrier Applied West. It’s not just complex equipment that is facing shortages. Even basic hardware and construction materials are seeing significant delays. Optical fiber can take six to eight months to arrive, and structural steel roughly a year. Meanwhile, contractors continue to encounter unexpected delays for relatively simple components like conduits and medium-voltage cables. These same hardware shortages also factor into delays in the production of more complex data center systems. Manufacturers say pumps, evaporators, fans, coils and heat exchangers used in cooling equipment are routinely sold out for a year or more, while basic components like breakers can slow the production of electrical systems. “The capacity the industry's taking down is outstripping the ability of the entire supply chain to keep up,” Johnson Controls Vice President Matt Kightlinger told DICE: Central. “It is absolutely an issue industrywide, all the way down to the component level.” Some of the pressure on the data center supply chain has been eased by delays elsewhere, panelists said. Projects derailed by grid constraints or local opposition have freed up equipment that had already been allocated, pushing scarce components back into the market. Even so, preventing procurement from becoming the pinch point on a project has required developers to rethink how they buy equipment and plan construction. Panelists said the ability to manage these constraints has become a key differentiator between firms that can actually deliver projects on schedule and those that cannot. One common strategy has been to stockpile long-lead equipment years in advance, effectively creating a strategic reserve of transformers and other critical equipment that can be deployed across multiple projects. It’s an approach that SkyBox Datacenters Executive Vice President Gordon Kellerman compared to “Covid panic-toilet-paper-buying.” But it's a strategy only open to major developers with deep balance sheets and large project pipelines, who can commit capital well before they know exactly where the equipment will ultimately be used. “We are definitely trying to buy multiple years out. That’s one of the advantages of having been around for a little longer and having a little more capital,” CyrusOne’s Cadell said. “I worked for a startup data center company, too, for a little bit, and this is a bigger challenge there.” Sophisticated developers are also sharing demand forecasts with suppliers as far as three years in advance, giving manufacturers greater visibility to plan production capacity.
