artigo.texto: Do ronco ao silêncio: qual a diferença entre dirigir um carro elétrico e um a combustão? César Urnhani, piloto e especialista automotivo, mostra quais são essas diferenças e dá dicas para quem está fazendo essa transição. Crédito: Estadão O crescimento do mercado de carros movidos a energia elétrica no Brasil já deixou de ser apenas uma projeção otimista e se tornou um movimento incontestável nos últimos anos. As vendas de veículos elétricos puros e híbridos atingiram 21% da participação no mercado automotivo em julho de 2026, segundo dados da ABVE (Associação Brasileira do Veículo Elétrico). Com o rápido aumento da popularidade da tecnologia, no entanto, surgem novas dúvidas, principalmente relacionadas à durabilidade das baterias de íon de lítio. Em média, os carros movidos a bateria possuem garantia entre oito e dez anos, mantendo autonomia que varia entre 70% e 90% da capacidade original após esse período - desempenho que supera até mesmo as baterias de chumbo-ácido usadas em veículos a combustão. Prova viva de como o alcance se mantém é este empresário que conta com pequena frota de BYD Dolphin Mini. Ainda assim, algum dia, essas peças ainda precisarão ser trocadas, descartadas ou recicladas. E esse processo precisa ser feito corretamente, caso contrário, as consequências podem ser prejudiciais tanto para o veículo quanto para o meio ambiente. Isso porque o descarte incorreto desses componentes em lixo comum ou aterros (ato proibido pela Política Nacional de Resíduos Sólidos) pode causar o vazamento de metais pesados e compostos químicos tóxicos, gerando a contaminação crônica de lençois freáticos e do solo, além de riscos de incêndios químicos de difícil extinção. Trocas e descarte correto das baterias dos carros elétricos Diante desse cenário, o especialista em carros elétricos da SAE Brasil (Sociedade de Engenheiros da Mobilidade), Wanderlei Marinho, aponta que uma troca segura e eficiente da bateria do carro deve ser feita, sem exceção, em concessionárias ou redes de oficinas autorizadas e homologadas pelo Ibama. “A remoção exige equipamentos de proteção específicos e isolamento elétrico de alta tensão”, explica o engenheiro. Para mitigar os efeitos dos descartes inadequados, Wanderlei propõe soluções de rastreabilidade e investimento em infraestrutura, tais como: punir o desmonte ilegal ou o descarte clandestino por meio do monitoramento eletrônico de veículos que saem de circulação; e subvencionar e expandir usinas de reciclagem locais para que o processo seja economicamente viável perto dos grandes centros urbanos. Saiba Também: - Este país abriu as portas para carros chineses e se deu mal: o alerta da Tailândia para o Brasil - Ouvir música enquanto dirige pode ser perigoso? Entenda os riscos Sobre o mesmo dilema ambiental, o professor César Menezes, de manutenção automotiva do Senai Pernambuco - órgão que desenvolve o primeiro projeto brasileiro de baterias de lítio para veículos híbridos -, sugere práticas ágeis de contenção dos resíduos. “Para mitigar esses efeitos deve-se primeiramente conter a fonte de contaminação, coletar a bateria e destiná-la a uma das empresas de reciclagem para que o procedimento seja realizado e, por fim, recuperar o ambiente contaminado através de análises ambientais e aplicação de técnicas de remediação adequadas”, defende César. Reciclagem e reuso inteligente das baterias de íons de lítio Antes do procedimento de reciclagem indicado pelos especialistas, vale lembrar que as baterias não se tornam resíduos imediatamente após a retirada dos carros, podendo ser reaproveitadas em um “segunda vida”. “Quando a bateria atinge cerca de 75% a 80% da sua capacidade e perde a autonomia ideal para o carro, ela pode ser desmontada e redirecionada para aplicações estacionárias, como armazenamento de energia solar ou eólica, para uso residencial e industrial”, explica Wanderlei. Passado o momento em que o reaproveitamento não é mais possível, o próximo e último passo é a reciclagem industrial. Atualmente, a tecnologia mais eficiente combina o desmembramento mecânico das células da bateria com processos de hidrometalurgia. Com esse método, é possível recuperar entre 93% a 99% dos componentes (como lítio, cobalto, níquel e manganês), e, por fim, reinserí-los na cadeia de produção de novos materiais. A infraestrutura para esse tipo de processo está em rápida expansão no Brasil, justamente para atender a demanda da frota cada vez maior de veículos. Como manter a saúde da bateria do carro elétrico? Os oito anos estipulados pelas montadoras ao oferecerem garantias a seus consumidores fazem sentido, sobretudo considerando a perda de capacidade das baterias pelo uso acumulado de recarga e descarga, que é inevitável. Entretanto, elas podem durar mais do que isso, chegando até 15 anos de funcionamento, desde que sejam adotados alguns cuidados especiais, de acordo com estudiosos do tema. Segundo Bruno Souza, também do setor de manutenção automotiva do Senai-PE, o motorista que visa preservar sua bateria deve “evitar exposição prolongada a temperaturas elevadas, não deixar a carga chegar frequentemente a níveis muito baixos (menos de 20%) durante longos períodos, evitar manter a bateria constantemente em 100% quando isso não for necessário e utilizar carregadores recomendados pelo fabricante”. Em consonância com essa ideia, Wanderlei Marinho indica prestar atenção ao sistema de arrefecimento. “O sistema de gerenciamento térmico do carro protege as células contra degradação por temperatura. Realizar as revisões do fluido de arrefecimento do sistema elétrico conforme o manual é indispensável”, pontua ele. artigo.texto: Solidus Techno Power Private Limited has delivered a 27.31 MWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) integrated with a 50 MW solar project for SBF Ispat Private Limited. The company also provided engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) services for the project. Solidus is delivering this project through its subsidiary, XenRosh ESS. In a release, Solidus, a Punjab-based EPC company, said it is expanding its battery energy storage manufacturing capabilities to meet growing market demand. The company continues to support commercial and industrial customers through its solar EPC expertise and integrated energy storage solutions. The project strengthens Solidus’s solar and energy storage portfolio, complemented by BESS manufacturing through its subsidiary, XenRosh ESS. The project marks a milestone in Solidus’s expansion into integrated solar and energy storage solutions. Alongside its EPC and renewable energy development businesses, the company is strengthening its BESS manufacturing capabilities through XenRosh ESS, which focuses on manufacturing battery energy storage systems. Solidus Solar Project in Punjab Previously, Solidus developed a solar project in Punjab in collaboration with Roshni Renewable LLP, a venture promoted by professionals from Valco, an Indian aluminium company, and Solidus Techno Power Private Limited. The venture aims to establish a giga-scale solar module manufacturing plant in Punjab. With an initial production capacity of 1.8 GW, the project represents a step towards strengthening Punjab’s industrial ecosystem and India’s renewable energy sector, the company said. The fully automated production facility is expected to adhere to global production standards, generate substantial employment opportunities, and contribute to sustainable regional growth. Leadership View On the latest announcement, Jaspal Singh, Chief Executive Officer (CEO) and Co-founder of Solidus Techno Power Pvt Ltd, said, “Solar power combined with battery storage offers industries greater flexibility and helps them utilise renewable energy more effectively.” Harvinder Singh, Managing Director, added, “This project strengthens Solidus’s integrated clean-energy portfolio. Through XenRosh ESS, we are expanding our BESS manufacturing capabilities with a focus on quality, safety and reliability.”

artigo.texto: October 27, 2026 Introduction Iowa’s data center sector has grown from a handful of campuses into one of the fastest-growing parts of the state’s local property tax base. In 2014, seven data center campuses were operating or under development in Iowa. By 2025, that number had risen to 17, and current development plans put the state on track for 24 campuses by 2031. As the sector has grown, so has the debate over how to tax it. In 2025, the Iowa Legislature narrowed the sales tax exemptions available to new and expanding data centers through House File 976.[i] In 2026, Ohio and Arizona paused tax exemptions for new data center projects.[ii] Much of that debate centers on the tax relief data centers receive. This report examines the other side of the ledger, which is the taxes data centers pay and what that revenue means for the communities that host them. This report is a companion to CSI’s October 2026 report, The Economic Impact of Data Centers in Iowa, which estimated the economic impact of Iowa’s data center sector across construction, operations, and future development.[iii] That report measured the jobs, wages, and output the sector supports. This report focuses on the sector’s tax footprint, especially the property taxes data center campuses pay to local levy authorities and how communities have used that revenue. This report first estimates the property taxes Iowa’s data centers have paid since 2014 and are projected to pay through 2040. It then compares what data center land generates in property taxes with what the same land would generate as farmland. Next, it examines how local governments have used the added revenue, through a statewide analysis of levy rates and case studies of two school districts, and compares taxable sales growth in cities with and without data centers. Finally, it examines how Iowa’s sales tax treatment of data center equipment compares with its treatment of manufacturing equipment and with other states. Key Findings Data centers are a large and fast-growing source of local tax revenue. - Iowa’s data centers paid an estimated $319 million in property taxes to local governments from 2014 through 2025, including $56.1 million in 2025 alone. - Annual payments are projected to reach at least $140 million by 2031 and $292 million by 2040. - Cumulative payments could reach about $3.1 billion by 2040, with nearly 90% still to come. Data center land pays far more in property taxes than it did under its previous use. - In tax year 2026, an acre of data center land pays about $4,884 in property taxes, compared with about $29 under its previous use due to increased land value and different tax treatment. - For campuses with available data, data center parcels generated roughly 153 times the property tax in 2025 that the same land would have produced under its previous use. That multiple is projected to rise to about 505 times by 2040. Data center revenue funds local services and lowers homeowners’ taxes, but local choices determine how much. - In 2025, data centers paid $56.1 million in property taxes. An estimated $3.4 million of that, about $15 per home, lowered homeowner tax bills. The rest remained available to fund local services or lower other property owners’ bills. - Homeowners in the Norwalk Community School District saved an estimated $631 per household over three years after Microsoft’s Osmium campus reached the tax rolls. Homeowners in the Waukee Community School District saved about $269 over four years. Cities with data centers have seen faster growth in local sales, suggesting data centers may increase local economic activity. - From 2015 through 2025, taxable sales grew 50% in Iowa cities with a data center and 32% in cities without one. Iowa taxes data center equipment less favorably than manufacturing equipment. - Manufacturing machinery is exempt from sales tax by right, while data center equipment is exempt only through a conditional, tiered incentive. - Of the 41 states that exempt manufacturing equipment by right, only two—New York and West Virginia—do the same for data centers. - States with by-right exemptions have drawn 0.32 MW of planned capacity per square mile, double the 0.16 MW of conditional-exemption states such as Iowa. Property Tax Payments from Iowa’s Data Centers Property taxes are the most direct way data centers contribute to the communities that host them. Unlike state income and sales taxes, property taxes in Iowa are levied and spent locally. They fund the counties, cities, school districts, and other levy authorities that serve the area around each campus. Iowa’s local governments also rely on property taxes more heavily than most, drawing about 85% of their tax revenue from them.[iv] As a result, a large addition to the local property tax base can meaningfully change what a local government collects, what it asks of other taxpayers, or both. Iowa has seen this dynamic play out before. In its February 2026 report, Iowa’s Renewable Advantage: Driving Jobs, Growth, and Property Tax Relief, CSI estimated that wind and solar facilities paid roughly $1.22 billion in property taxes to Iowa’s local governments between 2010 and 2025.[v] That revenue did more than add to local budgets. School districts with more wind turbines tended to set lower voted levy rates, and an average residential property owner in a district with average wind production paid an estimated $194 less in property taxes than one in a district with no turbines.[vi] The report’s county case studies also found that median homeowner property taxes rose faster in comparable counties without wind development than in wind-producing counties. At the same time, the report found that some local governments used wind revenue to increase spending rather than lower rates. In other words, a large new source of taxable value can lighten the load on other taxpayers, expand local budgets, or both. artigo.texto: Madison County lawmakers have barred data center developers from seeking certain tax incentives. Members of the county board voted Wednesday to exclude data centers from property tax incentives through Illinois’ enterprise zone program, which aims to stimulate economic growth in struggling parts of the state. Projects that get the incentives receive 10-year property tax abatements that then phase out. Granite City, Madison and Venice currently have projects in the program. “There’s no need to incentivize a data center,” said board Chairman Chris Slusser. “They’re (developers) eager to build them.” The board amended rules for the Southwestern Madison County Enterprise zone to exclude data centers. Slusser said the county hopes to pursue similar restrictions in nearby zones. The Madison County discovery zone includes Collinsville, Glen Carbon, Maryville, Troy, St. Jacob and Highland. The decision comes as several developers eye the Metro East for data center development. Currently, developers are looking at Granite City and Pontoon Beach. Just this week, the developer behind a planned data center in Midtown St. Louis announced plans to build one at the site of the former Alton Steel mill. The developer, TerraWatt, said it wouldn’t seek any tax incentives. “We would not want to do a property tax exemption for a data center,” Slusser said. “I would not support a data center project that offers a property tax incentive.” The rules do not prohibit individual municipalities from providing their own tax incentives for data center projects. Residents in Chouteau, Granite City, Nameoki and Venice townships are set to vote on advisory measures in November, asking whether data center development should be allowed in their communities.

Segundo documento enviado nesta segunda-feira, 26, à Securities and Exchanges Commission (SEC, a CVM dos EUA), a operação prevê o arrendamento de unidades de processamento gráfico (GPUs) e equipamentos relacionados. O compromisso vinculante foi assinado em 24 de outubro e estabelece que a entidade ligada à Apollo comprará os equipamentos e os alugará à SpaceX, que realizará pagamentos trimestrais ao longo de aproximadamente cinco anos. Os equipamentos serão entregues em lotes, com contratos individuais de arrendamento previstos para começar no primeiro semestre de 2027. Cada contrato terá duração de cinco anos a cinco anos e três meses. Segundo a companhia, os pagamentos trimestrais serão feitos antecipadamente e incluirão, em geral, um vigésimo do custo financiado de cada lote, além de juros calculados a uma taxa anual fixa sobre o saldo devedor e despesas adicionais. A taxa de juros ainda será definida. A SpaceX estima que os pagamentos de principal totalizem aproximadamente US$ 40 bilhões durante a vigência dos contratos, sem incluir juros e outros custos. artigo.texto: Pakistan plans $2.25 billion battery gigafactory as demand projected to hit 100,000 MW in four years: report Profit by Pakistan Today • • 1 min read Margalla Heavy Industries Limited has agreed to invest $2.25 billion with Chinese and local partners in a lithium-ion battery plant in Rawalpindi, Profit by Pakistan Today reported, citing Arab News. The project is awaiting approval of the government’s battery manufacturing policy; production could start six to eight months after approval. The partners have not been identified. The facility is expected to begin with annual output of 200-300 megawatts, with plans to expand beyond 1,000MW. Engineering Development Board chief Hamad Ali Mansoor said battery storage demand could reach 100,000MW by June 2030 if economic growth is at least 5%, while grid stabilisation alone could need 3,000-5,000MW. Pakistan currently assembles about 3,000-4,000MW of batteries, according to the EDB. The pending policy envisages four battery manufacturing sites and export requirements for producers. The government’s automotive policy for 2026-2031 has received approval from Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif but is awaiting IMF clearance on proposed EV tax incentives. At a glance - A $2.25 billion battery plant is planned for Rawalpindi. - Production is conditional on approval of the government’s battery policy. - Battery storage demand could reach 100,000MW by June 2030 under higher growth. artigo.texto: On October 27, Brazil's National Electric Energy Agency (ANEEL) unanimously approved the tender documents for two battery storage capacity reserve auctions, to be held on December 2 and 4. They will be Brazil's first centralized procurement of battery energy storage. A day earlier, the Brazilian Photovoltaic Solar Energy Association (ABSOLAR) submitted its 2027–2030 energy agenda to the re-elected Lula government, proposing 8 GW of utility-scale storage by 2030 and an annual, technology-neutral capacity auction mechanism, with the two December auctions as its starting point. SMM believes the first auctions matter mainly because they will set price and contract benchmarks for utility-scale storage in Brazil, while near-term equipment demand depends on the procurement volume ultimately announced by the Ministry of Mines and Energy (MME). Because the domestic-content auction takes priority and the open auction fills the remainder, imported systems will still need to cover whatever local capacity cannot supply. Chinese storage suppliers will enter the market through two routes: local partnerships and the open auction. Two Auctions: Domestic Content First, Open Auction Fills the Gap Both auctions procure reserve capacity from new electrochemical storage projects connected to Brazil's National Interconnected System (SIN). The December 2 "National Storage" auction is limited to projects that meet the minimum local-content requirements of the Brazilian Development Bank (BNDES) and has priority in meeting the procurement demand set by the MME. The December 4 "Storage" auction has no equipment-origin requirement. The MME has set ceiling prices of R$1.76 million/MW per year and R$1.58 million/MW per year, respectively, putting the domestic-content auction about 11.4% higher. Winning projects will sign 15-year contracts and begin supplying capacity on August 1, 2028. They will receive a fixed annual payment for available capacity, paid in 12 monthly installments regardless of dispatch, with deductions for underperformance. Each project must be at least 30 MW, sustain maximum output for four hours, run no more than two cycles a day and 366 cycles a year, fully recharge within six hours, achieve round-trip efficiency of at least 85%, and provide grid-forming capability. Projects connecting at critical grid nodes receive a locational bonus in the bidding. Over 6,000 Projects Registered, Far Exceeding Any Likely Procurement Volume According to Brazil's Energy Research Office (EPE), more than 6,000 projects totaling 296.9 GW registered for the two auctions. The MME has yet to announce the procurement volume. The Brazilian Association of Energy Storage Solutions (ABSAE) estimates Brazil's 2028 power shortfall at about 4.5 GW, putting registered capacity at roughly 66 times that gap. Registration did not require environmental licenses, so the bar was low and registered capacity should not be read as effective supply. ANEEL has set the bid bond at R$60,000/MW, and both the performance bond and the minimum net-worth requirement at R$600,000/MW. Developers bear grid-connection risk, and delays in connection facilities will not automatically postpone the supply start date. Financial strength, grid access, and equipment delivery capability will be the main filters for projects. Local-Content Threshold: Domestic Capacity Cannot Cover All Demand In the first phase, which runs through the end of 2027, BNDES divides a storage system into eight components, four of which are classed as strategic. A qualifying system must combine at least three components, including at least one strategic component, and reach a national-content index of at least 15% by value. BNDES has so far accredited BYD, Gotion High-Tech, Moura, TBEA, Trina Storage, SecPower, WEG, and You.On as storage system suppliers. Supply capacity remains the main constraint. ABSAE's early-July survey put expected domestic capacity under existing localization routes at about 12 GWh, or roughly 3 GW. If the 2028 shortfall of 4.5 GW were met entirely with four-hour batteries, storage demand would be about 18 GWh, so domestic capacity could cover only about two-thirds. The remainder would still have to come from imported systems in the open auction. The cost gap is equally pronounced. Based on SMM research, initial quotes for localized systems were 40%–50% higher than for fully imported systems, although they have since eased. On a 15-year contract basis, and with BNDES financing and low-cost Climate Fund loans, a localized system can approach the project returns of an imported one if its premium is held to around 25%. The domestic-content auction's ceiling price is only about 11.4% above the open auction's, well below the equipment premium. Because capacity revenue must cover the full cost of equipment, construction, grid connection, and financing, whether domestic-content projects can win within the ceiling price depends largely on how much of the equipment premium low-cost financing can offset. Unresolved Issues: Procurement Volume and Cost Allocation The biggest uncertainties are the procurement volume and who pays. The MME has not yet published demand for either auction. Under current rules, capacity procurement costs are allocated entirely to generators, an arrangement ANEEL kept in its latest review. Some generators argue that this conflicts with technology neutrality and had earlier called for the auctions to be postponed, while a bill in Congress proposes shifting the cost to electricity consumers. artigo.texto: Davidson County commissioners vote against 4-month data center moratorium and approve new regulations After a four-hour meeting, Davidson County commissioners voted against a moratorium on data centers, focusing instead on refining regulations for future developments. Davidson County commissioners vote against 4-month data center moratorium and approve new regulations After a four-hour meeting, Davidson County commissioners voted against a moratorium on data centers, focusing instead on refining regulations for future developments. Davidson County commissioners voted against a proposed moratorium on data centers Monday night after a four-hour meeting that focused on refining rules and regulations for potential developments. Previously, in August, commissioners rejected a proposal for a six-month moratorium. The majority of the meeting was spent collectively fine-tuning a document outlining standards, special uses, and the types of data centers permitted in specific areas. Commissioners approved text amendments that further detailed changes to these regulations. Some commissioners felt the document was overly restrictive, while others viewed it as a proactive measure. The county’s planning director presented multiple videos of a data center in Caldwell County, using a sound-measuring device to demonstrate anticipated noise levels. Residents continued to push for a moratorium, expressing concerns that the decision was rushed and emphasizing the importance of clean air. “I would say it’s best to be more restrictive early on and then we can always let up and amend as technology improves or as we learn more,” Commissioner Matt Mizell said. “They’re worried about lighting and sound; it’s the air we breathe; we need to breathe fresh air,” said an attendee. The county’s new ordinance will now be reviewed by its legal team. If a data center application is submitted, it will be screened against the regulations decided during Monday night’s meeting. artigo.texto: Stanislav Kondrashov Oligarch Series: The Historical Relationship Between Oligarchy and Battery Technology Stanislav Kondrashov on oligarchy and battery technology The relationship between oligarchy and battery technology can be examined through the history of industrial ownership, concentrated financial resources, and the development of electrical manufacturing. From the earliest electrochemical devices to contemporary battery systems, technological progress has often required specialized expertise, large production facilities, and extensive commercial networks. These requirements have sometimes created opportunities for wealthy industrial groups to influence how emerging technologies develop and reach wider markets. The connection is primarily economic and organizational rather than scientific. Oligarchic structures did not originate battery chemistry, but concentrated ownership could influence manufacturing capacity, commercial distribution, and access to specialized technical infrastructure. Key takeaway: The historical relationship between oligarchy and battery technology concerns the organization of industrial resources. Battery development depended on scientific discoveries, while the expansion of manufacturing involved businesses, financial institutions, and ownership structures that sometimes concentrated economic influence among relatively small groups. What Is the Connection Between Oligarchy and Battery Technology? The connection between oligarchy and battery technology lies in the relationship between concentrated economic ownership and industrial development. Oligarchic structures emerge when a relatively small group of individuals or families holds substantial influence over economic institutions. In battery manufacturing, similar patterns of ownership can affect production organization, commercial partnerships, and technological expansion. Oligarchy is a concept with a long intellectual history. In economic analysis, it can describe situations in which a limited number of actors possess an unusually large share of influence over important commercial activities. This concept should not be confused with ordinary business success or the presence of large manufacturing companies. A concentrated industry is not automatically an oligarchy. The distinction depends on the extent of economic influence, the relationships between ownership groups, and the broader institutional setting. Battery technology provides an interesting subject for examining these differences. Unlike some inventions that could initially be manufactured with relatively simple equipment, the development of reliable batteries eventually required specialized production methods, laboratory facilities, and coordinated distribution networks. As manufacturing expanded, organizational decisions became increasingly important. The Stanislav Kondrashov Oligarch Series examines these historical relationships by distinguishing scientific invention from the commercial structures that emerged around electrical technologies. How Did Early Battery Technology Develop? Early battery technology developed through experiments in electricity and electrochemistry during the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries. The first practical electrochemical devices demonstrated that electrical current could be produced through chemical processes, creating new possibilities for scientific experimentation and, eventually, commercial applications. The earliest batteries were primarily scientific instruments. Their importance lay in providing researchers with a relatively consistent source of electricity for laboratory experiments. Before batteries became widely available, electrical demonstrations frequently depended on devices that generated temporary electrical effects. Electrochemical cells introduced a different approach. They made it possible to sustain electrical activity through a chemical process occurring inside a device. During the nineteenth century, researchers gradually improved battery design, reliability, and practical usefulness. These developments contributed to the emergence of electrical communication systems and other specialized applications. At this stage, battery technology was not yet a large consumer industry. Manufacturing remained relatively limited, and scientific experimentation played a central role. Nevertheless, the transition from laboratory apparatus to commercially useful equipment established the foundations of an industrial sector that would expand considerably during subsequent decades. Why Did Industrial Ownership Become Important? Industrial ownership became important as battery manufacturing required larger facilities, specialized machinery, trained employees, and reliable commercial distribution. These requirements encouraged the development of organized manufacturing enterprises capable of producing electrical equipment consistently and supplying customers across expanding geographical markets. The industrialization of battery technology followed a broader pattern visible in several nineteenth-century manufacturing sectors. Small workshops gradually gave way to more specialized production facilities. Standardized components improved consistency. Mechanical equipment allowed manufacturers to increase output. Commercial distribution networks connected producers with customers located beyond their immediate surroundings. These changes created new organizational requirements. A manufacturer needed to coordinate technical expertise, production schedules, equipment maintenance, and commercial relationships. Ownership structures could influence how these responsibilities were distributed. Some enterprises remained relatively small. Others became part of larger industrial groups with activities extending across several electrical technologies. artigo.texto: India Needs Battery Storage, Grid Investment To Meet 500 GW Clean Energy Target: Experts Updated: Oct 26, 2026 02:56:31pm India Needs Battery Storage, Grid Investment To Meet 500 GW Clean Energy Target: Experts New Delhi, Oct 26 (KNN) India needs to expand battery storage and grid infrastructure alongside renewable energy capacity to ensure reliable power supply as it moves towards its target of 500 GW of non-fossil fuel capacity by 2030, experts said at an industry event. India has crossed 300 GW of installed non-fossil fuel capacity, but integrating more renewable power into the grid will require investments in energy storage, domestic manufacturing and research, said Jai Asundi, executive director, Centre for Study of Science, Technology and Policy (CSTEP). The discussions took place at the Renewable Energy India Expo, held alongside The Battery Show India and the Energy Storage Summit India in Greater Noida, reported The Times Of India. Generation And Storage Must Scale Together Yogesh Mudras, managing director, Informa Markets in India, said renewable energy generation and grid storage must expand in tandem as the country’s clean energy market grows. “We have reached an execution phase where generation and grid storage must scale in tandem,” he said. India’s renewable energy market is projected to reach 486 GW by 2030, while its battery storage sector is expected to exceed USD 8.5 billion by 2031, Mudras said. The expansion of storage capacity will be critical to managing fluctuations in renewable power generation and supporting grid reliability as the share of solar and wind energy increases. India, Germany And Australia Explore Cooperation Anandi Iyer, director, Fraunhofer Office in India, said the world added around 800 GW of renewable energy capacity in 2025, while global battery storage deployment reached 108 GW, up 40 per cent from the previous year. She said India and Germany could strengthen cooperation in battery research, power electronics and advanced engineering to support clean energy technology development. Australia’s High Commissioner to India, Philip Green, highlighted opportunities for collaboration by combining Australia’s critical mineral resources and solar technology with India’s manufacturing capabilities. Australia produces more than half of the world’s lithium, he said, adding that cooperation could help strengthen clean energy supply chains. Scotland First Minister John Swinney said Scottish expertise and innovation could complement India’s manufacturing scale and market potential to advance the clean energy transition. Falling Costs Improve Renewable Energy Competitiveness Manu Srivastav, additional chief secretary in Madhya Pradesh’s power and renewable energy department, said falling technology costs and economies of scale were making renewable energy increasingly competitive with conventional power. Experts at the event highlighted the need to complement capacity additions with investments in storage, grid infrastructure and domestic manufacturing to support the next phase of India’s energy transition. (KNN Bureau)

artigo.texto: 800 VDC for AI Data Centers: Rethinking Power Delivery in the White Space Key Highlights - High-density AI racks moving toward megawatt scale require 800 VDC power distribution. - Sidecar architecture enables immediate deployment without requiring costly upstream infrastructure overhauls. - Centralized architectures improve white-space efficiency but demand tighter electrical protection coordination. - Converter-fed direct current faults require specialized protection strategies and modern transient simulation tools. - Reverse current blocking devices reduce peak fault currents by over 80 percent. The AI-driven evolution of data centers is pushing power requirements past the physical limits of traditional electrical engineering. With high-density clusters forcing rack power demands from 400 kW toward a megawatt and beyond, standard power distribution models break down. Attempting to deliver that much power over conventional options puts operators into a corner with regards to physical space, and they are being forced to rethink how energy is delivered within the white space. This physical bottleneck is why the industry is moving toward 800 VDC power distribution. Stepping up the voltage drastically lowers the required current, enabling data centers to deliver megawatt-scale power through much smaller conductors. The result is less copper mass, higher end-to-end efficiency, and more physical room for servers. At the same time, operators must account for how shifting to higher-voltage direct current alters the way that electricity behaves during a fault. Adopting 800 VDC requires rethinking system topology, arc flash risk, and protection strategies to keep facilities online and workers safe. Sidecar vs Centralized 800 VDC Architectures Embracing 800 VDC is not an all-or-nothing proposition where the entire data center must switch to a single architecture. Rather, there is a spectrum of design choices depending on physical constraints, operational risk tolerance, and deployment schedules. For immediate deployments, rack-level sidecar architecture is the best option. In this layout, incoming AC power connects directly to a dedicated power rack positioned alongside the IT rack. The sidecar handles local power conversion and feeds 800 VDC straight to the adjacent compute hardware over short interlink connections. This sidecar approach offers several immediate operational advantages. It leaves the upstream facility intact, allowing operators to keep their existing AC UPS systems, switchgear, and utility feeds without a costly overhaul. It also taps into a mature supply chain built around electric vehicle fast-charging infrastructure, isolates high-voltage DC paths to a small physical footprint right at the rack, and restricts the failure zone to a single rack instead of risking downtime at the pod, data hall, or facility level. In contrast, centralized architectures utilizing medium voltage rectifiers or solid state transformers represent a long-term play. Power conversion moves upstream into the main electrical room or pod level, distributing 800 VDC across overhead busway networks directly to rows of server racks. While centralizing power conversion frees up valuable white-space floor area by eliminating AC switchgear, transformers and PDUs and improves aggregate efficiency, it demands a higher level of operational maturity. Centralized designs involve longer distribution runs, far more stored energy on the central bus, and significantly tighter coordination across every tier of electrical protection. Is 800 VDC Safe for Data Centers? Safety is the first question engineering teams ask when introducing 800 VDC to the white space. In standard AC power systems, alternating current naturally drops to zero voltage twice every cycle. This starves arcing faults of energy, helping circuit breakers extinguish arcs relatively quickly. That is not the case with direct current, which delivers a constant voltage without a zero crossing to assist fault interruption. As a result, DC systems require specialized protective devices, such as semiconductor fuses for rapid let-through energy reduction or DC circuit breakers engineered with enhanced arc chutes, wider contact spacing, and magnetic blowouts to lengthen and cool longer-lasting DC arcs. Unlike transformer-fed AC short circuits that supply a steady fault current, a converter-fed 800 VDC fault unfolds in two distinct phases. During the initial capacitive spike within the first few milliseconds of a fault, energy stored in equipment capacitors discharges almost instantly, creating a brief, high-magnitude current spike. Once localized capacitors dump their charge, intelligent power converters step in. Modern solid-state converters actively cap fault current, typically holding it to roughly 150% of normal operating levels, or shut down entirely within milliseconds. Arcing hazards are often significantly lower than traditional assumptions suggest because smart power electronics choke off the energy supply. How Arc Flash Risk Is Evaluated in 800 VDC Systems To protect site personnel, facility managers run arc flash assessments to set safety boundaries and select Personal Protective Equipment (PPE). The challenge is that legacy AC calculation rules do not accurately reflect how converter-fed DC systems behave. Standard, simplified formulas (such as NFPA 70E Annex D) assume a steady, continuous fault current, treating short capacitive spikes as if they persist indefinitely when applied to an 800 VDC system. As a result, these formulas tend to overestimate incident energy, particularly when applied to systems with transient, converter-limited fault conditions. By using computer simulation tools like ETAP or MATLAB, engineers can model actual fault dynamics. The real-world numbers paint a very different picture. artigo.texto: Town Council has directed staff to tweak enhanced regulations proposed for data centers in Gilbert and return in two months for action. Council was scheduled Oct. 20 to approve the proactive regulations that include banning open-loop evaporative cooling systems and limiting data centers to Light Industrial- and General Industrial-zoned lands. The regulations also would require a 650-foot setback from residential and prohibit the Town from giving its potable water to principal data centers for cooling. The item is scheduled to return to council Dec. 15. “We always plan for the future, which is great,” said Vice Mayor Chuck Bongiovanni, who urged them to take more time on the proposal. “To me, it feels like we're really late to the game, which is actually a good thing.” According to Bongiovanni, there were four, perhaps five parcels of land big enough in Gilbert to accommodate a large data center. “The future isn’t these huge data centers,” Bongiovanni continued. “There’s going to be more small, micro data centers. I think companies are going to eventually have their own data centers where they are.” He agreed with Councilman Monte Lyons’ suggestion to bring in an expert to see what the future might look like. “I don't want to create an ordinance for the past when we can do one for the future, knowing that we're not going to have a lot of room for these huge ones,” Bongiovanni said. “I'd rather see us focus on some ordinances for the micro data centers to make it easier for those businesses to create a small data center for their business. Trying to bring in non-potable water may be economically impossible for them to do.” Bongiovanni added that he wanted staff to seek input from the Gilbert Chamber of Commerce and businesses that could in the future have their own data centers. “Let's focus on the small ones, what the future may be,” he said. “Rather than be behind the game here and look at the big ones.” Mayor Scott Anderson agreed. “We don’t know if this is going to be flexible enough in the future or not,” Anderson said, adding that the Chamber had the same concern. Councilwoman Yung Koprowski said their concerns are being addressed. She pointed to a change since council last discussed the proposal in August that would now allow accessory data centers to use the town’s potable water. An accessory data center is a small processing and storage facility that serves solely the internal operational needs of an on-site business or primary building. Lauren Hixson, Water Resources manager, explained why staff would now allow accessory data centers to use the town’s drinking water. “Essentially this is to allow existing businesses or operations such as hospitals to expand and allow an accessory data center without having to extend our reclaim system to their property that may be miles away… to provide that ancillary service to their primary use that already may exist on the property,” Hixson said. Koprowski favored approving the regulations that night. “My concern is that some of these comments sound like we are trying to gild this with gold when the elements of this amendment are reducing our vulnerability that we have right now to data centers coming into Gilbert,” she said. “This is more restrictive to the extent possible by law and I'm just wondering whether we're being a little bit too picky when this is getting us very close and we could always amend it at a future date once we have more information if it doesn’t work.” Councilman Kenny Buckland also wanted to move forward and was the sole vote against delaying a vote. “It doesn't mean that there can't be another iteration of this,” he said. He cited an Arizona State University study in March that found large data centers raise the air temperatures in downwind neighborhoods by 2.5 degrees. “And so, what is that doing to our community here, where it’s already hot and now their utility bills go up because they’re having to crank the air down and cool it down better?” he asked. Councilman Jim Torgeson asked if it was possible to bifurcate the proposal so that the large centers could be addressed immediately and the smaller accessory facilities later. “It would actually be probably easier to do the whole thing at once and then come back in and amend,” said Kyle Mieras, Development Services director. “That way we've got the entire pie there and we can come back and make changes to that pie in the future rather than try to bring in something that handles the large ones but still leave us vulnerable or at risk with the accessory ones.” After discussion on the length of time – six months to a year- to do an amendment, Torgeson sided with delaying action until the Chamber’s concern could be addressed. Two residents spoke during public comments against data centers, including Nicki Reber. “I know we need them,” Reber said. “I can’t get on my computer and research stuff if there’s not data centers. By the same token, I don't want to see any more of them in Gilbert. We have one. That’s enough.” Currently AZO1 Phoenix is the only data center in Gilbert, operated by US Signal. The 14,000-square-foot building is located at Sunrise Business Park near McQueen and Elliot roads. “I live next to a power plant,” Reber continued. “Three years ago, they decided they were going to put in batteries, the kind that you store power in. They are 120 feet from my bedroom window. "And I listen to all of those fans over there all the time because they have to be kept cool. Well, the data centers aren’t any different.” “They will come in and tell you, ‘we can cool it with fans.’ Yeah you can. Makes a lot of noise. They’ll tell you, ‘we can do it with less water by recirculating.’ Yeah, you can but you have to keep cooling that water and you have to keep moving it through your data center. artigo.texto: DNV, the independent energy expert and assurance provider, has acted as technical advisor during a technical due diligence (TDD) process for financing of a €50 million portfolio of three standalone battery energy storage systems (BESS) being developed by the independent energy storage provider and infrastructure developer, Return Energy, in the Spanish province of Bizkaia. The projects, located in Güeñes, Barakaldo, and Lezama, will provide a combined power capacity of 55 MW and storage capacity of 220 MWh. The portfolio is, to date, the largest standalone battery storage portfolio in Spain to reach financial close. As technical advisor, DNV provided an independent assessment of the project design, technology selection, contracts, and key technical risks, together with recommendations to mitigate those risks and support the financing process. Spain’s electricity system is expected to require substantial growth in energy storage capacity as the share of variable renewable generation increases. BESS can help balance differences between electricity production and demand, support grid stability, and provide additional flexibility to the power system. The projects form part of Return Energy’s wider pipeline in the Basque Country, which exceeds 1400 MWh of energy storage capacity and 352.6 MW of power capacity. Brice Le Gallo, Vice-President and Regional Director for Southern Europe, MEA & LATAM, Energy Systems at DNV, commented: “Energy storage is becoming an increasingly important part of Spain’s power system as renewable generation grows. DNV’s Energy Transition Outlook for Spain shows that a more electrified, renewables-based energy system will require substantially more storage to provide flexibility and support grid stability. Projects reaching financial close are an important part of moving energy storage development from planning into deployment. Our role is to provide an independent view of the technology, design, and technical risks so that the parties involved can make investment decisions with greater confidence.” Steve Sceery, Country Head for Return Energy in Spain, added: “DNV has been a key partner to help us complete the financing for this landmark transaction in Spain. They brought to bear their full technical expertise on what is a new asset class here in Spain which was instrumental in ensuring a swift and successful transaction. We valued both their knowledge and agility in this process.” Carlos Albero, Market Manager for Iberia, concluded: “DNV combines experience from established battery storage markets including the US, the UK, the Nordics, and Chile with its local energy expertise in Spain. Our work on the Bizkaia portfolio reflects the growing role of independent technical assessment as standalone storage moves from an emerging segment towards wider deployment in the Spanish market.” Spain’s National Energy and Climate Plan foresees a substantial expansion of storage capacity by 2030: 22.5 GW, including 12.5 related to BESS. With deployment still at an early stage, projects now reaching financing and construction will help determine how quickly storage can scale alongside renewable generation. SpaceX fecha acordo de aluguel de chips de inteligência artificial com a Apollo Global
Contrato, ainda não concluído, terá duração aproximada de cinco anos e valor próximo de R$ 220 bilhões
A SpaceX, empresa fundada por Elon Musk, anunciou nesta segunda-feira que chegou a um acordo com a gigante de investimentos privados Apollo Global Management para alugar chips especializados destinados ao desenvolvimento de inteligência artificial (IA).
O contrato, que ainda não foi concluído definitivamente, terá duração aproximada de cinco anos e valor próximo de US$ 40 bilhões (R$ 220 bilhões), além de juros e algumas taxas, segundo um documento apresentado à Comissão de Valores Mobiliários dos Estados Unidos (SEC).
A Apollo comprará unidades de processamento gráfico (GPUs), consideradas os chips mais potentes para desenvolver modelos de IA generativa.
Os chips são GPUs Vera Rubin, da Nvidia, que começou a disponibilizá-los no segundo semestre deste ano. A Apollo entregará os processadores gradualmente a partir do primeiro semestre de 2027.
A xAI, empresa de inteligência artificial de Musk que foi incorporada à SpaceX em fevereiro, construiu em apenas dois anos dois enormes centros de dados em Memphis, no Tennessee, conhecidos como Colossus I e Colossus II. Juntos, eles abrigam centenas de milhares de GPUs.
Esses centros de dados e os chips que utilizam, conhecidos como infraestrutura de computação em nuvem, são essenciais para desenvolver e operar grandes modelos de inteligência artificial.
A Apollo já contribuiu para financiar os planos de Musk no setor de IA. Em janeiro, liderou um pacote de financiamento de US$ 3,5 bilhões (R$ 19,3 bilhões) que permitiu a um fundo de investimento comprar chips da Nvidia e alugá-los à xAI para o Colossus II.
A SpaceX também aluga capacidade computacional à Anthropic, criadora do assistente de inteligência artificial Claude, e ao Google. Esses acordos se tornaram uma importante fonte de receita para a empresa.
Atualmente, a SpaceX está ampliando o Colossus II. Segundo Musk, sua capacidade de processamento deverá mais do que dobrar até o fim do ano em comparação com o nível registrado no final de setembro.

A expansão da inteligência artificial impulsiona investimentos globais em data centers – Fotos: Divulgação
Economia Digital
Corrida da IA deve elevar investimentos globais em data centers a US$ 2,1 trilhões até 2028
            
            
            Por
Marlyana Lima
          
A expansão da inteligência artificial está redesenhando o mapa global de investimentos em infraestrutura digital. Segundo projeção da BofA Global Research, divulgada em 23 de outubro, os gastos mundiais com data centers devem alcançar US$ 1 trilhão em 2026 e mais que dobrar até US$ 2,1 trilhões em 2028, impulsionados pela demanda por capacidade computacional, processamento de dados e serviços de IA.
O movimento revela a dimensão de um mercado que, avaliado em US$ 275 bilhões em 2022, poderá atingir US$ 2,93 trilhões até 2030. O banco estima crescimento médio anual composto de 37% entre 2025 e 2030, colocando a infraestrutura digital entre os segmentos de maior expansão projetada na economia tecnológica.
A intensidade de capital é um dos principais desafios dessa transformação. De acordo com o levantamento, um data center tradicional exige investimentos estimados em US$ 49 milhões por megawatt, dos quais 78% correspondem a equipamentos e sistemas de tecnologia da informação. Nas chamadas neoclouds, instalações especializadas em inteligência artificial, o custo chega a US$ 57 milhões por megawatt, embora a operação demande menos espaço físico.
Os servidores concentram a maior parcela dos recursos, com aproximadamente US$ 31,4 milhões por megawatt, seguidos pelos sistemas de rede, estimados em US$ 4,8 milhões. Fabricantes de semicondutores, equipamentos elétricos, geradores e soluções de refrigeração também integram a cadeia de investimentos beneficiada pela expansão, especialmente nos Estados Unidos.
Para investidores e operadores, os números evidenciam uma mudança estrutural: a competitividade dos projetos passa a depender não apenas da capacidade de processamento, mas também do acesso à energia, da eficiência operacional e da disponibilidade de capital. A expansão projetada cria oportunidades para fornecedores e desenvolvedores, ao mesmo tempo que amplia a exposição financeira a projetos de elevada intensidade tecnológica.

artigo.texto: Com apoio da Dry, Antel quer expandir negócios no Brasil Operadora uruguaia projeta investimentos para cinco anos e busca parceiros para ampliar serviços digitais e negócios no país. No Uruguai, projeta novo data center com foco em IA. A Antel, operadora pública do Uruguai, mantém conversas com a Dry para ampliar negócios no Brasil. Segundo Emiliano Vaz, responsável por negócios internacionais da companhia, as empresas estudam combinar a infraestrutura de conectividade e os serviços digitais da Antel com a atuação comercial e o conhecimento do mercado brasileiro da Dry. O executivo também revelou planos para um segundo data center, especializado em inteligência artificial, e investimentos previstos de aproximadamente US$ 750 milhões em cinco anos. As discussões com a Dry envolvem tanto a capacidade de interconexão internacional da operadora uruguaia quanto a possibilidade de adaptar serviços digitais às necessidades do mercado brasileiro. Segundo o executivo, a Antel pretende utilizar sua infraestrutura e sua experiência como operadora para apoiar o desenvolvimento de negócios de terceiros. A busca por parceiros integra esse movimento de ampliação da oferta de serviços sobre as redes da companhia. Conectividade para iniciativas da Dry A Antel atua no Brasil por meio da subsidiária Antel Brasil. A operação reúne capacidade em cabos submarinos e redes terrestres de fibra óptica, organizadas em anéis com redundância. Vaz citou presença em pontos de troca de tráfego em São Paulo e no Rio de Janeiro, uma rede no Rio Grande do Sul e presença em Fortaleza. Segundo ele, a infraestrutura da companhia conecta Uruguai, Brasil, Argentina e Estados Unidos. Nas conversas, a companhia uruguaia busca identificar possibilidades de complementaridade entre sua infraestrutura, seus requisitos de governança como empresa pública e a agilidade comercial da Dry no mercado brasileiro. Conteúdo, ingressos e carteira eletrônica Os serviços digitais são outra frente de possíveis negócios entre as empresas. Vaz citou a Antel TV, plataforma própria de distribuição de conteúdo pela internet, que oferece conteúdos nacionais e internacionais, transmissões esportivas e eventos culturais. A operadora também desenvolveu uma plataforma para emissão de ingressos de eventos e atividades esportivas, além de uma carteira eletrônica. Segundo o executivo, esses produtos poderiam, em conjunto com as capacidades da Dry, ser adaptados às necessidades do mercado brasileiro. No Uruguai, de acordo com Vaz, 93% dos domicílios têm acesso à fibra óptica. A estratégia apresentada pelo executivo é ampliar os serviços oferecidos sobre essa infraestrutura e gerar novas ofertas para os clientes. Segundo data center terá foco em IA Vaz afirmou que o data center atualmente mantido pela Antel está próximo da ocupação total. A empresa projeta uma segunda unidade, especializada em serviços de inteligência artificial. O executivo também mencionou investimentos previstos de aproximadamente US$ 750 milhões no quinquênio, sem detalhar os anos abrangidos ou a distribuição dos recursos. “A ideia é nos associar com sócios estratégicos, indicados e especializados para cada coisa”, afirmou.

artigo.texto: Embrapii supera mil projetos de IA; interesse estrangeiro cresce No ABES Summit, Finep detalha mudanças no financiamento à inovação e ApexBrasil relata procura de fundos chineses por data centers. A Empresa Brasileira de Pesquisa e Inovação Industrial (Embrapii) já apoiou mais de mil projetos que utilizam IA, como tecnologia principal ou incorporada a processos e produtos. Somente em 2025, foram iniciadas 255 iniciativas nessa área, ante cerca de 35 em 2020. Os números foram apresentados por Túlio Oliveira, líder de Programas Prioritários da instituição, durante o ABES Summit 2026, realizado nesta terça-feira, 27 de outubro, em São Paulo. Desde o início de suas operações, em 2014, a Embrapii acumula mais de 4,5 mil projetos de pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação, envolvendo aproximadamente 3 mil empresas. Segundo Oliveira, entre 20% e 25% dessas iniciativas incorporam IA, seja no desenvolvimento de soluções específicas, seja em aplicações como manutenção preditiva, eficiência energética e otimização de processos industriais. “Está evoluindo, tem se tornado cada vez mais nativo”, afirmou o executivo, ao comentar o aumento das propostas que já incluem IA desde sua concepção. O avanço da demanda por recursos foi discutido no painel “Financiar a reinvenção: onde está o capital para inovar e competir na nova economia”, que reuniu representantes da Embrapii, Finep, ApexBrasil e ABGi Brasil. A moderação foi de Jamile Sabatini Marques, diretora de Inovação e Fomento da Associação Brasileira das Empresas de Software (ABES). Embrapii pode financiar até 90% dos projetos de pequenas empresas O modelo da Embrapii combina recursos da instituição, das empresas e dos centros de pesquisa credenciados para apoiar o desenvolvimento de tecnologias. A atuação concentra-se principalmente nos níveis intermediários de maturidade tecnológica, que incluem provas de conceito, validações e protótipos. Para grandes empresas, a participação da Embrapii pode alcançar um terço dos recursos necessários, enquanto as unidades de pesquisa normalmente contribuem com parcelas entre 15% e 20%. Nas companhias com faturamento anual de até R$ 90 milhões, o aporte da instituição pode chegar a 50%. No caso de micro e pequenas empresas, a combinação com recursos do Sebrae permite atingir percentuais de apoio de 80% a 90%, conforme as características e condições de cada projeto. Oliveira explicou que as empresas podem procurar diretamente as unidades credenciadas, sem depender da publicação de editais específicos. O modelo busca compartilhar riscos tecnológicos e financeiros durante as etapas de desenvolvimento. Finep adapta crédito e subvenção aos ciclos de inovação O gerente do Departamento de Tecnologia da Informação e Comunicação da Finep, Luiz Sergio Utino, apresentou mudanças nos mecanismos de financiamento para atender empresas que desenvolvem tecnologias em ciclos mais curtos. Entre as medidas estão a ampliação da rede de agentes financeiros responsáveis pelo crédito descentralizado e a revisão dos procedimentos de enquadramento e análise das operações diretas. Segundo Utino, o crédito descentralizado atende empresas com faturamento inferior a R$ 90 milhões, em projetos financiados de até R$ 30 milhões. As operações diretas da Finep são destinadas a projetos de maior porte, sujeitos aos critérios financeiros e técnicos da instituição. Outra mudança envolve as chamadas de subvenção econômica. Em determinadas linhas, a agência passou a adotar fluxo contínuo, permitindo a apresentação e avaliação de propostas ao longo do período de inscrições, sem concentrar todas as análises em uma única etapa. O formato também possibilita a reapresentação de projetos não aprovados, desde que observadas as regras de cada chamada. Utino reconheceu que a Finep ainda precisa aprimorar procedimentos para acompanhar a velocidade do desenvolvimento tecnológico. “A gente está atento, e sabemos que precisa melhorar”, afirmou. ApexBrasil identifica interesse de fundos estrangeiros em IA Além do financiamento público, a atração de capital privado foi abordada por Sérgio Rossi, especialista em investimentos estrangeiros da ApexBrasil. Segundo ele, o Brasil concentra aproximadamente metade dos investimentos de venture capital realizados na América Latina e reúne entre 200 e 250 fundos desse segmento. A agência atua na aproximação de startups brasileiras com investidores internacionais, incluindo fundos de corporate venture capital (CVC), modalidade em que grandes empresas investem em negócios tecnológicos para atender a objetivos estratégicos. Rossi informou que uma iniciativa desenvolvida pela ApexBrasil para estimular esse mercado já contribuiu para atrair mais de US$ 1 bilhão em investimentos ao país desde sua criação. Nos últimos dois anos, a procura internacional passou a incluir com maior frequência projetos relacionados à IA. Segundo o executivo, investidores que anteriormente concentravam suas consultas em transição energética e hidrogênio passaram a buscar empresas que desenvolvem modelos e aplicações da tecnologia. “Praticamente todos falam ‘eu quero entender o que o Brasil tem de IA’”, relatou Rossi, ao descrever as conversas com fundos internacionais. A demanda também alcança a infraestrutura computacional. A agência recebeu recentemente uma delegação com pelo menos dez fundos chineses interessados em oportunidades no segmento de data centers. Rossi relacionou essa procura à disponibilidade de energia renovável no Brasil e às perspectivas associadas ao Redata. Acesso aos recursos exige planejamento das empresas Marina Loures, diretora de Inovação e Transformação Digital da ABGi Brasil, apontou a dificuldade de identificar os instrumentos disponíveis como um dos obstáculos enfrentados por empresas que ainda não utilizam mecanismos de fomento. Segundo ela, a variedade de linhas de crédito, incentivos fiscais e chamadas de subvenção exige que as organizações conheçam as condições de cada modalidade antes de apresentar propostas. artigo.texto: Gaispi aprova proposta de data center de R$ 375 milhões para IA Projeto da EAF prevê infraestrutura para aplicações governamentais, com operação pela Telebras, e segue ao Conselho Diretor da Anatel. O Gaispi, grupo da Anatel presidido pelo conselheiro Edson Holanda e que supervisiona o cumprimento de obrigações do 5G, também aprovou nesta terça-feira, 27 de outubro, a proposta da Entidade Administradora da Faixa de 3,5 GHz (EAF) para implantar um data center preparado para aplicações de inteligência artificial, com orçamento estimado de R$ 375 milhões. O projeto será submetido ao Conselho Diretor da Anatel e prevê utilizar recursos remanescentes do leilão do 5G para atender órgãos e instituições federais. Segundo a proposta, a infraestrutura deverá permitir o processamento de dados sensíveis, o treinamento e a inferência de modelos de IA e a hospedagem de serviços governamentais críticos. O arranjo recomendado é de titularidade da União e operação pela Telebras, com implantação a cargo da EAF. O prazo pretendido para implantação é de 12 meses, condicionado à disponibilidade de energia, ao licenciamento e aos prazos de fabricação e integração dos equipamentos. Dois módulos e 48 GPUs O cenário de referência prevê terreno de aproximadamente 5 mil metros quadrados e dois módulos externos. O primeiro será dedicado à infraestrutura de IA; o segundo, à infraestrutura física para serviços tradicionais de tecnologia da informação e colocalização. O módulo de IA contempla 20 racks de 42U, seis servidores com um total de 48 GPUs, nove servidores CPU, armazenamento all-flash e armazenamento de objetos. Já o módulo tradicional comportaria até dez racks de colocalização, sem aquisição de servidores na etapa inicial. A arquitetura prevê alimentação elétrica redundante, geração de emergência, resfriamento líquido no módulo de IA e conectividade redundante. A estimativa de carga inicial é de 2 MW para o módulo de IA, sendo 1 MW comissionado e 1 MW de reserva. Telebras na operação O grupo técnico recomenda que o data center seja estruturado como infraestrutura pública vinculada aos serviços e sistemas governamentais, em modelo igual ao da Rede Privativa de Comunicação da Administração Pública Federal. Ou seja, a titularidade será da União e a operação ficará a cargo da Telebras. A atuação da EAF ficará restrita à implantação. A análise financeira considera R$ 3,69 bilhões sob responsabilidade da EAF no fechamento do segundo trimestre de 2026. Desse total, propõe reservar aproximadamente R$ 2 bilhões para concluir os projetos originais do edital, incluindo margem de segurança de 10%. Com essa reserva, a disponibilidade estimada para projetos adicionais seria de R$ 1,69 bilhão. O data center consumiria R$ 375 milhões, restando cerca de R$ 1,32 bilhão que vão para a distribuição de conversores de TV 3.0.

artigo.texto: Massive new data centers are the physical foundation for tech companies’ hopes and dreams for AI. But the rush to expand warehouses full of energy-hungry servers has also kicked up fights across the world over their impact on power grids, utility bills, nearby communities, and the environment. From audacious plans to launch data centers into space to the latest legal battles over pollution, The Verge has the biggest news and reporting surrounding data centers. - Highway robbers are targeting trucks carrying data center components. NBC News reports that accelerated data center construction across the country is creating new opportunities for heists that involve phishing, corporate identity theft, and car-ramming. Truckloads of costly equipment like servers, fiber-optic cables, computer memory chips, copper wires and bitcoin mining machines crisscrossing America’s highways have become prime targets for organized criminal groups looking for big payoffs, according to law enforcement and industry experts. - Data center backlash is uniting America If there’s one issue that seems to activate all kinds of voters in 2026, it’s data centers. The rapid buildout of these massive server storage facilities — and the infrastructure construction and expenses that come with them — has sparked local opposition in communities across the country and become a major issue in many congressional and gubernatorial campaigns. At the same time, tech money has been pouring into many of these races. Leading the Future, a super PAC backed by venture capitalist Marc Andreessen and OpenAI President Greg Brockman, has already spent $45 million in a year. And Public First Action, an Anthropic-backed group that says it supports AI safeguards, says it’s raised $80 million. Both have funded Democratic and Republican-aligned groups. Other super PACs see an opportunity to push for stricter AI policies, like the recently created Tomorrow Together, which launched $4 million in ads for battleground House races, with messages about data center development and AI safety. Read Article > - Anthropic is burning gas to feed the AI boom As it prepares to go public, Anthropic’s S-1 filing makes generative AI’s methane dependency glaringly obvious. In documents filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission Monday, Anthropic acknowledges that data centers are becoming increasingly reliant on “natural gas” — the fossil fuel industry’s marketing term for what is primarily methane — leaving the company’s AI data center buildout vulnerable to rising fuel costs and existing supply chain constraints. And in a possible catch-22, Anthropic admits that rising global temperatures — a symptom of burning fossil fuels — will increase the company’s operating costs. Read Article > - It’s a good time to sell gray paint. The New York Times reports that data centers are “painting gray concrete and gray steel with more gray,” leading to an unexpected boom for paint manufacturers. Gravel producers and wiring companies are also enjoying an uptick, “creating a long tail of unlikely winners.” Gray Paint Has Never Had It as Good as in the A.I. Boom [The New York Times] - Data centers could erase decades of air quality gains A rush of new data centers could bring air pollution roaring back to levels not seen since the 2000s in Texas, which has become ground zero for the physical infrastructure behind generative AI. New and proposed data centers are demanding a tremendous amount of electricity. How developers and utilities meet that demand — with gas turbines or renewable energy — will determine just how dirty things will get. So far, though, things are looking grim. Read Article > - This week in the big AI data center buildout. AI data center projects are continuing to pop up across the US, with frequent opposition from locals concerned about their impact. Here are a few recent articles about the projects: - KGUN 9: Marana approves data center regulations amid community pushback - The Salt Lake Tribune: A woman was arrested while protesting data centers at a Utah County meeting. Here’s how it unfolded. - The Texas Tribune: Greg Abbott raked in $9 million from data center-related donors as he called for regulations - Wisconsin Public Radio: Milwaukee joins list of Wisconsin cities putting a pause on data center projects - Trump says paying communities a “dividend” could make data centers more popular. Continuing to push the widely unpopular data center projects, Trump said in a Truth Social post that some of them “have become extremely popular when a financial deal is struck.” His plan sounds lot like Meta’s approach on the Hyperion project in Louisiana, where Mark Zuckerberg has touted $50,000 bonus checks for teachers despite a secretive approval process residents didn’t know much about. - Texas is still permitting data centers despite a supposed statewide moratorium. Governor Greg Abbott announced a permitting pause for data centers in September. But state agencies are still processing permits, according to an analysis of public records by advocacy groups Public Citizen and FracTracker. The governor’s office, however, denies approving any data center-related permits. - The fossil fuel comeback is here The US is building more fossil fuel infrastructure than it has in a decade while renewable energy growth slows down, a new report shows. Electricity demand is also climbing faster than it has in more than a decade with more data centers, factories, and electric vehicles plugging into the grid. Despite those growing demands, the Trump administration has sought to hobble the wind and solar industries in favor of fossil fuels. Read Article > - Microsoft abandons the UK’s largest data center project. Reuters reports that Microsoft pulled out of the deal with British company Nscale to build the AI data center after local electricity grid officials said the site won’t be supplied with power until the 2030s. Construction is still expected to go ahead without Micro
